volumes.nurj_title: Doula Care and the Role of Maternal Age in Reducing Maternal Morbidity Rates in the United States

blocks: Doula Care and the Role of Maternal Age in Reducing​
Maternal Morbidity Rates in the United States
Zora S. Warren
Global Health Studies Department, Northwestern University
Advised by Professor Sarah B. Rodriguez, Global Health Studies
Abstract
Background: Maternal morbidity rates and high rates of risky obstetric interventions remain a
problem in the United States. Birth doulas are a suggested solution to mitigate obstetric
interventions. Despite women of different maternal ages facing different risks during pregnancy,
research is not yet conclusive on whether the benefits of doulas may vary for different age
groups.
Methods: A literature review was conducted through PubMed and CINAHL with the inclusion
criteria that the article be published in English between 2000-2025, be about doula care and its
impact on cesarean sections and/or forceps-assisted deliveries, and include age as a measured
demographic. Articles must be from peer-reviewed journals. Literature regarding
forceps-assisted deliveries were parsed out.
Findings: Doulas likely reduce the risk of cesarean sections for adolescents (<20) by connecting
adolescents with needed resources and reducing stress. Stronger evidence exists showing doulas
reduce cesarean section rates for adults (20-34) by screening for maternal mental health, assisting
mothers in accessing needed resources, and providing culturally competent care. Inconclusive
literature was identified for pregnant people in the advanced age group (35+).
Conclusion: Existing literature has the strongest evidence that doulas reduce cesarean section
rates for pregnant women in the adult age category. More research must be conducted to confirm
the differences in degree of benefit between the age groups.
Introduction​
Maternal morbidity rates are a crisis in the United States, and studies suggest that
increased rates of medical interventions, such as cesarean sections and forceps-assisted births,
may be partially due to their associations with postoperational conditions such as hemorrhaging
and infection. To reduce the risk of maternal morbidity, researchers have suggested birth doulas
as a non-medical intervention to reduce the use of these obstetric interventions. Pregnancy risks
differ greatly between maternal age groups, and published research is inconclusive about the
benefits of a doula based on the age of the mother. This literature review seeks to determine to
what degree working with a doula during labor increases or decreases the risk of a cesarean
section or forceps-assisted delivery for women of different age groups in the 21st century.
Background
Doula Care
Birth doulas are trained professionals who provide emotional, physical, and informational
support during labor and the antepartum and postpartum periods (Mottl-Santiago et al., 2023, p.
467). Doulas are not clinicians, but nonetheless play a vital supportive role for pregnant people.
While hospital staff are typically able to spend about 21% of a person’s labor with the patients,
doulas provide continuous support throughout labor, as well as during prepartum and postpartum
visits (Kennell et al., 1991, p. 3). Doulas can assist in explaining procedures in terms that
pregnant people can easily understand, and they can facilitate communication between the
patient and their provider by encouraging the patient to speak up when they have questions or
concerns (Futch Thurston et al., 2019). Doulas provide both emotional and physical comfort
during birth via techniques such as counter pressure, position changes, and encouragement
throughout labor (Papagni K & Buckner E, 2006, p. 15). During the postpartum period, doulas
can assist with breastfeeding, household chores, and safe practices like proper car seat use (Hans
There are three models of doula care. The first is private practice: doulas who are hired
directly by the family, visit pre- and postpartum, and attend the labor (Thomas et al., 2017, p.
S61). The second is the hospital-based model, in which doulas are employed by the hospital and
are offered to families at a subsidized rate or no fee. Hospital-based doulas may not offer the full
breadth of services in the pre- and postpartum periods, and instead, their practice typically
centers around labor and delivery support (Lesser et al., 2005, p. 28). Finally, community-based
doulas serve primarily low-income families in their own neighborhoods and often share an
aspect of their identity with the mothers they serve; their services are typically offered to families
at no charge. In addition to providing home visits pre- and postpartum and during labor,
community-based doulas emphasize screening for social determinants of health such as access to
food, safe housing, and exposure to violence. Community-based doulas receive additional
training to help connect pregnant people whose needs are not being met to resources in the
community (Futch Thurston et al., 2019). Doulas are increasingly recognized as important
members of the healthcare team in labor, but according to the 2013 Listening to Mothers III
survey, the most recent survey available, only 6% of mothers in the United States used doula care
during labor (Declercq et al., 2013, p. 16). However, studies have found that doulas may be a key
to reducing maternal morbidity.
Maternal Morbidity in the United States
Maternal morbidities are the adverse consequences of pregnancy that affect a pregnant
person’s health and may include hemorrhaging, eclampsia, gestational diabetes, hypertension,
and puerperal fever. Severe maternal morbidity has increased over the past two decades, rising
from a rate of 146.8 per 10,000 births in 2008 to 179.8 per 10,000 births in 2021 (Fink et al.,
2023, p. 1). There are numerous risk factors for maternal morbidity: young maternal age or old
maternal age; being a person of color (largely specific to the U.S.); Medicaid enrollment; and
cesarean section (Fink et al., 2023, p. 14). Cesarean section in particular is associated with triple
the odds of severe maternal morbidity compared to vaginal delivery (Fink et al., 2023, p. 11).
Despite this statistic, there is an attitude in the US that vaginal delivery is inherently risky, while
cesarean sections can protect women from the risk of morbidity (Wolf, 2018, p. 134).
Misinformed attitudes have caused cesarean section rates to skyrocket in the United States.
While the World Health Organization recommends a cesarean section rate of 10-15% for optimal
benefit with minimized morbidity, in 2022, the U.S. cesarean section delivery rate was 32.1%
(Osterman et al., 2024, p. 40; WHO Statement on Caesarean Section Rates, 2015). Of particular
concern, severe maternal morbidity (morbidities with significant health impacts) rates associated
with cesarean section have increased during the 21st century, increasing from 252.4 cases of
severe maternal morbidity per 10,000 discharges in Q1 of 2008 to 312.1 per 10,000 discharges in
Q4 of 2021 (Fink et al., 2023, pp. 1–5). Many surgical morbidities are associated with cesarean
section, including sepsis, wound infection, bladder injury, hemorrhage, blood clots, and
increased risk of post-delivery complications such as wound separation, uterine tract infections,
gastrointestinal problems, and septic thrombophlebitis (Klaus & Klaus, 2010, p. 6; Quinlan &
Murphy, 2015, p. 178). Doulas reduce the chance of obstetric interventions during labor,
including cesarean section. In one study, women with doula care had a cesarean section rate of
only 13.9% compared to a 26.9% overall rate (Lesser et al., 2005, p. 30).
Forceps-assisted births are another intervention technique associated with maternal
morbidity. While less common than cesarean sections, they still pose a potential complication for
pregnant women. Forceps use is associated with severe birth trauma, including severe injury to
the peripheral nervous system and higher rates of severe postpartum hemorrhaging (Muraca et
al., 2019). Research suggests that continuous doula support during labor is associated with lower
rates of forceps assisted delivery; one study found forceps usage in patients with doula care was
8.2% compared to the control rate of 26.3% (p=0.0006) (Kennell et al., 1991, p. 4). The finding
that doulas may reduce the risk of cesarean sections and forceps-assisted births is significant,
especially considering heightened morbidity risks associated with maternal age.
Typically, when comparing risk between age groups, 25–29 years of age is used as a
comparison. Compared to 25–29 year olds,women under twenty years of age have a heightened
risk of endometritis, preterm delivery, and mild preeclampsia. Women ages 15–19, specifically,
have higher risks for severe preeclampsia, postpartum hemorrhage, and fetal distress. Women of
advanced maternal age (35+) are more likely to suffer from severe preeclampsia, preterm birth,
fetal distress, and hypertension (Cavazos-Rehg et al., 2015, p. 5). Older maternal age has also
been associated with higher risk of cesarean section. In 2022, women ages 40 and older had a
47.7% cesarean section rate compared to women ages 25-29 who had a 29.7% rate and women
under 20 with a rate of only 18.9% (Osterman et al., 2024, p. 40).
Doula Care to Reduce Maternal Morbidity
Doulas may help lower morbidities associated with cesarean sections and forceps assisted
deliveries. Continuous support from doulas has been hypothesized to reduce maternal anxiety
and thus reduce catecholamine levels, a class of molecules that can negatively impact delivery
outcomes by lowering the ability of the uterus to contract and decreasing blood flow to the uterus
and placenta  (Kennell et al., 1991, p. 5; Papagni K & Buckner E, 2006, p. 13). Doulas may help
women communicate their preferences for labor interference, avoiding unnecessary interventions
that may increase their risk of morbidity (Lesser et al., 2005, p. 31). Importantly,  the beneficial
findings of continuous doula care have not been replicated with the continuous labor support of
nurses or a patient’s partner, suggesting the doula’s care and training have unique and powerful
effects (Hodnett et al., 2002, p. 1373; McGrath & Kennell, 2008, p. 96).
Research has not yet been conducted on the degree of benefit of doula care for women of
different age groups, despite the different risks they face. Understanding the extent to which
doula care positively affects different age groups  would allow for more effective and timely
education of mothers on doula support and more effective referrals for mothers who may glean
the most benefit. It may also mitigate increased maternal morbidity risk associated with age.
Methods
To identify literature related to a doula’s differing effect on women of different age
groups, I searched PubMed and CINAHL (Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health
Literature) because of their emphasis on quantitative, peer-reviewed medical literature.
Beginning with the concepts of doulas, cesarean sections, forceps-assisted births, and age, I used
PubMed MeSH (Medical Subject Headings) terms to identify other potential key terminology to
account for all variations. These terms, along with the appropriate Boolean terms (i.e. AND,
OR), were combined into searches. At times when two MeSH variations were quite similar (i.e.
“cesarean delivery” and “cesarean section”), only the common part of the phrase was used in the
final search (“cesarean”), so it would identify results for both MeSH terms. Search terms can be
found in Table 1 in Appendix I. At times, I deployed different age group filters, since the
databases differed in their age-group filter options.
I then copied The searches into PubMed and CINAHL to gain a total of 3082 articles.
The articles were then filtered to exclude articles published before the year 2000, leaving a total
of 2955 articles. Articles were then de-duplicated, and articles were eliminated if they were not
written in English, or if they were clearly not related to pregnancy, doulas, or birth interventions
(i.e. articles about heart surgery). Articles I found manually through searching bibliographies of
previous articles were combined with the articles found in databases. After this stage, 346
articles remained. I then screened the articles by title and abstract; articles were eliminated if
they were not related to cesarean sections or forceps, if the study was done outside of the U.S., or
if the article was a recount of the author’s personal stories, rather than a formal research study or
review. I also eliminated Articles if they were not explicitly about professional doulas. 112
articles remained after this step. I then performed a full-text screening, eliminating articles if the
study was completed in another country, if the article was a review of literature that was already
collected for this review, if the article was not related to cesarean section or forceps rates and
doula care, if the data was theoretical, if the article was not from a peer-reviewed journal, or if
the full-text was not in English (1 article). This left 16 articles that I deemed eligible for analysis.
Included articles are detailed in Table 2 in Appendix I.
Originally, rates of forceps-assisted delivery were intended to be a measured variable in
this review. During screening, incredibly few articles were identified that included
forceps-assisted birth as an outcome. Due to this outcome, I broadened the search from
“forceps-assisted births” to all “assisted vaginal births,” which includes a vacuum assisted
delivery. A new round of searches was conducted, as listed in Table 3 in Appendix I. This new
search retrieved 201 articles. After removing duplicates, publication date check, and title
screening, 15 articles remained. After abstract screening, 8 articles moved on to full-text
screening. When this step was completed, one article did include data on assisted vaginal
deliveries, but was only applicable to women in the adult age group. Because of this, no analysis
based on age groups could be drawn, and data on assisted vaginal births with doulas has been
excluded from the body of this review.
Findings
The three age groups examined in this study are adolescent (pregnant people <20 years
old), adult (20-34), and advanced (35+).
Adolescents
Doulas, especially community-based doulas, may be particularly beneficial for pregnant
adolescents due to their ability to mitigate the heightened social determinants of health risks that
put adolescents  at greater risk for maternal morbidities (Cavazos-Rehg et al., 2015, p. 7). A
study showed that in a population of teen parents in Washington D.C., 37% did not access any
resources to assist with their food security, housing, or finances, pointing to barriers specific to
teens that keep them from essential  assistance (Smiley et al., 2025). Adolescents may also delay
or not seek prenatal care at all in an effort to avoid revealing their pregnancy, which could
potentially result in backlash from their vital support systems, negative stereotypes about their
sexuality, and tension with healthcare providers (Gentry et al., 2010, p. 25; Smiley et al., 2025).
Doula programs, especially those focused on serving a younger demographic , can bridge the gap
in resources for pregnant adolescents and refer them to necessary services/programs  (Smiley et
al., 2025). . For example, doulas can attend medical appointments with pregnant women and
assist them in enrolling in public support systems to ensure they have access to food, housing,
and financial support (Smiley et al., 2025).
Doulas can also attend to  adolescent parents’ mental health. The stress and trauma of
parenthood at a young age can result in an elevated risk for clinical depression (Gentry et al.,
2010, p. 25; Smiley et al., 2025). In one community-based doula program in Georgia, doulas
took baseline assessments of adolescents’ mental health and attempted to provide mental health
support and encouragement to help them cope and thrive in their pregnancy (Gentry et al., 2010,
p. 36). While this was perceived as beneficial by the participants, they also noted that doulas are
not mental health providers, and thus may be more impactful in  screening adolescent parents’
mental health  and referring them to professional mental health services rather than providing
direct support themselves (Gentry et al., 2010, pp. 36–37). Mental health screening and support
may play a role in reducing cesarean section rates, as perinatal mood disorders have been
associated with higher rates of primary cesarean sections (Zochowski et al., 2021, p. 6).
Separate from mental health services, adolescents in the Washington D.C. doula program
noted that childbirth education, access to social support systems, and encouragement to advocate
for themselves in clinical settings eased their stress around maternity (Smiley et al., 2025).
Advocacy is especially important, as some adolescents mentioned that they felt manipulated by
their obstetric providers to accept more medical interventions (Gentry et al., 2010, p. 34). A
doula’s stress-reducing support and encouragement to communicate desires and concerns likely
mitigates the risk of a cesarean section, per the outcomes of four studies. In a 2013 study of the
birth outcomes of 1,892 adolescents who were supported by doulas during labor, only 12.6% of
participants had a cesarean section, and only 2.5% of these cesarean sections were elective
(Everson et al., 2018, p. 140). According to the National Vital Statistics Report (NVSR) detailing
birth outcomes of adolescents without doula support from the same year, 21.8% of these births
were cesarean sections, a difference of 9.2% (Curtin et al., 2015, p. 4). The number of elective
deliveries is also important, as elective repeat cesarean sections make up 30% of the indications
of cesarean sections in North America (Quinlan & Murphy, 2015, p. 178). The Washington, D.C.
doula program found a cesarean rate of only 8% (1/12 participants), and community-based
program in Georgia found a cesarean rate of only 17% (53/314 participants), both of which were
lower than the national rate of 21.8% (Gentry et al., 2010, p. 29; Smiley et al., 2025). These
findings suggest that doula care can lower adolescent cesarean section rates.
The significance of doulas’ effects on adolescent cesarean section rates may also be
dependent on whether the adolescent parent is supported during labor, rather than only during
prenatal visits, and whether they are low risk and nulliparous . In one study of participants under
the age of 26 (with a mean age of 18.4 years old), no significant difference was found between
the doula care arm and the non-doula care arm (Hans et al., 2018, pp. S105–S107). The authors
of this study  hypothesized these results may have been because their population of young and
low-income mothers may have presented as more medically complex than expected/than the
program could support?? and only 75% of the doula treatment group actually received doula
support during labor (Hans et al., 2018, pp. S108–S110). In future studies, it may be helpful to
include a larger sample of pregnant adolescents who were randomized into doula and control
care groups and exclude samples in which the doula was not present during labor. It may also be
enlightening to compare doulas that provide care before, during, and after delivery  to labor-only
or prenatal-only doulas.
Adults
Unlike the adolescent age group, existing literature rarely reflected sample groups in
which every participant was within the adult age group of 20-34 years old. However, many
studies were concerned with populations whose means and standard deviations fell within the
adult age parameters. These studies, along with a study that had results distinct to the 20-34 age
group demographic, were used to investigate the adult age group. A total of 10 studies were
used.
Adults appeared to face some similar struggles to adolescents. Multiple studies noted that
doula programs specifically screened patients, sometimes more than once, for food insecurity,
intimate partner violence, and housing insecurity, three important social determinants of health
(Mottl-Santiago et al., 2023, p. 469; Thomas et al., 2023, p. S61). Doulas also screened patients
for depression and provided referrals to necessary mental health services, a factor that
adolescent-specific doula care was missing (Thomas et al., 2017, p. S61). Doulas worked with
pregnant women to identify their desires for their birth and educate them on how best to advocate
for themselves with their medical providers (Thomas et al., 2017, p. S61). This may help women
feel more confident in their decision if they intend to have a vaginal birth, reducing the rate of
elective cesarean sections. Discussing a comprehensive birth plan may also encourage the
pregnant person to speak up and continue to attempt labor if a cesarean section is suggested by a
medical provider during delivery l.
These doula interventions may be particularly effective for  women on Medicaid, many
of whom are also women of color. These women face the additional stressors of systemic and
interpersonal racism and poverty, and their communities bear disproportionate rates of chronic
health issues (Thomas et al., 2017, p. S60). Doulas are able to provide culturally specific care,
which may mitigate the impact of some of these stressors (Futch Thurston et al., 2019).
However, because Medicaid rarely covers doula services and private doula fees can range from
hundreds of dollars to around $2,000 (Futch Thurston et al., 2019; Kozhimannil et al., 2013, p.
118, 2016, p. 25), many pregnant women cannot afford doula care (Futch Thurston et al., 2019).
Several studies suggest doula support is effective at lowering cesarean rates for adult
patients in labor. Out of the 10 studies used for the adult age group analysis, four studies did not
return statistically significant results. However, all relevant studies showed a direct trend of
doula care reducing cesarean section rates (See Figure 1 in Appendix II). In the only study that
separated results for the adult age group, the study found that women with doula care had a
21.6% rate of cesarean section compared to women without doula support who had a rate of
29.3% (Gruber et al., 2013, p. 54). While this difference was not found to be statistically
significant to a p-value of 0.05, it does show a positive trend. The difference may have not been
significant because of the low power of the relatively small sample size (n=92) (Gruber et al.,
2013, p. 54). This trend was found in another study without exact adult age constraints, where
non-doula supported patients had a cesarean section rate of 33.3% and supported patients had a
rate of 31.9%, though the difference was not found to be statistically significant (Lemon et al.,
Other studies without a specific/explicit adult age sample group but with mean ages and
standard deviations within ages 20-34 showed a substantial decrease in risk for cesarean sections
when doulas were part of their healthcare team. For cesarean sections, adjusted odds ratios
(AORs) for a cesarean section with doula care were reported at 0.44 (95% confidence interval
0.39-0.49) (Kozhimannil et al., 2016, p. 23) and 0.41 (95% CI 0.18-0.96) (Kozhimannil et al.,
2014, p. 6), 0.59 (95% CI 0.51-0.68) (Kozhimannil et al., 2013, p. 116). Another study reported
a relative risk of 0.53 (95% CI 0.43-0.66) (Falconi et al., 2024, p. 1280) between patients with
and without doulas. For non-medically indicated cesarean sections, an even stronger association
was found with an AOR of 0.17 (95% CI 0.07-0.39) (Kozhimannil et al., 2014, p. 6).
Another finding was the ability of doula care to increase rates of VBACs (vaginal birth
after cesarean). In one study, the rate of VBACs for non-doula supported births was 18.8%,
while doula-supported births had a VBAC rate of 34.4% (p=0.002) (Lemon et al., 2025, p.
387.e5). Another study also reported that when doulas supported patients during delivery, they
were 116% more likely to have a VBAC delivery than their non-doula-supported counterparts
(Falconi et al., 2024, p. 1280). VBACs have been shown to result in fewer maternal morbidities
such as ruptured uteri, unplanned hysterectomies, and ICU admissions than repeat cesarean
sections, (Curtin et al., 2015, p. 1; Lemon et al., 2025, p. 387.e6). These studies suggest doula
care may play a substantial role in reducing rates of cesarean sections for adults.
Advanced Age
Women of advanced maternal age face significantly higher rates of cesarean section than
younger women? in the United States. While the overall cesarean section rate in 2022 was
32.1%, for women ages 35-39 years old, that number jumped to 40.0%, and for women 40 and
older, it jumped again to 47.7% (Osterman et al., 2024, p. 40). Women 35 and older have a
higher risk of developing maternal morbidities such as severe preeclampsia, superimposed
preeclampsia, and hypertension. Because of their elevated risk levels,  mothers of advanced
maternal age may benefit greatly from  doula care. However, women in the advanced age group
were less likely to have doula support compared to mothers ages 18-24 (Kozhimannil et al.,
2014, p. 5).  Unfortunately, no studies were identified for this review that considered the benefits
of doula care on advanced maternal age.
Comparing Benefits Between Age Groups
When examining AORs of cesarean section for women of different ages, it appears that
doula care may have a more significant benefit for adolescent and adult women than for women
in the advanced age category. According to a study published containing data from 2010-2014,
the AOR of cesarean sections, among all women with full term births in the study who had a
doula compared to those who did not, was 0.44 (95% CI 0.39-0.49)—showing clear benefit
(Kozhimannil et al., 2016, p. 26). When comparing between age groups, with ages 26-30 being
the reference age group (1.00), the AORs of women with full term deliveries having a cesarean
section (and 95% CIs) were as follows: ages 20 and under, 1.46 (1.38-1.53); ages 21-25, 0.90
(Kozhimannil et al., 2016, p. 26). If the degree of benefit of doula care for women of different
age groups was the same, it would be expected that the AORs between age groups would remain
the same when comparing doula care to doula care and non-doula care to non-doula care.
However, the data does not suggest this.
In order to compare data with as few confounding variables as possible, the control data
for this review was taken from the National Vital Statistics Report (NVSR) from 2012 so as to
stay within the timeframe of Kozhimannil’s study (2010-2014) reviewed above: the most recent
comparison between benefits to age groups. According to the National Vital Statistics Report
from 2012, the cesarean rates for the different age groups were as follows: ages 19 and under,
40-54, 49.7% (Martin et al., 2013, p. 51). While the NVSR does not provide AORs, a few
conclusions may still be made from the comparisons of the data.
Firstly, while the 19-and-under age group in the NVSR was 9.2% less likely to have a
cesarean section compared to women ages 25-29, Kozhimannil et al.’s study found that with
doula care, women under 20 have a higher risk of cesarean section compared to women ages
26-30. This suggests that, while doula care has been found to have a positive effect on birth
outcomes for adolescents, it is likely a smaller magnitude of benefit. There also appears to be a
smaller magnitude of benefit for women of advanced maternal age. The NVSR reported that
women ages 35-39 were 10.6% more likely, and women 40-54 were 18.2% more likely, to have a
cesarean section than women ages 25-29. However, that is a much smaller difference than AOR
presented in the study, which suggests that women ages 35+ are 4.67 times more likely to have a
cesarean section. This suggests that doula care has a much smaller impact (if both impacts are
positive) on the cesarean section rates of women of advanced maternal age.
This comparison is not ideal, given that it necessitates comparing data from different
sources and conditions. More research should be conducted that directly compares doula care to
a lack of doula care and age to limit cross-data set analysis and provide valid conclusions.
Strengths and Limitations
A strength of this review is that it specifically focuses on trained birth doulas. Lay doulas,
partners, and nursing staff who provide labor and prenatal support were excluded from analysis
to specifically identify  the impact of doula training. Another strength of this review is the
variety of studies that were analyzed, including both large quantitative studies using national
data, as well as smaller, interview-based qualitative studies—which allowed for closer
examination of how doulas cater their care to mothers of different age groups.
A major limitation of this review is the paucity of published literature on the effect of
doula care, maternal age, and forceps use, as well as a general lack of specific information on
advanced age pregnancies. There are no articles that break down cesarean section rates by age
group and compare them to the non-doula-care-control condition. This gap in the research led to
my need for comparing different data sets, which is not ideal. Another limitation of the studies
used in this review is the potential for selection bias, for most did not randomly separate
participants, but rather, they used data where pregnant women may have been referred to doula
care because of risk factors they faced or sought it out themselves (Falconi et al., 2024, p. 1276;
Kozhimannil et al., 2016, p. 26). This may have led to confounding factors such as the
populations in the study being at higher risk compared to non-study populations.
Conclusion
Published literature suggests that doula care has varying degrees of benefit to pregnant
people in reducing cesarean sections based on their age. This may be due to specific obstetric
risk factors that come with age, social determinants of health, or whether a specific age group
tends to have medically-indicated or non-indicated cesarean sections.
Future research, in addition to filling in the gaps identified in the Strengths and
Limitations section, may take a few different paths. One is to separate delivery outcomes into
medically-indicated and non-indicated cesarean sections to pinpoint whether doulas play a larger
role in medically indicated outcomes or elective delivery choices. Medical indications include
issues with the placenta, the baby being in the wrong position, fetal distress, and maternal health
conditions that make vaginal birth dangerous (Kozhimannil et al., 2014, p. 4). Further research
may also compare results between the different models of doula care.
Finally, more research should be conducted on insurance status and the impacts of doula
care. Many studies read for this review looked only at Medicaid-insured populations. Cost has
been shown to be a significant barrier to doula care access for all women, not just women on
Medicaid— and in one study, nearly three fourths of women reported that, if their health
insurance covered doula care, they would take advantage of this benefit (Mitchell et al., 2023, p.
187). This comes in stark contrast to the mere 6% of women who reported, in the most recent
data available, actually using doula care in the United States (Declercq et al., 2013, p. XI).
Studying, more specifically, the impacts of both private and public insurance covering doula care
may lead to significant policy action that can expand doula access for all women in the United
States.

obstetrics care and maternal mortality with a focus on midwifery under Professor Sarah
Rodriguez, which inspired Zora’s self-led project on doula care and maternal morbidity.

in Health Content
Asha S. Henry
Northwestern University
Advisor: David Rapp, Ph.D.
Second Reader: Galen Bodenhausen Ph.D.
Department of Cognitive Science, Northwestern University
School of Education and Social Policy, Northwestern University
Introduction
Since its inception in the early 2000s, social media has become a cornerstone of everyday
life for many people around the world, with 5.24 billion people estimated to have used social
media as of February 2025 (Statista). Sites such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X (formerly
Twitter), and Reddit have become international hubs for sharing news, art, and music, connecting
with friends, and building communities based on shared interests and hobbies. Exposure to
health and wellness content is frequent when a user spends any length of time on social media,
often with a near-immediate crossover to real-world impacts. Exposure can occur via influencers,
friends, news sources, sponsored content, and advertisements. Many social media users even
seek out sources of specific wellness content by following accounts that focus on niche health
topics (Lim & Molenaar et al., 2022).
The practice of sourcing information via social media is particularly prevalent in the case
of the app TikTok, a short-form video-sharing platform originally released in 2016. The app is
particularly popular among teens and young adults, with more than half of adolescents reporting
using the platform (Leppert & Matsa, 2024). The hope for social media to share information and
build community is nearly limitless; however, with an increase in digital consumption, the
simultaneous proliferation of health misinformation is visible and concerning.
The risk to public health has risen as social media increasingly has become a pathway
through which people consume health information. Many people, particularly youth, are
generally unfamiliar with how to identify trusted health sources online, making the credibility of
those accounts sharing health and wellness information particularly pertinent (Eysenbach, 2008).
Credibility checks of accounts sharing health and wellness information ensure that
misinformation does not spread as people are less likely to interact with sources they deem not
credible (Eysenbach, 2008). As social media has expanded, it has become a hotbed for
misinformation that can harm community health. Balancing the growth of social media alongside
the urgent need to combat misinformation will remain a life-and-death public health concern for
the healthcare industry, nations, and the global community.
Cognitive Consequences of Misinformation
Researchers have outlined the harmful effects of misinformation in the online context and
have explored how it impacts decision making. Misinformation is defined as “inaccuracies
generally conveyed through discourse, whether intentional or accidental” (Jia, 2020). Regardless
of intentionality, misinformation can cause people to retain falsehoods, and the resulting
confusion can contribute to misunderstandings of events (e.g., Butler et al., 2009; O’Sullivan et
al., 2022; Schiff et al., 2024; Umanath et al., 2012). Exposure to misinformation can cast doubt
on the credibility of outside sources (news media, podcasts, etc.), information dissemination
systems, and knowledge-based communities (Brashier & Schacter, 2020; Marwick & Partin,
2024; Westbrook et al., 2023). Even following minimal exposure to these inaccuracies, people
are more likely to be influenced by misinformation, rather than to spontaneously generate the
same ideas after accurate or unrelated information exposure (e.g., Appel & Richter, 2007; Butler
et al., 2009; Fazio et al., 2015; Gerrig & Prentice, 1991; Marsh et al., 2003; Marsh & Fazio,
2007; Rapp, 2016; Salovich et al., 2022; Salovich, Mason, et al., 2023). In cases wherein
participants previously held accurate understandings of information, exposure to inaccuracies
appeared to suspend and supersede the prior knowledge that participants previously held, with
falsehoods taking precedence (Hinze et al., 2014; Marsh et al., 2003; Salovich et al., 2022;
Salovich, Mason, et al., 2023;  Salovich & Rapp, 2023). Previous knowledge should have
allowed participants to rationally doubt and internally refute the inaccurate information presented
in the stimuli (Brashier & Schacter, 2020; Marwick & Partin, 2024). The fact that
misinformation can so easily dislodge prior accurate information among users portends a
worrisome future for public health, marked by both unintentional and malicious efforts that
spread misinformation.
Moreover, in the online environment, misinformation has exploited social media
algorithms, spreading misinformation to an ever-widening audience more rapidly than truths.
Vosoughi et al. (2018) investigated the spread of false information on the social media site
Twitter (now X), and found that falsehoods diffused faster than the truth. Falsehoods were found
to reach between 1,000 and 100,000 people, while the truth seldom reached more than 1,000
individuals. Furthermore, exposure to inaccuracies can result in confusion about what is the truth
and can foster doubt in previously held accurate beliefs, which causes additional reliance on
misinformation, (Rapp & Salovich 2018). The perceived credibility of the sources offering
information has also been proven to further impact the spread of misinformation. When
information is shared via sources that are perceived to be credible, such as an immigration
attorney speaking on common visa issues, people are more likely to learn and depend on the
misinformation presented to make decisions (Andrews & Rapp, 2014; Appel & Mara, 2013;
Ecker & Antonio, 2021; Heinbach et al., 2018; Nadarevic et al., 2020; Walter & Tukachinsky,
Health misinformation is defined as ‘health-related statements that are anecdotal
evidence, factually incorrect, or misleading due to a lack of scientific evidence’ (Suarez-Lledo &
Alvarez-Galvez 2021). Current work has found that engagement with videos—including clicks,
shares, views, comments and retweets—that include inaccurate information is higher than the
engagement with videos containing accurate information (Goobie et al., 2019; Selvi &
Baydilli, 2022; Xu et al., 2021). General online users, such as those who have lay knowledge of
health and healthcare, claim to receive health and wellness information from both credentialed
healthcare professionals and non-credentialed general users regularly (Kirkpatrick & Lawrie,
2024). However, the process of ascertaining expertise in online space is often based on
surface-level visual cues such as account username, number of followers, presence of a
verification check, profile photos, biography and other superficial details (Kirkpatrick & Lawrie,
2024). Although these sources may appear to be valid forms of account credibility verification,
visual cues can easily be changed, manipulated, or intentionally misrepresented to deceive
audiences. Experimental research has shown that exposure to videos that contain health
inaccuracies can result in changes in both behaviors and beliefs (Vraga et al., 2021). Given the
effectiveness of online media to influence thought and behavior, content creators can manipulate
users by projecting an image of credibility, which then increases the existence and impact of
health misinformation online.
In the online environment, much of the health and wellness information being
disseminated is through Social Media Influencers (SMIs), online creators with large followings
gained from the narration of their daily lives (Thompson, 2022). Health and wellness SMIs often
focus on niche topics such as reproductive health, dermatology, fitness training, or
Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and they often present on topics of interest to
their cultivated audience—including income-generating efforts to promote products and services.
These SMIs have a wide range of claimed expertise, from board-certified surgeons, specialty
nurses, and health researchers to naturopaths, and to those who may simply suffer from a
condition.
In general, Americans tend to have a high degree of trust in medical doctors and other
healthcare professionals, with 74% of Americans having a mostly positive view of doctors, and
68% having a mostly-favorable opinion of medical research scientists (Funk & Gramlich 2020).
Real-world trust overlaps with the online environment:the materials shared on social media via
influential users with expertise (i.e. the username @Dr.Smith) are proven to be more likely to be
shared and re-processed by other users than informational materials shared by general users
(Thompson, 2022). However, there has been a significant increase in anti-expertise rhetoric and
accompanying health misinformation by SMIs and a resulting proliferation of health-related
inaccuracies and myths online. Media theorist Mark Davis has critiqued that anti-vaccination and
other anti-expertise groups have fabricated and weaponized the ‘politicized’ agendas of
healthcare professionals to create an “us versus them” mentality between those with health
knowledge and those without. Under this framework, groups can conflate expertise with political
or ideological bias as a rationale for the promotion of supposedly harmful vaccines by healthcare
professionals (Davis, 2018). This process of demonizing healthcare professionals as supporters
of ideological bias encourages users to doubt those with traditional forms of expertise (education,
professional experience, board certifications) and to trust those that are perceived to be
ideologically pure and anti-expertise, even if their own authority on a topic is unfounded.
Short-form videos, typically less than one-minute long, have become one of the most
popular forms of media on apps such as TikTok (For You Page), Instagram (Reels), Facebook
(Shorts), and YouTube (Shorts), with each app creating their own version of short-form media
feeds within the larger app platform. Misinformation in these short form video feeds has not been
investigated in the field of cognitive psychology under experimental conditions. However,
observational studies of TikTok videos covering the Covid-19 pandemic found moderate
misinformation to be present in 22% of videos studied, which were viewed a median of 6.8
million times, and a high-level of misinformation to be present in 7% of of videos, viewed, on
average, 9.4 million times (Baghdadi & Coffey, 2023). Inaccuracies present in short-form videos
can be viewed in several modalities, including through speech, text, imagery, out-of-context
visuals or verbalizations, or artificial intelligence-generated images or videos (Rapp, Holohan, &
Withall, in press). In the present study, we have created experimentally controlled videos
modeled after those that one would find on social media containing speech misinformation.
Social Media and Misinformation
Unlike other models of communication, which utilize a vertical approach—those at the
top of the information hierarchy spreading knowledge down to the base—social media utilizes a
horizontal model, with anyone, regardless of positionality on the information hierarchy, sharing
knowledge equally with everyone (Fisher, 2022). Social media’s  transformation of the
communication model allows misinformation to be shared by anyone and to be viewed by any
number of users, with or without claims of expertise, or proof of knowledge. Social media apps
that utilize short-form videos are designed to capture the attention of the audience, with videos
that have garnered significant audience interactions (likes, comments, views, shares, etc.) being
boosted by the app’s algorithmic presentation, which then promotes high-engagement videos to
increasingly broader audiences, thus creating an exponential reach and potentially resulting in
the harmful spread of misinformation online. Furthermore, this algorithmic process means that
users sharing videos including misinformation out of alarm or dismay actually boost the reach
and impact of that misinformation.
Real-World Application of Research
Currently, there are significant gaps in the literature regarding misinformation in the
format of short-form videos in the cognitive psychology realm; however; this is an area that
should not be overlooked, for many hundreds of thousands of social media users are exposed to
health and wellness information daily, a significant proportion of which has been proven to be
misinformation. This misinformation is of critical concern because, as of early 2025, there is a
spreading outbreak of measles in many parts of the United States. The spread of measles likely a
result of current efforts by anti-vaccination groups, who incorrectly claim online that
vaccinations cause autism in children and who further question the efficacy of vaccines and their
long-term effects. The spread of vaccine misinformation in the digital age has resulted in the
eradication of prior national immunity due to widespread vaccination efforts, which resulted in
the elimination of measles from within the country in 2000 (CNN, 2025). As of October 2025,
the current outbreak has already caused the death of three unvaccinated children in, along with
hundreds of hospitalizations (U.S. Centers for Disease Control). Despite this, the National
Institutes of Health has terminated dozens of scientific grants for projects on the topic of vaccine
use and hesitancy, since this research has been considered to be unaligned with the Trump
administration’s priorities (PBS).
Current Study
The current study seeks to determine if the claimed expertise of the content creator has an
impact on the reproduction of health and wellness misinformation in the social media realm.
Participants viewed 12 short-form videos that shared both correct and incorrect health and
wellness information. Each video was presented along with an account username, which was
presented as either an expert (e.g., @Derm_Dr.Reith) or non-expert (e.g.,. @user124085). After
viewing the videos and completing a distractor task, participants answered questions about the
validity of the statements presented in the videos, along with several filler statements. Previous
work has shown that response accuracy decreases after exposure to inaccurate information as
compared to response accuracy after exposure to correct information, and we expect this typical
misinformation exposure effect to be replicated in the current study (Holohan & Rapp, in prep).
Furthermore, we expect that participants will be more likely to reproduce incorrect health and
wellness inaccuracies shared by a user with claimed expertise, as compared to non-expert users.
Method
Participants—We recruited one hundred and six (n = 106) undergraduate students via
Northwestern’s psychology subject pool. We excluded participants who had not completed the
survey, and we continued recruitment until the goal sample size of 100 was reached. This sample
size was chosen to roughly match the sample size in Salovich et al., (2022), which utilized a
series of three experiments to investigate if evaluative mindsets reduce the likelihood of the use
and influence of inaccurate statements. Salovich et al. (2022) included 80 participants per
within-subject condition, with a total of 160 participants to reach adequate power. Since all of
our variables were manipulated within-subjects, we determined that a sample of 100 participants
would be sufficient to achieve adequate power.
Design—This experiment used a 2 (exposure idea accuracy: accurate or inaccurate) x 2 (test item
accuracy: accurate or inaccurate) x 2 (username expertise: expert or non-expert) design with all
variables manipulated within-subjects.
Materials—24 videos were adapted from text vignettes created by Salovich et al. 2023 and
videos created by Holohan & Rapp, in prep. The vignettes contained information on various
topics that were considered to be true or false based on an accumulation of evidence, and the
health and wellness vignettes were selected to be made into short-form videos. A screenshot
from one of the videos can be found in Appendix A. The vital information in each vignette was
normed for the baseline rates, at which participants were able to correctly identify the accuracy
of each statement. Results from the norming study showed that the accurate assertions were more
likely to be determined to be as correct as compared to the inaccurate assertions. The script
dialogues were used to develop and record short-form videos, including a single individual
speaking about a topic (e. g., Vitamin C efficacy as a treatment for a cold) in a neutral setting.
Each video was between 29 and 46 seconds (M = 30.9 sec) in length. Two versions of each video
were created with the same actor discussing the accurate version of the stimuli (e.g. “Vitamin C
is an effective treatment for a cold”) and the inaccurate version of the stimuli (e.g. “Vitamin C is
not an effective treatment for a cold”). Each video contained a simple caption to model those
seen on short-form video platforms (“Vitamin C & Alleviating Cold Symptoms”).
Procedure
After providing consent, participants began the exposure phase of the study. Participants
viewed 12 videos, one at a time, presented in a different random order for each participant. Half
of the videos each participant viewed contained accurate information about various health and
wellness topics, and half contained inaccurate information about the same topics. Half of the
videos offered a tag that highlighted a source’s ostensible expertise in their username (e.g.,.
@Derm_Dr.Reith), and half of the videos included a non-expert username (e.g.,. @user124085).
Participants were required to watch each video in its entirety before a blue arrow popped up and
allowed the participant to click and view the next video. After watching the videos, participants
completed a mandatory 8-minute distractor task that consisted of simple math problems.
Participants were unable to advance until the eight minutes had passed, and they were
automatically advanced regardless of their degree of completion of the task once eight minutes
concluded/passed. Following the distractor task, participants began the judgement phase of the
task. Participants read 18 statements, 12 of which were related to the content of the videos, while
6 filler statements were also presented. Statements were presented in random order to each
participant. Participants were then asked to determine whether the statements provided were
“True” or “False,” then required to answer each statement before continuing onto the next
statement. After the competition of the judgement task, participants were asked to complete a
brief demographic questionnaire and were subsequently thanked and debriefed.
Results
Data analyses were run using logistic regression using generalized linear mixed effect
models (GLMER) with the statistics R package (R Core Team, 2025). All factors were contrast
coded. The model included the factors of Expertise (contrast coded: expert = -.5, non-expert =
.5), Exposure Accuracy (contrast coded: accurate = -.5, inaccurate = .5), and Test Condition
(contrast coded: accurate = -.5, inaccurate = .5), along with their interactions as fixed effects. The
model also takes into account the random effect of the participants. Accuracy analyses were
determined via the proportion of incorrect judgements yielded by each participant as a function
of accuracy of the content at exposure and test. Incorrect judgements (contrast coded: correct =
0, incorrect = 1) included cases in which participants identified inaccurate test statements as true,
and accurate statements as false. All means and standard deviations can be found in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Mean Proportions of Incorrect Judgments. Note: Mean proportions of incorrect judgements at test as a
function of expertise (expert or non-expert), exposure accuracy (accurate or inaccurate), and test condition (accurate
or inaccurate). Conditions were manipulated within subjects. Error bars represent standard error.
We observed a main effect of exposure condition, b = 1.74, SE = .14, z = 11.92, p < .001.
In line with predictions, participants made more incorrect judgments after having been exposed
to inaccurate information (M = .45, SD = .49 ), than after having been exposed to accurate
information (M = .13, SD =.34).
We did not observe a main effect of the test condition, b = .08, SE = 0.14, z = 0.62, p =
0.53. This indicates that participants did not make a significantly different amount of incorrect
judgments in the inaccurate test condition (M = .30, SD = .45) as compared to the accurate test
condition (M =. 29, SD = . 45). Further, we found no significant main effect of expertise, b =
-.01, SE = .14, z = -.07, p = 0.94. This indicates that there was no difference in incorrect
judgments after exposures to low expertise (M = .29 , SD=. 45) as compared to high expertise
(M = .30, SD = .45) usernames.
The analyses also revealed a marginal, three-way interaction between expertise, exposure
condition, and test condition, b = 1.12, SE = 0.57, z = 1.95, p = .05. Follow-up analyses revealed
that the interaction between exposure condition and test condition was reduced and inverted in
the expertise condition, b = -0.96, SE = 0.44, z = -2.18, p = 0.02, as compared to in the no
expertise condition, b = 1.72, SE = 0.20, z = 8.28, p < 0.001. These results indicate that, in the
expertise condition, after participants were exposed to inaccurate information, they made more
incorrect judgments when reading accurate test statements (M = .53, SD = .50) as compared to
inaccurate test statements (M = .39, SD = .49). However, in the no expertise condition, after
participants were exposed to inaccurate information, they made fewer incorrect judgments when
reading accurate test statements (M = .40, SD = .49) as compared to inaccurate test statements
(M =.51, SD =.50). No other interactions were significant (All ps > .05).
Results from this study replicate previous work, that exposure to inaccurate information
results in an increase in post exposure errors. Regardless of username expertise, participants
were equally as likely to replicate inaccurate information from an expert (e.g.,.
@Derm_Dr.Reith) as the non-expert (e.g.,. @user124085). A marginal three-way interaction was
found between expertise, exposure condition, and test condition, indicating that a combination of
these factors result in increased participant’s replication of inaccurate information.
General Discussion
When participants were exposed to inaccurate health and wellness statements, they are
more likely to produce errors at test. Expertise was a negligible factor in participants'
performance on judgement tasks, as participants replicated inaccuracies when shared by expert
users (e.g.,. @Derm_Dr.Reith) and non-experts (e.g.,. @user124085) at similar rates. However,
after exposure to inaccurate information, an engaging trend emerges. After viewing videos
shared by an expert user, participants made more errors when judging accurate test statements as
compared to inaccurate test statements, but after viewing videos with a non-expert username,
participants made more errors when judging inaccurate test statements as compared to accurate
test statements.
The proportion of errors after exposure to falsehoods in short-form videos replicated the
typical misinformation exposure effect found in previous studies (Appel & Richter, 2007; Gerrig
& Prentice, 1991; Rapp, Hinze, Kohlhepp, et al., 2014; Salovich & Rapp, 2021, Loftus et al.,
1992;). This indicates that when participants are exposed to incorrect stimuli via short-form
videos, they make more errors as compared to if they had been exposed to correct stimuli in the
videos. Exposure to inaccuracies can cause confusion and foster doubts about previous
knowledge, causing further reliance on inaccuracies (Rapp & Salovich, 2018). For example,
when participants are exposed to a video stating that “microwave radiation causes cancer,” they
may refer back to previously acquired knowledge and question if they have mis-remembered the
previous knowledge or the knowledge’s utility (Rapp & Salovich, 2018). The assertions used to
create the short-form videos in the current project were normed to ensure that participants had
some prior knowledge of the claims. Despite this, participants continued to make errors after
exposure to inaccuracies. These results are in line with previously reported literature, which
indicates that, even when people have accurate prior knowledge to disregard inaccurate stimuli
and respond with correct judgments, they still often continue to make errors (Ecker & Antonio,
2021, Anderson, J. R., 1981, Fazio, L. K., Barber, S. J., Rajaram, S., Ornstein, P. A., & Marsh, E.
Previous work on the perceived credibility and expertise of sources suggested that source
credibility has a significant impact on the extent to which information is encoded and relied
upon. Information shared by sources deemed to be unreliable is less likely to be encoded and
utilized to make decisions and solve problems than information deemed to be reliable (Andrews
& Rapp, 2014; Appel & Mara, 2013; Ecker & Antonio, 2021; Heinbach et al., 2018; Nadarevic
et al., 2020; Walter & Tukachinsky, 2020). However, the results of the current project indicate
that expertise had no effect on incorrect responses after exposure to inaccuracies in short-form
videos. This indicates that inaccurate information was relied on similarly across sources of
high-expertise and low-expertise. The results of the current study suggest that, unlike other forms
of social media, credibility determined via username expertise for short-form videos may have
little impact on the replication of misinformation. However, when further comparing the
proportions of incorrect judgements by condition, an interesting pattern emerges. Within the
expertise condition, when isolating solely for inaccurate exposure, we find that the proportion of
incorrect judgements was higher when judging accurate test statements, as compared to
inaccurate test statements. In the non-expertise condition, the proportion of incorrect judgments
was higher when judging inaccurate test statements compared to accurate test statements. This
reversal of trends may be a result of participants' willingness to use that information to combat
accurate claims when expert knowledge is assumed, but when the information comes from a
non-expert, they are more likely to only use the inaccuracies to support the same, inaccurate idea.
This pattern may be due to the exposure effect, where participants are unduly influenced by the
inaccurate knowledge at exposure (Appel & Richter, 2007; Calvillo & Smelter, 2020; Rapp &
Salovich, 2018). It is also possible that in the non-expert condition, participants are more likely
to defer to their own judgment and utilize prior knowledge rather than blindly believing the
knowledge shared by non-expert online users (Toth et. al, 2011). Another potential explanation
for this discrepancy is a lack of attention given to the username and source expertise by
participants, which can be a source for future research.
There are several factors that could have influenced the results observed. The sample size
(n = 106) was used to replicate that of Salovich et al., (2022), which used similar methods to
discover methods to reduce the influence of inaccurate statements; however, the limited sample
size can influence results. Future research related to this study includes how expertise was
represented in the videos. The claimed expertise of the short-form videos was presented in the
version of a username (e.g.,. @Derm_Dr.Reith or e.g.,. @user124085) located directly above the
video. Participants were instructed to pay attention to the username along with the content of the
videos, however it is possible that participants did not pay attention to the username, and as a
result, were unable to aptly encode the username along with the video. Future research could
include the modulation of the font size and placement of the username, which may draw
participants to place additional attention onto the expertise or lack thereof of the account’s user.
Under these conditions, it is possible that participants will pay increased attention to the
usernames in relation to the videos, possibly resulting in an increased effect of expertise.
Further research can seek to understand expertise as expressed through visual cues other
than username. Expertise can further be represented by the physical description of the person
speaking (e.g. wearing a white coat) as well as the setting and background of the video (e.g.
framed degrees or bookshelves). Will these forms of visual expertise result in similar rates of
inaccuracies as does the username? Further research can focus on understanding expertise
through cues other than username as potentially fueling misinformation. These cues can take the
form of the physical appearance of the individual speaking, an informational “bio” of the account
and user, overall content themes (e.g. an account solely posting content about adolescent
diabetes), or verbal claims of expertise. Alternative forms of expertise may impact the spread of
health and wellness misinformation online and can be an area of future research.
Results from this study replicated the misinformation effects from previous research in
the novel format of short-form videos commonly found on social media sites. A marginal
three-way interaction was found between expertise, test condition, and exposure, indicating that
a combination of these factors cause participants to produce errors. This is particularly alarming
as users online are not required by the sites to verify any form of credibility (education,
professional expertise, scientific basis for assertions, etc.), and it is the onus of the viewer to
determine the credibility of those sharing health and wellness information online.
When isolating within the expertise condition and inaccurate exposure, we found that, when
participants are exposed to inaccurate information shared by expert users, the proportion of
incorrect judgements was higher when judging accurate test statements, as compared to
inaccurate test statements. This may indicate that, after exposure to inaccurate expert statements,
users online may use that information to deny accurate information shared later on. However,
when exposed to non-expert inaccurate information, participants are more likely to replicate
inaccurate information, as opposed to the accurate test statements.
