blocks: Parenting with ADHD Symptoms:​
Investigating Warmth, Discipline, and Their Impact on Children with ADHD Symptoms
Samantha Hesekiel
Northwestern University, Department of Psychology
Advisor: Alissa Levy Chung, Ph.D., Department of Psychology
Abstract
Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition
characterized by persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity, often emerging in early childhood
and impacting social, emotional, and academic development. Given the high heritability of
ADHD, many parents – particularly mothers – of affected children also exhibit symptoms that
may, in turn, influence their parenting behaviors. This study examined associations between
maternal ADHD symptoms, parenting behaviors, and child behavioral outcomes. Eighty-eight
mothers of children aged 4-6 were recruited via Prolific and completed the Adult ADHD
Self-Report Scale (ASRS), the Comprehensive Early Childhood Parenting Questionnaire
(CECPAQ), and the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL). Results indicated that although more
boys (67.5%) than girls (44.7%) were diagnosed with ADHD, symptom severity did not
significantly differ by gender. Children diagnosed with ADHD showed significantly higher
internalizing behaviors, t(87)=2.22, p=.029, but not externalizing behaviors. Maternal inattention
was significantly associated with greater use of negative discipline, r(87)=.29, p=.01, though no
meaningful associations emerged with warmth or positive discipline. Additionally, positive
discipline was negatively correlated with children’s internalizing behaviors, r(87)=-.27, p=.01.
Findings suggest that maternal ADHD symptoms, particularly inattention, are linked to greater
use of negative discipline, which may contribute to child behavioral difficulties. The gender gap
in diagnoses, despite comparable symptom severity, further highlights potential diagnostic
biases. The use of a community, rather than clinical, sample may have influenced parent-reported
data and should be considered in future research.
Hesekiel, 1
Introduction
In 2022, an estimated seven million U.S. children aged 3-17 were diagnosed with
attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), marking an increase of one million diagnoses
since 2016.1 ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent patterns of
inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interfere with daily functioning.2
While many children outgrow some symptoms, untreated ADHD often persists into
adolescence and adulthood, making early recognition and intervention crucial.3 However,
diagnosing ADHD in young children is challenging because behaviors like high activity levels
are often typical for this age.4 This overlap requires a careful, nuanced approach to diagnosis.
Parenting Children with ADHD
Raising a child with ADHD presents unique challenges related to emotion regulation,
attention, and behavioral control. Managing these behaviors can be overwhelming for parents,
often draining their emotional resources5 and causing elevated stress. 6 In many cases, this
elevated stress increases the likelihood of harsher and more reactive disciplinary practices as
well, which not only fail to improve behavior but also weaken parent-child relations.7
7 Alizadeh, H., Applequist, K. F., & Coolidge, F. L. (2007). Parental self-confidence, parenting styles, and corporal
punishment in families of ADHD children in Iran. Child Abuse & Neglect, 31(5), 567–572.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2006.12.005
6 Lunkenheimer, E., Lichtwarck-Aschoff, A., Hollenstein, T., Kemp, C. J., & Granic, I. (2016). Breaking down the
coercive cycle: How parent and child risk factors influence real-time variability in parental responses to
child misbehavior. Parenting, Science and Practice, 16(4), 237.
5 Alizadeh, H., Applequist, K. F., & Coolidge, F. L. (2007). Parental self-confidence, parenting styles, and corporal
punishment in families of ADHD children in Iran. Child Abuse & Neglect, 31(5), 567–572.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2006.12.005
4 Egger, H. L., Kondo, D., & Angold, A. (2006). The epidemiology and diagnostic issues in preschool
attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A review. Infants & Young Children, 19(2), 109–122.
3 Lahey, B. B., Lee, S. S., Sibley, M. H., Applegate, B., Molina, B. S. G., & Pelham, W. E. (2016). Predictors of
adolescent outcomes among 4–6-year-old children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Journal of
Abnormal Psychology, 125(2), 168–181. https://doi.org/10.1037/abn0000086
2 National Institute of Mental Health (n.d.). Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder.
https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/topics/attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder-adhd
1 Center for Disease Control and Prevention. (2024b, October 23). Data and Statistics on ADHD.
https://www.cdc.gov/adhd/data/index.html
Hesekiel, 2
It is important to identify effective ways to support children with ADHD and
co-occurring conditions. This requires a deep understanding of parenting strategies that combine
emotional support with appropriate behavioral guidance. Evidence-based approaches tailored to
the child’s unique needs are essential for fostering healthier parent-child interactions and
improving long-term behavioral outcomes.
Warmth and Discipline in Parenting
Parenting research highlights two key dimensions linked to child development:  warmth
(referred to as support in this study) and discipline. Warmth involves acceptance, nurturance, and
positive reinforcement, while discipline encompasses strategies parents use to guide and manage
their child’s behavior.8 Though distinct, both techniques can coexist within an authoritative
parenting style that balances emotional security with behavioral control.9
This balance is particularly important for children with ADHD, who often struggle with
self-regulation and attention control. However, the stress of managing ADHD-related behaviors
makes it difficult for parents to sustain this warmth and consistency.10 As a result, parenting may
tilt toward a more controlling approach, often at the expense of support.
Impact of Parental Discipline
Not all forms of discipline affect children equally. Harsh or punitive approaches often
intensify behavioral problems rather than reduce them. Patterson’s research demonstrated that
coercive parent–child interactions can reinforce externalizing behaviors such as aggression and
10 Alizadeh, H., Applequist, K. F., & Coolidge, F. L. (2007). Parental self-confidence, parenting styles, and corporal
punishment in families of ADHD children in Iran. Child Abuse & Neglect, 31(5), 567–572.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2006.12.005
9 Garcia, O. F., Fuentes, M. C., Gracia, E., Serra, E., & Garcia, F. (2020). Parenting warmth and strictness across
three generations: Parenting styles and psychosocial adjustment. International Journal of Environmental
Research and Public Health, 17(20), Article 20. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17207487
8 Parmar, P., & Nathans, L. (2022). Parental warmth and parent involvement: Their relationships to academic
achievement and behavior problems in school and related gender effects. Societies, 12(6), Article 6.
https://doi.org/10.3390/soc12060161
Hesekiel, 3
defiance.11 When a child stops misbehaving after harsh discipline, the parent’s response is
inadvertently reinforced, perpetuating a negative cycle.
Children with behavioral or emotional challenges are especially vulnerable to these
dynamics. Those with ADHD, who already struggle with emotion regulation, may react more
strongly to harsh discipline and escalate conflict instead of learning self-control.12 Consequently,
punitive discipline can worsen defiance and strain relationships.
Impact of Warmth
While discipline supports behavior management, it must be balanced with emotional
support to be effective. Discipline without warmth often neglects children’s emotional needs,
which are central to healthy family dynamics.13 Research indicates that parental warmth, more
than discipline alone, has a stronger effect on improving behavioral outcomes.14
For children with ADHD, warmth plays a critical role. Research shows that higher
parental warmth at age five predicted fewer ADHD symptoms at age nine.15 Additionally, early
symptoms predicted reduced parental warmth later on. This bidirectional relationship shows how
warmth can buffer symptoms but may also decline as behaviors worsen. Overall, emotional
support addresses both immediate behavioral challenges and fosters improved well-being.
Parental Mental Health
15 Shelleby, E. C., & Ogg, J. (2020). Longitudinal relationships between parent involvement, parental warmth,
ADHD symptoms, and reading achievement. Journal of Attention Disorders, 24(5), 737–749.
14 Neppl, T. K., Conger, R. D., Schofield, T. J., & Donnellan, M. B. (2021). The influence of parental warmth and
harsh discipline on child behavior: A longitudinal study. Journal of Family Psychology, 35(4), 450–460.
https://doi.org/10.1037/fam0000812
13 Kirby, J. N. (2017). Compassion-focused parenting. In E. M. Seppälä, E. Simon-Thomas, S. L. Brown, M. C.
Worline, C. D. Cameron, & J. R. Doty (Eds.), The Oxford handbook of compassion science (pp. 129–140).
Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780190464684.013.8
12 Barkley, R. A., & Murphy, K. R. (2006). Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: A clinical workbook (3rd ed.).
The Guilford Press.
11 Patterson, G. R. (1982). A social learning approach: Volume 3 coercive family process. Multivariate Experimental
Clinical Research, 3(3).
Hesekiel, 4
As previously discussed, parenting a child with ADHD often leads to elevated stress
levels, disrupting a parent’s ability to remain consistent and emotionally available. These
challenges are often compounded when parents themselves experience ADHD symptoms, which
is common given the disorder’s high heritability. Approximately one-third to one-fourth of
parents of children with ADHD meet diagnostic criteria themselves.16 Parental ADHD
symptoms—particularly inattention, impulsivity, and emotional dysregulation—can impair
executive functioning, leading to inconsistent discipline and reduced warmth toward the child.17
Parental ADHD Symptoms and Parenting
Parental ADHD symptoms can further complicate the balance between support and
discipline. Maternal hyperactivity has been linked to lower levels of emotional support, as
impulsive and emotionally reactive behaviors can interfere with maintaining a nurturing attitude.
18 In contrast, maternal inattention is more closely associated with difficulties in enforcing
structured discipline.19 Challenges with focus, organization, and inhibitory control make it harder
to plan and apply consistent rules, leading to inconsistent parenting.
Current Study
19 Friedman, L. M., Dvorsky, M. R., McBurnett, K., & Pfiffner, L. J. (2020). Do parents’ ADHD symptoms affect
treatment for their children? The impact of parental ADHD on adherence to behavioral parent training for
childhood ADHD. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology, 48(11), 1425–1437.
18 Miklósi, M., Kovács, B., Janovicz, J., Lelki, F., & Kassai, R. (2024). Adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity
symptoms and parental cognitions: A meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 14.
17 Breaux, R. P., Brown, H. R., & Harvey, E. A. (2017). Mediators and moderators of the relation between parental
ADHD symptomatology and the early development of child ADHD and ODD symptoms. Journal of
Abnormal Child Psychology, 45(3), 443–456. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-016-0213-1
16 Chronis-Tuscano, A., Wang, C. H., Woods, K. E., Strickland, J., & Stein, M. A. (2017). Parent ADHD and
evidence-based treatment for their children: Review and directions for future research. Journal of Abnormal
Hesekiel, 5
This study focused on primary caregivers, recognizing that mothers are most often in this
role.20 Therefore, mothers of preschool-aged children were recruited to examine how maternal
ADHD symptoms relate to parenting behaviors. Additionally, parental ADHD symptoms were
measured dimensionally rather than categorically to capture subclinical traits that are
undiagnosed but may still affect parenting. This approach also accounts for the underdiagnosis of
women.21
Overall, the study explored links between maternal impulsivity and parental support, and
between maternal inattention and parental discipline, both in relation to children’s ADHD
symptoms. These focuses contributed to my primary research question: How do parental ADHD
symptoms (impulsivity vs. inattention) relate to both parenting behaviors and behavioral
outcomes in children with ADHD?
After investigating past research, I established three main hypotheses regarding the
relationship between parental ADHD symptoms, parenting styles, and child behavior outcomes.
1.​ Higher maternal impulsivity will be associated with lower parental support scores.
2.​ Higher maternal inattention will be associated with lower positive discipline scores and
higher negative discipline scores.
3.​ Children of more impulsive mothers will display more behavioral difficulties, as
impulsivity is tied to lower parental warmth, a key factor in positive outcomes.
Methods
Participants
21 Attoe, D. E., & Climie, E. A. (2023). Miss. diagnosis: A systematic review of ADHD in adult women. Journal of
20 Zimmermann, P., Mühling, L. E., Lichtenstein, L., & Iwanski, A. (2022). Still mother after all these years: Infants
still prefer mothers over fathers (if they have the choice). Social Sciences, 11(2), Article 2.
https://doi.org/10.3390/socsci11020051
Hesekiel, 6
Eligibility was described to participating mothers as those who had “a child between the
ages of 4 and 6 years old who presents with behaviors consistent with ADHD.” The study
focused on parent-reported symptoms rather than clinical diagnoses, given that these young
children likely have not yet received an official diagnosis. Prolific was used to recruit individuals
who met the specific eligibility criteria for this study.
Demographics
I recruited 88 participants, with an average age of 36.7 (SD = 10.5) and an age range of
22 to 77. It is important to note that the older participants, aged 73 and 77, may have been
biological mothers, but rather assumed the maternal role in the lives of the children. Additional
maternal demographics are included in Table 1.
The average age of children in the study was 5.0 years (SD = 0.72). The gender
breakdown was 53.4% female (n=57) and 45.5% male (n=40), with one participant missing
gender data. Regarding ADHD diagnoses, 54.5% (n=48) of the children were diagnosed with
ADHD, 44.3% (n=39) were not diagnosed, and one data point was missing.
Measures
Child Behavior Checklist
The Child Behavior Checklist is a caregiver-report tool designed to assess behavioral and
emotional problems in children aged 1.5 to 5 years.22 It includes 99 items across subscales
grouped into internalizing, externalizing, and other problem domains, with T-scores indicating
borderline (65-69) and clinical (≥70) levels (see Table 2). The CBCL demonstrates strong
reliability, with all subscales showing internal consistency alphas above 0.70 and good test-retest
reliability over one week.
22 Naar-King, S., Ellis, D. A., & Frey, M. A. (2004). Child behavior. In S. Naar-King, D. A. Ellis, & M. A. Frey
(Eds.), Assessing children’s well-being: A handbook of measures (pp. 123–145). Lawrence Erlbaum
Associates Publishers.
Hesekiel, 7
Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale
Parental ADHD symptoms were self-reported using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale
(ASRS v1.1), a validated 18-item screening tool developed by the WHO.23 The ASRS has two
subscales—inattention (10 items) and hyperactivity (8 items)—with questions rated on a 5-point
Likert scale from “Never” to “Very Often.” The inattention subscale assesses difficulties with
organization and focus, while the hyperactivity subscale addresses restlessness and impulsivity.
Scores range up to 36 per subscale, with scores above 24 generally considered clinically
elevated.24 The ASRS also demonstrates high test-retest reliability among adults.
Comprehensive Early Childhood Parenting Questionnaire (CECPAQ)
The Comprehensive Early Childhood Parenting Questionnaire (CECPAQ) assesses
parenting behaviors focusing on five domains: support, stimulation, structure, positive discipline,
and harsh discipline. This study used 29 items covering support, positive discipline, and negative
discipline, rated on a 6-point Likert scale. The subscales measure warmth and nurturing
(support), proactive strategies (positive discipline), and punitive responses(negative discipline).
The CECPAQ demonstrated good reliability, with Cronbach’s alphas of .88, .76, and .79 for
support, positive discipline, and negative discipline, respectively.25
Procedures
Qualtrics Survey
25 Verhoeven, M., Deković, M., Bodden, D., & Van Baar, A. L. (2017). Development and initial validation of the
comprehensive early childhood parenting questionnaire (CECPAQ) for parents of 1–4 year-olds. European
Journal of Developmental Psychology, 14(2), 233–247. https://doi.org/10.1080/17405629.2016.1182017
24 Corbisiero, S., Hartmann-Schorro, R. M., Riecher-Rössler, A., & Stieglitz, R.-D. (2017). Screening for adult
attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in a psychiatric outpatient population with specific focus on sex
differences. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 8, 115. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyt.2017.00115
23 Silverstein, M. J., Alperin, S., Faraone, S. V., Kessler, R. C., & Adler, L. A. (2018). Test–retest reliability of the
adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) v1.1 screener in non-ADHD controls from a primary care
physician practice. Family Practice, 35(3), 336–341. https://doi.org/10.1093/fampra/cmx115
Hesekiel, 8
The survey on Prolific was distributed via Qualtrics, another online survey tool. To
ensure consistency and reduce response biases, the survey was designed to prevent participants
from skipping questions or moving backward to previous sections. On average, it took
approximately 15 to 20 minutes to complete the survey. The structure of the survey began with a
demographics section, followed by the CBCL, ASRS, and CECPAQ. Informed consent was
obtained from all participants prior to their involvement in the study.
Results
Child ADHD Data
Gender and ADHD Diagnoses
A chi-squared test of independence revealed a significant association between gender and
ADHD diagnosis status (breakdown provided in Table 3). The analysis yielded a statistically
significant result: χ²(1, N=47)=4.55, p = .033. This suggests a significant association between
gender and ADHD diagnosis status, with a greater proportion of male children diagnosed
(67.5%) compared to female children (44.7%). However, female and male children did not differ
significantly in the severity of symptoms they exhibited. For internalizing behaviors, t(87)=-1.72,
p=.089, and for externalizing behaviors, t(87)=-0.58, p=.564 (breakdown provided in Table 4).
Internalizing vs. Externalizing Across Diagnoses
I also examined the differences in internalizing and externalizing behaviors across
diagnostic groups, shown in Table 5. Independent samples t-tests revealed that children
diagnosed with ADHD had significantly higher levels of internalizing behaviors than children
who were not diagnosed, t(87)=2.22, p=.029. There was no significant difference in externalizing
behaviors, t(87)=-0.06, p=.952. It is interesting to note that there was no significant difference in
attention problems between the two groups, t(87)=-1.38, p= .170, despite being a core symptom.
Hesekiel, 9
Interaction with Maternal Diagnoses
I also conducted a chi-squared test of independence to explore the relationship between
maternal and child ADHD diagnoses (breakdown shown in Table 6). The analysis did not yield a
statistically significant result: χ²(1, N=86)=1.01, p = .315, suggesting that there was no
meaningful association between parental ADHD diagnosis and their children’s diagnosis.
Maternal Data
After analyzing the children’s data, I examined the mothers’ characteristics. Table 7
shows descriptive statistics for mothers’ ADHD symptoms and parenting styles. Mothers
exhibited clinically significant inattention but subclinical hyperactivity. Parenting styles,
measured by CECPAQ (max score 6), revealed high warmth and positive discipline scores, with
relatively low negative discipline scores.
ADHD Symptoms
Before exploring the links between ADHD symptoms and parenting, it’s important to
note that hyperactivity and inattention were strongly positively correlated (Table 8). This means
mothers with higher hyperactivity also tended to report higher inattention, explaining that
parenting behaviors may not be fully independent.
Parental Hyperactivity. Contrary to my hypothesis, hyperactivity was not significantly
related to parental warmth but was positively correlated with negative discipline. However,
hyperactivity was positively correlated with negative discipline.
Parental Inattention. I expected a negative relationship between discipline and
inattention overall, assuming that greater levels of inattention would be associated with lower
levels of effective discipline. This was correct in the sense that there was a positive correlation
Hesekiel, 10
between inattention and negative discipline. However, there was no association between
inattention and positive discipline or warmth.
Associations Between Parenting Style Dimensions. Parental support was negatively
correlated with negative discipline. In contrast, parental warmth was positively correlated with
positive discipline.
Child Behavior Outcomes
I also conducted Pearson correlations between parenting strategies and child behavior
outcomes (Table 9), which suggested that maternal ADHD symptoms of inattention and
hyperactivity are positively related to externalizing behaviors, including sleep problems and
attention problems, but excluding aggressive behavior. However, they are not correlated with
internalizing problems.
Parenting Style
After linking parental ADHD symptoms to parenting strategies, the next set of analyses
explored how specific parenting strategies were linked to child behavioral outcomes. There was a
negative relationship between positive discipline in parents and internalizing behaviors in
children (displayed in Table 10), meaning higher use of positive discipline was related to fewer
internalizing symptoms. Interestingly, positive discipline was only negatively correlated with
some facets of internalizing behavior but not others (displayed in Table 11).
Discussion
Overview of Findings
This study examined associations among maternal ADHD symptoms, parenting styles,
and preschool-aged children’s behavioral outcomes. Maternal inattention and hyperactivity were
linked to greater use of negative discipline, but not to warmth or positive discipline. Positive
Hesekiel, 11
discipline was negatively related to children’s internalizing behaviors, suggesting that parenting
approaches may shape emotional adjustment—or that parents may respond more positively to
children with internalizing symptoms.
Children with ADHD showed higher internalizing symptoms than those without a
diagnosis, though no differences emerged in externalizing behaviors or attention problems.
Males were more likely than females to be diagnosed with ADHD despite similar symptom
severity, indicating possible gender-related diagnostic differences. Although many mothers
reported ADHD diagnoses or elevated symptoms, maternal and child diagnoses were not
significantly related.
Child ADHD Symptoms
Gender Discrepancy. Although existing literature suggests that boys are diagnosed with
ADHD more frequently than girls, I found that there were no significant gender differences in
actual behavior scores.26 Interestingly, despite this sample including more female children than
males, males still had a significantly higher rate of diagnoses. This difference highlights a
potential gender bias in diagnostic practices, in that both genders displayed the same levels of
behavioral difficulties, yet boys were still more frequently diagnosed.
Another important factor to consider is the age of the children in this sample. Many
preschool-aged children may not have received a formal diagnosis yet, despite the potential to
receive one later in life. Some children, especially girls, may be diagnosed later in life, which
could contribute to the lower rate of diagnoses observed among females at this stage. Literature
supports this, suggesting that the males are, on average, 1.7 years younger than females when
26 Center for Disease Control and Prevention. (2024b, October 23). Data and Statistics on ADHD.
https://www.cdc.gov/adhd/data/index.html
Hesekiel, 12
they receive their ADHD diagnosis.27 This later diagnosis in females can result in later treatment
and, as a result, more severe outcomes.
These findings highlight that ADHD symptoms may be more similar across genders than
previously assumed, yet diagnostic patterns suggest a gender bias in identification and referral.
Greater awareness of how ADHD presents in girls is essential to reduce underdiagnosis and
ensure timely support.
Diagnosed vs. Undiagnosed Children. In line with previous studies, children diagnosed
with ADHD in this study exhibited high levels of internalizing behaviors, such as anxiety,
depression, and somatic complaints.28 These align with the expectation that emotional
dysregulation often occurs alongside ADHD. Interestingly, however, children diagnosed with
ADHD did not differ from their undiagnosed peers in terms of externalizing behaviors, which are
core symptoms of ADHD as well.29 This result contrasts with the widely accepted view that
ADHD is primarily characterized by externalizing behaviors. Instead, the findings propose the
idea that emotional and internal struggles may play a larger role in how ADHD is experienced
early on.
Heritability. Another surprising finding was the lack of a significant relationship
between parental and child ADHD diagnoses. Children of diagnosed parents were not more
likely to have ADHD, though this measure reflects only diagnosed cases and may overlook
undiagnosed symptoms. This limitation, along with the children’s young age and the use of

27 Martin, J., Langley, K., Cooper, M., Rouquette, O. Y., John, A., Sayal, K., Ford, T., & Thapar, A. (2023). Sex
Differences in ADHD Diagnosis and Clinical Care: A National Study of Population Healthcare Records in
Hesekiel, 13
maternal data only, may explain the discrepancy from prior research highlighting the genetic
transmission of ADHD.
Maternal Data
ADHD Symptoms. The parent self-report data provided further insight into both ADHD
symptoms and parenting styles within this sample. Notably, mothers in this group reported
average inattention scores that exceeded the clinical cutoff, suggesting that these participants did
experience deficits in attention. However, the same was not true for hyperactivity, being that this
number did not exceed the clinical cutoff. Even so, both parental inattention and hyperactivity
interacted significantly with parenting style and child behavior outcomes in various ways.
It is important to first highlight the correlation observed between the inattention and
hyperactivity subscales of ADHD in this sample. Mothers who scored high in hyperactivity also
tended to score high in inattention. This relationship between inattention and hyperactivity in
adults might actually be causal, with inattention potentially driving hyperactive behaviors.30 This
perspective is particularly relevant to the current study, as it suggests that the observed parenting
challenges may be more strongly linked to the overall ADHD symptom profile.
An alternative explanation points to the progression of ADHD across the lifespan.31 Their
research outlines how hyperactivity is common in children with ADHD but tends to decrease
significantly as they grow older. However, while hyperactivity decreases, inattention often
persists into adulthood, manifesting in various ways. These symptoms, especially those relating
to executive functioning, can have a significant impact on parenting techniques and child
outcomes, as pointed out in this study.
31 Barkley, R. A., & Murphy, K. R. (2006). Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: A clinical workbook (3rd ed.).
The Guilford Press.
30 Sokolova, E., Groot, P., Claassen, T., Van Hulzen, K. J., Glennon, J. C., Franke, B., Heskes, T., & Buitelaar, J.
(2016). Statistical evidence suggests that inattention drives hyperactivity/impulsivity in attention
deficit-hyperactivity disorder. PLOS ONE, 11(10), e0165120. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0165120
Hesekiel, 14
Parenting Style. In terms of parenting styles, warmth and positive discipline were
commonly reported, whereas negative discipline appeared less frequently. These findings were
somewhat surprising given the high inattention scores, which previous research has linked to
increased parenting stress and less consistent parenting behaviors.32
Interaction Between Parental ADHD Symptoms and Parenting Style
A negative association was hypothesized between maternal hyperactivity and parental
warmth, but this was not supported. Similarly, although maternal inattention was not related to
positive discipline, it was significantly associated with greater use of negative discipline. This
suggests that mothers with higher inattention may engage in harsher or more reactive parenting,
possibly due to emotional regulation or planning difficulties.
Maternal hyperactivity was also correlated with negative discipline. Given the strong
correlation between inattention and hyperactivity, it is possible that the presence of ADHD
symptoms more broadly – rather than any single subtype – contributes to increased use of
negative discipline. This larger pattern suggests that negative discipline may be a common
behavioral outcome among parents experiencing elevated ADHD symptoms.
Further supporting these findings, associations between the two parenting style
dimensions revealed that parental support was negatively correlated with negative discipline and
positively correlated with positive discipline. These results suggest that parenting behaviors tend
to cluster in predictable ways: parents who are warmer and more supportive tend to use
constructive discipline strategies. In contrast, parents experiencing greater challenges, such as
32 Chronis, A. M., Chacko, A., Fabiano, G. A., Wymbs, B. T., & Pelham, Jr., W. E. (2004). Enhancements to the
behavioral parent training paradigm for families of children with ADHD: review and future directions.
Clinical Child and Family Psychology Review, 7(1), 1–27.
Hesekiel, 15
those associated with ADHD, may find it more challenging to sustain this support and instead
rely heavily on negative discipline and other, less constructive strategies.
Interaction Between Parental ADHD Symptoms and Child Behavior Outcome
My final hypothesis predicted a relationship between maternal hyperactivity and
behavioral deficits in the sample of children. However, because inattention and hyperactivity
ended up being correlated with one another, this hypothesis was more challenging to test.
Instead, it may be more informative to consider the broader impact of elevated parental ADHD
symptoms on child outcomes.
Across the board, both inattention and hyperactivity were significantly associated with
child externalizing behaviors but not internalizing behaviors. These findings suggest that
elevated ADHD symptoms in parents—regardless of the subtype—may contribute to increased
overt behaviors in children. Although the correlation with aggressive behavior did not reach
statistical significance, sleep problems and attention difficulties showed significant relationships,
indicating that these issues are still meaningfully associated with parental ADHD symptoms.
Research indicates that internalizing disorders like anxiety and depression show lower
heritability than externalizing disorders, which may explain the stronger link between parental
ADHD symptoms and children’s externalizing behaviors. Specifically, heritability is estimated at
49% for anxiety and 53% for major depression.33 These differences suggest that genetic factors
may play a larger role in externalizing outcomes, underscoring the importance of targeted
interventions for children of parents with ADHD.
Interaction Between Parenting Style and Child Behavior Outcome
33 Guffanti, G., Gameroff, M. J., Warner, V., Talati, A., Glatt, C. E., Wickramaratne, P., & Weissman, M. M. (2016).
Heritability of major depressive and comorbid anxiety disorders in multi‐generational families at high risk
for depression. American Journal of Medical Genetics Part B: Neuropsychiatric Genetics, 171(8),
Hesekiel, 16
Unlike the correlations with parental ADHD symptoms – which were strongly linked to
externalizing behaviors – the associations with parenting style were more related to internalizing
behaviors. Specifically, there was a negative relationship between parents who reported higher
levels of positive discipline and internalizing behaviors in children. This suggests that
supportive, nurturing discipline strategies may serve as a protective factor against internal
emotional difficulties in children.
Further analysis showed that positive discipline was negatively correlated with certain
internalizing subscales, including somatic complaints and withdrawn behaviors, but not with
emotional reactivity or anxious/depressed behaviors. This is noteworthy given that emotional
reactivity is often viewed as a core feature of ADHD, reflecting impulsive or intense emotional
responses. Its lack of association with positive discipline may indicate that emotional reactivity is
less influenced by parenting practices alone and may require more structured interventions.
Moreover, emotional reactivity may be more heavily influenced by genetic factors than
other internalizing symptoms. Some children may be more biologically sensitive to stress and
other emotional challenges.34 These children might exhibit more intense emotional responses
even in relatively mild situations, explaining why the positive discipline strategies used by the
parents in this study did not significantly correlate. Similarly, the lack of significant correlation
between positive discipline and anxious/depressed behaviors suggests that these symptoms also
may not be as easily mitigated through parenting practices alone.
This finding also highlights the nuanced ways that child behavior interacts with parenting
practices. While positive discipline may effectively fight against certain internalizing symptoms,
it may not be sufficient to address others. Alternatively, there may be a bidirectional relationship
34 Barzman, D. (2015). Review of the genetic basis of emotion dysregulation in children and adolescents. World
Journal of Psychiatry, 5(1), 112. https://doi.org/10.5498/wjp.v5.i1.112
Hesekiel, 17
here, with parents using gentler discipline with children who present in more vulnerable ways.
Understanding these distinctions is critical for targeting interventions for these children.
Limitations
While this study provides valuable insight into the links between maternal ADHD
symptoms, parenting styles, and child outcomes, several limitations should be noted. First, the
reliance on self-report measures may have introduced response bias. Additionally, the use of a
community rather than a clinical sample means that not all children had formal diagnoses, and
some symptoms may not have reached clinical levels. Nonetheless, many mothers reported
elevated internalizing symptoms, suggesting that community-based parents can still be highly
attuned to their children’s difficulties—though this may reflect the characteristics of parents who
chose to participate in the study. Future studies would benefit from using more observational
methods and potentially recruiting clinical samples to better understand the complex interactions
between parents and children experiencing ADHD.
Conclusion ​
Overall, this study aims to deepen our understanding of the complex effects that maternal
ADHD symptoms may have on parenting behaviors, particularly regarding warmth and
discipline in mothers of preschool-aged children diagnosed with ADHD. The findings revealed
that maternal ADHD symptoms, especially inattention and hyperactivity, are significantly linked
to negative parenting practices such as increased use of negative discipline. However, positive
parenting strategies, particularly positive discipline, were found to be protective against
internalizing behaviors in children, highlighting the potential benefits of supportive parenting.
Hesekiel, 18
In light of these findings, the study calls for more tailored interventions to address the
specific needs of children with ADHD and their families. Understanding the distinct ways that
parental ADHD symptoms and parenting styles interact with child behavior outcomes can
provide critical insights for clinical practices in the future.

blocks: A Nonparametric Approach to Market Sentiment and
M&A Deal Premiums in the United States
Mergers and acquisitions (M&A) are among the most strategically significant
transactions in corporate finance, often involving substantial premiums paid by acquiring
firms over the market value of target companies. Conceptually, M&A premiums are the
differences between the M&A prices and the fair values of the companies. These
premiums are influenced by a variety of factors, including firm fundamentals, strategic
synergies, and broader macroeconomic conditions. Amongst the latter, market sentiment
— often proxied by measures of volatility or risk aversion — plays a potentially
important but difficult-to-model role.
Prior research has extensively examined determinants of M&A premiums. For
instance, Rhodes-Kropf, Robinson, and Viswanathan (2005) explore how market
misvaluations influence merger activity, suggesting that periods of overvaluation can lead
to increased M&A activity with resulting higher premiums.1 Moeller, Schlingemann, and
Stulz (2004) analyze the impact of firm size on acquisition premiums, finding that larger
acquirers tend to pay lower premiums.2
However, the relationship between market sentiment and M&A premiums
remains less clear. While some might suggest that heightened market volatility may deter
M&A activity due to increased uncertainty, others might propose that such periods may
present opportunities for acquirers to negotiate lower premiums. The CBOE Volatility
2 Sreedhar T. Bharath and Guojun Wu, “Long-run Volatility and Risk Around Mergers
and Acquisitions,” University of Michigan, Department of Finance (2005): 1–43.
1 Matthew Rhodes-Kropf, David T. Robinson, and S. Viswanathan, “Valuation Waves and
Merger Activity: The Empirical Evidence,” Journal of Financial Economics 77, no. 3
Index (VIX), commonly referred to as the "fear index," serves as a widely recognized
proxy for market sentiment, capturing expected market volatility. Yet, empirical analyses
directly linking VIX levels to M&A premiums are limited.
This study aims to fill this gap by investigating the relationship between market
sentiment, as measured by the VIX, and M&A deal premiums using nonparametric
regression methods. Unlike linear regression models, nonparametric techniques allow for
flexible estimation of the conditional expectation of deal premiums without imposing a
specific functional form, accommodating potential nonlinearities and threshold effects.
The objective is to estimate the regression function:
𝑚𝑥
( ) = 𝐸𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑚𝑖𝑢𝑚|𝑉𝐼𝑋= 𝑥
and to assess the shape and properties of this function in order to understand how
acquirers adjust their bidding behavior in response to changing market sentiment. While
this primary analysis relies on nonparametric regression of deal premiums in VIX, the
investigation is further extended by incorporating robustness checks and complementary
analyses — including a percentage-based normalization of premiums and distributional
comparisons across different VIX regimes — to evaluate the statistical and behavioral
underpinnings of the observed patterns.
DATA
To investigate the relationship between market sentiment and M&A deal
premiums, a dataset is first constructed by combining manually-retrieved
transaction-level M&A data from S&P Capital IQ with market-level volatility data from
Yahoo Finance. The analysis focuses on completed U.S.-based acquisitions of whole
companies, announced between 1993 and 2025, with a reported deal premium.
The M&A data is then obtained using Capital IQ’s transaction screening tool,
restricted to deals with the following criteria:
●​ Geography: United States.
●​ Deal type: acquisition of the whole company (including majority stakes).
●​ Deal status: completed.
●​ Deal size: greater than $5 million.
●​ Premium paid: not N/A.
The extracted dataset includes the announcement date, premium paid (in millions
USD), transaction value, and parties involved in the transaction. For each deal, the
variables announcement_date and premium_paid are retained to serve as the basis for the
analysis. After cleaning and filtering for extreme outliers and incomplete entries, the
resulting sample consists of 3,662 M&A transactions from 1993 through early 2025.
Specifically, 30 deals that reported premium values below -100% are removed, as these
likely reflect data errors, highly distressed scenarios where the acquirer paid far below the
target’s pre-announcement market value, or possibly intra-group transactions used to
transfer assets within related entities, making them unsuitable for comparative analysis.
To measure market sentiment, the VIX is utilized, which serves as a widely used
proxy for market fear or uncertainty. Historical VIX data is primarily downloaded from
Yahoo Finance using the get.hist.quote() function in the software R. Because M&A deals
are typically negotiated prior to their announcement, each deal is matched with the VIX
level on the day prior to the announcement date. Missing values in the VIX series due to
holidays or weekends are imputed using the last observation carried forward.
The merged dataset provides a time-aligned panel of deal premiums and
corresponding pre-announcement market volatility, enabling nonparametric analysis of
how premiums vary with investor sentiment.
II.​
METHODOLOGY
To estimate the relationship between market sentiment and deal premiums,
kernel-based local linear regression is utilized. This nonparametric technique estimates
the conditional expectation function
without assuming a
𝑚𝑥
( ) = 𝐸𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑚𝑖𝑢𝑚|𝑉𝐼𝑋= 𝑥
specific functional form. This is crucial within this context, as prior literature and
intuition suggest that the relationship between market volatility and buyer behavior may
be nonlinear, exhibiting potential threshold effects or regime shifts. Although deal
premium is often expressed as a percentage of transaction value to normalize for deal
size, focus primarily lies on the raw premium (in USD) to capture the absolute dollar
magnitude of acquirer aggressiveness; robustness checks using percentage premiums are
included in subsequent analyses and yield consistent patterns.
Because deal premiums are highly right-skewed and include extreme outliers, a
log transformation of the form
is applied prior to estimating the
𝑙𝑜𝑔 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑚𝑖𝑢𝑚+ 1
regression function. This transformation is a common statistical approach that serves to
stabilize variance, reduce the influence of unusually large observations, and improve the
performance of local regression estimators in the presence of heteroscedasticity. In
nonparametric settings, such transformations are particularly useful when the response
variable exhibits heavy tails or nonconstant variance, as they help satisfy the conditions
under which kernel estimators perform most effectively. After estimating the regression
function in the transformed space, a back-transformation is applied to recover predicted
deal premiums on the original scale, thereby enhancing interpretability without
sacrificing estimation robustness.
Bandwidth selection is conducted via least-squares cross-validation to balance
bias and variance in the regression estimates. The final fit is then plotted over the scatter
of observed deals, using zoomed and transformed views to enhance interpretability.
III.​
REGRESSION RESULT: DEAL PREMIUM ON VIX
The estimated regression function reveals a non-monotonic relationship between
market sentiment and M&A deal premiums. In general, premiums are higher when VIX
is low, suggesting that acquirers are more willing to pay a premium during calm,
confident market conditions. As VIX rises above 30, the expected premium declines
significantly, consistent with the hypothesis that uncertainty depresses acquisition
valuations or limits buyer aggressiveness.
Figure 01. Back-Transformed Kernel Regression of Deal Premium on VIX, Zoomed In.​
Interestingly, the relationship is not strictly decreasing. Two local upward bumps
are observed in the estimated premium function — one near

dislocations, where confident buyers perceive mispriced targets and are willing to pay a
premium to preempt competition. Alternatively, they may signal shifts in buyer
composition or strategic objectives that become more salient under certain market
conditions. To assess the robustness of these features and better understand their drivers,
additional regression-based diagnostics are conducted, focusing on premium
normalization and volatility-regime-specific bidding distributions.

CONCLUSION
This project applies nonparametric regression techniques to examine the
relationship between market sentiment and M&A deal premiums, using the VIX as a
proxy for investor uncertainty. The results confirm an intuitive baseline finding: as
market volatility increases, acquirers generally offer lower premiums, likely due to
greater perceived risk and caution. However, the nonparametric framework reveals a

conditions. Future research could build on this work by examining acquirer
characteristics — such as whether the buyer is private equity or strategic, or whether
financing conditions differ across regimes — to better understand who drives these

blocks: The Kids Are Alright:
College Environments, Student Wellbeing, and the Role of Institutional Selectivity
Olivia Lauri
Northwestern University, Department of Psychology
Alissa Levy Chung
Primary Advisor
Ben Gorvine
Second Reader
Final Honors Thesis
Abstract
According to previous research, Generation Z undergraduate students, or students born
between 1997 and 2012, are experiencing unprecedented high levels of anxiety. Another study
investigated whether anxiety is more strongly predicted by undergraduate students’ cognition and
thought processes (internal factors) or the university environment (external factors), and whether
these factors play an equal role. Defined as highly ranked universities with low acceptance rates,
elite institutions may bolster anxiety levels due to the perceived environment, as suggested by
Role Strain Theory. Alternatively, anxious students may be self-selecting into elite universities,
as those with a high need for achievement and high avoidance goals experience more anxiety.
Participants within this study were undergraduate students who attended a wide range of
institutions, each with varying degrees of selectivity. They completed measures of anxiety
(state-trait, general), internal factors (goal orientation, fear of failure, and achievement
motivation), and external factors (class and professor perceptions). Results suggested that
internal factors, specifically fear of failure, were the strongest predictor of anxiety compared to
external factors. There were no significant differences between selective, moderately selective,
and less selective schools in overall anxiety when compared across three groups, but students at
the most selective schools were surprisingly less anxious than students enrolled in moderate and
less selective schools when those groups were combined. Altogether, the findings suggested that
internal factors – goal orientation, fear of failure, and achievement motivation – are the largest
determinants of undergraduate anxiety, compared to institutional selectivity and environmental
perceptions.
The Rise of Anxiety in Generation Z Undergraduates
For Generation Z, born between 1997 and 2012, anxiety is rising in prevalence,
especially in comparison to older generations, but why? Is the current generation of
undergraduate students innately more prone to anxiety? Is higher education causing higher levels
of mental distress? As prestigious universities become more selective and sought after,1 is there a
difference in the impact between elite and non-elite institutions on student anxiety? Existing
research postulates that the rise in anxiety could be due to a myriad of factors, such as
COVID-19, increased screen usage, or an overall generational difference due to more judgment
and societal expectations.2,3,4 As the current socioeconomic environment presents new challenges
that were not prevalent or even present before, Generation Z has been forced to grapple with
contemporary stressors that shape their current world, increasing anxiety levels overall.
Similarly, today’s undergraduate students are widely known as being the most anxious to date,
raising concern on a global scale. Recent mental health studies revealed that one-third of
undergraduate students are suffering from a possible anxiety disorder, with 10% of students in
the United States alone diagnosed with or treated for an anxiety disorder.5 The majority of

of stress in undergraduate students.11 Acting alongside these extrinsic, societal pressures, anxiety
is highly linked to internal bodily and mental processes, creating an interesting question about if
and how their interaction is related to higher contemporary rates of anxiety disorders.
Types of Anxiety
While reflecting contemporary cultural and social factors, the surge in anxiety among
Generation Z undergraduates also reveals important distinctions between the expression of
anxiety in individuals. State and trait anxiety, respectively, distinguish between situational
anxiety and baseline personality anxiety, while general anxiety is all-encompassing. Trait anxiety
is a measure of the personality trait that determines how people react to stress and difficulties.
High-trait anxiety describes a high level of baseline anxiety as one moves through daily life.12 If
an individual experiences high levels of trait anxiety, they operate through daily tasks and
situations with increased worry and unease, making smaller issues feel more threatening and
increasing the frequency of anxious feelings. As it is not driven by anxiety-provoking situations,
trait anxiety is largely stable and tends to be associated with the personality trait of neuroticism.13
On the other hand, state anxiety is a more acute, transitory form of anxiety and produces elevated
bodily arousal and mental distress, varying in intensity and complexity based on the catalyst
event. Situational and trait anxiety are both important factors in determining state anxiety.14
14 Endler, N. S., & Kocovski, N. L. (2001). State and trait anxiety revisited. Journal of Anxiety
13 Wu, X., Zhang, W., Li, Y., Zheng, L., Liu, J., Jiang, Y., & Peng, Y. (2024). The influence of big
five personality traits on anxiety: The chain mediating effect of general self-efficacy and
academic burnout. PLOS ONE, 19(1), e0295118. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0295118.
12 Endler, N. S., & Kocovski, N. L. (2001). State and trait anxiety revisited. Journal of Anxiety
11 Potter, D., Jayne, D., & Britt, S. (2020). Financial anxiety among college students: The role of
generational status. Journal of Financial Counseling and Planning, 31(2), 284–295.
While trait and state anxiety are not the same, they are intertwined, contributing to an
individual’s overall general anxiety levels together. Since high-trait anxiety is typically linked to
high-state anxiety, stress leads to more severe anxiety reactions for those with elevated trait
anxiety.15 Finally, general anxiety is a state of worry and panic due to the anticipation of a
stressful or threatening event.16 General anxiety merges the experiences of trait and state anxiety
in both individuals’ daily lives and in specific instances.
All three of these anxiety types help characterize the complexities in how anxiety
manifests for undergraduate students. Trait anxiety could be crucial to identifying self-selection
effects, as those with higher levels of innate stress may be more driven to attend a selective
institution and pursue higher achievement depending on factors like academic motivation and
personal standards. State anxiety relates more to the perceived environment, as the university
environment could influence levels of worry and stress through various factors. Both state and
trait anxiety paired with general anxiety provide a holistic representation of anxiety for
undergraduate students, exposing the possible contrasts between high-pressure environments
influencing anxiety versus high-anxiety students being drawn to such institutions. The
distinctions between anxiety types exhibit how differences between internal predispositions and
external drivers are important for understanding undergraduate anxiety.
Impact of College Environment: External Factors
Focusing on the impact of external drivers on anxiety, college can be a daunting change
for many students. Moving away from home, family, and friends into a place with new people

correlational study. Global Research Journal of Social Sciences and Management, 02(01), 01–12.

and new norms can be anxiety-inducing by itself. Once students are at school, the institution’s
academic culture can add stress by breeding harmful expectations and experiences that elevate
stress and anxiety. External factors within this study focus on the college culture, which includes
the social and academic experiences that shape perception of the environment. Because of
growing external and societal pressures for universities to emphasize performance and
achievement.17 Institutions and their expectations may intensify feelings of loneliness, academic
pressure, and competition, creating a negative perception of their environment. This phenomenon
reflects the Role Strain Theory, which argues that individuals experience higher levels of stress
due to the expectations associated with their position as students within the institution.18 Students
in a particular college environment may feel extrinsic pressure to meet a certain performance
standard, which then manifests in their perception of their classes and professors. Othman and
colleagues found that social stressors, like feeling judged and socially excluded, alongside
academic stressors, like obtaining the desired GPAs, were positively associated with depression
and internalizing disorders, indicating how both facets of an academic environment impact
students’ experience at an institution and their wellbeing. Thus, students’ subjective experience
of their daily environment, their classes, their peers, and their time on campus, is crucial to
understanding how academic environments can breed anxiety.19

https://doi.org/10.1037/cou0000269.
18 Posselt, J. R., & Lipson, S. K. (2016). Competition, anxiety, and depression in the college

Competition
The interaction between social situations and academic pressures are key components to
how a student experiences their classrooms, professors, and overall college climate, propagating
viewpoints surrounding difficult classroom structure and negative impressions of professors.
Students’ perceptions of their social and academic surroundings are crucial for how external
factors may shape their anxiety. A competitive environment where students feel more like rivals
can be harmful, especially in a learning situation where collaboration is vital for mental growth.
Within undergraduate programs, there are a myriad of settings in which students may feel
pressure to compete, including class performance, clubs and student groups, and job placement.
Since cooperation is more effective for learning than a competitive environment, undergraduate
programs with more peer competition cause negative habits and feelings surrounding learning
and classes.20 According to Posselt and Lipson’s findings, perceived peer competition not only
fails to foster a strong learning environment, but also leads to increased predicted levels of
anxiety and depression among students. Along with promoting divisive conflict in the classroom,
perceptions of competition within the institutional environment are linked to weakened
motivation, increased procrastination, and increased incidence of academic dishonesty.21, 22 These
findings suggest that peer competition may be a crucial contributor to an anxiety-inducing
environment.

Social Support vs. Loneliness
The pressure to compete also cultivates isolation, as students attempt to meet heightened
expectations with less social support and more demands to prove to both themselves and others.
When perceived competition is prevalent on campus, social support becomes limited as peers are
seen as rivals and not as possible friends, breeding isolation and amplifying mental health risks.23
Social support is key for life satisfaction, especially for college students who are going through a
life transition; as a result, less robust support networks can increase loneliness on campuses.
Perceived social support is linked to a decreased likelihood of depression and anxiety, especially
in times of high stress.24 If students experience a less welcoming undergraduate culture where
students are pitted against each other rather than inspired to work together, perceived social
support decreases and loneliness increases. Competitive curve grading, weed-out classes, limited
campus opportunities, and overemphasis on academic prestige all contribute to conditions of
competition and isolation that act as breeding grounds for anxiety.
While higher levels of social support, better self-esteem, and lower perceived levels of
stress lead to better adjustment to college,25 loneliness predicts the opposite, inspiring negative
perceptions of the social environment. These perceptions then influence negative cognitions,
including maladaptive coping, which are linked to student anxiety as well as the negative

perception of social support.26 If the college environment not only fails to foster social support,
but instead promotes a culture that increases loneliness, students’ anxiety is likely to increase as
a result of low perceived social support. The dynamic between competition and isolation is
crucial in the definition of a student’s perception of their learning environment, characterizing
how external elements may contribute to anxiety in undergraduate settings.
Academic Pressures
While loneliness and competition are crucial to the broader culture of all societies,
academic coursework is the main aspect of any college environment. Therefore, exams,
presentations, and papers may be the most obvious driver of stress and worry in students.
Academic pressures vary based on rigor, previous education, and institutional expectations, but
existing empirical findings illustrate that elite institutions often have undergraduate courses with
higher levels of cognitive complexity, increasing both academic pressures and anxiety.27 If
courses are more difficult due to the university environment and standard of achievement, overall
stress regarding completing assignments and performance increases. Regardless of national
ranking, environment and academic pressures have similar effects on anxiety in both public and
private institutions. For instance, community college students are more likely to struggle with
academics in a four year undergraduate program due to the new environments and expectations.28

All three of these examples demonstrate how undergraduate environments and
experiences fluctuate to affect perceived academic distress, achievement motivation, and anxiety
around it. One way academic distress could be linked to increases in anxiety is the increasing
numbers of college students entering undergraduate programs, as rising competition could
become overwhelming and stressful.30 Ultimately, the combination of loneliness, competition,
and academic pressures all interact to create a holistic experience of the institutional
environment, reflected in students’ perceptions of the classroom and professors. This research
examines whether students’ perceptions of their environment — shaped by peer contest,
isolation, and academic strain — are stronger predictors of increased levels of anxiety than
stable, internal factors.
Individual Differences in Cognitive Processes: Internal Factors
While external factors play a key role in undergraduate anxiety, the influence of internal
processes works parallel to shape the manifestation of anxiety. Internal factors are defined as
variation in mental processes that affect how an individual perceives and reacts to situations. To
be admitted to an undergraduate program, individuals must have a certain level of academic
motivation and goal-setting, as higher education institutions expect students to have a high GPA,
standardized test scores, and extracurricular involvement. Individual differences in internal traits,
30 Jones, P. J., Park, S. Y., & Lefevor, G. T. (2018). Contemporary College Student Anxiety: The
Role of Academic Distress, Financial Stress, and Support. Journal of College Counseling, 21(3),

polynomial regression analysis of the joint impact of the perceived learning environment and

such as goal orientation and achievement motivation, can impact how students experience their
environment, how difficult challenges seem to them, and therefore how they respond to that
difficulty. There is a wide range of impact these internal predispositions could have on students,
influencing their academic performance, social skills, and overall affect, including their
susceptibility to higher levels of anxiety. Regardless of external factors, goal orientation, need for
achievement, and fear-of-failure levels influence stress and how students cope with feelings of
anxiety. Simultaneously, internal factors also interact with external factors to alter how people
experience and cope with everyday life. To accurately identify the impact of external factors and
internal factors, it is essential to understand how they work independently first to then
understand their interaction with undergraduate anxiety levels.
Goal Orientation
Goal orientation is an internal factor that describes how students’ internal motivation
affects their behavior and initiative in goal approach efforts.31 Achievement goal orientation
defines how people respond and react to achievement situations, rendering it a key internal
process behind undergraduate anxiety levels. Within the main achievement goal framework,
there are two constructs — performance and mastery goals — that are differentiated by
conceptions of success, reasons for approaching achievement goals, and self-definition.32
Mastery goals focus on the value of learning and posit that effort leads to individually defined
mastery, which then defines success. In contrast, performance goals define success by
outperforming others; as a result, self-worth becomes linked to one’s ability to demonstrate

competence compared to one’s peers.33 Mastery goals are positively related to positive effects
and success in learning, while performance goals can have mixed influences, but mostly have a

success or failure is based on external evaluations of one’s competency.35
Within mastery and performance goals, the valence of competence is also largely
influential, creating another distinction between approach and avoidance goals. Approach goals
focus on demonstrating success or competence, while avoidance goals lean on the desire to avoid
failure or incompetence.36 Previous literature suggests that avoidance motivation is disruptive to
intrinsic motivation processes while approach goals activate success-focused processes.37
Avoidance goal orientations, which focus on the prevention of embarrassment or failure, are also
linked to higher levels of anxiety.38 Altogether, performance-approach and
performance-avoidance have been identified as harmful for self-worth and resilience due to the

Students predisposed towards performance orientations or avoidance orientations could
experience college life with a more anxiety-provoking outlook, as they use challenging events
and setbacks as defining factors for their self and ability. This relationship, too, may contribute to
the increased anxiety found in undergraduate students.
Need for Achievement
Individuals with high need for achievement are defined as those who have high standards
for their goals and attempts to accomplish trying tasks.41 Need for achievement is a stable motive
disposition that varies from person to person, contributing to the myriad of internal factors that
could influence anxiety. Need for achievement is highlighted as the interest in meeting or
exceeding standards, so individuals with high need for achievement thrive on feeling competent
and become more motivated as that feeling increases.42 Importantly, Schüler and their colleagues
found that if those with high need for achievement do not feel competent, they are less engaged

in, have weaker commitment to, and make less progress toward their goals. For individuals in a

of inadequacy, all of which could be linked to heightened anxiety.
Fear of Failure
Fear of failure is defined as the dispositional tendency to avoid failure in achievement
settings because of the shame associated with possible defeat, identifying how individuals define
failure and behave in related settings.43 It is an internal psychological factor, linked to a similar
dimension of the individual as goal orientation and the need for achievement. All three are tied to
individual differences in how students focus on outcomes and equate success with self-worth and
competency. For those high in fear of failure, a misstep carries more weight and impacts the
individual’s self-worth more compared to success, so tasks that risk possible failure increase
anxiety.44 While it stems from internal orientation, fear of failure also interacts with
environmental factors. The learning environment has an important influence on fear of failure,
interactions between internal goals and perceptions of external circumstances can increase such
fears. Institutions that emphasize receiving the highest score and encourage competition can
make students define personal success in comparison to others, which can increase
performance-orientation which is positively related to fear of failure.45 Therefore, certain higher
45 Chen, L. H., Wu, C.-H., Kee, Y. H., Lin, M.-S., & Shui, S.-H. (2009). Fear of failure, 2×2
achievement goal and self-handicapping: An examination of the hierarchical model of
achievement motivation in physical education. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 34(4),
44 Ibid.
43 Elliot, A. J., & Thrash, T. M. (2004). The Intergenerational Transmission of Fear of Failure.
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 30(8), 957–971.
pressure environments can worsen the fear of failure, particularly an environment that focuses on
performance like those of elite institutions.
However, the performance-oriented goals influence the fear of failure regardless of the
environment, as avoiding failure is likely linked to anxiety because of the threat posed by
possibly failing and being perceived as inadequate. All of these internal aspects of individuals
seem to be relatively stable over various environments and do not shift with external factors,46
which may provide an explanation as to why some students are more likely to be anxious than
others.
Selectivity of Institutions
Beyond the generational difference and broader social influences on anxiety, variation in
university size, type, and caliber impact a person’s experience of their college environment, with
some of the external factors that drive student experience being captured by school selectivity.
While some schools prioritize a diverse student body and teaching methods, some elite, private
institutions have increased focus on maintaining selectivity and placing focus on students to
participate in acquiring resources.47 The expectations promoted by prestigious universities focus
more on undergraduate students’ educational outcomes like GPAs, putting students under more
pressure to fulfill their roles in perpetuating the schools’ high-end reputation. If universities need
to maintain a low acceptance rate and high rankings to remain competitive and desirable
institutions, they could inadvertently reinforce expectations of students to produce achievement
47 Mahmoud, J. S. R., Staten, R. “Topsy,” Lennie, T. A., & Hall, L. A. (2015). The Relationships
of Coping, Negative Thinking, Life Satisfaction, Social Support, and Selected Demographics
With Anxiety of Young Adult College Students. Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychiatric
46 Halisch, F. (1987). Modeling and Achievement-Related Behavior. In F. Halisch & J. Kuhl
(Eds.), Motivation, Intention, and Volition (pp. 87–100). Springer.
outcomes that support those goals. This type of university-wide change can make mental health
of lesser importance to the institution relative to concerns about the institution’s academic
reputation, which has serious implications for the students and their mental health.
The external factors of a college environment along social, academic, and institutional
dimensions likely play a large role in increasing undergraduate anxiety, corroborating the Role
Strain Theory.48 With the increased pressure in the university environment, students are more
likely to experience higher levels of anxiety as they attempt to conform to standards imposed on
them by elite universities' culture and expectations. Simultaneously, being admitted into an elite
university requires much taxing work, but the end goal rewards the individual with prestige and
status, drawing people with a higher need for achievement. Achievement motivation and goal
orientation may inspire a self-selection effect into certain levels of selective institutions, as
students with a high need for achievement and predisposition towards avoidance goals may
pursue ambitious goals with a more negative mindset. Furthermore, the college environment may
interact with a student’s innate anxious predisposition in a feedback loop, where the
environmental expectations can then reinforce the students’ internal pressures, bolstering anxiety.
Ames identified that goal orientations can be elicited by different environmental demands to lead
to very different goal patterns.49 While it is clear that undergraduate students are experiencing
increased anxiety, the direction of the relationship remains underexplored. Are students who
attend highly prestigious schools just higher in trait anxiety, and would have higher anxiety
49 Ames, C. (1992). Classrooms: Goals, structures, and student motivation. Journal of
Educational Psychology, 84(3), 261–271. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.84.3.261.
48 Posselt, J. R., & Lipson, S. K. (2016). Competition, anxiety, and depression in the college
classroom: Variations by student identity and field of study. Journal of College Student
across all areas? Is the environment of prestigious institutions driving up anxiety in students
disproportionately, or is it a combination of the two factors?
Conclusion
My study delved into the anxiety levels of undergraduate students through the lens of
external factors, internal factors, and selectivity of institutions. I explored if
consistently-increasing anxiety could be due to the perceived environment — as some climates
have a culture of loneliness, academic pressure, competition, and perfectionism — which
influences classroom and professor perceptions,50 or if anxious students could be self-selecting
into universities, as those with a high need for achievement, high avoidance goals, and other
internal predispositions tend to experience more anxiety.51 I hypothesized that perceived
environments would be a stronger predictor of anxiety compared to internal factors, regardless of
school selectivity. In addition, I hypothesized that individuals with a performance-approach goal
orientation would be less anxious than those with a performance-avoidance goal orientation.
When accounting for selectivity, I hypothesized that elite institutions would influence higher
levels of anxiety in undergraduate students over less elite institutions. There were key
correlations between anxiety and both internal factors and external factors, specifically fear of
failure and classroom avoidance. Fear of failure was found to be the strongest predictor of
anxiety, supporting the conclusion that internal factors are driving up anxiety for college
students. Finally, selectivity did not have the expected relationship with anxiety. The results
51 Halisch, F. (1987). Modeling and Achievement-Related Behavior. In F. Halisch & J. Kuhl
(Eds.), Motivation, Intention, and Volition (pp. 87–100). Springer.
50 Mahmoud, J. S. R., Staten, R. “Topsy,” Lennie, T. A., & Hall, L. A. (2015). The Relationships
of Coping, Negative Thinking, Life Satisfaction, Social Support, and Selected Demographics
With Anxiety of Young Adult College Students. Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychiatric
showed that students at less selective institutions had increased fear of failure and classroom
avoidance compared to those at selective institutions. There was no significant relationship
between selectivity and anxiety levels. My findings conflicted with the idea that the institution’s
environment is more important for anxiety, illustrating that internal processes have a stronger
relationship, specifically fear of failure. Notably, fear of failure and classroom avoidance were
significantly different between selective and less selective institutions, with less selective having
higher reported levels of both. While adding to the expanding body of research on undergraduate
anxiety and its predictors, this thesis provides valuable information for universities and their
efforts to combat increasing anxiety through various interventions and resources and hopefully
assists in cultivating a healthy collegiate environment and experiences for all universities,
regardless of selectivity.
