“When did the depictions
become worse than the
reality?”: Black Trauma Porn
and The Black Horror Genre
in Television and Film
by Karina Karbo-Wright
Department of African American Studies
Faculty Adviser: Barnor Hesse
Abstract
The American film industry is inextricably tied to the history of racism
in the United States; thus, Black representation in film and T.V. has been
a topic of rigorous academic and public debate. Most recently, that debate
has circulated around the topic of “Black Trauma Porn” (BTP). Emerging
on social media in 2016 during the Black Lives Matter movement, Black
thinkers used the phrase “Black Trauma Porn” to articulate the nuanced
complexities of the phenomenon, specifically sharing police brutality videos
and the production of films and T.V. series with similar themes. Many piec­
es have received extreme backlash, and BTP became loaded with negative
connotations, labeling the pieces as exploitative and harmful. However, as
the phrase gained popularity, the analysis of these movies and T.V. shows
became derivative and uncritical, instigating the need to investigate if the
phrase properly articulates what authors were utilizing it for. To interrogate
BTP, it is necessary to explain the impact of film on the spectator and engage
the history of race in Hollywood in order to conclude that BTP is actually a
modernist subgenre of Black horror. This conclusion is supported through
an analysis of white versus Black horror as well as a deep-dive into what
“trauma” and “porn” mean individually and within this context. Reframing
and usurping the phrase BTP provides the beginning to a new framework
for analyzing Black historical horror films and answering larger questions
about Black representation in film and T.V.
Introduction
Unlike everyone else I knew, I did not
see Get Out (2017) until two years after its
release. At the time, I could not exactly
pinpoint why I had no desire to see it.
When asked, I would just say that I was
not interested, or that even though I loved
Key & Peele (2012), I did not think this
movie would be my speed. Shortly after,
I read the phrase “Black Trauma Porn”
on my social media, and I felt an over­
whelming sense of relief. It put a word to
the feeling of fear that kept me from the
theater and the uneasiness I experienced
when I saw videos of police violence. In a
way, it served as validation that remedied
much of my guilt toward not watching
movies that dealt with anti-Blackness. It
was not because I did not like Black movies
— Jumping the Broom (2011) and Barbershop
(2002) were my favorite childhood films —
but there was a sense of guardedness that
I had learnt from previous experiences of
watching unsettling media that kept me
from watching certain films. When I saw
the phrase BTP, I felt validated and com­
forted in the fact that I would not watch
Get Out or any other movie of which I was
wary. After this point, any movie or series
I saw labeled as BTP became unwatchable
to me.
The BTP issue has emerged in tan­
dem with the Black Lives Matter move­
ment, beginning in the early 2010s with
the murder of Trayvon Martin in 2012
and the success and notoriety of 12 Years
a Slave (2013) shortly afterwards. This is
when the conversation began to emerge.
However, the first articulation of the term
1 Nkumane, Z. (2016). No longer will I partake in Black trauma porn. OkayAfrica.
2 Wear Your Voice Magazine 2016; [Very Smart Bros]. (2016). Yeah, I’m Finished With The Black Suffering Trauma Porn Of Orange Is
The New Black -- by @inomallday
was not until 2016 in a South African ar­
ticle by Nkumane,1 which describes the
conflicting impact of consuming videos of
white supremacist violence against Black
people. The article recognized how these
videos force necessary conversations but
also incite terror among viewers. This
article, along with equally popular articles
entitled “Orange is the New Black is Trau­
ma Porn Written for White People” and
“Yeah, I’m Finished With The Black Suf­
fering Trauma Porn Of Orange Is The New
Black,” was widely circulated across Twit­
ter in the summer of 2016.2 This spurred
a mass increase in the use of the term to
describe the phenomenon at hand: videos,
films, and T.V. shows that depict extreme
violence by white civilians or state officials
against Black people are disseminated for
mass public consumption and/or mass
entertainment, which impacts white and
Black spectators differently, despite being
distributed with the assumption that some
amount of pleasure is extrapolated from it
by the general viewing public.
What followed was a seemingly
correlated increase in the visibility of an­
ti-Black police brutality and the creation
and popularity of films and T.V. shows
that depicted white supremacy and the
Black experience, the most notable of these
being Get Out. The discourse surrounding
this phenomenon focuses on three main
concerns with the purpose and effects of
depicting violence against Black people in
movies and T.V.: the immense violence
inflicted on the Black characters within
these films and T.V. shows is unnecessar­
ily incessant and an exploitative derivative
of real-life Black trauma, the traumatic
impact of violent anti-Black depictions
on Black spectators, and the pornifica­
tion of these violent depictions by white
spectators who are believed to gain some
form of pleasure or gratification from the
visualizations.3 In other words, these ten­
sions exist around negotiations of violence
against Black people and the subsequent
Black/non-Black spectatorship of those
depictions. This centering of Black specta­
tors is commendable and unprecedented in
mainstream film analysis, but it seems that
the nuances that contextualize Black story­
telling are not a part of these critiques.
It is always necessary to interrogate
the terms which we use to critique our
own culture’s creations. In the case here,
BTP could be used to further censor and
marginalize the already racially gatekept
world of film. Black storytelling has im­
mense power and ability to be able to
communicate and negotiate matters of cul­
ture and identity. I hope that by exploring
this phenomenon, this paper will mediate
questions of Black representation and bring
awareness to the necessity of intentionality
and analysis when forming opinions on
Black T.V. and film.
The History of Film and the
Horror Genre
There have been many historical instances
of immense violence which impact entire
societies of people, like the Transatlantic
Slave Trade, World Wars I and II, The
3 Braxton, G. (2021, April 19). Media images of Black Death have a cost, experts say. many viewers are fed up. Los Angeles Times.; Cha­
risma, T. (2021, June 18). Trauma porn and the commercialisation of Black Pain. tmrw.; Giorgis, H. (2021, April 18). Who wants to watch
Black pain? The Atlantic.; Muhammad, M. (2019, June 2). Getting off: What black trauma porn is and why we hate it. Medium.
4 Elm, Kabalek, K., & Köhne, J. B. (2014). The horrors of trauma in cinema : violence void visualization. Cambridge Scholars Publishing.
5 Ibid., 4
6 Ibid., 4
7 Ibid., 4
8 Ibid., 4
9 Crouthamel, J. (2016). The Horrors of Trauma in Cinema: Violence Void Visualization. Film & History, 46(2), 86–89.
10 Ibid., 4; Bernardi. (2007). The Persistence of Whiteness : Race and Contemporary Hollywood Cinema. Taylor & Francis.
Holocaust, and the occupation of Pal­
estine; through the collective trauma of
these events, the perpetrators and victims
are relationally linked together in what
Elm et al. calls a “traumatized society.”4
One of the ways by which a traumatized
society may cope or heal from the trauma
is through cinema, which can give “expres­
sion to trauma and violence for a wounded
[community]” through the visualization
and actualization it provides.5 As a medium
of mediated realistic reenactment,6 film
can act as a preserver of traumatic history
and can provide catharsis and healing for
those within the traumatized society who
create and view the film. Film can also aid
in individual and collective7 memory re­
tention as well as in cultural preservation,
revealing levels of history and memory
which, for societies that have experienced
trauma through destruction, can be vital
in protecting cultural history. However, it
can also be used as a tool of suppression or
cover to erase and rewrite history for po­
liticized propaganda-like efforts,8 and this
is most often seen through an analysis of
Hollywood and its relationship with race.
Elm et al. proposes that the horror
genre is one of the best genres for success­
fully encapsulating a historical trauma nar­
rative on film.9 Horror is able to portray
the tenacity of the violence experienced
in historical trauma while also providing
the cinematic tools to unpack that violence
within the horror narrative.10 Through the
analysis of historical trauma film, I believe
that several Contemporary Black stories in
film are current iterations of Black horror.
In that account of historical trauma films,
Elm et al. explains the benefit of using
horror to communicate impactful stories
of historical trauma.11 As a tool of com­
municating Black history in the present
U.S. that is largely sculpted by collective
and historical traumas as well as a tool for
critiquing and commenting on white hege­
mony through horror genre tropes, these
contemporary Black stories in film utilize
the genre of horror. In order to character­
ize this thesis, an exploration of the Black
and white horror genres will provide the
necessary groundwork for my argument.
Horror is a genre of “literature, film,
and T.V. that is meant to scare, startle,
shock, and even repulse audiences” where
the “story and characters are just as import­
ant as mood and atmosphere.”12 Because of
the horror story’s ability to “[shock] and
[provoke] with its exploration of the un­
known,”13 it is a great tool for cross-genre
productions and social impact, including
matters of race.14
11 Ibid., 4
12 MasterClass, & Stine, R. L. (2021, September 7). What is horror fiction? learn about the horror genre, plus 7 classic horror novels you
should read - 2022. MasterClass.
13 Ibid., 12
14 Curtis. (2008). Dark places : the haunted house in film. Reaktion.
15 Clasen, M. (2021). On the psychology of Horror movies. Psychology Today.; The Psychology of Fear: Concordia University, St. Paul
online. CSP Online. (2021, October 21).
16 Jóhann, B. (2020, September 14). A brief history of Hollywood’s racism, sexism, and homophobia. Medium.

(2015). Race, Gender, Hollywood: Representation in Cultural Production and Digital Media’s Potential for Change. Sociology Com­

What can be considered horror is
extremely vast because what scares one
spectator may not scare another.15 How­
ever, the staple elements of a horror film
are the central elements of violence and/
or fear.16 Psychologist Dr. Glenn D. Wal­
ters theorizes three main aspects of horror
films that establish the genre and produce
audience attraction.17 The first aspect is
tension. Created by the techniques of film
highlighted in horror — dialogue, sudden
perspective changes,18 unsettling shots that
are either too quick or very slow,19 sound
and music, and lighting — tension comes
through suspense, mystery, intrigue, ter­
ror, gore, and shock.20 Often, this is under­
stood to be “universal relevance,” referring
to the fears “everyone” has — specifically
“the psychology of fear of death and the
unknown, or cultural relevance of social
issues” — but it may refer to personal rel­
evance as well.21 The final result is that
cinema provides us with what Walters
calls “unrealism.” This means that despite
the validity of the content of the piece, the
spectator is still consuming the narrative
Film can act as a preserver of traumatic history
and can provide catharsis and healing for those
within the traumatized society who create and
view the film.
and is not within it. To enjoy viewing
horror films, the spectators must also feel
physically and mentally safe in order to de­
tach themselves from the film.22
While horror films, like all films, are
deeply influenced by the spectator’s reac­
tion, there are also important impacts felt
from the content of these films. As a central
part of social life, films have a specific and
influential role in shaping what emotions
look and sound like;23 horror films have
the unique role of defining what is fear
and what is fearful. In a study on the so­
cial experience of horror films, Renda ex­
plains, “Scariness is not (only) an attribute
of the film content but is said to stem from
cognitive factors such as the individual’s
empathy with film characters or person­
ally held moral beliefs and expectations.”24
This socially constructed factor of fear is
central to horror movies, but the complex
genre’s norms also include the engagement
with taboos and rupture of boundaries, the
unfamiliar penetrating the familiar, the
resistance of typical bounds and flow of
narrative creations, and the challenging of
the rational.25 It is this intentional disrup­
tion aspect of these norms and the horror
films’ oscillations between the spectrum
of good and evil that crafts what is and is
not scary. However, as a genre created and
continued by Hollywood, I would like to
reframe horror films as the determination
and identification of narratives centering
on what horrifies white people.
I make this assertion because what
is understood as conventional horror was

24 Ibid., 23
25 Ibid., 16; Ibid., 23
26 Ibid., 12
27 Bogle. (2001). Toms, Coons, Mulattoes, Mammies, and Bucks: An Interpretive History of Blacks in American Films, Fourth Edition.
Burns & Oates Imprint.; Hill Collins. (2014). Black feminist thought: knowledge, consciousness, and the politics of empowerment (Revised
tenth anniversary edition.). Routledge.; Ibid., 16; Nittle, N. K. (2021, March 6). The 5 most common black stereotypes in TV and film.
ThoughtCo. The Take (2020) “A History of Black Stereotypes Onscreen” Youtube.
created through white storytelling from
popular horror writers like Edgar Allan
Poe and pivotal texts like Mary Shelly’s
Frankenstein (1818) or Bram Stoker’s Drac­
ula (1897).26 These stories are not only
populated largely by white creators but also
within the narrative; the stories privilege
white experiences, fears, and losses and
further bolster them as universal.27 Because
Hollywood is a segregated tool of white
storytelling, the horror stories present in
film and T.V. most often follow those of
white individuals; thus, conventional and
mainstream horror is about what horrifies
white people.
If Black stories in
horror films are
narratives “about Black
experiences and
Black cultural
traditions” ... then the
Black horror genre
will refer to what
horrifies Black people.
For example, in Scream (1996), the
fear is centered around the killers’ ability
to forcibly enter the house, a space that
is supposed to be safe, and their complete
control over whether the victim lives or
dies, stripping the victim of their agency
over their life. Forcibly entering the home
can be equated to white community’s fear
and consequent disgruntlement with in­
tegration, but the fear stemming from the
loss of agency is most terrifying. This claim
is supported by the role of white women in
the film, who historically have been used
to identify what is most fearful. This theme
can be tracked through almost all (white)
horror films popular in Hollywood, in­
cluding the three listed above — that a loss
of white agency, whether through murder,
paranormal possessions, or psychological
torture, is the real fear. This film is white
horror because the story told features spe­
cific circumstances in which only white
people lose their sense of agency. If cinema
is playing on the fears of white people for
conventional white horror, then the ques­
tion remains: what is Black horror?
Because of horror’s ability to “[shock]
and [provoke] with its exploration of the
unknown,”28 it becomes a ripe place for so­
cial commentary and critique, especially on
matters of race.29 This unique engagement
of commercial value, peculiar narrative,
and fluctuating aesthetic has made horror
extremely useful for debating “dilemmas of
difference.”30 If Black stories in horror films
are narratives “about Black experiences
and Black cultural traditions — a Black
28 Ibid., 12
29 Curtis. (2008). Dark places : the haunted house in film. Reaktion.
30 Ibid., 27
31 Ibid., 27
32 Ibid., 27
33 Bellot, G., Cox, R., & Mckinney, D. (2021, November 10). How black horror became America’s most powerful cinematic genre. The
New York Times.
34 Breznican, A. (2020, August 3). Black storytellers are using horror to battle hate. Vanity Fair. 14 chilling African American horror
novels. UNC Chapel Hill Libraries. (2021, October 28).
cultural milieu and history swirling around
and impacting Blacks’ lives in America”
communicated through the horror genre,31
which conceptualizes the surrounding so­
cial and political worlds through the Black
gaze, either actively or passively critiquing
white hegemony and centering Black sto­
ries, then the Black horror genre will refer
to what horrifies Black people.
In the Black horror genre, Black art­
ists are looking to spark “sociopolitical dis­
courses … through representations about
… Blackness” that “‘speaks’ difference” to
and interrogates whiteness by reversing
white horror’s placement of Blackness as
the “Other.”32 Horror has long been in the
history of Black storytelling and oral tradi­
tions. Black folklore about ghosts and oth­
er mythologies that stretched the African
continent followed enslaved Black people
to the Americas; the oral tradition helped
craft the origins of the Black culture we
know today.33 Memory served as a form of
resistance, and these tales began to trans­
form into stories about revolution and
freedom. Black cultural productions were
working through various newspapers,
films, novels, and storytelling that fea­
tured horror or horror aesthetics.34 What
Black horror cultural productions have in
common is the engagement with the Black
experience throughout Black history.
As it exists in tension with the strug­
gle to tell stories about Blackness, Black
storytelling must make the link between
depicting Black culture within horror
and answer the question, “What horrifies
Black people?” The answer is the horrors
of Black history. For Black people around
the world, because of the immense history
of unthinkable violence and the structural
positions that continue that violence, there
may be nothing more horrifying for Black
people than the past.35 From the brutali­
ties of dehumanization to social death and
physical mutilation,36 slavery began this
cycle of the horrors of Black history. The
Black horror genre through time proves
that what horrifies Black people are the
horrors of Black history. The Black horror
genre in film and T.V. as it stands today
begins to emerge in conversation through
films like Get Out (2017) and Us (2019). The
current subgenre is what is being contested
in the larger argument of this thesis.
The Black horror genre, then, is able
to provide a critique of white hegemony
through film and subverts (white) horror
norms by setting whiteness in Black his­
tory as the antagonist, as proposed by the
theory of historical trauma films.37 The
Black horror genre conveys that Black his­
tory is filled with horror, and these films
are depicting Black history through Black
horror. These issues of the relationship
between the horrors of Black history and
Black horror genre necessitate the interro­
gation of what is being critiqued with the
BTP phenomenon, and what specifically
BTP is supposed to explain.
Black Trauma Porn: Current
Debates and Positionings
The question of Black horror has recently
been taken up by critics who complain

of BTP. The issue of BTP is the videos,
films, and T.V. shows that depict extreme
violence by white civilians or state officials
against Black people that are then dissemi­
nated for mass public consumption and/or
mass entertainment, which impacts both
white and Black spectators differently,
despite being distributed with the assump­
tion that pleasure is extrapolated from
it by the general viewing public.38 It has
generated questions about who Black me­
dia is made for.39 Despite existing in films
and T.V. shows throughout the twentieth
century, the argument around the usage of
Black experiences and anti-Black violence
was reignited by Jordan Peele’s social
thriller, Get Out. The pieces depicting
anti-Black violence fit into four thematic
categories which reflect the various pe­
riods of time that indicate major events
in Black history: slavery, segregation/
Jim Crow, mass incarceration, and police
brutality.40 Developed out of those who
were opposed to it, BTP was to refer to a
negative phenomenon.41 However, even
in its first iterations, it was unclear exactly
what BTP carried in its meaning. In order
to understand if BTP is really describing
what it is meant to allude to, I will present
the critiques of the films and T.V. shows
to which it refers and unpack the words
comprising the phrase to decipher if BTP
is the best term to describe the phenome­
non at hand.
There are three main critiques of
what is being called BTP: the incessant
violence against Black characters in these
depictions and the visual exploitation of
Black trauma, the possible harm these de­
pictions have on Black spectators, and the
consumption of these violent depictions by
white spectators.42
The first critique about the BTP phe­
nomenon is the belief that the violence
depicted in these films and series is unnec­
essary and excessive.43 In a comparison of
Little Marvin’s Them and Jordan Peele’s Get
Out, author Maryann Erigha says that Get
Out gets the depictions of white supremacy
right without the violence:
There’s a subtlety with that film, which
is why it was so successful … People
understood the message without the
film having to show physical trauma.
But in Them, the message is being
lost when you take it to that level of
violence. I don’t think you need to see
brutalization happening in order to
understand the brutality of racism or
anti-Blackness.44
Erigha’s sentiment is shared throughout
other films and T.V. shows at the center
of the critique of BTP.45 Film and T.V.
are most often seen as entertainment, so
critics believe that this violence holds a
different weight when presented as “es­
capist fare” because for Black people, “it’s
not entertainment.”46 This critique is what
foregrounds the others.
The second critique is that these
depictions harm Black spectators.47 The
concern is that since the stories reflect real
events in Black life, their presentation as

entertainment is triggering and traumatic
for the Black viewer.48 Author Hannah
Giorgis says that Black films invite more
speculation around intent than white
films, and this will cause Black spectators
to consider the impact of the medium in
a specific, shared way, especially when it
comes to anti-Black violence in horror.49
Thus, “in the case of Them, the sheer inten­
sity and meaninglessness of the cruelty on
display lends credence to arguments that
Little Marvin didn’t anticipate how the
show might affect Black audiences, many
of whom view it as a bloodied funhouse
mirror of an already-horrifying reality,”50
even though according to Marvin himself,
he only thought of Black spectators during
the creative process.51 The critique is deep­
er than just creator intent; the concern is
that Black people are being reduced sole­
ly to their trauma and pain.52 This then
prompts the question of spectatorship and
who these films are for: “‘But as a Black
horror artist, I have to ask myself, Who
would that be for?’”53 This is where the fi­
nal critique rests.
The final critique is that white specta­
tors are granted too much access to depic­
tions of the Black experience and extract
some form of pleasure from the violent de­
pictions.54 If the goal is to generate atten­
tion or gain recognition through increased
viewership, then instances of Black trauma
are being exploited to satisfy that desire.55
Another concern is that Black experiences
are exploited for the purpose of educating
non-Black people on anti-Blackness and
appeasing white guilt at the expense of
Black consumers, who will be harmed by
seeing their trauma visualized.56 More ne­
fariously, some fear that white audiences,
continuing the traditions of lynchings, are
either sadistically “getting off” on the de­
pictions of anti-Black violence by living vi­
cariously through the white aggressors on
screen, voyeuristically “exploring” Black­
ness, attempting to ease their white guilt,
or gratifying their obsession with moni­
toring Blackness.57 While it is relevant and
radical to center the experience of the Black
spectator and critique that of the white
spectators in an otherwise white-centered
world, what the BTP perspective fails to
examine is the relationship between Black
history and its horrors and the importance
of witnessing and engaging with that.
I am calling into question the very
term and definitions of BTP itself, posing
these pieces of media as necessities rather
than trauma exploitation. I am concerned
with the extent to which the horrors of
Black history are being addressed by the
critics of BTP and whether some of these
critics see these films as developing the
Black horror genre. To discuss these ques­
tions, it is necessary to unpack the words
which comprise the phrase BTP.
Through an analysis of traumatic
film, vicarious trauma, and spectacle hor­
ror, the idea of BTP can be problematized.
The term itself does not encapsulate the
intended meaning because the utilization
of the term does not take into account the
analysis of and historical engagement with
55 Safford, D. (2019). “How to Use Three-Act Structure to Write a Story Readers Can’t Put Down,” The Writing Practice.
56 Ibid., 3
57 Ibid., 3
Black trauma and traumatic film, and it
does not critically engage with the entirety
of the Black experience in which vicarious
trauma happens, particularly because Black
history and Black trauma are inextricably
linked. We cannot witness our history
without also vicariously experiencing in­
sidious and collective trauma. This means
that, in tandem with the understandings
of trauma and memory, that Black trauma
is Black history. However, Black history is
not Black trauma. What is then relevant
to the BTP critique is that Black trauma
is Black history, and Black history is Black
horror – thus Black trauma is Black horror,
or what horrifies Black people.
I propose that it is not BTP and the
exploitation of Black trauma taking place,
but a new articulation of the Black horror
genre – that these films are depicting, in
their entirety, what horrifies Black people
in Black history. For this analysis, I’d like
to rename this new subgenre of the Black
horror genre, Black historical horror, to
replace BTP as a title. This new interpre­
tation of the Black horror genre capitalizes
on the new space for Black art in society
and uses the popularity and cultural force
of the cinema industry to depict and dis­
seminate the suppressed realities of Black
history as a necessary liberatory technique
with the contemporary power to unsettle
whiteness and white supremacy.
Conclusion
There is a significance in being able to
provide nuance to Black narratives that
are being analyzed without doing so in
the public sphere. Throughout this thesis,
I have aimed to argue that the BTP argu­
ment is an unnuanced approach to what I
“Black storytelling is an extremely expansive
discipline, and to analyze it without nuance is
to further subjugate Black narratives.”
have called Black historical horror. I have
discussed the basis for where this argu­
ment emerges from, where I believe it sits,
and the analysis to support it.
The impact of film and T.V. is im­
mense, as is the reality that Black creations
no longer exist within a vacuum. From
this, it is clear that Black thinkers are trying
to conceptualize the benefits and setbacks
of this impact on racial conceptualizations
of whiteness and Blackness. Because of the
current historical positioning in culture
allowing more space for Black films and
T.V. shows, there is contention over what
types of Black stories should be shared.
Out of these tensions, I wanted to see what
exactly BTP is trying to describe and un­
derstand how that might affect the Black
stories being told. In order to do so, this
paper explained Hollywood’s history of
violence against Black characters through
white storytelling in film and T.V. Then,
I discussed how this necessitated the de­
velopment of the Black gaze and a distinct
Black storytelling in film and T.V. This
history provided the necessary background
for understanding the role race has played
in American cinematic history and fore­
grounded and characterized this phenome­
non. This thesis explained the combination
of what is called “historical trauma film”58
and Black film to yield the basis for un­
derstanding BTP to be a new articulation
of the Black horror genre: Black historical
58 Elm, Kabalek, K., & Köhne, J. B. (2014). The horrors of trauma in cinema: violence void visualization. Cambridge Scholars Publishing.
horror. By dissecting what the white and
Black horror genres entail and applying
that analysis to the historical trauma film,
I positioned the BTP phenomenon as ex­
isting between the storytelling of Black
horror genre and the horrors of Black his­
tory. Following this, the paper discussed
contentions surrounding the BTP issue
and interrogated how these contentions
related to the interrogation of the terms
“trauma” and “porn.” These examinations
proposed the guidelines for rearticulation.
I found it almost ironic that when I set
out to do this analysis, I personally agreed
with the arguments I worked against. Black
storytelling is an extremely expansive dis­
cipline, and to analyze it without nuance is
to further subjugate Black narratives. The
main conclusion from this thesis is that film
is an incredibly powerful tool that has rev­
olutionary power when used to commu­
nicate stories of Blackness. Experiences of
the representation of Blackness in film and
T.V. and the vicarious trauma that may be
experienced when viewing those represen­
tations may vary widely from spectator to
spectator. However, whether or not Black
critics enjoy or loathe the creation, it is still
necessary to analyze the purpose and im­
pact of the film or series’ message and pon­
der the question: if we don’t tell our stories,
who will? The BTP debate is negating the
tensions between violence against Black
people on the screen, white and Black
consumption of that violence, and what
contemporary Black representation should
or should not look like. By labeling pieces
of Black film and T.V. as BTP, critics are
inflicting unforeseen consequences against
Black cinema, which may severely limit
progress and continue to erase narratives
of the horrors of Black history and Black
trauma. By usurping the phrase BTP and
developing a new framework for analyzing
Black historical horror and questions
about Black representation in cinema, this
thesis provides the foundational grounds
for unearthing new answers for questions
of Black representation in contemporary
film and T.V.◆

On the surface, life in a university seems like a straightforward process.
Teach. Research. Publish. However, the reality is that the world of aca­
demia is a beautiful mess of hard work, passion, and luck. Professor Bry­
an Hunter recently moved from Harvard University to teach chemistry
and continue his research in the Hunter Lab at Northwestern University
(N.U.). In this interview, he speaks about his research on sustainability and
reflects on his personal journey thus far.
By Andrew Lu
Serendipity and Struggle:
Reflections on the
Social Dynamics of Research
[This interview has been edited for
brevity and clarity.]
What sort of research does
your lab do?
My lab is interested in sustainability and
renewable energy. What I do on a day-to-
day basis is to look at important reactions
in the world, which are typically [done]
through catalysis. You have some material
or substance which permits a reaction to
happen at a lower barrier, so it’s kineti­
cally more favorable. A lot of these reac­
tions take place at high temperatures and
high pressures, such as the Haber–Bosch
process. These are inherently inefficient
reactions because entropy losses occur in
the process of moving to high tempera­
tures and pressures. So, we’re interested
in converting these reactions into electro­
chemical reactions that are done at room
temperature, with ambient pressure, and
often in solution. To do this, you need to
develop a new class of catalysts — catalysts
that are electro-catalysts. We develop
and produce materials and molecules that
serve as electro-catalysts for a variety of
reactions. Additionally, we’re interested
in water splitting, carbon dioxide reduc­
tion, ammonia production, [and] things
like that.
Do you see many practical
applications for your re­
search?
Yes, we’ve made some major contribu­
tions to water-splitting catalysis. These
have been incorporated and integrated
into water electrolyzers, which are com­
mercially available — that technology
FEATURE
is used. It’s not yet used on a large scale
because we don’t have, currently, the de­
mand for a huge amount of clean hydro­
gen. However, I think that there will be
demand for it in the future, and making
improvements to those technologies now
is pertinent and timely.
We’ve patented several things, such
as this catalysis for C-H bond activation
that has applications in pharmaceuticals
and some technology that uses electro­
chemistry in medical settings. We’ve been
able to repurpose some of the catalysts
that we’ve used for water splitting to
generate local pH changes in tissue. Then,
we patented this methodology of being
able to reshape stiff tissue just by passing
an electrical current through it with an
appropriate catalyst.
You patent things because you think
it’ll be useful in industry. You never know
what exactly the impact of your research
is going to be. Particularly for fundamen­
tal research in chemistry, [the] majority
of people are doing basic research, which
is stuff that is one more step removed
from real world applications. But you
never know.
What was your decision be­
hind pursuing graduate edu­
cation?
I knew I loved research, and I had always
had a dream of getting my Ph.D., but it
seemed really far off — it seemed like an
impossible thing to do. I remember in col­
lege, as an undergraduate, putting myself
in that mindset … because of that, I didn’t
go directly to graduate school after under­
graduate degree.
I would say up until maybe the sec­
ond semester of my senior year, I wasn’t
sure what I was going to do. I then met a
recruiter for Teach For America, and he
had done the two-year commitment [in]
teaching – this guy was just amazing. He
really inspired me about the mission of
Teach For America and the effect I could
have just out of college. So I applied, and I
got accepted. I taught chemistry in south­
east Los Angeles for two years. While
I was doing that, I obtained a master’s
degree in teaching. And then, somewhere
in that process, I really thought about
what it is that I still wanted to do. I kept
getting drawn back to graduate school. So,
I used an additional gap year to apply to
graduate school, make some connections,
do some research, and by the next fall, I
was enrolled in the California Institute of
Technology working for someone I had
always really admired. Taking those years
off really did some good for me. I learned
a lot about myself.
I think people feel like they have to
be 100% a medical school student or 100%
a chemistry graduate school student in
the future, even as freshmen. It’s okay to
explore many career paths and ultimately
be sure of what you’re doing. Everyone is
different and operates on their own time­
line. There’s nothing wrong with taking
longer — there’s nothing wrong with do­
ing something else and then returning to
something you’re really passionate about.
Why did you choose N.U.?
N.U. is obviously a fantastic school, and
in particular, the Chemistry Department
at N.U. is this jewel. It’s remarkable how
quickly it has grown to being a top 10
department — and certainly I think a top
5 department — in the country. Some of
it’s just that it worked out, timing wise. I
was ready to make an arrangement for my
next step after Harvard University, and
N.U. was hiring during COVID when no­
body else was hiring. They really [wanted]
to grow and improve. There’s no place I
would’ve gone instead.
So there was a mix of ser­
endipity and hard-work that
worked out for you?
A lot of it is serendipity — that’s a good way
to put it. A lot of it is somewhat a roll of
the dice. So much of it is you’re in the right
place at the right time. That’s also a major
source of frustration. You can work as hard
as someone else, but you don’t get lucky. It’s
not like industry, where you get rewarded
for doing a good job. Academia is a little
different. You need to be exceptional at
all times, and even then, you’re just doing
your job. You won’t be rewarded.
There are a lot of things out of your
control. Most of the things in your control
are your attitude and work ethic, and if
you can really work on those things, you
can set yourself up for success. But, there’s
still this aspect of luck. Every part of your
life has a luck component.
Were there any challenges
moving around a lot, pur­
suing your education, and
research?
At the highest level of research, you fol­
low the science. You look at what’s going
to stimulate you intellectually, and you
make the sacrifice. It’s particularly tough
if you’re in a relationship or married or
with somebody close … breaking those
relationships and putting them on pause is
really tough. They call this in academia the
two-bodied problem, which is that you ar­
en’t just worried about yourself. You can’t
just pick up and leave.
That part is really tough. And being
in a new city, especially as a postdoctoral
fellow, which are shorter periods of time
where you’re doing an intense amount of
research — it can be lonely. But I think if
you are enjoying what you are doing, that
brings a lot of comfort. You know that at
the end of the road, you’re going to take a
position that’s a permanent position, and
you’ll finally get to settle down. That kind
of makes that settling down very sweet,
because you’ve earned it.
Any advice for undergradu­
ates seeking research?
If there’s not a spot, don’t take things
personally and don’t let that discourage
you from reaching out to someone else. At
the end of the day, this is a profession of
people. Research doesn’t do itself. There
are personnel-type things that have to
come into play.
My advice to undergraduate students
is to put yourself out there. Do the leg­
work to show that you’ve actually done
some background research and then put it
on them. Ask them if there are opportuni­
ties for you to be involved. Get integrated
into the culture of the group. Graduate
students are your best friends. Get a desk
in the lab and do your homework there
instead of the library so that you get to be
a part of the group. Get the experience of
being a part-time researcher, and that’s
how you know if that’s the life for you.
Defeating the Dragon:
Epistemic Injustice Towards
Asian/ American Women
by Olive Liu
Departments of Asian American Studies and Philosophy
Faculty Advisors: Sanford Goldberg and Ji-yeon Yuh
Abstract
Epistemic injustice, and testimonial injustice specifically, is a type of dis­
crimination that occurs when a person suffers a credibility deficit because of
an identity-based prejudice. This is an issue that affects many marginalized
groups and can have larger repercussions on one’s perception of self, loss of
resources and opportunities, and continued mistreatment, both epistemically
and non-epistemically. My project explores this phenomenon in relation to
Asian/American women, which I identify to be an at-risk group for system­
atic, testimonial injustice. Through the course of this thesis, I discuss how
stereotypes about Asian/Americans, and Asian/American women in partic­
ular, were created and how these stereotypes negatively impact the perceived
credibility of Asian/Americans, both historically and currently. The goal of
this is to problematize the dominant images of Asian/American women and
to show how this idea is not informed by actual Asian/American women
but by dominant and oppressive forces such as white supremacy, patriarchal
power, and Western exceptionalism. Furthermore, I argue that testimonial
injustice against Asian/American women can reproduce and maintain these
negative images and that the discrediting of this group can lead to further,
non-epistemic harms like physical and sexual violence. Because of this, how
we conceptualize justice for Asian/American women socially and politically
is deeply tied to epistemic justice, which serves as a method I discuss for
overall resistance to violent powers.
Introduction
On Mar. 16, 2021, Robert Aaron Long en­
tered three different spas in Georgia with the
intention to kill. His eight victims included
six Asian-American women: Xiaojie Tan,
Douyou Feng, Soon Chung Park, Hyun Jung
Grant, Suncha Kim, and Yong Ae Yue. When
interrogated by the police, Long said that his
shootings were an attempt to eliminate the
“temptations” of his “sexual addiction.”1
Although Long never admitted that
his crimes were racially-motivated, it is no
mistake that his targets were Asian-operated
spas. The perceived connection between
Asian/American women and hyper-sexu­
ality is something that has been forged and
maintained through long histories of discrim­
inatory laws, American military occupation,
and derogatory representations of Asian/
American women in Western media as docile,
submissive, and emotionally uncaring.
While violence against Asian/Amer­
ican women is perpetrated in many ways,
this project aims to uncover the impacts of
epistemic injustice, specifically testimonial
injustice.2 My intention is to understand how
knowledge production can be discriminatory
and how excluding and discrediting certain
groups can contribute to continued oppres­
sion and violence.

a relevant topic to Asian/American wom­

However, one’s understanding of these
social categories is not objective. In Truth and
Method, Michel Foucault discusses the cycle
between power and knowledge, writing
that “truth isn’t outside of power, or lacking
in power … Each society has its regime of
truth.”5 In other words, those in power can
produce and circulate knowledge that justi­
fies their dominance while also derogating
their inferiors. Such understandings are
often institutionalized through education,
politics, and other systems, making them
difficult to disrupt and question.
This kind of dominance can be seen
in the idea of controlling images, which Pa­
tricia Hill Collins introduces in her work,
Black Feminist Thought. Controlling images
are negative characterizations of minority
groups that detract from their humanity,
“mak[ing] racism, sexism, poverty, and
other forms of injustice appear to be more
normal, and inevitable parts of everyday
life.”6 In this sense, controlling images
often conceal the truth of the histories of
oppression certain groups have faced by
making their marginalized position seem
self-evident. It is important to note that
these controlling images will probably not
reflect the actual lived experiences of the
group they describe. Thus, one may ask
why these ideas were formed without in­
terruption, despite the actual violence that
they may cause. I believe that these ques­
tions can be answered by explaining the
function of epistemic injustice, specifically
testimonial injustice.
According to Miranda Fricker in her
seminal text, Epistemic Injustice: Power and
Ethics of Knowing, testimonial injustice occurs
when a speaker “receives a credibility deficit
owing to identity prejudice in the hearer.”7
Note that I am focusing on systematic testi­
monial injustice, which occurs when some­
one unjustly discredits their interlocutor, not
because of the content or context of their tes­
timony, but because of their social identities
like race and gender. Here, one can see how
the relationship between knowledge and
power is important to testimonial injustice:
if one is made to believe that a certain iden­
tity group is inferior, they are likely to grant

Beyond Fricker’s concept of testimo­
nial injustice, Kristie Dotson points out ad­
ditional kinds of epistemic injustices in her
paper titled “Tracking Epistemic Violence,
Tracking Practices of Silencing.” The first is
testimonial quieting, in which “an audience
fails to identify a speaker as a knower.”8 She
directly links this sort of violence to Hill
Collins’ idea of controlling images, as these
images detract from their perception as
knowers and their level of credibility.9 The
second is testimonial smothering, which
occurs when a person limits their testimo­
ny if they feel that their listener may not
consider their knowledge fairly because of
the content of their account or because of
prejudices against their identity.10
As a group, Asian/American women
are particularly at risk for these different
testimonial injustices because of a history of
racially gendered violence, harmful stereo­
types, and exclusionary policies. Thus, to un­
derstand how epistemic injustice manifests
and affects Asian/American women, I want
to provide a brief analysis of three major
factors that have influenced dominant con­
ceptions of this group: Orientalism, overseas
occupation, and domestic oppression.
Section 2: Camptown
Women, Lotus Blossoms, and
Dragon Ladies
Before delving into the more specific histo­
ries of Asian/American women, I want to
introduce the framework of Orientalism,
which was first coined by Edward Said to
describe the relationship between the West
(the Occident) and the East (the Orient). Al­
though Said is writing about the relationship
between Europe and the Middle East specif­
ically, the idea of Orientalism can still offer
us a useful framework for understanding
power and knowledge and how it influenced
the identity of Asian/American women.
According to Said, the Western conception
of the ‘Orient’ or Asia is largely a construc­
tion invented by Europe, which he calls the
Occident.11 In essence, the way the Occident
understands the Orient is integral to its
perception of itself and its superiority, as the
Orient defines the West as being an inferior
“image, idea, personality, experience.”12 Be­
cause of this, people identified as ‘Orientals’
are perceived as being inherently lesser than
their Western counterparts, an idea that un­
dergirds many stereotypes directed towards
Asian/American women.
For instance, the Page Act of 1875
(henceforth referred to as the Page Act),
while explicitly banning the entry of coerced
laborers, convicted felons, and prostitutes
from Asia, implicitly prevented the immigra­
tion of Chinese women to the U.S. by gener­
alizing them as sex workers.13 Using language
like “lewd and immoral” as justification to
deny their entry, the Page Act perpetuated
the popular racist sentiment that Chinese
women were impure and hyper-sexual.14 The
role that testimonial injustice played in the
denial of Chinese women from immigrating
to the U.S. was also premised on these beliefs.

as prostitutes — this time, to fill the camp­

abundance of camptown clubs cannot be

women, the attitudes that American soldiers
had toward these women cannot be ignored.

stereotypes of Asian/American women
depicted in popular media to identify some
additional harms Asian/American women

that of camptown women influence ideas of
Asian/American women today. For this pa­

by Renee E. Tajima in “Lotus Blossoms
Don’t Bleed”: the Lotus Blossom and the
Dragon Lady. The former is characterized
as “a sexual-romantic object” who is “utter­
ly feminine [and] delicate” and “exist[s] to
serve men,” especially white men.21 A popu­
lar example of this is Kim from the musical
Miss Saigon, a Vietnamese sex worker who
is seemingly ‘saved’ from her profession by
an American soldier, Chris. Consistently
characterized as virginal and pure, Kim falls
in love with Chris, only to commit suicide
once she discovers that he has re-married
after leaving Vietnam. This reveals that
Kim’s character exists only as the object of
Chris’ sexual desires, being discarded when
she no longer serves her purpose.
While the Lotus Blossom presents an
innocent and submissive image of Asian/
American women, the Dragon Lady subverts
this idea, placing Asian/American women in
a position of sexual dominance. She is char­
acterized by her “excessively dangerous sex­
uality” and “Oriental femininity,” which are
weaponized as tools of manipulation.22 Yet,
this overt sexuality often masks the emotion­
ally cold and cruel intentions of the Dragon
Lady, which are often antagonistic against
white and male power. Perhaps one of the
most famous examples of this character is
O-ren Ishii in Kill Bill Vol. 1. Portrayed by
Lucy Liu, O-ren’s cold demeanor juxtaposes
the excessive violence she wreaks through­
out the movie, using her femininity as a tool
to seize power and seek revenge. This char­
acterization may imply that Asian/American
women as lacking fundamental humanity
— they are willing to cross moral boundaries
and weaponize deeply personal things, such
as sex, to get what they want.
Section 3: Epistemic Injustice
and its Effects on Asian/
American Women
Using both the stereotypes and the history
of camptown women that I have previ­
ously explored, I will now sketch out the
justifications one may use when commit­
ting an act of testimonial injustice against
Asian/American women. The Lotus Blos­
som is perhaps the clearer one to dissect:
because they are directly characterized as
shy, submissive, and docile, it is easy to see
why they may be seen as having low credi­
bility. Their perceived tendency is to defer
to their male counterparts, and as a result,
they often have things decided for them and
not with them, thus being treated more like

On the other end, the Dragon Lady is often
perceived to be powerful, and even dom­
inant over men. While this might seem
like it awards them an adequate amount
of credibility, it is important to note that
this power comes from their sexuality and
cruelty.23 Because they use immoral means
to procure their position over others, their
testimony is often seen as untrustworthy
or manipulative.
The negative effects of this are also
seen when American servicemen justify
their involvement with military prosti­

Asian countries. The implication is that
Asian women are inherently hyper-sexual,
and should be used and treated as such.
When camptown women spoke up about
the violence that they faced at the hands of
G.I.s or club managers, their line of work,
gender, race, and class called their integrity
and credibility into question.
With this information, I offer this
account of what epistemic, and specifically
testimonial, injustice looks like for Asian/
American women: Asian/American wom­
en are likely to suffer instances of testimo­
nial injustice when their audience holds
a prejudiced idea about them that stems
from the controlling images of Asian/
American women as sexual, subservient,
untrustworthy, and passive. These stereo­
types directly detract from their status as
knowers by undermining their credibility,
particularly in situations relating to sex,
intimate relationships, and personal harm.
Furthermore, Asian/American women,
and especially those who are lower-class,
immigrants, or in other disadvantaged
groups, are at risk of smothering their
testimony because the content of it often
puts them at risk for violence, either in­
terpersonally or from the state. This often
results in epistemic oppression, which
Kristie Dotson defines as the “persistent
epistemic exclusion that hinders one’s
contribution to knowledge production.”24
Because of this consistent exclusion and
silencing, the testimonies and experiences
of Asian/American women often do not
shape the knowledge surrounding them,
allowing for the continued epistemic, so­
cial, and political violence against them.
This account can best be thought of
through the concept of a positive feedback
loop, in which the result of an initial action
causes more of that action to occur. With
testimonial injustice against Asian/Amer­
ican women, the initial event is often the
development of prejudice against them,
including traits that take agency away from
Asian/American women, such as how
the Lotus Blossom trope portrays Asian/
American women as submissive and docile.
This may invite people to think about these
women in a way that dismisses their needs
or experiences in favor of their own.
This leads to an increased potential of

American women, as these views are likely
to detract from their credibility as know­

will likely confirm the original prejudice,
especially because any resistance to the act

of testimonial quieting due to a lack of
credibility. This creates a positive feedback

previously points out, controlling images

of everyday life, and not something to be

Section 4: Epistemic Justice:
How People Can Do Better
Through this analysis, it becomes clear
that testimonial injustice can be used as a
tool of epistemic, sexual, and psychological
harm. Thus, it is important to develop a
method of epistemic justice as a form of re­
sistance. In their book, The Epistemology of
Resistance,  José Medina proposes the idea
of meta-lucidity, which is the awareness of
one’s social position and how it relates to
the identities, histories, and beliefs of oth­
ers.28 In doing so, one is better equipped
to identify the gaps in their knowledge or
diagnose certain beliefs as inaccurate or
problematic, which will affect how they
assign credibility to others in the future.
The goal in doing so is to expand and fill
the gaps in one’s knowledge by “pursu[ing]
interventions and transformations aimed
at instilling new attitudes and habits.”29 In
other words, it is not enough to become
aware of one’s epistemic practices — peo­
ple must work to correct them by directly
interacting with the groups that are affect­
ed by their beliefs. This is done through
epistemic interactions, particularly in­
teractions that create epistemic friction,
which can be understood as “experiencing
resistance from significantly different
perspectives in social interaction.”30 By
attempting to correct one’s own and learn
new beliefs, people develop a “kaleidoscop­
ic consciousness that remains forever open
to being expanded,” which pushes one to
“acknowledge and engage new perspec­
tives” in relation to their own knowledge.31
In terms of how this relates to testi­
monial justice, I argue that practicing this
kind of reflection with one’s identity and
willingness to change one’s perceptions
of others will make people more open to
learning about different identities and less
motivated to make assumptions about
other groups. A kaleidoscopic conscious­
ness can also help someone recognize that
some communities have been systemically
excluded from contributing to collective
epistemic resources, as their accounts
might have critiqued and detracted from
the authority that racial, gendered, and
other social powers have. Because of this,
people can assess whether their ideas about
others are harmful and question the validi­
ty of such beliefs, making them more open
to change when they encounter epistemic
friction with them. This can address the
prejudices that inform acts of testimonial
injustice, as Medina’s model pushes people
to question why such beliefs are formed,
how they reify current structures of power,
and how people can rectify these gaps in
their knowledge.
Like epistemic injustice, epistemic
justice can also exist in a positive feedback
loop. As I explained previously, one’s re­
alization that their perceptions of others
are problematic should be followed by
attempts to unlearn these beliefs. For in­
stance, in Section 2, I discussed how Ori­
entalism often characterized Asian people
as less human than their Western counter­
parts. If a person learns about this history,
they should be more critical of the current
idea that Chinese people are responsible
for COVID-19 because they consume
non-traditional animals like bats or dogs.
They might realize that the rhetoric that
the media uses is prejudiced against Chi­
nese people, which should push them to
realize how things like the news reproduce
certain racist biases. Thus, when they view
news articles like those that characterize
Black Lives Matter protestors as violent
looters, they will probably be less likely to
accept this at face value and instead seek
out the experiences of those who were
actually a part of these movements. The
cause (recognizing one’s own harmful be­
liefs) leads to the effect (trying to learn and
repair one’s knowledge about the group
they are prejudiced toward), which leads
back to the cause, increasing the number of
things that one might identify as problem­
atic. Of course, not every individual will
undergo such a process when unlearning
certain prejudices and stereotypes. The
importance of epistemic justice is that it
cultivates a certain sense of curiosity about
how certain concepts came to be and how
others see these ideas and the world.
Conclusion
My intention throughout this thesis has
been to illuminate an issue that many
people face and to give others the language
and tools to identify these types of
It is not enough to
become aware of one’s
epistemic practices —
people must work to
correct them by directly
interacting with the
groups that are affected
by their beliefs.
injustices in their own lives. In doing so,
I hope that more people will recognize
how their perceptions of Asian/ American
women might be harmful, which will
encourage them to seek out the stories
and histories of these women. By learning
about these experiences, I believe people
will question and be more critical of the
oppressive forces that informed their ini­
tial prejudices, which will hopefully strip
these powers of their dominance. This is
the ultimate future that epistemic justice
can lead us to. The knowledge that one
possesses and uses is constantly changing
and responding to different influences
and experiences in our lives. We should
consider it a powerful tool that can push
us towards a better world — one in which
we are no longer objects of domination,
but instead are subjects of positive change.

Throughout my academic, profession­
al, and personal journeys, I have always
believed in the power of community and
care. That being said, I am very thankful
for the community that came to my sup­
