craft as a tattoo artist — if she experiences
discrimination that her male counterparts
do not, how she is perceived differently
than tattooed men in Korea, and how
marginalized communities and activism are
related to South Korean tattoo history and
culture. To my surprise, however, C would
often respond by telling me that there was
no such clear difference between men and
women in many cases, and she incorporat­
ed gender into her responses in ways that
I had not anticipated. Instead, I found that
many of C’s responses reflected her own
negotiations of identity as a female South
Korean tattoo artist — how she perceived
tattoos in relation to Korea’s tattoo history
and the way that Koreans negatively view
heavily tattooed women. I focus on two
themes present in her responses: historical
associations between tattoos and crime
in Korea, and C’s negotiation of her own
body and identity in relation to shame (or
lack thereof).
I began by asking C about the sto­
ries she has heard about Korea’s tattoo
history. C started by recalling the practice
of penal tattooing in the Chosŏn dynasty
(1392—1897 CE), noting that tattoos were
used to punish criminals. According to C,
the wounding of one’s skin by engraving
these letters was “the most shameful insult”
that one could receive at the time.14 The
Korean word for tattoos, munshin, could
be translated as letters engraved onto the
body (mun meaning letters or writing and
shin meaning body).15 Korean scholar Kim
Hyŏng-jung traces such punishment back
to Korea’s Koryŏ period, in which penal tat­
toos became legalized. These tattoos would
permanently mark a criminal’s face or body
with letters indicating the type of crime
committed.16 Particularly due to the grow­
ing influence of Confucianism in Korea at
the time, wounding of the body received
from one’s parents was viewed as a betray­
al of filial piety.17 Chosŏn dynasty rulers
favored harsh tattoo punishments, deliber­
ately marking criminals’ faces to make their
past crimes visible to the public.18
When recalling Korea’s tattoo his­
tory, C immediately began with the cruel
practice of penal tattooing, focusing on
strong associations between tattoos and
crime; however, she was not specifically
prompted to do so by my questions. In
fact, when I conducted my second oral
history interview a month later with artist
“H,” I got a response comparing pre- and
post-social media tattoo culture, centering
on technological development rather than
criminality.19 However, it cannot be denied
that since the end of the penal Chosŏn dy­
nasty tattoo punishments, tattoos continue
to be associated with the illegal activities
of gangsters and prostitutes, which C also
mentioned in her personal timeline of Ko­
rean tattoo history.
The image of tattooed gangsters in
South Korea, while considered outdated
by some, does not come from a place of
mere speculation.20 i-D’s mini-documen­
tary features Grace Neutral speaking to a
self-identified current gang member, Mr.
Kim, who has just received a large back tat­
too. Mr. Kim estimates that “if 100 [gang­
sters] have tattoos, then only one would not
have one.”21 Associations between tattoos

At some point in the middle of our

C if she ever hides her tattoos, however,
she expressed that she felt it was unneces­

Identity Negotiation: C’s
Understanding and Display
of Her Tattooed Body
All three women I interviewed reported
some instance of covering their tattoos in
certain settings. However, each artist qual­
ified these statements, expressing that they
do not “hide” (sumgida) or want to hide
their tattoos from family or the public,
but that they might “cover” (karida) them
up or choose to not show them in certain
contexts.28 C particularly emphasized that
this covering of tattooed flesh is not an
act of shame, for having tattoos is nothing
shameful to her.29 While I find it encour­
aging that C does not view her tattoos as
shameful, it cannot be ignored that she
makes a conscious choice to cover her tat­
toos in certain social contexts. If C is un­
ashamed of her tattoos, why cover them in
any situation? Certainly, C’s choice to limit
the display of her tattoos around elders
alone does not necessarily indicate that she
feels a sense of shame as a heavily tattooed
South Korean woman. How, then, could
we (or should we) interpret the negoti­
ation of identity through the covering of
tattoos? How is this different from “hiding”
one’s flesh? And, finally, considering that
this covering is not done out of shame,
what are some other emotions that may be
driving this action? Although all of these
questions cannot be fully answered, I do
think they are significant in understand­
ing the unique identities and experiences
of each artist. I find that in these social
situations, C does not hide her tattoos in
shame but rather practices an intentional
negotiation of identity that relates to her
own understanding of tattoo history and
culture in Korea.
This concept of negotiation is dis­
cussed by scholars who interviewed North
American women with tattoos using oral
history methods similar to mine. Scholars
Michael Atkinson and Victoria L. Pitts
both express that their interviewees’ bodies
should be understood not as sites of agency
or conformity alone but rather as sites of
an ongoing negotiation.30 As Victoria L.
Pitts notes, “Women’s marked bodies ex­
emplify both the praxis of culturally mar­
ginal body projects and the limits of that
praxis. As I see it, they highlight the female
body as a site of negotiation between pow­
er and powerlessness, neither of which are
likely to win fully.”31 Considering this defi­
nition, I suggest that C’s body is also a site
of negotiation, being displayed or covered
according to context rather than sites of
complete subversion of or submission to
Korean societal norms.
Moreover, through examining all
three oral history narratives, I find that
the negotiation of one’s tattooed body and
flesh is incredibly nuanced and varies on an
individual level. Each negotiation is per­
sonal and is not only based on larger social
hierarchies or norms but also on personal
identities, relationships, and interactions. In
addition to the works of Atkinson and Pitts,
I also frame my understanding of identity
30 Atkinson, “Pretty in Ink”; Pitts, In the Flesh: The Cultural Politics of Body Modification.
31 Pitts, In the Flesh: The Cultural Politics of Body Modification, 81.
32 Deaux and Ethier, “Negotiating Social Identity,” 301.
33 Atkinson, “Pretty in Ink,” 229.
negotiation around Deaux and Ethier’s defi­
nition: “agentic identity work carried out in
response to contextual demands.”32 Essential
to this definition is the agency of the identity
negotiator, as well as the demands which ne­
cessitate a negotiation of identity. Given C’s
responses, it is clear to me that her covering
of tattoos is a conscious choice that depends
heavily on contextual elements; thus, I
would like to frame her as an agent rather
than an object of discrimination.
To some, exercising agency exclusively
looks like uncovering one’s flesh and show­
ing it at all times for the world to see. As
scholar Michael Atkinson notes in his own
oral history interviews with tattooed Ca­
nadian women, several believe “that tattoo
body projects intended for social resistance
must be visible to be effective”; otherwise,
if the tattooed body remains concealed
in certain circumstances, “no discernable
challenge to established understandings of
the body can be established.”33 However, I
find that covering or even hiding parts of
the body, whether influenced by shame or
some other emotion, can also function as
an exercise of agency. While the act of cov­
ering one’s own body is not total resistance
against forces of gender and legal oppression
faced by South Korean female tattoo artists,
it should also not be characterized simply
However, I find that covering or even hiding
parts of the body, whether influenced by shame
or some other emotion, can also function as an
exercise of agency.
as an act of conforming to societal norms.
Rather, the different ways in which each
woman I interviewed intentionally covers
or uncovers her tattoos can be understood
as acts of agency negotiated to fit within
current social and legal boundaries.
One of my most interesting findings
was that the three women I interviewed
chose to negotiate their identities in very
specific, distinct social contexts. Contrary
to what I had expected, there was no clear
distinction between the artists’ negotiation
of identity in public versus private spaces,
around young versus old people, inside or
outside of the family, etc., that was con­
sistent across all three narratives. Rather,
each woman negotiates the display of her
tattooed flesh, as well as her identity as a
tattoo artist, in relation to specific individ­
uals or groups with whom they interact.
In other words, they negotiate differently
depending on the relationship between
their individual, intersecting identities,
and their own everyday social interactions.
As stated previously, C said that she
does not cover up her tattoos in front of
family or in public but will sometimes cov­
er them if she is suddenly around elders at
an event like a wedding. The social and cul­
tural contexts which inform C’s negotiation
are not broadly defined such as public or
private, or between friends versus in front
of strangers. Instead, C specifically identi­
fied elders as the group of people in front
of whom she conceals her tattooed body.
Moreover, C stated that she covers her tat­
toos when she ends up going to places with
many older people and gives a wedding as
an example of a setting in which she may
encounter elders and negotiate the display
of her tattoos accordingly. This suggests
that C generally does not cover her tattoos
in circumstances where she might encoun­
ter smaller, sporadic numbers of older
people, such as when she is simply walking
outside or going to the store. The formality
of a large gathering and ceremony such as a
wedding also seems to influence C’s nego­
tiation of her tattoos. C asserted that when
she chooses to refrain from showing her
tattoos, she does not do so out of shame.
Combined with her consideration of her
relation to others’ ages, it is possible that C
instead negotiates her display of tattoos as
a way to show respect for elders.
Looking at all three cases of identity
negotiation together highlights how de­
cisions to negotiate identity vary across
individuals. While the method of covering
up tattoos and the language used to describe
this act are similar throughout all three oral
history narratives, the contexts which each
woman feels demand this negotiation are
very different. The differences in contexts —
the nuances of the spaces and people which
necessitate a distinct display or covering of
one’s tattooed body in Korean society — also
suggest that motivations behind identity ne­
gotiation can differ from person to person.
Covering one’s tattoos in certain contexts
becomes a conscious negotiation influenced
by care, respect, and/or the consideration of
others’ gaze. Care and concern for family,
respect for elders, and a consciousness of
what is expected of mothers in particular
settings — practiced by artists Y, C, and H,
respectively — shape South Korean female
tattoo artists’ daily existence within the
Korean tattoo industry and Korean tattoo
culture more broadly.
Conclusion
Ultimately, the three oral history narra­
tives told by South Korean female tattoo
artists C, H, and Y inform current un­
derstandings of women’s roles in Korean
tattoo history and culture by providing
nuanced accounts of the evolution of Ko­
rea’s tattoo scene as well as the gendered
dynamics within it. Moreover, these nar­
ratives demonstrate how each individual’s
understanding of Korean tattoo culture is
distinct. The timelines, social perceptions,
and gender dynamics connected to Korean
tattoo culture are presented differently by
each artist. Together, these unique narra­
tives also suggest that each artist negoti­
ates her own tattooed identity in specific
contexts related to her own understanding
of Korean tattoo history and culture.
The full version of my thesis aims to
answer questions relating to both the in­
terpretation of oral history more broadly
and what each individual narrative reveals
about different experiences of South Ko­
rean female tattoo artists. When looking
at the oral history process itself, how does
each woman narrate Korean tattoo culture
and history in relation to her own personal
identities and experiences? How can we
read their narratives in a way that values
what they chose to say but also acknowl­
edges and carefully considers what was left
out of their accounts? When considering
the specific content in each narrative and
how all three narratives are distinct yet

connected, what can we discover about
the different roles and experiences of fe­
male South Korean tattoo artists? How do
these artists make sense of their own iden­

Interviewing C gave me a sense of
direction for the rest of my senior thesis
project, leading me to the concept of iden­
tity negotiation and shaping the questions
that I would later ask artists Y and H. Af­
ter completing all three narratives, I found
that each woman not only narrates her own
understanding of Korean tattoo history and
culture as well as how they shift over time;
she also situates herself within contempo­
rary Korean society and reveals how gender
dynamics do or do not exist in Korea’s tat­
too scene. Ultimately, each artist tells a story
not only of the evolution of Korea’s tattoo
culture but also how historical and cultural
context shape the display of their tattooed
bodies and flesh in Korean society.34
Given the small scale of this project
and the depth of information available

a distinct display or covering of one’s tattooed

from only three oral history narrators, I
imagine there is great potential for success
in using oral history to record more wom­
en’s perspectives of tattoo history and cul­
ture in Korea. As Namgung Ho-sŏk notes
in his retelling of Korean tattoo history,
current archives privilege particular narra­
tives, such as that of penal tattooing prac­
tices in the Koryŏ and Chosŏn dynasties,
while leaving out other possible functions
of tattoos over time.35 While our ability to
make up for the missing pieces of written
records is limited, making an effort to col­
lect narratives from current tattoo artists
and tattooed people in South Korea will
diversify future historical records. Con­
sidering the absence of women’s voices in
particular, I hope to continue communi­
cating with other South Korean women
about Korean tattoo culture in the future.
Through oral history projects such as this
thesis, the roles of marginalized people’s
roles in Korean tattoo culture can be ex­
plored and recorded in depth.
In present-day Korea, tattooing is
still a criminalized act; yet it has become a
marker of individuality and agency. Since
the Koryŏ dynasty, tattooing has trans­
formed from a form of state control of the
body and flesh to an underground indus­
try operating against the law. In his own
research on tattoos, Korean scholar Kim
Hyŏng-jung characterizes the state’s crimi­
nalization of tattoo artists, as well as differ­
ent forms of discrimination tattooed Ko­
reans face from the government and older
generations, as a method of modern tattoo
punishment that evolved from the penal
tattoos executed in the Koryŏ and Chosŏn
dynasties.36 With this in mind, what does
it mean for South Korean female tattoo
paper; however, it is an important consideration that I plan to incorporate into future research.

artists to strategically negotiate the display
of their tattooed flesh? To wear the marks
that have marked slaves, criminals, gang­
sters, and prostitutes throughout Korean
history? To mark their flesh and the flesh
of others through a criminalized practice?
To enjoy the freedom of a freelance career
despite the constant danger of a fine and
prison sentence?
Through this thesis, I have at­
tempted to partially answer the first of
these questions, but the rest require fur­
ther research. As I contemplate what fu­
ture research on this topic will look like,
I return to the ways in which these three
artists’ responses to my questions subvert­
ed many of my expectations, particularly
in relation to gender dynamics. Although
I expected that one or possibly even all of
the artists would find ways in which their
female identities shaped their work as tat­
too artists, none of them had reflected on
how their work might connect to their Ko­
rean womanhood. This makes me wonder
if my focus on gendered differences — such
as varying perceptions of men and women
with tattoos, different challenges faced by
male versus female tattoo artists, etc. —
was an effective way to frame my oral his­
tory questions. If these gender dichotomies
of male/female and masculine/feminine
experiences within Korea’s tattoo culture
are not the most helpful aspect of Korean
tattoo culture to analyze, what questions
would be more productive? The difficulty
of centering women’s voices and a gendered
analysis while also capturing the significant
elements shaping Korean tattoo culture be­
came very apparent through this research.

FEATURE
By Zaina Karim
How We Can Ensure
Success in STEM:
Professor Marcel Vinces
In the fall of 2021, 4,204 students
at Northwestern University
(N.U.) were enrolled in the
Weinberg College of Arts and
Sciences. A significant portion of
these students pursued, and continue
to pursue, majors in biological or
pre-health-related fields, making
participation in an introductory biology
class inevitable. For many, starting biology
courses at N.U. will be the first experience
that they have with a collegiate level of
biological sciences, and therefore, hold
great importance for a student’s attitude
toward success in biology and beyond.
With this in mind, it would behoove N.U.
students, faculty, and administrators to ask,
“What can be done to ensure the optimal
outcome of introductory biology classes?”
This is exactly what Professor Marcelo
Vinces, a Weinberg academic advisor, has
worked to answer during his time at and
before N.U..
By closely examining and
evaluating the teaching and student
reception of introductory biology
courses, Professor Vinces and his
colleagues at Oberlin College were able
to pinpoint the distinction between
unsuccessful “teacher-centered learning”
and constructive “problem/project-based
learning.” Many students made the decision
not to continue science-related degrees
following introductory biology courses,
raising questions about
what different variations
of class structures might lead
to more students persisting
in STEM fields. Traditionally,
biology classes are taught with a
lecturer speaking, students quietly
taking notes, and then the students taking
two midterms and a final. However,
when asked about this approach, Vinces
emphasized the much more effective
learning outcomes of “problem-based
learning, where instead of the professor
just talking and the students taking notes,
students are given problems in the class,
often in groups.” This, he said, causes
students to “engage more deeply with
the material,” and provides the practical
foundation needed to retain information
and apply knowledge on exams.
While problem-based learning
is better for students in the long run and
leads to improved performance later,
it might cause a degree of discomfort
in the moment. In looking at students’
perception of their own learning,
students felt like they were learning
more when being lectured, rather than
doing problems and engaging in project/
problem-based learning. Although
students who use problem-solving and
group skills to acquire information encode
knowledge on a deeper level, they often
feel uncertain about their own retention
because they are not being explicitly
told the information. In his research,
Vinces worked to identify a way that
this initial resistance to problem-based
learning, what he described to be a type
of “culture shock,” could be remedied.
Eventually, with student survey reports
and interviews, he was able to identify
that through gradual acclimation and
realization of the benefits, students
grow comfortable with the approach
and persist longer in biology and other
STEM fields. With continued exposure
to practice problems, group work, and
opportunities to earn better grades,
students will soon become intrinsically
motivated to participate in class, work
with others, and push themselves to
showcase their expertise. One way in
which this can be implemented is by
giving students rewards for participation,
group work, and practice, and then
gradually transitioning them to taking
part in these activities for their benefit
and without reinforcement.
It is crucial for N.U. not to neglect
this issue. Weinberg advisors such as
Professor Vinces experience firsthand
the struggle that some students endure
with courses such as Introductory
Biology. Vinces mentioned that students
in separate sections of a single class at
N.U. have expressed dissatisfaction with
the fact that their peers had instructors
offering a higher frequency of graded
assessments such as homework and
quizzes, as opposed to their own
curriculum that relies on midterms and
a final examination. He continued by
stating that some classrooms exhibit a
“climate where students can more easily
ask questions.” These disparities can
be easily addressed at our school with
communication between teachers and a
focus on the benefits of demonstrative
and problem-based learning. With the
addition of the recently acquired grant
aimed towards furthering research on
various types of learning settings, N.U.
can work towards these improvements in
Introductory Biology, and all classrooms.
Through gradual acclimation and realization
of the benefits, students grow comfortable
with the approach and persist longer in
biology and other STEM fields.

Monstrous Masculinities,
Male Angst, and
Adolescent Development
in the Twilight Saga
by Juliet Jacques
Department of English
Faculty Adviser: Nick Davis
Introduction
Over the past two decades, the Twilight
series has become a staple of popular
culture, with an enormous and dedicated
fanbase. The “vampire versus werewolf”
or “Edward versus Jacob” debate is almost
universally recognizable, especially among
fans of 2010s Young Adult (Y.A.) media.
However, fans and critics alike miss a
crucial element of analysis (or obsession)
in Twilight. Inseparable from this study
of masculinity is the related issue of ra­
cialization, which is especially salient for
werewolf and love interest Jacob Black
— Edward’s chief rival in the franchise
from both a romantic and species (coded
as racial) standpoint.
Twilight may at first appear as an un­
usual object of literary analysis. The saga
has attracted no lack of criticism, ranging
1 See Melissa Click’s Bitten by Twilight for a comprehensive collection of essays on Twilight’s influence on fandom culture, Holly­
wood teenage idols, and the commodification of literature.
all the way from its depiction of unhealthy
teenage relationships to the quality of its
writing. However, the series has had a
profound impact on the entire Y.A. genre
of popular culture. Many scholars cred­
it Twilight as paving the way for other
popular franchises such as Fifty Shades of
Grey, which originated as Twilight fanfic­
tion, and other teenage romances such as
The Hunger Games, which has continued
Twilight’s revival of the Y.A. genre’s in­
terest in tropes such as love triangles and
strong, independent, teenage heroines.1 It
is clear that the series has had an enduring
effect on popular culture, cementing it as a
cornerstone of Y.A. literature. Due to the
immeasurable impact of both the original
novels and the multimedia phenomenon
they launched, Twilight deserves its own
field of scholarship. Millions of readers
and viewers have seen and internalized the
saga’s surprisingly new themes surround­
ing gender roles and masculinity. Literary
analysis of Twilight’s language, character
construction, recurring metaphors, and
Gothic antecedents can uncover the spe­
cific themes and messaging that have made
Twilight such an enduring, influential, and
beloved series. Furthermore, it can help us
to understand the way that Y.A. literature
engages with and reshapes representations
of adolescent masculinity.
Analysis of the Current State
of Twilight Scholarship
The field of Twilight scholarship is quite
young, with scholarship beginning around
2010 after the first of the novels were
published in 2006 and the first film was
released in 2008. Even so, in the decade
since the start of the field, there has been
enormous growth in scholarship and
perspectives surrounding Twilight, with a
growing confidence in approaching this
series through various modes of literary
analysis. Thus far, Twilight scholarship has
followed two main avenues: close-reading
analyses that examine the language and
rhetoric of the texts independently as well
as more sociological approaches that think
about elements of the series in conversa­
tion with the success and reception of the
franchise. The field is, in general, con­
flicted about how much these approaches
should overlap or rely on each other. It
appears as if the inclination to analyze the
Twilight novels as literary texts separately
from their corresponding cultural impact
only came later in the 2010s. After all, it
2 It is interesting that many of the first books on Twilight were published by McFarland, including a third book, Wilson’s Seduced by
Twilight. The publisher is especially known for its books on popular culture and media.
takes courage to admit to studying this
series as literature.
The first books and essays written on
Twilight focus heavily on the sociological
and cultural aspects of the series. For ex­
ample, Amy Clarke’s The Twilight Mystique
(2010) and Parke and Wilson’s Theorizing
Twilight: Critical Essays on What’s at Stake
in a Post-Vampire World (2011) explore
the overall series through the lens of its
recent success.2 The essays in these books
are often reflexive in that they think both
about how Twilight is influenced by popu­
lar culture norms and stereotypes as well as
how it influences them in return. Thus, in
these earlier books, it is harder to separate
literary analysis from sociological analysis.
These articles act almost as primary sourc­
es because they differ so much from the
intricate, detailed analyses of language and
theme that come later. In fact, early authors
such as Benning (2011) acknowledge that
they are writing at the very beginning of
the field and suggest many potential topics
for later authors. These older articles often
cover both a sociological analysis of the
readers and culture surrounding Twilight
as well as more literary elements of the text
itself, particularly genre tropes and influ­
ential literary predecessors. However, this
seemingly comprehensive approach actu­
ally weakens the literary analysis because
scholars are unwilling to look at Twilight’s
language and themes for their own merit,
separately from the ensuing reception and
sociological aspects. To better understand
the success and appeal of the series and its
legacy in Y.A. fiction, we should also view
the textual elements themselves as insight­
ful and intentional.
Indeed, as more articles were writ­
ten and published, the field became more
varied and more accommodating of
close-reading methodologies. For exam­
ple, Anne Morey’s collection Genre, Recep­
tion, and Adaptation in the ‘Twilight’ Series
(2012) looks and reads much differently
from earlier collections in its willingness
to analyze the literary aspects of the series
separately from the sociological. Claudia
Bucciferro’s collection The Twilight Saga:
Exploring the Global Phenomenon (2014) also
demonstrates this growth, though it is no­
table that studies of Twilight remain con­
fined to para-academic publishers and not
major university presses. Overall, these
later books divide the two types of analysis
more than previous collections — a trend
that only grows throughout the rest of the
decade. Morey’s introduction separates the
articles by subject matter: first looking at
genre and narrative within Twilight, then
turning to the reception of Twilight as a
cultural phenomenon, and finally study­
ing adaptation and film. Significantly,
Morey emphasizes the importance of
studying novels in the romance genre — a
well-established practice within literary
and cultural studies, especially in the
wake of Janice Radway’s foundational
text Reading the Romance (1991), but not
previously applied to Twilight, at least in
print. As with Morey’s, Bucciferro’s book
is divided into sections for articles on spe­
cific areas of study, such as fandom and
reception, gender in Twilight, and looking
beyond the franchise. This last section is
particularly interesting, as it recognizes
Y.A. novels as their own genre that de­
serves analysis by examining common

Other clear patterns emerge as schol­
arship on Twilight evolves. Early literature
focused on critiquing antifeminist and mi­
sogynist aspects of the series, arguing that
Bella was forced to submit to a dominant
patriarchal culture.3 After this initial ap­
proach, and likely in response to the cul­
tural backlash and hatred for the series, an
opposing, postfeminist movement arose,
wherein scholars began to look at the
ways in which Bella could still represent a
progressive, autonomous character. These
two reactions formed the basis for the field
of scholarship, but authors then quickly
moved beyond these “good” and “bad” bi­
naries, and scholarship began to be more
detailed, intricate, and creative. Twilight
scholarship became more diversified as
authors looked beyond the more obvious
aspects of the series, such as the portrayal
of unhealthy teenage relationships, to take
a more nuanced look at gender roles and
relationships, albeit with a predominant
interest in the female gender. Scholarship
also began looking at Twilight as a coming-
of-age series or bildungsroman in which
Bella finds her place and identity in the
world.4 Whereas earlier authors wrote
broadly about the series, later authors
began filling in the gaps, finding more
intricacies and subtleties. For example,
Nicole Willms, writing in Bucciferro’s
collection, discusses race, masculinity, and
rivalry in the series, and Sara Day, as a
contributor to Morey’s anthology, argues
that Bella’s increasing passivity can be un­
derstood through the lens of what she calls
“narrative intimacy” and her weakening
relationship with the reader as the series
progresses. Both of these articles lay the
key groundwork for readings I pursue later
in this thesis.
The Limits of Current
Approaches to the Study of
Gender and Masculinity
Within this emerging field of Twilight
literary scholarship, one subfield looks at
portrayals of gender and masculinity using
two common approaches. The first refer­
ences Gothic tropes and historical charac­
teristics in relation to gender and sexuality.
For example, Budruweit (2016) argues
that Twilight sanitizes Gothic monsters,
instead making women’s uncontrolled
bodies into the primary sites of the “mon­
strous.” In contrast, Moruzi (2012) gives a
postfeminist reading of Bella, arguing that
the incorporation of Gothic characteristics
intensifies the romance, adding danger
and allowing Bella to explore her desires
and identity, which can be messy without
being monstrous. Moruzi argues that as­
pects of Edward such as self-discipline, in­
experience, and “vegetarianism” (Twilight’s
language for vampires who refuse to feed
off humans) shift the power dynamics of
their relationship, obligating the male part­
ner to the stereotypically feminine task of
relentless self-monitoring, and by contrast
allowing Bella more control and autonomy.
These two examples demonstrate
the common elements scholars often de­
fer to when talking about the Gothic in
conjunction with Twilight. These generic
tropes, whether physical (blood), moral or
behavioral (self-control), affective (desire),
or specifically sexual (including queerness,
5 There is a large, in-depth body of literature on this Gothic tradition, especially for Twilight’s 19th century vampiric counterparts
as Stoker’s Dracula (1897) and Le Fanu’s Carmilla (1872). Just a few of the essays on this topic include Craft’s “Kiss Me with those Red
Lips”: Gender and Inversion in Bram Stoker’s Dracula (1984), Signoretti’s Repossessing the Body – Transgressive Desire in “Carmilla” and
“Dracula” (1996), and Schaffer’s “A Wilde Desire Took Me”: The Homoerotic History of Dracula (1994).
or an alleged lack of queerness) can be cat­
egorized as disparate yet closely connected
aspects of the Gothic, all of which center
the body in some way. Desire for blood and
desire for sex always go hand in hand in this
tradition: The act of desiring and drinking
blood is often erotic, representing other
sexual desires, usually those deemed devi­
ant.5 For example, scholars such as Moruzi
(2012) and Lindén (2013) argue that the
desire for blood is replaced or subordinated
by the desire for sex in these more recent,
Y.A.-style reinterpretations of vampirism.
However, this approach again fails to look
at major, masculine characters such as Ed­
ward as individuals who confront other
conflicts and wrestle with their own stages
of development, separate from their ro­
Beyond short-changing
the texts under review,
these Bella-centric
approaches to the
series lead scholars
to ignore masculine
characters’ questions
and anxieties about their
own performance of
masculinity and the way
male identity relates to
the supernatural.
mantic relationships. Thus, critical lenses
such as postfeminism and others that pre­
vail in Twilight scholarship may not do full
analytical justice to these characters.
Within this Gothic approach, schol­
ars also look at Twilight in terms of its po­
tential historical influences from 19th-cen­
tury British novels and their often Byronic
heroes. Common comparisons in studies
such as Nancy Reagin’s Twilight and Histo­
ry (2010) include the love interests from
Pride and Prejudice (1813), Jane Eyre (1847),
and Wuthering Heights (1847).6 These texts
are often chosen because of overt refer­
ences in the Twilight novels. However,
scholarship too often conflates Twilight’s
themes and internal dynamics with those
of its famous predecessors without paying
enough attention to their differences or,
once more, thinking more forwardly about
masculinity and male characters. In other
words, while literary-historical analysis
foregrounding 19th-century antecedents
of Twilight is an interesting and fruitful
approach, there is a gap in that literature
connecting these historical perspectives
with how Edward thinks of himself, his
masculinity, and his quasi-filial relation to
his vampire “creator,” Carlisle. In addition,
there is a dearth of scholarship that reads
Twilight with its more monstrous, Gothic
predecessors, an issue that will be discussed
more in Chapter 2. Because Bella is the pri­
mary narrator, scholars are more likely to
think critically about her actions and moti­
vations while taking Edward’s at face val­
ue, even if he is Twilight’s clearest anchor
within the Gothic tradition specifically and
perhaps in 19th-century character tropes
more broadly.
6 For a variety of articles on this topic, see Parke and Wilson’s Theorizing Twilight (2010), specifically the second part of the col­
lection titled: Once Upon a Twilight: Fairy Tales, Byronic (Anti) Heroes, Post-Feminist Romance, and Growing Up in a Twilight
World.
The other common approach to
looking at gender and masculinity moves
away from literary and cultural paths to
argue that characters such as Edward are
most interesting for how they embody the
characteristics and desires of current soci­
ety. This approach, whether or not it re­
flects the sociological and reception-based
tendencies in early Twilight criticism, also
considers the way Twilight both influences
and is influenced by societal values. For
example, Christensen’s article Blood Absti­
nent Vampires and the Women Who Consume
Them (2013) argues that these 21st-century
vampires represent a desirable Other, an
antiseptic epitome of consumer culture in
explicit contrast to Gothic messiness. In
Twilight, the Cullen family is inhumanly
beautiful and perfect: a collective para­
gon, to which other characters, as well as
readers, aspire. In Mukherjea’s My Vampire
Boyfriend: Postfeminism, “Perfect” Masculini­
ty, and the Contemporary Appeal of Paranor­
mal Romance (2011) she argues that these
vampire boyfriends present a “perfect” mix
of masculinity, embodying white, old-fash­
ioned, gentlemanly, and protective values
without crossing a line into patriarchal
creepiness or overtly controlling behavior
(in Twilight alone, Bella describes Edward
as “perfect” over 30 times). Characters such
as Edward also juggle values from multiple
eras and classes. This combination allows
female characters to perform patriarchal
norms of femininity while also gaining
freedom from societal values and explor­
ing their own independence. Once again,
articles like these omit any focus on mas­
culinity or male angst, instead centering
anxieties around postfeminism and how to
be feminist. The two examples I have cited,
though seemingly very different, get close
to the issue of men’s anxiety around mas­
culinity and growth, specifically Edward’s,
but never actually address it. Christensen
focuses only on the 21st-century aspects
of vampires, without thinking about their
influences from previous eras. Mukherjea
acknowledges that characters like Edward
are juggling values from multiple eras but
focuses only on how that confusion affects
their romantic partners. They argue that
Edward and other male characters always
portray masculinity “perfectly” without
considering how this pressure to perform
may affect them internally, even though the
original novels clearly indicate that struggle.
Midnight Sun further confirms that there are
more elements at play in the series than Ed­
ward’s relationship with Bella.
Beyond short-changing the texts un­
der review, these Bella-centric approaches
to the series lead scholars to ignore mas­
culine characters’ questions and anxieties
about their own performance of mascu­
linity and the way male identity relates
to the supernatural. More broadly, these
interpretive angles perpetuate patriarchal
assumptions and norms around the in­
fallibility and confidence of cis-heterosex­
ual men. Much of Edward’s inner conflict
centers around his own relationship with
vampirism, aging, and eternal adolescence,
rather than being focused solely on Bella.
Distancing our analysis of Edward from Bel­
la’s perspective will reveal his own deep dis­
comfort and insecurity, foregrounding his
intense self-scrutiny rather than Bella’s sec­
ond-hand and often idealized observations.
In reality, as a very old vampire, Ed­
ward is navigating both these historical
values and current ones. The messiness
of these past and present pressures reveals
how some forms of masculine and patriar­
chal anxieties have not changed completely
for men over this long historical timespan.
The past and present often unstably coexist
for Edward, although Twilight criticism of­
ten does try to partition the past from the
present. We need to look at how maturity is
portrayed within an unchanging but eter­
nal vampire body and how Edward views
his maturation in relation to both humans,
such as Bella, and other vampires, like
Carlisle. Edward’s relationship to growth
is fraught because his expected character
development and societal pressure contrast
As a subject of analysis, masculinity regularly
receives less focus than women and
feminism, with particular gaps around cis,
straight, masculine characters. By paying
attention to these gaps and studying these
types of masculinities, we can gain a better
understanding of how these characters
internalize and perpetuate toxic patriarchal
norms, but also offer alternative masculinities
that already exist.
with his allegedly “perfect,” unchangeable,
and impermeable exterior. In other words,
as Edward’s life changes and society chang­
es around him, his appearance cannot also
change in parallel. The mythology around
vampires as unchanging and set in stone
both physically and psychologically at
the age they are “turned” (when they are
bitten) contributes to his general anxiety
and insecurity about his inhumanness and
inability to change. Because scholarship
focuses on Bella’s relationships and char­
acter growth, we are currently missing an
understanding of how Edward has his own
anxieties around morality and masculinity
and how being a vampire not only “freez­
es” his development, but also prompts his
constant uneasiness and self-questioning.
This pattern within Twilight scholarship
also points to a broader gap in masculinity
scholarship within the field of gender stud­
ies as a whole, including its engagement
with literature. As a subject of analysis,
masculinity regularly receives less focus
than women and feminism, with particular
gaps around cis, straight, masculine char­
acters. By paying attention to these gaps
and studying these types of masculinities,
we can gain a better understanding of how
these characters internalize and perpetuate
toxic patriarchal norms, but also offer al­
ternative masculinities that already exist.
To gain a fuller understanding of Ed­
ward and the diverse — and perhaps con­
tradictory — ways masculinity is presented
within the series, we need to think of him
as an independent and fallible character
rather than only as an ideal romantic inter­
est for Bella. This, of course, is inherently
difficult because Bella’s voice offers our
only direct access to Edward’s headspace
until Midnight Sun directly engages his per­
spective. But even before that point, when
we consciously step back from Bella’s nar­
ration and cast doubt on her omniscience,
the first Twilight novel does offer ways to
take stock of Edward’s feelings and conflicts
in ways that are not solely about Bella. By
decentering Bella, even in the texts she nar­
rates, we can glean suggestive information
about Edward’s other relationships, such as
the father-son or perhaps creator-creature
relationship with Carlisle, whom he often
looks to as a role model.
In tandem with this new approach,
we need to turn to other, often ignored
Gothic aspects to understand Edward as an
independent, three-dimensional character.
As mentioned earlier, Twilight scholarship
always reverts to Gothic vampiric tropes
associated with sex and desire. Instead, we
should also look at Gothic elements such
as the interior versus the exterior, the du­
ality of identity, and the monster within.
Midnight Sun’s emphasis on the monstrous
Gothic solidifies Twilight’s connections to
foundational novels like Dracula, as well as
revealing its nods to other kinds of Gothic
novels, such as Robert Louis Stevenson’s
Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
(1886) and Oscar Wilde’s The Picture of
Dorian Gray (1890).
Twilight’s complex masculine love
interests and characters are at odds with
the traditional heroes of romance novels
by even being allowed to grow and change,
rather than offering a fantastical, uniform,
and “perfect” symbol of masculinity. Twi­
light’s massive, global readership means
that the themes and characters within the
series have an incalculable influence on
fans, pop culture, and the genre of Y.A.
fiction. Studying Edward well outside the
terms of his romantic relationship with
Bella serves not just to help us better un­
derstand his character, but to provide a
whole new lens through which to under­
stand all masculine characters in the series.
“Twilight’s complex masculine love interests and
characters are at odds with the traditional heroes of
romance novels by even being allowed to grow and
change, rather than offering a fantastical, uniform,
and ‘perfect’ symbol of masculinity.”
Although it is easy to see Edward and Jacob
as the pop cultural movement tends to por­
tray them, and which is exacerbated by the
films, particularly New Moon and Eclipse,
they are so much more than two dimen­
sional, hypersexualized, and idolized love
interests.7 As the franchise has emphasized
and commercialized the love triangle,
the characters themselves are forced into
stereotypical roles to portray hegemonic,
toxic representations of masculinity. In
parallel, the seemingly equal competition
and dislike between the werewolves and
the vampires is unbalanced and entirely
due to the actions of the Cullens. When we
take a closer look at the novels, we see a
much more complex version of these char­
acters, many of whom do not fit into the
masculine tropes that critics often assume
the series to be arguing for, as well as a
more nuanced portrayal of race.
Ultimately, all the masculine char­
acters in Twilight, both supernatural and
human, are part of a complex system of
social dynamics, each navigating their own
relationship to masculinity and patriarchal
norms, and each invites and deserves more
attention and investigation than we often

foundational book Our Vampires, Ourselves

it needs” (145).8 Edward is certainly one
of the most prominent vampires of this
generation and so analyzing his own trials
and tribulations with adolescence, matu­
ration, and the performance of masculin­
ity will perhaps help us understand why
so many people gravitate toward Twilight,
and what about the teenage experience in
the 2000s has made it such an influential
and beloved series.◆

The Center: Where Art
and Science Converge
by Maggie Rose Baron
FEATURE
In one of the thousands of art muse­
ums around the world, an onlooker stands
in front of an oil painting and notices tiny
blisters on the surface of the artwork. The
surrounding paintings may be affected in a
similar way, but to a degree imperceptible
to the human eye. In either instance, the
study of these damages is vital to the choic­
es that conservation scientists make to
protect and restore works of art. So, what
causes the bubbles that form beneath the
surface of oil paintings?
The Center for Scientific Studies in
the Arts (hereafter referred to as “the Cen­
ter”), a collaboration between Northwest­
ern University (N.U.) and the Art Institute
of Chicago, tackles these kinds of questions
through the incorporation of technologies
from a range of fields including materials
science, engineering, and chemistry.
Professor
Aggelos Katsag­
gelos, co-director
of the Center and
professor of Elec­
trical and Computer
Engineering at N.U., says
the Center’s goal is “to serve
the cultural heritage and general
community … but along the way, [we] es­
tablish scientific methodology that can be
of use in many other fields: scientific fields,
fields of investigation.”
The Center’s research is object-based,
which Senior Scientist and Associate Re­
search Professor Maria Kokkori describes
as “an art historical method that centers
physical study of a work of art as a primary
text.” This kind of research, Kokkori says,
“can provide information about the chem­
ical composition … as well as insights into
artists techniques, and damages and repairs
over an artwork’s lifetime.”
Take the oil painting question.
Through the use of X-Ray and fluores­
cence techniques, as well as the chemical
analysis of the materials used by artist
Georgia O’Keeffe in her oil paintings, re­
searchers determined that the blisters in
these paintings are caused by metal soaps
that form through chemical reactions in
the paint.
The discovery prompted the research­
ers to develop a hand-held tool that can
map works of art for these protrusions to
determine the conditions that may cause
them to change. The project, while
inspired by a physical work of art,
impacts far more than simply the
understanding of soap bubbles
on a single O’Keeffe painting.
Projects have ranged from
the investigation of different
painting pigments and techniques
To serve the
cultural heritage
and general
community
… but along
the way, [we]
establish scientific
methodology that
can be of use
in many other
fields: scientific
fields, fields of
investigation.
to the discovery of ancient Roman writing
hidden in bookbinding. With each project,
the Center expands the breadth of knowl­
edge in areas of conservation science and
develops new technologies and techniques
for broader applications.
According to Kokkori, the Center
provides training and mentorship in con­
servation science to students and early-ca­
reer researchers in an effort to “lead the
next wave of advances” in the field.
The advancements are bolstered by
the Center’s collaborative nature. While
the scientific techniques, technologies,
and expertise are mostly housed within
N.U., outside institutions can also tap into
these resources to explore their own ques­
tions and projects. According to Katsag­
gelos, the Center aims to “democratize”
the technology by giving museums and
libraries access to N.U.’s physical instru­
ments as well as the algorithms devel­
oped by Center researchers.
The Center is, quite fittingly, at the
center of a range of disciplines. They might
seem unconnected in other contexts, but
without each and every field included
within the institution, the Center’s work
would not be possible.
“This field of conservation science
and the Center … is a unique contribution
to sometimes make the invisible visible,”
Kokkori says. “But also to make us think, in
a broader, different way, what our knowl­
edge, no matter from which discipline we
are coming from, can contribute to expand
our knowledge on the study of art.”
Currently, the Center is funded by
the Mellon Foundation. However, as that
funding draws to a close, the faculty at
the Center are working to keep it thriv­
ing long-term. According to Katsaggelos,
establishing permanent faculty positions
within the Center may be key to its future.
“We can be here for the very long run,”
Katsaggelos says. “It’s endless, the number
of problems … that one can address.”
The [disciplines] might seem
unconnected in other contexts, but
without each and every field included
within the institution, the Center’s
work would not be possible.”
God, Absurdism, and Law:
Suffering and Meaning in
the Works of Nietzsche,
Dostoevsky, and Camus
by Violet Decker
Department of Comparative Literary Studies
Faculty Adviser: Jonas Rosenbrück
Introduction
There are three powers, only three
powers on earth, capable of conquering
and holding captive forever the
conscience of these feeble rebels, for
their own happiness — these powers
are miracle, mystery, and authority.
— Fyodor Dostoevsky, The
Brothers Karamazov
In “The Grand Inquisitor,” a story told by
the character of Ivan Karamazov in The
Brothers Karamazov and one of Dosto­
evsky’s most celebrated passages, Christ
is reprimanded for his choice to give
human beings free will. In turn, says the
Inquisitor, humanity is destined to suffer:
“Without a firm idea of what he lives
for, man will not consent to live and will
sooner destroy himself … There is nothing
more seductive for man than the freedom
of his conscience, but there is nothing
more tormenting either” (Dostoevsky
254). Through its transforming characters,
religious and judicial themes, and elaborate
musings of life and death, Dostoevsky’s
novel is an account of both the depths and
heights of humanity when faced with an
existence of freedom. 77 years later, Albert
Camus’ monological novel The Fall draws
upon these same themes of freedom,
judgment, and faith to also showcase the
madness that results from total freedom
and the dissonance between the legal
system and man’s true nature. Each work
calls to find reconciliation between these
disparate needs — though we desire feeling
as though our lives embodied freedom
and had meaning, we require some kind
of unifying system to live under, without
which we find existence lacking all sense.
Ultimately, Dostoevsky points to faith in
Christ and practicing active love as the
only solution to this paradox. Camus urges
an acceptance of the paradox with no
finality (“the Absurd”) as fuel to continue
man’s instinct towards art and rebellion
— a mindset that will best allow for both
progress and relief.
Both Dostoevsky and Camus stand
in a relationship with one of modernity’s
most trenchant thinkers of the links be­
tween suffering, freedom, and meaning:
Friedrich Nietzsche. Nietzschean propos­
als, notably the exigency to find meaning
in suffering and the will to power, create a
foundational claim for our need for limit­
ing systems despite the blatant inadequacy
and self-denial found in judicial and reli­
gious frameworks. His assertion that one
must undergo personal transformation in
order to reach self-fulfillment and meaning
further the notion that preconceived sys­
tems limit this search, and it is this notion
to which Dostoevsky and Camus both re­
spond in their literary works.
Nietzsche
Freedom and The Three Metamorphoses
Nietzsche’s The Three Metamorphoses out­
lines his basis for a meaningful existence
— the continual creation of new ideals
and ways of life. Nietzsche affirms that
this must come from personal experience:
“Breaking with the norms of the past is
meaningful for us only if we had previ­
ously valued them … Otherwise, we are
merely dressing the norms of the past in
new clothing” (Gordon).
Central to this transformation is his
depiction of three distinct stages of de­
velopment: the camel, the lion, and the
1 The Nietzschean concept of “the Great Dragon” is those values and beliefs culturally upheld that are given to us as moral and
right, without demanding personal experience to find agreement with them. They serve as temptation of the natural inclination
for a guiding framework — but “the rebel resists this temptation by embracing uncertainty” (Illing 34). He recognized that in these
pre-existing frameworks that have a hold on morality, law, culture, religion, and science, there does exist something mankind
needs in order to survive: a limiting model in which to point our creative, intellectual, and emotional energies. However, without
continuing to reflect on and modify these frameworks through personal introspection and experience, they render society and the
individual stuck and suffering.
child. One begins as the burden-seeking
camel, both consciously and unconscious­
ly searching for experiences that give rise
to suffering. This asserts existence, while
starting the drive to find meaning in suf­
fering, which for Nietzsche is the major
intent of life and a bandage for the wounds
of total freedom.
The camel then becomes a lion when
a more aggressive, freedom-seeking ethos
comes to the forefront. The lion demands
victory and becomes its own master: “‘Thou
shalt’ is the name of the Great Dragon.1 But
the spirit of the lion says ‘I will’” (Nietzsche,
2006, 17). The lion embodies an intent to­
wards freedom, creation, and autonomy
that moves beyond the search for suffering.
Finally, the lion becomes a child by
reclaiming humility and a childlike sense
of wonder that can give rise to new poten­
tialities: “Why must the preying lion still
become a child? The child is innocence
and forgetting, a new beginning … a first
movement” (Nietzsche, 2006, 17). It is nec­
essary, then, to access a childlike spirit in
order to free oneself from the chains of ex­
ternal systems and allow for new creation.
Mercy
Mercy remains … the prerogative of the
strongest … Whenever a community gains in
power and pride, its penal code becomes more
lenient, while the moment it is weakened or
endangered the harshest methods of the past
are revived.
— Friedrich Nietzsche, The Birth of
Tragedy and the Genealogy of Morals
It is paramount to note Nietzsche’s rec­
ognition that the law operates in tandem
with its nation’s current social and polit­
ical landscape. Because the law operates
as a universal system, its treatment of the
individual depends not squarely on the
accused’s behavior or circumstance, but
on a larger framework embodying aspects
outside of any individual’s control. The
above quote recognizes that the legal sys­
tem asserts dominance over its members
in times of strife by minimizing leniency
and exercising its domination in full.
In such scenarios, despite the law’s
supposed aim of enforcing universal safety
and morality for the betterment of society,
this notion of separateness and disconnect
permeates the courtroom and legal system:
the courtroom as separate from the exter­
nal world, the judge as separate from the
criminal, and the accused as separate from
the accuser. If mercy is given more fre­
quently in times of political and social ease,
there is a split between the framework of
law and the assertion of universal and hu­
manistic values.
The Will to Power and Morality/
Law/Religion
According to Nietzsche, he who wants to
be a creator of good and of evil, must first
destroy all values.
— Albert Camus, The Rebel: An Essay on
Man in Revolt
The self-exploration and individual per­
spective involved in breaking past “the
Great Dragon” is, in essence, the asser­
tion of the self. Those already in power
achieved their position through the will,
and therefore, it was a solitary act that then
makes it impossible to ensure that societal
laws can account completely for the good
of the universal. This is why Nietzsche
stresses the importance of individual re­
flection and rebellion against pre-existing
2 “To behold suffering gives pleasure, but to cause another to suffer affords an even greater pleasure” (Nietzsche, 1956, 198).
systems. By doing so, one asserts their own
will to power, which Nietzsche sees as a
major solution to the paradox and distress
of freedom.
This driving force is a major element
of both The Brothers Karamazov and The
Fall. Dostoevsky’s characters in particular
“are engaged in a desperate and unending
struggle to disentangle their own image of
themselves from the world’s image of them
as preliminary to achieving an attitude to
themselves independent of the world’s at­
titude” (Jones 100). In both novels, charac­
ters attempt to assert their own existence
and dominance by seeking superiority and
action both within and against the legal
system. The desire both for and against
justice is therefore seen as a mere illusion
that is fundamentally the will to power.
Rebelling against these systems, which
affirm the collective but destroy the indi­
vidual, is an assertion of our consciousness
and autonomy as individuals.
Suffering and Meaning
Nietzsche asserts that we enjoy both
experiencing and inflicting suffering,2 for
it operates from our will to power. For
example, monks suffer through self-denial
and thereby gain a prideful kind of pleasure
in which they view themselves worthy of
judging others for not living by the same
asceticism. Through this lens, the powers
which Dostoevsky writes could “conquer”
people’s consciences are really frameworks
that give meaning to suffering. They
attempt to impose meaning onto our per­
plexing experience of freedom and pain.
In actuality, “what makes people
rebel against suffering is not really suffer­
ing itself but the senselessness of suffering”
(Nietzsche, 1956, 205). With this in mind,
the frameworks (religious, legal,
intellectual, and creative) may be consid­
ered a sort of bearable comprehension for
meaningless suffering. Nietzsche claims,
for example, “the ascetic ideal arises from
the protective and curative instinct of a life
that is degenerating and yet fighting tooth
and nail for its preservation” (Nietzsche,
1956, 256). By accepting religious ideals,
one can find a reason to live despite an
otherwise miserable or ill existence.
Nietzsche also insists that suffering
best finds release in mechanical or creative
activity. Note how the specific environ­
ments of a prisoner in jail, a criminal in a
courtroom, or a novice in a monastery are
subdued and involve little movement or
mental stimulation. Without any release,
one may be more inclined to search for
meaning in the framework of legal or
religious ideas. Religion and law may then
serve as “safety valves” for overwhelming
emotion and suffering (Nietzsche, 1956,
276): it places limits on existence to make
sense of the body and current circum­
stance. This necessitates living by creation
rather than denial: “Nietzsche … belonged
to the party which envisioned a society
where judges would no longer rule, but
where artists/creators would reign” (Du­
vall 551).
Dostoevsky
The Brothers Karamazov and the
Characterization of Existential Strivings
In The Brothers Karamazov, the character of
a cold, loveless, and ultimately murdered
father Fyodor Karamazov can be seen as
the depths from which his sons attempt
to escape. His three sons Dmitri (who
chooses to live by instinctual passion and
3 Nietzsche expressed similar sentiments when speaking of all beliefs and systems we follow: “how can we ever hope to find what
we have never looked for? … Our thoughts should grow out of our values with the same necessity as the fruit out of the tree” (Ni­
etzsche, 1956, 150). The ideal path for both Nietzsche and Dostoevsky ought not to be one of ease and following, but the intractable
and strong desire to empirically discover our own values, which calls upon the gamut of emotional and practical experience.
desire), Ivan (who chooses to live solely
by rational and intellectual thought), and
Alyosha (who follows the path of faith as
a novice monk) present three different
guiding life frameworks.
Dmitri, the eldest, pursues excesses
and pleasures of life. It is notable that he
refers to his own self as the “fallen man”
(Dostoevsky 107), and similar to what
will be examined later in Camus’ The Fall,
this references the Bible’s Genesis story of
man being relegated from innocent and
faithful to disobedient and distanced from
God/unity.
Dostoevsky critiques this choice by
presenting Dmitri’s arrest for the murder
of his father. The impulsive way of life
Dmitri has chosen leads to his inevitable
downfall, for though it satisfies the self’s
desire for pleasure and joy, it neglects the
full portrait of life and other people. This
results in ostracism and more suffering,
and Dostoevsky uses Fyodor’s murder and
the legal system to flesh out this realization.
Because he has not in fact committed the
act, this storyline accomplishes two other
distinct aims of Dostoevsky’s work: one, to
display the inexorably nonsensical and cru­
el nature of the justice system, and two, to
demonstrate through Dmitri’s transforma­
tion — which takes place after the accusal
and his time of suffering in the legal system
— that the move from disbelief to faith can
only be transcended through suffering and
must come from personal experience.3
When Dmitri is finally declared
guilty, he proclaims, “I swear by God and
by his terrible judgment, I am not guilty
of my father’s blood! Katya, I forgive you!
Brothers, friends, have pity on the other
woman!” (Dostoevsky 753). It is greatly
significant that Dmitri first calls out to God
when he learns of his fate, for the novel
starts with him living solely for himself.
Additionally, he speaks of the others in­
volved in the murder case to show his ex­
istence is now one more aligned with unity
than separation.
Dostoevsky’s style often points to the
multifaceted aspects of man, sometimes
showcasing opposites actually existing
more in tandem than typically considered.
Phrases such as “the kind of hatred that is
only a hair’s breadth from love” and “do
you understand that one can kill oneself
from a certain kind of ecstasy?” exempli­
fy his point that systems relying on strict
rules and judgments, specifically the legal
system, cannot possibly accurately account
for the complex and contradictory states
of human nature (Dostoevsky 114, 115).
The act of imprisonment itself can then be
concluded to be a type of judgment that re­
stricts man’s character into something that
can never reflect the multiple traits and
emotions within.
Meanwhile, Dostoevsky’s “furnace of
doubt was itself receiving its most memo­
rable fictional expression in the person of
Ivan Karamazov” (Jones 25). Ivan, the mid­
dle brother of the family, experiences a tur­
bulent struggle regarding the acceptance of
God. He rejects viewing the nature of the
world through the lens of faith primarily
due to his inability to reconcile the atroci­
ties and suffering of life with an all-loving
and all-powerful God. This rational dis­
belief within Ivan makes him a character
of metaphysical rebellion.4 He seeks unity
between all, similar to people of faith, but
has justified a move away from religion be­
cause of it, and instead pursues the avenue
4 This term first appears in Camus’ The Rebel over 70 years later, but distinctly defines a man protesting not against a specific or
temporary condition, but against his inescapable condition of living and the whole of creation — a protest against the intrinsic
sufferings of existence: “Camus was drawn to figures like Ivan Karamazov because he understood metaphysical revolt as a negation
of reality” (Illing 206).
of intellectualism and reason. He similarly
does not understand the tenets that Christ
preached, such as universal love, stating, “I
never could understand how it’s possible to
love one’s neighbors … occasionally from a
distance, but hardly ever up close” (Dosto­
evsky 236). This kind of impersonal focus
on the collective as opposed to the unique
individual is the same philosophy found in
the legal system.
The novel hints that intellectualism
leaves much to be desired, which explains
Ivan’s lengthy grappling with this subject
and eventual descent into madness. He rec­
ognizes the “absurdism” of reality, yet after
the arrest of his brother, he cannot find
peace in man-made attempts to reconcile
this absurdism. Dostoevsky makes a point
of characterizing Ivan as a man of youth
The superiority of any
system can only be
rightfully known and
recognized when one
personally rebels against
it or experiences its
breakdown.
who revels in this, even stating, “By the
age of thirty, I will probably drop the cup
[give up on life], even if I haven’t emptied
it, and walk away … But until my thirtieth
year, I know this for certain, my youth will
overcome everything” (Avramenko 230).
Though seemingly self-assured, Ivan has
not found a guiding principle that he is
confident will support him through his life.
Serving as a foil to Ivan’s stark practi­
cal intellectualism, Alyosha is the youngest
son who chooses to go in the direction of
faith and live in a monastery. In a pivotal
scene, he is told by his elder Zosima to at
once leave the monastery in order to see
and experience more of life:5 “You will have
to endure everything before you come back
again … You will behold great sorrow, and
in this sorrow you will be happy” (Dosto­
evsky 77). He is told that leaving will equip
him with the right experiences and suffer­
ing to further unite him with mankind and
deepen his faith. It becomes clear through
the journeys of each character in the novel
that Dostoevsky does not wish for religion
to be a dictatorial system like the legal sys­
tem: it is necessary that the universal love
he sees as emblematic of Christ is realized
on a personal level.
The Necessity of Collapse and Tragedy
Karamazov or Nietzsche only entered
the world of death because they wanted to
discover the true life. So that by a process of
inversion, it is the desperate appeal for order
that rings through this insane universe.
5 “The elder sent me to reconcile and unite” (Dostoevsky 196).
6 Grushenka, a young and vivacious woman in the novel, “falls into one of those illnesses that, in Dostoevsky’s works, are at once
— Albert Camus, The Rebel: An Essay on
Man in Revolt
Due to Dostoevsky’s notion that personal
experience and transformation is necessary
to experience Christ, we see each brother
undergo a collapse of the previous self and
ideology in some way to attain something
larger. This is referenced not only through
characterization but also through smaller
anecdotes and quotations: “Othello’s soul
is simply shattered and his whole world
view clouded because his ideal is destroyed”
(Dostoevsky 380). Destruction is implicat­
ed in the novel as a necessary ingredient to
enlightenment and personal connection
to universal love. Dmitri’s imprisonment,
Ivan’s breakdown, and Alyosha’s encour­
agement to leave the monastery all involve
religious experience following a collapse
of the ideologies that have carried each
brother to adulthood. This also builds on
Nietzsche’s encouragement to practice
personal rebellious thinking, for the supe­
riority of any system can only be rightfully
known and recognized when one per­
sonally rebels against it or experiences its
breakdown.6 All characters are forced to
undergo a transformative event in order to
directly experience this kind of universal
love, or Christianity.
Camus
Camus and the Absurd
While Dostoevsky sees religion as the
preferable opposition to law, Camus places
By choosing an imposed collective value system,
we sacrifice the individual search for and
understanding of truth and meaning.
religion in the same category as the law:
seeking to confine mankind when our
very nature resists that at every turn. He
renounces this false consolation, turning
instead to the only sort of solutions he
believes would prevail: “Art and rebellion
will only die with the death of the last man
on earth” (Camus 1951, 270).
His concept of the Absurd is no more
aptly demonstrated than in The Fall, where
Camus points out the contradictions and
inadequacy of the justice system to account
for man’s true nature. The novel, referenc­
ing the Genesis story, demonstrates the
crumbling of the illusion of the moral and
obedient self; the protagonist Jean-Baptiste
Clamence, a retired lawyer, comes to terms
with his true nature, which lies at odds
with justice.
Once an esteemed lawyer and judge in
Paris, Clamence grapples throughout the
novel with an event in which he had the
opportunity to save a woman from death
after witnessing her jump from a bridge,
but chose not to. Clamence hides behind
a veneer, acting as someone who imposes
morality and fairness upon all of society.
Yet again, this references the concept dis­
played in The Brothers Karamazov: that by
choosing an imposed collective value sys­
tem, we sacrifice the individual search for
and understanding of truth and meaning.
Our response to the absurd can be total ni­
hilism, extricating oneself through pre-ex­
isting systems, or rebellion and art.
Clamence lives with neither grace nor
justice yet acts as though he is enforcing
the latter. He kills without directly partak­
ing in the action of killing and embodies
the Nietzschean concept of the will to
the sign of intense spiritual conflict and the harbinger of renewal. After five weeks of suffering, during one of which she is uncon­
scious, she emerges ‘very much changed’” (Paris 129).
7 “When I see a new face, something in me sounds the alarm. ‘Slow! Danger!’ Even when the attraction is strongest, I am on my
guard” (Camus, 1956, 11).
power. The criminal and the judge, much
like the rebel or intellectual and the intel­
lectual or religious ascetic, are divided in
their aims. One works within a system, and
one attempts escape by living by their only
personally relatable value: the assertion of
their self-consciousness and existence.
Away from the court, Clamence expe­
riences a total lack of unity with, and fear
of, people around him.7 He states that he
has desired his job in order to feel superior:
“If fate had forced me to choose between
work at a lathe or a roofer, don’t worry,
I’d have chosen the roofs and become ac­
quainted with dizziness. Coalbine, ships’
holds, undergrounds, grottoes, pits were
repulsive to me” (Camus 1956, 24). This
admittance is noteworthy because Cla­
mence’s job is supposedly one that instills
equal treatment and punishment as well as
works to maintain a moral and just society,
but he himself desires domination. When
Clamence does not go after the women,
this strengthens his admittance of feeling
so comfortable being both literally and
metaphorically above others that he does
not mind if others are harmed or even
killed in the process of getting him there.
Further, in order for Clamence to continue
acting as the role of judge he depends on a
continual supply of others who are to “fall”
and be punished: one cannot exist without
the other.
The Fall as Legal and Ascetic Critique
Clamence is presented as a protagonist
who has full awareness of himself and his
motives. He contrasts heavily with the
character of Ivan, who professes “I made
up my mind long ago not to understand”
(Dostoevsky 243). Whereas one witnesses
at first glance the battle between good
and evil in The Fall, the battle appears
to be between the devil and God in The
Brothers Karamazov.
However, “Clamence seems to speak
for Camus in denouncing the religion of
Christ as a merciless cult of Judgment,
which has made of the cross a kind of
judge’s gavel” (Sharpe 155). Clamence
has accepted his duplicity and has full
self-awareness of the gulf between his true
self and the imposed rules and morality
his career has him follow. Because of this
awareness, he hoists himself to a position
in which he sees himself as a rightful judge.
He knows, as preached by Zosima in The
Brothers Karamazov,8 that he is equal to the
criminal. By acknowledging his own du­
plicity and guilt, he makes the move from
being a singular to universal figure, and can
then by his logic judge others, because he is
simultaneously judging himself. It is pre­
cisely this awareness that seems to make a
mockery of both the justice system and re­
ligion. Clamence’s reflections allow him to
stand outside both systems, asserting that
the only truthful and knowable element is
his own drive and consciousness.
Conclusion
Clamence’s ability to see the totality and
duplicity of himself offers a self-knowledge
not demonstrated by any character in The
Brothers Karamazov.9 He is able to assuage
himself of guilt by fully understanding
himself. Camus presents this as a possible
means to “salvation” (salvation meaning,
in this sense, freedom from the awareness
of Absurdity).
8 “Make yourself responsible for all the sins of men” (Dostoevsky 320)

than everyone else and that they all take me for a buffoon —  so let me indeed play the buffoon, because all of you, to me, are lower
and stupider than I am” (Dostoevsky 86). While he does not acknowledge his own duplicity or contradictory nature, he immerses
himself in the ‘play,’ giving himself over to the illusory mask of his personality.

Zosima claims that “as soon as you
sincerely make yourself responsible for
everything and for all men, you will see at
once that it is really so, and that you are
to blame for every one and for all things”
(Avramenko 20).10 Clamence does precise­
ly this, and by acknowledging his baseness,
he finds personal redemption that allows
him to then play the part of a judge. The
justice system, however, while claiming
to seek unity, separates people from each
other, puts guilt only on the trespasser, and
locks him away, enforcing an overarching
disconnect that gives rise to more univer­
sal suffering and search for meaning. The
characterization of Clamence shows his
true nature to operate entirely outside of
this belief system — he represents an un­
derstanding that human nature is bigger
than the systems it finds itself existing
under. This proves to be his true salvation.
He goes so far as to say that Jesus, too, was
not altogether innocent, which is why he
accepted his crucifixion.
For Camus, artistic creation and the
act of rebellion both operate as ideal guid­
ing frameworks for humanity and best
solve our desires for structure, meaning,
and individual freedom. What Dostoevsky
sees as a call to faith, the absurd “anguish
of ignorance and indecision” (Dostoevsky
392), is precisely what Camus proposes we
embrace in order to reconcile our unan­
swerable questions. And what Dostoevsky
would interpret as the “blows of fate [that]
are the means by which God manifests his
power” (Paris 130), Camus sees as absurd­
ism, which is precisely the space of limbo
and puzzlement that acts as a catalyst for
rebellion and creation. While Dostoevsky
has his characters go through contradic­
tion and suffering to create a new person,
in The Fall, there is no certain transfor­
mation other than Clamence accepting
an irreconcilable discordance between the
truth of the self and the desire for higher
value and morality. “After prolonged re­
search on myself,” he says, “I brought out
the fundamental duplicity of the human
being” (Camus, 1956, 84). It becomes im­
possible, Clamence demonstrates, for us to
be accurately embodied in any generalizing
system of strong boundaries, for we are
contradictory by nature. Absurdism paves
the way for a morality that is moreso a
“creative action” as opposed to a given set
of unchangeable tenets (Bowker 170). Be­
cause of this, it can also work in tandem
with new ideas and progress and is not
constrained by itself.
Both rebellion and art still operate de­
pendently on a system, which is why they
are successful means to assuage the suffer­
ing and chaos found in freedom. “The first
thing that a landscape painter does is to
square off his canvas” (Camus, 1951, 225):
they still represent a need for unity and a
coherent system. They provide limitations
and order, which relieve us of the burden
and perplexity of total expansive freedom.
They reflect parts of ourselves back to us,
marking our existence and value while
supplying us with a sense of unity.
These solutions are a never-ending
process. The duality that exists within us
can therefore find expression and relief in
rebellion and art: art says, “Be like me, the
Original Mother, who, constantly creat­
ing, finds satisfaction in the turbulent flux
of appearances” (Nietzsche, 1956, 102).
In this way, the continual creations of art
and rebellion are more pure and accurate
manifestations of the self. They seek to be
expressions of truth, not implementations
of constraints.
The paradox of justice lies in its desire
for unity and peace despite its denial of all as
intrinsically connected. The characters who
reject this interconnectedness are doomed
to isolation, anxiety, and despair, but the
recognition of this brings enlightenment,
peace, and reconciliation. The fixed nature
of law and religion can be alleviated and
ultimately changed through rebelling in
order to experience and understand what
these systems lack, and the expression of
difficult and complex truths through liter­
ature and art. Without choosing mystery,
we choose to avoid full realization of the
self. The goal must not be to encourage vi­
olence, generalizations, or limitations, but
rather to become Nietzsche’s “child” and
challenge the impersonal systems of law
and dogmatic religion, opening up new
and creative means to handle social conflict
while encouraging all to go in the direction
of art and rebellion.◆
“The fixed nature of law and religion can be
alleviated and ultimately changed through rebelling
in order to experience and understand what these
systems lack.”
