FEATURE
In 2015, 196 parties, including the
U.S., signed the Paris Agreement, mark­
ing a global commitment to limit global
temperatures to 2.0°C above pre-indus­
trial levels. In the seven years since, the
parties’ actions toward this commitment
have proved deficient as global tem­
peratures continue to soar. Based on the
International Panel on Climate Change’s
(IPCC) estimates, in a “business-as-usu­
al” scenario, temperatures are likely to
rise to 2.7°C above pre-industrial lev­
els by the end of this century, and, in
a worst case scenario, they may even
rise 4.4°C. (Hausfather et al., 2020).
The IPCC thus reported that simply
cutting greenhouse gas emissions is no
longer enough – we now must actively
remove carbon dioxide from the atmo­
sphere for any chance of fulfilling the
Paris Agreement (IPCC, 2021).
This burgeoning field of carbon
dioxide removal (CDR), alongside solar
radiation management, where sunlight
is blocked to decrease global tempera­
tures, has been dubbed “geoengineering.”
Increasing scientific interest in geoengi­
neering has created a vast menu of op­
tions, including mechanically capturing
atmospheric carbon dioxide (direct air
capture), using rocks to react with and
trap atmospheric carbon dioxide (min­
eralization), adding certain compounds
into the ocean to increase its absorption
of carbon dioxide (alkalinity enhance­
ment), and even releasing giant mirrors
into space.
The decision of which of these op­
tions to implement and how looms ever
closer, but with geoengineering research
only beginning, it is a politically, legally,
socially, and ethically fraught choice.
Herein lies Environmental Policy and
Culture Visiting Professor Dr. Wil Burns’
current area of research: navigating geo­
engineering under international law.
As Professor Burns tells it, his career
has been a series of “serendipitous” mo­
ments, taking him from studying biology
and political science as an undergraduate,
to forming an international wildlife law
think tank, to working in climate change
litigation. Professor Burns recounts the
particular serendipitous moment that
first introduced him to geoengineering:
“I had been asked to be a visiting scholar
at Williams College, and I was flying
there to start teaching … international
environmental law to undergraduates. I
discovered that instead of 16 weeks, which
is what I thought the semester was, it was
17 weeks. I said, ‘Yikes, I don’t have a topic
for another week.’ I was getting ready to
get off the plane, and the guy next to me left
his ‘USA Today’ on the seat … There was
a small article on climate geoengineering,
and I thought, ‘Oh, that’s an interesting topic
combining science and technology and law
and politics and ethics. I bet by Week 17,
I could have a lecture on this for the
students.’ And I did.”
Re-engineering the Planet,
Legally
By Lynna Deng
At the time, geoengineering was truly
in its infancy. “There weren’t many people
in geoengineering, full stop, but there was
nobody on the social science side,” Profes­
sor Burns says. When he and a colleague at
American University founded their research
center, the Washington Geoengineering
Consortium, in 2013, it was the first working
on the social science of geoengineering.
Now, as the field has flourished under
the interest of researchers, start-ups, and
investors, it has become clear that deploying
any geoengineering technique will have a
global impact. Yet, with geoengineering only
being seriously considered in the past few
years, most existing international law doesn’t
directly govern the practice. Thus, Professor
Burns’ current work seeks to understand
how the international laws and customs cur­
rently in place would affect geoengineering’s
deployment, as well as what new legislation
needs to be enacted to fully regulate it. This stands in
stark contrast to many others’ work in international
law, including Professor Burns’ former work in in­
ternational wildlife law, where legislation is specifi­
cally aimed at the issue of interest. On comparing the
two, Professor Burns says:
“On
one
hand,
[international
law
for
geoengineering is] daunting and frustrating. On
the other hand, that’s kind of an interesting role
for a lawyer … When it comes to these fields,
where they’re relatively new, I think you can
play a role in helping to establish that foundation,
figuring out how we repurpose some of these
laws to fit, or identifying what gaps we have that
we’re going to have to fill with more law or more
regulatory provisions in the future. And that’s
fun to do.”
With such a lengthy list of geoengineering
options, there is an equally lengthy list of interna­
tional laws and customs that could apply to each.
Professor Burns explains that, when he sifts through
the options to select what
to research, his choice is a
“judgment call.” He clarifies,
“You have to … make your
own decisions about where
you focus based on your in­
terest, your expertise, and
whatever criteria you estab­
lish.” For him, those criteria
are, “Is [the geoengineering
technique] economically vi­
able? Is it relatively low risk?
… Might [the public] look at
this and say, ‘Yeah, we could
live with this’?” Designating
these criteria allows some
options, such as alkalinity
enhancement, to rise to the
top for Professor Burns.
As geoengineering has
gained prominence, people
outside of academia have
begun seeking out Professor
Burns’ 15 years of expertise.

representatives and law firms, to speak­
ing with reporters, to consulting for
start-up companies, to running a pod­
cast and webinar series, he finds that
being a social scientist makes him well
equipped to give such explanations and
recommendations. “In some ways, [it’s]
easier … than having a scientist com­
municate because scientists sometimes
just can’t break it down. [Scientists]
don’t know what [others] don’t know,”

The aforementioned decision of
which geoengineering technologies to
use and how relies heavily on this com­
munication. Professor Burns says that,
based on a new study from the Univer­
sity of Oxford, the number of people in
a given country who report they know
about carbon removal “ranges from
four or five percent, maybe up to 18%

mean] when they say they know about
carbon removal; there’s no reason for
most people to know about this, right?”
(Smith et al., 2023).
Indeed, perhaps most people feel
they have no reason to stay informed
about geoengineering, but as our un­
willingness to make drastic emission
cuts catapults us toward a terrifying
future, we all certainly need to. Pro­
fessor Burns’ work in geoengineering
research and education thus only grows
in urgency and importance.

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
The trope or “type” of the ingenue, the
expectations it creates for teenage girl­
hood/young womanhood onstage, and the
impact of those expectations on theatre
artists and audiences.
How did you come to your research topic?
As a young female theatre artist often
considered for “ingenue” roles, I had
found the type limiting and untruthful,
and was interested in investigating how to
interface with this “type” while telling the
kind of stories I wanted to tell. Research,
particularly community conversations,
soon showed me that my frustrations rep­
resented only a small, shallow portion of
the ramifications of ingenue expectations.
Where do you see the future direction
of this work leading? How might future
researchers build on your work, or what
is left to discover in this field?
I would hope that this work would further
push a shift in mindset in the theatre
industry toward greater respect and rec­
ognition of each artist as a full, agentive,
creative individual, allowed to express the
fullness of themselves onstage and unlim­
ited by reductive, untruthful, exclusive
notions of what it is to be a young wom­
an. My combined process of traditional
academic reading, ensemble discussion,
and performance as research could be in­
credibly generative if applied to different,
similar, or even the same topic with a dif­
ferent core ensemble of individuals. While
I focused on the demographic of teenage
girlhood and the “type” of the ingenue,
there is much exciting research and cre­
ative work to be done around expectations
for other ages, genders, and “types”/cate­
gories of role onstage, and what processes
and texts can tell each of our stories with
the most truth and positive impact.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
I’ll be staying in Chicago to work profes­
sionally as a theatre artist, particularly
focused on performance, choreography,
and direction. I can’t wait to continue to
pursue my passions of healthy artist ex­
periences and meaningful, collaborative,
positively impactful storytelling!
Emily Brooks

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
My research seeks to find textual support
and connections in specific works of
Friedrich Nietzsche, Albert Camus, and
Fyodor Dostoevsky regarding the purpose
and nature of the legal system and religion
in society. The thesis seeks to explore,
through literary works and the lives of
the respective authors, the drives toward
strict religious and/or legal beliefs and
the larger result of this on both personal
development and society at large.
How did you come to your research topic?
In my reading of French and Russian lit­
erature through my major of Comparative
Literary Studies, I noticed a repetitive
theme of the legal system and the common
threads of its portrayal in numerous nov­
els. I became interested in exploring this
further to seek practical understandings
of how these portrayals might guide us
in revising relevant legal frameworks, or
creating new frameworks that might lead
to better personal and societal fulfillment
and meaning.
Where do you see the future direction
of this work leading? How might future
researchers build on your work, or what is
left to discover in this field?
I see much more to dissect regarding the
legal system’s portrayal in world literatures
and how that, in time, could translate to a
greater understanding of some of its pit­
falls and challenges. Because literary works
focus so richly on human nature in a way
the legal system alone cannot, it
brings a new dimension to our under­
standing of judgment and law. Any por­
trayal of character involvement with (or
against) the legal system in fictional works
in world literature can help enhance these
understandings.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
I am preparing for an M.F.A. in Creative
Nonfiction writing.
Violet Decker
God, Absurdism, and

Meaning in the Works of
Nietzsche, Dostoevsky,
and Camus
In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
My thesis is centered around studying
representations of masculinity for adoles­
cent characters in the Twilight Saga. This
global book series and movie franchise has
had an incalculable effect on the genre of
Young Adult fiction as a whole. I argue
that despite its seeming banality as a
romance novel, it is actually doing some­
thing new and important in the way that it
portrays teenage boys’ fraught relationship
to patriarchal standards of masculinity.
After discussion with my advisor, I
submitted the introduction of my thesis to
the NURJ. In this, I summarize the field of
Twilight scholarship, trace the way that it
has evolved over the past decade, and ar­
gue that there is a gap in the study of mas­
culine characters. I argue that this is also
representative of a larger trend in literary
and gender studies, which tend to focus on
feminist studies without a parallel under­
standing of the way that men, especially
during adolescent, are also necessarily a
part of and affected by patriarchal systems.
I then go on to outline my arguments for
the three chapters of my thesis and con­
clude with the importance of this research.
How did you come to your research topic?
I’ve been a Twilight fan since middle
school, but only recently have begun to
not be embarrassed about it! I feel strongly
about defending seemingly silly romance
novels, which because of the way they are
marketed towards women, get a hugely dis­
proportional amount of hate and criticism.
Where do you see the future direction
of this work leading? How might future
researchers build on your work, or what is
left to discover in this field?
I feel that my work on masculine
characters in Twilight is only the
beginning. I focus on two main primary
characters, but I argue that all characters
within the series are interacting with
masculinity in different and interesting
ways, and all would be fruitful objects of
analysis. I also think that the frameworks
I have developed for thinking about these
characters can definitely be applied to
other novels in the genre.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
University of Wisconsin-Madison Law
School with a full scholarship

I am looking at what is meant by “Black
Trauma Porn” and if the best phrase to
describe the phenomenon is being used
specifically in relation to television and film.
How did you come to your research topic?
Professor Hesse and I were chatting about
research topics and he brought up Black
Trauma Porn and asked my opinion on it.
When I gave it, which was pretty much a
regurgitation of what is online, he asked
me if I’d be willing to interrogate it. As a
film lover, I thought it was a great idea!
Where do you see the future direction
of this work leading? How might future
researchers build on your work, or what
is left to discover in this field?
I would LOVE to continue this work in a
graduate study program. In the conclusion
of my full thesis, I say that there are other
avenues within Black horror and within
other Black genres that I could explore.
I also proposed the idea of engaing with
how colorism and interracial relationships
play a role in these films as well. I would
love to explore Black horror more. I
think that besides the authors mentioned
throughout the thesis, there is not a ton
work on Black film genres, especially
horror, with it’s impact on current con­
ceptualizations compared to other fields
in Black studies. I’d love to see how people
could expand on these ideas in analysis
of other Black genres, Black performance
fields, and Black creations.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
I currently work at Vivacity Tech PBC
as a Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Spe­
cialist, however, I would very much like
to continue my study in a Black studies

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
Epistemic injustice, and testimonial injus­
tice specifically, is a type of discrimination
that occurs when a person suffers a cred­
ibility deficit because of an identity-based
prejudice. This presentation seeks to
understand testimonial injustice and its
relevance to Asian/American women.
Through the course of this project, I
explain what prejudices influence acts of
testimonial injustice against Asian/Ameri­
can women, tracing both their historical and
theoretical roots. I will also discuss the po­
tential effects of testimonial injustice, which
consists of two main types of harm: sexual
and psychological. Finally, I present the idea
of epistemic justice as a counter to epistemic
injustice and how it can be practiced.
How did you come to your research topic?
In the winter quarter of my junior year,
I took a course on the topic of epistemic
injustice with my advisor, Sanford Gold­
berg. Throughout this class, I realized
that testimonial injustice was something
I had experienced for most of my life as
an Asian/American femme. There was a
huge sense of relief in being to describe
this kind of discrimination, and have the
tools to combat it in my own life. Because
of this, I became interested in how the
influencing factors of testimonial injustice
towards Asian/American women have
been shaped and influenced throughout
histories of racially gendered and colonial­
ist violence.
Where do you see the future direction
of this work leading? How might future
researchers build on your work, or what is
left to discover in this field?
As it stands, epistemic injustice is a
relatively new concept within Philosophy.
Yet, for most of the people I spoke with
throughout this project, it was something
they had experienced frequently. Thus, I
Defeating the Dragon:
Epistemic Injustice
Towards Asian/
American Women
think that one of the goals of this project
was to provide the language and tools for
people to identify and combat this kind
of injustice in their own communities. In
terms of the future direction of this work,
I think that the development of a more
specific account of testimonial injustice
for different groups would be valuable,
especially in thinking about how specific
communities can work against and heal
from epistemic injustice. Even further,
I’m curious to see how epistemic injustice
changes depending on the intersections
of certain identities, shifting cultural
contexts, and modes of communication,
like digitally.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
Currently, I am working at Chicago Pub­
lic Schools as a NU Public Interest Pro­
gram Fellow. After the program ends, I
hope to continue my research by applying
to Ph.D. programs in either Philosophy
or Ethnic Studies.
In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
The role of women in South Korea’s tattoo
history and culture, as well as the experi­
ences of South Korean female tattoo artists.
How did you come to your research topic?
As a female tattoo collector myself, I
wanted to investigate the experiences of
women in South Korea’s tattoo scene. I
noticed many female tattoo artists in South
Korea who were popular, but not a lot of
research on them apart from writings on
beauty tattooing (such as tattooing semi
permanent makeup).
Where do you see the future direction
of this work leading? How might future
researchers build on your work, or what
is left to discover in this field?
I am hoping to interview more artists
as my Korean proficiency continues
to improve. I’m hoping that other
researchers in my field will consider the
usefulness of ethnographic methods
such as oral history to supplement exist­
ing research that focuses on literature or
other sources.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
I’m currently taking a gap year at home,
spending time with my mom, little broth­
er, and cats. I hope to earn a master’s and
PhD in my field and eventually become a
college professor.
Kiana Staples

I see the findings of this work and

blocks: RAND and the Development of U.S. Nuclear Thought in the Early 1960’s
80 years after Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the world has yet to experience another atomic
bomb. During the Cold War, however, the United States and Soviet Union (USSR) came
dangerously close during the Berlin Crisis of 1961 and the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962. The
heavily anti-communist Kennedy administration oversaw the successful navigation of these
crises, all the while maintaining an uncompromised nuclear position and deterring the Soviet
Union from military action. At the behest of the Research and Development (RAND)
Corporation, the United States’s nuclear plans became more aggressive, confrontational, and
malleable. In the early 1960s, the United States’ strategic nuclear policy shifted drastically in
favor of flexibility and offensive capabilities due to the efforts of one institution: the RAND
Corporation.
The Kennedy administration marked a turning point in American defense thought. In
1958, the United States possessed an estimated 7,345 nuclear warheads. By 1964, that number
quadrupled to more than 29,000.1 Military assistance to South Vietnam and the failed invasion of
Cuba lent evidence to a bold, new strategy: confrontation. The most important change in
American policy was ‘behind closed doors’, though. During the Berlin crisis of 1961, Kennedy
and the Joint Chiefs of Staff secretly planned a nuclear first strike against the Soviets.2 The
Kennedy administration was convinced “that there was a ‘fair probability’ of success; it was ‘a
plan to wage rational nuclear war.”3 This first test of Kennedy’s administration demonstrated a
sharp departure from prior strategy. Not 10 years prior, General MacArthur was famously fired
3 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001)
https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.
2 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001)
https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.
1 Max Roser, Bastian Herre, and Joe Hasell, Nuclear Weapons (Our World in Data, August 6, 2013)
https://ourworldindata.org/nuclear-weapons.
by President Truman for even suggesting the tactical use of nuclear weapons in the Korean War.
Kennedy’s serious consideration of nuclear first strike — and insistence that it could be
successful — indicated a deviation from the conventional wisdom of mutually assured
destruction, or that nuclear war would unquestionably result in worldwide desolation. The
principle of mutually assured destruction was entirely defensive in nature, as it denied even the
possibility of one side emerging victorious, thereby removing an offensive incentive. Moreover,
Kennedy’s openness to an offensive strike required a greater degree of flexibility in the event of
nuclear conflict — the President needed to be able to successfully initiate both a small, targeted
first-strike and a retaliatory second-strike. His actions during the Berlin Crisis implied that not
only was nuclear war probable, but also winnable. So impactful was the administration’s plan
that Secretary McNamara altered the Single Integrated Operational Plan (SIOP-63) to include
Kennedy’s suggestion of a potential first strike aimed at strategically paralyzing Soviet nuclear
capabilities.4
In 1959, the U.S.’s first operational intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) enabled the
successful implementation of a militant and adaptable nuclear strategy. ICBMs permitted the
United States to drastically increase its nuclear delivery system; payloads could be deployed up
to 8,700 miles away without the same logistical issues which plagued bomber-based nuclear
weapons. Despite Soviet claims of ICBM superiority, “by 1959 there was a missile gap…
widening steadily in favor of the United States.”5 American ICBM buildup coincided with the
general increase in nuclear weapons seen during the Kennedy administration, indicative of an
aggressive shift in U.S. strategy. General Curtis LeMay — Chief of Staff of the Air Force from
5 Neil Sheehan, A Fiery Peace in a Cold War: Bernard Schriever and the Ultimate Weapon (New York, NY: Random
4 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001)
https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.
1961 to 1965 — was a chief proponent of the new ICBM program, and regarded it as “the
ultimate weapon.”6 LeMay relished in the thought of “reduc[ing] the Soviet Union to cinders,” a
sentiment shared by many in the American government.7 Enthusiasm for nuclear offense and
confrontation was evident, and the ICBM helped the ideas of persons such as LeMay and RAND
come to fruition. The introduction of the solid-fuel Minuteman ICBM to the Strategic Air
Command in 1962 further enabled American destructive capabilities. Uncoincidentally, Kennedy
“had come into office railing about a ‘missile gap’ that was giving the Soviets a dangerous
edge,” and the initial Kennedy plan for a general nuclear strike against the “Sino-Soviet Bloc”
relied heavily on ICBMs.8 The United States of the early 1960s was ready to fight — and win —
a nuclear war against the Soviet Union if necessary.
Established in 1948 by Curtis LeMay and others, the RAND Corporation provided
analysis and research to the United States military and played an integral role in the new
aggressive nuclear strategy of the United States. After Kennedy took office, McNamara hired a
list of defense experts from the RAND Corporation to help shape the future of nuclear policy.
Among these were Carl Kaysen and William Kaufmann, and they exercised significant influence
over America’s new nuclear strategy. Kaufmann found that despite Soviet claims of a significant
ICBM stockpile, they had only eight operational missiles.9 But, instead of assuaging fears of
Soviet nuclear capability, Kaufmann saw an opportunity. He believed that through an isolated
attack, the Kennedy administration “could knock out the whole Soviet nuclear arsenal” and
9 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001)
https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.
8 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001)
https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.
7 Neil Sheehan, A Fiery Peace in a Cold War: Bernard Schriever and the Ultimate Weapon (New York, NY: Random
6 Neil Sheehan, A Fiery Peace in a Cold War: Bernard Schriever and the Ultimate Weapon (New York, NY: Random
effectively win a nuclear war.10 Kaysen’s — and newly-recruited RAND consultant Henry
Kissinger’s — subsequent agreement with Kaufmann again alluded to a fundamental change in
defense thought: that a nuclear war was winnable, and that aggression would be advantageous to
the United States. Kissinger specifically instructed National Security Advisor McGeorge Bundy
“to submit a plan for graduated nuclear response,” in a memo on July 7, 1961.11 Bundy informed
the President of RAND’s suggestion, and Kaysen “took charge of organizing the first-strike
plan.”12 RAND not only had a direct connection to the Kennedy administration and the
development of the new flexible first-strike plan, but also directly influenced the administration’s
nuclear policy during and after the Berlin Crisis.
Arguably the most famous employee of RAND was Herman Kahn, who in 1960
published On Thermonuclear War — a controversial book discussing the possibility of atomic
warfare. Also in 1960, Kahn published an article entitled The Nature and Feasibility of War and
Deterrence in which many of the same principles were discussed, namely how the United States
could ‘win’ a nuclear war with the Soviets. Kahn argued that the United States must “stand up to
the threat of fighting a [nuclear] war and to credibly threaten to initiate one.”13 Kahn correctly
assessed that deterrence hinged upon the United States’ willingness to execute a nuclear strike
and suffer casualties of its own. For U.S. nuclear strategy to work, the Soviets needed to believe
the United States was capable of vast destruction at any moment. Implied in his article was the
complete failure of mutually assured destruction, or that nuclear combat did not necessarily
result in immediate worldwide ruin. The United States could possibly launch a successful first
13 Herman Kahn, The Nature and Feasibility of War and Deterrence (Santa Monica, CA: RAND Corporation, 1960),
12 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001)
https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.
11 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001)
https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.
10 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001)
https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.
strike on the USSR, as Kennedy prepared to do after Berlin. But, in the event of a Soviet
first-strike, the United States needed second-strike capability, or the ability to deliver a lethal
blow to the Soviets no matter how well-planned the initial attack — an idea echoed by many at
both RAND and in the Federal government. This second-strike was to be tripartite; B-52’s
carried nuclear bombs, submarines (SSBN’s) carried ballistic missiles, and mainland missile
silos housed ICBM’s. The general principle was to disperse American nuclear capability in order
to best preserve the United States’ ability to strike back in the event of an attack.
Kahn’s work at RAND concurred with the nuclear buildup of the Kennedy
administration, and perhaps the former explained the latter. Kahn and RAND’s message was
clear: the United States “must look much more dangerous as an opponent than as a collaborator”
to the Soviets.14 This was an ‘aggressive defense’, so-to-speak; in the minds of those at RAND,
more nuclear weapons meant a greater second-strike deterrent. And, even in the event of an
attack, Kahn’s plan gave the United States the greatest chance of victory — a sentiment realized
in the Kennedy administration’s first-strike proposal in 1961. Kaysen, Kaufmann, and
Kissinger’s proximity to President Kennedy, the National Security Council (NSC), and the
Department of Defense (DoD) certainly supported this theory. But some of the most convincing
evidence came from Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara. By the mid-1960s, McNamara
“had come to believe that the U.S. deterrent capability, the nation’s strategic offensive forces, not
the damage-limiting strategic defense forces, protected American society.”15 Moreover, he
believed that a smaller, pointed nuclear strike benefited the United States more so than all-out
15 Keith B. Payne, The Great Divide in U.S. Deterrence Thought (Strategic Studies Quarterly 14, no. 2, 2020), 22.
https://www.jstor.org/stable/26915276.
14 Herman Kahn, The Nature and Feasibility of War and Deterrence (Santa Monica, CA: RAND Corporation, 1960),
warfare.16 His beliefs were similar to those of Kahn: that offensive capabilities served to protect
the balance of peace, and reflected Kaysen, Kaufmann and Kissinger through advocating for a
flexible, strategic nuclear response. McNamara implemented the RAND mode of thinking in the
1961 plan under Kennedy. The McNamara-RAND label of nuclear warfare was “calculated,
[and] deliberate” through extensive use of precise statistics to determine success; McNamara
held that a U.S. strike — either preemptive or retaliatory — required at least 55 million Soviet
deaths.17 Kahn similarly explored the possibility of widespread Soviet urban evacuations, in
which only five to 10 million Soviet citizens would be killed in a U.S. retaliatory strike — a
number insufficient for both deterrence and nuclear victory.18 Though defense was important,
McNamara reflected Kahn’s use of offensive nuclear capabilities to ensure that a) The United
States could ‘win’ a first-strike scenario; b) the Soviets would be deterred by a devastating
second-strike; or c) neither side would use nuclear weapons for fear of mutually assured
destruction.
RAND’s plan — though radical — was both innovative and effective, a fact recognized
by both the Kennedy administration and military personnel such as Curtis LeMay. People such as
Kaysen, Kaufmann, and Kissinger communicated directly with the NSC and DoD, and Secretary
McNamara implemented many of Kahn’s ideas. RAND’s plan for nuclear deterrence and
potential victory hinged upon sufficient nuclear stockpiles and a demonstrable willingness to
initiate nuclear warfare — it ensured a ‘peace through strength’. Though counterintuitive, this
‘offensive defense’ was successful. For instance, the Soviets might not have been compelled to
remove missiles from Cuba if not for a credible threat of nuclear war with the United States. The
18 Herman Kahn, The Nature and Feasibility of War and Deterrence (Santa Monica, CA: RAND Corporation, 1960),
17 Keith B. Payne, The Great Divide in US Deterrence Thought (Strategic Studies Quarterly 14, no. 2, 2020), 22.
https://www.jstor.org/stable/26915276.
16 Keith B. Payne, The Great Divide in US Deterrence Thought (Strategic Studies Quarterly 14, no. 2, 2020), 22.
https://www.jstor.org/stable/26915276.
evidence supporting RAND’s responsibility for the change in nuclear policy was overwhelming;
the Kennedy administration and McNamara replicated the ideas of Kaysen, Kaufmann,
Kissinger, and Kahn and made them official policy. Almost 80 years after Hiroshima and
Nagasaki, no nuclear conflict has occurred. Perhaps, then, RAND deserves credit for preventing
a nuclear war during a time of great international volatility — the early 1960s.

Quarterly, 2(14). https://doi.org/https://www.jstor.org/stable/26915276

Retrieved March 2022, from https://ourworldindata.org/nuclear-weapons

Weapon. Random House.

blocks: Methodology
In order to determine how Louisiana lawmakers discuss Targeted Regulation of Abortion
Providers (TRAP) legislation, this study examines and codes video footage showcasing the
House and Senate committee meetings where TRAP bills were deliberated. This study consists
of a total of six TRAP bills and 12 corresponding videos, as each TRAP bill was argued both in a
House and Senate committee. Notably, most TRAP bills were sent to the Health and Welfare
Committee to be discussed, and that committee appears the most throughout the study. Although
other abortion-related laws were introduced and passed within the time frame of this study, these
six TRAP bills were my sole focus as they posed the greatest threat to abortion clinics in
Louisiana. The study spans from 2014 to 2020, corresponding to the year that House Bill 388, an
admitting privileges law, was passed and the year it was struck down by the Supreme Court in
June Medical Services L.L.C. v. Russo.1 I watched these hearings and paid special attention to the
language choices used by lawmakers when they discussed abortion, women, fetuses, and the
Supreme Court, which resulted in an open coding of the footage. This careful inspection and
coding were used to highlight any societal gender-based stereotypes present in the passing of
these TRAP bills, examine the Louisiana legislature’s attitudes about the Supreme Court, and
obtain an insight into law-making in a pro-life state.2
Results
The first bill in this study, introduced in 2014, was House Bill 388. HB388 established
admitting privileges for physicians who performed abortions, mandating that any abortion
physician must be able to admit patients to a nearby hospital. As mentioned above, this bill was
2 A 2019 study found that 60% of Louisiana residents believe abortion should be illegal in most or all cases. “The
State of Abortion and Contraception Attitudes in All 50 States,” PRRI (blog), accessed March 7, 2022,
https://www.prri.org/research/legal-in-most-cases-the-impact-of-the-abortion-debate-in-2019-america/.
1 “18-1323 June Medical Services L.L.C. v. Russo (06/29/2020),”
https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/19pdf/18-1323_c07d.pdf.
struck down six years later by the Supreme Court in June Medical Services v. Russo (2020).3 The
next two TRAP bills— House Bill 488 and House Bill 815 — were introduced in 2016. HB488
mandated that abortion physicians must be board-certified, or if they are currently enrolled in a
residency program, must obtain on-site supervision from a physician who is board-certified.4
HB815 regulated the ways in which abortion clinics could dispose of fetal remains after
abortions were completed, requiring abortion providers to sign contracts with funeral homes to
either bury or cremate the fetal remains.5 Senate Bill 325, introduced in 2018, established
criminal penalties for abortion clinics that intentionally destroyed records, performed an abortion
on a minor, or completed patient forms in advance of a patient’s appointment.6
The last two bills in this study, House Bill 484 and House Bill 133, were both introduced
in 2019. HB484 imposed regulations on the storing of medical documents — mandating that
physicians, medical directors, and owners of an abortion clinic would all be responsible for the
retention of records. Additionally, the bill established longer retention periods and imposed
penalties for violations.7 HB133 expanded the meaning of “abortion” to include medical
abortions, mandating that the abortion pill could only be dispensed at a licensed facility.8 All six
bills were signed into law within a few months after their introductions.
My analysis is split up into several key themes that emerged from the 12 legislative
hearings on TRAP bills — negative treatment of opposition, the woman-protective argument,
8 Louisiana State Legislature, “House Bill 133 by Representative Frank Hoffmann,” 2019 Regular Session,
https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?s=19RS&b=HB133&sbi=y.
7 Louisiana State Legislature, “House Bill 484 by Representative Raymond Crews,” 2019 Regular Session,
https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?s=19RS&b=HB484&sbi=y.
6 Louisiana State Legislature, “Senate Bill 325 by Senator Milkovich,” 2018 Regular Session,
http://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?s=18rs&b=SB325&sbi=y.
5 Louisiana State Legislature, “House Bill 815 by Representative Julie Stokes,” 2016 Regular Session,
http://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?s=16rs&b=HB815&sbi=y.
4 Louisiana State Legislature, “House Bill 488 by Representative Katrina Jackson,” 2016 Regular Session,
http://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?s=16rs&b=HB488&sbi=y.
3 Louisiana State Legislature, “House Bill 388 by Representative Katrina Jackson,” 2014 Regular Session,
http://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?s=14RS&b=ACT620.
descriptions of fetuses, descriptions of women, and mentions of the Supreme Court. Throughout
all 12 hearings, 23 individuals spoke in favor of these TRAP bills, while 15 voiced their
opposition. House Bill 388 notably had the greatest number of people wishing to give testimony,
as it was arguably the most detrimental to Louisiana women’s access to abortion. On top of
supporting linguistic themes within the existing literature and highlighting the Louisiana
legislature’s attitudes about the federal legality of abortion, this study also offers an insight into
law-making in a conservative and anti-abortion state.
Negative Treatment of Opposition/Pro-Choice Sentiment
Throughout all 12 hearings, it was apparent from the attitudes of the Louisiana legislature
that pro-life sentiment was the norm, and any TRAP bill that did not explicitly scoff in the face
of the Court’s rulings, therefore inviting costly lawsuits, would be passed with little to no
opposition. The Louisiana legislature expressed pride in their pro-life stances, as demonstrated
when Rep. Pope (R) began his introduction to SB325 by saying, “I think it’s been very very
evident throughout the last years that this committee has taken a very strong stance against
abortion.”9 Upon hearing this, the chairman of the House, Rep. Hoffmann (R), responded with an
emphatic, “No doubt.”10 Similarly, in his opening remarks on HB133, Rep. Hoffmann claimed,
“We are very proud of Louisiana being a pro-life state.”11 This pro-life bias was especially
apparent in the treatment of pro-choice voices during these legislative sessions. Although not all
hearings included pro-choice voices, when opposition did present itself, opposers of TRAP bills
were noticeably silenced and critiqued at a greater rate than anti-abortion activists.
11 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 04/24/19,”
https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2019/apr/0424_19_HW, (1:02:29-1:02:35).
9 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Committee on Judiciary C Meeting 04/17/18,”
https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2018/04/041718JUDC_0, (1:39:07-1:39:15).
The most notable examples of this occurred in discussions of HB388. While pro-choice
lawyer Ellie Schilling explained her opposition of the bill, she was interrupted by Rep. Simon
(R) with a question of, “Can we wrap this up please?” When she agreed and began to finish her
sentence, he repeated, “You have one more minute, ma’am.”12 Notably, this was the first time in
this hour-long discussion where the aspect of time constraint had been mentioned. The
representative also told a second opponent of the bill, Sylvia Cochran, to “wrap it up” before she
was finished speaking.13 Another significant interaction with this bill occurred when Carrie
Wutten, a representative for Louisiana Progress Action, stated strongly that each legislator in the
room would be complicit in the deaths of Louisiana women who would inevitably die after being
forced to obtain an abortion illegally.14 In response, Rep. Simon angrily exclaimed, “We face
decisions like this daily, and for somebody to come here and make a statement like that is just
absurd…none of us take it lightly. And I speak on behalf of my members that we don’t
appreciate that type of talk around here.”15 Lastly, when Rep. Simon read out the red cards in
opposition of this bill at the end of this discussion, he seemed entirely uninterested and even
refused to correctly state some of the names. As he read the cards, for example, he said,
“Bethany VanCamping…uhhh…Louisiana Students for Reproductive…Whatever,”16 which
elicited a chuckle from Representative Jackson (D).
In the Senate discussion of HB388, Ellie Schilling claimed that it would be difficult for
an OBGYN in a rural area to find a hospital within 30 miles where they could obtain admitting
privileges. Sen. Nevers (D) responded by asking for documentation to back up that statement, a
12 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 03/18/14,”
https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2014/Mar_2014/0319_14_HW,
question that had not been asked of anyone else so far in this discussion.17 When Schilling
responded by saying that her statement was based more on common sense than statistics,
claiming that rural areas have less hospitals in general, Sen. Nevers countered by saying, “Well, I
just, you know, because you’re sworn to tell the truth and–and you know, when you sign the
witness card, I just wanted to be sure that if you–that you tell us if you have data that supports
that statement or not. And right now, you don’t have that data.”18 This quote from Sen. Nevers
was quite shocking, as no anti-abortion advocates had been asked to provide specific data to back
up their claims in this discussion, even after several proponents of HB388 were proven to have
misrepresented Louisiana’s existing admitting privileges laws earlier in this senate discussion.19
These clear examples of bias from the Louisiana legislature suggest that with morality policies
such as abortion, it is extremely difficult for legislatures to be impartial.
Describing Abortion: The Woman-Protective Argument
The woman-protective argument that Siegel chronologizes in her work appeared
commonly in the Louisiana legislature’s debates on TRAP legislation — it was mentioned in
every video included in this study.20 Anti-abortion advocates relied heavily on this argument to
promote adding additional regulations to Louisiana abortion clinics. Imposing stringent
regulations on abortion clinics was framed as a necessity due to the dangers of abortion
procedures. In reality, abortion is a remarkably safe procedure, with the World Health
Organization calling it a “safe and simple health care intervention” as long as it is performed
legally and with proper sanitation.21 The protective paternalism that emerged in Greubel’s study
21 World Health Organization, “Abortion,” accessed March 11, 2022,
https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/abortion.
20 Reva B. Siegel, “The Right’s Reasons: Constitutional Conflict and the Spread of Woman-Protective Antiabortion
Argument,” Duke Law Journal 57, no. 6 (2008): 1641-1692.
17 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 05/07/14,”
https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2014/05/050714h~w, (2:23:38).
was also present during these discussions, with many anti-abortion advocates promoting
Louisiana TRAP bills on the basis that the state has the right to protect women from incompetent
physicians who would fall under Greubel’s definition of “bad players.”22
Anti-abortion advocates utilized the “bad players” argument in several ways, highlighting
cases of supposed malpractice within Louisiana abortion clinics as well as using the case of
Kermit Gosnell to argue that women need protection from malicious physicians. Gosnell, the
Philadelphia abortion doctor currently serving a life sentence for running an unsanitary clinic and
murdering three infants born after failed abortions, was mentioned a total of 10 times throughout
these 12 legislative hearings.23 Greasley points out the logical fallacies of using Gosnell as an
anti-abortion argument, as making legal abortion harder to access will most likely result in a
greater quantity of illegal abortion cites and subsequently a greater amount of dangerous
abortions performed.24 Louisiana’s legislature and anti-abortion advocates clearly disagreed with
Greasley’s argument, using Gosnell to advocate for stricter regulations on abortion providers.
Ryan Verret, representing Louisiana Right to Life, highlighted the Kermit Gosnell case in
his advocacy for HB488, using Gosnell’s clinic as an example of “the tragedy that abortion
imposes on women and unborn babies.”25 Verret was one of many anti-abortion advocates who
used the Gosnell case to extrapolate and describe all abortions as highly dangerous. In several
legislative hearings, connections were made between the Delta Clinic of Baton Rouge and
Kermit Gosnell, with Deanna Candler notably naming Eileen O’Neill, who left the Delta Clinic
25 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 03/30/16,”
https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2016/mar/0330_16_HW, (17:28-17:33).
24 Kate Greasley, “The Pearl of the ‘Pro-Life’ Movement? Reflections on the Kermit Gosnell Controversy,” Journal
of Medical Ethics 40, no. 6 (2014): 419–23.
23 Sarah Hoye, “Gosnell Sentenced to Life in Third Baby’s Death,” CNN,
https://www.cnn.com/2013/05/15/justice/pennsylvania-abortion-sentences/index.html.
22 Amanda Greubel, “Benevolent Sexism in the Targeted Regulation of Abortion Providers (TRAP): A Case Study
of Texas House Bill 2,” Sex Roles (2021): 650-660. Greubel defines “bad players” as “doctors and clinics who
commit egregious harm in their practices of abortion” (655).
and “surrendered her medical license, claiming that she had Post Traumatic Stress
Disorder…After that, she went to practice without a license in the Philadelphia abortion clinic of
Kermit Gosnell.”26 While many other claims about the dangers of abortions were impossible to
corroborate, the grand jury report on the Gosnell case does include this information on O’Neill,
who was subsequently sentenced to six to 23 months of house arrest on conspiracy and
corruption charges.27
The “bad players” argument manifested itself through descriptions of malpractice in
Louisiana abortion clinics, as well as claims of abortion clinics’ alleged connections to the sex
trafficking industry. In his advocacy for SB325, Sen. Milkovich (D) accused abortion facilities of
falsifying their records, adding that these facilities were allegedly concealing “abortions
performed on minors and potentially abortions performed to support the sex trafficking
industry.”28 The Senator offered no tangible proof to back up this intense claim. As the
Committee on Judiciary C meeting went on, Sen. Milkovich brought up the Delta Clinic in Baton
Rouge as an example, alleging that “women would be screaming, and they would not give them
proper medical care…they were re-using the instruments over and over and over again and they
were filthy.”29 These vivid and repugnant descriptions of the Delta Clinic are arguably
descriptions of torture, with Sen. Milkovich essentially claiming that abortion physicians at this
clinic knowingly abused their patients. In a similar way of thinking, Richard Mahoney, an
independent citizen, also attacked the Delta Clinic, stating, “The Delta Clinic pre-signed and
28 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Committee on Judiciary C Meeting 04/17/18,”
https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2018/04/041718JUDC_0, (2:57:45-2:57:59).
27 R. Seth Williams, District Attorney, “Report of the Grand Jury,” Pennsylvania,
https://operationrescue.org/pdfs/GrandJuryWomensMedical.pdf; Emad Khalil and Vince Lattanzio, “Tearful Gosnell
Associate: I Just Wanted to Give Care,” NBC10 Philadelphia,
https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/national-international/gosnell-associate-gets-house-arrest/1963884/.
26 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 05/07/14,”
https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2014/05/050714h~w, (1:48:56-1:49:25).
pre-checked the forms before they even saw their victims.”30 While Sen. Milkovich heavily
implied that women who visited the Delta Clinic were abused, Mahoney explicitly referred to
these female patients as victims, framing the clinic as an evil antagonist.
Rep. Crews (R) introduced HB484 by explaining that it was born out of necessity after an
abortion clinic, Bossier City Medical, “unlawfully shredded patient records after the state
documented that it failed to notify law enforcement of a 14-year-old girl’s reported rape. So, she
reported rape, and then these records get shredded.”31 Rep. Crews’ word choice heavily suggests
that the abortion clinic was knowingly complicit in the sexual crime committed through their
shredding of the patient records. Rep. Crews similarly ended his testimony by saying, “This
really is a women’s and sadly a child’s bill. We’re trying to stop trafficking and predatory
practices and without records, what do you do?”32 His language establishes a sense of urgency,
implying not only that abortion clinics are complicit in the continuation of sexual crimes, but
also that clinic records are imperative to solving sex trafficking crimes. This implication that
abortion clinics are perpetrators of crimes was taken a step further by Richard Mahoney, who
stated that he was testifying against “the egregious medical malpractice and child molestation
cover-up by the abortion cartel for 38 years in this state.”33 Mahoney’s strong statement was not
backed up by any evidence, but his statement dramatically furthered the woman-protective
argument by explicitly defining abortion clinics as criminal organizations.
The most common occurrences of the woman-protective argument were generalized
statements of the dangers of abortions, with a heavy focus on the procedure’s possible health
33 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 05/07/14,”
https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2014/05/050714h~w, (1:43:35-1:43:46).
31 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Wellness Committee Meeting 04/24/19,”
https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2019/apr/0424_19_HW, (5:55:42-5:56:06).
30 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 05/07/14,”
https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2014/05/050714h~w, (1:43:45-1:44:00).
complications. Kathy Kliebert, representing the Dept. of Health and Hospitals, highlighted the
“clear health risks associated with an abortion,” such as “pelvic infection, blood clots, and other
serious complications like perforation of the uterine wall, which is reported in 1 out of every 500
abortions” in her discussion of HB388.34 Dr. Damon Cudihy, a board-certified OBGYN, claimed
that surgical abortions “have several known complications that are inherent in the procedure
itself, not necessarily the result of an incompetent physician, or any sort of malpractice.”35 Dr.
Cudihy’s language provides a twist on the above portrayals of protecting women from evil or
incompetent physicians, as he stigmatized abortions by maintaining that even the best physicians
cannot save women from experiencing dangerous complications. In both discussions of HB133,
Dorinda Bordlee, the Senior Counsel of Bioethics Defense Fund, used imagery from a film to
add a vivid description of the dangers of medical abortions, saying, “If any of you have seen the
movie ‘Unplanned,’ it kind of opens up with that scene and how painful that is where she’s
passing that baby at home in the shower.”36 Bordlee’s use of this film provided a visual to go
along with the medical descriptions of abortion complications, furthering the classification of
abortions as painful and dangerous procedures.
Accompanying their descriptions of abortion dangers and complications, many
anti-abortion advocates made broad and factually incorrect claims about the deadly nature of
abortions. Kathy Kliebert stated in her defense of HB388 that Louisiana “has a strong history of
enacting strong laws to protect the lives of women and children.”37 Cindy Collins, the founder of
37 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 03/18/14,”
https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2014/Mar_2014/0319_14_HW,
36 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 04/24/19,”
https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2019/apr/0424_19_HW, (1:04:32-1:04:41).
34 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 03/18/14,”
https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2014/Mar_2014/0319_14_HW,
Louisiana Abortion Recovery, used her testimony to further this notion, exclaiming, “Women
deserve the care that they need to save their life.”38 Dorinda Bordlee also claimed, “Abortion is a
violence against women that commonly takes their lives.”39 Bordlee took the deadly abortion
argument one step further by claiming that abortion is not only “violent,” but that
abortion-related deaths are common-place. In discussions of SB325, Mike Johnson, an
independent citizen representing himself, went on to describe Louisiana’s Delta Clinic by saying
that this facility “risked the lives of every woman who went there for an abortion.”40
As proven in the beginning of this section, abortions have a very low complication rate,
and dying from an abortion procedure is extremely uncommon. The above rhetoric was clearly
meant to inspire fear of abortion clinics and physicians — a motive that may have disastrous
consequences for Louisiana women. Influencing the women of Louisiana into losing trust in
abortion clinics will not stop abortions, but might convince women to seek more dangerous,
at-home methods of abortion. After all, why would women pay hundreds of dollars at an
abortion clinic if doing so could result in the same complications they would receive from opting
for a cheaper, street-market abortion method? Low-income women who desire an abortion for
their own valid reasons might end up choosing cheaper, illegal methods of abortion if they
believe that clinics cannot give them a higher standard of safety.
The Woman-Protective Argument: Mental Health
While most descriptions of the dangers of abortions were physical, mental health also
played a notable part in this discussion, with anti-abortion activists maintaining that abortion
inflicts mental trauma and distress upon women. In support of HB388, Cindy Collins stated, “I
40 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 05/08/18,”
https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2018/may/0508_18_HW, (1:35:01-1:35:05).
have been helping women recover from the trauma they’ve experienced due to abortion for the
past 28 years.”41 Collins returned to testify in support of HB133 and made several other
statements that described abortion as mentally dangerous to women, saying, “We have many
broken women in our state…and the damage to women is increasing also.”42 Collins’ description
of women who obtain abortions as “broken” highlights the psychological emphasis on the
woman-protective argument —anti-abortion advocates focus on possible feelings of regret
following an abortion, implying that women who make this choice suffer a great psychological
burden afterwards.
When a pro-choice opponent argued that a previously cited abortion-related death had not
actually resulted from the abortion pill but from an unconnected drug overdose, Rep. LeBas
explicitly mentioned this feeling of regret, alleging that, “Sometimes, when you deal with these
people and they begin to suffer and have second thoughts, sometimes they revert to drug
overdoses. The drug overdose may have been due to the abortion in that way.”43 Through his
immediate speculation that this drug overdose must have occurred as a result of post-abortion
depression, Rep. LeBas reveals the main mental health assumption of anti-abortion advocates —
that it is extremely rare for a woman to feel good about her decision post-abortion. In the Senate
discussion of HB388, Sen. Nevers asked the question of, “What’s the percentage of mental
complications that we have following an abortion?” Alice Chapman, a medical student at LSU,
responded by saying that she was aware of a study which “found better outcomes for women
who sought an abortion and were able to obtain their abortion than they did for women who
43 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 03/18/14,”
https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2014/Mar_2014/0319_14_HW,
42 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 04/24/19,”
https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2019/apr/0424_19_HW, (1:08:12-1:08:37).
41 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 03/18/14,”
https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2014/Mar_2014/0319_14_HW,
sought an abortion and were unable to obtain it.” Sen. Nevers responded negatively to the
mention of this study, stating, “Well that’s in your opinion. I–I mean, I’ve heard just the opposite,
so I don’t know which one’s right. I mean, if we had the data, we could see it.”44 Not only does
this short interaction provide further support for the showcased earlier in this study, it also
highlights how real, tangible data is mostly ignored by the Louisiana legislature in favor of
anecdotal evidence that favors their political opinions.
44 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 05/07/14,”
https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2014/05/050714h~w, (2:32:40-2:33:30).
