blocks: Running head: GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
Gendered Messages in The Handmaid's Tale: Offred's Evolution, 1985 - 2017
Kayan Khraisheh
MIT 398: Feminist Media Historiography
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
In 1985, Canadian author Margaret Atwood released a novel titled The Handmaid’s Tale,
which follows the chilling story of a Handmaid named Offred. In the dystopian society of Gilead,
there are very few remaining fertile women, as a result of environmental pollution and radiation.
The protagonist, Offred, is one of the few women left with the ability to bear children. Her duty
as a Handmaid is to give birth to children from upper-class men. If she fails to do so, she is
labeled an “unwoman” and destined to a horrible fate. Gilead’s oppressive system functions due
to the imprisonment and brainwashing of women (Septiawati & Darma, 2014). Offred’s story is
explicit and harrowing, and does not have a happy ending. It has been the subject of extensive
feminist analysis. Atwood’s novel was adapted to the screen twice, first as a film in 1990, and
later as a TV series in 2017. The three versions of this story differ significantly and have been
received very differently by critics and audiences. There is an abundance of feminist and media
discourse regarding whether these different versions of The Handmaid’s Tale are pro-feminist
and empower women, or anti-feminist and promote sexist narratives.
While several scholarly articles analyze the individual media artifacts from a feminist
perspective, few studies, if any, compare the three versions in terms of gender representations.
Therefore, in this paper, I will be analyzing the differences in the gendered messages conveyed
in the three versions of The Handmaid’s Tale to date: the 1985 novel by Margaret Atwood, the
1990 film adaptation directed by Volker Schlöndorff, and the 2017 TV series by executive
producer Bruce Miller. For the TV series, I will primarily focus on Season One, as the following
seasons extend beyond the events of the novel. I will highlight the changes in feminist narratives
with an awareness of the different contexts at the time of each artifact’s release. This paper will
also examine the historical reception of these artifacts; special attention will be paid to the 1990
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
movie adaption which is greatly overlooked and lacks in popularity compared to the novel and
the show.
This paper concludes that the three versions of The Handmaid’s Tale differ narratively -
through the prominence of Offred’s voice, her agency, and her motives - but also in terms of
visual portrayal. In the film, these changes reduce the complexity of her character and the
emotional depth of the story, resulting in a negative reception by audiences and critics. However,
in the show, the changes made suit the contemporary context while still resonating with
Atwood’s original portrayal.
Historical Contexts
Before diving into an analysis of gendered messages, it is necessary to look at the
different historical contexts at the time of each artifact's release. This will help in understanding
the reasons for the changes made from medium to medium. The novel by Atwood was released
in 1985, near the end of second-wave feminism. Some scholars analyzing Atwood and her work
have determined that The Handmaid’s Tale is a critique of second-wave feminism. Although
Atwood was politically active in advocating for human rights and social equality for women
beginning in the early 1960s, her beliefs did not always align with those of second-wave
feminists. She believed that second-wave feminists frequently advanced a single issue at the
expense of all the others, rather than confronting the multitude of socio-economic issues that
women faced; this meant that women with different goals were often at odds with one another,
with feelings of resentment and distrust more common than feelings of unity (Callaway, 2008).
Atwood was also strongly critical of radical feminism, a branch of second-wave feminism which
advocated for the annihilation of sex roles and a complete revolution in terms of gendered
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
oppression on all fronts. Atwood found this approach to be antagonistic towards men and
thought that this kind of fear and aggression could undermine the successes of the women’s
liberation movement (Callaway, 2008).
Thus, The Handmaid’s Tale is frequently perceived to be exploring a potential outcome of
radical feminism. Atwood even said in an interview, “if practical, hardline, anti-male feminists
took over and became the government, I would resist them” (Neuman, 2006). This can be tied
easily to the events of the novel, as it centers on the protagonist’s exploration of rebellion in a
society where women are enslaved and oppressed. In “‘Just a Backlash’: Margaret Atwood,
Feminism, and The Handmaid's Tale”, Shirley C. Neuman states that specific scenes within the
novel - namely the birthing scene and the brothel - are manifestations of the call of radical
feminists for a ‘woman’s culture’ (Neuman, 2006). Over the years, Atwood has grappled with
the definition of feminism and whether she considers herself and her work to be feminist, as
demonstrated by her various published interviews. In a 1982 interview, she described the term
feminism as “one of the all-purpose words”, saying feminist positions can range from “people
who think men should be pushed off cliffs to people who think it's O.K. for women to read and
write” (Callaway, 2008). In another interview, she claimed that her definition of feminism is a
“belief in the rights of women... [as] equal human beings”, concerned with freedom of choice
and distinct from notions of feminist or doctrinaire separatism (Neuman, 2006). While her
understanding of feminism has evolved over the years, she has remained firm on her opposition
to radical feminism.
Atwood claimed that she invented nothing in Gilead, as the events of the novel were
directly influenced by events occurring in the world in the early 1980s. Atwood studied and
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
integrated the actions of governments including Iran, Afghanistan, the Philippines, and Romania.
Some of the aspects of the novel that were inspired by real-life occurrences in these countries
include the use of electric prods in beatings, the murder of dissidents, the monitoring of women
monthly for pregnancy, the linkage of women’s wages to childbearing, the outlawing of birth
control, and more (Neuman, 2006). It is also important to note that in the United States, the
1980s were marked by Ronald Reagan’s presidency, and he ushered in a new conservatism to
American politics during his eight years in office. Abortion in particular was under attack in the
US, with abortion clinics being bombed, Medicaid halting the funding of legal abortions, and
state laws being passed prohibiting even the supply of information about abortion (Neuman,
The Handmaid’s Tale film was released in 1990, just five years after the release of the
novel, during a time in which feminism was entering a new phase. A number of film critics
commented on the film’s plausibility considering the context. One critic stated: “It's not entirely
unbelievable that a government of fanatical fundamentalists could come to power. (After all, it
happened in Iran.)” (Jacobs, 1990). Most interesting is how vastly different the director’s
interpretation of the film was from how Atwood perceived it. While Atwood appeared to oppose
the idea of a war between the sexes and emphasized the political context that informed the
society of Gilead, Schlöndorff stated that the film was about ''the war of the sexes much more
than any religious/political war” (Johnston, 1990). He claimed that it was about women’s
sexuality, and their fear of sterility and a loss of independence. Atwood responded by stating: “I
don't think the book is that at all, and I don't think the film is that. He must have been very
worried that people would think of it as just a political film” (Johnston, 1990).
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
As with both the novel and the film, the political context at the time of the TV show’s
release in 2017 was politically charged, particularly considering the post-election atmosphere.
The year was marked by the start of the Trump era, during which President Donald Trump
immediately issued a number of executive orders, many of which restricted the rights of minority
groups. Reproductive rights were once again under attack, with restrictions being imposed on
abortion and access to birth control, and the impending threat of legalized abortion being
reversed (Mulkerrins, 2017). The #MeToo movement was also going viral in late 2017, with
people all around the world speaking out against sexual abuse and sexual harassment. This social
movement influenced a number of the decisions made in the show, particularly during the
transition to Season Two, which extends beyond the events of the novel (Bhuvad, 2018).
Differences
There are numerous changes involving other characters and the establishment of Gilead
that were made between the novel, film, and TV show. However in this paper I will focus on
changes regarding the protagonist Offred, over time and across different media.
Offred’s Voice
The first key difference between the three media texts is the prominence of Offred’s
voice. The novel is narrated by Offred’s perspective, and Atwood frequently includes long,
expressive internal monologues that provide valuable insight into her perspective. Having access
to her thoughts helps communicate how she defies social expectations and expresses rage
towards her situation, but also how she has been brainwashed to believe certain things. In an
article comparing the novel and the TV show, Saartje Gobyn asserts that, at the start of the novel,
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
Offred’s internal monologues are the only method through which she can express her resistance
and defiance of the regime (Gobyn, 2019). One of many examples is when she watches the
Commander whose house she resides in and imagines spitting out the window or throwing
something at him. “I don’t feel like being kind”, she says (Atwood, 1985, p. 59). There are
countless other examples in which Offred outwardly behaves but inwardly scorns or criticizes the
people around her. However, Gobyn explains, Offred’s internal monologues also highlight how
she is “slowly but surely indoctrinated by the ideas that she was initially opposed to” (Gobyn,
2019). Her resistance lessens over the course of the novel, and she begins to behave more
passively, a change which is only evident through the progression of her thoughts. Thus, Offred’s
internal monologues are essential in understanding her character.
The film omits Offred’s internal monologues completely, with no substitute provided to
replace this look into Offred’s thoughts. According to Gobyn, Offred’s internal monologue is the
primary narrative technique used to represent her search for identity, her resistance, and the
collapse of her resistance (Gobyn, 2019). The removal of such an important aspect of the novel
strips away much of the complexity of Offred’s character. Additionally, the film has a fairly
minimalist script, meaning not a lot is verbalized. Offred has nearly the same amount of lines as
the other characters. One scene which demonstrates the impact of this change is the scene in
which Offred takes notice of a Handmaid who is pregnant. In the film it is quite a short scene, no
more than 20 seconds, and Offred speaks only a few words. Ofglen, Offred’s neighbor and
shopping partner, says, “she must be a very happy girl”, in reference to the pregnant Handmaid,
and Offred replies with, “praise be” (Schlöndorff & Pinter, 1990, 0:34:30). The tone of her voice
is neutral and the look on her face is blank, failing to reveal her true thoughts and feelings. The
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
other Handmaids clap respectfully and smile, but do not speak. In the book, however, it is a
fascinating scene that highlights how the women have endured months of indoctrination.
Although Offred does not speak out loud at all, unlike in the film, her thoughts are very
expressive. She refers to the pregnant Handmaid as an “object of envy and desire” (Atwood,
1985, p. 29). This is followed by a description of how the Handmaid is victorious and flaunts her
pregnancy in public, earning the jealousy of the Handmaids who have yet to become pregnant.
One other Handmaid hisses “showoff”, and in response Offred thinks, “this is true” (Atwood,
1985, p. 29). In the novel, Offred’s thoughts, her choice of language, and the way she reacts to
people around her much more thoroughly communicate both her internal resistance and the
extent of the brainwashing that she has been through. There are instances in which she criticizes
the regime, and instances in which she does not resist and simply expresses a desire to survive.
As the film’s audience had to rely only on Offred’s actions and dialogue to form a judgment of
her character, they likely surmised that she is obedient and conformist. Her character was viewed
by many critics as passive and flat, and the omission of the internal monologues is probably a
key reason as to why (Gilbert, 2015).
In the show, a crucial decision is made to include voiceovers to reflect Offred’s inner
monologues. As with the internal monologues in the novel, they help to convey the extent to
which Offred’s thoughts and actions can - or cannot - be policed. Offred is more spirited and
rebellious in the show - which will be discussed in more detail in later sections - but she is
externally obedient and subservient, at least initially. The voiceovers, frequented by sarcastic or
witty comments, provide insight into her anger and frustration. An example is when she is
grocery shopping with the other Handmaids, and they encourage her to take some oranges. She
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
obeys silently, but her voiceover reveals her true feelings: “I don’t need oranges. I need to
scream. I need to grab the nearest machine gun” (VanArendonk, 2017). While Offred is more
spirited in the show compared to the novel, this moment does not seem out-of-character, as it
echoes some of the violent thoughts Offred has in the novel; for example, at one point she eyes a
knife in the kitchen, thinking: “[it] is sharp and bright, and tempting. I would like to have a knife
like that” (Atwood, 1985, p. 49). Gobyn argues that while the internal monologues in the novel
highlight the collapse of her resistance, the voiceovers in the show do the opposite,
communicating how she grows stronger and more rebellious as time passes (Gobyn, 2019). As a
result of the creative choice to include Offred’s internal monologues as voiceovers, her voice is
much more prominent in the show compared to the film, and her character is perceived as more
three-dimensional and sympathetic, as it was in the novel.
Offred’s Agency
In the novel, Atwood strikes an interesting balance with Offred’s agency, as she is
depicted as being both powerless and powerful. On the one hand, she is enslaved, separated from
her husband and her daughter, and forced into being a Handmaid. She is also a somewhat passive
character; although she has thoughts about rebellion, her priority is survival, and she does not
actively support the resistance. On the other hand, she is treated with some level of respect and
reverence due to her status as one of the few fertile women left. Moreover, Neuman warns us not
to perceive Offred as an unmitigated heroine, as she indulges in “her own small exercises of
power, however ignoble” (Neuman, 2006). In one scene, the young male guards lust after her,
and she takes advantage of this, sauntering in front of them. She is dressed conservatively, in an
ankle-length skirt with full sleeves, gloves, and wings to conceal her face. Still, as these men are
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
not yet permitted to touch women, and her red clothing easily identifies her and announces her
‘purpose’ to the public, she wields the power of sexual appeal. She simultaneously enjoys the
power she holds and feels ashamed for baiting them, because she believes her situation is not
their fault - they all have roles to play in Gilead’s system (Atwood, 1985). Another example of
Offred’s power lies in her influence over the Commander. After they have spent many evenings
together, she discovers that she can use his desire for companionship to her advantage. She
begins with small requests, such as hand lotion. As her confidence grows, she capitalizes upon
her position, asking about the Handmaid that came before her, and about the political situation in
Gilead. His feelings and desire for her grow, which she notes: “It’s difficult for me to believe I
have power over him, of any sort, but I do” (Atwood, 1985, p. 200). She also realizes that she
holds a kind of power over his wife, Serena Joy, although she does not know it, by way of these
secret evenings with her husband. While Offred’s character is inarguably powerless in some
regards, she has moments of defiance both internally and externally, and her unusual position
allows her to wield small amounts of power over those around her.
In the film, this is not the case. While the film features moments of how she uses her
budding relationship with the Commander to her advantage, the scene with the guards is not
included. Moreover, without Offred’s internal monologues and that look into her thoughts, a
majority of her character’s depth is lost. As established, in the novel her moments of resistance
typically occur internally, through her thoughts. As the film omits the internal monologues, her
inner moments of agency and defiance are not communicated to the audience. This leaves them
with the externally obedient Offred. Rather than a balanced depiction of Offred as both powerful
and powerless, she primarily appears to be powerless and dependent on others. She seems to
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
passively accept her situation and does not attempt to fight or join the resistance. There is no
sense of her anger at her unjust situation or her criticism of the regime, which were so prevalent
in the novel. The one moment of agency she is given in the film is when she kills the
Commander, which does not occur in either the book or the show. This decision might have been
made in order to fulfill the expectations of mainstream films: that the antagonist is defeated, the
protagonist escapes her dire circumstances and finds freedom. It is important to note that Offred
is instructed to kill the Commander by a member of the resistance and is provided with the
means to do so - a knife. While this can be perceived as a moment of true agency in response to
her oppressive treatment, I would argue that she is still being used as a pawn, just by a different
group. Due to the lack of insight into Offred’s thoughts, there is little sense of how strongly the
desire to kill the Commander came from her, or whether she was just acting as instructed. Had
she decided to kill him by herself, in an attempt to find freedom, this might have had different
implications.
Offred is a more headstrong and feisty character in the TV show. She exercises increased
agency and participates in the resistance against Gilead’s regime. In later seasons she becomes a
freedom fighter, but even in Season One which follows the events of the book, she plays more of
an active role. Atwood recognized this, stating in an interview that “the Hulu team made their
Offred more active than my Offred” (Vineyard, 2017). One example is the Salvaging ceremony,
in which Handmaids are given permission to attack and kill criminals accused of crimes such as
rape. In the book, Offred is intensely disturbed by the viciousness of the women attacking the
man and does not participate. In the show, she is one of the first Handmaids to attack the man.
Similarly, in the book, Offred encounters some Japanese tourists and struggles to answer their
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
question about whether she is happy. She remains silent. In the show, however, she speaks to one
of the ambassadors and her assistant, asks for their help, and secures their assistance in
delivering a note to her husband. One final example occurs near the end of Season One, when
she is presented with a way to help the resistance (by collecting a package) and she makes an
attempt to do so. As explained above, in the book she does not actively aid the resistance efforts.
Series creator Miller explained part of his intentions behind the transformation of Offred’s
character, stating that the Offred from the book was a woman from a different time. He wanted
Offred in the show to represent a woman of her age in today’s world, an everyday hero that
exemplifies the “heroism of just doggedness”, of getting up every time you are knocked down
(Stanford, 2019). As a result, he decided to juxtapose Offred’s internal and external monologues
- done in part through the contrast between her actions and her thoughts, conveyed through the
voiceover - resulting in a combination of obedience and indignance (Dockterman, 2017). Thus,
Offred’s increased agency stems from the contemporary context, motivated by the desire for the
show’s protagonist to resonate with the growing group of women speaking out against sexual
abuse, gender oppression, and more. The change happens gradually, with Offred growing more
defiant and taking on a more active role in later seasons. This means that Offred in the show is
not completely different from Offred in the novel, but her underlying rebellious characteristics
are closer to the surface. Rather than growing less resistant, she demonstrates increased
determination in resisting the regime as time goes on.
Names
One key change made between the three media texts that plays into the idea of Offred’s
agency is the name she is given. In the novel, the Handmaids are never referred to by their birth
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
names. The protagonist is known as Offred, meaning Of Fred - property of Fred. The reader
never learns her actual name. Regardless of this fact, Offred’s real name is given a lot of
significance. She thinks of it often, as something that was taken away from her. In one of her
internal monologues she ruminates, “I tell myself it doesn’t matter, your name is like your
telephone number, useful only to others; but what I tell myself is wrong, it does matter. I keep the
knowledge of this name like something hidden, some treasure I’ll come back to dig up, one day. I
think of this name as buried” (Atwood, 1985, p. 84). Sure enough, when she begins to trust her
love interest, the chauffeur Nick, she confesses to him what her real name is, still without
revealing it to the reader. “I tell him my real name, and feel that therefore I am known” (Atwood,
In comparison, in the movie, Offred is referred to frequently by her birth name, Kate.
This erases the depth and significance surrounding the idea of ownership and agency, which I
believe was a compelling aspect of the novel. In the novel, there is a powerful scene involving
Ofglen, one of Offred’s friends. Near the end of the story, Ofglen kills herself and a new
Handmaid takes her place. When Offred asks where Ofglen went, the woman replies, “I am
Ofglen” (Atwood, 1985, p. 268). This highlights how replaceable the women are, “a national
resource” as Offred says in the book (Atwood, 1985, p. 67). This scene does occur in the film,
but unfortunately it is not as impactful. It is a very short scene, barely 15 seconds long, and
Offred does not say anything in response to the new Ofglen’s statement. Her facial expressions
are also neutral (Schlöndorff & Pinter, 1990). Moreover, the fact that Offred’s birth name is
utilized by other characters reduces the significance of the scene, as it undermines the idea that
all Handmaids are replaceable resources. This scene does not occur in the show, as the character
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
of Ofglen is given a backstory and a role in coming seasons. In short, I disagree with the decision
made by the film director to provide Offred with a name. The idea of these women as property
with no agency or freedom is more impactful when they lack a basic human right: a name of
their own.
In the show, Offred’s birth name - June Osborne - is also revealed at the end of the first
episode. This does in part reduce the significance around the concept of agency, as continuously
referring to the Handmaids as property of upper-class men emphasizes their cruel treatment.
However, the show does at least create a sense of mystery and importance surrounding Offred’s
name, which is something that the film does not do. The Handmaids use their birth names as a
type of currency, sharing them amongst one another as a way to connect and secretly keep tabs
on each other. While the show unfortunately did not adopt Atwood’s powerful use of names, the
director at the very least ensured that the Handmaids’ names were a significant aspect of the plot.
Also, Gobyn perceives this particular change as indicative of Offred reclaiming her identity. This
makes sense in the context of her argument that Offred grows more resistant in the TV series,
thus reconstructing her identity and reclaiming her name, whereas she does the opposite in the
novel (Gobyn, 2019). Additionally, the show adapts an important aspect of the book, which - in
conjunction with the use of names - further emphasizes how the Handmaids are property. In the
novel, numbers are tattooed onto each Handmaid to identify them, similar to how prisoners in
Nazi concentration camps had numbers tattooed onto their arms (Harrington, 2017). Offred states
that the numbers “guarantee that I will never be able to fade, finally, into another landscape”
(Atwood, 1985, p. 67). In the show, the Handmaids are identified by ear tags, which also
function as trackers. This change from tattoos to ear tags is reasonable considering that the show
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
is set in more modern times and involves a greater use of technology. Like the tattoo, the ear tags
are a cruel and inhumane method of distinguishing the Handmaids and preventing their escape.
In Season Two, Offred removes the tag by cutting into her ear, losing a chunk of cartilage and
causing blood to drip everywhere. In contrast, to identify the Handmaids, the film uses bracelets
that are easily removed and leave no visible mark on the women. This is another way in which
the film reduces the impact of what should have been a chilling story of gendered oppression.
Ending
Another change that will be highlighted is the ending of each respective media artifact, as
they vary in terms of emotional depth and reflect Offred’s differing motives. In the novel, the
ending is quite ambiguous. Offred is rescued from the household where she works by Nick and
the Eyes - Gilead's secret police - although she has no way of knowing what they will do with
her. The epilogue is the famous ‘Historical Notes’ ending, which takes place in 2195,
approximately two hundred years after the events of the novel. A professor is lecturing about
Gilead, which fell long ago. He is unsympathetic and dismissive of Offred’s struggles. He says
that her fate is unknown - she may have escaped, or she may have been recaptured or killed. It is
never revealed what happens to her afterward. Although she suspected that she might be
pregnant with Nick’s child at the time of her escape, she was not certain and it is never
confirmed (Atwood, 1985). This epilogue is highly significant in many of the discussions
regarding the novel, as it hints at the idea that a society like Gilead’s is not as far off or
implausible as we may think.
In the movie, Offred is also rescued by Nick and the Eyes, but only after she kills the
Commander. She is shown to be living in a trailer in the mountains, pregnant with Nick’s baby
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
and hopeful for the future. Although her future is uncertain, there is less of a mystery
surrounding it, and it is essentially a ‘happily ever after’ ending. The exclusion of the powerful
‘Historical Notes’ ending further strips the film of the novel’s deeper implications. As with the
bracelets, this ending undermines the significance of all that Offred has been through. It has been
referred to as an attempt to “mute tragedy or horror”; while this ending may be appropriate for a
typical Hollywood film, it is not suitable for an adaptation of one of Atwood’s novels, which are
known for their darker narratives and more open endings (Nischik, 2010). Additionally, one
scholar claimed that this ending features a reintroduction of the male patriarch, which is an
inappropriate conclusion to a story about the enslavement of women (Bodelson, 2006). This
choice was likely made to appeal to audiences, as the ambiguous ending of the novel might not
have been perceived as satisfying in a mainstream Hollywood film.
In the show, Season One ends on the same note as the novel, with Offred disappearing
with Nick and the Eyes. The show then flashes forward and depicts the ‘Historical Notes’
ending, relatively similar to the one described in the novel, where scholars debate Offred’s
unknown fate (Keaney, 2017). A number of other events unfold over the course of Season Two,
until Offred is given the opportunity to escape Gilead. Instead, she chooses to stay. Over the next
few seasons, Offred becomes more involved in the fight against the regime and eventually
becomes a freedom fighter. This decision transforms Offred’s character and her desires; in the
novel and the movie, she fluctuates between wanting to escape the oppressive regime and
wanting to stay so that she can be with Nick. In the show, she actively makes the choice to stay
and fight back. While the decision to let Offred stay and fight could likely be attributed in part to
the desire to continue the show, it was also greatly influenced by contemporary feminist
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
activism. The same can be said for Offred’s increased agency and transformation from a passive
character to an active one. Elisabeth Moss, co-producer of the show and the actress who plays
Offred, spoke in an interview about how relevant themes such as female empowerment and
resistance would feature heavily in Season Two. Another actor on the show spoke about how the
show has converged with the momentum of the #MeToo campaign and similar movements, and
how the character of Offred would represent that (Chuba, 2018). As Offred’s transformation is
gradual and her motives evolve over several seasons, it does not feel unnatural or out of
character. Miller builds on Atwood’s initial characterization of Offred, slowly drawing out her
more rebellious characteristics as time passes.
Offred’s Eroticization
One final difference is how Schlöndorff’s visual portrayal of Offred eroticized her in a
way that neither Atwood nor Miller did. In “Redemptive Restrooms: Moments of Utopic
Possibility in Volker Schlöndorff's Film Version of The Handmaid's Tale”, Amery Bodelson
explores how the film can be viewed through the lens of phallocentrism, in which the male
sexual organ and the image of castrated women give meaning to the world. She explains that the
male gaze is a film device used to capture the power dynamic between the sexes. In particular,
Bodelson says that the director eroticized the film’s poster and still shots, encoding “erotic visual
clues that the novel never suggests” (Bodelson, 2006). For example, the film poster depicts a
beautiful, youthful, tanned Offred, with flowing blonde hair and a red robe clutched to her naked
body. Her eyes are submissively downcast, but she does not look troubled or afraid, which is
strange considering that this is a film about the enslavement of women. Another example is the
German poster promoting the film, which features just the naked backside of a woman, with her
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
arms bound behind her back. This is an explicitly submissive pose, and the poster hints at
masochistic eroticism. With her head and her feet cut out of the frame, she has been reduced to a
sexual object (Bodelson, 2006). There are numerous versions of the book cover and the TV
series poster, but none of them sexualize Offred to this extent. They typically portray Offred in
her conservative Handmaid attire, looking pensive or defiant.
Another example of Schlöndorff’s eroticization that I identified is the ceremony scene, in
which Offred must have sex with the Commander as his wife watches. In the novel, this is not
Offred’s first ceremony, as she has been a Handmaid to other families in the past. It is described
quite dispassionately and the whole process is brisk and impersonal. She lies still and detaches
herself from the situation until it is over. Once back in her room, she changes into her nightgown,
uses some stolen butter as a lotion for her face and hands, and attempts to go to sleep (Atwood,
1985). The TV series mirrors the book closely in its portrayal of the ceremony. Offred lies
passively on the bed, face blank as she likely disengages from the present until the ritual is over.
She also returns to her room afterward and attempts to sleep. In the film, however, this scene
becomes akin to a violent rape scene. It is Offred’s first ceremony and she sobs and gasps
throughout the process. Once she returns to her room, she lashes out as she cries, breaking a cup.
She then pulls off her clothes and presses her naked body against the window, gasping for air.
Although it is initially a long shot, the camera zooms in until Offred’s naked body is in the center
of the frame. Nick, her future love interest, also catches sight of her in this moment (Schlöndorff
& Pinter, 1990). This is an example of the fetishistic camera work that Bodelson mentions in her
article. By transforming the clinical ritual into a violent rape scene and including the close-up of
Offred’s naked body, Schlöndorff amplified the erotic cues for the male gaze (Bodelson, 2006).
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
Interestingly enough, in a 2017 Buzzfeed article, Anne Helen Petersen praises the TV series for
its “female glance”, as opposed to the typical male gaze that is present in most mainstream
media, including Schlöndorff’s The Handmaid’s Tale. As opposed to the obsessive male gaze,
she states that the female glance is “constantly vigilant… it observes, with patient detail, the
moments of a woman’s world that often go unnoticed” (Petersen, 2017). This highlights how the
visual framing of the film (particularly in comparison to the show) drastically impacted audience
reception, especially considering that the focus of the story is the sexualization and exploitation
of women.
Reception
The novel and the TV show were both received positively by critics and general
audiences. The novel was perceived by most as powerful, compelling, and well-written; it was
nominated for and granted multiple awards between 1985 and 1987. A 1985 article in The
Toronto Star just a week after the novel’s publication claimed that it was “riding a wave of rave
reviews” (Adachi, 1985). The excitement surrounding the novel was not limited to the weeks
after its release; in a 1986 book review in the Los Angeles Times, Elaine Kendall declared Offred
to be a “spirited and engaging narrator”, and stated that “the power of the book comes… from
[Atwood’s] deliberate subjugation of imagination to demonstrable fact” (Kendall, 1986). In other
words, Kendall’s primary praise for the novel was that it was based on actual events occurring at
the time, making it feel more realistic than fictional. The bold and shocking ideas contained
within the book continue to spark discourse amongst scholars and academics until today.
The show similarly resonated with audiences all across the world; women in the US,
Ireland, Poland, Argentina, and more have donned the Handmaid’s costumes in sexual assault,
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
abortion, and anti-Trump protests, to name a few. The Handmaid’s Tale became a powerful
symbol of resistance as a result of the show’s popularity (Gulf News, 2018). Critics have called
the show “brilliant, terrifying television”, “a total stunner of a series”, and the “most chilling
Trump era series”, amongst other praise (Brittany, 2017). Other reviews have remarked on the
show’s timelessness and allure; an IndieWire review called the show “a haunting confluence of
tenses… one of the best shows of the year so far, at times hard to watch but impossible to
ignore” (Miller, 2017). It made history as the first streaming series to win Best Drama awards at
the Emmys and the Golden Globes (Katz, 2018).
In comparison, the film was incredibly unsuccessful, grossing less than $5 million against
its $13 million budget (Gilbert, 2015). The movie’s lack of success is likely attributed to
Schlöndorff’s execution, as criticism of the film was mainly aimed at the director’s choices or
the actors’ performances, rather than the actual premise of the novel. Indeed, a number of critics
wondered why a film about women being dominated by men had been directed by a male rather
than a female (Nischik, 2010). In a 1990 review in the Chicago Tribune, renowned film critic
Dave Kehr stated that the film “comes to seem less feminist than frankly misogynistic” (Kehr,
1990). In other historical newspapers from 1990, numerous critics found fault with the film,
claiming that it was exploitative of women, stating that the audience was distanced from the plot
rather than immersed into it, and even reporting that the preview audience found it humorous, as
they were snickering during the preview (Johnston, 1990; Jacobs, 1990). This could partly be
explained by a 1989 interview in which Schlöndorff explained that he believes the novel and the
film share a “sense of humor” that is often overlooked, as the horrific events are often described
as hilarious (Forsberg, 1989). However, evidently the horrific nature of the story did not come
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
across to audiences in this way if they felt distanced from the plot and unsympathetic towards the
characters. While the book and the show both successfully (according to audiences and critics)
convey a chilling story of women forced into sexual servitude, the film lacks this emotional
depth. The shock factor was more surface-level, featuring in the violence and the rape scene
rather than in the story about severe gender oppression and sexual enslavement and its impact on
Offred.
Conclusion
In this paper, I explored the changes in gendered narratives communicated in the three
versions of The Handmaid’s Tale. They differ narratively, with the novel and the film
highlighting Offred’s internal resistance and unique moments of agency. The internal
monologues, featuring as the voiceovers in the show, were essential in forming Offred’s identity
and making her a sympathetic character. While the novel and the TV show demonstrate different
progressions in Offred’s motives - she grows less rebellious in the novel, but more rebellious in
the show - the changes made in the TV show highlight and build upon aspects of Offred’s
character hinted at in the book, rather than taking away from her character or making her
unrecognizable. The changes made suit the modern context, as Offred’s increased agency and
active resistance reflect contemporary feminist activism and social movements at the time.
By omitting this narrative technique, the film portrays Offred as a more passive, obedient
character who lacks complexity and depth. The novel and the show both communicate a
powerful story of sexual enslavement, using various plot elements (the names, the tattoos/ear
tags, and the ‘Historical Notes’ ending) to emphasize the idea of the Handmaids as property of
Gilead. Schlöndorff omits a number of these elements, opting for a more Hollywood-ized
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
approach, with Offred killing the commander and having a ‘happily ever after’ ending. In doing
so, the film undermines Atwood’s messages, lessening the emotional impact of the story. One
final reason why the film did not resonate with audiences in the same way that the novel did just
five years earlier is Schlöndorff’s visual portrayal of Offred; by catering to the male gaze and
employing fetishistic camera techniques, the film eroticizes Offred and reduces her to a sexual
object.
There are many other differences made between the three texts that could be analyzed,
including the costumes and the development of supporting characters such as Ofglen, Nick, and
Moira, Offred’s closest friend. (In the novel and the show, Offred and Moira have been friends
since adolescence, whereas in the film they meet for the first time at the Handmaid's training
center.) One other detail excluded from the film is the concept of Unbabies: babies suffering
from birth defects or physical deformations that are ‘disposed’ of by authorities in Gilead
(Atwood, 1985). This subplot is very significant in the novel and the show, and can be linked to
the historical contexts regarding abortion and reproductive rights.
“The personal is political” is a key phrase used in the women’s liberation movement,
especially during second-wave feminism (Dore, 2014). As Neuman asserts, “nowhere is the
personal more political than in Gilead” (Neuman, 2006). In Atwood’s dystopian society, every
choice a woman makes is rooted in the political context, from the decision to be a Handmaid
rather than suffer a fate in the Colonies, to their often violent actions during the Salvaging
ceremonies. Released near the end of second-wave feminism, Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale is
a cautionary tale that hits close to home for many, considering its generous use of real-life events
as inspiration for the horrors of the story. Not only does it comment on gender oppression, it also
GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE
envisions the implications of religion, race, and sexuality in a dystopian society. The film and TV
series adaptations were similarly released in highly politically-charged situations, in which
earlier accomplishments in the women’s liberation movement were being challenged. The film’s
failure highlights how drastically the story’s themes can be misinterpreted, whether
unintentionally or deliberately. Correspondingly, the success of the TV show over three decades
after the novels’ release demonstrates how Atwood’s powerful exploration of radical feminism
remains relevant across a range of historical contexts. As one of the key texts that has been
analyzed by scholars in the fields of gender and media, it is essential to consider the different
interpretations of the messages encoded within The Handmaid’s Tale, as it is a story that has
resonated strongly with audiences for decades, and will continue to do so for years to come.

volumes.nurj_title: Geospatial Evidence for Diversification Effects in Branch Banking Deposit Stability: A Case Study in Fracking

blocks: Northwestern University
March 17, 2021
Geospatial Evidence for Diversification
Effects in Branch Banking Deposit Stability:
A Case Study in Fracking
JACOB WIESENTHAL
Abstract
The heterogeneity of regional economies in the United States provides branch banks with
plentiful opportunities to mitigate risk through geographic diversification. This paper
introduces natural geography to the discussion of diversification in branch banking in
order to examine the dynamics of deposit stability in the context of an economic shock.
By developing a microeconomic index of geographic diversity by county, I assess how
the emergence of hydraulic fracturing or “fracking” in the early 2010s impacted industry
concentrations across five distinct regions. A regression discontinuity framework is
applied to counties who concurrently began fracking operations and, as a counterfactual,
the counties with which they share a border. Positive spatial autocorrelation of deposit
variances between proximate branches is estimated to quantify the degree to which
deposit stability is derived by location. Given the exogeneity of natural gas shale play
discoveries, I construct a difference-in-differences model that identifies the directionality
in which geographic diversity augmented the effect of fracking on deposit stability. My
analysis reveals that geographically diverse branches mitigated the shock’s impact on
deposits and in some cases even became more stable. I conclude that geographic
diversification is positively associated with deposit stability, and that both interstate bank
consolidations and online banking services are uniquely positioned to leverage this
diversification advantage.
Keywords: banks, geographic diversification, deposits, fracking
JEL Classification Codes: C3, C58, G11, G21, L71, Q33, R1
1 Introduction
Federally-insured banking in the United States is inherently
shaped by the vastly diverse regional geographies of which it
serves. Historically, intrastate branch banks have existed and
adapted on a microeconomic level, optimizing each branch to
synergize with the unique profiles of their local populations.
With the passage of the Riegle-Neal Act in 1994, which enabled
bank holding companies (BHCs) to acquire branches outside of
their
headquartered
state,
interstate
banking
was
able
to
capitalize on this heterogeneity by inducing diversification
through mergers and acquisitions. Hughes et al. (1999) examine
the
mass
interstate
consolidation
of
banks
following
the
Riegle-Neal Act and identify significant gains in performance
attributable to these mergers.1 Akhigbe and Whyte (2003) build
on this theory and provide evidence that these gains are derived
from a decrease in risk due to larger and more diversified branch
portfolios.2
It is well understood that lending risk can be mitigated through
the diversification of industries represented in a portfolio, and
that doing so generally increases profitability. Demsetz and
Strahan (1997) suggest that large BHCs are able to increase their

and

more
profitable
loans
because

“diversification advantage” in which the heightened risk of such
operations
is
counterbalanced
by
the
stabilizing
effect
of
diversified portfolios.3 However, there may also be diseconomies
to interstate expansion in lending. Acharya, Hasan, and Saunders
(2006) find evidence that a lack of localized lending experience,
an
inability
to
specialize,
and
potential
complications
in
monitoring distant branches can offset the risk-based advantages

through diversification-enabled leverage is understood to be
contingent on the idiosyncratic management of BHCs.
However, unlike lending, geographic diversification as it pertains
to branch deposits has not been the subject of sizable research
following the rise of interstate banking in the United States. This
paper seeks to reconcile the insights of previous literature on
lending diversification with evidence concerning deposit stability
as it relates to the geography of branch banks. In particular, I
assess whether the geographic diversity of a regional economy is
negatively associated with deposit variability in local branches,
and
by
extension,
whether
geographically
diversifying
a
portfolio of branches induces aggregate deposit stability for a
bank.
Ascertaining an answer to these inquiries will complement our
lending-based understanding of how diversification impacts
bank performance. This is because the financial leverage of which
diversification is found to enable may be the result of either
increased stability in loan earnings or increased stability in the
deposit bases on which leverage is measured. Maintaining a
stable deposit base is critical to justifying enhanced leverage and
is thus equally worthy of inspection.
Identifying the effects of geographic diversification on deposit
stability is a more unidirectional problem than that of lending
because, unlike loans, soliciting deposits from a more diverse
clientele
does
not
introduce
significant
diseconomies
of
expansion.
Whereas
information
asymmetry
and
poor

profound in disrupting the stability of a branch’s deposit base.
For this reason, evidence of diversification effects in deposit
stability
would,
in
combination
with
our
lending-based
understanding of interstate banking, suggest that geographically
diversifying may be advantageous to branch banks in both
lowering risk and increasing profitability.
Two key contributions to the econometric evaluation of this
dynamic are made in this paper. First, geographic diversity is
measured at a more microeconomic scope than in previous
studies, adding precision to its description of regional economies.
Second, deposit stability is assessed in the context of an economic
shock (the emergence of hydraulic fracturing) in order to

1.1 Literature Review
Previous literature attempting to measure the implications of
geographic diversification in banking has procedurally become
more microeconomic but is generally limited to metrics of
distance and quantity. Rivard and Thomas (1997) conducted one
of the earliest studies to segment interstate banking presence by
Federal Reserve Bank district in addition to a dummy variable
representing whether a bank operates across states.5 Their results
suggest that the advantages of geographic diversification in
lowering risk are not only derived from an interstate presence,
but also differ depending on which particular regions the bank’s
branches are located in. This approach was expanded by Berger
and DeYoung (2006) in estimating the efficiency of BHC branches
by controlling for individual state fixed effects, as well as
introducing a measurement of distance between each branch and
the BHC’s headquarters.6 Deng and Elyasiani (2008) measure
geographic diversification with an emphasis on this relationship
between branch and headquarters, employing a Cobb-Douglas
function of both distance and geographic dispersion.7 It should
be noted, however, that while distance is a sensible predictor of
difference, their connection is far from absolute. In a human
geography as dispersed as that of the United States, it is not
uncommon for greater distance from one city to, at some
inflection, begin approaching another city more similar than any
rural areas between the two. Therefore, there is an argument to
be made that distance should not be relied on as a strict indicator
of diversity.
Following Deng et al. (2007), a Herfindahl-Hirschman Index
(HHI) is constructed to represent the state and Metropolitan

5 Rivard, R. J., & Thomas, C. R. (1997). The effect of interstate

A key development in Deng and Elyasiani’s second iteration of
the measurement is the accounting of deposit dispersion, in
which the HHI is weighted by the deposits held by each branch.
This method calibrates the measure of geographic diversification
to reflect the relative importance of each branch to the bank,
assigning less weight to small branches and more weight to
branches which represent a majority of the bank’s deposit base.

1.2 Assessing Diversification in the Context of an
Economic Shock
As
previously
mentioned,
the
inspection
of
geographic
diversification in the context of economic shocks closer resembles
the true dynamic by which diversity interacts with volatility.
While simple measures of distance and quantity can approximate
the risk mitigation of local industry exposures, the geography of
banking is clustered, human-dependent, and ever-changing.
Because deposit stability is a product of time, it can be thought of
in terms of temporal changes in deposit bases as a result of
economic growth and decline. The distinction of a stable deposit
base is therefore most pronounced in the face of a transitional
economic shock. Yet strictly financial analysis of economic shocks
in banking typically either restricts implications of causality (due
to endogeneity of the shock) or requires an instrument that limits
predictive accuracy.9
Fortunately, the study of geography is uniquely disposed to
present us with an abundance of natural experiments in which
the
resulting
shocks
can
be
understood
as
exogenous.
Interpreting a shift in geographic diversification as an exogenous
product of a natural, geographical event allows for its predicted
effect on deposit stability to be causally attributed. This paper
introduces insights from natural geography to the discussion of
diversification
in banking by examining the emergence of
hydraulic fracturing or “fracking” in the early 2010s. During this
period, banks were unable to proactively account for the rapid
growth of the fracking industry, given the discovery of new
technology, natural gas shale plays, and estimates suggesting
unforeseen volumes of productivity.10 As such, the disruption to
regional employment caused by the fracking industry can be
translated into shifts in geographic diversity for proximate
branches. Likewise, the degree to which our diversification
measure was affected by fracking can be causally linked to
patterns observed in these branches’ deposit stability.

2.1 Stratifying Counties by the Presence of Fracking
To identify the effects that these new wells had on their regional
economies in the context of geographic diversity, I transform the
data collected by the EPA into a collection of counties which saw
at least one new well begin fracking operations within their
borders during 2012. This group of counties includes both those
which had fracking activities take place within their borders
prior to 2012 and those for which the observed wells were the
county’s first instance of fracking. Because our analysis isolates
the consequences of the operations in 2012 in particular, this
distinction is negligible. Counties included within this group are
hereafter referred to as “fracking counties” to simply denote their
classification.

3 Hypothesis Development
Given the literature on geographic diversification as it pertains to
lending risk and the mechanisms by which industry diversity
may be tied to deposit stability, it would intuitively follow that
there is some relationship between the geographic diversification
of a bank’s branches and the stability of their deposits. Namely, a
low concentration of industries in a county is likely to mitigate
the effect of any industry-dependent microeconomic shock on the
deposits in proximate banks. This dynamic necessitates that
deposit stability be at least partially derived from its geography,
and therefore I expect to observe spatial autocorrelation in
deposit stability across all counties. As such, I will test the
following hypothesis:
H1: Deposit stability is positively spatially autocorrelated between
branches.
If, in fact, spatial autocorrelation is observed in the deposit
stability between counties, then it would be appropriate to
regress deposit stability on a geographically-based index such as
my modified HHI. More specifically, in the context of fracking, I
expect the emergence of fracking to have variable effects on the
measured diversity of fracking counties, depending on whether a
county was previously concentrated in the energy sector. The
dynamic effects on deposit stability of the treatment of fracking
can then be translated into bank-level insights. Based on the
arguments given above, I expect this relationship to be positive
and causal. In other words:
H2: Geographic diversification is positively associated with deposit
stabilization.
Not only this, but by taking the economic shock of fracking as
exogenous, this relationship can be inferred as causal, proposing
geographic
diversification
as
a
tool
by
which
banks can
intentionally mitigate variability and potentially increase their
leverage of deposits.

in both fracking counties and bordering counties, this model will
identify the causal treatment effect of being located within a
fracking county in 2012 on a branch’s subsequent change in
deposit stability. Using the natural log of deposits_cv to interpret
percentage changes in deposit stability as a log-linear function of
the treatment and its covariates, I estimate the following model:
𝑙𝑛_𝑑𝑒𝑝𝑜𝑠𝑖𝑡𝑠_𝑐𝑣𝑖𝑡= β0 + β1 * 𝑝𝑜𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑡+ β2 * 𝑓𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑘𝑖𝑛𝑔𝑖𝑡+ β3 * 𝑏𝑟𝑎𝑛𝑐ℎ_𝑑𝑖𝑣𝑖𝑡+
where αi is the branch fixed effect and μt is the year fixed effect.
Of most importance are the coefficients of β4 and β7, which can be
interpreted as the treatment effect of fracking in 2012 on a
branch’s deposit stability and the degree to which this effect
differed by the geographic diversity of that branch’s county,
respectively. In particular, the coefficient of the triple interaction
term postit*frackingit*branch_divit will indicate the directionality in
which geographic diversity impacts deposit stability for branches
and, by proxy, for their parent banks.

Descriptive statistics of the sample dataset are given in Table 1.

for the deposits and deposits_cv variables are 613,475.3 and 17.119,
respectively,
indicating that the collection of fracking and
bordering counties include branches of a wide spectrum of size
and stability.

5.2 Difference-in-Differences Model
Annualized trends in deposit stability by geography can be
visualized in Figure 5, which plots the median deposit variance
for both fracking counties and bordering counties by year. The
parallel trend assumption is assessed for the years 2010 to 2015,
as banking diagnostics in 2009 were exogenously impacted by
the global financial crisis of that year. As illustrated in the line
plot, deposit stability in both fracking counties and bordering
counties experienced parallel shifts across all years except 2012,
in which fracking counties became more stable while bordering
counties became less stable. This inequality was sustained for all
years following 2012, as the median deposits_cv in fracking
counties remained roughly 3% less than that of bordering
counties.

The estimation results of my difference-in-differences model are
outlined in Table 2, including robust standard errors and
coefficient indicators of statistical significance. Consistent with
Figure 5, these estimation results imply a negative effect on
deposits_cv
for
all
counties
post-2012,
and an additionally
negative effect for fracking counties in particular. The coefficient
estimate for the treatment effect post*fracking is positive and
statistically significant at the 0.1% level, suggesting that the
emergence of fracking in 2012 caused deposit instability for
branches in counties with little to no geographic diversity.
However, much if not all of this instability is mitigated by the
effect of geographic diversity on the treatment. The coefficient
estimate
for
post*fracking*branch_div
is
negative
and
also

counties saw less deposit instability as a result of fracking, and in
some cases even became more stable as a result. Whereas a
macroeconomic, observational model would seek to identify the
coefficient estimate for branch_div, a measure of diversification
effects outside of the context of economic shocks, the focus on its
triple interaction with the treatment effect yields much more
explanatory results. At a glance, the magnitude of diversification
effects in the context of the economic shock of fracking is
estimated to be roughly eight times greater (and far more
statistically discernible) than its magnitude as estimable without
considering the shock.
To assess the robustness of the model, I first test the null
hypotheses that the covariates bhc and brsertyp are equal to 0 and
calculate the two leftmost results of Table 3. Likewise, I test the
null hypothesis that the year fixed effects are jointly equal to 0
and calculate the rightmost result of Table 3. The covariates bhc
and brsertyp are determined to be different than 0 and statistically
significant at the 5% and 0.1% levels, respectively. The year fixed
effects are determined to be different than 0 and statistically
significant at the 0.1% level. Thus, the model is justified in
including these covariates and fixed effects.
Noteworthy is the strongly positive coefficient corresponding to
branches with the FDIC branch service type of 23, representing
drive-through offices. The estimate suggests that, as compared to
typical brick and mortar offices, branches offering drive-through
depositing services are much more prone to deposit instability,
especially in the face of an economic shock such as fracking. This
makes intuitive sense given the relatively low opportunity costs
to clients of making drive-through deposits and withdrawals
without having to physically enter the branch.

As an additional robustness assessment, a second model is
estimated with random effects in place of branch fixed effects
and compared against the original model in accordance with the
Hausman (1978) econometric model specification test.17 The
results of the specification test are given in Table 4, which rejects
the null hypothesis that there is no systematic difference in the
estimated coefficients given either fixed or random effects.
Therefore, the inclusion of branch fixed effects in my model is
justified. An important intuition as to why branch fixed effects
are key covariates in modeling geographic diversity lies in their
derivation. Since a branch will be located within the same county
for all years observed in the dataset, the fixed effects of its county
are inherited within the branch fixed effects when absorbed. By
including branch fixed effects, the model not only controls for
static characteristics of each branch such as locational advantages
and management style, but also controls for static characteristics
of each branch’s county such as demographics and, to an extent,
its competitive landscape of banking.
Together, the treatment effect and its triple interaction with
geographic diversity are substantiated by the above statistical
robustness analysis. More importantly, it tells a story consistent
with
both
the
proposed
underlying
mechanisms
of
diversification and the existing literature on branch banking,
exogenous economic shocks, and the industry of fracking. As
hypothesized, the introduction of fracking as an exogenous
economic shock was an industry-specific destabilizing event
whose effect on deposit stability was augmented by geographic

Econometrica, 46(6), 1251.
diversity, where a greater level of diversity generally lead to
more overall stability.
While the magnitude of the coefficient estimates are ambiguous
in their relation to a bank’s total deposit stability as a product of
geographic
diversification,
their
statistical
significance
and
directionality in the context of this model are transferable. That
is, since changes in branch geographic diversity and deposit
stability are positively proportional to their corresponding effects
on bank geographic diversification and deposit stability, the
insights of this model can be applied at a bank level as well. The
estimated values infer that the effect of geographic diversification
on a bank’s total deposit stability is positive and significant.
Therefore, H2 is affirmed: geographic diversification is positively
associated with deposit stabilization.
6 Conclusions
Since every county poses a unique risk profile to the branches
located within it, it is crucial to account for the differences in
their economic profiles when measuring geographic diversity.
Further, as the geographic diversification of a bank relies on a
portfolio of branches with low concentrations of local industry
exposures,
analyzing
trends within individual branches as
opposed to entire banks is a valuable tool. This insight can likely
be transferred to other individually subtle but aggregately potent
banking dynamics. By taking this approach in the context of an
economic shock, we arrive at several interesting results that
would be unobtainable from a macro-level, non-panel analysis.
The extent to which we observe positive spatial autocorrelation
in deposit stability between branches is predominantly among
neighbors less than 25 arc distance miles apart. An alternative
interpretation of this statistic is that past 25 arc distance miles,
branches share no discernable spatial autocorrelation in deposit
stability. Given that the smallest state in the United States, Rhode
Island, stretches 37 miles in width, the notion of taking each state
to represent a single risk profile is misguided since, in each, there
are at least two uncorrelated spatial clusters of deposit stability.
Adapting the previous literature on geographic diversification in
branch banking to index counties rather than states, and to
represent
both
rural
and
urban
regions,
is an important
development that the results of this paper corroborate.
Contrary to their connotation, economic shocks can often provide
a source of stability for the regions which they affect. The
emergence of fracking in the early 2010s and its effects on deposit
stability is an excellent case study in substantiating this thought.
Branches in fracking counties with a low industry concentration
of energy employment could be said to have benefited in terms
of stability by the introduction of fracking, since the employment
it spurred increased the county’s industry diversity. However, it
may be more advantageous to think of the treatment effect of
fracking as quadratic, with an inflection point at which its energy
industry employment equals the mean level of employment
among all present industries. If fracking employment were to
surpass this inflection point, the county’s measured diversity
would actually decrease along with its branches’ predicted
deposit stability. Therefore, it should be prefaced in further
discussion of economic shocks in banking that shocks are not
necessarily destabilizing events, but rather their effects on
stability are augmented in either direction by the shock’s
corresponding impact on each affected region’s risk profile.
While the case study in fracking does not prove any universal
relationship—perhaps shocks to other industries impact deposit
stability differently—its study does aid us in our comprehension
of
the
microeconomic
mechanisms
by
which
geographic
diversification may be an important consideration for growing
banks.
Altogether, these understandings form a compelling story for the
types of diversification advantages proposed by Demsetz and
Strahan (1997).3 For banks seeking to improve predictability and
leverage of their deposit bases, opportunities to expand towards
geographically diverse and dissimilar regions may prove an
effective means to do so. In particular, mergers and acquisitions
of smaller, regional banks may principally provide economies of
experience and localized knowledge of markets that mitigates
risk in lending, but may also serve to diversify the deposit base of
the parent bank as a whole. The mass consolidation of banking
institutions
following
the
Riegle-Neal
Act
in
was
predominantly fueled by an interest in the former advantage, but
future consolidation may likely be encouraged from further
discovery of diversification effects and their potential benefits to
leverage and subsequently profitability.
Diversification
advantages
may
also
belong
in
the
macroeconomic discussion of the United States banking sector in
its entirety, especially when compared with the banking sectors
of more geographically homogenous countries. In the first major
global recession since the passage of the Riegle-Neal Act in 1994,
the United States economy and banking sector in particular was
able to recover far quicker in the years following 2009 than were
European countries like Italy, Spain, and Greece.18 Much of this
disparity was due to debt-related policies governing bankruptcy
and credit, however the results of this paper propose another
reason embedded in differences in geographic diversity. Given
the vast geographic heterogeneity of the United States and its
numerosity of distinctive regional economies, its interstate banks
had more opportunity to mitigate the deposit instability caused
by the financial crisis through diversification than did banks in
the smaller and more homogenous countries of Europe.
Finally, a discussion of diversification in banking, even when
rooted in physical geography, cannot overlook the contemporary
migration toward online banking as a primary deposit servicing
medium. The rapid growth stories of fintechs over the past
decade have challenged the predominant trends in branch
banking
on
which
most
research
is
founded,
largely
by
minimizing overhead costs and maximizing client access in an
unprecedented fashion. Despite not conforming to any physical
plane of geography, the digital presence of online banking is
actually
quite
relevant
to
the
analysis
of
geographic
diversification.
Because
online
banking
extends
access
to
populations across the country regardless of their proximity to
physical branches, its potential for geographic diversification is
elevated to a ceiling beyond that of any physical branch banking
portfolio.
The
identification
of
diversification
effects
in
facilitating deposit stability may even premise that fintechs can
be leveraged to a point beyond that of traditional branch banks
without any greater risk of insolvency. Considering geographic
diversification is therefore a vital piece to understanding why
fintechs are optimally positioned to disrupt the modern banking
sector.
18 Schildbach, J., & Wenzel, C. (2013). Bank performance in the US
and Europe. Current Issues, Global financial markets, B. Speyer, Ed.,
Frankfurt am Main, Germany: Deutsche Bank Research.
In learning from the dynamics of the more than 146,000
FDIC-insured branch banks across the United States, further
research on the topic of geographic diversification will serve as a
foundation on which innovation in branch banking, both digital
and physical, can continue at the remarkable rate that it has. By
taking advantage of diversification effects, fintechs especially
may continue to triumph in growth and profitability over
traditional
banking
while
maintaining
both
stability
and
solvency. If preparedness for an uncertain future of economic
shocks and disruptions is a key to success in the speculative
business
of
banking,
then
knowledge
of
the
underlying
mechanics through which uncertainty interacts with risk is the
toolkit by which the banks of the future will reign most lucrative.

Introduction
Growing up in Vietnam, I was haunted by a proverb, Nhất nam viết hữu thập nữviết vô,
which roughly translates: “Having one son means having a child, having ten daughters means not
having any child.” I learned it from the textbooks; I heard it in conversations; I saw
manifestations of it in the way parents relentlessly tried to have more babies in order to beget a
son, regardless of their preparedness. The implicit lesson, both inside and outside of the
schoolroom: being a girl meant I was deficient compared to boys.
Several years later, in a college Renaissance Literature class, I noticed with both
amusement and chagrin that the notion of the defective female not only spans hemispheres,
cultures, and eras, but also bleeds into scientific pursuits. According to Galen, the ancient Greek
anatomical structures, but “[women’s] lack of vital heat—of perfection—…result[s] in the
retention, inside, of structures that in the male are visible without” (Laqueur 4). This means,
among other things, that women’s genitalia and men’s are structurally homologous—with the
vagina and ovaries corresponding to the penis and scrotum—except that women’s organs fail to
extrude. In other words, women are men turned outside in. This model, later termed the “one-sex
model” by Thomas Laqueur, makes it clear that maleness is the default, the product of successful
gestation, while femaleness is incomplete, defective, faulty.
While this model consolidates male superiority, it also introduces a prominent issue of the
early modern period: if men and women are anatomically parallel, how can gender differences be
enforced? Jean E. Howard explains, “Because by this [Galenic] account male-female difference
was less grounded in ideas of absolute bodily difference than is typical today, much emphasis
was placed on behavioral differences and on distinctions of dress” (1619). More specifically,
early modern England relied on education to generate these behavioral differences that would
distinguish boys from girls: “Renaissance humanists… sought to gender young children through
pedagogy” (Wall 61). As Caroline Bowden puts it, “the provision of education in the family was
gendered, with girls receiving less tuition than boys, and in some cases it is clear that girls gained
only very basic skill” (90). The location and content of their education also differed: while boys
left home at the age of seven to receive formal training in Latin, rhetoric, grammar, logic, and
mathematics at grammar school, girls remained at home for domestic and religious lessons. As
education aimed to condition learners into virtuous citizens, Danielle Clark argues, it “inculcated
social values, acculturated the individual, and provided the learning deemed appropriate to the
social status held by the pupil,” directing boys toward a vocation and girls toward a “discourse of
containment” (19). In other words, the early modern educational model served to produce and
reinforce social and gender roles: men trained to become powerful and eloquent state leaders
while women prepared to become chaste, silent, and obedient wives, mothers, and mistresses of
the house. There was also an emphasis on women’s education not as an opportunity for
self-edification but rather as a preparation for fulfilling their matrimonial and household duties.4
Walter Ong specifically examines Latin language training as an enforcement of a
gendered education. In his influential paper “Latin Language Study as a Renaissance Puberty
Rite,” Ong considers the early modern teaching of Latin as a “puberty rite” through which young
4 See Vives; Bowden 88-90; Moncrief and McPherson, Chapter 1.
3 This is not to discredit the significant content of the female education “track.” As Wendy Wall’s work on
domesticity reveals, the “mistress of the house” needed expertise in multiple fields, including cooking, medicine,
pharmacology, nursing, food preservation, and home budgeting and economics.
2 For further discussion, see Moncrief and McPherson, Chapter 1.
