boys were inducted into a male tribe—an “extra-familial life which involve[s] a sense of break
with the past … together with segregation from the family and from those of the other sex, and
chastisement under the direction of elders for didactic purposes” (106). In essence, the cleavage
between Latin and vernacular English mirrors the division between an exclusively male world
and a domestic world with (and of) women. To become full members of the learned society, boys
must leave the company of women for the social milieu of powerful preceptors.
Implied in Ong’s argument is the notion that masculinity requires socialization in the
right environment, while femininity is the state that can be informally taught within the domestic
setting. This claim offers another model for understanding maleness and femaleness that may, at
first, appear to be in conflict with Galen’s, but Galen’s is a model for sexual, gestational
difference while Ong’s emphasizes differences that result from separate gender training. Early
modern sex and gender, then, undergo divergent (yet interconnected) processes of construction.
This important distinction between early modern sex and gender resonates with the modern
understanding of the sex/gender distinction proposed by Judith Butler, building on Simone de
Beauvoir’s generative argument in The Second Sex. In her analysis of de Beauvoir, Butler
contends that de Beauvoir’s powerful formulation, “One is not born, but rather becomes, a
woman” (de Beauvoir 301), suggests that gender and sex are separated, and that gender is an
aspect of identity acquired over time. Butler expounds, “sex is understood to be the invariant,
anatomically distinct, and factic aspects of the female body, whereas gender is the cultural
meaning and form that that body acquires, the variable modes of that body’s acculturation”
(Butler, “Sex” 35). Being “female” and being a “woman” are distinct modes: one is born into a
5 For further discussion of this argument, see Hartstock 133-52.
sexed body but grows into one’s gender during the process of socialization and cultural
acclimatization. However, neither Butler nor the early modern is strictly binary: Butler addresses
the instability of the binary distinction between sex and gender as well as the instability of the
male/female distinction even in biological sex; early modern philosophers made sense of
anatomy through the lens of social expectations (gender) even as they were performing
dissections. Vesalius’s illustration of the vaginal canal, reproduced below, reflects Galen’s
erroneous belief and makes a powerful statement about how much our beliefs and expectations
regulate our perception. Although it was produced after Vesalius operated on real human
cadavers, the illustration looks more like a penis (without testicles) than a vaginal canal.
6 For example, Butler writes, “If the immutable character of sex is contested, perhaps this construct called ‘sex’ is as
culturally constructed as gender; indeed, perhaps it was always already gender, with the consequence that the
distinction between sex and gender turns out to be no distinction at all.” See Butler, Gender Trouble, 10-11.
Image 1. Vesalius’s illustration of the vaginal canal
Due to the significance of education in the imposition of gender, the “relative
democratization of learning” for groups that had previously enjoyed little access to education,
and the wealth of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century printed texts on pedagogical methodologies
and the value of education for both boys and girls, among other reasons, early modern education
blossomed “on both the stage and page” (Moncrief and McPherson 1-2). Several playtexts
display explicit concern with education, as suggested by Rosaline’s question, “Shall I teach you
to know?” (Love’s Labor’s Lost IV.1.103) and Bianca’s statement, “I’ll not be tied to hours nor
‘pointed times/ But learn my lessons as I please myself” (The Taming of the Shrew III.1.19-20).
7 For a few examples, see Vives; Elyot; Ascham; Salter; Mulcaster; Batt; Pritchard; Kempe.
Interestingly, Renaissance playwrights sought to challenge the very education that shaped them
and to destabilize the deep-rooted framework of gender through their dramas. It is not difficult to
find examples of female characters from this period who “suggest both an awareness of the
constructed and performed nature of gender roles, and a desire to problematise and complicate
the classifications typically available as ways of seeing women” (Kamaralli 1123). In her
investigation of names in The Taming of the Shrew, Laurie Maguire points out that even when
Katherine sanctions Petruchio’s right to name everything, she still finds the space to slyly
reassert the full form of her own name, which Maguire interprets as an act of resistance.
Similarly, Patricia Parker contends, Bianca establishes herself as an independent scholar who
masters her own masters by flaunting fluency in Latin and demanding to study “as [she] pleases
[herself].” Anna Kamaralli offers an excellent reading of the four female characters in John
Webster’s The White Devil and Shakespeare’s The Winter’s Tale and their performance of
traditionally masculine traits, thereby calling into question the definability of womanhood. Janet
Adelman identifies in the characterization of Cleopatra in Shakespeare’s Antony and Cleopatra a
tension with the phallogocentric parameters according to which women are faulty men. These
characters also invite us to upend the teacher-pupil roles and imagine women not as passive
students but powerful instructors, an invitation that I will later take up in this thesis.
These plays, along with copious early modern instructional texts—such as Juan Luis
Vives’s Instruction of a Christen Woman (1529), Roger Ascham’s The Scholemaster (1570), and
William Kempe’s The Education of Children in Learning (1588)—also testify to the
inextricability of education, the construction of gendered and hierarchical social configuration,
and the (re)production and performance of both masculinity and femininity. The early modern
stage was, according to Moncrief and McPherson, a “key pedagogical site” to examine how
educational practices disciplined students as representatives of their social station and gender (4).
Nevertheless, scholarly discussions of early modern education until the first decade of the
twenty-first century gave only minimal attention to the matter of gender and almost none to the
ways in which pedagogy and performance intersect: Rebecca Bushnell’s The Culture of
Teaching: Early Modern Humanism in Theory and Practice offers a thorough discussion of the
advent and development of humanism throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries but
neglects its interplay with gender; Jeff Dolven’s Scenes of Instruction in Renaissance Romance
attempts to formulate a “poetics of pedagogy” by studying instructional scenes in prose
romances rather than the drama of the age; and a variety of texts concentrate on women’s
literacies in the early modern with little to no consideration of gender and performance. Moncrief
and McPherson’s edited collection goes furthest in exploring the rich intersection of gender,
pedagogy, and performance. The essays in this collection examine a variety of Renaissance
instructional and literary texts to illustrate that early modern pedagogy, especially the teaching of
gender, is explicitly performative. Moncrief and McPherson also examine the inseparability of
performance on stage and performance of gender in everyday life. As aforementioned,
distinctions of dress were meant to signify male-female differences, and crossdressing, “however
playfully undertaken, always threatened to expose the artifice of gender distinctions by showing
how easily one sex could assume the clothes and ape the behavior of the other” (Howard 1619).
As we know, early modern stage performances licensed crossdressing in plays that do and do not
thematize gender, since female parts were played exclusively by young boys during this time.
Nevertheless, not enough attention has been paid to scenes of (sexual and gender)
pedagogy in which women rise to the role of educators and men are relegated to studenthood.
What occasions women to teach? What conditions must be satisfied for women to safely
transition into an instructional role? What does it take to educate a man into manhood? In the
first part of my thesis, Love’s Cure offers an excellent platform to entertain these questions,
especially in its portrayal of budding romantic relationships. The play’s attempt to realign the
gender performance of its two protagonists, who are both transvestites, with their biological sex
sparks a complex series of educational imperatives that simultaneously deconstruct and
reconstruct its understanding of sex and gender. For the purpose of this thesis, I will focus only
on Lucio and his relationship with Genevora, for two reasons. First, Lucio regards himself as a
woman at the beginning of the play and maintains his femininity almost until the end. As my
research aims to examine gender presentation not as equivalent to biological sex but rather as the
product of social acculturation partially distinct from sex, I view Lucio as gender-fluid and
fruitful for the scope of my study. Second, this relationship features a female pedagogue. In my
analysis, I read Genevora as simultaneously a mother, a lover, and a teacher, and thus as a
challenge to Walter Ong’s proposition that early modern masculinity was only learned in the
closed male schoolroom. Lucio’s character arc illustrates a masculinity taught in the domestic
setting by a woman to a male-born student originally alienated from male society. More
importantly, I contend that while Genevora adopts a similar pedagogy to other male characters
who attempt to transform Lucio, her successful tutelage results from her acknowledgment and
encouragement of Lucio’s gender fluidity and performativity. Instead of viewing his femininity
9 That said, I will follow the playtext in using he/him/his pronouns for Lucio and she/her/hers for Clara throughout
this thesis for ease of reference.
8 And arguably transgender, though I am aware of my anachronism in using both terms here.
as an ignominious property to be cast off, Genevora is interested in the various gender
expressions that Lucio occupies and commands him to assume different gender roles as they suit
her needs.
The second part of my thesis shifts into a discussion of Shakespeare’s As You Like It.
Although this is a canonical text, there are surprisingly few materials written on Rosalind’s role
as an educator in the play. A large body of scholarship on As You Like It comments on her
crossdressing and the effect that it has on surrounding characters and the dramatic plot. My thesis
briefly explores her transvestism, but only in the service of a larger investigation into the
opportunities that playing a man opens up for Rosalind in her education of Orlando. More
specifically, I argue that under the guise of the young man Ganymede, Rosalind performs the
dual roles of a teacher and a physician, both versions of the “doctor.” Throughout the play, she
assumes these two “doctor” roles in parallel to bolster her authority and to exact a “transgressive
reinscription,” to borrow a term from Jonathan Dollimore: using irony or parody as “a mode of
transgression which finds expression through the inversion and perversion of just those
preexisting categories and structures …; a mode of transgression which seeks not an escape from
existing structures, but rather a subversive reinscription within them—and in the process a
dis-location of them” (Dollimore 57).
In other words, instead of striving for transcendence, this
version of transgression takes the form of upending or destabilizing ideological, “natural”
categories. For Rosalind, this transgressive reinscription means establishing her position in
traditionally male-dominated fields so as to effectively infiltrates the patriarchal order and
destabilizes the extant epistemological paradigm.
10 I mention this notion in passing in my examination of Love’s Cure, but will employ it more substantially in my
chapter on As You Like It.
As a whole, this project endeavors to disrupt the narrative of uninterrupted early modern
patriarchy. Love’s Cure and As You Like It tells the stories of women who upset the power
differential between the sexes and claim authority they could not ordinarily assume. These plays
explore and interrogate the theater and the classroom as sites where gender performance can
vitiate entrenched power structures. By examining the gendered pedagogical dynamics in these
plays, I hope to reveal how every instance of teaching and learning offers opportunities for
shifting the grounds of power and authority. They always allow for the possibility of resistance,
transgression, and subversion—incrementally, perhaps, but no less powerful for that.
Chapter 1: The Case of Male Pupil and Female Pedagogue in Love’s Cure
Who is the average schoolteacher in the United States? A 43-year-old white woman with
over a decade of teaching experience, according to data published in April 2020 by the U.S.
Department of Education (Tai and Westat). While it is true that the demographic of
schoolteachers (excluding higher education) is now predominantly female, this has not always
been the case. Up until the common school movement of the late 1830s, men dominated the
teaching profession (Provenzo). During the early modern period, it was at best bizarre and at
worst transgressive to imagine women as pedagogues. More often than not, early modern literary
works, especially playtexts, position women as students who need instructions from male
masters. Highly canonical examples include Shakespeare’s The Taming of the Shrew, which
features two sisters as students and three male suitors acting as teachers, and The Tempest, in
which Prospero teaches Miranda about the male species for the first time.11
However, the multiplicity of female student figures in literature does not imply that there
was no attempt to question the standard male-tutor-with-female-pupil dynamic. Just as modern
society questions the pay gap between men and women undertaking the same work, or the
tendency for women to end up in lower-ranking and untenured positions in higher education,
several early modern dramatists interrogate the gender dynamics and politics in their scenes of
instruction through educational, social, and ontological lenses. One salient example appears in
Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher’s Love’s Cure, or The Martial Maid. The main plot deals
with the gender transformation of two siblings—Clara and Lucio—who have been brought up
separately as members of the opposite sex—Lucio raised by their mother Eugenia and Clara by
11 As I will briefly mention later, ballads and pornography more often portray women as the dominant and
experienced participant, in keeping with their exploration and inversion of social norms. Dramas are the opposite:
women in early modern drama tend to be delicate tabulae rasae.
their father Alvarez. Twenty years later, the family is reunited, and the siblings are commanded
to conform to their expected gender behaviors. This play offers a divergent narrative in its
construction of the relationship between its male lead Lucio and his love interest Genevora, a
noblewoman. The pedagogical dynamic between the lovers skews toward the woman: Genevora
appears to be simultaneously an experienced woman showing a naïve man the “sexual ABCs”
and a mother teaching her child the tenets of (wo)manhood (Traub 295).
These two possibilities interweave closely, as is evident from the ambiguous diction in
Genevora’s speech at the double duel. In this final scene, Vitelli and his second Lamorall prepare
to duel against Alvarez and his son Lucio to resolve their long-running feud. When the time for
combat comes, the intended duelists are interrupted by Clara (Alvarez’s daughter and Vitelli’s
lover), Genevora (Vitelli’s sister and Lucio’s lover), and Eugenia (Alvarez’s wife), who plead
with them not to fight. Genevora declaims:
Oh Lucio!
Be thou more mercifull: thou bear’st fewer yeers,
Art lately wean’d from soft effeminacy,
A maidens manners, and a maidens heart
Are neighbours still to thee: be then more milde,
Proceed not to this combat; bee’s thou desperate
Of thine own life? yet (deerest) pitty mine:
Thy valour’s not thine owne, I gave it thee,
These eyes begot it, this tongue bred it up,
This breast would lodge it: doe not use my gifts
To mine own ruine: I have made these rich,
Be not so thanklesse, to undoe me for’t. (V.3.110-121, emphasis mine)
The Oxford English Dictionary defines “wean” as the act of “accustom[ing] (a child or young
animal) to the loss of its mother’s milk” (OED, “wean” v., 1). This word immediately recalls a
mother-and-child dynamic in the interactions between the lovers. In fact, Genevora’s speech is
littered with language of parenting, italicized in the quotation above: “to beget” means to bring (a
child) into existence (OED, “beget” v., 2.a), while “to breed” not only implies the environment in
which one grows up but also connotes the education of young persons (OED, “breed” v., I.10.b).
By employing these verbs, Genevora firmly establishes her position as a mother without whom
there will be no masculine Lucio. In other words, she imagines Lucio as the feminized infant
who comes to be through her parturition and requires her parenting.
Genevora is not the first theatrical character to acknowledge the necessity of women in
the formation of masculinity, however. In fact, her speech harks back to a moment in
Shakespeare’s Love’s Labor’s Lost, when Lord Biron (or Berowne) declares:
[For] women’s sake—by whom we men are men—
Let us once lose our oaths to find ourselves,
Or else we lose ourselves to keep our oaths. (IV.3.334-6)
Here, Biron relinquishes the definition of masculinity as an exclusive single-sex academy and
acknowledges that “masculinity is expressed only in relationship” (Moncrief 123).
That is, men
do not gain masculine honor and self-enhancement through isolated study but through
interactions with and positioning relative to women, for whose sake (and by whose maternal
offices) “men are men.” Of course, Biron might just be referring to the fact that we are all born
of women—an interpretation that Love’s Cure certainly takes advantage of. But Biron does not
claim that “people are people” or “babies are babies” or “boys are boys,” but specifically “men
are men,” insisting that women play a role in boys’ maturation into men, not just their existence
as human beings. Love’s Cure is essentially making the same claim, but the play takes its
“transgressive reinscription” a step further by having Genevora proclaim her own significance.
As opposed to Love’s Labor’s Lost, what we witness in Love’s Cure is not a reflection by the man
12 For an excellent analysis of this speech, see Moncrief, “‘Teach Us, Sweet Madam’.
but an explicit assertion of authority by the woman: Genevora knows herself to be the master and
claims her role: “Thy valour’s not thine owne, I gave it thee.”
Interestingly, Love’s Cure proposes more than one way “we men are men” by women.
The first, as we have identified in the use of “wean,” is through the narrative of motherhood,
which signals that Lucio’s manhood results from the entire process of Genevora’s gestation,
parturition, and parenting. Another route interprets “to breed” not as parenting but as copulation
and reproduction: not only has Genevora birthed and raised Lucio, but she also breeds with him,
thus conflating the parental and erotic dynamics between the two. This word, along with
previous scenes in the play, explicitly spells out sexual education as the catalyst for Lucio’s
gender transformation. For the first half of the play, Lucio presents as a young, innocent boy/girl
so ignorant of the “sexual ABC’s” that he expresses surprise at the prospect of desire beyond a
kiss. He is not exceptional in his cluelessness. Valerie Traub makes a case that “Renaissance
texts are populated with women and men who simply do not know what other people seem to
know; and more often than not, this lack of knowledge consistently evokes a pedagogical
imperative that is elided or refused or fails” (295). In the case of Love’s Cure, the “pedagogical
imperative” that springs from Lucio’s lack of knowledge, his initiation into the arts of love,
officially begins with Genevora’s erotic instructions. Their kiss in Act 4, Scene 4 communicates
new sexual knowledge that leads to “strange new motions” and “alteration,” which serve as a
turning point for Lucio’s gender formation (IV.4.12-14). Shortly after this kiss, in response to
Genevora’s chiding for not protecting her love token, Lucio exclaims:
My womanish soul, which hitherto hath govern’d
This coward flesh, I feel departing from me;
And in me by her beauty is inspir’d
A new, and masculine one: instructing me
What’s fit to do or suffer; powerful love
That hast with loud, and yet a pleasing thunder
Rous’d sleeping manhood in me, thy new creature,
Perfect thy work so that I may make known
Nature (though long kept back) will have her own. (IV.4.54-62, emphasis mine)
This monologue details Lucio’s most conscious utterance of his gender transformation from a
“womanish soul” into a “masculine one.” Crucially, this transformation relies heavily on
Genevora’s beauty, which Lucio claims to have “inspir’d” a new soul into him. Etymologically
derived from the Latin prefix “in–” and the verb “spīrāre,” which means to breathe, “inspire”
imagines the couple’s kiss as the literal act of Genevora breathing out and Lucio breathing in.13
This literalization signifies that Lucio’s soul, be it “womanish” or “masculine,” is not an inherent
element within his natural body but rather a property obtained through and gendered by his
participation in an erotic act. Intriguingly, Lucio’s sexual socialization, particularly his
description of the kiss as Genevora “instructing [him]/ What’s fit to do or suffer,” bears a striking
resemblance to that of the hapless male lover, Tomalin, in Thomas Nashe’s narrative poem “The
Choise of Valentines.” Tomalin, just like Lucio, is “clueless about the mechanics of sex,
specifically about how to pleasure a woman” (Traub 114-15). On the whole, their experiences fit
into the larger sexual narrative, which employs the compelling trope of naiveté that invites
tutelage from the more experienced woman who performs the role of instructor. In Love’s Cure,
Lucio and Genevora’s sexual encounter inaugurates a pedagogical process, or at least a
pedagogical dynamic, that Lucio identifies in this soliloquy and that conforms to Genevora’s
speech in the dueling scene cited above. In this fashion, Lucio’s gender transformation is
“revealed to be the result of a particular social production, a process of knowledge construction,”
13 Interestingly, the image of Genevora breathing into Lucio harks back to the biblical account of the creation of
men: “And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and
man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7 identify which translation you’re using here). This parallelism solidifies
Genevora’s position of power, possibly at the expense of the erotic dimension of the relationship.
one that relies heavily on education through participation in sexual acts (Traub 117-18).
What these two scenes illuminate is that whether she plays the role of a mother or a
romantic partner, Genevora undeniably activates Lucio’s integration into masculinity through her
(sexual) tutelage. This proposition stands in contrast with Walter Ong’s influential observation
that the departure from domestic life into Latin training was a kind of male “puberty rite” (Ong
103). In fact, Lucio has never fully entered the exclusively male society and remains entirely
foreign to it, until Genevora’s interposition. We see this in Alvarez and Bobadilla’s futile attempt
to redeem Lucio’s manliness:
Alvarez.
Thou hast made me mad: and I will beat thee dead
Then bray the in a morter, and new mold thee
But I wil alter thee.
Bobadilla.
‘Twill never be:
He has bin three days practicing to drink,
Yet still he sips, like to a waiting woman,
And looks as he were murdering of a fart
Among wild Irish swaggerers. (IV.3.25-31)
Bobadilla highlights Lucio’s status as an outcast who fails to enter the male world by comparing
him to “a waiting woman,” a sneer at not only Lucio’s womanly behavior, but also the
accompanying threat of downward social mobility. Furthermore, while the play is set in Spain, it
is performed to an English audience well aware of English colonialism in Ireland. Ireland, like
many others colonized countries, was often feminized, “increasingly imaged in wifely terms” in
direct contrast with England, her masculine imperial master (Valente 190).
In positioning Lucio
“among wild Irish swaggerers,” Bobadilla relegates him to the world of uncultured, unlearned
(wild) women (Irish) who lack proper, courtly behaviors (swaggerers). All three layers of
otherness—in terms of gender, class, and race and ethnicity—simultaneously pronounce the
14 For further discussion of the English colonial discourse about Ireland, see also Stevens et al.
danger of Lucio’s wanting manliness and confirm the men’s desperation and inability to
transform him. When all their efforts prove to no avail, they resort to rage, carnality, and
violence:
Ther’s only one course left, that may redeem thee,
Which is, to strike the next man that you meet,
And if we chance to light upon a woman,
Take her away, and use her like a man,
Or I wil cut thy hamstrings. (IV.3.37-41, emphasis mine)
While Anne Duncan cites this passage as an example of “the connection between rage and the
performance of masculinity,” I am more concerned with the implication that sexual knowledge is
an agent or catalyst of manly honor (399). We have seen in Lucio’s soliloquy above that it is not
rage that “rous’d sleeping manhood” in him; it is his kiss with Genevora. In other words, sexual
experience, rather than violence, triggers this process of masculinization. However, as Valerie
Traub makes clear, “eroticism isn’t just something that people do (…); it is something that
people learn; it requires initiation, experimentation, education, [and] practice” (119). In that case,
Alvarez’s appeal to a final “course,” a term with forceful pedagogical connotations, does not
terminate where he imagines it would: at a single lewd act of “[using] her like a man.” Instead, it
(unintentionally) marks the beginning of Lucio’s courtship with Genevora and thus occasions an
erotic educational process. Ironically, this educational process at once echoes and fundamentally
differs from the one implemented by the men themselves. As a pedagogue, Genevora chides as
the men have chided: “Nay you are rude; pray you forbeare; you offer now/ More then the
breeding of a Gentleman/ Can give you warrant for.” (IV.4.1-3). She instructs as the men have
instructed: both parties adopt the learning-by-doing approach, Genevora with desire and kissing
and Alverez with fighting and violence. Finally, when Lucio’s indecisiveness causes him to lose
her “favour”—that is, her gloves, which were given as a love token—to another suitor, she
resorts to “torment” in the same manner as Alvarez has threatened to “bray [Lucio] in the
morter”:
For thy torment,
If my poore beauty be of any power,
Mayst thou doat on it desperately: but never
Presume to hope for grace, till thou recover
And weare the favour that was ravish’d from thee. (IV.4.45-52, emphasis mine)
In other words, Genevora employs similar pedagogical techniques as Alvarez and Bobadilla.
And yet, she yields the desired outcome as the men could not. Lucio’s successful education in
masculinity, then, results not from the method of instruction but the instructor and the content.
Instead of drinking and “strik[ing]” with men, Lucio thrives under the sexual tutelage of a
woman. More broadly speaking, he moves from one domestic scene—where he finds in his
mother Eugenia a model for imitation—into another—where he learns from his mother-like
fiancée. Contrary to Walter Ong’s argument, what the men fail miserably to do can be achieved
rather seamlessly by two women: Eugenia teaches him to be a woman, and Genevora allegedly
turns him into a man.
What exactly renders Genevora a more proficient educator than Alvarez and Bobadilla? I
contend that Genevora’s success is attributable to her disinterest in the binary caricature of
masculinity; on the contrary, she acknowledges that Lucio has the wisdom of all the different
gender roles that he has played and employs her various roles to capitalize on this fluidity and
capaciousness. A salient manifestation of this practice is in her speech at the double duel where
Genevora at once establishes her position as the mother and reasserts her power as the instructor.
“[B]e then more milde,” she commands her lover, asking him to temporarily reassume his “soft
effeminacy,” which Lucio has practiced in his feminized infancy. Her directive encourages us to
read “effeminacy” and by extension “masculinity” as a performance that one dials up and down
rather than something that can be wholly eradicated and superseded. Her use of “soft
effeminacy” in conjunction with “wean’d” also reinforces this idea of gender performativity, for
the definition of “wean” as the act of “accustoming to” anticipates Butler’s language of
acculturation and a “contingent construction of meaning” (Butler, Gender Trouble 139). In other
words, gender in Love’s Cure is neither innate nor constant, but a series of possibilities to be
performed as convenience and/or ethics dictate. To Genevora, Lucio’s earlier childhood
femininity is not something shameful; instead, it contains useful information for him to draw on
to become more expansive, more compassionate, and an altogether better partner for her. Thus,
what makes Genevora stand out from Lucio’s other instructors is her cognizance of what we
might now call the performativity of gender, her appreciation of Lucio’s various qualities of
different genders, and her awareness of the significance of her presence. As a result, Lucio’s
change of gender depends not on his will but hers: when she is upset that he cannot protect her
love, he assumes masculinity; when she is upset that he is about to harm her family, he is
compelled to revert to softness. Ultimately, Lucio’s gender is not only a performance; it is a
series of performances cultivated and authorized by a female director and pedagogue.
In looking at Lucio’s gender transformation, which results from his accumulation of
sexual knowledge, I have illustrated not only that, and how, a woman can occupy the role of an
educator, but also the efficacy of her tutelage. Throughout Love’s Cure, Genevora weaves
together motherhood and professorship, and in so doing, successfully trains Lucio to become a
man—a considerable feat that other male figures in the play fail to do. What is remarkable is that
Genevora adopts a similar approach to teaching as Alvarez and Bobadilla do, with an emphasis
on instruction, punishment, and practice, but yields vastly different results. Her favorable
outcome, then, must be attributable to her ability to perceive Lucio as both the feminized,
helpless infant and the masculine partner who has adult sexuality and can relate to her with
desire. By understanding this simultaneity and by imagining her authority as both motherly and
teacherly, Genevora asserts her claim to the result—Lucio’s honorable manliness/ manly
honor—in both familial and academic terms: she simultaneously begets his outstanding qualities
and trains him to develop a full consciousness of and mastery over those qualities. Consequently,
she also reserves the right to revoke those characteristics and skillfully manipulates Lucio’s
gender performance, calling on him to privilege his masculinity or femininity as she sees fit.
Read this way, the play is as invested in recording Genevora’s growth as a pedagogue as it is
keen on the notion of gender as a performance, or the actual erotic content and training that
contributes to Lucio’s increasing masculinity. Whatever the case, Love’s Cure undeniably
compels its audience to interrogate and dismiss patriarchal assumptions about who can be a
teacher, and what it means to be, become, or perform a gender.
Chapter 2: Doctor Rosalind Dismantles Patriarchal Authority in As You Like It
In December 2020, Joseph Epstein wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal, calling for
First Lady Jill Biden to drop her honorific. “‘Dr. Jill Biden’ sounds and feels fraudulent, not to
say a touch comic,” writes Epstein, suggesting that only physicians with M.D. are entitled to,
well, the title. Dr. Biden only earned an Ed.D., a Doctor of Education, “through a dissertation
with [an] unpromising title,” so she should think again and “forthwith drop the doc.” Never mind
that it reeks of misogyny and sarcastic condescension; the piece leaves me questioning whether
Epstein fully comprehends what the doctorate signifies. The term “doctor” was originally a
linguistic derivative of the Latin verb docēre, meaning “to teach.” Over time, it gained use as an
academic title when the first doctorates were conferred in Europe, for those who have obtained a
doctorate were qualified to teach or express an authoritative opinion. A physician, who had gone
through a long university education,
would therefore also be referred to as a “Doctour of
Phisyk” (documented in Chaucer, Canterbury Tales Prol. l. 413) or “doctour of deth”
(documented in Langland, Piers Plowman B. xviii. 362), to distinguish from their colleagues in
church (Doctor of the Church) and law (Doctor of Law). Throughout its history, the term
“doctor” has accumulated nuances, each becoming more or less salient depending on the context
in which the term appears. These nuances are not mutually exclusive—on the contrary, they are
closely connected, and the activation of one does not inhibit or negate the (linguistic) validity of
others. So, Mr. Epstein, the answer to your question is yes, not only is there a doctor in the White
House, but women have also presumed upon the title and role of doctor for centuries.
15 Not every medical practitioner in early modern England earned the title of doctor. In fact, only physicians, who
had received extensive training and schooling in universities, were singled out for the appellation. This was because
university education not only transmitted knowledge about healing but also trained students in cultivating and
exercising their good judgment and advice, two crucial concepts in establishing professional authority. For further
discussion, see Cook.
The inquiry into these varying resonances of the term “doctor” and their interplay is not
merely a twenty-first century phenomenon: we can also see manifestations of it in early modern
literature. The present chapter concentrates, in particular, on the maneuvering of the role and its
various forms of authority in Shakespeare’s pastoral comedy As You Like It. In this play, the main
character Rosalind is a witty woman with a delightful tongue-in-cheek sense of humor. When she
meets her love interest, Orlando, in the forest, she pointedly performs—literally so, for she
remains in disguise as the young, male Ganymede during the majority of her interactions with
Orlando—as both a teacher and a physician to shape him into the lover she desires. Throughout
the play, she uses the two most prevalent resonances of “doctor”—physician and teacher—in
parallel as roles to mutually bolster her authority and to infiltrate the patriarchal order. By doing
so, Rosalind effectively ridicules and destabilizes the existing epistemological paradigm.
One salient moment in this pattern appears as soon as Rosalind sees Orlando in the forest,
when she asks about the time and then demands to “tell” him about how time functions
(III.2.314). Rosalind unapologetically rejects the Renaissance trope of “the swift foot of time,”
which is often cited in early modern literature, especially in Shakespeare’s sonnets,
and
proceeds to explain that time moves at different speeds for different people. Her seemingly trivial
question becomes highly productive when considered in conjunction with Jaques’s earlier
musings on time and the different stages of maturation:
All the world’s a stage,
And all the men and women merely players.
They have their exits and entrances,
And one man in his time plays many parts,
His acts being seven ages. At first the infant,
16 Two examples: Shakespeare’s Sonnet 19: “Make glad and sorry seasons as thou fleet,/ And do whate’er thou wilt,
swift-footed Time”; and Sonnet 65: “O fearful meditation! where, alack,/ Shall time’s best jewel from time’s chest lie
hid?/ Or what strong hand can hold his swift foot back?” (emphasis mine).
Then the whining schoolboy …
And then the lover,
Sighing like furnace, with a woeful ballad
Made to his mistress’ eyebrow. (II.7.146-156, emphasis mine)
In this passage, “time” refers to one’s lifetime, which can be divided into seven stages: infant,
schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon (or foolish old man in pantaloons), and finally,
“second childishness and mere oblivion” (II.7.172). Thus, the concept of time in Jaques’s model
refers to not only a point of existence measured in hours or minutes, but also to the broad idea of
time as the continued progression of existence and events. This progression is not linear but
circular; humans ultimately return to a second iteration of “childishness” and then finally quietus.
Subsequently, Rosalind’s question can be understood as partially a query about where Orlando is
in the stages of men: it is not just “what is ’t o’clock?” but “what is ’t o’clock with him?” The
phrase “o’clock” is also apt to evoke the cyclicity of time: etymologically an abbreviated form of
“of the clock,” both the letter “o” and the image of the physical clock suggest a circular contour
and movement. Read this way, Rosalind is feeling out what her role is going to be in making the
clock move forward, essentially giving Orlando a placement test before writing a curriculum.
This curriculum, it is hinted, is not going to be straightforward, for time itself is not linear, nor
will Orlando’s progress be. Furthermore, if we use Jaques’s multi-stage model of time to assess
Orlando’s level and progress, then Rosalind’s proposition to “give him some good counsel” is
appropriate. Jaques’s description of a lover here aligns with what Rosalind later cites as cues to
“know a man in love” (III.2.376-377). By dismissing Orlando’s claim to “loverness”—I offer my
detailed analysis of this dismissal below—she positions him as a “whining schoolboy,” the stage
immediately preceding lover (for it is clear he is no longer an infant “mewling and puking in the
nurse’s arms” [II.7.151]). If this is so, Orlando’s earlier poetic declarations of love can be
regarded as “whining,” and he the schoolboy “unwillingly to school.” This taxonomy provides
the pedagogical imperative for Rosalind to rise to the role of the doctor (teacher) who can mentor
Orlando to the next stage: lover.
At the same time, this opening motif of time initiates Rosalind’s process of “transgressive
reinscription,” the term Jonathan Dollimore coined to the subversive inversion or reversal of
ideological categories.
In rejecting the conventional understanding of time as swift-footed and
constant, and in providing humorously realistic evidence for her argument, Rosalind inaugurates
her own system of knowledge independent of masculine poetics and courtly parameters. In this
system, the foundation of Renaissance humanist education—that is, Latin language learning—is
not the “puberty rite,” the required condition for young boys to be inducted into an exclusive
male tribe, as Ong would have it. Instead, Latin training is degraded into “the burden of lean and
wasteful learning”—something that offers little reward for abundant effort (III.2.329). This
trivialization
of Latin also serves as a vicarious critique of institutionalized masculine learning
and its various pedagogical methods as impractical and ineffectual in imparting transferable
knowledge and skills.
In Rosalind’s system of understanding, the “natural” categories of male and female are
also problematized, curiously, through the establishment of the categories of “lover” vs.
non-lover (or “loving yourself”). As I explained in the introduction, the Galenic model of
anatomy proposes that men and women share the same anatomical structures, the only difference

“one-sex model” contends that maleness is the telos of gestation, while femaleness is a form of
incompletion. A sloppy or lay interpretation of this model, which disregards anything invisible or
intangible as irrelevant, is the (in)famous use of “nothing,” such as in Much Ado About Nothing,
as a slang for a woman’s private part, for she has “no thing” or lacks a penis. This phallocentric
discourse perpetually confines women within a negative
space: always lacking, always
needing.
In her conversation with Orlando, Rosalind sets out to invert this use of the negative:
ROSALIND, as Ganymede
There is none of my uncle’s marks upon you. He taught me how to
know a man in love, in which cage of rushes I am sure you are not
prisoner.
ORLANDO
What were his marks?
ROSALIND, as Ganymede
A lean cheek, which you have not; a blue eye and sunken, which
you have not; an unquestionable spirit, which you have not; a
beard neglected, which you have not … Then your hose should be
ungartered, your bonnet unbanded, your sleeve unbuttoned, your
shoe untied, and everything about you demonstrating a careless
desolation. But you are no such man. You are rather point-device
in your accouterments, as loving yourself than seeming the lover of
any other. (III.2.380-391, emphasis mine)
Here, instead of repudiating this patriarchal theory of women, Rosalind delegates the negative
space to Orlando. In describing his not-a-lover mien, she reiterates the phrase “which you have
not” four times and attaches the negative prefix un- to almost every adjective, emphasizing the
lack that is, ironically, glaringly present in his accouterments. In the same way that Galen and
other prominent early modern anatomists define the female body strictly in relation to its male

a non-lover who exists wholly in the un-s and the have-nots. Most interestingly, Rosalind’s
standards for a proper lover, according to which she is critiquing Orlando, is a list of
stereotypical images. After all, early modern English literature “abounds with examples of
melancholy lovers, who burn with passion, die of breaking hearts, or simply waste away”
(Dawson 12). Rosalind mocks both the (non-)lover (here, Orlando) and the trite depictions of a
lover in their “careless desolation.” In the time of Shakespeare, Lesel Dawson explains, “while
the clothing and bearing of the lovesick individual suggest that the symptoms of erotic
melancholy were privately felt, the fact that this inwardness is expressed through recognizable
conventions of posture, dress, and behaviour indicates the way in which lovesickness was a role
performed as well as an emotion experienced” (34).
That is to say, one must look and dress the
part if one wishes to be considered as a serious lover. By using the popular lovesick tropes
curated and often employed by male poets, Rosalind is not only ridiculing the superficiality of
early modern expressions of love, but she is also using the master’s tool to dismantle the master’s
house—that is, using the rhetorical devices of the male lovers against one of its own
representatives (Lorde 110). This subversion of power is even more impressive when we recall
that Rosalind is dressed as a man in this scene. While it comes at the (temporary) expense of her
feminine expression, this male costume enables her to enter the male society and effectively
manipulates masculine authority in her favor. As the plot progresses, Rosalind becomes even

more explicit in her criticism of the tropes of lovesickness and the poetic rhetoric of attributing

Eventually, Rosalind concludes that Orlando appears to be “loving yourself than seeming
the lover of any other,” condemning his expressions as rooted in narcissistic infatuation rather
than love. One may note that the few characters whom Orlando speaks of and/or interacts with in
the first act are all men: his father, brothers, their servant Adam, Charles the wrestler, Duke
Frederick, and Le Beau. There is no mention of a mother or any female figure before his
acquaintance with Rosalind and Celia in Scene 2.
Thus, as far as we can observe from the text,
Orlando has always been contained within a male circle; and yet, he was never truly a part of that
exclusive community, for he lacks “all gentlemanlike qualities” (I.1.68). Already, even as a man
in this “man’s man’s man’s world” (in the words of singer James Brown), Orlando is a liminal
figure who fails to be positively defined: though he tries to assert himself as the son of a Sir
Rowland de Bois, others—including the audience—know him as a man who lacks gentlemanlike
behaviors and therefore a social position. Rosalind’s suggestion about his narcissism might
therefore be underscoring Orlando’s confinement within the masculine homosocial circuit,
thereby implying that the socially constructed wall of masculinity is accountable for his
“negativeness.”23
At the same time, Rosalind’s conclusion about Orlando’s neat appearance also hints at her
reason for remaining cross-dressed even in the safety of the forest. As Marjorie Garber suggests,

“As the lessons she gives to Orlando immediately testify, Rosalind does not have to learn much,
if anything, about love, or the quality and depth of her own feelings” (Garber 104). In fact, it is
Orlando who needs an education, who must learn “what ‘tis to love” (V.2.87). By electing to be
“caparisoned like a man,” Rosalind upends the expected patriarchal pattern of a father or
husband educating his wife and daughter and offers a reverse paradigm of the female
schoolmaster and male pupil. She dresses in male attire so that she can be liberal with her
criticism and fashion Orlando into the lover that she desires, rather than a “point-device” man
primarily concerned with “loving [him]self.” The phrase “point-device,” which appears most
frequently in relatively staid texts of the period, such as chronicles of monarchs or discourses on
scripture, connotes the quality of being “perfectly correct or precise, esp. in matters of dress or
appearance; scrupulous, neat, fastidious” (OED, “point-device” adj.). Nevertheless, there seems
to be significant support for reading “point-device” as a double entendre: “point” being a
possible euphemism for the phallus and “device” meaning “will, pleasure, inclination, fancy,
desire”—as in “leave one at one’s own device” (OED, “device” n., 3.a). Combined, this phrase
could mean punctilious, neat, and meticulous, but it could also be interpreted as “at the pleasure
of your penis.” The disconcerting implication that follows is the association of perfection and
correctness with phallic desire: the receiving partner in a sexual act is somehow deficient, and
her “no-thing” can only be made perfect through the presence of the phallus. By this logic, we
may understand Rosalind’s mockery of Orlando’s appearance as, indirectly, a double critique of
phallocentricism and narcissism. Once again, we see how Rosalind wields her new masculine
power to undo the inveterate mindset of male prerogatives for her benefit.
Through their conversation in Act 3, Scene 2, Rosalind also makes clear her intention to
draw on the medical connotation of “doctor” and perform as a physician in their relationship.
When asked to recount some of the “principal evils that [God] laid to the charge of women,” she
immediately refuses: “No, I will not cast away my physic but on those that are sick.” However,
she also opens up an opportunity for Orlando to enlist her help: “If I could meet that fancy
monger [who worships Rosalind], I would give him some good counsel, for he seems to have the
quotidian of love upon him” (III.2.364-372). Here, not only is Rosalind claiming to possess some
“physic” that she will bestow upon the “sick,” she is also diagnosing Orlando with the “quotidian
of love,” in which “quotidian” is short for the quotidian fever or quotidian malaria. Figuratively,
“quotidian” also denotes a state of emotional or nervous agitation (OED), a fitting understanding
of love in physiological terms. Then she goes on to validate her diagnosis and qualifications as a
physician by listing the symptoms of love in the passage cited above. The seeming medical
check-up concludes with her naming the disease (“Love is merely a madness” [III.2.407]) and
offering a treatment plan (“Yet I profess curing it by counsel” [III.2.412]). This entire exchange
follows an almost methodical process of medical examination, further highlighting Rosalind and
Orlando’s dynamic as doctor and patient.
Importantly, Rosalind also invokes Galenic physiology later when detailing her proposed
cure: “… and this way will I take upon me to wash your liver as clean as a sound sheep’s heart,
that there shall not be one spot of love in ’t” (III.2.429-431, emphasis mine). Her reference to the
liver recalls humoral theory, which “assumed connections among bodily fluids, the four
elements, and the seasons, leading to a theory of temperaments or bodily dispositions and
psychosomatic phenomena” (Baltussen). During the Renaissance, lovesickness was considered a
serious physiological affliction. Galen himself treated love as a disease. Lovesickness was said to
have resulted from an imbalance of the humors, especially excessive heat and blood. In the scene
in question, Rosalind’s invokes the Galenic understanding that blood was produced exclusively
by the liver. Shakespeare could also have been influenced by Marsilio Ficino’s model of
lovesickness as a pathological form of desire. According to Ficino, lovesickness is the result of
an “enchantment” or “bewitchment,” a pathological sequence of erotic melancholy in which
the eye, wide open and fixed upon someone, shoots the darts of its own rays into the eyes
of the bystander, and along with those darts, which are the vehicles of the spirits, aims
that sanguine vapor which we call spirit[.] Hence the poisoned dart pierces through the
eyes, and since it is shot from the heart of the shooter, it seeks again the heart of the man
being shot, as its proper home; it wounds the heart, but in the heart’s hard back wall it is
blunted and turns back into blood. This foreign blood, being somewhat foreign to nature
of the wounded man, infects his blood.
(Ficino 160)
Thus, the lover becomes sick with alien blood, which must be cleansed through the liver. What
we learn from Galenic humoralism and Ficino’s explanation of the origin of lovesickness is that
the liver is a key organ in the understanding and cure of the malady, and that by promising to
“wash your liver as clean as a sound sheep’s heart,” Rosalind simultaneously demonstrates her
in-depth knowledge of Galen and consolidates her prestige and authority as an erudite doctor
(physician) fluent in the medical language of the time.
Having successfully asserted her position, Rosalind takes advantage of her medical
authority as leverage for her role as an educator: she proposes to cure “by counsel,” which is to
say, by instruction.
This recommended remedy appears to run counter to Galen and the
humoralists. During the early modern period, there were four prominent ways to redress

However, Rosalind’s
trickeryis innovative (and perhaps even poses a counterargument to Galen) for three reasons.
Firstly, Rosalind’s proposal to help Orlando is anything but altruistic, nor is her goal necessarily

preferences in love, thereby training him to become lovelorn in the particular way that will suit
her. Secondly, Rosalind requests that Orlando view her (posing as Ganymede) as his beloved so
that he can practice wooing her (Rosalind), and she can teach and give feedback on the spot.
Their play-acting courtship serves as exercise in the art of love; it adds an experiential
component, which Jeff Dolven has illustrated to be potentially powerful.
Thirdly and most
importantly, Rosalind’s cure by instruction brings in the pedagogical overtone of “doctor” in
conjunction with the present medical connotation of the term. In this manner, Rosalind appeals to

These two resonances of doctor prove to be mutually reinforcing and conducive to
Rosalind’s transformation of Orlando. In the popular scene of instruction in Act 4, Scene 1, she
returns to the topic of lovesickness in her lesson:
ROSALIND, as Ganymede
No, faith, die by attorney. The poor world is almost six
thousand years old, and in all this time there was not any man died in his own person,
videlicet, in a love cause. Troilus had his brains dashed out with a Grecian club, yet he
did what we could to die before, and he is one of the patterns of love. Leander, he would
have lived many a fair year though Hero had turned nun, if it had not been for a hot
midsummer night, for, good youth, he went but forth to wash him in the Hellespont and,
being taken with the cramp, was drowned; and the foolish chroniclers of the age found it
was Hero of Sestos. But these are all lies. Men have died from time to time and worms
have eaten them, but not for love. (IV.1.99-113, original emphasis)
As part of her lecture on love, Rosalind debunks the myth that love can lead to death, as poets
and medical practitioners of the time contended. In her system of knowledge, men die because of
love only by proxy—that is, lovesickness might instigate actions that lead to death, such as
“[having one’s] brains dashed out with a Grecian club” or “being taken with the cramp and …
drowned” when swimming. Ironically, she exploits her title as a doctor in the Galenic tradition to
debunk the Galenic myth about the fatal power of lovesickness. Simultaneously, this comment
reinforces her expertise as a teacher and extends her earlier criticism of the overused lovesick
tropes. Now going beyond merely listing clichéd representations of the lover, Rosalind employs
her knowledge of the poetics and calls out the histrionic romance heroes by name: Troilus of
Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida (and/or of Chaucer’s Troilus and Criseyde) and Leander of
Christopher Marlowe’s Hero and Leander. It’s especially tempting to understand Rosalind to be
including Shakespeare among the male poets whose exaggerated rhetoric she mocks: an
authentic moment of master’s tools dismantling the master’s house!
Rosalind also goes so far as to label the “chroniclers of the age” foolish and their
depictions of lovelorn men as “all lies.” There might also be a sexual double entendre in the
word “die,” for orgasm is also termed la petite mort, or “the little death.” With this definition,
Rosalind’s concluding remark could be interpreted as a lampoon of men’s carnal desire: they
have attained sexual release from time to time, but they have never done so for love (rather than
for pure pleasure). Moreover, I identify in her speech a subtle commentary on gender discourse:
women would be blamed for the tragedies of men, even if they “had turned nun.” Speaking as a
woman, Rosalind might be dismissed as transgressive, defensive, or even hysterical. Speaking as
a man, however, she can meaningfully exercise the prerogatives exclusive to the male society to
push back on gender discrimination. Her successful masquerade as Ganymede attests not only to
the gender-specific nature of early modern pedagogy but also to Rosalind’s mastery over what
she teaches and to her strategic understanding of when different gender performances are
conducive to her aims. Once again, she employs the master’s tools to dismantle the master’s
house; however, this time, the employment is threefold: a Galenic doctor refuting a Galenic
doctrine, a schoolmaster mocking poetic banality, and a man ridiculing masculine clichés.
In dressing up and performing as a man, in assuming the varying postures of professional
authority subsumed under the umbrella term doctor, all of which were exclusively male
prerogatives, Rosalind fashions a new pedagogical and epistemological system that works to
overturn existing patriarchal beliefs through transgressive reinscription. In the same way
Genevora performs multiple roles in Love’s Cure, so too does Rosalind perform multiple genders
and positions. Her characterization foregrounds the contingency of performance: she chooses to
be a man or a woman, a teacher or a physician, depending on context. Through her arrogation of
the multiple roles of “doctor,” Rosalind exerts a subtle but meaningful shift in the power
dynamics of romantic and pedagogical interactions, and invites us to question our normative
assumptions about power and authority in early modern relationships, both erotic and
instructional.
Coda
When I first started this project, I wanted to study female education. What kind of
pedagogy did women receive? How did education shape understanding of femininity and female
gender and sexualities, undermine or support female agency, and challenge or perpetuate
patriarchal orders? I had imagined writing about women as astute pupils, transgressively
educated to know and to become. Yet, as I dug deeper into Love’s Cure, it dawned upon me that
Clara the student was not the only female character who deserved the spotlight; Genevora the
teacher did, too.
Thus began my journey into the world of female pedagogues, where I learned that female
education does not consign women to the role of passive students. The Genevora and Rosalind
that I have come to know are so much more than that: they are witty, they are compassionate,
they are powerful. But most of all, they offer diverse (re)presentations of women as
teachers—while both assume at least one other role, each takes a markedly different pedagogical
approach: Rosalind cross-dresses and plays the physician while Genevora remains overtly
feminine and performs as a mother as well as a lover. Naturally, their “transgressive
reinscription” also carries markedly different implications. Rosalind temporarily relinquishes her
femininity, establishes her credentials in two quintessentially masculine fields, and exacts her
subversion from within. She dismantles—or at least, destabilizes—the master’s house using the
master’s tools. This is a conscious decision on her part: she chooses to cross-dress as much as
she chooses to teach. In fact, the success of her entire pedagogical agenda hinges on the fact that
she is performing a masculine role, for Orlando has always been confined within an exclusively
male world, and therefore only knows the principles perpetuated by men. Her transgression,
then, lies in her endeavor to erode the epistemological system of gender from within.
On the other hand, I suspect that Genevora does not initially intend to teach, but when the
occasion arises, she embraces the challenge beautifully and confidently. Unlike Rosalind, she
loves as a woman and teaches as a woman. The question then becomes: what licenses
Genevora’s educational authority if not transvestism? The answer lies in another intriguing
distinction between the two plays. In As You Like It, the characters’ genders are always clearly
defined: Orlando performs the man, Rosalind the woman. Even when Rosalind is deceiving
Orlando, the audience can identify, at any given moment, all the layers of her gender
performances: she is a boy actor playing a woman playing a man playing a woman. In Love’s
Cure, we deal with a much more complicated ambiguity: Lucio’s gender is entirely unintelligible
to his contemporaries because the gender he is socialized into is incongruent with the gender
associated with his sex at birth. Based on this premise, Love’s Cure probes into how this
unreadability might challenge or transform teacherly authority and offers Genevora as a potential
answer. She urges Lucio to embrace both his feminine and masculine sides and selectively to
perform the gender that would be most suitable for each situation. This tutelage is in itself a
Butler-style manifestation of transgressive reinscription, for it destabilizes the idea of gender
dimorphism and divulges how limited our set of gender categories has been.
In this regard, I find that As You Like It and Love’s Cure both offer wisdom to modern
educators: whether they employ transvestism or celebrate gender fluidity, Rosalind and Genevora
always have their students in mind; they tailor their approach to connect meaningfully with their
students. In other words, our female pedagogues meet the students where they are. In them, we
see a model for effective education: educators must be able to recognize, acknowledge, and
encourage all the qualities that students possess (Genevora) and identify potential room for
improvement (Rosalind).
