blocks: A Pipeline Flows Both Ways: Contradictions of an Activist Trajectory
Lucy London
Senior Honors Thesis, Department of Performance Studies
April 2023
In the Beginning: Maple Syrup Spring

In the beginning there was sap. It was late March, just around Zisbawktoke Gises—the Maple Sugar Moon[1]—and spring was starting to warm the ground. I had traveled up to northern Minnesota for my spring break with two comrades from Chicago and Madison. We pulled up to the Welcome Water Protectors camp in Aitkin County. Signs along the road read “Water Is Life,” “Land Back,” and “Honor the Treaties.” Things were quiet as we entered camp. A kind woman explained that Enbridge was waiting to drill until the ice melted, the ice blanketing the Mississippi. Water protectors who usually kept up camp were using this hiatus as a time to rest or go home to family. We were eager to help out, and asked what needed to be done around the camp. She offered us the task of going down to the Mississippi River, just a short stroll from camp, to see if the ice had melted and if the river was flowing yet. She said it would be coming soon— any day now. As we walked there we passed another sign: “Down to the River to Pray.” I started humming the Allison Krause tune and my companions joined in. As we came upon the Great Mississippi, we saw movement. My stomach dropped.

Water was flowing. Never had I dreaded so much the end of winter. Pieces of ice floated away on ripples of water, and the river was coming alive with the turn of the season. The awakening of spring meant the hiatus was over; drilling was to begin.

We sat by the river for a while. It was the first time I had seen the Mississippi and I was surprised at how narrow it looked compared to the grandness of its reputation. We were near the northern tip of the Great River, the river of all rivers. The river that is the main freshwater source for 15 million people along its path,[2] the river that Enbridge drilled underneath, twice, to install a tar sands oil pipeline.

We walked solemnly along the river through the trees until we came to a streak of bald earth that signaled the impending path of the pipeline. Eerily straight, the trees along this chunk had been demolished, signs forbade trespassing and the site was marked off with orange tape. In its path, by the side of the river, a traditional Anishinaabe lodge stood ground, proclaiming the land rights of its people to this territory protected by treaty and opposing in sacred prayer the construction of this pipeline.

We returned to camp with the news of spring, and in accordance with the turn of the season, a group was huddled around a large, steaming pot smelling of smoke and maple. They were making maple syrup out of the freshly tapped sap! We stood by the boil down, taking turns stirring and flirting with the direction of the smoke.

An Anishinaabe elder exited the main cabin to have a smoke. I was told her name was Tania Aubid and that she had just broken a 38 day hunger strike in protest of the pipeline.[3] 38 days. Over a month of not eating. Seeing Tania and hearing her story moved me to feel the gravity of this fight, part of a chain of historical Indigenous resistance, environmental justice and manifestations proclaiming sovereignty. In this moment, Line 3 felt like more than just a strategic “campaign”—it represented a struggle for actual livelihood and survival. Tania’s hunger strike represented a moment of clarity for me in understanding the depth and seriousness of the movement. Little did I know that 5 months later Tania and I would be arrested together and briefly share a jail cell.

When we left that first day of spring, folks at the camp offered us the special gift of freshly boiled down maple syrup. We accepted the three jars with gratitude, knowing that they contained far more than just syrup.

Coming back home after this brief trip to Minnesota I wept: tears I didn’t know how to explain, tears that my roommates couldn’t understand. I didn’t know how to process the experience or who to process with. I wrote a letter to myself and decided to fast the next day, inspired by Tania’s hunger strike. As I reflected on why I was heavy with emotion, I realized that I had felt a sense of alignment being up north, a sense of the change and uncertainty of life that I had felt mostly removed from my whole life, and felt especially estranged from in the protective bubble of college. There was something vivid, connected, and directly affected by both the elements of nature and the real consequences of oil projects like Line 3. The activism I had been doing for years seemed distant and removed from the actual realities of the projects I was trying to stop, the realities these Indigenous people were living every day. My glimpse of this type of on-the-ground resistance work seemed to present a way to live into my values more deeply and led me to spend my summer up at Line 3 in different Indigenous-led resistance camps along the pipeline route. My commitment to the movement that followed unveiled some key alignments and contradictions of changework and fostered me through a variety of episodes in my ideology and theory of change. Recounting some of those episodes here, I will demonstrate how I’ve both grown through them and simultaneously continue to hold each one as true in my present understanding of dialectical, multiple truths.
My Whiteness Is a Cloud

My whiteness is a cloud I can’t always see. It extends beyond my skin into every interaction, into every relationship, into every footstep I take, have taken, and will take. It clouds my own vision of myself.
My whiteness is a cloud made of guilt, shame, taking and separating. It clouds my sense of spirit, my connection with all things.

My whiteness is a training, and a lifelong untraining, an aloneness, a “forgive me” from my most well-meaning ancestors and a “redeem me” from the more ignorant. My whiteness is a lost child, without story, without culture, forgotten somewhere overseas. My whiteness is blank, a white page, a canvas.

I am ruled by my whiteness, by the fear I’ve been trained to contain as a white femme. Fear of confrontation, of sounding stupid, of being ridiculed, of causing harm. In most situations I get by by remaining a quiet bystander, politically correct in the not-saying.

I have been taught as a woman to be quiet and demure. I tiptoe around difficult subjects for fear of offending. I don’t want to be called racist, even though I know that I am the expression of a racist system. I don’t want to hurt anyone, but sometimes by not addressing difficult subjects I cause more harm than good. I am conflict-avoidant, and that is a tenet of white supremacy.

As a principle of movement work I have learned to prioritize taking leadership from the most impacted. This often looks like striving to take everything a person of color says to be true, fact, and right. Although it is critical to listen to and trust those who have been historically oppressed, I believe there is a complexity to it that I don’t always see. People of color are not a monolith. Even within resistance spaces with the same goal of stopping a pipeline, Indigenous leaders have differing ideas of what needs to be done.

Looking back at my journals from my time living at camp Namewag, I am remembering how uncomfortable it felt much of the time. Distrust was the dominant attitude, fear of infiltration made relationships testy, and security culture meant to protect also sometimes was used to gate-keep. Leaders were often stressed, angry and demoralized, which led to some manipulative attitudes surrounding arrests and a lack of full consent regarding risk level during actions. With the dominant strategy being to “put our bodies on the line” to stop construction, actions began to feel self-sacrificing and bodies were being regarded as resources, with the full humanity of each subject not always fully acknowledged.

It can be difficult to strike a balance between showing up in full capacity to trust in whatever Indigenous leaders call for, and prioritizing, or at least accounting for, my own agency and wellbeing. On the one hand there is the decentering of the self, the regard for Indigenous futurity over settler futurity, and the understanding that this fight isn’t about me. And on the other hand there is the real acknowledgement that my stake in this movement only goes so far as I believe in the cause I am fighting for, knowing that I am fighting for the liberation of all beings and that that liberation includes me. Although I likely won’t live to see a completely liberated society, I strive to perform into existence the type of liberatory care and pleasure that I hope all beings can someday experience. I believe in a more joyful militancy, one that builds bridges rather than burns them. I believe in the success of a movement rooted in love, with a regard for the humanity and agency of everyone, even our enemies. I believe in the strategies of joy over guilt, learning and honest communication over shame, and repair and transformative justice over revenge. Grappling with my whiteness is full of contradictions that I will continue to struggle through and rehash, but for now I strive to embody a commitment to the liberation of all, understanding that this means trusting in my own body and agency while simultaneously decentering myself.
Things Have Come to Be the Way They Are Right Now
“Out beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing there is a field. I’ll meet you there.”
- Rumi[4]

I sat on the cushion, my legs stiff from the last 4 days of meditating 10 hours a day. I was trying to breathe through my physical discomfort, feeling a mix of impatience, sleepiness, melancholia, and wonder. I visualized these feelings in my body as colors and shapes, observing how they played with me. I was trying to practice acceptance, allowing my thoughts and feelings to pass through me, minimizing my suffering by letting go of my attachment.

Then one of the teachers said something that stuck with me, a phrase I used as a mantra throughout the rest of the retreat. In her Dharma talk, Bruni had reminded us of the historic fatefulness of all things: things have come to be the way they are right now, she said. Things have come to be the way they are.

History is intentional, fateful, created by the agency and choices of “things”. Things have not simply fallen into place like this—rather, they have come to be this way. This knowledge opens up in me an appreciation for how unique and specific and destined this moment is, and how each thing had agency in its path to get here, creating the current reality.

This, of course, doesn’t mean that it’s good, or that it can’t change. That’s just it; it’s always changing. It’s not good or bad, just the way it is. The negative brings in the positive and the positive gives rise to the negative. There’s always a struggle for balance.

This is the view of eternity I like to hold. Everything has come to be like this. Not fate or destiny in a way that robs us of our agency. Rather, we are God building Change, we create the reality in company with every being and force on this Earth. All is well in this universe. We must not be ruled by fear. And yet, there is an understanding of the ephemerality of this moment, the malleability of the future, the deconstruction of time and the force of every contradiction creating change.

Although some may think that the Buddhist way is training to accept the conditions of the moment as they are, I think there is a nuance, and perhaps a contradiction: Buddhist practice invites us to let go of our clinging in order to accept the force of change. Suffering comes from clinging: clinging to the past, to a relationship, to an idea. What if we let go of that attachment and accept the fluidity of everything? What would that do for movement spaces?

I think movement spaces tend to operate best when there is an idea that people can get behind and get excited about, but at the same time there must exist the wisdom of knowing when to let go, change paths, and let emerge another iteration or a different thing. “How we live and grow and stay purposeful in the face of constant change,” writes adrienne maree brown, “actually does determine both the quality of our lives, and the impact that we can have when we move into action together.”[5]

The Line 3 fight was successful in many ways: it radicalized hundreds of young people and trained them in frontline direct action. It forged connections and networks that are now showing the beginnings of a constellation of chained actions and campaigns, inspired and supported by one another.

But the Line 3 fight made a lot of mistakes. One of the main pitfalls was the attachment to the tactic of direct action before all else. There had been legal and legislative fights to stop the pipeline already, all of which had failed. Direct action was considered both the last resort and a physical representation of the movement’s strength and people power. As a tactic, direct action can be very impactful, but in the Movement to Stop Line 3 the same types of actions were overused, forfeiting the element of surprise and losing the attention of the media. Over and over people locked themselves to construction equipment, on almost a daily basis during the summer. And the result was maybe an hour or two of delayed construction and the water protector(s) being thrown in jail. In my opinion, clinging to the ideals of direct action—or at least the same type of action—as the worthiest tactic was part of what caused us to lose the fight.

In Joyful Militancy, carla bergman and Nick Montgomery coin the term “rigid radicalism” to describe this phenomenon in movements. Participants tend “towards mistrust and fixed ways of relating that destroy the capacity to be responsive, creative, and experimental.”[6] This dynamic is created on the relational level and creates rigidity in the flow of tactics and strategies at an organizational level. “It is the pleasure of feeling more radical than others and the worry about not being radical enough; the sad comfort of sorting unfolding events into dead categories; the vigilant perception of errors and complicities in oneself and others; the anxious posturing on social media and the highs of being liked and the lows of being ignored; the suspicion and resentment felt in the presence of something new; the way curiosity feels naïve and condescension feels right.”[7] These attitudes ring true to my experience, and, I’d propose, mostly stem from a common fear of change, the clinging to a certain idea of radicalism. It is also the human need to form packs, to corroborate our opinions, the need for certainty in the inevitably uncertain work of changemaking.

Upon acknowledging this root and its unfortunately prevalent consequences, how might we train ourselves to recognize and unlearn these attitudes? Joyful Militancy provides some helpful ideas: they suggest working non-ideologically, not privileging morality but instead listening to the milieu of different truths and experiences and using common understandings to guide decisions, accepting uncertainty, and holding ambivalence. I hope to continue to remind myself of these important nuances and ideas and embody them in my presence in movement spaces to come, as this is a major step to prefiguring the world we wish to create.
On the Hill in Santa Clara

“If everything has come to be the way it is right now, how can I justify my desire to make change?” I asked my friend Jeremy, an ardent Marxist. “Can I be both righteous and recognize that this is just one truth, one side of the whole, one small argument in the complex trajectory of the universe?”

We were climbing a hill overlooking Santa Clara, the city that housed the final historic battle of the Cuban Revolution. I was trying to make sense of the many contradictions of changemaking that had been nagging at me lately. Ever since I went full force planning an all-night Earth Day “teach-out” the past April, I had been extremely burnt out, unmotivated, and disillusioned with movement work. The added toll of the conflict in my defendant group left me feeling unsupported and unequipped to participate in the difficult work of rebuilding trust. I felt angry at the dogmatic righteousness that seemed to guide many leftists and alienate anyone who dared to disagree. I was also processing the Vipassana meditation retreat I had attended in the summer where I was reminded of the alignment of the universe and the synchronicity of each thing. Between disillusionment and encouragement of the broader picture, I was perplexed by the tension between my belief in change as a guiding force and my complicated relationship with movements and the motivation necessary to create that change. I brought these feelings and questions with me up this hill, and a formative dialogue helped me unwind them.

Jeremy queried my assertion of the inherent rightness of the universe. “Things are what we make them,” he asserted, “in accordance with the conditions at hand.” He doesn’t think we can believe in fate to the point of quelling our sense of agency, for our subjectivity is a part of the force of change, the flow of nature. Perhaps it's the feeling of control that we can let go of; we can’t control many things, and it doesn’t help us to worry about controlling them, but we can try to shape change in most situations. I accept this nuance. I go on:

I think it is not just that things are as they are meant to be, but that within every opinion, every experience, every human story there is a seed of influence for the building or destroying, creating or critiquing of the new world. Regardless of whether someone is conservative, liberal, progressive or leftist, regardless of whether they are ignorant or wise, well-read or out-of-touch, they have a place in the ecosystem of things. For example, I think of my friend who is a radical leftist, quite critical of almost everything, sometimes, I think, too critical, but with very original and well-argued critiques. I think he has a strong role to play in the making of a better world because, even if people don’t agree with him all the time, he stretches those around him into new ways of thinking; he pulls us further left because he stands his ground and is smart, loveable, and unapologetic in his views.

Then I think of my dad, a somewhat nutty man who lives alone in his RV and is deep into conspiracy theories. Some, like my mom, are apologetic of his behavior, or that I don’t have a more responsible father, but I wouldn’t have it any other way. He has shown me ways to live life outside of the constructs of society, taught me to challenge dominant culture and be skeptical about mainstream stories and news. My father has a role in the ecology of things as an outsider, a weirdo, an influencer of those related to him and those he interacts with to think a little differently.

There’s my Cuban grandfather, the republican Trump supporter who “disowned” me after I posted a blog post with the word “eco-socialist” in it. His views, coming from a place of unhealed trauma from his adolescence when his wealthy family fled the communist revolution, show me another side of how people experience change. My relationship with him has been a difficult one, but I see it as a rehearsal for dealing with conflict in the greater arena of societal changemaking. We can’t have a revolution unchallenged.

All these roles either stretch us in some direction or teach us to stand our ground. They serve to diversify us, for we can’t have a society where we all think homogeneously. But this can be a lot to grapple with for those of us trying to figure out what we believe (which, I think, is most of us). With influences and messaging coming at us from all angles, how are we to parse out what we think, what feels right to us as individuals coming into the movement or just trying to live life? How do we discern our truth in a world with multiple truths? How can we regard other beings with a radical understanding of their whole story that has led them to this point, with a compassion that bridges divides, while also holding true to our theory of change? How much should we accept the continued replication of counterproductive forces/people in society, and how much can we assert our ideologies and try to change people?

Jeremy responded to my rant with the brilliance of Marxist dialectics: of course, the view of the necessary ecology of things has its happy opposite, he noted. Contradicting the plurality and indiscernibility of truths is the other, equally true notion that if we are to make change, we must believe in some right way. We cannot make change by justifying everyone’s position. Rather changemakers must act to change circumstances that change people. Sometimes, they must get carried away in the righteousness of their own path and assert their opinions over others.

Jeremy’s point brought me to another, more personal question: why am I doing changework? Why do I feel like I can/should assert my righteousness and try to change others? If I can just as easily justify stepping away to “be in the rightness of eternity,” what is continually bringing me to this work?

I know that I am oppressed, as a subject of the American education system, as a young person, as a woman, as a consumer and a product of capitalism, and as a member of the oppressive white race (as Nelson Mandela writes, “the oppressor must be liberated just as surely as the oppressed”).[8] I know that my liberation is tied up with the liberation of all beings. I know I am a human in a historical moment and I have the ability to influence change. But I also know I could, and have the privilege to, accept things as they are. I often get a strong urge to escape or retreat, go live in a commune or a van, climb mountains and fulfill my adventure spirit. I could learn to live without actively shaping change in the world, in the sense of committed organizing. What is stopping me from retreating like that?

I have a sense of responsibility. A sense of faith in the idea of change as a divine force—“God is Change,” as Octavia Butler writes in Parable of the Sower.[9] A sense of the meaning I’ve created for myself in changework, a feeling of truth in the philosophies of dialectical materialism and the exciting opportunity present for change in the historical moment we are living in. An alignment with the prefigurative embodiment of recognizing ourselves within the ecology of things, the decentering of the self and of the human, the construction of practices to remember the inherent truths of change and interconnectedness.

I won’t kid myself by claiming that I need any of this to live. Depressingly, I think it does all boil down to something to stave off the chilling and stagnating force of boredom. But in alignment with the values I’ve been taught and what brings me joy and energy, changework is the meaning I’ve chosen to imbue my life with. In the words of a dear friend and lover, Emma Lohman, with regard to the Line 3 fight:
We who went back where
we failed to stop construction
can't say what it means.
We don't even know what to ask.
Maybe it's a better way than most to get older.[10]
We began to head down the hill. On our way down, Jeremy explained to me the laws of dialectics, the second of which proved to be particularly relevant to my questions. In his words (emphasis mine):

2) the unity and conflict of opposites means that in certain conditions seemingly "opposite" things in our world are interconnected and struggle together to produce change. for example, proletariat and bourgeoisie are "opposites" but are bound together within one total system (capitalism) and could not exist without the other as categories. their struggle (class struggle) produces change, the proletariat overthrows capitalism and therefore abolishes itself as "proletariat" along with all class distinctions. The point is that things that seem "opposite" to one another shouldn't be thought of as rigidly isolated from one another, but interpenetrate and struggle which produces change

This is intriguing. How do we hold both the necessity of contradictory, opposing, polarizing forces while also fighting for one side? What does our vision of an ideal society look like when we recognize that contradictions will inevitably persist? I think this principle of the unity and conflict of opposites calls on us to devise a new orientation towards changemaking: instead of aligning ourselves with “leftism” or with any vision of utopia, what if we align ourselves with the divine force of change itself that contains and challenges both political sides and negates any utopic endpoint? Perhaps some diversity is required: some of us must maintain this cosmic alignment, while some hold to the left and some to the right, some fight for a vision and some accept the conditions at hand. Together we change, through contradiction, systems and cultures and people.

blocks: Putting the Brain on Trial: Diving into the Genesis of Crime with Dr. Robert Hanlon
By Rebecca Chen
With the rise of mass shootings and horrifically incomprehensible crimes in recent years that
have burdened the hearts of many students today, whether it be at Michigan State University, or
in a closer case, Highland Park in Illinois, the question that we often ask is “why?” Forensic
psychology puts the brain on trial, using a scientific approach in answering this question.
Dr. Robert Hanlon, a Professor of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and co-director of forensic
psychology at Northwestern Medicine, speaks about his work on the interaction between
neurocognition, emotion processing, personality traits, and socioecological factors in the genesis
of violent behavior, raising ethical questions that pave the way for a jurisprudence and legal
theory that is more biologically informed.
[This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.]
What inspired you to pursue forensic psychology?
I’m a clinical neuropsychologist that specializes in traumatic brain injury (TBI). As a
neuropsychologist, I was interested in impulsive aggression in individuals who have sustained
TBI. That clinical interest led me to pursue empirical research on criminals who committed
violent crimes. Then, I received a lot of referrals from attorneys in the criminal justice system to
evaluate violent criminal offenders to assess their neuropsychological status and see if there were
deficits or impairments that would or wouldn't be important to their defense, possibly allowing
them to have a lesser degree of prosecution.
Since there are different parts of the brain implicated in different kinds of neurocognitive
deficits, does that correlate with the type of crime that is committed?
To some extent. There is a region called the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Lesions in the
dorsolateral prefrontal cortex are not particularly associated with criminal acts or acts of
aggression. There’s also an area called the ventral medial prefrontal cortex, which is known to be
involved in individuals who have a lack of moral information processing.
What makes people become murderers? Do you think all crime stems from some kind of
neurocognitive deficit in the brain?
No, not at all. Well, it depends on whether you believe or adhere to the notion and the idea that
psychopathy and personality disorders are brain disorders. I’m not particularly of that camp; I
don’t really believe that those are brain disorders. I think those are subtypes of personality that
fall within the spectrum of human personality. It’s well established that 2-3% of males in the
overall population manifest antisocial personality disorder. And then of that group, there's about
25% of those that are actual psychopaths who don’t possess the same emotional spectrum that
you and I do. In one of my studies, I examined neuropsychological differences in individuals
who had planned and committed predatory types of crimes, like mass shootings. Those types of
individuals we found in our study are quite different neuropsychologically from individuals who
commit impulsive types of murders, as they tend to be more intelligent and do not manifest
significant neurocognitive deficits.
You worked on a book that is from the view of a real murderer, “Survived by One.” What
was that experience like?
It’s the story of an individual named Tom Odle, who murdered all members of his family in the
mid-1980s, in a small town in southern Illinois. He did this over the course of about eight hours,
and it was strategic. With Odle, I conducted an evaluation of him at the request of his attorneys
while he was on death row. As a result of more men being exonerated while on death row than
had actually been executed, a moratorium on executions in Illinois was set. If that hadn’t
happened, Mr. Odle would have been executed. At about that time, he contacted me and wrote
me a letter, saying that he was interested in trying to understand more about antisocial
personality disorder, and why he had committed the crime that he had. After a few exchanges of
letters, I said to him, I mean, if you're interested, I’m willing to help you try to engage in
therapeutic self-analysis, and increase your understanding of why you did what you did. It
proceeded that way. Over time, this sharing of communication and this relationship that I had
developed with him just evolved into a book. It’s rather exceptional that someone on death row is
interested in engaging in reflection. Part of it, in my opinion, is because he was imminently
facing execution. And then as a result of the moratorium, suddenly, he's not going to be executed.
He was going to spend the rest of his life in prison, and he was still a young man in his 30s.
What kind of prevention strategies do you think would block something like this from
happening?
The types of crimes that do have the potential for prevention are domestic homicides. There are
multiple domestic homicides that occur every day, but there are often signals and markers that
can be identified that predict those types of crimes that are not readily available in many other
types of murders. Victims are often so enmeshed in the situation with the murderer that they
might not even be able to observe signals or the changes in behavior, but other people who know
the victim often perceive those signals and changes in behavior. So it’s a matter of identifying,
being aware of what those are, and assisting the potential victim in removing them from the
situation. But like most aspects of human behavior, it’s not simple, which is why we still have
the massive volume of domestic homicides that occur in this country.
Do you see this changing in the future? Do you think that technology could play a role in
creating prevention strategies?
It’s possible. But people have rights, and they have a right to not have their personal information
disclosed. You see it in this country, you see it every week now, or sometimes multiple times a
week— the problem with mass murders in elementary schools, high schools, universities,
shopping centers, and workplaces. It’s a massive challenge to try to get information that would
help prevent some of those types of crimes. I would hope that there may come a time when some
technological advances or communication systems may be in place to facilitate the sharing of
that information.
What do you wish more people knew about? What do you think is most important for our
undergraduates to know about your field?
In these types of violent crimes, particularly homicides, there is a multitude of motives that are at
the basis of why people commit these types of crimes. There are multiple different factors
regarding brain function and psychological function that contribute to these crimes. No crime is
alike. They’re often characterized by very different factors. So, with the idea being that these are
complicated social phenomena, I think it’s important for people like me to spend our professional
time trying to increase our understanding of some of these factors and educate the public about
these things. For me, providing information and publications to the literature that have the
potential to increase the understanding of crime has been the most rewarding thing in my career.

blocks: Loopholes in the Fourth Amendment:
Predictive Policing and the Threat of Data Brokers
Flora Tian
Political Science 395: Politics in the Digital Age
Professor S. Sara Monoson
March 17, 2023
Abstract
The rise of big data surveillance and predictive analytics has transformed the capabilities
of law enforcement and created new forms of big data policing. Police departments (P.D.s) have
increasingly used algorithms to analyze massive amounts of information in order to forecast and
investigate potential criminal activity, such as Chicago P.D.’s Strategic Subject List (SSL). State
governments have also adopted surveillance technologies such as facial recognition and acoustic
sensors in their crime-reduction efforts. This has raised many concerns about individuals’
constitutional rights of privacy, as well as the adverse impacts on marginalized communities.
More alarming, however, is the role of data brokers in allowing law enforcement agencies to not
be held liable for these violations. These for-profit companies aggregate individuals’ personal
data and sell it to the largest bidders. This is not only concerning but also unconstitutional as
these purchases bypass the Fourth Amendment through the third-party doctrine. Yet, Congress
has still not passed a federal data privacy law addressing these loopholes.
As such, this paper explores the impacts of predictive policing programs and argues for
the necessity of policy intervention on data brokers in three parts. First, it provides an overview
of big data policing and its evolution in light of new predictive technologies. Second, it analyzes
how predictive policing challenges the constitutional protections under the Fourth Amendment
and the role that commercial data brokers play in this process. Finally, the paper concludes by
highlighting the need for new legislative solutions to maintain these protections and regulate the
data brokerage industry.
Introduction
Steven Spielberg’s film Minority Report follows detective John Anderton in a futuristic
society as he swaps out his eyes with new forward-thinking technology that tracks people and
scans their activity. The central concept is simple: A new “precrime” unit in Washington, D.C.
has solved the problem of crime control by predicting murders using computer algorithms before
they happen.1 Police arrest individuals who have broken no law but will in the future. This is met
with triumphant success — until the program predicted that Anderton himself will murder
someone in the next 36 hours. While it was filmed in 2002, it may be one of Spielberg’s most
prescient work.2 Now, the surveillance-state future is closer than ever before. From new facial
recognition software to what Cathy O’Neil terms weapons of math destruction, dazzling
technologies have infiltrated our everyday lives, constantly collecting our information. Data
privacy has become a big area of concern that touches on many spheres of life and big issues
come especially crisply into focus when one looks at policing. The evolution of predictive
analytics and data collection tools has transformed the landscape for crime control, which raises
the question: To what extent has law enforcement agencies used sophisticated new technologies
to amass individuals’ personal data and what roles do data brokers play in the endangerment of
civil rights afforded by the Fourth Amendment?
I.
Big Data Policing and How It Is Used in Law Enforcement
a. The Evolution of Predictive Policing
Digital information is readily available in the age we live in. The ability to gather, store,
process, and analyze huge amounts of data provides the end user with a wealth of information
2 Ibid.
1 Sims, D. (2022, June 14). ‘Minority Report’ Tried to Warn Us About Technology. The Atlantic.
https://www.theatlantic.com/culture/archive/2022/06/minority-report-spielberg-movie-tom-cruise/661274/
about individuals, from what they ate for breakfast to where they work. This process is now
leveraged by law enforcement agencies to transform capabilities of crime prevention and create
what is called “Big Data Policing.”3 Today, a data-driven surveillance state is no longer a
futuristic idea. Predictive analytics, social media scraping, “heat lists” of subject lists, and
real-time facial-recognition software are just the beginning of how policing will evolve with big
data.4 Crime data and gang statistics are mined for patterns while victims and perpetrators of
violence are mapped in social networks. Personal tracking data is used to watch our movements
and study our behavior for any suspicious activity. Soon, a possible suspect is identified from a
real-time automated license-plate reader fishing the city for data about the trails of every vehicle.
This is the real world of big data policing — no longer in its infancy but now in full swing to
prevent and prosecute crime across the nation.
So far, these policing methods have been passive. But now, police departments in some of
the largest cities in the U.S. are experimenting with predictive policing as a new way to actively
forecast criminal activity. Similar to existing practices, predictive policing uses algorithms to
analyze massive amounts of data — from historical crime data, gang associations to a web of
surveillance and sensor data — to make decisions about patrol deployment and identify
individuals that are deemed likely to commit or be a victim of crime.5 This is where the scenes
from Minority Report come to reality. An example is seen in the story of Robert McDaniel. On a
weekday, McDaniel heard a knock on the door. He did not expect to see anybody but was instead
met with two police officers who stopped on his street in Austin, Chicago, a neighborhood that
5 Ibid.
4 Ibid.
3 Ferguson, A. G. (2017). The Rise of Big Data Policing: Surveillance, Race, and the Future of Law Enforcement.
NYU Press.
makes up almost 10 percent of the city’s homicide rate in 2020.6 McDaniel was caught off guard,
he only had small arrests for drug-related offenses and no history of violence on his record.
When the officers came in, they explained that McDaniel was identified by an algorithm from
the Chicago Police as a potential “party to violence” based on his location and associations with
shooters.7 But what the police did not know was what side he would be on. McDaniel could be
the shooter or the victim. Either way, he was at risk and the police had the right to make a stop
and “investigate.” This is just the beginning of what predictive policing looks like.
b. The Strategic Subject List (SSL)
The algorithm the police officers referenced is what is known as Chicago P.D.’s SSL
program. The SSL, also known as the “heat list” program, was first tested in 2012 and compiled
a rank-ordered list of individuals it believed to be most likely to engage in gun violence. The
algorithm was developed by researchers at the Illinois Institute of Technology, who were inspired
by epidemiological models used in disease research at Yale University.8 The earlier versions of
the list used variables such as whether or not the individual has been a victim of aggravated
battery or assault, age at most recent arrest, social circles/gang affiliation, number of prior drug
arrests, number of prior violent offense arrests, etc. It was used mainly in Chicago from 2014
before it was suspended in 2020 due to complaints from civil rights groups and a report from
Chicago’s Office of the Inspector General that found it to be overly reliant on arrest records.9
9 Ibid.
8 Lau, T. (2020, April 1). Predictive Policing Explained | Brennan Center for Justice.
https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/predictive-policing-explained
7 Ibid.
6 Stroud, M. (2021, May 24). An automated policing program got this man shot twice. The Verge.
https://www.theverge.com/c/22444020/heat-listed-csk-entry
According to a police superintendent, in 2016, “officers, social workers and community leaders
[had] gone to the homes of more than 1,300 people with high numbers on the list.”10 During its
operation, the SSL was intended to improve public safety and more effectively address higher
crime neighborhoods.
c.
“Dirty Data” and Risks of Bias
However, predictive programs such as the SSL leverage massive amounts of individual
data that run significant risk of being biased. Yet, these programs are often used to provide the
“reasonable suspicion” that is required for any stops by the police and help justify nonsensical
searches.11 This is troubling for minority communities as they are simultaneously overpoliced
and underserved and are thus more likely to become targeted by these programs. A 2019 study
conducted by the AI Now Institute draws attention to this very issue. In an analysis of thirteen
jurisdictions that have used these predictive policing tools, Richardson et al. found that police
departments overly rely on data “derived from or influenced by corrupt, biased, and unlawful
practices” or what they call “dirty data” that is often biased and discriminatory in nature.12 In the
SSL data specifically, over 50 percent of Black men under the age of 30 in Chicago had a risk
score while more than a third of the people on the list have never been arrested or a victim of a
11 Richardson, R., Schultz, J., & Crawford, K. (2019). Dirty Data, Bad Predictions: How Civil Rights Violations
Impact Police Data, Predictive Policing Systems, and Justice (SSRN Scholarly Paper No. 3333423).
https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=3333423, p.192
10 Davey, M. (2016, May 23). Chicago Police Try to Predict Who May Shoot or Be Shot—The New York Times.
https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/24/us/armed-with-data-chicago-police-try-to-predict-who-may-shoot-or-be-shot.
html
crime.13 In addition, a study conducted by RAND Corporation found that not only was the SSL
ineffective in reducing gun violence, but it also raised significant concerns about privacy and
civil rights.14 In its implementation, the SSL also did not focus on social service interventions but
was only mostly used for police contact. This was largely due to the fact that Chicago P.D.
officers were not at all trained to use the SSL predictions adequately, which only resulted in
officers increasing their contacts with individuals on the list.15 Therefore, much evidence showed
predictive programs such as the SSL pose significant risks of bias and reinforce the over-policing
of minority communities.
II.
The Fourth Amendment and the Introduction of Data Brokers
a. Constitutional Concerns of Privacy
On top of the disparate impacts of “big data” and predictive policing programs, legal
experts argued that these programs endanger the rights afforded by the Fourth Amendment,
which protects individuals against “unreasonable searches and seizures.”16 Specifically, the
Fourth Amendment says that any warrant issued by the police must have probable cause
“supported by oath or affirmation, and particularly describe the place to be searched, and the
persons or things to be seized.”17 This probable cause must also be demonstrated before a judge,
17 Ibid.
16 Volkwein, C. E. (2022). Digitizing The Fourth Amendment: Privacy in the Age of Big Data Policing, p.3
15 Richardson, R., Schultz, J., & Crawford, K. (2019). Dirty Data, Bad Predictions: How Civil Rights Violations
Impact Police Data, Predictive Policing Systems, and Justice (SSRN Scholarly Paper No. 3333423).
https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=3333423, p.210
14 Hollywood, J. S., McKay, K. N., Woods, D., & Agniel, D. (2019). Real-Time Crime Centers in Chicago:
Evaluation of the Chicago Police Department’s Strategic Decision Support Centers. RAND Corporation.
https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR3242.html
13 Ibid. p.209
who then makes an informed decision regarding whether the warrant is granted. However, there
are exceptions to this requirement. In some cases, law enforcement is allowed to conduct a
search without a warrant such as in a “stop-and-frisk,” where the police can temporarily detain
and question an individual, if there is “reasonable suspicion of criminal activity.”18 And it is
precisely this rule that is often exploited by law enforcement to extend their policing powers and
exhibit biases, a process also known as “racial profiling.” As defined by the American Civil
Liberties Union (ACLU), it is the “discriminatory practice by law enforcement officials of
targeting individuals for suspicion of crime based on the individual’s race, ethnicity, religion or
national origin.” Now, this practice is further augmented by new capabilities of predictive
policing as the scope of interpretations of “reasonable suspicion” is broadened by the new
algorithms and technologies used in the absence of warrants.
In Katz v. United States, 389 U.S. 347 (1967), the Supreme Court established that an
individual has a reasonable expectation of privacy that cannot be violated without a warrant
under two conditions, subject to certain exceptions. The conditions hold that if an individual has
a reasonable expectation of privacy in a given setting and society generally accepts the
reasonableness of that expectation, then that expectation is upheld and cannot be violated without
a warrant.19 In the context of surveillance technologies used by law enforcement, the Court also
determined in Carpenter vs. United States, 138 S. Ct. 2206 (2018) that the retrieval of location
information on a particular individual for the duration of a week more requires a warrant.
Specifically, the Court recognized that the tracking of individuals’ movements over time is
highly invasive and that individuals should have a reasonable expectation of privacy regarding
19 Katz v. United States, 389 U.S. 347 (1967)
18 Ibid.
their cell-site location information (CSLI), which is generated by a user’s cell-phone providers.20
However, while Carpenter set the precedent for law enforcement’s digital access and prevented
the police from directly retrieving individuals’ personal data, there are still multiple avenues
from which law enforcement agencies can legally obtain information on individuals, one of them
is through what is called the third-party doctrine.
b. The Third-Party Doctrine and Data Brokers
The third-party doctrine is a principle that informs the Fourth Amendment and states that
if an individual voluntarily shares information with a third party, then that individual’s
reasonable expectation of privacy associated with that information is void and a warrant would
no longer be required for law enforcement to access that information.21 As a case in point, in
Smith vs. Maryland, 442 U.S. 735 (1979), the Court decided that there was no violation of the
Fourth Amendment when the local law enforcement agency installed a pen register that records
numbers dialed from a telephone on defendant Michael Smith’s telephone without having
obtained a warrant. The opinion reasoned that Smith was not entitled to a reasonable expectation
of privacy because he voluntarily shared those numbers with his telephone company, and as such
assumed the risk that the company might share that information.22 Therefore, law enforcement’s
retrieval of this information without a warrant is reasonable under the Fourth Amendment and
police departments can bypass the warrant requirement by purchasing commercially acquired
information from third-party data aggregation companies, or “data brokers.”
Now, the third-party doctrine is widely used across law enforcement and predictive
policing, where agencies are amassing individuals’ personal information without their
22 Smith vs. Maryland, 442 U.S. 735 (1979)
21 Volkwein, C. E. (2022). Digitizing The Fourth Amendment: Privacy in the Age of Big Data Policing, p.4
20 Carpenter vs. United States, 138 S. Ct. 2206 (2018)
knowledge nor direct consent by partnering with commercial businesses in the private sector.
These data brokers are for-profit companies that collect and manage personal information from
individuals, including people’s search histories, which medicines they take, where they drove to
last and more.23 They are now part of a huge, lucrative industry, generating about $200 billion in
revenues a year.24 Much of this data is then analyzed collectively to predict users’ movements
and behavior, and then sold to the largest bidders. This is seen in some of the largest scandals in
tech of the past decade, such as the Cambridge Analytica scandal after the 2016 elections. As
such, data brokers are playing an increasing role in exploiting users and turning them into
merchandisable data points. A notorious example is Clearview AI, a company that provides
facial recognition tech and boasts having one of the world’s largest databases of people’s faces.25
Its clients include the U.S. Justice Department, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
(ICE), New York P.D., and some of the largest retailers in the U.S., such as Walmart.26 Their
databases, which store billions of pictures of people’s faces, are used to create possible matches
and serve the basis for arrests. However, these matches are often inaccurate and can lead to many
false arrests or even unwarranted jail time. Furthermore, these algorithms were found to be
especially flawed on Black and Asian faces and led to the wrongful arrests of many people of
26 Sarkesian, L., & Singh, S. (2021, January 6). How Data Brokers and Phone Apps Are Helping Police Surveil
Citizens Without Warrants. Issues in Science and Technology. https://issues.org/data-brokers-police-surveillance/
25 Heikkilä, M. (2022, May 24). The walls are closing in on Clearview AI. MIT Technology Review.
https://www.technologyreview.com/2022/05/24/1052653/clearview-ai-data-privacy-uk/
24 Ibid.
23 Sarkesian, L., & Singh, S. (2021, January 6). How Data Brokers and Phone Apps Are Helping Police Surveil
Citizens Without Warrants. Issues in Science and Technology. https://issues.org/data-brokers-police-surveillance/
color, such as in the case of two black men — Robert Williams and Michael Oliver, who ended
up suing over the disproportionate harms it had on the Black community.27
While Clearview AI and others have faced scrutiny in the UK and the rest of Europe, it
has not been as scrutinized in the US due to the lack of a federal data protection law.28 Instead,
due to the third-party doctrine, the business of data brokers allows law enforcement to skirt past
the Fourth Amendment and gain access to vast amounts of personal data on individuals without
any restraints. A recent example of this pattern is Detroit City Council’s contract with
ShotSpotter, a company that provides gunshot-detection technology by installing sensors in
typically low-income neighborhoods.29 While ShotSpotter and other similar companies advertise
themselves as public-safety platforms, they really are another set of “data brokers” that exchange
data for monetary gain. The contract alone with Detroit asked for $7 million, which is a
significant allocation of funds from the city council for what is nothing more than information
about loud sounds in their local neighborhoods.30 Not only is this data overpriced, but it is also
arguably poorly collected as ShotSpotter’s microphones detect all sounds that are of a certain
range in decibels and are often deployed in marginalized neighborhoods. Another example is
seen in the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) prosecutions of the Capitol Breach of 2021 that used a
lot of aggregated information from commercial data brokers. In a federal court filing, the DOJ
admitted to using “location history data for thousands of devices present inside the Capitol” that
30 Ibid.
29 Vogel, E. (2023, February 1). Police Surveillance Firms Are Just Data-Brokers by Another Name—The Appeal.
https://theappeal.org/police-surveillance-firms-are-just-data-brokers/
28 Ibid.
27 Heikkilä, M. (2022, May 24). The walls are closing in on Clearview AI. MIT Technology Review.
https://www.technologyreview.com/2022/05/24/1052653/clearview-ai-data-privacy-uk/
were obtained from sources such as Google and other data aggregation companies.31 Thus, there
has been no clear limit on commercially acquired data that law enforcement agencies have used,
which calls for intervention at a federal level.
c.
Geofence Warrants
How is this practice of data brokerage further manifested in everyday policing practices?
The answer is through geofence warrants. Now, law enforcement agencies not only can access
individuals’ personal data through commercial means, but they can also act on it. Geo-fence
warrants, also known as “reverse location searches,” are warrants that allow the police to identify
individuals that were in a specific area and during a given time frame — such as for the purposes
of locating a suspect in a crime — and conduct sweep searches through digital databases that can
ultimately to arrest.32 For instance, in January 2020, Zachary McCoy received notice that he was
a suspect in a local burglary. The reasoning was that his RunKeeper app, which keeps a record of
his bike rides around his neighborhood in Gainesville, Florida, placed him at the crime scene.
After getting a lawyer for a few thousand dollars, McCoy was able to block the release and not
go to court.33 However, McCoy is not alone. Thousands of innocent people are made “suspects”
through geofence warrants, which imposes significant financial and mental burden on the
individuals. Yet, no evidence shows any utility in these warrants in actually catching
perpetrators. Instead, they are only “fishing expeditions” that violate the very expectations of
privacy that the Fourth Amendment seeks to protect.34 Sadly, court oversight has also not been
34 Ibid.
33 Geofence Warrants and the Fourth Amendment. (n.d.). Retrieved March 15, 2023, from
https://harvardlawreview.org/2021/05/geofence-warrants-and-the-fourth-amendment/
32 Volkwein, C. E. (2022). Digitizing The Fourth Amendment: Privacy in the Age of Big Data Policing, p.13
31 Grand Jury Action No. 21-20 (BAH), 2021
strict due to the lack of transparency around the technical details of the searches such as the
scope of coordinates. Lastly, the number of geofence warrants issued is escalating as police
departments expand their requests to not just coordinates and geolocations but also keyword
search histories. However, despite it being categorically unconstitutional in many interpretations,
the dangers of geofence warrants are not widely known. Furthermore, lack of judicial scrutiny
regarding these warrants has led it to become an evolving practice of policing and crime control.
III.
Conclusion and Recommendations
The need for intervention on the ever-expanding practice of predictive policing is evident.
As shown previously, the Fourth Amendment effectively contains a loophole that allows law
enforcement agencies to violate individuals’ constitutional rights of privacy by acquiring
commercially obtained information from data brokers. This critical shortcoming needs to be
tackled through the introduction of new data protection bills or amendments to the existing
privacy act. Particularly, the lack of transparency around government purchase orders and the
role of data brokers in helping law enforcement agencies circumvent violations under the Fourth
Amendment needs to be addressed.
While many predictive policing programs, such as Chicago P.D.’s SSL, have been
ultimately suspended, the market for commercial data brokers and the commodification of
individuals’ personal data still remains wide open. Law enforcement agencies still have access to
large amounts of geolocation data without any warrants, a practice that Sen. Ron Wyden has
called a “backdoor to throw the Fourth Amendment in the trash can.”35 While a few members of
35 Robertson, A. (2020, August 4). Donald Trump trying to control the FCC is a “disaster,” says Sen. Ron Wyden.
The Verge.
https://www.theverge.com/2020/8/4/21354244/ron-wyden-fcc-nomination-section-230-trump-order-vergecast-interv
iew
Congress have begun paying more attention to the operations of data brokers in the U.S., there is
still a lot of unclarity on the rest of the big data ecosystem.
Earlier in 2021, Sen. Wyden, D-Ore., and 18 others announced the Fourth Amendment is
Not for Sale Act, a piece of bipartisan legislation that strives to close the loophole that allows the
government to obtain commercially acquired data from individuals without any warrants or court
oversight36. This bill would be a first step in addressing the constitutional privacy concerns and
uncovering the role of data brokers and has already received support from many coalitions and
privacy organizations. Separately, states should enact stricter transparency rules and legislation
that requires data brokers to register with the state to gain more insight into their practices.
Examples include the 2018 Vermont law and the California Privacy Act that requires a data
broker registry. All of these efforts are necessary and should work towards a more
comprehensive data privacy law including the regulation of data brokers that should be instituted
by Congress at the federal level. It is only then can we begin to address the loopholes in the
Fourth Amendment, the unregulated data broker industry, the disparate impacts of predictive
policing, and not let Minority Report become a reality.

blocks: A Rolling Stone Gathers No Moss:
Comparing Rolling Stone Magazine and A Brief History of Seven Killings
Kalycia Hodge
English 397: An Empire of Islands
Professor Jules Law
April 20, 2023
Abstract

This paper intends to use commentary from Marlon James’s A Brief History of Seven Killings to evaluate the representation of Jamaica in Rolling Stone magazine, particularly as it pertains to the Jamaican politics of 1970. The rising popularity of Rolling Stone corresponds to a significant amount of pop-cultural influence over the American public; the perception of Jamaica in America can be largely attributed to the magazine at this time. This makes representation significant, for the sake of Jamaica being appropriately presented to magazine consumers. Literary analysis of these articles shows a significant level of racism, infantilization, and exoticization of Jamaica, at the fault of reckless writing from Rolling Stone.

1970s Jamaica featured extreme violence and national insecurity. This period was highly publicized, most notably through musical publications, as reggae music began to reach an international audience. A Brief History of Seven Killings, by Marlon James, provides a fabricated narrative of the violence surrounding the attempted assassination of Bob Marley and the Wailers. James’s account depicts a politically divided Jamaica from multiple different perspectives, mostly Jamaican, though also featuring a few outsiders, most relevantly fictional Rolling Stone reporter Alex Pierce. Although James’s novel offers fictionalized reports of this time, there is an uncanny resemblance between Pierce’s articles and those of topical 1970s Rolling Stone. Of the few articles Rolling Stone released about Jamaica, most focused on the politically charged events of the 1970s with a disingenuous “counterculture” perspective. “Counterculture,” for the purposes of this paper, involves any specifically political ideology that supports marginalized identities, against a more popular oppressive regime (anti-establishment, etc.). The magazine commodified Jamaica and dehumanized its people for the purpose of their own success and popularity.

1972 was a historically significant year for Jamaican politics, marking a shift in international political alliances (Adams 2018, 100). During this period of uncertainty in Jamaica, two distinct political parties aggressively opposed one another: the People’s National Party (PNP) and the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP). “...[W]hile the JLP’s leader Edward Seaga was aligned with the capitalist ideas of the US, the PNP charted a new path, which leader, Michael Manley, declared as Democratic Socialism in 1974” (Adams 2018, 100).  However significant the political fight and public discernments between both parties became, the overall retrospective sentiment argues that their supportive audiences had such significant overlap, that “…both of them, when saddled with the responsibility to govern, adopted roughly similar methods to attain roughly similar ends” (Foner 1973, 54). The PNP and JLP constantly usurped each other as the main holder of political power, with JLP leading from 1962-72, and PNP winning the 1972 election (Foner 1973, 53).

It is around this time, the 1970s, that Rolling Stone magazine experienced their first major rise in popularity. Most of this was highly attributed to major events within the United States, such as the Summer of Love in San Francisco during 1967. The 60s and 70s served as a catalytic period for the magazine, where the combination of music and political movement allowed founders Jann Wenner and Ralph Gleason to easily cover a significant amount of popular, relevant bands, while simultaneously being minimally controversial through the slight reference of current politics. The main musical focus of the magazine was (and still is) rock; specifically, rock in the continental United States, and the bands that played there. This expands to include bands from outside of the country with substantial American audiences. Reggae music, or any other genre, just as we might see now, were minorities in comparison. Therefore, the addition of reggae music to the Rolling Stone roster seems a suspiciously calculated choice.

Rolling Stone was wary of being genuinely divisive in their approach, sufficiently being controversial enough to state countercultural takes, but not to adopt a counterculture identity, which would offer the magazine up for negative scrutiny and opposition. Jann Wenner himself stated, in “A Letter from the Editor” from one of Rolling Stone’s very first installments, “You’re probably wondering what we’re trying to do. It’s hard to say: sort of a magazine and sort of a newspaper. The name of it is Rolling Stone, which comes from an old saying: "A Rolling Stone gathers no moss…” (Wenner 1967, 2). This perfectly encompasses the non-committal, politically allusive, musical report Wenner and Gleason ended up creating.

Within A Brief History of Seven Killings, fictitious Rolling Stone reporter Alex Pierce finds himself exhibiting a strong indifference to Jamaican tragedy. He describes having a tokenized, preconceived expectation of what Jamaica will be like, only for this to be disrupted by its similarities to the America he just left.

But hey, it's Jamaica. At least everybody should be pumping some Big Youth and Jimmy Cliff. And yet when I get here, first time in a year, the only thing playing on the radio is More More More, How Do You Like It How Do You Like It, and I’m thinking this rep is bogus, … Even Abba gets more play than reggae here. (James 2014, 59)

Though Pierce is meant to be a fictionalized imagination of a Rolling Stones reporter, his attitude parallels that of a real article. He lacks the integrity to write about Jamaica the way he experiences it, criticizing what he finds, and disrespecting a country he does not understand, for the sake of a misguided expectation. There is an apathetic disappointment that Pierce approaches his articles with, as he finds ways to make the Jamaica that he experienced align better with the one he is finding ways to sell.

Pierce’s apathy is animated in the 1976 Rolling Stone article “The Rastas Are Coming the Rastas Are Coming!” by Michael Thomas. The article title comes across as insensitive but fitting, considering its content; an inappropriately comedic recount of the shooting of Jamaican PNP official, Michael Manley’s chauffeur. The article sports multiple instances of ill-fitting, indifferent, and frankly crass writing, such as, “Probably some JLP (Jamaica Labour Party) sportboy did it, although plenty of people had reason….” (Thomas 1976, 32). Thomas makes a mockery of this political conflict, reducing it to the effect of a random drive-by, and not making a point to explicitly express the dangerous reality of the situation. “Inter-gang warfare was a postcolonial political phenomenon engineered by a segment of the emerging national political class. Inter-gang warfare was thus from its genesis, political warfare,” (Hutton 2010, 29). While the prevalence of gang-behavior is significant, and rampant at this time between the PNP and JLP, Thomas fails to appropriately report the culturally relevant importance of this event.

Later in the article, while attempting to elaborate on the reasons that Manley’s chauffeur could have invited this violence upon himself, Thomas wrote, “Apparently this cowboy used to pull it out wherever he was – at a cocktail party, or at a King’s House reception for the Cuban hospital committee…” (Thomas 1976, 32). His writing turns the death into a spectacle that is grossly implied to be deserved. The article isn’t meant necessarily to be sympathetic for the actual victim. Rather, it is a clear attempt to reference political official Michael Manley and cover events of significance that satellite him. However, it somehow still finds a way to be actively reductive and uncompassionate to the event itself.
The depths of Alex Pierce’s apathy are furthered by the article he later begins to write, which takes on a much darker, uncompassionately voyeuristic tone. A portion of it reads:

The Third World slum is a nightmare that defies beliefs or facts, even the ones staring right at you. A vision of hell that twists and turns on itself and grooves to its own soundtrack. Normal rules do not apply here. Imagination then, dream, fantasy. You visit a ghetto, particularly a ghetto in West Kingston, and it immediately leaves the real to become this sort of grotesque, something out of Dante or the infernal painting of Hieronymus Bosch. It’s a rusty red chamber of hell that cannot be described so I will not try to describe it. It cannot be photographed because some parts of West Kingston, such as Rema, are in the grip of such bleak and unremitting repulsiveness that the inherent beauty of the photographic process will lie to you about just how ugly it really is. Beauty has infinite range but so does wretchedness and the only way to accurately grasp the full, unending vortex of ugly that is Trench Town is to imagine it. You could describe it in colors, red and dead like old blood, brown like dirt, clay or shit, white like soapy water running loose down a too narrow street. Shiny like new zinc holding up a roof or a fence right beside old zinc, the material itself a living history of when last the politician did the ghetto a favor. Zinc in the Eight Lanes shines like nickel. Zinc in Jungle is riddled with bullet holes and rusted the color of Jamaican rural dirt. To understand the ghetto, to make it real, one should forget seeing it. Ghetto is a smell. (James 2014, 81)

It is clearly a reimagination, and it is easy to assume that the real article would be less direct, however the language so staunchly matches that of Rolling Stone through the embellishment of poverty and accentuation of squalor. Nonetheless, Pierce reflects on this writing, allowing Marlon James to produce a commentary and not simply a satirical parody of Rolling Stone’s reporting. Pierce rebuts his own writing: “Fucking hell. Shit sounds like I’m writing for ladies who lunch on Fifth Avenue. Unending vortex of ugly? Holy sensationalism, Batman! Who the fuck am I writing for?” (James 2014, 82).

Written without any self-reflection, reporter Ed McCormack opens his 1976 Rolling Stone article, Bob Marley with a Bullet, with a quote presumably written in Jamaican vernacular. “It I dream, mon, every Rastamon’s dream, to fly home to Ethiopia and leave a-Babylon, where de politicians doan let I an’ I brethren be free an’ live we own righteous way,” (McCormack 1976, 37). The necessity of this is unclear, as the alternative might have the negative effect of changing the original voice of the quote. Though, this use of vernacular pervades the rest of the article which appears to take on a mocking tone towards the men McCormack interviews. The article begins with a conversation between McCormack and “Chris Blackwell, the young Jamaican Caucasian heir to a tea and spice plantation who founded Island Records, and Michael butler, the “hip millionaire” who backed ‘Hair’...” (McCormack 1976, 37).  Butler is quoted saying “New Yawk” (McCormack 1976, 38), instead of “New York”, which hardly appears necessary to the integrity of the individual in the way the opening quote might arguably be. Instead, it leaves a crude impression, as though the presence of Butler’s accent is something magazine consumers should be entertained by. There is a portion of the article later where McCormack covers the movement to legalize marijuana, and ventriloquizes a local Jamaican term, “ganga” (more commonly spelt, “ganja”), and it blares obviously and awkwardly from his voice in the article.

Aside from the uncomfortable tone-deaf nature of McCormack’s quotes throughout the article, he frequently evokes language similar to “poverty porn,” describing the “squalor” he observes throughout the streets of Jamaica. Ed McCormack wrote:
“Is this the area they call Trench Town?” I asked the cab driver, gawking out the back

window at the endless pathetic claptrap shanties and tin-roofed shacks. “Noooooo, mon,” he said, swerving to avoid a stray goat, “Trench Town is a bad place. Dat be in de ghetto.” Unfortunately, the distinction was lost on me. For not even the most strident protests of Marley, Tosh and other reggae artists, or the reggae cult film, The Harder They Come, had prepared me for the absolute squalor I saw along the narrow Casbah thoroughfares where sullen Caribbean Staggerlees stood on Catfish Row corners outside funky, blasting juke-joints with paint-potched Red Stripe Beer signs dangling down. Nothing had done justice to this pace, I realized, staring dejectedly out the window at too many ragged urchins with spidery limbs and swollen bellies swarming through the Casbah swelter, scattering all my palmy tourist-brochure preconceptions along that dismal roadside. Then, my spirits lifted momentarily when the first real live Rastafarian I had ever seen breezed by on a motorbike, dreadlocks flying like freakflags. (McCormack 1976, 39)

Much of the cruelty in this quote lies in that not only does McCormack’s writing accentuate and call attention to the unfortunate state Jamaica finds itself in at the time, but it also simultaneously disrespects the home in which Jamaicans were presently living. He treats it like a zoo, looming out of his window at the icky misfortune outside, claiming that he has no ability to differentiate between what his driver refers to as the “bad part of Jamaica” and the part he is viewing at the time. His depiction of this conversation implies the driver is unintelligent. The jarring contrast in speech between McCormack and his driver, through the abrasive uses of vernacular, imply that he must be too dumb, or used to his life in Jamaica to recognize that the area they are driving through seems undesirable.

Although McCormack is explicitly not referencing the ghetto, his inability to differentiate makes this quote applicable, “The current confinement of the lower stratum of the Kingston population into ghettos that are “chamber[s] of hell” speaks to the enduring plantation rationale of denying basic necessities because of a belief in their animality, idleness, and immorality, not to mention a corresponding belief in the insanity of their unreasonableness…” (Lettman 2022, 132). The quote is drawn from a much more nuanced argument regarding philosophical analysis of the epigenetic colonized consciousness; it still functions to expose a darker connotation of McCormack’s representation. It shows that the language used to represent Jamaica in this article has the lasting effect of reinforcing post-colonial colonized mindsets, and the racist fantasy stereotypes of minorities that continue to pervade modern society.

In addition, McCormack describes likely impoverished Jamaicans as “ragged urchins with spidery limbs.” This is excessively dehumanizing, as he refers to them through the lens of animals, insects, and anything but people. Disappointed that it doesn’t live up to its vacation destination reputation, McCormack continues to make a spectacle out of Jamaica and her people, referring to a Jamaican man as a “real live Rastafarian.” The phrase “real live” implies a sense of mythicality, and although few of us outside of Jamaica are frequently conversing, or simply seeing, any Rastafarians, they are not any less people. This only furthers the significance of the Lettman quote in this reading, as the rampant racism covert in McCormack’s article proves to be extraordinarily harmful.

Rolling Stone magazine’s representation of Jamaica is irresponsible, supporting the dehumanization, infantilization, and unfortunate commodification of a community not often heard from. When given the opportunity to represent a country experiencing a substantially troubled time, not necessarily in need of anything but compassion and human connection from the rest of the world, Rolling Stone squanders it. Instead, they appeal to the problems the country is facing for entertainment. This reckless writing in turn communicates to Rolling Stone’s growing audiences that Jamaicans are unintelligent and slovenly; in the same breath asserting that they are too unintelligent to be aware that the state they are living in is uncomfortable. The magazine’s unfeeling imperialistic journalism does not go unnoticed by Jamaica, but surely it is overlooked in favor of an advantageous approach to editorial, supporting Rolling Stone in creating a strong and ever-present successful magazine.
