that is driven by the West. Anderson
questions the implications of these com­
munities on the people existing within
(or outside) them. I am taking the ideas
brought forward in his book and applying
them to my concert analysis. In doing so,
I will highlight the imagined community
created after the fall of the Berlin Wall and
will question the narrative that is furthered
and the ideals that are presented as being
those of a (seemingly) reunified Germany.
In this condensed thesis, I will explain
my analysis of one of three reunification
concerts that took place in Berlin between
November 1989 and January 1990. The
analysis of this concert will serve as the basis
for better understanding the themes pre­
viously outlined and will begin to answer
the posed questions about how the Berlin
orchestras are representative of greater
German society during the Wendezeit.
Brotherhood and Freedom:
the Leonard Bernstein
Concerts
In what was one of the most public and
globally—recognized
musical
displays
of the German Reunification, Leonard
Bernstein led an orchestra consisting of
members of the former East and West
Germany, as well as members of combat­
ive nations involved in World War II —
Great Britain, France, The United States,
and The Soviet Union. Two concerts were
held in December of 1989 — one for the
citizens of the former GDR and the other
for those in the West with the most well—
known concert taking place in the Konzer­
thaus Berlin in the Gendarmenmarkt. These
concerts were broadcast to nearly 20,000
onlookers into the streets of the old West
through speakers on the roofs of buildings
on Kurfürstendamm (Dennis 1), as well as to
hundreds of thousands of people in more
than 30 countries around the world (Berlin
Celebration Concert). The target audience
for this concert appeared to extend beyond
those in Berlin, as demonstrated by the
numerous forms of media broadcasting
and recording this event and the large
international audience, which again raises
the question of the curation of the image
presented to the world about the “true”
values of a reunited Germany.
This ad hoc orchestra, which came
together for only two days, played Bee­
thoven’s Symphony No. 9 to celebrate the
recent fall of the Berlin Wall. Historically,
this orchestral work is deeply symbolic of
“hope, unity, and fellowship — across bor­
ders and through conflicts” (Johnson and
Suchtet). In fact, since 1985 the “Ode an die
Freude” section of the last movement, has
acted as the official anthem of the European
Union because “in the universal language
of music, [it] expresses the European ideals
of freedom, peace, and solidarity” (‘Euro­
pean Anthem’).
The combination of the many con­
nections back to a time of great German
cultural significance (i.e., the emergence
of the narrative as das Land der Dichter und
Denker) and the highly publicized nature
of this event is not coincidental. It seems
to project exactly the desired image of a
reunited Germany with ties to a specific
cultural heritage — but in presenting an
orchestrated image to the world that fur­
thers the narrative of the West and over­
writes that of the East, this cannot be an
accurate representation of German society
because it is exclusionary by nature.
In these concerts, a large emphasis
was placed on the concept of Brüderlich­
keit — not only between East and West
Germany but also between the countries
with a presence in Berlin after World War
II. It was as if this concert symbolized the
act of setting aside long—standing tension
in celebration of not just the reunification
of the German states, but also the global
implications that came with it. Leonard
Bernstein even famously changed the word
Freude to Freiheit in the final movement of
the symphony to commemorate this joyous
occasion. While the act of changing the
text of Friedrich Schiller’s poem is often
credited to Bernstein, this gesture has ties
to the late 18th Century when the “German
rebels appropriated the poem during the
French revolutionary era for the use as the
text of a political Lied, sung with the word
Freiheit replacing Freude” (Dennis 26). In
claiming this seemingly small change to
the poem as his authentic reaction to the
displays of freedom in Berlin (despite the
greater implications of this gesture and by
“The highly
publicized nature
of this event is not
coincidental. It
seems to project
exactly the desired
image of a reunited
Germany with ties
to a specific cultural
heritage.”
ignoring the important connections back
to the French Revolution), Bernstein’s
decision to claim this revision as his own
is quite questionable, as his Western, US—
American perspective is overwriting a sig­
nificant and unique German cultural refer­
ence. In presenting an orchestrated image
to the world that furthers the narrative of
the West and overwrites that of the East,
it cannot be an accurate representation of
German society if not everyone is included.
The location of the concert in the
Gendarmenmarkt — an important historical
square with a Konzerthaus designed by the
German architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel
with a towering statue of Schiller directly
in the middle of the plaza — is a crucial
element to consider when remembering
this historic event. It is no coincidence
that Bernstein’s concert takes place di­
rectly behind the famous statue of Schil­
ler — whose poem “Ode an die Freude ‘’ is
the basis for the final movement of Bee­
thoven’s Symphony No. 9. Additionally,
Schinkel was an architect who was “dafür
verantwortlich, Berlin in eine repräsen­
tative Hauptstadt umzugestalten”3 (von
Treptow). The aesthetic of Schinkel’s
architecture served as the foundation
for the literary aesthetic of the Weimarer
Klassik with Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
and Schiller as its main representatives
(Snodin et al 39). Therefore, on a funda­
mental level, this concert building was
not only a part of the movement to make
Berlin the center of arts and culture but
also part of the inspiration and foundation
for one of the most recognizably “German”
literary movements. Once again, there is a
strong tie back to the ideals and triumphs
of 18th and 19th century Germany.
3 Schinkel was an architect who was responsible for transforming Berlin into a representative capital city
4 The idea of a Gesamtkunstwerk can be found in the architectural theory of E.—L. Boullée with the design of Idealstädte, which was
supported by the French Revolution
This multidisciplinary event that was
broadcast into the streets of Berlin and to
the world also has a tangible connection
to the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk. This
term, meaning “total artwork” describes a
work or process in which the combination
of different art forms creates a cohesive
whole: generally, Gesamtkunstwerke con­
tains elements of music, drama, poetry,
architecture, or painting (Mühlenberend
282). Not only does this concert combine
artistic elements (such as instrumen­
tal music, choir, poetry, sculpture, and
architecture) in a way consistent with a
Gesamtkunstwerk, but this very concept has
a strong connection with the ideals of the
French Revolution and the development
of “ideal” cities4 (Mühlenberend 282). In a
way, the connection between the Leonard
Bernstein concert being a Gesamtkunstwerk
and the greater implication of this term
strengthens the narrative being created
after the fall of the Berlin Wall. Berlin was
an ideal city, not only in the sense that an
idealized reunified Germany was being
projected but also in the idealized possibil­
ity of the reunion of two halves of a city
that embodied (and continued to embody)
such different political and cultural ideolo­
gies. Berlin is an Idealstadt in the sense that
it overcame such difficulties of separation,
and yet this centuries—old narrative of
deep cultural importance still survived.
The connection between Beethoven’s
works and the ideals of the French Revo­
lution mirrors the creation of Germany
through the birth of the nation—states
and official recognition as a country in
1871. These ideals — Freiheit, Gleichheit,
Brüderlichkeit — served as the basis for the
emerging political and cultural changes.
The ideals associated with the Weimarer
Klassik were primarily shaped and created
by Goethe and Schiller, and the ideological
basis for the emergence of Weimar Clas­
sicism was the French Revolution and its
impact on public life in Germany (Stephan
186). The Schiller statue was unveiled in
the Gendarmenmarkt plaza in 1871, which
shows just how intertwined the newly
established nationhood of Germany and
the great Dichter and Denker are. This is
particularly relevant because Goethe and
Schiller are the poets and thinkers ref­
erenced in the expression of das Volk der
Dichter und Denker, and there is a strong
connection between Goethe and Schiller
and the birth of the German nation states:
”Die Deutschen, die die Goethezeit als die
Epoche ihrer Klassik bezeichneten, zei­
gen ein verändertes Klassikverständnis
an, das auch im Zusammenhang mit der
Herausbildung der modernen Nation­
alstaaten gesehen werden muss”5 (Stephan
233—234). It is essential to recognize the
interconnectedness of these important fig­
ures in the history of the development and
establishment of Germany as a nation and
as das Land der Dichter und Dichter.
It is no coincidence that three of the
main proponents of Weimar Classicism
— Goethe, Schiller, and Schinkel — and
the music of Beethoven all simultaneously
occupy the space in the Gendarmenmarkt
during this concert, and that this is the
5 The Germans indicate a changed understanding of classicism — one that must be seen in the context of the formation of modern
nation states.
image that is chosen to be broadcast for the
world to see. The striking ties to German
cultural history around 1800 are pres­
ent in the concert venue, and these links
significantly impact the reception of the
orchestrated ideal conveyed through the
Gesamtkunstwerk.
Beethoven and das Land der
Dichter und Denker
Beethoven’s music is noticeably very pres­
ent post—German reunification — par­
ticularly in the reunification celebration
concerts. Nearly every concert contains
one (or more) of his works, and there are
even greater connections to established
cultural traditions that go deeper than
the explicit contents of the music. There
is an important relationship between the
increased presence of Beethoven’s music
and the narrative of the ideals of the for­
mer West Germany, as well as in the pull
towards an ideal identity of Germany as
das Land der Dichter und Denker.
Throughout modern German histo­
ry, Beethoven has been synonymous with
and representative of the German iden­
tity. His role within German culture has
changed throughout the last two centuries;
however, what has remained constant
is his music being “symbolic of its [the
society’s] particular vision of the German
future” (Dennis 6). This remains true for
“Berlin is an Idealstadt in the sense that it
overcame such difficulties of separation,
and yet this centuries—old narrative of
deep cultural importance still survived.”
the role of Beethoven in the Wendezeit, as
his music helped project an idealized soci­
ety within Berlin.
To understand the relevance of Bee­
thoven’s music during the Wendezeit, we
must first go back to the point in history
when his music became synonymous with
the ideals of the French Revolution and
became deeply intertwined with and rep­
resentative of German culture. During
the celebrations of Germany becoming
a country in the late 19th century, Bee­
thoven’s music was used for parades and
celebrations (this coincided with the hun­
dredth anniversary of his birth). The use
of his music for these occasions set the
precedent for the use during the German
reunification in 1989, and “the evocations
of Beethoven in nineteenth—century Ger­
man political culture — particularly those
before unification in 1871 — enhance our
understanding of the early development of
a German identity based on cultural, and
in large part musical, nationalism” (Dennis
Bonn is often regarded as Beetho­
ven’s city, being that it is his birthplace
and hometown. Beethoven — who is often
hailed as not only one of the greatest com­
posers of all time but also as one of the most
“German” — is celebrated there frequently
through festivals and memorials. Interest­
ingly, Bonn was the capital of the Bundesre­
publik — and this says something about the
remembrance culture during the German
reunification when reminders of the West
were constantly overshadowing all other
viewpoints and experiences. There is a
clear connection between the program­
ming of Beethoven’s music and what Bonn
represents to the Bundesrepublik. This city
distances itself from the complicated his­
tory of twentieth—century Germany and
reminds the audience (whoever that may
be) of the ideals of the (especially West)
German people:
Throughout the Cold War, Bonn
epitomized the image that West
Germany wanted to project to a
suspicious world — pleasant, provincial,
even a little bit boring … Bonn’s most
celebrated son [Ludwig van Beethoven]
also suited West Germany’s public
image — classless, liberal, international.
Since reunification, his significance has
grown and grown. In a country where
so many cultural icons are tainted by
association, Beethoven presents no
problems. He has none of Wagner’s
baggage. He is a hero Germans can
celebrate without apology or shame
(Cook 67).
With Beethoven, and therefore
Bonn, representing West German ideals,
the expression of the cultural formation
and heritage of those in the East tends to be
overwritten. The subtle programming and
pushing of the narrative of the old West
seems to work against the established com­
mitment to equally preserving elements of
both cultures. This supports the idea that
the “imagined community” created after
the German Reunification centered on
only one group of people and projected an
idealized version of society onto the others.
Conclusion: Greater
Implications of German
Reunification
The reunification of Germany led to a
return to a specific set of cultural tradi­
tions: i.e., a resurgence of the ideals of the
Weimarer Klassik and the implications of
the French Revolution on German politics
and culture. Many connections to the past
can be observed in the celebration concerts
during the Wendezeit. In taking a critical
look at the preservation of both the former
East and West German cultural identities,
an idealized narrative of reunified Berlin
was projected onto the Berliners. The idea
of “presenting East German identity as a
danger to German unity implies that unity
can only occur if Eastern identities cease to
exist, which suggests that German identity
is akin to West German identity” (Clark
and Wöfel 144). This reveals a kind of
Leitkultur within German society — with
proponents of this idea believing that
“the so—called German Leitkultur should
dominate as the core cultural identity in
Germany … that is to say that East German
identity should be considered problematic
because it does not fit in with their con­
cept of Germanness” (Clark and Wöfel
145). This concept was not only present
in greater society but it can also be clearly
observed in the idealized and curated
image from the orchestras within Berlin at
this time.
In the time since the Fall of the Wall,
shocking statistics about the unequal
impacts on the orchestras in the former
East and West have been released — with a
striking difference in the loss of orchestras
in the former East:

besonders deutlich: Von 168 Orchestern

gesamtdeutschen

der Landkarte verschwunden. Ganz
überwiegend im Osten, vereinzelt im
Westen. Damit verschwanden auch
fast 3000 Musikerstellen6 (Mertens 10).
It is entirely expected that orches­
tra positions and entire orchestras would
be lost during the reunification process.
However, what is so striking is the dis­

parity between the impact on the former
East and West. A vow was made to pre­
serve both cultures equally; however, the
reality of the situation protected the values
of the West, overshadowing the cultural
institutions of the former East. After the
fall of the Berlin Wall, the majority culture
favored the ideas and culture tying back to
an ideal of Germany as das Land der Dichter
und Denker. As previously mentioned, the
strong pull towards these values reflects
an effort to reclaim a German identity that
has not been entirely soiled by National
Socialism. Again, it is simply naïve to
attempt to return to this idealized version
of society without acknowledgment of the
impact of the horrors of the 20th century.
The fall of the Berlin Wall had an impact
on more than just the narrow view of what
was constituted as “German enough,” and
the furthering of a narrative that does not
acknowledge this is problematic.
“A vow was made
to preserve both
cultures equally;
however, the reality
of the situation
protected the
values of the West,
overshadowing the
cultural institutions
of the former East.”
The orchestra is a microcosm of
German society during this period of tran­
sition, and the impact of reunification on
the orchestras, as shown through statistical
data, intentional concert programming,
and curated concerts, mirrors the larger
social and political changes occurring
not only in Berlin but also throughout
Germany. When considering the effects
of the fall of the Berlin Wall, it is essential
to question who controlled the narrative,
to recognize who the audience was during
the Wendezeit and after the official reunifi­
cation, and to examine what impact these
decisions had on the people in Berlin. ◆

Research in Translation:
A Conversation with
Dr. Alissa Levy Chung
By: Felicia Mou
Dr. Alissa Levy Chung, an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology, is a practicing
clinical psychologist with over 20 years of experience working with people of all ages. Dr. Chung
received a PhD from the University of Minnesota with a dual degree in child development and
clinical psychology, and she completed an internship and post-doctoral program at the University
of Illinois Chicago Department of Psychiatry. In the following conversation, Dr. Chung talks
about the role of research in clinical psychology, its limitations, and the current trajectory of the
field.
[This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.]
FEATURES
“Some of that depends on the kind of training program clinical psychologists
do. In order to be called a clinical psychologist, you do need to have either a
PhD or a PsyD. In a PsyD program, that is mostly geared toward people who
want to practice psychology. While they do a little bit of research and some
kind of dissertation, research is not really the emphasis of the program. In
PhD programs, research is the core of what students are doing and the clin­
ical piece is the lesser part; the idea is that they’re really training people to be
clinical scientists. They will potentially also learn how to be practitioners, but
it’s more geared toward preparing people for academic careers. The majority
of your time is spent on your research, and you’re researching any area that
could be germane to clinical psychology. That could be anything from an inter­
vention study to see if a new intervention works to trying to understand how
different disorders develop or what’s the underlying biology of the disorder. It’s
a broad umbrella of understanding anything that explains psychopathology.”
What role does research play in the training of clinical psychologists?
How are research findings communicated to clinical psychologists?
“This is a problem. The number one problem is that research findings end up
in journals. When you’re practicing by yourself, you don’t have access to any of
them. The only journals you can access are the ones you paid for out of your own
pocket or open access journals. That means that you’re severely limited in the
research you can even read once you go out into practice. It would have to matter
enough to you to spend at least several hundred dollars to get access to a data­
base in order to download any article you wanted. Then you’re going to have to
find the time to read them, and you have no protected time to do research when
you’re in practice. We do have to do continuing education to keep a license active,
which means you have to get a certain number of hours going to conferences
or reading things and doing quizzes to show that you actually read them, talks,
and those kinds of things that can give you your continuing education hours. It’s
usually the literature review version of journal articles where you’re not assessing
the quality of the research itself. It’s pretty separated, unfortunately, and it really
has to be up to the initiative of the clinician to go pursue the research findings
that the researchers do because it rarely goes the other way. Researchers are not
usually saying, “I found this really interesting thing. Let me go find all the clini­
cians in my community and have a dialogue with them about implementing it.”
What are the challenges of integrating research into clinical practice?
“In order to do “good science”, sometimes it means that people have to reduce
the number of confounding variables in their study. Let’s say you want to un­
derstand something about your intervention and whether it helps people who
are diagnosed with depression. A common way of doing that would be to do a
clinical interview and find a sample of people diagnosed with depression. If they
have another problem, they usually get ruled out of the study. That scientifically
makes sense, but most clinicians would say we almost never have clients who
only have one problem. Often people ask, “Will this literature generalize?” The
average person who walks into my office doesn’t have just one “pure” problem
or they don’t exactly meet criteria for something, so the real clinical world can be
messy. We have to have faith that our interventions will generalize or it would be
up to the clinician to marry two different interventions and try to figure out how
to layer those, even though the literature doesn’t exactly do that for you. On the
clinician side, there are clinicians who think that their clinical judgment exceeds
the science. Sometimes there’s resistance to using science if it isn’t intuitive or
requires someone to change something that they’ve been doing for a long time.”
How do research findings guide your formulation of treatment plans?
“I think this would vary by clinicians. There are some clinicians that use much
more manualized treatments, where they’ll take something that was used in a
research trial and use that manual to implement the intervention. What interests
me the most is the mechanisms of change so that I can figure out which parts
of the treatment are most essential for people. For example in CBT, at first
people thought that you had to get people to change their thoughts and believe
new ones. Now the evidence suggests that maybe that is less of the case and
more that they just have to recognize that their thoughts may not be accurate
or valid. We’re also learning that developing distress tolerance is probably a
more realistic goal for people than getting rid of all their distress. Those prin­
ciples help guide me in thinking about what’s most important for my clients,
how do they make real progress, and how can I equip them with skills that
they can take with them. I also use a ton of developmental literature because I
work with people of all ages including children which informs where I’m going
to intervene, what my target is for how I want the person to be functioning,
whether or not I think something is a problem at all, and breaking down what
it is I think the person needs to do. Sometimes reading qualitative literature
where the people themselves get to talk about how they experience the world
is really helpful to me to give up on things we used to think were working or
helpful, and it turns out at best they did nothing and at worst they were hurtful.”
How do clinical psychologists contribute to research?
“Once you’ve gotten through the training, people either become academics or go
into practice. There’s not a lot of overlap in that population. There’s some people
who do both academia and private practice, but most commonly people will go into
private practice, and they don’t really do research anymore. So then the question
is what are they doing with the research. At best, they’re just reading it. There’s
certainly people who do intervention research where they’re both clinicians and
researchers or people who run clinics and do research in the clinics, often in med­
ical schools. Tangibly, I would think you would contribute to research only if you
get recruited to be one of the clinicians in someone’s study, are willing to admin­
ister someone’s treatment, or be their control group. Often treatment as usual is a
control treatment, and that means that your control group will just be people get­
ting therapy in the community that someone is being compared against. Not that
anyone ever wants to be someone’s control group because the implication there is
that whatever you’re doing isn’t as good as what someone else could be doing. At
the same time, I think we need to not be threatened by stuff like that and recognize
that if somebody can find something better than what I’m doing, that only helps
me be better at my job. Instead of being afraid of that, we need to be open to that.”
In what direction is research moving in the field of clinical psychology?
“I don’t know if we have one direction in which we’re heading in. Certainly for a
long time, things have been moving more into neuroscience to try to understand
what’s going on in the “black box” that is somebody’s head. We haven’t gotten
very far in identifying candidate genes involved in different disorders. If we can
actually understand what’s going on in the “black box” that is somebody’s head,
whether that’s coming up with better medications that are more appropriately
targeted or therapies to understand what systems we’re trying to act on, I think
that could be very helpful. It could also help with diagnostics because it could
well be that we’re grouping together disorders that don’t belong together and not
grouping together disorders that do. If we could understand the common neu­
robiology of different outcomes, we might have a very different understanding
of disorders. In terms of practice, mindfulness is hot right now so there’s a lot of
research on mindfulness. We’re also focusing more on intersections with public
health disparities and how mental health is experienced, diagnosed, and treated
in communities depending on the resources and opportunities people have.”
Motivation
Research and development of III-Nitride semiconductors have led to promising, and
increasingly important, optoelectronic applications ranging from light-emitting diodes
(LEDs) to photodetectors (PDs). Previous developments in the III-Nitride material
system have given rise to blue and green LEDs, while future advancement will allow for
ultraviolet (U.V.) LEDs. Perhaps the most promising application is solar-blind deep-
U.V. avalanche photodiodes (APDs) in Geiger mode for single photon detection, with
high quantum efficiency (QE) and gain and low dark current. P.D.s in the U.V. range
allow for precise control of furnaces via monitoring U.V. heat signatures within the
civilian market [1]. The U.S. military has also conveyed its desire for solar-blind deep-
U.V. APDs, operating between 200 and 250 nm for the detection of bio-chemical weap­
ons, explosive signatures, and missiles, as well as for covert space communications [2].
Due to the nature by which organic material characteristically fluoresces under
U.V. light, PDs have also lent themselves to the detection of pathogens, bacteria, and
chemicals such as Anthrax, Smallpox, Marburg, Ebola, Plague, and Tular [3]. With the
advent of COVID-19, the focus of deep-U.V. APD-based detection is shifting to a new,
more prominent threat in a pandemic-stricken society, and it is believed that these APDs
will allow for the detection of this virus’ U.V. fluorescence with high-accuracy. Ulti­
mately, this technology will allow for the simultaneous fluorescence and detection of
COVID-19 through portable U.V. LEDs and APDs.
Structural Characterization
via X-Ray Crystallography of
III-Nitrides for APDs
by Michael Richards
Faculty Adviser: Dr. Manijeh Razeghi
Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
Background
The III-Nitride semiconductor material
system — formed from the combina­
tion of group III elements with group V
Nitrogen — consists of AlN, GaN, InN,
and their alloys. The most important
property of III-Nitride semiconductors
is their wide and direct bandgap energy.
The wide bandgap allows for short, high
energy wavelengths in the green, blue,
and U.V. regions of the electromagnetic
spectrum; the direct bandgap is ideal for
optoelectronic applications as energy tran­
sitions do not require a momentum shift
in k-space, which translates to stronger
absorption and emission as optical transi­
tions will more readily occur [1]. AlN has
a particularly large bandgap energy of 6.2
eV, which allows for bandgap engineering
of solar-blind AlxGa1-xN epilayers accord­
ing to Vegard’s Law (Equation 1).
Within the U.V. range of the
electromagnetic spectrum exist three sub-
bands: long-wavelength U.V.-A (315-400
nm), medium-wavelength U.V.-B (280-
315 nm), and short-wavelength U.V.-C
(100-280 nm), of which only U.V.-C is
solar-blind [4]. The solar-blind region is
critical for photodetection as it is the range
at which the Earth’s ozone layer com­
pletely absorbs all solar radiation, leaving
only artificially generated electromagnetic
radiation. The solar-blind nature of III-
Nitride-based deep-U.V. APDs is crucial
to detection due to their single-photon
sensitivity, as extraneous sun-originated
radiation would detrimentally impact the
signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).
Preceding the sophistication and
development of the APD, the industry
has relied on P.D.s such as the Schottky
Metal-Semiconductor-Metal (MSM) pho­
todiode and the p-i-n photodiode. The
MSM photodiode consists of two Schottky
contacts on an intrinsic (undoped) semi­
conductor layer. These contacts operate
through the rectification of a difference
in work functions between metal and
semiconductor through an electrostatic
barrier, and carrier transport is fueled by
thermionic emission [5]. This photodiode
is easy to fabricate and is fast and efficient;
however, it requires a high absorption co­
efficient, does not have a sharp cutoff or
band-pass response, and may only operate
via front-illumination. The p-i-n photodi­
ode, instead, makes use of doping to create
n- and p-type regions separated by an in­
trinsic region, which has a low free-carrier
density and high resistivity [5]. For this
reason, it is capable of high-speed opera­
tion with low noise and low dark current.
The main drawback of the p-i-n junction is
its poor sensitivity under low reverse-bias
conditions.
“The focus of deep-U.V.
APD-based detection
is shifting to a new,
more prominent
threat in a pandemic-
stricken society, and it
is believed that these
APDs will allow for the
detection of this virus’
U.V. fluorescence with
high-accuracy.”
Design
Despite the merits of other photodiodes,
the APD is optimal for applications in
deep-U.V. single-photon detection for
its high speed and extremely high gain,
which benefits sensitivity. Unfortunate­
ly, there are many difficulties associated
with the APD, including high sensitivity
to defects and dislocations, high doping
requirements, and leakage paths, which
reduce the noise equivalent power (NEP)
and therefore detectivity. The crux of
APD design is to achieve high external
quantum efficiency (EQE) and internal
gain (M) while maintaining low dark
current.
The APD is essentially a strongly re­
verse-biased p-i-n junction. This bias has
the effect of causing an avalanche effect via
impact ionization, wherein released charge
carriers are accelerated and collide to gen­
erate additional electron-hole pairs (EHPs)
in the active region resulting in a cascade
(avalanche) of EHPs due to a single photon
[5]. The carrier type that dominates the
ionization is given by the ionization ratio
(k) and dictates the performance of the
device, with k>>1 being hole-dominant
and k<<1 being electron-dominant [5]. An
ionization ratio of approximately 1, mean­
ing that both carriers ionize effectively, is
undesirable as the excess noise factor (F)
increases linearly with internal gain (M),
demonstrated in Figure 1. For the APDs
designed at the Center for Quantum De­
vices (CQD), an ionization ratio of k<<1 is
desired for its electron-dominance.
A III-Nitride ternary alloy, AlxGa1-xN,
is selected for the p-i-n heterostructure of
the APD due to its tunable bandgap be­
tween 3.4 eV and 6.2 eV, allowing for so­
lar-blind detection. Pertaining to the doped
region of the p-i-n, p-AlxGa1-xN is doped
with Mg while n-AlxGa1-xN is doped with
Si. The p-i-n is grown on highly doped n+-
AlxGa1-xN, which itself is grown on pulsed
atomic layer epitaxy (PALE) AlN on a
low-temperature (LT) AlN buffer [6]. GaN
is used as a capping layer. These epitaxial
layers are grown on a wurtzite/sapphire
(Al2O3) substrate on the (00.2) plane. The
APD structure is shown in Figure 2. The
AlxGa1-xN epilayers have high dislocation
densities due to the large lattice mismatch
with the sapphire substrate and the high
Al-content AlxGa1-xN, which comprise the
APD, has low doping efficiencies. Both act
to the detriment of the necessary high gain
and sharp avalanche breakdown.
Growth
The epitaxial growth of APDs is per­
formed using CQD’s AXITRON metalor­
ganic-chemical-vapor-deposition (MOC­
VD) system. This growth technique is
used for its capability for high-quality,
thin-film deposition with atomic layer
precision and abrupt interfaces [5]. The
MOCVD system consists of a gas handling
system, reactor chamber, exhaust system,
and safety apparatus for toxic gas moni­
toring, the schematic of which is shown
in Figure 3 [5]. Necessary for high-qual­
ity, low-defect, and single crystalline
epilayers is precise control of the growth
pressure, temperature, and III/V ratio.
The group III sources are trimethylalumi­
num (TMAl) for Al and trimethylgallium
(TMGa) for Ga, while the group V source
is NH3 [7]. The Ga dopants are silane
(SiH4) for n-doping with Si and DCpMg
for p-doping with Mg [7].
Structural Characterization
X-Ray Diffractometry
X-ray crystallography is the experimen­
tal field wherein the molecular structure
of crystalline materials is determined by
the diffraction pattern of incident X-ray
beams. Since X-ray electromagnetic ra­
diation is on the same order as the lattice
spacing of the crystal structure (on the
order of 1 Å), the resulting interference
pattern from the incident beams is unique
to the crystal and can reveal information
regarding its structure and properties [8].
At CQD, X-ray crystallography is
performed using the X-ray diffractometer
(XRD). X-rays of approximately 1.54 Å are
created by bombarding a water-cooled cop­
per target with electrons, introduced with
a current of about 40 mA and accelerated to
20-50 keV [8]. This process, known as the
Bremsstrahlung effect, is responsible for
the generation of X-rays via electron-neg­
ative acceleration upon interaction with
the copper nucleus’ Coulomb field. The
X-rays are then filtered and collimated into
a coherent, monochromatic beam. The co­
herent X-ray beam is diffracted through
the crystalline sample and the interference
pattern, dictated by Bragg’s Law (Equation
2), is recorded as the angle of incidence is
varied [8].
Characterization of many of the
III-Nitride
semiconductors’
structural
properties can be determined by XRD.
Bragg’s Law is used to determine the lat­
tice constant of the crystal. If the rocking
curve is narrow and the wavelength of the
X-ray is known, the lattice constant may
be determined by measuring the epilayer
omega peak position relative to the sub­
strate reference peak [1]. Lattice mismatch
between epilayers or substrate is indicative
of the strain or relaxation present in the
crystal [8]. The size of the rocking curve’s
full-width
at
half-maximum(FWHM),
which can be easily obtained from a sym­
metric XRD scan, is inversely related to
the number of dislocations in the epilayer
and therefore an indicator of film quality
[3]. The composition of alloy III-Nitrides
can be determined from Vegard’s Law
using the lattice constants calculated from
the XRD. Though traditionally achieved
through more destructive or involved
characterization techniques, XRD has
even been shown to provide an accurate
estimate of mosaicity and defect densities
within crystalline materials using a tech­
nique known as Williamson-Hall plots.
The thickness of epilayers and superlattice
periods can be determined by the distance
between satellite peaks on either side of the
principal peak, known as Pendellösung os­
cillations, while the intensity and number
of satellites are indicative of film quality.
CQD uses a Philips HR-XRD system
for structural characterization. The X-ray
half-beam intensity is kept at 30,000 steps
for III-Nitride scans. For sample adjust­
ment, the X-ray is left in standby mode, 5
mA and -35 kV, and the shutters are closed;
however, for performing scans of the sam­
ple, this is increased to 35 mA and the shut­
ters are opened. Important parameters,
which must be controlled by the system,
include the angle the sample stage makes
with the incident beam (ω), the angle the
detector axis makes with the incident beam
(2θ), the tilt about the intersection of the
plane of scattering vectors with the plane
of the sample holder (φ), and the rotation
about the surface normal (χ). In symmetric
diffractometry, the angle of incidence, ω,
is equal to the angle of detection, θ, which
allows for probing of the sample normal,
yielding information such as the c-plane
family (00.1) in wurtzite crystalline struc­
tures; whereas in asymmetric diffractom­
etry, the angle of incidence, ω, is not the
same as the angle of detection, θ, allowing
for probing of a multitude of planes, unob­
tainable through symmetric geometry such
as the (10-15) plane.
Williamson-Hall
Williamson-Hall (W-H) plots allow for
an estimated analysis of the mosaicity
of epitaxial layers — including tilt angle
(αtilt), heterogeneous strain (ε┴), lateral
coherence length (L║), and perpendicular
coherence length (L┴) — via symmetric
X-ray crystallography of three orders of
[9]. W-H plots take the form of in-plane
or perpendicular, with the former being
the plot of βω-2θ(sinθ)/λ vs. (sinθ)/λ and
the latter being βω-2θ(cosθ)/λ vs. (cosθ)/λ,
where βω-2θ is the full-width at half-max­
imum (FWHM), θ is the diffraction peak
angle, and λ is the wavelength of the
values are plotted according to these axes
and a linearly fit line is drawn. For the
in-plane W-H plot, the lateral coherence
length takes the form of the y-intercept
of the linearly fit line, in angstroms, while
the tilt angle takes the form of the slope
of this linearly fit line, in degrees. For the
perpendicular W-H plot, the perpendic­
ular coherence length takes the form of
the y-intercept of the linearly fit line, in
angstroms, while the heterogeneous strain
takes the form of the slope of this linearly
fit line.
The above four parameters, which
describe the mosaicity of epitaxial layers,
are essential to understanding the crys­
talline structure and quality of the III-Ni­
trides used at CQD for the development of
APDs. Due to a large mismatch in lattice
constants between the sapphire substrate
and epitaxial layers, as well as a difference
in thermal expansion coefficients, III-Ni­
trides take on a mosaic structure of discrete
wurtzite grains due to the breaking of crys­
talline periodicity [10]. Figure 4 models
the III-Nitride mosaicity, described by the
four parameters estimated by W-H plots.
The lateral and perpendicular coherence
lengths describe the average mosaic grain
size, which is dictated by epilayer thickness
[9]. The tilt angle describes the angular
distribution of mosaic grains normal to the
c-plane, while the heterogeneous strain
describes the strain along the c-plane
(growth plane) due to mismatch between
differing epitaxial materials [9].
W-H plots may also be used to es­
timate the screw (threading) dislocation
density of epitaxial layers. Screw disloca­
tions occur when one side of the crystal
undergoes shear stress and is displaced at
least one lattice plane, while the other side
is held fixed, modeled in Figure 5 [8]. Using
the tilt angle, in radians, determined by the
slope of the linear fit of the in-plane W-H
plot, Equation 3 may be used to determine
the screw dislocation density, where αΩ is
the tilt angle in radians and bc is the screw
dislocation Burgers vector, particular to
each epitaxial material [11]. The screw dis­
location Burgers vector (b = [00.1]) for AlN
is 20.1 Å and 10.7 Å for GaN. The Burgers
vector for AlxGa1-xN can be determined for
its mole concentration using Vegard’s law
(Equation 1). III-Nitride reference screw
dislocation densities are readily available
in the literature, with AlN on the order
of 107 cm-2 and AlGaN on the order of 108
cm-2. The magnitude of increase between
epilayers is inversely proportional to the
quality of growth, wherein a small change
in dislocation density from one epilayer to
the next is preferable.
Thickness & Pendellösung Oscillation
In the case of high-quality epitaxial
growths, X-ray crystallography may be
used to calculate epilayer thicknesses.
This is done via measurement of the
Pendellösung oscillations which may be
observed on one shoulder of an XRD
epitaxial diffraction peak. These oscilla­
tions originate from the sharp interfaces
between epilayers of high-quality growth,
often the interface between the epilayer
and substrate [12]. The epilayer thickness
may be calculated according to Equation
4, where λ is the X-ray wavelength (~1.54
Å), Δθ is the Pendellösung period of oscil­
lation (the angular distribution between
Pendellösung peaks), and θ is the diffrac­
tion peak [12].
Mismatch
Sapphire (Al2O3), used as a substrate, and
the III-Nitrides used in the APD design
have wurtzite crystal structure. This, cou­
pled with sapphire’s transparency to the
deep-U.V., makes sapphire an ideal choice
of substrate. The only major drawback
of sapphire is its large lattice mismatch
with III-Nitrides - an approximately 13%
mismatch with AlN, which is shown in
Figure 6 [3]. Large mismatches can result
in semi-coherent or incoherent interphase
boundaries, subject to strain-induced
cracks, edge dislocations, and other defect
structures. A III-Nitride substrate such as
AlN would significantly reduce the mis­
match present; however, AlN is not prac­
tical due to its high cost and defect-related
luminescence [13].
The relative difference in the in-plane
lattice parameters of an interface boundary
is used to determine the mismatch. In the
case of wurtzite grown in the (00.1) ori­
entation, the a-planar family is in-plane.
The hexagonal lattice parameter equation
(Equation 5) is used to first determine the
c-plane lattice parameter from the (00.2)
diffraction peak angle and then the a-plane
lattice parameter from the (10-15) peak
XRD Findings
AlN on Sapphire (Al2O3) Substrate
W-H plots are used to determine the
mosaicity and screw dislocation density
of AlN samples grown on sapphire sub­
strates. The W-H plots calculated for one
sample (R6-13036) are shown in Figure
7(a), for in-plane, and Figure 7(b), for
perpendicular. This growth has a tilt, αtilt,
of 0.1301° and a heterogeneous strain, ε┴,
of 0.0176. The growth has a lateral coher­
ence length, L║, of approximately 222 nm
and a perpendicular coherence length, L┴,
of approximately 445 nm. Using the tilt
angle and the AlN screw Burger’s vector,
the screw dislocation density could be
determined according to Equation 3. The
screw dislocation density was found to be
2.9328×107 cm-2, which agrees with the
expected value for AlN on sapphire.
The epilayer thicknesses of partic­
ularly high-quality AlN samples grown
on sapphire (00.1) can be determined by
measuring the period of the Pendellösung
oscillations observed on ω scans of the
(00.2) diffraction peak. The AlN epilayer
thickness is calculated according to Equa­
tion 4 and then compared to more direct
measurements of the epitaxial cross-sec­
tion using scanning electron microscopy
(SEM). The Pendellösung oscillations (top)
and SEM imaging (bottom) are shown for
two samples in Figure 8. A discrepancy of
8-9% relative to the average of multiple
measurements taken from SEM imaging
is reported. This represents a difference
of tens of nanometers on calculated thick­
nesses of 186 nm for sample R6-13024 in
Figure 8(a), an 8.4% discrepancy, and 244
nm for sample R6-13025 in Figure 8(b), a
9% discrepancy.
The mismatch between the AlN
epitaxial growth and the sapphire sub­
strate can be determined by the in-plane
(a-plane) lattice parameters. To measure
this, the difference between mismatched
(AlN on sapphire) and no lattice mismatch
(AlN on AlN) samples are compared.
No mismatch AlN has an a-plane lattice
parameter of 2.94 Å (5.5% error), while
mismatched AlN has an a-plane lattice
parameter of 3.37 Å (8.1% error). This rep­
resents a mismatch of 14.5% with the AlN
epilayer under strain, which is higher than
expected. The large error of the a-plane
lattice parameters is assumed to be a result
of the Philips HR-XRD system, and more
steps will have to be taken to optimize θ to
improve accuracy.
AlN on AlN Substrate
W-H plots are used to determine the
mosaicity and screw dislocation density of
an AlN sample grown on an AlN substrate
(R6-12731), shown in Figure 9(a), for in-
plane, and Figure 9(b), for perpendicular.
This growth has a tilt, θtilt, of 0.0144° and a
negligible strain, ε┴, of 0.0011, due to the
nature of the homoepitaxial growth. The
growth has a lateral coherence length, L║,
of approximately 2.1 μm and a perpendic­
ular coherence length, L┴, of approximate­
ly 2.9 μm, owing to a thick AlN growth.
The screw dislocation density was found
to be 3.607×105 cm-2, which is two orders
of magnitude less than that for AlN on a
sapphire substrate indicating a substantial­
ly lower-defect growth.
AlxGa1-xN/AlN/Al2O3
W-H plots are used to determine the
mosaicity and screw dislocation density
of an AlxGa1-xN/AlN/Al2O3 growth (R6-
13056), shown in Figure 10: (a) and (b)
are the in-plane and perpendicular plots
for AlN, respectively, and (c) and (d) are
the in-plane and perpendicular plots for
AlxGa1-xN, respectively. This growth has
a tilt, θtilt, of 0.1547° for AlN and 0.4034°
for AlxGa1-xN. It has a heterogeneous
strain, ε┴, of 0.0114 for AlN and 0.0282 for
AlxGa1-xN. The lateral coherence length,
L║, is approximately 195 nm for AlN and
83 nm for AlxGa1-xN. The perpendicular
coherence length, L┴, is approximately
268 nm for AlN and 83 nm for AlxGa1-xN.
The screw dislocation density was found
to be 4.15×107 cm-2 for AlN and 4.86×108
cm-2 for AlxGa1-xN, which aligns with the
expected values.
XRD mapping is performed on Alx­
Ga1-xN/AlN/Al2O3 to assess sample unifor­
mity. W-H plots are used to calculate the
dislocation density, tilt, strain, and lateral
and perpendicular coherence lengths of
each epitaxial material at each point on
the wafer. Additionally, bandgap energies,
lattice parameters, and mole compositions
of AlxGa1-xN are mapped across each lo­
cation. Figure 11 shows the aerial (a) and
cross-section views (b) of an AlxGa1-xN
sample (R6-13039), on which four loca­
tions, each 1 mm apart, were selected in
uniformity mapping.
The AlxGa1-xN and AlN epilayers
show good uniformity across the wafer
for each measured parameter. Figure 12(a)
shows the screw dislocation densities of
each material at each of the four mapped
locations; the mapping reveals a change
in dislocation density of only about one
order of magnitude between the AlN and
AlxGa1-xNepilayers, which is highly desir­
able. Figure 12(b) shows the tilt angle and
Figure 12(c) the heterogeneous strain at
each mapped location, which were extrap­
olated from the slopes of the in-plane and
perpendicular W-H plots, respectively. It
should be noted that the tilt angle and het­
erogeneous strains are both slightly larger
for the AlxGa1-xN epilayer, owing to the na­
ture of the epitaxial layering. Figure 12(d)
shows the lateral coherence lengths and
Figure 12(e) the perpendicular coherence
lengths at each mapped location, which
were extrapolated from the y-intercepts of
the in-plane and perpendicular W-H plots,
respectively. Since the coherence lengths
represent the average grain size and are
indicative of the growth thickness, it is ex­
pected that the thicker AlN epilayer should
have a larger coherence length.
APD
XRD mapping is performed on the final
APD epitaxial structure to assess sample
uniformity. W-H plots are used to cal­
culate the dislocation density, tilt, strain,
and lateral and perpendicular coherence
lengths of each epitaxial material at each
point on the wafer. Additionally, bandgap
energies, lattice parameters, and mole
compositions of AlN, AlxGa1-xN, and GaN
epilayers are mapped across each loca­
tion. Figure 14 shows the aerial (a) and
cross-section views (b) of the APD struc­
ture (R6-12164C), on which four loca­
tions, each 5 mm apart, are selected in the
investigation into uniformity.
Each epitaxial layer shows good uni­
formity across the wafer for each measured
parameter. Figure 15(a) shows the screw
dislocation densities at each of the four
mapped locations; the mapping reveals a
change in dislocation density of only about
one order of magnitude between the AlN
and AlxGa1-xN epilayers and less than one
order of magnitude between the AlxGa1-xN
and GaN, which is highly desirable. Figure
15(b) shows the tilt angle and Figure 15(c)
the heterogeneous strain at each mapped
location, which were extrapolated from
the slopes of the in-plane and perpendic­
ular W-H plots, respectively. It should be
noted that the tilt angle and heterogeneous
strains are both slightly smaller for the
AlN epilayer, while those for AlxGa1-xN
and GaN epilayers are similar, again ow­
ing to the epitaxial structure wherein AlN
is on the sapphire substrate. Figure 15(d)
shows the lateral coherence lengths and
Figure 15(e) the perpendicular coherence
lengths at each mapped location, which
were extrapolated from the y-intercepts of
the in-plane and perpendicular W-H plots,
respectively. Since the coherence lengths
represent the average grain size and are in­
dicative of the growth thickness, it makes
sense that the thicker AlN epilayer should
have a larger coherence length than the
AlxGa1-xN and GaN epilayers.
Mapping also allows for analysis of
the variation of the bandgap energy, lattice
constant (c-plane), and mole composition
of the epilayer materials at each location.
Figure 16(a) shows the bandgap energy (in
both eV and nm) vs. the lattice constant for
the III-Nitride epilayers of the APD struc­
ture at each of the four mapped locations.
Figure 16(b) shows the variation of the
four AlxGa1-xN epilayers as well as the AlN
and GaN bandgap energy and lattice pa­
rameter, with the center point represent­
ing the average of the four locations and
the error bars indicating the minimum and
maximum extrema. The findings unilater­
ally point to a high degree of uniformity
within each epitaxial layer, while also con­
firming values consistent with those found
in the literature for each material and the
expectations from the MOCVD growth
parameters. Particularly with regards to
the four AlxGa1-xN epilayers, the observed
high-Al concentrations are highly desir­
able for the deep-U.V. APD application.
This successful material characterization of
the APD structure predicts the capability
of high-quality diodes with a high level of
uniformity in performance from one diode
to the next, across the device – important
to the efficacy of APD development and
device yields.
Conclusion
The ultimate objective of the research
conducted is to achieve solar-blind deep-
U.V. APDs in Geiger mode for single pho­
ton detection, with high QE and gain and
low dark current. Most important to un­
derstanding the performance of the APD
devices is a deep understanding of the
foundational materials used in their fabri­
cation. Due to the highly reversed nature
of APDs, they are inherently extremely
sensitive to defects. Material character­
ization of high-quality heteroepitaxial
growths is a crucial precursor to the fabri­
cation of high-performance APD devices.
The result of the XRD investigation into
the structural properties of III-Nitrides is
significant: using a non-destructive char­
acterization method, information about
the quality, composition, and uniformity
of growths used for the fabrication of real,
tested APDs are obtained.

Located just across the street from Jones Hall at 1801 Hinman Avenue, the Office
of Undergraduate Research (OUR) is a resource for all undergraduate students looking
to take the next steps to get involved in research. Director Peter Civetta first helped
found the office in 2012 in an effort to provide additional support and guidance for those
interested in doing research, especially those with no previous experience.
The office provides many different resources, such as the Undergraduate
Research Assistant Program (URAP), where students get paired with faculty
members during the fall quarter to help conduct research in various labs, and
Undergraduate Research Grants (URGs), eight-week programs that fund inde­
pendent student projects, both during the academic year and the summer.
URAP specifically targets first- and sec­
ond-year students who have no prior research
experience. While research grants
have historically had the most
involvement
from
juniors
and seniors, one of the office’s
goals has been to get students
involved in these experiences
earlier on during their college
experience.
Beyond the
Classroom: Finding
Opportunities for
Undergraduate
Research
By: Allison Kim
FEATURES
“We know that these experiences
have an incredibly high impact. That’s
a well-documented thing in the field
that students doing their own independent
research is incredibly valuable,” Civetta said. “But we
also know that they don’t know how to do it. Not because
they’re idiots but because we haven’t taught them yet. So part of the goal,
and the work of this office, is to teach them that process.”
For both programs, the process starts with scheduling a meeting with an adviser on
the OUR website. The office looks over resumes and cover letters for those looking to
get paired through URAP. For those who wish to start the process of writing a grant pro­
posal, applicants working with advisers have a much higher success rate as they provide
support throughout the various steps of creating a successful research project.
With URGs, the first hurdle in the process is going from big ideas and interests
to specific questions that students can focus on answering through their work. Civetta
often directs students to look inward to help narrow down their topics.
“One thing that’s guaranteed is that we’re gonna be overwhelmed by the amount of
options there are. This can cause us to freeze or turn to faculty members and ask, what
should I do?” Civetta said. “We want students to be deeply self-reflective. That’s going to
lead you. There are so many damn problems in the world. So, what do you want to work
on? Where do you feel like you can make a difference? What’s important to you?”
The next steps often include connecting students with faculty members who are
experts in their field of interest so they can progress with working on other aspects of
the proposal, such as literature reviews and methodologies. Sometimes, the OUR looks
outside of their own programs to help students find the resources that work the best for
them.
“I joke with students saying that I’m not paid on commission. I’m not trying to push
students into my programs. If you come to me and say you want to do something, and
I know that someone else does that already, I’m going to point you there,” Civetta said.
“Universities are really complicated. No one expects a student to understand how to find
all the resources. We try to be a real central place where you can come in, and if our
grants are relevant for you, we’ll help you with that, but if another program or another
unit might be more helpful, we’ll direct you towards that.”
Civetta said staying connected to all the resources across all corners of Northwestern’s
campus has been crucial to the success of the OUR. Especially, in regard to the office’s
goals of growing involvement in research from fields in the arts and humanities.
“It’s much more obvious in lab settings what research is, but there’s research in
every field. That has exploded, and for the last three years, 25% of all the summer grants
have creative arts or journalism outputs,” Civetta said. “Last year, we had record involve­
ment from first- and second-year students, record involvement from Bienen students,
Medill students, Comm students, which traditionally were not very involved. At the
same time, we were continuing to fund labs at the highest rate ever, so we didn’t take
grants away from one department to fund another. We’ve been creating more opportu­
nities throughout.”
Alongside the OUR’s focused efforts to diversify the areas of research students were
conducting, Civetta said the office has also been working to improve their outreach
methods to increase demographic diversity as well, hoping to reach first-generation
and/or low-income (FGLI) students and students of color.
“We had our highest number of FGLI, BIPOC students last year as well,” Civetta
said. “Those things have been incredibly rewarding just to see students get to do what
they want to do and have these incredibly meaningful experiences.”
Following these new developments in the program, the OUR is looking to continue
its work with programs such as the Emerging Scholars Program which focuses specif­
ically on serving communities that are underrepresented in academic research and
supporting research centered around issues of social justice, diversity, equity, and
inclusion. Additionally, the office is looking toward new areas for growth moving
forward.
“The new frontier for us in the last couple of years has been more wrap­
around support. We’ve been very good at helping students get started, helping
them learn how to write grants, and giving away money. What we’ve real­
ized is that once you get the money to do the grant, research can
be really confusing,” Civetta said. “Figuring
out what to do with research at the end of
the experience can also be really hard.
[...] We work to find how
we can use this as a way to
learn more about what you
might want to do in the
future. Through this, we’re
looking to support students
more broadly in what they
do.”
Baby got Bac:
Associations Between Maternal Psychosocial
Stress and Infant Gut Microbiotaa in Cebu,
Philippines
by Rebecca C. Wu
Faculty Adviser: Katherine Amato
Department of Anthropology
Introduction
Health is affected by a variety of both biological and sociocultural factors. While
previous research has focused largely on biological factors, sociocultural determinants
of health have also gained attention in recent years. These sociocultural components are
related to structural disparities in health, including access to quality healthcare (Saluja
& Bryant, 2021; Shavers, 2007), stress induced by socioeconomic status (SES) (Baum et
al., 1999; Kapuku et al., 2002), and quality of physical environment (Evans, 2006; Wil­
son et al., 2004). While these factors can affect health through the course of one’s life,
an important point of focus lies in the early-life environment, which includes both the
prenatal environment experienced by a mother and fetus and an infant’s postnatal envi­
ronment. Specifically, maternal experiences, including energetic deprivation (Wu et al.,
2004), climatic stress (Rylander et al., 2013), and psychosocial stress (Davis & Sandman,
2010) can have physiological consequences that are passed on to an infant in utero and
during birth.
Maternal psychosocial stressors can impact maternal and infant immune responses
(Ruiz & Avant, 2005), epigenetic activity (DeSocio, 2018; Thayer & Kuzawa, 2011), and
microbiome composition and diversity (Jašarević et al., 2015, 2017). Infant cognitive
development has been associated with stressors through changes in composition of the
microbiota (Vogel et al., 2020). However, despite known links between maternal stress
and infant gut microbiota composition
(Jahnke et al., 2021), as well as the gut
microbiota and physical health (Thursby
& Juge, 2017), infant physical health out­
comes related to the microbiota remain
understudied. In order to better understand
pathways between maternal psychosocial
stress, the microbiota, and infant health
outcomes, the relationships between these
variables were studied in Cebu, Philippines
in a subset of 43 mother/infant dyads from
the Cebu Longitudinal Health and Nutri­
tion Survey. Results shed light on potential
connections between maternal psychoso­
cial stress, the infant gut microbiota, and
infant health outcomes.
Background
Allostasis and Stress
Allostasis is a term used to describe
the efficient regulation of physiolog­
ical processes through the biological
“anticipation” of needs in an environment
(McEwen & Gianaros, 2011; Sterling,
2004) and represents a shift from the
traditional homeostatic model (Cannon,
1929). Importantly, allostatic processes
occur in response to neurological predic­
tion, and thus, this concept can be used
in better understanding stress. Stress is
a broad term that encompasses a variety
of physiological and psychosocial factors
affecting allostasis, including nutrition,
environment, and sociocultural factors. An
accumulation of stress, sometimes termed
allostatic load (McEwen & Stellar, 1993),
can have negative effects on physiological
systems, eventually resulting in disease.
Psychosocial stress, which arises from
stressors relating to sociocultural variables,
as opposed to those that arise from physi­
cal phenomena (Elder Jr. et al., 1996), has
gained increasing attention in recent years.
It can stem from a wide variety of factors
across cultures, including SES, interper­
sonal relationships, and identity-based
expectations (Taylor & Aspinwall, 1996).
In particular, identity-based marginaliza­
tion, including racioethnic discrimination,
can increase psychosocial stress for indi­
viduals in marginalized groups (Collier et
al., 2013; Spruill, 2010). These stressors
disproportionately affect individuals in
underprivileged groups; thus, stress is
often further exacerbated through a com­
pounding of several interrelated physical
and social factors.
Developmental Origins of Health and
Disease and the Human Gut Microbiota
Research shows that early-life differ­
ences in nutrition, environment, and stress
can contribute to variable health later in
life. This field of research is related to the
Developmental Origins of Health and Dis­
ease (DOHaD) hypothesis, which posits
that factors contributing to infant mor­
tality could also lead to morbidity later in
life (Barker & Osmond, 1986). Research on
mechanisms of DOHaD has largely focused
on epigenetic effects (Bianco-Miotto et al.,
2017; Kuzawa & Sweet, 2009), but the gut
microbiota has received increasing atten­
tion as a potential pathway through which
early environments can affect health.
The human gut microbiota refers
to the collection of microorganisms, or
microbes, that inhabit the human gastro­
intestinal tract (Ursell et al., 2012). The
microbiome, by contrast, refers not only to
the microbes themselves, but the genetic
information possessed by the microor­
ganisms in a particular community. These
microorganisms are integral to bodily
functions, including provision of nutri­
ents, support of the immune system, and
protection against pathogens (Thursby
& Juge, 2017). Changes in microbiota
composition, termed dysbiosis, have been
associated with a variety of morbidities, in­
cluding but not limited to Type 2 diabetes
(Sharma & Tripathi, 2019), obesity (Ley,
2010), and Crohn’s disease (Wright et al.,
The microbiota is initially acquired
at birth, either through the vaginal tract
and maternal fecal during vaginal birth, or
from the mother’s skin and environment
in the case of Cesarean section (C-section)
(Dominguez-Bello et al., 2010). It is re­
sponsive to changes in the environment,
especially in the first two to three years
of life (Rodríguez et al., 2015). Dysbiosis
of the gut microbiota in infants, including
changes resulting from C-section, anti­
biotic use, and environmental exposures,
have implications for early life, as these al­
terations have been associated with future
disease risk (Tamburini et al., 2016).
The Gut Microbiota and Stress
In addition to its environmental sen­
sitivity, the gut microbiota sits at the inter­
face between stress and physiology, as it is
sensitive to both physical and psychosocial
stressors. Gut microbiota composition is
associated with neurocognitive develop­
ment in infants (Carlson et al., 2018; Vogel
et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2016). Neurode­
velopmental disorders often coexist with
physical health problems like gastrointes­
tinal issues, headaches, and asthma (Alabaf
et al., 2019), suggesting that stressors per­
turbing the infant microbiota can impact
physical health later in life.
Recent research has combined analy­
ses of maternal stress, the maternal micro­
biota, and infant health outcomes. Increas­
es in potentially pathogenic bacteria in the
maternal gut have been correlated with
high stress that alters the immune system
(Jahnke et al., 2021). Infant gut microbial
composition is also associated with levels
of maternal psychosocial stress (Hechler et
al., 2019). Despite this, research on the spe­
cific pathways connecting these variables
in human populations has been limited.
Studies have focused on similar topics, but
have centered on pregnancy-related stress
(Dunlop et al., 2015) or utilized mouse
models (Jašarević et al., 2017).
While mouse studies have provided
strong evidence for pathways between
maternal stress and the infant gut micro­
biota (Bowers & Yehuda, 2016; Jašarević
et al., 2015), the physiologies of mice and
humans, as well as the diversity of psy­
chosocial stressors that are experienced by
each, differ greatly. Additionally, despite
known connections between lower SES
and higher levels of chronic stress resulting
from social and environmental conditions
(Baum et al., 1999), little work in this area
has included robust information on SES
and its related factors. Thus, while these
studies provide valuable insight, studies
in socioeconomically diverse human pop­
ulations are an important future step in
understanding these pathways.
Health Disparities and Broader Impacts
While issues of stress and health are
ubiquitous across populations, these effects
are particularly significant in underprivi­
leged groups. Differences in ability to ac­
cess resources and prevalence of psychoso­
cial stressors can contribute to disparities
in health outcomes across populations. In­
dividuals in socioeconomically underpriv­
ileged groups not only experience poorer
access to healthcare and food (Kapral et al.,
2002; Zhu et al., 2020), but also must cope
with the compounded psychosocial stress
resulting from these factors and discrim­
ination (Saluja & Bryant, 2021). It is im­
portant in scientific research, particularly
when attempting to understand health
inequities, to contextualize these within
social environments and lived experiences.
Studying differences in stress experience
and their potential impacts on the mi­
crobiota, stress, and inflammation allows
research to contribute to the broader body
of race-conscious literature to improve
understanding of health in minoritized
groups.
Research Questions and
Hypotheses
1. How is stress associated with the mater­
nal and infant gut microbiota?
Hypothesis One: It was hypothesized
that higher levels of perceived maternal
stress, as determined by validated stress
surveys, would be associated with lowered
microbial diversity in mothers and their
infants at two weeks and six months. It was
also hypothesized that different microbial
taxa would be enriched or decreased de­
pending on levels of maternal stress.
2. How is composition of the infant gut
microbiota associated with infant health
outcomes?
Hypothesis Two: It was predicted
that higher levels of maternal stress would
correspond with a higher prevalence  of
adverse health outcomes at both two weeks
and six months, and that higher infant mi­
crobial diversity would be associated with
a lower incidence of adverse health out­
comes. Additionally, it was hypothesized
that the abundances of different microbial
taxa would be enriched or decreased with
the prevalence of illness outcomes at two
weeks and six months.
Materials and Methods
Surveys
Data for this project were collected as
part of the Cebu Longitudinal Health and
Nutrition Survey (CLHNS), a cohort study
based in Metro Cebu, Philippines since
1983. Data for the CLHNS were originally
collected from 3,327 mother/infant dyads
in 1983 and 1984 (Adair et al., 2011). Spe­
cific data for this study were collected from
a subset of the original study. The moth­
ers in this study, who were infants in the
original 1983/1984 study, were contacted
for follow-up in 2017 and 2018 to gauge
interest in this sub-study. Interviews were
conducted in Cebuano with 51 pregnant
mothers from the cohort during their
third trimester of pregnancy. Answers to
interview questions were coded in English.
Follow-up to these original interviews oc­
curred at two weeks and six months post­
partum and included surveys of birth and
infant health.
Survey questions included topics on
diet, stress, medication, and other lifestyle
factors. Stress was quantified using modi­
fied versions of the Perceived Stress Scale
(PSS) and Center for Epidemiologic Stud­
ies Depression Scale (CES-D). The PSS is
the most widely used validated survey for
measuring stress in individuals (Cohen et
al., 1983). The CES-D, another widely used
scale, typically consists of 20 questions re­
lating to potential depressive symptoms
(Radloff, 1977). The modified questions
and frequencies of responses are recorded
in Tables 1 and 2.
Using data from both scales, stress
levels were indexed as follows: questions
relating to positive emotions were re­
versed, as is typically done in both surveys,
and numbers were summed both separate­
ly for the PSS and CES-D and together
across both scales. Larger numbers indi­
cated higher levels of perceived stress or
depressive symptoms. The possible range
of PSS scores was 0 to 40, while the range
of CES-D scores was 16 to 48. These scores
were also divided into low, medium, and
high tertiles (Figure 1) for analysis.
Additionally, data on income and
SES were collected and analyzed to better
understand stress in relation to SES. Av­
erage monthly income over the past three
months was directly reported in 15 out
of 43 households, with a range of 450 to
34,000 pesos per month (8 to 614 USD).
An index of SES was generated using rel­
evant measures of social class previously
used in Cebu (Desantis et al., 2015). Pos­
sible scores in this index ranged from 1 to
12, with higher values representing higher
SES. Actual scores ranged from 1 to 10,

Microbiome Analysis
Fecal samples were collected as a
proxy for the gut microbial community
of mothers and infants in the community.
Mothers were instructed to collect a fe­
cal sample from their most recent bowel
movement before the time of the inter­
view. Infant fecal samples were collected
by mothers at two weeks and six months
of age from soiled diapers. Samples were
stored in ethanol and containers were
stored away from direct sunlight and warm
temperatures until they were picked up by
researchers between six and 12 hours after
sample collection. The samples were stored
at 4 °C until shipment to the Amato Lab­
oratory in Evanston, Illinois, where they
were stored at -80 °C until DNA extraction.
Microbial DNA was extracted from
fecal samples using the QIAGEN Powersoil
Kit following manufacturer instructions,
with some modifications to incubation
times and centrifuge speeds and times. Af­
ter extraction, the V4-V5 region of the 16S
rRNA gene was amplified using polymerase
chain reaction and the 515Fa/926R primer
set (Mallott & Amato, 2018; Walters et al.,
2015) and following the Earth Microbiome
Project protocol (Thompson et al., 2017).
Each set of extractions and each PCR plate
was run using a negative control to pro­
tect against contamination of samples by
foreign DNA. Grouped amplicons were
sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq V2 plat­
form at the DNA Services Facility at the
University of Illinois Chicago.
Paired-end sequences were processed
in QIIME2 v2020.2 (Bolyen et al., 2019).
For each set of samples (maternal, two
week, and six months), sequences from
mitochondria and chloroplasts were re­
moved. Maternal samples resulted in a
