44,686). Using the dada2 plug-in, amplicon
sequence variants (ASVs) were obtained
and clustered.
Statistical Analysis
After processing in QIIME2, micro­
biome data were further analyzed in R us­
ing the phyloseq, ANCOM-BC, and vegan
packages, which are designed for use with
microbiome data. Using the vegan pack­
age, permutational multivariate analysis
of variance (PERMANOVA) tests were
run for two week, six month, and mater­
nal microbiome data and the following
variables: maternal PSS indexed scores,
maternal CES-D indexed scores, maternal
total stress score, infant health outcomes,
and SES scores. Health outcomes were
tested both as individual symptoms (fever,
diarrhea, runny nose, sore throat, ear dis­
charge, nasal discharge, or other illness)
and total illness frequency. Antibiotic use
was included as a covariate in the two-week
model. Maternal antibiotics, antibiotics
at six months, breastfeeding, and delivery
mode — all previously shown to impact
microbial composition (Kurilshikov et al.,
2021) —  were not significantly associated
with microbial composition in this sample
and were therefore not included in any
models.
Microbial alpha diversity, or diver­
sity within each community of microbes,
was measured at two weeks, six months,
and the maternal third trimester using
the Shannon Diversity Index (Kim et al.,
2017). These values were tested for cor­
relations with the following: maternal PSS
indexed scores, maternal CES-D indexed
scores, maternal total stress, infant health
outcomes, quantified as above, and SES
scores. Similar to the PERMANOVAs,
antibiotic use was included as a covariate
at two weeks, while no covariates were in­
cluded at six months or with maternal data.
Finally, differential abundances of
microbial taxa were tested using Analysis
of Compositions of Microbiomes with Bias
Correction (ANCOM-BC) (Lin & Peddada,
2020) at the phylum, class, order, family,
genus, and species levels. The significance
of aforementioned covariates was tested at
each level, and only infant antibiotic use at
two weeks at the phylum level and delivery
mode at the species level at two weeks were
found to be significant. Maternal PSS and
CES-D levels were divided based on pre­
viously mentioned tertiles. Frequency of
infant illness symptoms, individual symp­
toms, and presence or absence of illness
were also tested. Results were interpreted
based on q-values — measures of statistical
significance controlled for the false dis­
covery rate — and log-fold change (LFC)
values, where positive values indicate an
increase in abundance, while negative val­
ues indicate a decrease in abundance in a
condition.
Results
Maternal Stress and the Microbiota
PERMANOVA tests were run be­
tween maternal stress scores (PSS, CES-D,
and combined) and weighted unifrac dis­
tances for mothers and for infants at two
weeks and six months. Neither the mod­
els that controlled for covariates nor the
unadjusted models showed any statistical
significance in associations with microbial
composition. However, pseudo-F values
for maternal stress on all three scales and
maternal microbiota composition were all
lower than values for maternal stress and
infant microbiota composition, suggesting
that maternal stress may be more strongly
related to infant than maternal microbiota
composition (Figure 2).
Maternal alpha diversity was signifi­
cantly negatively associated with CES-D
scores (p = 0.044), and higher total stress
levels showed trends toward lower di­
versity (p = 0.055), but diversity was not
significantly associated with PSS scores (p
= 0.188). At two weeks, infant microbial
diversity was significantly correlated with
maternal CES-D (p = 0.030), maternal PSS
(p = 0.037), and maternal total stress (p =
0.017). This association was not evident
with the CES-D score (p = 0.475), PSS
score (p = 0.299), or total stress (p =  0.288)
(Figure 3).
ANCOM-BC analysis showed that at
the phylum and class levels, medium CES-D
level was associated with an increase in
Spirochaetes abundance when compared
with low CES-D level. Medium CES-D
level was associated with an increase in
abundance of Bacillales, Staphylococcace­
ae, and Staphylococcus at six months of in­
fant age. Medium PSS levels corresponded
with a decrease in abundance of the family
Ruminococcaceae at six months of age and
showed trends toward a lower abundance
of the genus Faecalibacterium and species
Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. Results are
displayed in Table 3.
Maternal Stress, SES, and Infant Health
Outcomes
PERMANOVA testing showed that
SES levels were correlated with maternal
microbiota composition (p = 0.025), but
not composition at two weeks (p = 0.0564)
or six months (p = 0.499). SES levels were
associated with income (p = 0.004), but not
with maternal or infant microbial diversity.
At two weeks, sore throat was significantly
associated with infant microbiota compo­
sition (p = 0.025). Other symptoms and
total frequency of illness symptoms were
not associated with microbiota composi­
tion at two weeks. At six months, neither
individual health outcomes nor total illness
symptoms were associated with microbio­
ta composition.
Most health outcomes were not as­
sociated with infant microbial diversity,
but notably, “other illness” at two weeks
was associated with microbial diversity (p
= 0.031) at two weeks. ANCOM testing of
microbial taxa showed no significant asso­
ciations at any taxonomic levels, though
the genus Megamonas trended toward dif­
ferential abundance between ill and non-
ill infants at 6 months (q = 0.094). Health
outcomes results are found in Table 4 and
Table 5.
Discussion
Maternal Stress, Maternal Microbiota Com­
position, and Infant Microbiota Composition
Despite previous research pointing to
associations between maternal perceived
stress, maternal and infant gut microbiota
composition, and infant health outcomes,
few results were significant using PER­
MANOVA testing in our sample. Mater­
nal stress was associated with  infant gut
microbial diversity at two weeks of age,
while maternal gut microbial composition
was associated with infant gut microbial
diversity at six months of age. It was pre­
dicted that high maternal stress would be
associated with low alpha diversity. How­
ever, it was only strongly associated with
microbial diversity in infants at two weeks
and showed trends towards lower diversity
in maternal samples. It is therefore possible
that, while maternal stress is an early pre­
dictor of microbial diversity, as an infant
is exposed to more environmental fac­
tors and spends more time outside of the
womb, other variables confound this rela­
tionship. Maternal stress, while associated
with diversity, was not associated with
composition at any time points, suggesting
that these differences in diversity may be
small compared to overall composition.
Another explanation that is consis­
tent with concepts in DOHaD is that ma­
ternal stress is “passed down” to the infant
through a mechanism that is not the mi­
crobiota; that is, epigenetic modifications
or changes in hormonal levels are passed
to the infant in utero, signaling to the
infant that high stress should be expected
after birth. The infant may then need to
adapt to the corresponding immunolog­
ical challenges predicted in utero, leading
to a quicker increase in diversity at two
weeks that is less evident at six months.
Furthermore, at two weeks, the infant im­
mune system has not yet developed, while
a functioning immune system exists at six
months (West 2002). The microbiota plays
a role in the development of the immune
system, which influences composition of
the microbiota (Martin et al., 2010), sug­
gesting that the connection between these
factors in intergenerational effects of stress
and health has not been fully explored.
ANCOM-BC results also support
the hypothesis that increased maternal
stress affects the immune system of the in­
fant. Enrichment of Staphylococcus at six
months in infants of mothers experiencing
higher stress suggests differences in im­
mune function. Staphylococcus has been
implicated in immunological challenges
(Pietrocola et al., 2017), and colonization
by Staphylococcus in early life is associ­
ated with risk for atopic disease (Vael &
Desager, 2009) and allergy (Björkstén et
al., 1999), supporting its potential impacts
on innate immunity.
Similarly, bacterial species Faecali­
bacterium prausnitzii, which is in the fam­
ily Ruminococcaceae, was decreased at six
months in infants of mothers with higher

to be reduced in intestinal disorders (Lo­

reduction of F. prausnitzii decreases one’s
ability to defend against inflammation
(Parsaei et al., 2021). These results, in con­
junction with the enrichment of Staphylo­
coccus, which can increase inflammation,
suggest that infants of more highly stressed
mothers may experience immunological
challenges as they age.
Importantly, differences in enrich­
ment and depletion of microbial taxa were
most significant in infants at six months.
Given that diversity measures are less
strongly associated with maternal stress at
six months than two weeks, this suggests
that changes to the immune system be­
tween two weeks and six months contrib­
ute to specific selection of microbial taxa
at six months, while a different physiolog­
ical pathway may contribute to decreased
diversity of the infant microbiota at two
weeks.
Health Outcomes
Health outcomes at two weeks, mea­
sured as a variety of physical health symp­
toms in the 14 days prior to survey, were
only somewhat related to maternal stress at
microbiota diversity at two weeks. Despite
statistical significance, only one infant had
a sore throat at two weeks, and only three
infants exhibited a fever. It is therefore
possible that neither maternal stress nor
infant microbial diversity was truly predic­
tive of infant illness at two weeks.
The only significant associations were
found between sore throat and fever and
microbial diversity at two weeks, and these
associations were notably absent in infants
at six months. This is likely explained by
the timing of survey data. At both two
weeks and six months of infant age, moth­
ers were asked about the symptoms of their
infants in the 14 days prior to the survey,
which excluded approximately five months
of health data between two weeks and five
and a half months. Given this missing time
frame, data on illness at six months were
not indicative of overall infant health up to
the point of the survey.
Furthermore, most health outcomes
that have been associated with gut micro­
biota composition in the past have been
later-life morbidities like diabetes, obesity,
and heart disease, few of which are found
in infants. Previous studies of the microbi­
ota and DOHaD have shown that early-life
environments can predict later-life risk for
non-infectious disease, but work on in­
fectious disease susceptibility is lacking in
the intersection of microbiota and DOHaD
research. The early immunological func­
tions of the gut microbiota must therefore
be explored to better understand how
differences in colonization can modulate
susceptibility to infectious disease in early
life before the establishment of the infant
immune system.
Future Directions
An increased timespan of this lon­
gitudinal study could shed more light on
the later health outcomes of infants in

environments can

for non-infectious
disease.”
this cohort. Given that data collection
occurred in 2017 and 2018, follow-up in
the present (five to six years later) could
provide insight on the neurodevelopmen­
tal and physical health outcomes previ­
ously shown to be present in children of
highly stressed mothers. It would also be
beneficial to collect data on blood pressure,
cholesterol levels, and other future predic­
tors of non-infectious disease. Given the
likely role of the immune system in mod­
ulating — and being modulated by — the
gut microbiota between two weeks and
six months of age, valuable insight could
be gained through longitudinal measures
of immune activation and inflammation.
These data from mothers and infants, in
conjunction with microbiome data and
data on frequency of infectious illness,
could shed light on potential immune con­
sequences of intergenerational effects of
stress.
Conclusions
This
project
supports
ongoing
research on the intergenerational effects
of maternal stress on infant health.
Importantly, it was discovered that mater­
nal stress was associated with microbiome
diversity at two weeks and microbiome
composition at six months, though it was
not associated with diversity at six months
or composition at two weeks. These
seemingly contradictory results point to
the timing of immune development as a
critical point from which to further study
the impacts of maternal stress on the
microbiome and infant health. While few
significant results were found with infant
health outcomes in relation to microbiota
diversity or composition, this may be due
to the timing of survey data. Future work
should have more comprehensive data on
health outcomes — including pathogenic
and non-pathogenic disease — and should
incorporate markers of inflammation and
immune activation to improve under­
standing of specific pathways to the inter­
generational transmission of stress. ◆

“Beauty Sickness”:
Dr. Renee Engeln on
Researching Body Image
and Vigilance
By: Izzy Pareja
FEATURES
Body image, defined as the way in which someone perceives their own body, has become an
increasingly popular topic of conversation, especially with the rise of social media and photo
editing platforms that make it easy to promote unrealistic appearance standards.
Both historically and currently, women have been especially susceptible to pressures sur­
rounding appearance. Margaret Atwood, award-winning author of The Handmaid’s Tale,
attempted to describe the intense relationship women have with their bodies in her 1993 novel
The Robber Bride: “. . . pretending you’re unseen, pretending you have a life of your own, that
you can wash your feet and comb your hair unconscious of the ever-present watcher peering
through the keyhole, peering through the keyhole in your own head, if nowhere else . . . You
are your own voyeur.”
With the field of body image research experiencing a growth like never before over the last
decade, the idea that Atwood presents, one of a constant, second-nature vigilance extended by
women towards their bodies, seems to have gained much empirical support.
Dr. Renee Engeln, a Northwestern
professor and Director of the Body
and Media (BAM) Lab, is one
researcher dedicated to investi­
gating this phenomenon. In her
book Beauty Sick: How the Cultural
Obsession with Beauty Hurts Girls and
Women, she identifies a trend in
which “women’s emotional energy
gets so bound up with what they
see in the mirror that it becomes
harder for them to see other aspects
of their lives,” which is sustained by
“a culture that focuses on women’s
appearance over anything else they
might do or say or be.” She calls
this sensation “beauty sickness,” a
term that encapsulates one of the
prominent issues at the core of her
research.
“In general, what we look at are factors in our culture, broadly, that make it hard to
feel okay about your body,” Engeln said while describing her lab’s agenda. “We mostly
focus on women, but we also do some work in particular on sexual minorities and body
image that is more gender inclusive.”
Her lab’s research goals are highly oriented around those of her research assistants
and the relevance of certain topics.
“To some extent, what we’re focusing on at any given time just has to do with
what’s going on with students’ research projects, but also just what’s going on in the
world that’s interesting,” Engeln said.
While Engeln and her team have managed to contribute various extremely
relevant findings to the field of body image research, that doesn’t mean she and other
researchers haven’t experienced their fair share of challenges.
“It’s a hard topic to study because a lot of people don’t take it seriously.” Engeln
described an experience listening to a methods in psychology podcast episode in which
the hosts critiqued a journal article published in the journal Body Image. “The two
podcasters, who were both men, said ‘Wait, what journal is this in? Body Image? How
could there be a journal called Body Image?’ . . . They just immediately dismissed it.”
Engeln finds this sentiment particularly frustrating, especially since there is ample
evidence of damaging appearance-related messages present in every-day life.
“Look at the diet industry, look at the beauty industry, look at rates of eating disorder
behavior, and then tell me that body image doesn’t matter.”
Engeln is also concerned with producing research that is more representative of
different kinds of bodies and people, especially since the field has historically neglected
to do so.
“Early on, a lot of work in this area was about pretty much privileged white women
with anorexia,” Engeln said. “That was sort of what people thought of body image
struggles.”
Despite its necessity, this effort has presented its own set of obstacles that have been
difficult to overcome in a traditional research setting.
“One of the broad challenges we face is how to be more inclusive,” Engeln said.
“Both in terms of what we’re studying, who we’re studying, where we’re getting our data,
dealing with real limits in terms of the money we have to pay research participants—a
very small amount, right—or the access we have to different populations to study.”
Issues surrounding body image have become popular topics for discussion as well,
especially on social media platforms like TikTok. The popularity of movements promot­
ing body positivity and mental health maintenance in recent years have also increased
conversation surrounding the subject. This, too, comes with its own set of challenges, as
Engeln points out.
“There are a lot of well-meaning people who are trying to have a positive impact on
body image who are doing things for which there is no empirical support.”
Despite the misinformation circulating through social media apps, stigma against
body image as a valid research area, and struggle to implement more inclusive research
frameworks, the field continues to grow stronger as researchers gain a deeper under­
standing of how women develop relationships with their bodies. This alone has been
a success for researchers like Engeln, who began their work during a time where issues
women often experienced with body image were written off as matters of confidence or
vanity.
“We do a much better job now,” Engeln said. “Realizing that there’s more going on
than that, realizing that body image isn’t just something that happens in you, in your
head, but it’s something between you and your culture that is deeply interpersonal.”
Abstract
Over the last decade, public schools have seen a dramatic rise in the use of visible school
security measures, including metal detectors, security cameras, and security personnel
(Tanner-Smith & Fisher, 2015). Although several studies have examined the impact of a
school security presence on students’ academic outcomes, only a few studies have looked
at how a security presence impacts school climate and student wellbeing, largely focus­
ing on quantitative analyses. The lack of more qualitative approaches that offer in-depth
descriptions of students’ lived experiences limits the scope of assessments examining
school security presences. The present study seeks to fill these gaps by examining the
relationship between school security and school climate through the lens of student
wellbeing. A survey was completed by 97 Northwestern first-year students, assessing
their high school’s climate with or without a school security presence. Afterward, 10
students were selected for follow-up interviews. The semi-structured interviews con­
sisted of items related to dimensions of school climate and adolescent wellbeing, and all
selected interviewees graduated from a high school with a security presence. Findings of
the study included the impact of school violence on a student’s relationship with their
school’s security and administration and its consequences for school climate and student
wellbeing; direct impacts of school security on student wellbeing; how different security
types elicit different perceptions in students; how student identity impacts the relation­
ship between a student and their school’s security presence; and how a lack of adequate
support affects student perception of school climate and student wellbeing.
The Impact of School
Security on Student
Wellbeing
by Jacob Geil
Faculty Advisers: Dr. Timothy Dohrer and Dr. Regina Logan
School of Education & Social Policy
Introduction
Public schools over the last decade have
seen a dramatic rise in the use of visible
school security measures, including metal
detectors, security cameras, and security
personnel (Tanner-Smith & Fisher, 2015).
In response to several high-profile school
shootings in the 1990s, federal and state
legislation began establishing a security
presence in schools that continues to grow.
This has prompted a fierce debate.
Supporters argue that a security presence
protects against school violence and helps
to improve relationships between young
people and security personnel. Opponents
rebut that security in schools is disruptive
and criminalizes student behavior with
disproportionate damage done to minority
students and students with disabilities.
Several studies have examined the
impact of school security on student out­
comes. However, only a few studies have
looked at how a security presence impacts
school climate and student wellbeing,
largely focusing on quantitative analyses.
This leaves gaps in what to date has been
observed and reported. The lack of more
qualitative approaches that offer in-depth
descriptions of students’ lived experiences
limits the scope of assessments examining
school security presences.
School climate plays a critical role
in a school’s efforts toward meeting goals
and resolving problems, as students ex­
periencing a positive school climate show
stronger academic performance and lower
rates of absenteeism, truancy, and drop out
than that of students experiencing a nega­
tive school climate (Norton, 1984; Payne,
2018). Furthermore, schools have an enor­
mous impact on a student’s development,
especially during adolescence, which is an
important and complex period of the lifes­
pan, characterized by significant physical,
psychological, and social transitions (PRB,
2014). Considering this importance, a
thorough understanding of the elements of
school climate and the factors that might
be negatively impacting perceived school
climate is essential to achieving academ­
ic goals, as well as promoting positive
emotional and behavioral outcomes for
students.
Additionally, this research, in exam­
ining school security through the lens of
school climate and student experience, will
help to establish a better understanding
of how previously researched inequities
related to school security and punishment
manifest in student experiences and out­
comes, and what their consequences are
for students of color. These findings could
be informative to educators and adminis­
trators as they contemplate equity-based
changes to their school security and school
climate procedures.
This study examined the relationship
between school security and school climate
through the lens of its extended conse­
quences for student wellbeing. Through
its methodology, it collected and examined
student experiences of stress, safety, fear,
and discomfort, assessed how they mani­
fested in anxiety, depression, and other
mental health challenges among students,
and explored their connection with the se­
curity presence at the student’s high school.
Review of Literature
Violence Within Schools
School violence can encompass a mul­
titude of behaviors, including bullying,
fighting, verbal threats, weapon posses­
sion, physical aggression, and acts of sexual
violence, including harassment and assault
(Turanovic & Siennick, 2022). Regardless
of its form, school violence has been found
to have a traumatic impact on everyone
within a school community, most of all
students, who are especially vulnerable to
many of its consequences, including lone­
liness, low self-esteem, depression, anx­
iety, suicidality, self-harm, and fear (NIJ,
2022). Furthermore, due to the sensitivity
of adolescence, experiencing violence in
school during this period of development
can have long-term effects on a student’s
health, such as reactive attachment dis­
order, obesity, diabetes, heavy alcohol
or substance use, and other poor health
outcomes, in addition to the emotional
consequences listed above (Ferrara et al.,
Increase in School Security Presence
In an attempt to mitigate threats of school
violence, public schools over the last de­
cade have seen a rise in the use of visible
school security measures (Tanner-Smith
of public primary schools and 75.2% of
public high schools had a regular security
presence. By 2017-2018, these numbers
had inflated to 51.4% for public primary
schools and 84.3% for public high schools.
School Resource Officer (SRO) programs
refer to the permanent placement of law
enforcement officers within schools, and
as a response to increasing rates of school
shootings, SRO programs have grown in
both size and mission over the last two
decades (Ryan et al., 2017). As of 2017-
2018, 36% of public primary schools and
72% of public high schools had armed law
enforcement stationed on campus (NCES,
Nonetheless, evidence has shown that
a school security presence does not neces­
sarily prevent school-based violence nor
lead to increased school safety (Kupchik &
Farina, 2016). Although some researchers
have reported positive impacts of an SRO
presence in schools (Johnson, 2016), based
on a report by the National Center for
Education Statistics (2022), the 2020-2021
school year saw the highest number of
school shootings in two decades, despite a
rise in the use of school security.
Impact of School Security on Student
Outcomes
Several studies have critically examined
the impact of a school security presence on
students’ academic outcomes and educa­
tional futures, finding that the presence of
school security can lead to increased rates
of student suspension and arrest (Finn &
Servoss, 2014). The consequences of in­
creased suspension, expulsion, and arrest
rates of students are severe, as any policy
that removes a student who misbehaves
from the classroom creates an “educational
disruption” that prevents that student
from receiving the protective effects of
education on misbehavior or crime, there­
by predisposing that student to further
misbehavior, disciplinary infractions, or
incarceration (Passero, 2022).
Furthermore, researchers have found
that race and gender play a large role in
the frequency and severity of punishment
received in schools (Pentek & Eisenberg,
2018). Research has shown a severe discrep­
ancy in who is punished, how frequently
they are punished, to what severity they are
punished, and the lasting consequences they
might face. Black students, and Black female
students in particular, experience dispro­
portionately high suspension and expulsion
rates (Morris & Perry, 2017). Considering
how law enforcement, other security mea­
sures, and punitive policies have created an
avenue for student incarceration, the conse­
quences of these disparities and the implicit
bias they affirm are severe.
School Climate
School climate refers to the combination
of beliefs, attitudes, and values that shape
interactions between students, teachers,
and administrators (Mitchell et al., 2010).
It is the atmosphere and personality of
a school, including its norms, values,
expectations, and social characteristics
(Brookover et al., 1978; Anderson, 1982).
School climate has been linked to many
student outcomes, such as academic
achievement, discipline problems, and
rates of absenteeism, truancy, and student
dropout (Mitchell et al., 2010; Norton,
1984; Payne, 2018). Furthermore, the per­
ceived quality of school climate has been
associated with behavioral and emotional
adjustment in adolescents, with a negative
perception contributing to declines in aca­
demic performance, self-image, perceived
social support, and perceived quality of
school life (Kuperminc et al., 1997).
School Security, School Climate, and
Adolescent Wellbeing
The use of certain visible security mea­
sures has been found to lead to a signifi­
cant decrease in students feeling safe while
in school (Perumean-Chaney & Sutton,
2013). Even after controlling for the
school’s level of violence, the use of metal
detectors, security guards, or locked doors
in a school is highly correlated with height­
ened levels of student fear (Gastic, 2011;
Bachman et al., 2011). Particularly among
students who have previously experienced
victimization, research shows that visible
security measures may magnify fear,
promote distrust, and serve as a reminder
of the threat of violence (Bachman et al.,
2011). The stress, fear, and discomfort that
may result from the use of certain visible
security measures all impact dimensions of
school climate.
There are five proposed domains of
adolescent wellbeing: good health and op­
timum nutrition; connectedness, positive
values, and contribution to society; safety
and a supportive environment; learn­
ing, competence, education, skills, and
employability; and agency and resilience
(Ross et al., 2020). These five domains
are meant to encompass both subjective
and objective constructs of wellbeing,
which include personal experiences and
individual fulfillment, as well as quality of
life indicators, such as material resources
and social attributes (Ross et al., 2020). As
we consider the impact a school security
presence might have on school climate, in­
cluding increased levels of perceived fear,
discomfort, or lack of safety, as well as the
behavioral and emotional repercussions
for a negatively perceived school climate,
the extended consequences for student
wellbeing are clear.
Methodology
For data collection, this study incorporated
a mixed methods approach. I collected
quantitative data from a Qualtrics survey,
distributed to students at Northwestern
“Research has shown a severe discrepancy
in who is punished, how frequently they are
punished, to what severity they are punished,
and the lasting consequences they might face.”
University. These data were then sorted to
only include responses from first-year col­
lege students who graduated in the last year
from high school. Additionally, I collected
qualitative data from interviews conducted
with first-year students at Northwestern
University who graduated the previous
year from a high school with a security
presence. “Security presence” was defined
as a school’s use of police, security guards,
security cameras, metal detectors, or any
combination of the four. The quantitative
method allowed me to identify potential
trends in the relationship between school
security and school climate, which I then
built upon with personalized and detailed
participant perspectives through the quali­
tative method.
Quantitative data was collected first,
via the Qualtrics survey. I obtained 97 via­
ble responses to use in my analysis, which
provided a sample size of about 5.7% of
Northwestern University first-year stu­
dents. From the 2,039-person class of
2026, I subtracted an approximate number
of Northwestern first-year students who
took a gap year (based on national trends),
as well as students who transferred from
another university, as these students,
despite being in their first year at North­
western, graduated from high school more
than one year prior (Northwestern Admis­
sions; Hadden & Kaplan, 2020). See Table
1 for demographic details of the 97 total
participants, including race, gender, type
of high school attended, how many of the
students’ schools had a security presence,
and various types of security utilized by the
students’ schools.
The survey began with demographic
questions, questions about the school from
which the student graduated, and questions
about the security presence (or lack thereof)
in said high school. From there, students
were presented with 11 questions assessing
school climate and wellbeing. A Likert-type
scale ranging from one (Strongly Disagree)
to five (Strongly Agree) was used to as­
sess students’ emotional reactions to these
prompts, which included themes such as
safety and comfort at school, instances of
harassment or abuse, and experiences of
mental health challenges. At the end of
the survey, participants were asked if they
were willing to be contacted in the future
for an interview. See Appendix A for a full
list of survey questions.
The quantitative data were analyzed
using linear regressions, frequency tests,
and one-way ANOVA tests through the
program JASP. These analyses allowed me
to identify potential relationships between
school security and elements of school cli­
mate that negatively impact student well­
being, such as stress, discomfort, fear, and
lack of safety, as well as ensure statistical
validity and control for confounds. The
trends established through these analyses
informed the questions I asked in my in­
terview protocol and were used as support
for themes that emerged in the interviews.
Interview participants were selected
based on their indicated willingness from
the survey. I interviewed 10 individuals,
which ensured that proper data saturation
“Black students,
and Black female
students in particular,
experience
disproportionately
high suspension and
expulsion rates.”
was reached (Guest et al., 2006), and in­
terviews took place over Zoom, due to the
ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. Although
there were no specific demographic re­
quirements for interviewees, I recruited a
target population that was diverse in terms
of personal and high school demographics
based on the survey responses. The final
sample of interviewees was Elizabeth,
Alice, Emily, Jack, Elise, Deva, Marianna,
Abby, Landon, and Maya. Nine were public
school graduates, and one, Elizabeth, was a
private school graduate. Alice, Elise, Jack,
and Abby are white, Elizabeth is Black,
Emily is East Asian, Deva is South Asian,
Marianna is Hispanic/Latine, and two stu­
dents were multiracial: Maya is Black and
white, and Landon is Hispanic/Latine and
white. Alice, Elise, Abby, Elizabeth, Emily,
Marianna, and Maya are female-identify­
ing, Jack and Landon are male-identifying,
and Deva is non-binary/non-conforming.
Among the 10 interviewees, every possible
response to the student’s assessment of
their school climate on the survey was rep­
resented, ensuring a diverse sample both in
terms of student identity, as well as student
perception of their school and its security.
The interview protocol consisted of
10 questions and followed a semi-struc­
tured approach. By using semi-structured
interviews, I was able to introduce new
concepts based on an interviewee’s re­
sponse. The semi-structured interview
protocol consisted of original questions,
drawn from previously researched mea­
sures of school climate, and informed by
trends established via the quantitative sur­
vey (Bernhardt, 1998). It began with ques­
tions regarding the student’s high school
and its security presence, including the
type of security present, its visibility to stu­
dents, and the systems of support the high
school offered in conjunction with the
security presence. From there, questions
pertained to interactions with and emo­
tional reactions and feelings as they related
to the security presence. See Appendix B
for a copy of the semi-structured interview
protocol.
Qualitative data were organized and
analyzed following a grounded theory
framework. As a methodology designed to
uncover explanatory theories grounded in
data, utilizing this framework not only al­
lowed for a potential relationship between
a student’s wellbeing and their school’s se­
curity presence to emerge, but also helped
create a buffer for the biases that could oth­
erwise influence my interpretation (Chun
Tie et al., 2019).
Findings
In assessing each student’s impression of
their school’s security, the level of school
violence experienced or witnessed by the
student emerged as a predictor. Students
such as Alice, Maya, Deva, and Marianna,
who reported the most negative percep­
tions of their school’s security, were also
the students who reported experiencing
or witnessing the most violence on a reg­
ular basis within their school. This finding
stands out, as Maya, Alice, Deva, and
Marianna would theoretically have the
most to gain from the presence of school
security, considering the intention behind
security measures is to protect students
from the violence that these students were
experiencing and witnessing. However,
Maya, Alice, Deva, and Marianna spoke of
a gap between the intention of the school
security, the funding that it required, and
the actual effect, or lack thereof, on the
school climate and their feelings of safety
as a main reason behind their negative
perceptions of their school’s security. They
witnessed the violence that contributed to
the hiring of their school’s security pres­
ence; they experienced the security, took
notice of the resources it consumed, and in
some cases, experienced harm as a result;
and they failed to see its promised changes
in either mitigated acts or threats of vio­
lence or positive effects to their wellbeing.
Similarly, the students who had
the most positive reactions toward their
school’s security, as well as the students
who were mostly indifferent toward their
school’s security, all reported low levels
of violence within their schools and con­
sistent feelings of safety. Two students
remarked that their school’s security offi­
cer felt like a member of the school com­
munity. Although there were a number of
characteristics of the officer contributing
to this perception that these students list­
ed, such as frequent, positive interactions
and conversations with students, as well
as active involvement in school events,
the fact that none of these students had to
encounter violence presents an alternative
explanation as to why the security presence
could exist purely as a community mem­
ber; neither student had to experience the
security presence outside of that context.
Their interactions could entirely consist
of greetings and friendly questions, and
the interactions they had to witness only
revolved around standard school rules,
which both students thought were fair.
Furthermore, neither student had to ex­
perience a situation of violence by which
to assess the security’s effectiveness at its
intended protection, in the way that the
students with negative reactions did.
For some students, the type of securi­
ty that was present proved a big distinction
in the student’s perception of said security.
Different types of security include passive
measures, such as cameras, and active mea­
sures, such as bag checks, security guards
or paraprofessionals, and SROs or police.
When asked about their school security
presence, regardless of which types were
present within the school, students more
often brought up active measures than
passive measures. Similarly, when asked
about various consequences of the secu­
rity presence, either positive or negative,
students more often defaulted toward
commenting on security personnel, such
as security guards/paraprofessionals or
SROs/police. It may be the case that stu­
dents think of passive security measures
either differently than active measures or
not at all, due to differences in frequency
and type of encounter between the two
types of measures.
Many students reported having posi­
tive impressions of and relationships with
the security guards or paraprofessionals
at their school, regardless of their gener­
al reaction toward security. For students
who reported negative feelings related to
features of the security, such as them be­
ing armed, or to harm committed by the
security presence, such as instances of
racial profiling and targeting or especially
forceful or punitive protocols, the students
differentiated between SROs/police and
security guards/paraprofessionals when
the two contrasted in these features or
behaviors. This was amplified when, as it
was in many of these cases, the security
guard or paraprofessional did not resemble
what one might imagine a typical security
presence to be, such as one student de­
scribing her school’s paraprofessionals as
“old ladies”.
Every male-identifying interviewee
reported a positive or neutral percep­
tion of their school security, and only
female-identifying and non-binary in­
terviewees reported negative reactions.
Additionally, only interviewees of color
discussed instances of racism when an­
swering questions about the impact of
their school’s security on the school cli­
mate. Thus, it may be the case that cer­
tain kinds of violence are only included
in assessments of school security when
the assessment is being conducted by stu­
dents of certain identities, emphasizing
the need for diverse perspectives on the
matter. Furthermore, as only students of
certain identities can speak firsthand to the
emotional, mental, and physical impact of
instances of discrimination or prejudice,
it is critical that we include diverse voices
in our conversations, if we hope to get a
complete picture of the impact of school
security.
Several students described witnessing
or experiencing acts of racism from their
school’s security. These included racial
profiling, targeting, microaggressions, and
acts of violence against Black and brown
students. For these students, all of whom
are students of color, these observed and
experienced acts of racism shaped the
student’s view of and relationship with
security, as well as greatly impacted their
wellbeing as a student within the school.
When describing their high school
experience, many students mentioned
the necessity of mental health support,
speaking on behalf of both themselves and
their peers. However, despite this stated
significance of mental health challenges in
a student’s experience at and perception of
their school, the majority of the students
describing mental health challenges faced
by themselves or their peers followed those
sentiments with reports of inadequate re­
sources and care. Several of the students
remarked on how this lack of support
amplified their frustration toward their
school and its security. They saw the se­
curity presence growing, absorbing more
and more of their school’s resources and
funding, and they continued experienc­
ing and witnessing violence, all the while
seeing students suffer without adequate
support. Several students also mentioned
that they saw mental health support as key
to addressing the violence and conflicts
they witnessed or experienced within their
school. Especially for the students who saw
security measures as punitive, reactionary,
and ultimately ineffective, they described
mental health support as an opportunity to
address school-based conflicts and violence
at their source before they turned more
severe.
Discussion and Analysis
As we consider the relationship between
security, school climate, and student well­
“. . . as only students
of certain identites
can speak firsthand
to the emotional,
mental, and physical
impact of instances
of discrimination or
prejudice, it is critical
that we include
diverse voices in our
conversations, if we
hope to get a complete
picture of the impact of
school security.”
being, the greatest reported impact from
the interviewed students came from the
security’s perceived ineffectiveness. The
students that encountered regular violence
experienced a negative impact on their
school climate caused by said violence
that had ramifications for their wellbe­
ing. Additionally, when acts of violence
disproportionately affected Black and
brown students, as was the case in some
schools, we see an even greater disruption
in the school’s climate for these (Black
and brown) students. These disruptions
had an emotional and mental toll on these
students, as they navigated intense feelings
of fear and lack of safety.
With the addition of school security,
the impact was amplified. In some cases,
this came from acts of violence and racism
committed by security officers. However,
for many of these students, it came from
the security’s perceived ineffectiveness
at addressing the violence in the schools:
the safety it failed to ensure, the emotion­
al and mental stress it failed to remedy,
and the frustration toward the school, its
administration, and the security presence
that it prompted. Many students explained
that they saw security as a failure on their
school’s part to protect them from the
threats, both internal and external, that
they were experiencing. It communicat­
ed a lack of care and support on behalf
of the school, regardless of whether this
was the school’s intention. Furthermore,
these students were already experiencing
intense anxiety and fear related to actual
and perceived threats to their safety, and
this added an additional layer, where these
anxieties and fears were not eased, and
students now felt as though they could not
trust their school to support them. In con­
junction with inadequate systems of men­
tal health support, students described situ­
ations spiraling, feelings of frustration and
lack of trust in the school, and a collective
hopelessness at the idea of receiving help
or support from the school, all of which
contributed to a negative perception of the
school’s climate and thus, facilitated the
negative consequences of a poor percep­
tion of school climate for these students.
For many students, there was a dis­
tinction made between different types of
security, particularly security guards or
paraprofessionals and SROs or police. This
finding is somewhat supported by current
research but also presents an opportunity
for future research. Some studies differ­
entiate between school security measures
through characteristics such as visibility, in­
trusiveness, and rigidity, which aligns with
the distinction between active and passive
measures found in this study (NCES, 2012;
NASP, 2018). However, most research
assessing the impact of school security
“They saw the security presence growing,
absorbing more and more of their school’s
resources and funding, and they continued
experiencing and witnessing violence,
all the while seeing students suffer
without adequate support.”
categorizes all security measures within
the same definition of security or only
focuses on the measures often associated
with most people’s conception of school
security, such as metal detectors, security
guards, and police. There have been few
studies examining how different types of
security may affect students differently, but
based on this study, this could be an area
of research worth exploring, particularly
for schools that wish to maintain a security
presence.
Throughout the study, students of
different gender and racial identities de­
scribed varying perceptions and impacts
of their school’s security, revealing how
students of different identities can have
different experiences within the same
school climate and, thus, will form unique
impressions and bear unique consequences
of their school’s security and climate. This
is supported by current research, which
has found that race and gender play a large
role in the frequency and severity of pun­
ishment for subjective infractions in school
(Pentek & Eisenberg, 2018; Morris & Per­
ry, 2017), and presents an area for future
research. A thorough understanding of
the role of intersecting identities in school
punishment and discipline is critical for a
complete assessment of school security and
its impact: on students, their perception of
their school’s climate, and their wellbeing.
Conclusion
This study attempted to fill in the gaps in
current school security literature by exam­
ining the impact of a school security pres­
ence on school climate through the lens of
student wellbeing. In this study, student
wellbeing was assessed through student
experiences with stress, perceived safety,
fear, and discomfort, as well as how these
emotional outcomes manifested in student
experiences with depression, anxiety, and
other mental health challenges. Findings
of the study included the impact of school
violence on a student’s relationship with
their school’s security and administration,
and its consequences for school climate
and student wellbeing; direct impacts of
school security on student wellbeing; how
different security types elicit different per­
ceptions in students; how student identity
impacts the relationship between a student
and their school’s security presence; and
how lack of adequate support affects
student perception of climate and student
wellbeing.
Hopefully, these findings will pave
the way for future research on the matter,
as well as meaningfully contribute to the
current literature. As threats and acts of
violence within schools continue to affect
student learning and wellbeing, and as an
unprecedented number of schools resort to
security measures and security personnel,
it is critical that we continue to study the
best ways to support our students, protect
them from threats, and promote their
long-term wellbeing. Furthermore, it is
imperative that we acknowledge that these
answers will only emerge once we begin to
not only include but center student voices
and experiences in this conversation.◆

Finding an Equilibrium
in Life: An Interview
With a Chemistry
Graduate Student
By: Hannah Xu
FEATURES
Luis Sierra Ossa is a first-year Ph.D. student from Cali, Colombia. After completing his B.S. in
Chemistry at Universidad del Valle, he began his graduate studies at Northwestern University.
He is currently a graduate researcher in The Tempelaar Team, which focuses on exploring
quantum and classical theories and developing hybrid models that implement both.
[This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.]
What was your undergraduate education like?
I was born and raised in Colombia, and I went to a public university called Universidad
del Valle for my Bachelor’s degree in Chemistry. My undergraduate education was five
years long, which is common in Colombia. During the last three years, I did research in
a theoretical chemistry group at my undergraduate institution, developing theories on
entanglement in low-dimensional systems. This research is what I wrote my undergrad­
uate thesis on.
In my last year, I had the incredible opportunity to do research as an international
student in the iScholar program at the University of Rochester. In my research group
there, I did theoretical chemistry research, using programming to simulate the optical
and electrical properties of materials. It went very well, and that opened the doors for
me to apply to Ph.D. programs, including the one here at Northwestern.
What made you interested in pursuing a Ph.D.?
Everyone has a different journey, but for me, it was easy to decide that a Ph.D. was the
best option. I have a lot of passion for research, and while I love my country, I wanted
to do a Ph.D. somewhere with more opportunities for scientists. I also felt that pursuing
a Ph.D. was a challenge that was valuable for my personal development, as it involved
moving to a new environment, meeting new people, and learning new things.
How did you identify your research interests?
I knew very early on that I was interested in theoretical chemistry. I remember taking
general chemistry my first year with the professor who was my undergraduate thesis
mentor. I was amazed not only by how physics can tell you what is happening in chem­
ical processes, but also by the fundamental questions asked when exploring theory in
chemistry. I always wanted to understand the fundamental concepts in chemistry, so it
felt natural for me to pursue theory.
What was the Ph.D. application process like?
Before applying, I made a long list of all the Ph.D. programs I could be interested in.
I looked into each program, and I narrowed the list down to only the nine I applied
to. I took this very seriously, as doing a Ph.D. is a major life opportunity. I sent emails
to 25twenty-five professors whose research I was interested in, which was important
to make a good first impression. Around half of these professors responded, including
Prof. Roel Tempelaar at Northwestern. After talking to some of them, I submitted my
applications, and I did a few interviews in which I talked about myself and my research,
among other things. In the end, I received my decision notifications between December
and February.
This was simply my experience applying to Ph.D. programs, and it may be slightly
different from others’ experiences because I am an international student in theoretical
chemistry. Even within chemistry, the interviews can be different if you are an ex­
perimentalist rather than a theorist, and it can also depend on the professor you are
interested in working with.
How did you decide between Ph.D. programs?
I was accepted to five schools, but Northwestern stood out to me because of two main
reasons: the structure of the program and my research mentor.
I like the structure of Northwestern’s graduate program because it places a lot more em­
phasis on research than classes. Northwestern requires graduate students in chemistry
to take six classes their first year, but then students are free to dedicate their time fully
to research. Some schools emphasize classes more, so students there are required to do
more than one year of classes. This can be beneficial for some students because you learn
more background from classes before doing research. However, I believe that having
more time to do research is important because what you learn through your research is
often far more complex than what classes can teach. Apart from the program structure,
I also came to Northwestern for Roel Tempelaar, whose research aligns well with my
interests.
Could you describe your research?
Could you describe your research?
My research is in theoretical chemistry. These two words may seem odd together be­
cause chemistry is largely experimental. What is theoretical chemistry? Essentially, we
use mathematical and physical tools to study chemical phenomena. When theoretical
insights match experimental results, they provide a fuller explanation of phenomena.
For example, the orbital is a very interesting concept that was made by theorists, and
orbitals are now used by experimentalists to explain many chemical processes.
In my research group, we aim to develop these kinds of tools for everyone in the field
to use. My project focuses on mixed quantum-classical dynamics, developing theories
to understand what is happening to electrons in materials in the presence of phonons,
which are crystal vibrations. We begin with a model, develop theories to understand
the model, and then use computer programming to run theoretical simulations. The
theoretical results can be compared to lab results, which tells us if our theories provide a
plausible explanation for what is observed.
What are your responsibilities as a first-year graduate student at
Northwestern?
The first year is challenging in the sense that you need to adjust to a new lifestyle, develop
new skills, and manage your time well. There is also a wider variety of responsibilities in
the first year, which includes taking classes, doing research, and teaching undergraduate
students. During my first year, I am taking two classes each quarter so that I also have
time to do research for at least one hour every day, but I will be able to dedicate more
time to research once I am done with classes at the end of this year. I will also be a
teaching assistant for five quarters during the Ph.D. program. As a teaching assistant, I
discuss content with the professor, grade assessments, prepare review sessions, hold of­
fice hours, and am there for students. It is a lot of work sometimes, but I enjoy it because
I think the best way to fully understand the depth of a topic is to teach it. Explaining
concepts in simpler terms is incredibly beneficial because it is difficult and it requires me
to think about them in different ways. Outside of these responsibilities, I try to find an
equilibrium in my life through my hobbies.
What do you plan on doing after your Ph.D.?
I don’t know, actually. Anything can change during a Ph.D. I would love to keep work­
ing on research, not necessarily as an assistant professor, but maybe in an institution.
But it is also important to be realistic. Academia is hard, even more so for international
students. My goal for now is to develop a complete set of skills that enables me to choose
whatever path I want after my Ph.D., whether it’s industry, academia, opening a bakery,
or anything else. This is why I feel like a Ph.D. is a life opportunity—at the end of the
day, it will help me develop strong skills so that I have more options when I need to
make a decision.
Do you have any advice for undergraduates who are interested in
pursuing a Ph.D.?
Life is too short to not do a Ph.D.
Naturally, it’s not for everyone. A Ph.D. opens a lot of doors, but it closes others. The
most important thing in a Ph.D. is your research, and making sure that it’s something
you love to do. Asking questions about the universe, interpreting your findings … if
you’re passionate about these things, a Ph.D. is a very good opportunity to deepen your
understanding of your field and discover what you want to do with your life. Discover
your signature. It even helps you develop as a person because you constantly approach
problems differently, encounter failures, and try to solve them. Nothing is black and
white here—everything is colorful. You put yourself completely in your work, and you
learn a lot about yourself through your research. Every challenge is beneficial for you,
and it helps you develop both your research and your life skills, teaching you how to
improve your time management, balance your responsibilities, and find equilibrium in
your life.

Abstract
BeReal grew rapidly in popularity throughout 2022. Created as a response to social
media platforms where idealized images and higher usage are encouraged, BeReal takes
a different approach. Valuing authenticity, BeReal asks users to post a daily front and
back-facing picture within a random two-minute time slot and provides a short daily
feed of BeReals from friends. In an online survey, U.S. college students 18-23 years old
were studied in two groups: BeReal users (n = 100) and non-BeReal users (n =100).

Are People “Real” on
BeReal? Perception and
Authenticity in Utilization of
Social Media App
With over 10 million daily users and
53 million downloads, BeReal claims to be
“a new and unique way to discover who
your friends really are in their daily life”
(BeReal). Created as a response to social
media platforms like Instagram, where us­
ers tend to post picture-perfect images on a
never-ending feed, BeReal takes a different
approach. The app shows a limited daily
feed of friends’ BeReals, taking up only a
small part of the day.
The overall objective of this app is to
“be real.” A BeReal user gets a notification
at any point during the day and has two
minutes to take a front and back-facing
camera picture. If they do not post within
that time frame, the delayed time is shown;
for example, “10 minutes late” or “8 hours
late.” Users are discouraged from posting
later when they may be doing something
that is more appealing to their audience.
Users cannot see their friends’ BeReals for
the day until they post one themselves.
BeReal does not show the feature of likes
or followers but instead has “reacts” where
users can respond to a BeReal with a pic­
ture, emoji, or comment. Users can only
see friends’ BeReals from that day and not
from past days to keep users’ feeds short
and up to date. All these aspects combined
could potentially eliminate the popularity
aspect of other social media platforms,
such as comparing numbers of followers,
likes, and other interactions. The main
goal of the app is for users to see what their
friends are up to while mitigating the neg­
ative effects of other social media platforms
such as Instagram and Facebook. Due to
the novel popularity of BeReal, there is no
current literature studying this platform.
“While the app
was designed to
promote authenticity
by keeping users
accountable, actual
users were more
forgiving with
these inauthentic
behaviors.”
Given its widespread usage among college
students and younger adolescents, looking
into how people use and perceive BeReal
could reveal unintended negative conse­
quences to using the app and/or show that
it is a social media app that connects people
in a positive manner.
Existing Authenticity in Social Media
Platforms
Before BeReal’s prominence, authen­
ticity on social media platforms was en­
couraged in other ways. For example, on
Instagram, users often have a main account
and a “finsta” or a “fake Instagram.” The
main account is where users post their best
pictures for a more general audience, while
the finsta is where users post less polished
photos, emotional photos, archival photos,
funny moments (Kang & Wei, 2020), and
unfiltered thoughts to a small group of
friends (Huang & Vitak, 2022). Despite this
push for authenticity by using Instagram in
this manner, young adults and children still
may face certain pressures to “perform” on
these finstas since there are a set of norms
as to what content is posted and how often
(Dewar et al., 2019).
Looking even further into the past,
blogging in a personal journal or diary
form on platforms like MySpace and
Tumblr has allowed users to vent and
seek feedback on difficult situations or
everyday life situations by giving users an
online platform where it is appropriate
and encouraged to share personal experi­
ences and seek support from a community
(Baker et al., 2008). Certain social con­
straints hinder people from bringing these
situations up in face-to-face conversations.
When comparing bloggers on MySpace to
nonbloggers, bloggers’ social integration,
reliable alliance, and friendship satisfaction
all increased compared to nonbloggers’,
suggesting that blogging may have benefits
in perceived social support (Baker et al.,
2008). Blogging could even be used as a
form of self-therapy (Tan et al., 2018).
Despite the push for authenticity
in previously existing social media using
these two methods, BeReal remains dis­
tinct. BeReal is a photo & caption-based
platform with authenticity as a focus
throughout the design process. Finstas and
blogging on MySpace are features embed­
ded in the larger overall platform. People
use Instagram and MySpace for purposes
other than finstas and blogging on those
respective platforms, so there could still be
several other features on the platform that
could negatively affect how authentic users
are.
Authenticity, despite its nuances, is
important to study because past research
has shown that authenticity is related to
a lower risk of developing social media
addiction (Monacis et al., 2021). In addi­
tion, authentic self-expression is associated
“Despite this push for authenticity by
using Instagram in this manner, young
adults and children still may face certain
pressures to ‘perform.’”
with greater reported life satisfaction
compared to self-idealized self-expression
(Bailey et al., 2020).
Self-Presentation & Authenticity
False or adapted self-presentation
and inauthenticity in portraying one’s
life and emotions is a frequent problem
with certain social media platforms (Gil-
Or et al., 2015). Even with the measures
against false self-presentation and push for
showing the true self on BeReal, like the
two-minute time limit and the randomized
time a user gets a notification to post for
the day, there is still an opportunity for
inauthenticity through retakes, not post­
ing on time, and not posting at all. If the
first photo is bad, the user might retake the
photo to get a better angle of themselves. If
the user feels like they are not doing some­
thing interesting enough, they could wait
to post until later. And there is always the
option of not posting at all if they do not
want to show themselves for that day.
The number of friends a user has
on social media could push users to in­
crease positive self-presentation regardless
of whether the user is doing well or not
(Kim & Lee, 2011). BeReal shows friend
counts in increments after a certain point.
For example, if a person has 68 friends on
BeReal, it is displayed as 50+ instead of
that specific number. It is possible that the
relationship between audience and false
self-presentation is hindered by the lack of
specificity in BeReal of how many friends a
person has added. However, there are lim­
itations to studying the effect of this spe­
cific feature due to other factors affecting
false self-presentation like the presence of
photos (Gil-Or et al., 2015) and the makeup
of the audience (Rui, 2013). And it is still
possible that those with more friends may
still display more false self-presentation
behaviors than those with fewer friends on
BeReal.
Despite research showing that
authentic self-expression can be positive, it
is also important to note that there could
be moments where authenticity can be
negative. For instance, “vague-booking”
is defined as when people go on Facebook
to post a true but vague message about
their current feelings that elicits a response
from other users (Astleitner et al., 2023).
Vague-booking may mediate the rela­
tionship between personality and mental
health and is linked to suicidal ideation
(Berryman et al., 2017). It is possible that
sometimes going to social media to com­
municate and seek support may not be the
best form of action, and it may be better to
reach out to personal networks instead.
Social Media & Fear of Missing Out
Past studies suggest that an increase
in social media usage is correlated with
lower self-esteem (Jan et al., 2017; Hawi
& Samaha, 2016). Lower self-esteem is
associated with lower life satisfaction
(Hawi & Samaha, 2016). A phenomenon
where social media users feel left out of
specific social events is known as the Fear
of Missing Out (FoMO). Studies have
shown that the negative impacts of social
media sites leading to lower self-esteem
are mediated by FoMO (Salim et al., 2017).
Higher levels of FoMO were also related to
increased social media presence through
behaviors like updating their status more
often or posting more pictures. BeReal
aims to avoid FoMO by showing when
users post late as an accountability fea­
ture. That way, people cannot only post
their most interesting social interactions
because they need to post when prompted
to avoid “being late.” However, FoMO may
still be prominent since users will likely see
if they were left out of a social gathering
on BeReal.
Social Media & Psychopathology
Several studies have implicated
more time spent on social media as a risk
factor for developing an anxiety disorder
(Keles et al., 2020; Vannucci et al., 2017).
Increased social media use has been linked
to depression and anxiety, particularly
when there is greater emotional invest­
ment in social media (Woods & Scott,
2016). Since BeReal is designed to take up
a relatively short amount of time per day
(~10 minutes), it is possible that users who
primarily use BeReal and no other social
media platforms have a reduced risk of
developing psychopathology due to the
minimal time spent on the app. In addi­
tion, if users utilize BeReal in an authentic
manner, it is possible BeReal use mitigates
the relationship between social media use
and negative outcomes.
Research Questions
This study will explore the ques­
tions: (1) Does BeReal usage mitigate the
link between time spent on social media
and anxiety, fear of missing out (FoMO),
public self-consciousness (PSC), and au­
thenticity? (2) How do people use BeReal,
and what do they think BeReal’s intended
purpose is compared to other social media
apps? (3) Are inauthentic BeReal behaviors
such as retakes, posting late, and skipping
related to greater anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and
inauthenticity?
Main Hypotheses
My hypothesis is that BeReal use
moderates the link between total time
spent on social media and anxiety, PSC,
FoMO, and authenticity. Past research has
shown a link between total time spent on
social media and increasing anxiety, FoMO,
and self-consciousness and decreasing
self-esteem and authenticity (Monacis et
al., 2021). BeReal’s push for authentic use
could potentially mitigate these negative
outcomes.
In open-ended questions about BeRe­
al, participants are expected to report ben­
efits like functionality (which limits time
spent on the app), the encouraged lower
friend count, the refreshed daily feed, and
the spontaneity of posting. Some disadvan­
tages participants may bring up are FoMO,
opportunities for inauthenticity often re­
ferred to as “being fake,” and the random
notification during the day being at an
inconvenient time. I expect there to be a
greater positive attitude toward BeReal
compared to other social media platforms.
Those who have more BeReal friends
and exhibit more inauthentic behaviors
such as greater average number of retakes,
posting late, and skipping posts despite
seeing the notification on time may have
greater anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and less au­
thenticity. Those who have greater anxi­
ety, PSC, and FoMO, and less authenticity
may care more about how they look during
the two-minute window than remaining
authentic, so they may retake their BeReal
more often and skip or post late instead of
showing what they are doing at the time
of notification. A greater percentage of
time spent scrolling through feeds may
be correlated with higher levels of anxiety
and FoMO due to a greater likelihood that
a user may see other friends spending time
with each other, while a greater percent­
age of time spent interacting with friends’
BeReals may be correlated with greater
authenticity and lower FoMO.
Methods
Participants
Undergraduate college students of all
genders, races, and ethnicities who are En­
glish speakers (n = 650) aged 18-23 years
old across the United States were surveyed
about their TikTok, Instagram, and BeRe­
al usage on the research platform Prolific.
This screening on Prolific was used to sep­
arate participants into two groups. Group
1 participants (n = 100) did not use BeReal
(less than once every two weeks for one
month). Group 2 participants (n = 100) did
use BeReal (at least once every two weeks
for one month). Additional participants
for the BeReal survey were sought out
from the Northwestern University under­
graduate community due to the low num­
ber of qualifying BeReal users (n = 158).
Participants in Group 2 (n = 100) were a
mix of Prolific users (n = 75) who were
compensated and Northwestern students
(n = 25) who were not. Participants were
only asked what college they go to in the
demographics section since Prolific pro­
vides data on age, race, ethnicity, gender
identity, year in school, and region.
Questionnaires
The survey included a question on
college attended, questions on general so­
cial media usage across different platforms,
questions about their perception of each
social media platform (purpose, affect,
etc.), questions specific to BeReal, the Gen­
eral Anxiety Disorder-7 Scale (Spitzer et
al., 2006), Public Self-Consciousness Scale
(Scheier and Carver, 1985), the Fear of
Missing Out Scale (Przybylski et al., 2013),
and Authenticity Scale (Wood et al., 2008).
General Anxiety Disorder Scale
The General Anxiety Disorder-7
(GAD-7) was used to measure anxiety in
the current state (Spitzer et al., 2006). This
short questionnaire utilized a Likert scale
of 0-3 (not at all, several days, more than
half the days, and nearly every day) with
prompts like “Feeling nervous, anxious, or
on edge” and “Worrying too much about
different things.” Scores were calculated
by summing the numerical score of each
item for a final score. For this study, scores
were treated as a continuous variable. A
greater score is indicative of greater anx­
iety. Cronbach’s α for the GAD-7 scale in
this sample is 0.938 (n = 191). The GAD-7
Scale is widely used in clinical settings and
was shown to be reliable and valid (Spitzer
Public Self-Consciousness Scale
Public Self-Consciousness (PSC) re­
fers to the tendency to think about aspects
of self in the matter of public display. Only
the PSC Scale from the overall Self-Con­
sciousness Scale (Scheier and Carver, 1985)
was utilized as this form of self-conscious­
ness may be particularly relevant to BeReal
usage. The seven-item questionnaire gave
prompts like “I am concerned with my style
of doing things” and “I usually worry about
making a good impression,” which are an­
swered on a 0-3 Likert scale (not like me at
all, a little like me, somewhat like me, a lot
like me). Scores were averaged to obtain an
overall score. A higher score is indicative
of greater PSC. The PSC Scale was shown
to be reliable and valid (Scheier and Carv­
er, 1985). Cronbach’s α for the PSC Scale in
this sample is 0.846 (n = 191).
Fearing of Missing Out Scale
The 10-item FoMO Scale was used to
measure the degree to which someone fears
missing out on social events and uses social
media to remain hyper-connected using a
5-point Likert scale (not at all true of me,
slightly true of me, moderately true of me,
very true of me, and extremely true of me)
with prompts like “I get worried when I
find out my friends are having fun with­
out me” and “I fear my friends have more
rewarding experiences than me.” Each
item’s score from 1-5 points was summed
to a total score, and an average between all
answers provided a final score. A greater
score is indicative of a greater fear of miss­
ing out. The FoMO Scale was shown to be
reliable and valid (Przybylski et al., 2013).
Cronbach’s α for the FoMO Scale in this
sample is 0.897 (n = 191).
Authenticity Scale
The 12-item Authenticity Scale mea­
sured authenticity in knowing oneself,
expressing emotions in a way that is con­
gruent with values and beliefs, and staying
true to personal beliefs despite external
influences (Wood et al., 2008). There were
four items for each of the three subscales:
Self-Alienation (AS), Authentic Living
(AL), and Accepting of External Influences
(AE). Participants were given prompts like
“I feel as if I don’t know myself very well,”
“I live in accordance to my values and be­
liefs,” and “I am strongly influenced by the
opinions of others,” which were answered
on a Likert scale of 1-7 (does not describe
me at all to describes me very well). The
AS and AE Subscales were reverse-scored.
The final authenticity score was the sum of
the reverse-scored subscale items and AL
Subscale items. In the overall Authenticity
Scale and AL Subscale, a greater score was
indicative of greater authenticity. For the
AS and AE Subscales, a lower score was
indicative of greater authenticity. The Au­
thenticity Scale and Subscales were shown
to be reliable and valid (Wood et al., 2008).
