General Social Media Questions
This nine-item section was repeated
for every social media platform partic­
ipants indicated they use. Participants
were asked which social media platforms
they used, percentage breakdowns of the
amount of time spent on each platform,
how often they used each platform (daily
or almost daily, 2-3 times per week, 1 time
per week, 1-2 times per month, <1 per
month), average amount of time spent per
day, how they used each platform (catch
up with friends, scroll through feed for en­
tertainment, scroll through feed for news,
post about own life, make entertaining
content, other) and percentage breakdown
of time spent on those options. They were
also asked open-ended questions about
what they thought the intended purpose of
this platform was and whether the benefits
outweigh the disadvantages.
BeReal Questions
Group 2 participants (n = 100) who
were active users of BeReal (at least once
every two weeks for a month) were asked
a separate set of questions (28 items). They
were asked how many friends they have on
BeReal, the percentage of time they post,
the percentage of time they are on time
when they post, the percentage of time
they retake their BeReal before posting,
the percentage of time they retake 1, 2, 3,
or 4 times, the motivation behind retak­
ing BeReals, what percentage of time they
scroll through the feed after they post, the
percentage of time they skip the BeReal
despite seeing the notification on time,
the percentage of time they skip the Be­
Real after seeing the notification late, the
percentage of time they interact with their
friends’ BeReals, and when they do inter­
act with friends’ BeReals, the percentage
of time they utilize face react compared to
emoji compared to comment. The last two
questions gauged when users thought the
latest someone could post and the maxi­
mum number of retakes that they would
consider to be socially acceptable to them.
Plan of Analysis
We ran a linear regression to com­
pare total time spent on social media and
the four numerical dependent variable
scores. BeReal use is expected to moderate
the correlation between total time spent
on social media and the four DVs, so hours
spent on social media per week and BeReal
use acted as independent variables and an
interaction term between hours spent on
social media per week and BeReal use was
included in the model. Pearson correlations
were run between separate IVs (number of
friends, percent of times posted, percentage
of late posts, percentage of retakes, average
number of retakes per BeReal, percentage
of skips despite seeing BeReal on time, per­
centage of skips after seeing notification
on time, percentage of time spent scrolling
through feed after post, percentage of time
they interact with friends’ BeReals) and
the four DVs to determine further correla­
tions. Qualitative data was coded for the
top five occurrences.
Results
Data Cleaning & Scoring
Participants were removed from the
data if they did not meet certain criteria
(n = 9). For both the General Survey and
the BeReal Survey, those who did not
complete the questionnaires about anxiety,
PSC, FoMO, and authenticity were re­
moved (n = 3). Those who took the BeReal
survey and did not post at least twice in the
last 30 days were removed (n = 5). Partic­
ipants who had given out-of-range data
(e.g., over 24 hours of social media use per
day) were also removed (n = 1). 191 par­
ticipants remained: 93 BeReal users and 98
non-BeReal users.
Social Media Usage
Results are based on hours spent on
social media per day and on what specific
apps are shown (Table 1). On average, par­
ticipants used apps like TikTok, Instagram,
and YouTube for a greater amount of time.
For the BeReal group, the mean time spent
on social media was 4.0 hours (SD = 2.3)
per day. The BeReal use percentage mean
was 4.96 (SD = 5.86), ~12 minutes a day.
TikTok and Instagram percentages
were higher for the BeReal group, with a
slightly lower YouTube percentage (Table
2). We see that Facebook percentages are
low across the board for college students.
Many participants thought the intended
purpose of Facebook is to connect with
friends and family of the older generation
or for event invites and notifications.
How social media was used greatly
differed depending on the platform. Par­
ticipants generally used BeReal to scroll
through their feed or stories to see what
people in their network were up to (M =
51.7%, SD = 35.5%) and post or create con­
tent (M = 27.8%, SD = 32.9%). Participants
primarily scrolled through their feed for
entertainment on TikTok (M = 72.4%, SD
= 26.6%)) and YouTube (M = 72.0%, SD
= 35.3%), while Instagram was used in a
greater variety of ways: scrolling through
the feed to keep up with network (M =
36.8%, SD = 27.3%), scrolling through the
feed for entertainment (M = 31.0%, SD
= 25.8%), and directly interacting with
friends (M = 21.9%, SD = 22.6%). Face­
book’s main usage was scrolling through
the feed to keep up with their network (M
BeReal Results
In the BeReal data set, participants
posted a BeReal 78% of the time. Of our 93
participants, 55 provided insight as to why
they skipped posts (Table 3). Participants
posted late on average 53.8% of the time
(SD = 29.3%). The most occurring reasons
for posting late were inconvenient times,
perceived interest, and apathy (Table 4).
Out of our 93 participants, 84 participants
provided qualitative data on reasons for
posting late. The mean percentage they re­
took their BeReal before posting was 37.5%
(SD = 30.8%). When participants retook
their BeReal, they tended to retake it only
once (M = 74.2%, SD = 24.6%) or twice (M
= 19.4%, SD = 18.9%). Most users retook
BeReals for unclear photos, appearance of
self, and because it did not include desired
content (Table 5). Out of our 93 partici­
pants, 90 participants provided qualitative
data on reasons for retaking BeReals.
The mean percentage of participants
interacting with friends’ BeReals was 56.5%
(SD = 38.1%). The methods participants
used to interact with friends on BeReal
were Face React (M = 60.3%, SD = 37.0%),
Comment (M = 19.4%, SD = 25.1%), and
Emoji React (M = 12.6%, SD = 25.8%).
Face React, or taking a selfie response, was
the most popular. The median number of
friends users had on BeReal was 47 (SD =
15). In users’ opinion, the mean max hours
a user should post late is 11.9 with a me­
dian of 10 hours (SD = 8.8), and the mean
max number of retakes a user should take
is 3.7 with a median of 3 retakes (SD = 2.6).
Primary Analyses
We ran Pearson correlations be­
tween time spent on social media and
anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and authenticity and
found a positive correlation between time
on social media and anxiety (Table 6). Cor­
relations between the four scales were all
significant. Anxiety, PSC, and FoMO all
had moderate positive correlations with
each other, while anxiety, PDC, and FoMo
had moderate negative correlations with
authenticity (Table 6).
To test if BeReal use moderated the
relationship between total time spent on
social media and anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and
authenticity, four linear regression models
were run with those four variables as the
DVs. Hours spent on social media per week
and BeReal use acted as independent vari­
ables, with an interaction term between
hours spent on social media per week and
BeReal use included in the model. There is
no evidence that BeReal use mitigates the
relationship between total time spent on
social media and the DVs (Table 1A-4A).
Analyses were also run to test the
BeReal group and see if authentic vs. in­
authentic BeReal use moderates the rela­
tionship between total time spent on social
media and anxiety. Authentic BeReal use
was defined as practical reasons for not us­
ing BeReal as intended. If a participant said
that they could not take the BeReal on time
because they were in the shower or in class,
that reasoning would be coded “authentic.”
If a participant said they could not take the
BeReal because they were doing something
boring and would do something more in­
teresting later, then their reason was coded
“inauthentic.” Similar reasoning was ap­
plied to reasons for retakes and skipping
the BeReal. Authentic usage did not mod­
erate the relationship between total time
spent on social media per week and the
four DVs (Table 5A-7A).
Secondary Analyses
Percentage of late posts had a positive
correlation with the authenticity scores (r
= 0.279, p < 0.003) and a moderate negative
correlation with the self-alienation authen­
ticity score (r = -0.429, p < 0.001). In this
subscale, the higher the score, the greater
self-alienation and decreased authenticity
in that aspect. The percentage of late posts
also had a slight negative correlation with
the GAD-7 anxiety score (r = -0.306, p <
0.003). Percentage of skips had a positive
correlation with the PSC score (r = 0.208, p
< 0.046). See Table 8A for full results.
Discussion
Summary & Interpretation of Results
In terms of general social media use,
we found that apps that have an entertain­
ment aspect, like TikTok, Instagram, and
YouTube, were used for a greater duration.
Time spent on BeReal is generally low (Ta­
ble 2). BeReal was mainly used to keep up
with people in users’ networks and post or
create content that has a greater social or
community aspect.
We found that BeReal use does
not mitigate the link between time spent
on social media and anxiety, PSC, FoMO,
and authenticity. In addition, out of the
four possible correlations between time
spent on social media and the four DVs,
only time spent on social media and anx­
iety had a significant positive correlation.
Descriptive statistics showed that among
those who use BeReal, the average user
posted 78% of the time. When users post­
ed, they tended to post late 52% of the time
and retake their BeReal at least once 37%
of the time before posting. It is possible
that because users did not always adhere to
the intended use of BeReal, no moderating
effects were observed, as users only spent
12 minutes on BeReal every day. A shared
understanding that it is okay to post late
or retake your BeReal despite the counter­
measures built into BeReal shows that it
was not being used in the intended way.
Anxiety, PSC, and FoMO all had
moderately positive correlations with
each other, while anxiety, PSC, and FoMO
had moderate negative correlations with
authenticity. This result showed those
with either high anxiety, PSC, or FoMO
may have higher scores in the other two
variables as well. The percentage of late
posts has a positive correlation with the
Authenticity Scale and a moderate neg­
ative correlation with the self-alienation
authenticity scores, which differed from
the hypothesis. We expected that those
who exhibited more inauthentic behavior
would show lower authenticity scores.
Those who posted late may be more likely
to be engaging in in-person activities in­
volving others, which suggests authentic
living outside of the app. The percentage
of late posts also had a negative correla­
tion with anxiety, which could possibly be
“We found that BeReal use does not
mitigate the link between time spent on
social media and anxiety, public self-
consciousness (PSC), fear of missing out
(FoMO), and authenticity.”
explained by the idea that those with less
anxiety may not be as vigilant about post­
ing on time. If a user cares a lot about how
they are seen by the public, then they may
have opted to skip BeReal altogether even
when they are available to post late, which
explains the positive relationship between
percentage of skips with PSC score.
Limitations
In the data collection process for au­
thentic usage in retakes, posting late, and
skipping, participants were asked for rea­
sons why they retake, post late, and skip,
which we coded as authentic or inauthen­
tic. While the number of participants who
listed each reason was obtained, data were
not collected longitudinally to see the fre­
quency of each reason in specific instances.
Although some may have listed authentic
or inauthentic reasons, we still do not know
how often they are engaging these behav­
iors for authentic or inauthentic reasons
and whether some users fall somewhere in
the middle in terms of authentic use. More
detailed studies on BeReal use with a great­
er sample size are necessary to gain a better
understanding of this relationship.
Future Direction
The predicted mitigation effect of
BeReal was hypothesized under the as­
sumption that BeReal would largely be
used in the intended manner. We found
that this was not the case. However, since
we collected a great deal of data on how
BeReal is used, that can be helpful in cre­
ating and designing further BeReal studies.
The most recent update on BeReal
showed a significant change in design.
Now, users can post up to three BeReals if
they post their first BeReal on time. They
likely made this decision because, as this
study shows, adherence to BeReal rules is
low. However, this does defeat the original
purpose of the app, which was for users to
show what they are doing at any given time
during the day. This new update makes
BeReal more of a mix between the original
app and Instagram, where you post your
highlights. Although some may argue that
the new BeReal update is still better than
Instagram since users must post on time
to unlock the extra posts, there is a possi­
bility that this could lead to more FoMO
since BeReal is already an intimate view
into one’s life as a daily task. Now, with the
added option of posting up to three times
a day, there is even greater visibility. Re­
searchers must adapt to these changes to
fully understand the relationship between
social media and psychopathology. ◆

Learning to juggle:
Undergraduates balance
research with busy lives
Izzy Mroczek
Ashley Brobbey
FEATURES
Classes, work, sports, pre-professional organizations, extracurricu­
lars, and volunteer hours. A typical undergraduate Northwestern student
is pulled in a thousand different directions, and some find the time to add
another item to their plate: research.
“It’s really fascinating to me, because you can ask questions, and answer
them,” third-year Izzy Mroczek said of her research. “You’re constantly stim­
ulating a new topic and kind of solving puzzles in ways that really matter.”
Mroczek is a double major in biological sciences and Slavic language and
literature. Since June of 2022, she has worked as an undergraduate research
assistant in the Shilatifard Lab, an epigenetics cancer lab at Northwestern’s
Feinberg School of Medicine.
Research can take many forms for a Northwestern undergraduate,
from working in a physical laboratory with scientific experiments, to sifting
through archival texts on a computer or in a library. Mroczek’s work is the
former: she studies the degradation of a protein that transcribes DNA to
RNA, and her specific project is part of the Shilatifard Lab’s overall focus on
mutations in transcriptional machinery and how those mutations are linked
to cancer.
“You’re really contributing, even if it’s in a small way as an undergrad
with a small little project,” Mroczek said. “It still makes a difference, so I find
that really cool.”
Commuting to Feinberg, which is located in Chicago, gives Mroczek
a different experience than other undergraduate researchers who stay in
Evanston.
“It’s kind of harder since I do have to … commute to the city,” Mroczek
said. “I don’t have as much freedom with my experiments as I’d like because
there’s only so much I can do within the two days.”
Nonetheless, Mroczek said that her lab’s location within Feinberg offers
her opportunities she would never have if she did research on the Evanston
campus. She has been able to attend seminars, learn about research outside
of her own field and get connected to faculty and medical students. Since
Mroczek plans to go to medical school after undergrad, these experiences
have been invaluable to her.
For students in other fields of research, being part of a lab can offer
similar opportunities for mentorship and support.
“They will support you as you do your own projects in their lab,” said
Ashley Brobbey, a third-year majoring in psychology and global health stud­
ies who works in the Personality Across Development Lab (PADlab). “They
guide you not only in undergraduate but also through graduate, because
they are really your mentors and they’re here to help you do your PhD path
or your grad school path, whatever it is you want to do with your future.”
The PADlab studies developmental psychology and the psychology
of personality, and Brobbey, who started as an undergraduate research
assistant in the summer of 2023, specifically studies how the personalities
of children are shaped by their environment and their socioeconomic and
racial statuses. She was drawn to the PADlab both because of her interest in
their research and because of the flexible and supportive environment the
lab embodies.
That flexibility is important to Brobbey in part because she has so many
other involvements on campus. Brobbey is a member of Northwestern’s
cheerleading team and holds positions in Black Formal, Society of Women
Engineers, Minority Association of Pre-Med Students and Physicians for
Human Rights.
“I like this lab because you can work part time when your schedule is
busy,” Brobbey said. “And then come back to full time, or even take a full
quarter break from lab until you want to come back.”
Brobbey stressed the importance of having good time management and
sticking to a schedule when balancing lab work with the rest of her life.
“I do all of my lab work on Fridays, so I can just go in and just knock it
all out, and that way I can focus on the rest of those other commitments.”
Mroczek, who works in her lab around 13 hours a week on top of her
classes and involvement in Quest+, Matriculate and Physicians for Human
Rights, said she has been lucky that her many commitments have not clashed.
Like Brobbey, she emphasized the importance of a consistent schedule. For
Mroczek, this means commuting to Feinberg every Monday and Friday, a
routine she has been able to keep up throughout her time at the Shilatifard
Lab.
While research is a commitment that busy undergraduate students
may have to juggle with the rest of their lives, both Brobbey and Mroczek
encouraged students who know they want to do research to get involved
early, even if that means joining a lab that does not entirely align with their
interests.
“The most important thing is to get involved in a lab that will support
you and give you the opportunities to grow,” Mroczek said. “If you join a
lab where it’s possibly something you’re interested in but maybe not to the
fullest extent, but they really do support you and give you a place to grow …
I think that’s the biggest thing to look for when looking at research groups
to join.”
Visualizing Empire
After decades of battle, the Aisin-Gioro clan from Manchuria officially became the
sovereigns of Imperial China after conquering Beijing in 1644, establishing the Qing 清
dynasty. Among the 10 rulers of the dynasty, the Qianlong 乾隆 emperor (r. 1736–95)
reigned the second-longest and oversaw China at its geographic peak. During his 60-
year tenure, the ruler immersed himself in administrative and artisanal affairs, serving
“as conqueror and empire builder, aesthete and sponsor of culture, poet and artist, grand
ruler over the world’s largest society.”1
A series of military campaigns from the 1740s to 1790s doubled the geographic
size of the Qing empire, extending from Mongolia to Myanmar and Xinjiang to Tai­
wan (Figure 1). This expansion also brought numerous ethnic groups into the empire’s
domain. To celebrate this success, the Qianlong emperor instructed his court to create
the Huang Qing zhigong tu 皇清職貢圖 [Qing Imperial Illustration of Tributaries], which
historian Laura Hostetler describes as a “cultural cartography of empire.”2 The Huang
Qing zhigong tu contains image likenesses and textual descriptions of over 300 groups
of people within the mid- to late-18th century Qing domain. Upon imperial behest,
court artists made several versions, leading to the circulation of ethnographic tropes,
including nakedness, animalistic qualities, and ‘uncultured’ mannerisms.
1 Mote, Imperial China, 900-1800, 912.
2 Hostetler and Wu, Qing Imperial Illustrations.
Illustrating Indigeneity:
Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu and the critical
reevaluation of its depictions of aboriginal
Taiwanese peoples, 1751–1775 and 2006–2022
by Grace A. Wu
Faculty Advisers: Dr. Yuthika Sharma and Dr. Peter J. Carroll
Department of Art History
Although the genre of zhigong tu histori­
cally depicts people who paid tribute to
the Chinese court, the large number of
figures—who did not all pay tribute—in
the Huang Qing zhigong tu reflects the
scope of the Qing domain. Empire is as
much of a visual project as a material one,
and the Qing utilized cultural cartography
to supplement topographical maps they
created.
The National Palace Museum’s il­
luminated handscroll version of the Huang
Qing zhigong tu, attributed to court artist
Xie Sui 謝遂 (hereinafter “Xie Sui scrolls”
or “NPM scrolls”), has distinct formal
attributes, such as its brilliant illumination
(Figure 2). The four Xie Sui scrolls are
unique out of surviving editions of the
Huang Qing zhigong tu (Appendix A) due
to their frequent public display in Tai­
wan’s National Palace Museum (Appendix
C). Curators’ decision to regularly exhibit
these scrolls highlights their curatorial
and educational importance in 21st centu­
ry Taiwan, which I discuss further in the
conclusion.
The Qing-Imagined World
The genre of zhigong tu 職貢圖 first
emerged during the Liang 梁 (502–57)
dynasty. Zhi 職 is used in phrases relating
to duty and responsibility; gong 貢 is
shorthand for gongfu 貢賦, or tribute.
Together, zhigong expresses the obligation
to respectfully submit, obey, and present
things to someone higher in the hierar­
chy. Tu 圖 describes an image, illustration,
or map. Zhigong tu, or illustrated tributary
documents, is unique from textual docu­
mentation of tribute because it contains
the supposed visual likeness of the indi­
vidual or group.
3 Zheng, “Tribute Bearers to the Liang Court,” 36.
4 Zhigong manifested in three types of relationships: “from tributary states to the Qing empire, from regional governments to the
court, and from individual officials above a certain rank to the emperor.” The Qing tributary system was complex and flexible to
changing conditions. In this thesis, I focus on the foreign relations aspect of this system. Ko, The Social Life of Inkstones, 45.
Throughout Chinese history, the imperial
court leveraged zhigong tu to celebrate the
dynasty’s influence within and outside of
its domain. Their high-quality materiality
and careful documentation suggest only
the highest-ranking officials viewed them,
celebrating their political and diplomatic
successes. The earliest-known zhigong tu,
Tribute Bearers to the Liang Court (c. sixth
century), depicts full-length portraits of
the actual ambassadors who paid tribute
to the Chinese court (Figure 3). Despite
the envoys’ formalized stiff poses, each of
the over two dozen illustrated figures ex­
hibits individualized characters with emo­
tions and personalities. An accompanying
textual description of their respective
polity details its topography, customs, re­
lationship with the Liang, and the tributes
presented to the court.3
Zhigong tu supplemented chaogong tixi
朝貢體系 [the tributary system].4 With
rudimentary origins during the Han 漢
dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE), the Chinese

claims of faithful
representation, the
provincial and court
artists inevitably

of people into

tributary
system
reinforced
imperial
suzerainty by organizing people by their
perceived civility. The frequency of tribute
paid to the center vaguely determined the
groups’ positionality.5 The Qing codified
the tributary system, conducting foreign
relations through this “abstract creed of loy­
alty.”6 Although not all polities interpreted
the practice of zhigong as demonstrating
loyalty to the Chinese emperor, the Qing
perceived their submission as such; the in­
clusion of European countries in the Huang
Qing zhigong tu serves as a prime example
of this difference in understanding.
The Qing viewed the tributary system
as a method for foreigners and ethnic mi­
norities to gravitate towards the court out
of admiration of the political, military, and
cultural supremacy of the Chinese state.
As a visual reflection of these beliefs, the
Huang Qing zhigong tu exhibits the dynas­
ty’s narrative of its superiority within and
beyond its borders.
Content evolved from individu­
alized portraiture to ethnographic repre­
sentations that delineated the dress and
habits of the other 12 centuries after the
first known zhigong tu’s creation. Instead
of documenting male ambassadors who
physically were at court, the Huang Qing
zhigong tu depicts male-female stock pairs
who lived far from the imperial center.
This shift to male-female pairs reflects an
attempt to know ‘all’ people of a group.
As the distance widens between the Qing
court and their subjects, the illustrations
in the Huang Qing zhigong tu become more
exaggerated and archetypal.

番. Though its meaning is nuanced, fan

The handscroll versions of Huang
Qing zhigong tu offers a unique viewing
experience for the audience. The viewer
would first lay the scroll flat on a table;
then, they would unroll about a shoul­
der-width section of the tributary scroll to
simultaneously view one to three entries.
To progress further along the handscroll,
the viewer would roll the right roller end
while unrolling the left, bringing more
figures into his gaze. This interactive na­
ture of a constant progression brings the
viewer on a journey throughout the Qing
domain without leaving Beijing.
Creation and Layout of the
Huang Qing zhigong tu
In 1751, the Qianlong emperor issued
edicts to governor-generals within
the empire detailing the imperial
ethnographic and encyclopedic project
that later became known as the Huang
Qing zhigong tu:
My dynasty has united the vast
expanses. Of all various peoples from
within and beyond [neiwai miaoyi 內外
苗夷] our domains, there are none who
have not sincerely turned toward Us and
been transformed. As for their clothing,
caps, appearance, and bearing, each has
its differences. Now although we have
likenesses from several places, they are
not yet uniform and complete. Gather
together the several models that we now
have, and deliver them to each of the gov­
ernors and governors-general near the
borders. Order them to take the Miao, Yao,
Li, and Zhuang within their jurisdictions,
as well as the myriad Yi and Fan beyond,
and according to these examples copy
their appearance, bearing, clothing,
and ornaments, make illustrations
and send them to the Grand Council
for classification and arrangement for
presentation and inspection.8
Incumbent government officers
across China mobilized upon receiving
this decree. As the governor-general of
Fujian and Zhejiang, Karjišan 喀爾吉
善 quickly instructed his subordinates
to create detailed visual likenesses of “all
various peoples” with whom they crossed
paths with, such as during trade.9 Other
Fujian provincial officials sent the sketches
to Karjišan’s office, where workers created
final drawings. After an official envoy
approved them upon detailed inspection,
workers decorated the compiled album for
presentation to the Qianlong emperor.10
To accompany the drawings sent to Bei­
jing in 1752, provincial officials included
a written addendum presenting the illus­
trations to the emperor, describing the
people’s clothing, accessories, facial char­
acteristics, culture, preferences, and geo­
graphic jurisdiction. The Grand Council
in Beijing received and finished compiling
the submissions from across the empire in

drawings to the emperor for inspection
before handing them to court artists.11
This process of creating and approving
the illustrated likenesses at different levels
of the government reflects how deeply
the Qing administration involved itself in
every step of the Huang Qing zhigong tu’s
creation.
The Qianlong emperor personally
appointed a master court painter to work
on each of the four scrolls: Ding Guan­
peng 丁觀鵬, Jin Tingbiao 金廷標, Yao
Wenhan 姚文瀚, and Cheng Liang 程梁,
respectively.12 As part of their roles, these
painters analyzed the provincial albums
and finalized the colored likenesses. To
fulfill the Qianlong emperor’s wish to have
his empire recorded for posterity, other
court artists—including Xie Sui—triplicat­
ed each scroll and created a polished album
folio of each figure (Appendix A).13
Each of the NPM handscrolls is
roughly one-foot tall, and their lengths
vary from 46- to almost 60-feet long.14
The expressive title of each scroll written
on the orange frontispiece celebrates the
power of the Qing court through its col­
lection of tributary subjects (Appendix B).
Poems appear at the beginning and end of
each scroll, praising the prosperity of the
multi-ethnic Qing-ruled society and claim­
ing the information in the scrolls—spe­
cifically the illustrations—as accurate and
trustworthy.15 Despite the claims of faith­
ful representation, the provincial and court
artists inevitably generalized millions of
people into 300 male-female paradigmatic
types. However, the Qianlong emperor’s
approval signals these drawings were good
enough for the Qing’s self-admiration.
Hundreds of vertical sections, with
varying widths between six- and 12-inch­
es, lie between the bookend colophon
poems. Each section, or entry, depicts a
group of people associated with a foreign
polity or Qing administrative region. In
the upper register of the scroll, text in
the Qing’s official languages, Chinese and
Manchu, identifies the group and describes
their social customs. Sometimes the text
explicitly mentions tribute being made to
the Qing court, which would have been
performed by ambassadors or carefully se­
lected representatives.
Illustrated figures that correspond to
the text occupy the lower register. In al­
most all the entries, an archetypal male and
female pair in generalized local dress rep­
resents the group. The figures are roughly
five- to six-inches tall and interact with
a quotidian object, local crop, or animal
mentioned in the text. Some figures stand
erect, and others contort their bodies while
engaged in an activity or turn away from
the viewer. The figures seemingly float
on the paper with no painted background;
clearly, the focus of the object is on people’s
visual likeness, dress, and other local cus­
16 Wei, “‘Huang Qing zhigong tu’ chuangzhi shimo,” 11.
17 See “Balebu Headman with Servant” entry in the first scroll. Olivova, “Tobacco Smoking in Qing China,” 236.
18 Skoggard, The Indigenous Dynamic in Taiwan’s Postwar Development, 10.
toms. In a compendium of over 300 entries
and 100,000 words,16 the diversity of dress,
pose, and color visually displays the cultur­
al heterogeneity and geographic span of
the Qing empire. The Qianlong emperor
then viewed the final product, claiming all
of these subjects in his domain by stamping
important personal seals onto the scroll.
Xie Sui worked on the scrolls between
1751 and 1775, though sections were add­
ed up to 1790—likely not by the same artist
due to differences of artistic rendering and
male-male pairs. 17
Taiwan in the Huang Qing
zhigong tu: A Case Study
From the founding of the Qing dynasty
in the seventeenth century until the
early 19th century, Taiwan had “an
uprising each three years, a rebellion
every five” largely due to both Ming
loyalists attempting to subvert the
Qing dynasty and inter-ethnic conflicts
between Han Chinese settlers and
Indigenous Taiwanese communities.18
In 1684, the Qing annexed Taiwan into
Fujian Province—naming it “Taiwan
Prefecture”—in hopes of directly
combatting future threats emerging from
the island (Figure 4).
Documents like the Huang Qing zhi­
gong tu demonstrate the Qing continued to
“The entries’ text and image mutually
reinforce Qing notions of savagery
yet sometimes diverge on their extent,
creating conflicting portrayals of fan.”
view Taiwan as liminal and savage a centu­
ry after the annexation through their ter­
minology, text, and illustrations. Although
fan became a general term for unaccultur­
ated people, three specific subdivisions of
fan became closely associated with Taiwan:
shoufan 熟番, guihua shengfan 歸化生番,
and shengfan 生番. The terms sheng 生
and shou 熟 literally translate to “raw” and
“cooked,” respectively, with connotations
of “wild” and “tame” or “unacculturated”
and “acculturated.”19A third term, guihua
shengfan 歸化生番 [naturalized raw fan],
or huafan 化番 for short, refers to a middle
designation where wild fan affirm their al­
legiance to the Qing court through tribute
and taxes. The representation of the sub­
divisions fan in the Xie Sui scrolls demon­
strates tension between the arguments that
the Taiwanese aboriginals can become
assimilated into Chinese society but also
have less developed ways of living, such as
a reliance on hunting and eating raw food.
In the second NPM scroll, 13 Tai­
wanese male-female pairs appear in the
Fujian Province section, and their titles all
contain the “fan” label.20 The entries’ order
is organized by a perceived decline in cul­
tural refinement; there are eight shoufan
followed by three huafan and two shengfan
(Appendix D). Savagery is most visually
apparent through the male figure’s pose,
dress, and facial expression while the fe­
male figures are more passive, have fairer
skin, and dressed more modestly than their
male companion.21 The details in the text
and illustrations complement and refer­
ence one another, though some differences

By 1747, Qing records included 299
aboriginal villages by name. The consol­

male-female pairs in the Xie Sui scrolls is a
deliberate one; the title of each entry sug­

D).22 The Huang Qing zhigong tu reflects an
ethnographic framework by documenting
Taiwanese society through specific cate­
gories—such as housing, food, costume,
marriages, burials, and tools—though the
depth of detail varies depending on the
Qing’s familiarity with that group.23 This
structure, organization, and emphasis re­
flect Qing administrative and cultural log­

The seventh Taiwanese entry doc­
uments the shoufan of Dehua and other
communities in Danshui Subprefecture in
northwest Taiwan (Figure 5). These shou­
fan are among the most modestly dressed,
and their upright pose and direct gaze fur­
ther connotes their civility and humanity.
An excerpt of the accompanying text de­
scribes the terrain and people:
Their lands are very swampy be­
cause they are close to the ocean. They
therefore use thatch or wooden boards
to make their dwellings. They eat mil­
let together with a mixture of fish and
shrimp prepared in a spicy broth. Both
men and women wear short upper gar­
ments bound at the waist with a strip of
cloth. They work hard at farming and
they also fish and hunt. They play flutes
and zithers made of bamboo for enter­
tainment in their spare time.24
The text portrays the shoufan as
adaptable and resourceful, with the con­
junction “therefore” to explain the logic
of using construction materials suitable
for the swampy environment. The sho­
ufan also utilize local natural resources,
catching fish and shrimp from the ocean
to sustain themselves. Reflecting their shou
[“cooked”] and acculturated nature, their
food involves cooking with fire. The text
also notes that these fan have gustatory re­
finement: they add spices to this dish and
mix different flavors and textures together
in their food.
The pair’s illustrated costume departs
from the text. Instead of wearing “short
upper garments bound at the waist,” both
figures wear embroidered and woven cloth
shirts that loosely extend beyond their hips
and cover their arms. Though the text does
not mention leg garments, the pair wears
long flowy skirts that cover the entirety
of their legs. This length of skirt would
be highly impractical while farming and
fishing in swampy surroundings; this dis­
connect shows the artist’s creative liberty
in rendering costumes without seriously
contemplating the textual description. The
man holds a bamboo flute in his hands
and eagerly offers it in the direction of
his female companion, who gazes to her
right towards the next entry while hold­
ing a hoe and basket. The text notes that
the shoufan sustain themselves through
farming, fishing, and hunting, but the
artist only included agricultural tools. The
deliberate exclusion of weaponry elevates
the shoufan’s perceived civility through

the textual description and illustrations
work together to portray this group as

The second case study pair, the huafan
in Zhuluo County (Figure 6) have customs
that situate them in the Qing imaginary as
unacculturated fan. The figures’ concentric
bracelets and leg wrappings highlight their
exoticness and distance from the Manchu
Qing. A portion of the accompanying text
documents their living habits:
They dwell in mountainous earth­
en caves. Their dress and diet are similar
to those of Shanzhumao and other com­
munities. They are not well versed in
farming, only raising sweet potatoes
and taro in cracks in the rock. They
use bow and arrow to hunt river deer for
food. Their feet are like chicken claws,
allowing them to climb steep surfaces as
if they were flat. They annually submit a
head tax of more than 30 silver taels.25
In contrast to the more resourceful
shoufan who build their residences, the
text says the huafan live in “earthen caves”
in the mountains. The huafan’s practice of
growing food “in cracks in the rock” fur­
ther signals the group’s liminal position
between developed civilization and the
wilderness placing themselves on a lower
register in the Qing imagination.
In the bottom half of the entry, the
man and woman face one another, stand­
ing upright. They both wear sleeved deer­
skin jackets and patterned woven skirts
with fabric belts. The man holds a barbed
spear in his right hand, and he carries a
bow, quiver, and basket filled with flowers
on his back. The text does not discuss
hunting spears; the addition of this weap­
on in the image depicts these people as
potentially threatening. The combination
of collected flowers and weaponry simulta­
neously asserts the huafan as primitive yet
potentially hostile. In line with the text, the
male figure has long, claw-like nails on his
feet. In contrast, the female figure has nor­
mal-length toenails, and she displays the
group’s craftsmanship by holding a beaded
circle and wearing a beaded necklace. This
artistic insistence of expressing savagery
through the male figure while simultane­
ously refining the female reflects the Qing
perception of wild fan and Chinese values
of the demure woman. This visual repre­
sentation demonstrates the nuanced Qing
understanding of fan as having the poten­
tial to assimilate into Chinese society yet
perpetually far from civilization.
The last Taiwanese entry in the sec­
ond scroll, the shengfan of Youwunai and
other wild communities in Danshui (Fig­
ure 7), contains the most-nude figures out
of the 13 pairs. In Chinese visual culture,
women are rarely portrayed bare-chested;
the Qing perceived these people to be so
savage that the artist broke cultural norms
to illustrate an exposed female chest. The
accompanying text purportedly reports the
shengfan’s untamed living habits:
The Shengfan live in the moun­
tains. Men and women both bare their
bodies. Some wear deerskins or use
leaves for clothing. They eat raw food.
Their nature is strong and fierce. They
kill for a living. In winter when the grass
and streams dry up they shoot deer. They
can climb tall trees and run as if they are
flying.26
The text’s tone differs greatly from
the shoufan and huafan in the scrolls. The
mentions of mountains, nakedness, un­

Working with—yet sometimes departing
from—the text, the artist created a literal
image of Indigenous Taiwanese who are
wild and hostile.
Throughout the three case studies of
Taiwanese fan, image and text collaborate
to create a supposed authoritative record
of those who are refined versus barbaric.
The representations of savagery are most
explicit through the males’ costumes, asso­
ciation with weaponry, corporal pose, and
grotesque facial features. The males’ cloth­
ing encapsulates the progression of barba­
rism from tame fan to wild fan: the shoufan
of Danshui wears layers of woven textiles,
the huafan of Zhuluo dons a deerskin jack­
et and a woven patterned skirt, and the
shengfan of Danshui is the least-clothed in
his deerskin costume. The male figures’
object-interactions become increasingly
threatening, from the shoufan presenting a
musical instrument to the huafan carrying

weapons to the shengfan actively spearing
an unspecified target. All three men have
untied, freely flowing hair in sharp contrast
to the braided Manchu queue hairstyles
required in the empire, highlighting their
cultural distance from the Qing. None of
the Taiwanese figures wear hats nor shoes,
further indicating their primitiveness. The
diet of these three groups literally reflects
the categories of “cooked” fan and “raw”
fan: the acculturated “cooked” fan makes
broth for himself, and the wild “raw” fan
eats raw food. The entries’ text and image
mutually reinforce Qing notions of savage­
ry yet sometimes diverge on their extent,
creating conflicting portrayals of fan. The
Huang Qing zhigong tu emphasizes this
framework of tiered savagery through the
Taiwanese entries’ visual representations,
reflecting Taiwan’s liminal position in the
Qing empire.
The Twenty-first Century
Afterlife of Xie Sui’s Huang
Qing zhigong tu
Chinese settler-colonialism of Taiwan
continued to grow through the Qing era
and into the present; people of aboriginal
descent comprise 2.28% of present-day
Taiwan’s 23-million population.27 Despite
their small proportion in society, Indige­
nous Taiwanese have been the subject of
growing public interest in recent decades.
This increased respect towards and signif­
icance of Indigenous culture and history
stems from a desire to distinguish Taiwan­
ese identity and nationality from China,
including the modern-day Communist
state and the Chinese imperial past.
Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu
resided in the imperial Qing collection
upon its completion in the eighteenth cen­
tury.28 After the fall of the Qing dynasty in
1911, portions of the imperial collections
formed the collection of the newly estab­
lished, state-operated Palace Museum in
Beijing. To safeguard the museum’s most
culturally valuable objects from military
threats—from the Japanese in the 1930s
and from the Chinese Communists in the
1940s—the Chinese Nationalist govern­
ment evacuated thousands of crates filled
with these objects around the country and
then to Taiwan, respectively. Alongside
the Nationalist government’s retreat to
Taiwan, these select portions of the Qing
imperial collections found their new
home in the National Palace Museum in
Taipei’s Shilin District in 1965. Today, the
museum is internationally acclaimed for
its extensive collection of imperial Chinese
artifacts, and the Xie Sui scrolls serve as
strong visual references for postcolonial
discussions of Taiwanese Indigeneity.
In the early 2000s, aboriginal national
legislator Kung Wen-chi 孔文吉 urged the
NPM to develop more programming rele­
vant to Taiwan’s Indigenous communities;
the public echoed his sentiment, as former
NPM Director Wu Mi-cha 吳密察 said
in an interview.29 Wu Mi-cha elaborated
on the museum’s best efforts to meet pub­
lic interest, saying, “it is difficult to make
interesting exhibitions” that highlight ab­
original Taiwanese society from the muse­
um’s Qing archives because the collection
contains mostly text manuscripts.30 Thus,
the exhibitions discussing Taiwanese Indi­
geneity often incorporate the second Xie

Wu Mi-cha noted a crucial step in
facilitating present-day people’s compre­
hension of Qing archives: clarifying Qing
terminology.31 “Fan” carries a derogatory
connotation in modern-day Taiwanese
society, and the 2022 exhibition What is
“Fandz”? Taiwanese Indigenous Peoples in
Historical Documents of the Qing Empire32 not
only gave museumgoers an opportunity
to understand the Taiwanese aboriginals’
liminal positionality in the Qing empire,
but also encouraged them to recenter
Indigenous perspectives in imperialist
archives through “write back” exercises.33
The Xie Sui scrolls served as an education­
al tool, providing visual references for each
Qing-imagined category of fan: shoufan
(tame fan), guihua shengfan (wild fan who
pay taxes), and shengfan (wild fan).
Museum staff utilized the Taiwanese
figures in several aspects of the exhibi­
tion to not only highlight the association
between the Qing-imagined savage and
Taiwanese fan, but also call attention to
the imperial prejudice and ethnographic
oversimplification within the displayed
documents. The main decal in the 2022
exhibition hall (Figure 8) features some
of Xie Sui’s aboriginal figures—including
the male-female shengfan from Danshui
(Figure 7)—transposed on a Qing map of
Taiwan. The original figures in the Huang
Qing zhigong tu sit on a blank background,
so giving them an illustrated backdrop
modifies their meaning. This addition
affirms Indigenous presence in Taiwan;
they inhabited real spaces on the island
and did not aimlessly float in ethnographic
documents.
To accompany the Fandz exhibition,
the curatorial staff created a website titled
“Nixie Qingdiguo 逆寫清帝國” [“Write
back the Qing Empire”] (Figure 9). Nixie
逆寫 [“write back”] encourages the public
to share new interpretations of Xie Sui’s
fan figures through postcolonial interven­
tions, such as summoning collective mem­
ory and rejecting the language of the colo­
nizer.34 This method draws upon the work
of several British, Indian, African, and ab­
original Taiwanese postcolonial theorists,
which encourage the reconstruction of the
(historically marginalized) subject through
embracing Indigenous theory and replac­
ing imperialist terminologies and ste­
reotyped motifs.35 The website currently
features seven “write back” pieces by high
school and graduate students in Taiwan,
along with an aboriginal author. These
short historical fiction essays draw inspi­
ration from Xie Sui’s Taiwanese figures,
offering imagined interactions between
the Indigenous Taiwanese and the Qing
scribes who recorded their likenesses.36
The first-person narratives include: diary
entries of a court painter in Beijing during
the production of the Huang Qing zhigong
tu, the dog accompanying the shoufan of
Dadu witnessing a Qing official command
his subordinates to sketch the dog’s owner,
and an aboriginal individual criticizing the
Qing’s failure to depict her culture’s shawl

Public engagement with “write back”
also extends to this thesis: in this academ­
ic project, I chose to consider the Xie Sui
scrolls in not only their historical context,
but also of the present. I critically studied
the textual description and formal repre­
sentation of three paradigmatic Taiwanese
fan types in Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu,
noting discrepancies and how they visually
assert the Qing-imagined savageness of
Taiwanese aboriginals. While understand­
ing Qing imperialist ideologies shines
valuable light on why the Taiwanese rep­
resentations take the form they do, study­
ing them without considering their pres­

the weight of these harmful narratives.
Thus, this conclusion embraces the post­
colonial “write back” methodology by also
analyzing how people in the present-day
think about these objects, emancipating
the scrolls from solely holding historical
significance. People residing in the 21st
century, myself included, boldly “write
back” to the Qing empire that its view of
Taiwanese fan does not have the last say in
our collective history and understanding
of Taiwan’s original peoples. ◆

By: Avery Morawa
Hypercapnia and Immune
Suppression with
Dr. Peter Sporn
FEATURES
Hypercapnia, an excess concentration of carbon dioxide in the blood­
stream, is often used as a marker of adverse outcomes in clinical practice
for patients with advanced lung disease such as COPD, asthma, acute lung
injury, or cystic fibrosis. At this stage, patients often succumb to infection,
but the association between contagion and hypercapnia wasn’t clear. Peter
Sporn, a professor at the Feinberg School of Medicine, began to wonder if
hypercapnia plays a causal role rather than an associative role in the infection
rates of patients with advanced respiratory complications. This problem is
extremely pertinent to clinical care: investigating the relationship between
these two factors could potentially change the way that medical care systems
approach the treatment of lung disease.
Through the Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine at Fein­
berg, Sporn and his research team began exposing cells in an in vitro envi­
ronment to high levels of CO2 to model hypercapnia. They found that excess
CO2 concentration inhibited a number of phages important to host defense
and innate immunity as well as inhibiting cytokine secretion, phagocytosis,
and respiratory burst, which all play a role in defending the body from mi­
croorganisms. Hypercapnia was shown to have suppressive effects on both
cell groups and the total organism as mice in hypercapnia in the study died
more quickly and had a higher mortality rate, but this left Sporn with more
questions. Hypercapnia certainly played a causal role in developing an infec­
tion, but would it make infection worse?
Sporn and his group performed a genetic screen on drosophila fly genes
in order to identify genes whose expression was required for CO2 mediated
immunosuppression. Although the drosophila genetic code is primitive in
comparison to mammalian heredity, there are various mammalian homo­
logues and genes related to the drosophila genes that have similar effects on
the organism and its cells. ZFH2, a gene that encodes transcription factors
for cellular development and hypercapnic immune response in drosophila,
was identified and the group developed flies with ZFH2 knockout. Flies with
the knockout gene were protected from the immunosuppressive effects of
hypercapnia, so the group looked to the homologue ZFHX3 gene in mice to
investigate the impact of this conserved gene on mammals. However, the
study was presented with an interesting problem: due to its role in mamma­
lian cellular development, this gene was an embryonic lethal mutation. In
order to create mice with the knockout phenotype, the knockout could only
be present in the myeloid cell line to prevent embryonic death.
The treatments and results indicated that the ZFHX3 gene was central
to hypercapnic immunosuppression. Mice with the ZFHX3 myeloid defi­
ciency were reported to have had less lung injury, reduced burn, and partial
protection against hypercapnic suppression, establishing ZFHX3 as the first
known mammalian mediator of hypercapnic immune suppression.
Sporn’s research group will conduct further research on the molecular
mechanisms by which hypercapnia signals through ZFHX3 to impact im­
mune function. They have begun searching for potential CO2 sensors or
receptors that signal to ZFHX3 or incite cellular pathways that interact with
the gene. Once these receptors or pathways are identified, research can be
conducted on their role in various cell types present in the lungs and this can
guide the development of a treatment for hypercapnia induced immunosup­
pression. “If there are ways to interrupt hypercapnia’s suppressive effects, we
can reduce the patients’ resistance to infection or improve their outcomes if
they are infected,” Sporn noted, hoping to see a future where his impactful
work can save lives.
By: Caroline Guerra
[This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.]
Interviewer: Could you tell me about your research in graduate school?
Professor Gesmundo: I did research in graduate school at the University
of North Carolina (UNC), and I worked for Professor Joseph DeSimone. One
of the projects that I started reading a lot about was nanoparticles for cancer
therapeutic delivery, which was one of the things I was really interested in his
research group. Joe’s research group was very interdisciplinary. We had people
from the chemistry department, the school of pharmacy, biology, NC State’s
College of Engineering, and a couple of empty Ph.D. students. It was a really
wide range of people. I believe the lab had 65 members at the time I joined, so it
was really big. However, I was the only analytical chemist in the lab at that time,
so I was concerned when I started reading about the project and the work that
he was doing on it that I would end up being kind of a go-to analyst to solve
problems for other people’s projects. So, even though I was really interested
in the oncology group, I was a little hesitant to join without having a project I
could truly own myself.
FEATURES
Nanotechnology & Medicine with
Dr. Katie Gesmundo
I ended up starting a new type of project for the group, which was really a cool
avenue. Joe was interested in delivering nanoparticles in different ways, not just through
traditional oral systemic delivery, but using the technology his lab was really good at to
deliver drugs transdermally, or through the skin. Hearing about this project and wanting
to have something that was my own niche, I was really interested in it. We also discussed
at the time if the project could have a cancer application, which was very much possi­
ble, so I started working on that. I worked on creating microstructures using the same
technology that we use to create nanoparticles, and adapting the platform for a larger
particulate shape was a little bit of an engineering challenge that was really fun. We
started loading chemotherapeutics into the microparticles once we actually had proof of
concept. As much as I was passionate about that project, it had a lot of hurdles to get it to
pass a mouse-modeled type of avenue. So we ended up doing an even more fundamental
study of trying to figure out what types of molecules we could deliver with these micro­
particles that went through the skin.
My thesis turned out to be a lot of fundamental studies of loading larger and larg­
er therapeutic surrogates into microparticles and looking at how they would be trans­
formed through the skin barrier using mostly mice models. We looked at small molecules
of fluorophores, protein therapeutics, and nanoparticles, which are kind of packaged into
these microparticles. I guess the main conclusion of my research is that it was possible
to deliver all of these things with our technology. The microparticles are part of a field
called microneedle patches, and so after showing proof of concept from small molecules
to nano particulates, we could really get this type of technology working to deliver drugs
to the body.
Interviewer: Have you seen your research on microneedle patches be used practically
or commercially?
Professor Gesmundo: Yeah, there are a few labs that have advanced them quite a bit
further than what we were doing at the time when I was working on this research. We
were working on a very specific application of microneedle patches. We were looking
for something that could be completely soluble, so our approach was like thinking of a
Band-Aid with a bunch of spikes, but the spikes were so short that they entered your
skin without touching your pain receptors. Our vision was using water to dissolve the
backing; there would be no waste, ultimately kind of contained in a Band-Aid-like
packaging, and we were thinking that this would be something that could be really
useful for self-administration. You wouldn’t need medical professionals to do that.
There’s an advertisement for a flu vaccine with an absurdly small needle, which is
technically a microneedle technology. It is just one that would require a nurse or
some medical professional to actually still administer. There are some products on
the market that have needles involved in them that are in clinical trials right now.
I don’t think any of them have really met that need of completely soluble that I was
working on, but there are definitely pieces of this technology that exist today.
Interviewer: How did you decide to pursue graduate school?
Professor Gesmundo: So, I went to college to be a high school teacher, and I picked
a university that had a really great college of education. I envisioned myself teaching
high school chemistry and physics, so I picked that specialization when I went into
college. Picking that specialization was really useful because it put me in chemistry
courses over things like biology courses in my first year of school, so I could take
some of the more advanced chemistry courses earlier in my degree, and that’s how I
realized that I really liked chemistry.
I started doing undergraduate research with the professor who taught me or­
ganic chemistry. He was taking students, and he wasn’t necessarily scared away by
the fact that I was not a chemistry major. I really thank him for that. I was very, very
lucky that he took a chance on letting somebody do some research over the course
of my first three years. I really did like teaching, but I spent more of my time doing
research than I did probably any other extracurricular activity. When I was a junior
in college, finishing up my third year of research, he asked me if I had considered
graduate school. I said no, I’m not really considering that, I’m thinking of going into
teaching. He basically said, I don’t think you should turn down the option to try to
learn more about chemistry; you really like this, and I had to agree with him. I really
did. He talked to me about what it meant to be a professor in chemistry and what
types of teaching opportunities I would have if I was more committed to teaching
than I was to high schoolers. There was an avenue for me to learn more about chem­
istry but still keep teaching in my future career. I thought that was really powerful.
At that point, after three years in college, I added a major in chemistry, which is a little bit
nuts. But it was possible to finish my degree since I started taking upper-level chemistry
courses out of curiosity. After I applied to graduate school and was accepted, I did some
visit weekends, and I got really excited about this option. I took a chance on graduate
school once I was accepted to UNC, which was pretty much my dream school.
Interviewer: From my understanding, your organic chemistry professor served as a
mentor to you; having someone who can encourage you and inspire you is very valuable.
Professor Gesmundo: I really cannot thank those professors enough. You can’t really
oversell how important it is to have someone in your corner when you’re thinking about
what to do with the rest of your life. One of the things that I love about working here
is that I do get to have conversations with a lot of people about what their future might
look like. I know how valuable a professor was for my personal experience, so I really
don’t take it lightly when I talk to people about what they want to do. I think it’s one
of the joys of being a faculty. I am pretty grateful that I have the opportunity to do for
somebody else what was so powerful for me.
Interviewer: What are some valuable lessons you have learned along your journey
in academia?
Professor Gesmundo: That’s a hard question. The first thing I learned about academia
was when I was sitting as an undergraduate thinking about what it meant to be a chem­
istry professor. I had one thing in mind of what it looked like to be a chemistry professor,
and it turns out that there are a lot of different ways to work in higher education as
a chemist. I went to a small liberal arts college, so the role of a professor is to teach
undergraduate courses and do undergraduate research. Occasionally you go to present
your work or publish a few papers. That’s not what my role is now. At Northwestern,
which is considered a research one university, R1 faculty members and their research
labs are mostly populated by graduate students and postdocs. A majority of their publica­
tions don’t involve undergraduates. I really wanted to work with undergraduates; that’s
something that was important to me. I didn’t really see how I would fit in a big school if
I wanted to work with undergraduates. My role as a teaching faculty member at North­
western is a little bit different than both of those. What I am expected to do for most of
my job is instruct undergraduate courses, but I also work with graduate student TAs. I
also work with the larger curriculum committees to kind of map out what it means to be
a chemistry major at Northwestern. I teach chemistry courses like the freshman seminar,
which helps me understand what it means for a Weinberg College first-year student to
feel prepared to keep going through the rest of their journey. That type of role is really
unique. I didn’t know about that role when I went to graduate school.
My first teaching job was at Ohio State, which is quite a large university. Part of my
role in that teaching job was to work with graduate students and help them learn to be
good teaching assistants. I absolutely loved that part of my job. I really love working with
graduate students, and I have a unique background in teaching and pedagogy that a lot
of people didn’t have. I love sharing that knowledge and helping graduate students learn
about a job like mine because I didn’t know about it at all.
When I was looking for a job in the Chicago area, I was really attracted to North­
western because it would allow me to instruct undergraduates and keep working with
graduate students. Those were the two things that I found I was most passionate about
in my career, so my first lesson is that academia is not one size fits all. There are a lot of
different roles that you can have. Exploring what those roles look like and what types
of jobs are available is something that I would recommend to anyone who might want
to work at a university. There are more options than I ever thought when I was an
undergraduate.
I’ll do one more lesson. One thing that is really important when you’re working at
a university is to keep everyone’s identities in mind when approaching your work with
them. All of the different populations of people that I work with have unique needs.
They are individuals that come to the table with different motivations. I try really hard
to keep policies that keep my students in mind, but no policy is completely custom­
ized to an individual. Allowing yourself to recognize everyone’s individual differences,
concerns, and needs in the moment is really important when working at this level. It’s
something that I spend a lot of time thinking about, and I really think that all students
benefit when you not only consider their status as a student, but you also consider them
as an individual. Keeping that in mind when advising students or organizing courses is
really important to me.
Introduction
“How do Northwestern undergraduate students with chronic physical conditions inte­
grate their health status into their identities?”
I interviewed Northwestern undergraduates who have been physically ill for the
past six or more months to understand how they have or have not integrated their health
status into their identities.1 In this sense, “identity” refers to a part of someone’s sense of
self that they either disclose or choose not to disclose in different settings. My interview
guide covered a wide array of situations, from intimate, private conversations between
friends or family to very public settings such as at work, on medical forms, in govern­
mental surveys, and so on.
Part of making an accessible world is first studying how disabled individuals and
communities understand themselves and relate to society. However, there is a gap in the
literature regarding the intersection of disability studies and identity formation when it
comes to ill young adults. Identities are impactful and important: they help dictate who is
excluded or included in a group, help build a sense of community and alliance, and help
people publicly express their internal experiences. Since the 1980s, the queer community
has experienced a proliferation of labeling, including the reclamation of some words and
the rejection of others, which sociologists have studied to better understand the queer
community and its needs on a social policy level. My study aims to do parallel work
within disabled spaces.

Literature Review
My study investigates how Northwestern
undergraduate students with long-term
illness(es) form an identity around their
health and how they think about, express,
and label their health during that process.
There is an abundance of sociological
research on identity formation, and many
studies empirically apply this theory to
chronically ill communities. My study
specifically aims to understand the unique
experiences of young adults in college.
Identity Formation
Psychologist and psycho-analyst Erik
Erikson popularized identity formation as
a social science subcategory in the mid-
to-late 20th century. Heavily influenced
by Freudian thought, Erikson developed
a “psychosocial construct of identity for­
mation” (Herman 2011) that he labeled the
theory of ego (Erikson 1950). This theory
proposed that young adulthood was a time
of self-reflection and individualization
where young adults either developed a
unique, individual identity or failed to do
so and then struggled to become full adults.
Even before Erikson, Charles
Cooley was the first to specifically discuss
identity formation in the context of sociol­
ogy (1902). He proposed the looking-glass
self theory, which argued that individuals
create a sense of self and identity by con­
sidering how they are perceived by others
and by society writ large. In other words,
people use how they think others think
about themselves to determine how they
view themselves.
George Herbert Mead and Charles
W. Morris furthered sociological thought
with their symbolic interactionism theory
(1934). Symbolic interactionism proposed
that conversations, interactions, and expe­
riences with other people informed how
someone built their identity and how they
viewed themselves. Thus, it constructed
the individual from a sociological per­
spective by studying “how the individual
internalizes the self and its roles from in­
teractions with others” (Brekus 2020).
Erving Goffman added to identity
formation theory by coining the term
“social identities,” which suggested that an
individual’s identities might change based
on social context (1959). Goffman specif­
ically employed a drama allegory to relate
different social contexts to different acts in
a play. Just like actors might change their
behavior or comportment for different
scenes, people might act differently and
even think about themselves differently
depending on their current social context.
Anthony Giddens critically built upon
identity formation by conceptualizing it as
a reflexive process between the individual
and their social environment. He argued
that society shifted from low to high with
the advent of mass-mediated communica­
tion via the internet, late-stage capitalism,
and globalization. As a result, identity for­
mation became both active and political:
individuals taking up or refusing certain
identities shifted larger social institutions’
perception of those identities, which could
influence social processes such as individ­
uals’ future identification, social relations
between people with different identities,
politics, and so on (Giddens 1991). In re­
sponse to their changing worlds, individu­
als increasingly and repeatedly reconstruct
their identities to match their environment
and create a stable life story.
Most studies that consider identity
formation theory’s specific application to
physical health conditions are interviews
and surveys that researched how respon­
dents felt their illness impacted their life or
how they manage their illness in academic,
medical, personal, and other settings. The
most influential thinker on this topic is
Michael Bury (1982; 1911), whose early
work on chronic illness as “biographical
disruption” provided the foundations for
an identity-based approach within med­
ical sociology. Biographical disruption is
the idea that becoming chronically ill is so
life-changing that it can alter or disrupt the
ill individual’s other identities and sense of
self.
Sociological interrogation of Bury’s
theories can be found in recent studies,
like the Oris et al. study that investigated
how chronically ill adults had or had not
integrated their illness into their identities,
using four potential stages: engulfment,
rejection, acceptance, and enrichment
(2018). The study did not ask how labels
inform or intersect with the four stages.
However, the four stages have been em­
ployed in other studies, such as one on
how youth handled their Type 1 Diabetes
diagnoses (Raymaekers 2019).
A few leading studies consider illness
identity formation specifically in the con­
text of young adulthood. Ceri Wilson and
Jennifer Stock’s research noted that phys­
ically ill young adults reported experienc­
ing a mixture of emotions related to their
health, including personal empowerment,
depression, anxiety, and “being different”
(2019). Spencer et al. studied the experi­
ence of chronically ill college students, in
particular how each participant felt their
illness impacted their daily life, how they
explained their illnesses to both them­
selves and to their peers, and how they
tried to manage their health alongside all
of the other pressures of university (2021).
My study aims to build upon this body of
knowledge.
Motivation
The motivation behind this project is
threefold: sociological, current relevance,
and personal. On the sociological level,
outlined above in the literature review,
there are few studies that specifically con­
sider young adults with long-term illness
and how their health might impact their
identity, making my research topic both
interesting and significant.
Secondly, this topic is timely and
increasingly relevant in the context of
COVID-19, the looming threat of another
pandemic, climate change, and other so­
cial health hazards that disproportionately
impact and create chronically ill people.
These social and medical catastrophes
pushed conversations about disability and
disabled people to the forefront of national
discourse, albeit temporarily. One conver­
sation focused on how hospitals should
triage COVID-19 patients when they had
limited ventilators: disabled people were
often the first to be deprioritized (Chen
and McNamara 2020). Another discussed
who should qualify to receive a COVID-19
vaccine in the first few waves of distribu­
tion: people with very specific diagnosed
conditions were prioritized, but many
other disabled people were not. Largely
missing from both of these conversations
were the voices of disabled people. Thus, re­
search on how this population understands
their health and how they choose to frame
it in different engagements with society is
incredibly pressing and necessary. I believe
my research will positively impact the so­
ciological and chronically ill communities.
Finally, my interest in this topic is
also deeply personal. As a person with
chronic physical health conditions, my
own experience reflects a roughly linear
trajectory from engulfment to enrich­
ment. Throughout my thesis, I was aware
that my personal experiences might skew
my interpretation of data collected in the
interviews, mistakenly and erroneously
pushing my data closer to my hypotheses.
I implemented a couple of mechanisms in
place to counteract my bias. First, I was
aware enough of my bias to be able to name
and recognize it, making it easier to identi­
fy moments where my assumptions might
have overridden the data directly collected
through the interviews. Second, I worked
with two faculty members and a cohort of
other seniors writing theses whose feed­
back and review helped me identify and
counterbalance my biases. Third, I was a
competitive debater in high school and
now coach debate, so I have ample practice
divorcing my personal feelings and attach­
ments to my professional work. Further­
more, I believe my personal experience
with my research material also benefited
my project: I strategically and succinctly
self-disclosed my health status at times
during interviews, allowing me to relate
to respondents on a level that encouraged
more fruitful and lush answers.

sample size of Northwestern students. I
was primarily interested in the thought
processes and experiences that shaped and
influenced each participant’s health identi­

quantitative.
My interview guide started with a
short introduction about myself and my
study, a reminder that participants can
skip questions or stop the interview at

The interview’s second phase consist­

the thought processes and experiences that
influenced and shaped the participant’s
responses to phase one. The open-end­
ed questions started with their internal
health identity, progressed to more private
expressions of their health identity, and
ended on more public displays. While I
could not guarantee my participants told
me the truth, I made it clear throughout
the interview that participants were free to
skip questions if they found them too pri­
vate and also tried to read the participants’
body language. If they seemed too uncom­
fortable with a line of questioning, I would
switch to a different topic that would hope­
fully make them feel more comfortable and
more likely to tell me their truth.

Interviews lasted anywhere from 30

On average, I spoke for 10% of the inter­

Initial Empirical Analysis
As an inductive study, its purpose was
to identify key emergent themes in how
Northwestern students with long-term
health conditions understood and labeled
their health. Thus, analysis throughout
the data collection period was critical
because it informed how I guided future
interviews to gather data relevant to the
emerging themes. My intended sample
size was 10-20 participants, so I conducted
my first round of preliminary analysis
after the first 4 interviews. I uploaded the
transcripts to ATLAS.ti, a software for
analyzing and coding qualitative data. It
was advantageous because I could input
my codes and easily apply them to quotes,
search all transcripts by codes or key­
words, and highlight critical passages for
later review. It also provided small-scale
quantitative data, such as how often I used
each code, that helped me quickly identify
patterns.
My analysis section had two parts that
corresponded with the interview’s two
parts. First, I turned to the data collected in
the interview’s statement section. I tallied
the participant’s points in each category
and then computed each category’s aver­
age score: average scores above three in
any category indicated that the participant
identified with that stage of identity forma­
tion, and scores below three denoted a lack
of identification with the respective stage.
Scores close to three indicated ambivalence
while scores notably higher or lower than
three indicated a stronger feeling.
Second, I analyzed the respondents’
answers to the open-ended questions, tak­
ing note of patterns and creating relevant
codes in my codebook. The first major
codes I imputed into ATLAS.ti were still
the four health identity integration phases
from the Oris et al. study: engulfment
(coded 76 times), rejection (34), acceptance
(218), and enrichment (66). As I started
coding and potential themes emerged, I
then added other codes: accommodations
and school (85), interactions with others
(72), managing health/treatment/coping
mechanisms (88), interactions with med­
ical institutes (48), explicit mentions of
label preferences (74), explicit or implicit
mentions of perceived illness validity (55),
and mentions of illness’s visibility or in­
viibility (58).
See Appendix II for details about each
participant.
Findings
The analysis revealed some of the shared
experiences of Northwestern students
with chronic physical health conditions.
It supported the theory of four stages of
health integration but complicated my
hypothesis that students would prog­
ress linearly through the stages. While
participants did report a roughly linear
progression in terms of how they thought
about and mentally understood their
health, their actual health symptoms did not
always improve linearly. As a result, some
participants reported being mentally in the
acceptance or enrichment stages while also
scoring highly in the engulfment stage due
to their burdensome daily symptoms.
It is noteworthy but not surprising
that none of my participants scored in the
“rejection” stage as their primary catego­
ry: students who were actively rejecting
their health conditions were least likely to
self-select to participate in a study explic­
itly about their health status. Most partic­
ipants scored primarily in the acceptance
stage, which would explain their willing­
ness and comfort in participating in an
interview about their health. Participants
mentally and physically in the engulfment
stages tended to be diagnosed the lon­
gest, suggesting that time since diagnosis
increased their comfortability in talking
about their health despite their persistent
and pronounced challenges. Supporting
my secondary hypothesis, I did find a cor­
relation between the participants’ mental
integration stage and their preferred labels.
Finally, I also identified other emergent
themes, social identities, and experiences
that directly influenced participants’ health
identities and can inform future research.
Four Stages & Linear(ish) Progression
My findings support the validity of
the four stages of identity integration: par­
ticipants who scored highly in engulfment
spoke about feeling overwhelmed by their
health during the open-ended questions,
participants in acceptance affirmed their
peace with their illness, and so on. Par­
ticipants who scored highly in the engulf­
ment stage most often reported a lack of
social support and all-encompassing daily
symptoms:
On feeling engulfed as a child: I was so
used to pain…so all of that was going
on for years and…my dad refused to
take me to a doctor and my dad is a
doctor, but he couldn’t fathom the idea
of something being wrong with his
kid…so he did not take me to a doctor,
even when I literally couldn’t move my
hands very much for years…it finally
got really, really bad and then my dad
agreed to take me. (Participant 4)
As explained above, none of my par­
ticipants scored highest in the rejection
stage, which makes sense given that peo­
ple rejecting their health probably would
not self-select to participate in a study on
chronic illness. On the other end of the
spectrum, people who scored highly in the
acceptance or enrichment categories talked
about their health and its impact on their
life in less emotionally charged or negative

While my data supports a linear pro­
gression in terms of mental models around
participants’ health identities, I also discov­

One iteration was the mental engulfment
depicted in the above analysis. The second
was physical rather than mental engulfment.
Participants who were physically engulfed
had such severe daily symptoms that they
scored highly in the engulfment stage. Still,
they also scored highly in the acceptance or
enrichment stage as they more accurately
reflected their current mental model:
