Thus, my data supports the four-
stage theory of identity formation, com­
plicated slightly by the two different forms
of engulfment. This formation process also
proved to be approximately linear, encour­
aged by factors such as manageable daily
symptoms and a strong social support net­
work. I will next analyze how label prefer­
ence intersects and reflects a participant’s
current stage of identity formation.
Discussion
Aside from its small size, a few other
factors potentially made my sample more
biased and less representative. First is
self-selection bias. My participants con­
centrated more on the acceptance and
enrichment end of the identity formation
spectrum, and none identified with “rejec­
tion” as their primary stage. Second, my
main recruitment method for this study
was an informational email sent from
AccessibleNU to students who currently
receive accommodations due to a physical
illness they have experienced over the past
6 or more months. Thus, my recruitment
methods themselves limited my potential
participants to people who have already
disclosed their health conditions to the
school and their professors.
As an inductive study, it created more
questions than answers, such as the poten­
tial relationship between perceived visibil­
ity and feelings of validity. Hopefully, larg­
er and more resourced studies in the future
can help fill some of the gaps in my study.
It would be helpful to more actively recruit
participants who are less confident in their
health, more recently ill, and who hold
other marginalized identities to under­
stand how those variables impact one’s un­
derstanding of their health and their health
identity. It would also be advantageous to
conduct studies with larger sample sizes
that might be generalizable and to examine
how populations other than young adults
in prestigious academic environments re­

Overlap in Env Sci and EPS Majors
at Northwestern
By: Gabrielle Walthour
The living and the dead. The environment and the Earth. Two sides of the same
coin. At Northwestern, environmental science “prepares students to address one of soci­
ety’s greatest challenges: preservation and stewardship of the natural world”1 and Earth
and planetary science is the study of “ the past, present, and future of the Earth and other
planets [and helps] scientists address fundamental scientific questions important for un­
derstanding the Earth and society’s connection to it.”2 Both are majors at Northwestern.
Although they both deal with the environment, fundamental distinctions lead to
major differences in curriculums. Within the environmental science program, there are
two pathways: science and policy. The science track is interdisciplinary and students can
choose to focus on sciences like biology and chemistry. The policy track is more eco­
nomics-focused which can be misleading. Within the environmental science major, it
is expected that students take two environmental policy classes, but for students more
interested in policy, Weinberg offers an environmental policy and culture adjunct major
and minor.
FEATURES
The Earth and planetary major also has different concentrations: Earth materials,
geochemistry, seismology, geology, climate/paleoclimate, geophysics & planetary, and
geobiology. Students must take courses from at least four of the seven subdisciplines
leading to interdisciplinary work. A plus is that the general requirements for the two
majors are mostly similar so first-year students have the whole freshman year to decide
which major they want to pursue.
Even though there are fundamental differences between the two majors there is
much collaboration between the two departments. For example, there is much collabo­
ration between the leadership in both departments, and multiple teachers are affiliated
or related faculty with both programs. Also, it is not uncommon to learn about topics
pertaining to one major in a class for the other, because they are related topics, both
involving the environment.
While there are major differences in the curriculum at Northwestern, the two ma­
jors are close to each other regarding careers and the future. Both majors can lead to jobs
in industry, government, or academic work. There is even overlap with students major­
ing in Earth and planetary science getting a higher degree in environmental science. The
interdisciplinary work that students do for both majors can lead to similar job work, but
it is important to note that each major’s coursework prepares students for certain jobs
differently.
1 Northwestern Environmental Science website: https://envsci.northwestern.edu/about/
2 Northwestern Earth and Planetary Science website: https://www.earth.northwestern.edu/about/
Shattering the Finance
Ceiling & Breaking Boundaries:
By: Rebecca Chen & Ellen Liu
Fintech’s Female Frontier
In the bustling world of quantitative
finance, the clinking of numbers and
the whirlwind of algorithms form
the backdrop of high-stakes deci­
sion-making, yet diversity remains a
crucial but often elusive goal. How­
ever, individuals like Whitney Chen,
a sophomore majoring in economics,
are challenging the status quo with fer­
vor and innovation. At Northwestern
University,
her
impact
extends
far beyond her academic pursuits.
Within the Kellogg School
of Management, Chen is research­
ing leadership and organizational
behavior, striving to uncover effec­
tive strategies for navigating complex
dynamics in quantitative finance.
“My research centers on understanding how leaders can negotiate with stakeholders
to enact meaningful change within their organizations,” she explains. Through meticu­
lous study and analysis, Chen explores the intricate interplay between power dynamics,
communication strategies, and organizational structures. Her work not only sheds light
on the nuanced art of negotiation but also offers valuable insights into fostering trans­
formative change within modern workplaces and organizations, with a particular focus
on empowering women in finance.
Chen’s research has far-reaching implications for the finance industry. By eluci­
dating the intricacies of negotiation dynamics, she offers actionable insights and strat­
egies to navigate challenging organizational landscapes, particularly in terms of gender
inequality, and drive positive change. Through her research, Chen’s focus on female
empowerment within quantitative finance highlights the pressing need for diversity and
inclusivity in traditionally male-dominated fields.
The most rewarding aspect of Chen’s research journey lies in its potential to affect
real-world change. “The fact that the insights that I uncover in my research have the
FEATURES
possibility of making an impact is what is
most rewarding for me” she reflects.
Northwestern University Fintech
(NUFT) aims to prepare students for
competitive industry roles in quantita­
tive analysis and research, training their
members in quantitative analysis and
research skills while exposing members to
a top-tier pre-professional environment.
As the General Manager of NUFT, Chen
has focused on taking initiative to increase
female participation in a traditionally
male-dominated space.
“One of the challenges we faced was
the lack of representation,” she explained.
“Women often felt sidelined or intimidated,
leading to a significant gender disparity in
club participation.”
In response to this challenge, Chen
took decisive action by spearheading a
series of initiatives within NUFT. From
the start, her goal was clear: to empower
and educate women interested in Fintech,
fostering an environment conducive to
their growth and success. “We wanted to
shatter the glass ceiling one initiative at a
time,” Chen emphasized during our inter­
view. Her words resonated with a sense
of purpose; with each endeavor, Chen is
steadfast in her previous commitment,
paving the way for a more inclusive future.
When asked what event was most
effective in promoting female involve­
ment, Chen replied “Definitely the series
of training workshops and networking
events tailored specifically to the needs of
women in Fintech, such as inviting women
who are already leaders in the field to speak
about their experiences.” According to
Chen, “this provided mentorship and con­
nections that extended beyond the event,
which is immensely helpful in navigating
and thriving in a male-dominated field like
finance.”
“Representation
matters,”
Chen
stressed, “and by showing success stories
of women in finance [through panel dis­
cussions and networking events], we can
inspire others to follow suit, forming the
next generation of female leaders.” She
further emphasized, “Right now, diversity
and inclusion are major missions of tech
culture.” As a result, Chen’s commitment
to promoting diversity and inclusion mir­
rors the evolving landscape of the tech and
finance industry.
Chen, in recognizing the vital sig­
nificance of outreach and recruitment,
took proactive steps to increase NUFT’s
exposure to women interested in the field.
By having NUFT participate in events
like Women in Computing, and actively
engaging with attendees, Chen not only
shares the club’s mission but also creates
a welcoming environment, encouraging
women to explore opportunities within
the club.
“Recruiting more women into the
club was very important to me,” Chen
explained. “It is not just about increasing
numbers or meeting a quota. For me and
many others, it is about fostering a sense
of belonging and creating a space where
women feel empowered to pursue their
passions in Fintech.”
The impact of Chen’s initiatives has
been visible, as there has been a significant
increase in female membership and partic­
ipation in executive roles within NUFT.
“Seeing more women actively engaged and
making their voices heard has been incred­
ibly rewarding. There is still so much work
to be done in terms of fostering diversity
and inclusion within the finance industry,”
Chen remarked. “But we are just getting
started.”

Eden Stargardt
The Lasting Legacy of a
Divided City:
The Berlin Orchestras as a
Microcosm for Germany during
the Wendezeit
In a nutshell, what is your
research topic?
Orchestras are important cultural institu­
tions and as such they are representations
of greater socio-political movements. They
often act as mirrors of political, social, and
cultural landscapes, and reflect the greater
values and beliefs within a given time. After
the fall of the Berlin Wall, the greater themes
of Germany during the Wendezeit were
reflected in the activities of the orchestras,
musical institutions, and concert program­
ming in the orchestras in Berlin and acted
as representations of cultural politics during
this transitional period. By examining three
significant reunification concerts that oc­
curred in Berlin between late 1989 and early
1990, my research explains the ways in which
the orchestras in Berlin acted as a microcosm
for the greater German society. Through
these analyses, I highlight the unequal
preservation of cultural institutions in the
former East Berlin and the Bundesrepublik
and will explain the resurgence of the ideals
of the French Revolution and Germany as
das Land der Dichter und Denker that is in­
tertwined with it. I illustrate the connections
between the large presence of Beethoven’s
music, the idea of the Gesamtkunstwerk,
and the influence of figures such as Johann
Wolfgang Goethe, Friedrich Schiller, and
Karl Friedrich Schinkel on the curated image
of the reunification concerts in Berlin. I also
question who controlled the narrative in this
period of transition and who the collective
audience is after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
How did you come to your
research topic?
I came to my research topic after taking
Professor von Holt’s class entitled Berlin and
the Culture of Democracy. I was looking
for a way to combine my two areas of study
(German and music performance) and want­
ed to create a project to culminate my time at
Northwestern. In her class, we learned about
the impact of the German Reunification on
other artforms (i.e., popular music, dance,
film), but I noticed that there was not wide­
ly-available literature explaining the impact
on classical music and the orchestras. I trav­
eled to Berlin on a Summer research grant
and discovered that the materials existed but
had not been translated into English. This
discovery served as the basis for my project.
Where are you heading to
after graduation?
I will be continuing my studies at Northwest­
ern this fall and will be starting a graduate
degree in music performance at the Bienen
School of Music.
Jacob Geil
In a nutshell, what is your
research topic?
My research is on the impact of school secu­
rity on student wellbeing. It examined how
attending school alongside a security pres­
ence affects school climate, and its extended
consequences for student wellbeing, includ­
ing student experiences of stress, safety, fear,
and discomfort, and how they manifested in
anxiety, depression, and other mental health
challenges.
How did you come to your
research topic?
I attended a high school with a large and very
visible security presence, including armed
police officers, metal detectors, cameras,
and weekly drug tests. Assuming this was
typical, I did not question this security pres­
ence while a high school student. However,
after getting to Northwestern and learning
that not all high schools operate like this, I
began wondering how this sort of regular
exposure to intense security measures might
have been affecting mine and my peers’ day-
to-day experience as students, as well as the
learning environment my school was trying
to foster. This inspired my research topic.
Where do you see the
future direction of this work
leading? How might future
researchers build on your
work, or what is left to
discover in this field?
I am excited to see how this research con­
tinues to develop. I believe there are many
future directions for this research to take,
including a broader sample size; incorpo­
rating students of various age groups and
periods of development; further research
into the role of identity and intersectionality
in this relationship; and further research into
the kinds of support that are most effective
for students and how to make this support
accessible to schools.
Where are you heading to
after graduation?
I will be working as a Higher Education An­
alyst with Huron Consulting Group in New
York City.

Structural Characterization
via X-Ray Crystallography
of III-Nitrides for APDs
In a nutshell, what is your
research topic?
Using a piece of equipment to determine the
structural (physical) properties of a particu­
lar type of semiconductor using x-rays and
subsequent analysis. This seminconductor
family (III-Nitrides) is very good for optical
applications in the UV region and is capable
of high sensitivity, provided we minimize
defects during growth.
How did you come to your
research topic?
I found my lab, CQD, after taking EE223
with Prof. Razeghi my sophomore year. I
began exploring III-Nitrides there and began
my journey with structural characterization
using the XRD there. Since then, I have also
explored the electrical and optical properties
and got more involved in the APD device
fabrication.
Where do you see the
future direction of this work
leading? How might future
researchers build on your
work, or what is left to
discover in this field?
Semiconductor photodiodes are undoubt­
edly the future of optics and detection. In
the UV region in particular, which is what
III-Nitrides are good for, is huge for a lot of
sensitive-detection applications, which now
include the quick and accurate detection
of pathogens and viruses like COVID-19.
These devices start with a better understand­
ing of the materials they are made of so that
higher quality devices can be made - and this
requires further research using characteriza­
tion tech like XRD.
Where are you heading to

After graduating in 2024 with my BS & MS

In a nutshell, what is your
research topic?
My research involves looking at the effects of
maternal prenatal stress on the composition
and diversity of the infant gut microbiome
and infant health outcomes.
How did you come to your
research topic?
I became interested in the human gut micro­
biota after joining Dr. Katie Amato’s lab at
the end of my freshman year. As a former
pre-med, I was interested in how health
inequities manifested through stress-based
pathways, and the microbiota is at the center
of stress and physiology, which led naturally
to my research topic
Where do you see the

leading? How might future

Amy Fan
Are People
“Real” on BeReal?:
Perception and Authenticity in
Utilization of Social Media App
In a nutshell, what is your
research topic?
My research study focuses on how college
students use the social media app BeReal. Be­
Real claims to be “A new and unique way to
discover who your friends really are in their
daily life” (BeReal). Created as a response to
social media platforms like Instagram where
users tend to post picture perfect images on
a never-ending feed with ads, BeReal takes
a different approach. As an app designed to
value authenticity from its users with a limit­
ed daily feed of BeReals from friends, it takes
up a minimal part of a user’s day. The main
goal of the app is to provide a platform for
users to stay in touch with their social circle
while reducing inauthenticity. I studied how
college students use the social media app
BeReal compared to other social media apps
and whether BeReal is effective at promot­
ing authenticity and reducing negative links
often related to social media usage. Looking
into how people use and perceive BeReal
could reveal unintended negative conse­
quences to using the app or determine that
it is indeed a social media app that connects
people in an authentic, positive manner.
This study explored the questions (1) does
BeReal usage mitigate the link between time
spent on social media and anxiety, fear of
missing
out, public self-consciousness, and authen­
ticity (2) how do people use BeReal and what
do they think BeReal’s intended purpose is
compared to other social media apps, (3) do
inauthentic BeReal behaviors such as retakes,
posting late, and skipping posts correlate
with greater anxiety, public self-conscious­
ness, and fear of missing out and vice versa?
How did you come to your
research topic?
Watching BeReal grow in popularity, I
saw an opportunity to investigate if the
design of BeReal allowed users to act more
authentically on the app. Through research,
my friends and fellow peers who use the app
would become more knowledgeable about
the technology we are engaging in every
day and be able to make informed decisions
based on the results.
Where are you heading to
after graduation?
After spending a gap year working as a
medical assistant, I hope to attend medical
school to become an OB/GYN, contributing
to the community through primary care and
patient outcomes research.
Grace A. Wu
In a nutshell, what is your
research topic?
My research centers around an eigh­
teenth-century Qing illuminated handscroll
that contains written and illustrated ethno­
graphic descriptions of different groups of
people in the Qing empire. I explore how
“fan 番,” or those who are “barbaric” or
“savage,” is expressed in the thirteen depic­
tions of aboriginal Taiwanese male-female
pairs, in addition to notions of savagery
versus imperial and cultural superiority. I
also bring this object into the present and
analyze not only how twenty-first century
Taiwanese curators have thought about and
exhibited this handscroll in the National
Palace Museum in Taiwan, but also how the
public has engaged with this object through
a postcolonial lens.
How did you come to your
research topic?
I knew I wanted to write an art history
senior honors thesis about Taiwan, so I
connected with Professors Yuthika Sharma
(Art History) and Peter J. Carroll (History)
to brainstorm ideas. Professor Carroll
mentioned seeing one of these scrolls at the
National Palace Museum years ago, and it
immediately piqued my interest because of
its themes of imperialism, construction of
race/Otherness, and inclusion of Indige­
nous Taiwanese communities. The National
Palace Museum’s 2022 special exhibition of
the scroll was also on view during this time,
which made me realize I could also inves­
tigate the contemporary attitudes toward
this manuscript and compare/contrast them
with eighteenth-century Qing perspectives.
Where do you see the
future direction of this
work leading?
While the ethnographic depictions in the
handscroll are unique for their brilliant
illumination and frequent public display,
other versions of the same content exist in
other media, such as woodblock-printed
books and illuminated albums. Some of the
books were destroyed in conflict, but a book
is currently in the Library of Congress in
Washington, D.C., and some illuminated
album folios are in the Bibliothèque natio­
nale de France in Paris, France. No scholar
has yet written in English how these man­
uscripts left China or what non-Manchu
people thought about its contents, which
would be an exciting future direction of
inquiry.
Illustrating Indigeneity:
Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong
tu and the critical reevaluation
of its depictions of aboriginal
Taiwanese peoples, 1751–1775
Sierra Erdman-Luntz
The Health Identities of
Northwestern Students with
Chronic Physical Health
Conditions
In a nutshell, what is your
research topic?
My research considers how college students
with long-term illnesses integrate their
health status into their personal identities.
How did you come to your
research topic?
While I have been sick since I was 16, it took
years for me to identify as chronically ill and
disabled, and I only recently started advocacy
work for my conditions. I was curious how
other students in similar positions to mine
navigated being sick as a young adult.
Where do you see the
future direction of this work
leading? How might future
researchers build on your
work, or what is left to
discover in this field?
There are so many aspects of identity and
circumstance that might influence one’s
health integration journey that I was unable
to explore in my study due to time and sam­
ple size constraints. Future researchers could
look at how class, age at diagnosis, gender
identity, type of diagnosis, geographic loca­
tion, sexuality, and race could impact how
someone does or does not integrate their
health into their identity. My full thesis also
considered how labeling theory intersects
with identity development, which is current­
ly a large gap in the literature.
Where are you heading to
after graduation?
A few years gap and then law school.

LETTER FROM THE
ADVISERS
Dear Readers,
We would like to welcome you to the Volume 17 of the Northwestern Undergraduate
Research Journal (NURJ). This 2021-2022 issue is the product of a year’s work by
the students who lead and contribute to the NURJ, a student-produced annual print
publication funded by the Office of the President and the Associate Provost for
Undergraduate Education. This year marks our first as advisors for the NURJ following
in the footsteps of the late Professor Allen Taflove, who was with the NURJ for its first
18 years. We have seen incredible work done this year, all of it in Taflove’s honor, and
celebrate the students who have made this publication possible, particularly the Editors-
in-Chief Shreya Sriram and Jenna Greenzaid.
This past year has been the first that students have been able to work together again
in person, and the creations by the NURJ, including this journal, has been a product of
coming together again. In addition to this journal, our students were able to create an
outstanding online package by interviewing student researchers in person, continue to
make new episodes on the NURJ Talks Podcast, and find new ways for student researchers
to share their work and experiences across campus.
The NURJ staff continues to grow, expanding to 70 members, all of who study a
wide variety of subjects. The convergence of different backgrounds has allowed the
NURJ to continue to grow and prosper by creating a more collaborative, creative,
and passionate community where new ideas are welcomed. We have been lucky to see
these new ideas come to life and become staple parts of the work this organization
puts together, from this print edition to the Archives project, interactive online
publications, and everything in between.
As you continue through this Volume 17 journal, you’ll find the intersection of excellent
research and excellent media, all done by and for Northwestern students.
Best,
Dr. Peter Civetta and Patti Wolter

Q&A with Northwestern President
Morton Schapiro
Our late faculty adviser, Professor Allen Taflove, had a list of faculty names whom he fondly
referred to as his “VIPs.” These were members of the Northwestern University community
who were hand-picked to receive a special copy of the NURJ’s annual Print Edition. As a
dedication to Professor Taflove, we have created “Taflove’s VIPs” — a place for us to talk
with some of our fellow exceptional Wildcats, both on and off the initial list. We hope to
establish this as an annual feature, such that Professor Taflove’s vision and dedication can
be eternally celebrated.
To commence this tradition, we thought it only fitting to present a special sit-down with
Northwestern professor, economist, and departing president of 13 years, Morton Schapiro.

NURJ: What were some of your

see if I can try to bring them together as
much as I could.” And that’s what I’ve tried

western, we do a very good job providing

orton Schapiro has been the president of Northwestern University

Black-Owned Small
Businesses in Englewood,
Chicago:
by Sophie Boorstein
School of Education and Social Policy
& Department of Statistics
Faculty Advisers: Prof. Jonathan Guryan, Ph.D.,
Prof. Reuel Rogers, Ph.D., & Prof. Elizabeth Tipton, Ph.D.
The year 2020 was characterized by
insurmountable losses for communities
around the world. Amid the global
COVID-19 pandemic and the largest
recession since the mid-20th century in
the U.S., the Black Lives Matter (BLM)
movement rose to a global scale and
brought the epidemic of police brutality to
the public eye. All aforementioned events
in the United States disproportionately
impacted Black communities, amplifying
pre-existing racial health, income, and
social disparities.
News media reported that Black-
owned businesses were severely financially
impacted by 2020’s crisis events. From
February to April 2020, the number of all
active business owners in the United States
dropped by 22%. During the same period,
the number of active Black business own-
ers dropped 41% (Leatherby, 2020). When
BLM protests erupted in all 50 American
states in response to George Floyd’s mur-
der and the unjust murders of countless
other Black victims, a minority of protest-
ers, including individuals not associated
with the protests, looted local businesses
in several cities across the country.
Englewood, a neighborhood on the
South Side of Chicago, was identified as
one of the areas severely damaged by loot-
ing and the COVID-19 pandemic (Bayne,
Documenting the Effects of
COVID-19 and the Black Lives
Matter Movement in 2020
Background
2020). The area of Englewood, for the pur-
poses of this paper, contains two adjacent
neighborhoods: West Englewood and En-
glewood. Of Englewood’s 75,000 residents,
approximately 90% are Black (“Household
Income in Englewood,” 2020). The median
household income in Englewood is $28,000,
which is half of Chicago’s overall median
household income, and at least 30% of its
residents live below the poverty line. Ac-
cording to Englewood activists’ testimonies,
COVID-19 restrictions and looting activity
exacerbated many hardships that Engle-
wood community members already faced.
Yet, policy responses inadequately
addressed Black-owned businesses’ height-
ened vulnerability in 2020. The federal gov-
ernment attempted to remedy the effects of
the recession on all small businesses through
the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), a
$669 billion loan program from the Small
Business Administration (SBA). However,
structural characteristics of the PPP disad-
vantaged Black-owned small businesses’
access to loans (Abramson, 2020; Selvam,
2020). Even prior to the contingencies and
concerns exacerbated by COVID-19, Black-
owned small businesses were at higher risk
of financial hardship compared to white-
owned small businesses. Although 32% of
Chicago residents are Black, in 2017, Chica-
go had only 1,875 Black-owned businesses,
comprising only 3.7% of all Chicago busi-
nesses (Marotti & Elejalde-Ruiz, 2020). Sys-
temic racism in financial institutions, which
have become systems that maintain white
supremacy, is one cause of racial financial
inequities. Historically, non-white business
owners have had disproportionately low
access to bank credit, and lower-income,
minority neighborhoods have suffered
from lower lending rates than higher-in-
come, white neighborhoods (Blanchard et
al., 2008). Due to racial disparities in credit
access, the majority of small businesses in
Chicago that have fewer than two weeks of
cash reserves are in majority-Black neigh-
borhoods (Leatherby, 2020).
Historical crisis events reveal poten-
tial direct and indirect effects of the 2020
crises on Black-owned small businesses in
Englewood. After the riots in Ferguson,
Missouri, following the 2014 murder of
Michael Brown, businesses in Ferguson
suffered up to 50% in profit losses, re-
gardless of whether they were physically
damaged (Hackman, 2014). Literature
has documented indirect damages of ri-
ots during the Civil Rights Movement,
and the effects were particularly signifi-
cant for Black-owned properties because
the majority of cities’ Black populations
resided in riot-affected areas. Further,
economic recessions disproportionately
affect minority and low-income commu-
nities due to predatory lending and low
cash reserves among family units and lo-
cal businesses (Williams et al., 2013).
Despite the significant challenges that
Black business owners face, scholars have
found that Black-owned business develop-
ment is an effective strategy to create job
opportunities in urban areas, and Black
business owners exhibit higher political
activity and a stronger commitment to
community development than white busi-
ness owners. Black-owned small business-
es can politically and financially support
their community amid crisis events, as
Black-identifying
businesspeople
have
leadership abilities that can influence lo-
cal political institutions and strengthen
human capital in disadvantaged neighbor-
hoods (Ferleger & Lavallee, 2018).
To better understand how Black-
owned businesses can succeed and pos-
itively impact their communities, the
present research aims to understand the
effects of combined 2020 crisis events on
Chicago’s minority-owned small busi-
nesses, using Englewood as a case study.
The work builds upon topics covered by
scholars examining natural disasters, riots,
and recessions, which have to date sig-
nificantly impacted low-income and non-
white communities like Englewood. Using
a mixed-methods approach, I address the
research question: how were Black-owned
businesses in Englewood economically im-
pacted by COVID-19 and the BLM move-
ment in the spring and summer of 2020?
More specifically, I examine two secondary
research questions:
1. How was Englewood economically
impacted according to foot traffic
data records?
2. How was Englewood economically
impacted according to business own-
ers’ accounts?
Methods
Quantitative Methods
For quantitative analyses, I employed
mobile phone data from SafeGraph, Inc.,
a commercial entity that offered free
datasets in 2020 to aid scholarly research
on the COVID-19 pandemic. SafeGraph’s
compiled mobility datasets used ano-
nymized cell phone location records and
governmental open data to capture weekly
population movements at the census block
group (CBG) level. Two datasets provided
foot traffic data on visitations to respective
points of interest (POI), defined as locations
at which a consumer spends money or time.
Quantitative analyses focused on two
events of interest in Chicago: (1) the Illinois
stay-at-home order declared on March 21,
2020, and (2) the murder of George Floyd
on May 25, 2020. I aimed to determine if
there existed significant differences in busi-
ness visitation following the two events of
interest between (1) majority-Black Chica-
go neighborhoods as compared to majori-
ty-non-Black Chicago neighborhoods and
(2) Englewood as compared to other major-
ity-Black Chicago neighborhoods. Because
majority-Black neighborhoods have higher
rates of Black business ownership, examin-
ing foot traffic on the CBG-level provided
information on foot traffic at Black-owned
businesses, and demographic variables
served as a proxy to examine the research
questions (Frey, 2018; Safegraph, 2020). A
difference in difference analysis with two

outcome variables, raw visit counts and
raw visitor counts, was determined as the

disproportionate changes in the foot traffic

significantly in the spring and summer of
2020, confirming that business visitation
declined in Englewood. Furthermore,
participants’ descriptions of decreased
business visitation and the effects of these
drops on profit are likely consistent with
the experiences of business owners in other
majority-Black neighborhoods in Chicago.
Analyses for Event 2, the murder of
George Floyd, showed that after May 25,
2020, majority-Black neighborhoods ex-
perienced a smaller increase in visit count
and visitor count as compared to majori-
ty-non-Black neighborhoods. This was
true when comparing (1) neighborhoods
0-33% Black with neighborhoods 66-100%
Black and (2) neighborhoods in Cluster 1
with those in Cluster 2. Figure 3 shows
that business visitation increased dispro-
portionately in majority-non-Black neigh-
borhoods as compared to majority-Black
neighborhoods after May 25, 2020, and
that total visitor counts in neighborhoods
indexed as 0-33% Black rises at a higher
rate around and after May 25, 2020, as
compared to neighborhoods indexed as 33-
66% Black. The significant findings align
with analyses 6 and 9, and Table 3 displays
the point estimates and significance levels.
While foot traffic increased dispro-
portionately in majority-non-Black neigh-
borhoods after George Floyd’s murder on
May 25, 2020, there were no differences
in visit or visitor count in Englewood as
S Figure 2. Visitor Count Pre- and Post-Lockdown
compared to other majority-Black neigh-
borhoods after May 25, 2020. Thus, En-
glewood is statistically similar to other
majority-Black neighborhoods in terms
of business visitation after the murder of
George Floyd. Business owners in the pres-
ent study’s sample explained that generally
few protests occur in Englewood: “I think
a lot of times protests come from groups
that have a little bit more than what we
have. We’re more in survival mode than
we are in changing mode.” News media
also confirms that thousands of individu-
als rallied in majority-non-Black Chicago
neighborhoods to protest for causes asso-
ciated with the BLM movement. Because
quantitative data indicates that Englewood
is comparable to other majority-Black
neighborhoods after May 25, 2020, it can
be reasonably concluded that the increase
in total visit counts and visitor counts in
majority-non-Black neighborhoods rela-
tive to majority-Black neighborhoods can
be attributed to higher protest activity in
majority-non-Black neighborhoods.
Qualitative Results
Although quantitative data indicates a
disproportionate decline in business vis-
itation in Chicago’s majority-non-Black
neighborhoods, interviews show that
the majority of businesses in the Engle-
wood sample experienced declines in
business visitation after the March 2020
stay-at-home order, which participants
attributed to customer fear of contracting
COVID-19. At the time of the interviews,
the majority of participants said that visi-
tation was at 50-60% of the pre-pandemic
volume. In fact, COVID-19 exacerbated
the challenges of acquiring and retaining
customers among the participants sam-
pled. Customer health concerns about
the virus were likely amplified by poor
public health infrastructure and high
COVID-19 positivity rates in Engle-
wood compared to other neighborhoods
in Chicago (“COVID-19 Community
Mobility Report,” 2020). Participant 7
stated that before the pandemic, most of
his customers lived in majority-white,
north-side Chicago neighborhoods. After
the stay-at-home order, Participant 7
noticed that these customers “haven’t
been calling.” Participants said that even
prior to COVID-19, “acquiring a custom-
er was much harder than in a different
neighborhood” in Chicago due to public
perception of Englewood as dangerous,
and customers from outside of the neigh-
borhood were less likely to patronize
businesses in Englewood.
COVID-19 precautions also increased
business costs and decreased revenue through
modes other than business visitation. For
S Figure 3. Visitor Count Pre- and Post-May 25
example, Participant 3 stopped making food
for delivery services like DoorDash due to
“problems where delivery people didn’t
want to wear masks.” Sanitation supplies
to address COVID-19 were costly, and
shortages early in the pandemic contribut-
ed to high expenditures on the sanitation
supplies. Participant 5 explained, “Say you
made about five or six hundred dollars for
the week. Now, you have to take $100 of
that just for sanitation. That’s not including
your lights, your gas, your product.” The
majority of participants were forced to bal-
ance cost and revenue streams by decreasing
the number of days their business was in
operation, lowering service prices, or let-
ting go of employees. It is important to note
that business success after the stay-at-home
order varied by industry; the funeral home
and hardware store had higher customer
visitation than before 2020. However, such
improved business performance was due
at least in part to implications of the stay-
at-home order, including increases in bike
riding and home repairs. And, even with
unharmed revenue streams, the COVID-19
pandemic affected these businesses’ interac-
tions with customers due to mask mandates
and storefront capacity limits. Participant 2,
whose profit was not affected by the stay-
at-home order, recounted his concern with
employee and customer health: “We talked
with employees about the importance of
not only keeping them safe and healthy, but
also keeping the public safe. And that we
were concerned about them as our staff. We
were concerned about their family.”
All participants’ businesses were at
least partially re-opened by June 2021 after
the initial economic shock from COVID-19
restrictions. However, Participant 5 ex-
plained that just after her business re-opened
in June, looting occurred in Englewood.
She said, “It was very heartbreaking for that
damage of all breaking in and stealing stuff
and destroying stuff. It was really tough. Es-
pecially mixed in with this pandemic.” The
two participants whose storefronts experi-
enced looting damage assumed additional
financial obligations for repairs. Participant
5’s costs amounted to over $25,000, with
90% of products and “countless” pieces of
equipment stolen. Looters broke Participant
3’s doors and windows in an attempt to steal
the ATM machine. Business owners who
did not experience direct effects of looting
reckoned with the destruction of their com-
munity. Participant 4 explained that looters
“burnt down a lot of stores and bust out
windows around the Englewood area.” Par-
ticipant 3 told me that she “watched some-
one’s business being destroyed for eight
hours” and that at the liquor store across the
street from her business, looters took “about
$6 or $7 million worth of alcohol.”
Business owners were unable to control
“Clearly, political protests — and police presence
— are more salient in Chicago’s majority-non-Black
neighborhoods, while majority-Black neighborhoods like
Englewood are deprived of the political infrastructure to
manage or prevent looting.”
looting activity themselves, and police failed
to protect their storefronts during the loot-
ing. While participants stayed in their busi-
nesses as long as possible, sometimes the
entire night, many returned home to sleep,
at which point the looting occurred. Unpro-
tected and vulnerable to the physical dam-
age of their storefronts, the consequences
of looting in Englewood amid pre-existing
financial hardship represent the racial and
socioeconomic discrimination inhibiting the
success of Black-owned small businesses.
Physical damage from looting asso-
ciated with the BLM movement after the
murder of George Floyd negatively affect-
ed participants’ businesses and emotional
well-being, but participants reported some
positive consequences of the BLM move-
ment itself, which helped counteract the
negative effects of the pandemic. After
losing customers in majority-white neigh-
borhoods, Participant 7 began posting ad-
vertisement flyers in the Englewood area to
attract new customers. Now, the majority of
Participant 7’s customers live in Englewood,
and he has a higher proportion of Black cus-
tomers. He said, “Ever since COVID, a lot
of Black people have been trying to look
for a Black computer repairman.” BLM
affected Black customers’ patronization of
Black-owned businesses, demonstrating in-
tra-community asset-building. Therefore,
participants revealed BLM as an avenue to
bolster economic capital in addition to po-
litical capital.
As expected from the accounts of
decreased profit and increased costs,
participants in the sample demonstrated
considerable financial need in 2020. Some
business owners in Englewood, explained
Participant 4, were not “able to pay the
landlord their rent” due to “losing their
business” in 2020. Participant 3 explained
that what she needed most right now was
“financial aid,” and half of the participants
reported using out-of-pocket or personal
funds to support their businesses in this
“time of need.” Additionally, rather than
discussing expansion or business strate-
gy, most participants explained that their
most important “business goal for 2020”
was “to stay open.” This data indicates
that positive effects of the BLM move-
ment on patronization of Black-owned
businesses did not remedy the financial
crises that participants faced in 2020. Ul-
timately, Englewood’s Black-owned busi-
nesses faced immense socioeconomic and
emotional hardship throughout the crisis
events in 2020.
Discussion
Numerous circumstances in 2020 interacted
to affect the experiences of Black-identify-
ing business owners in Englewood. In sum,
their experiences, hardships, and perspec-
tives are not quantifiable. While the effect
of the stay-at-home order was more sta-
tistically significant in majority-non-Black
neighborhoods, business owners in Engle-
wood reported significant economic dam-

ages from COVID-19. Statistical analyses
suggested that participants’ descriptions of
decreased business visitation and the effects
of these drops on profit are consistent with
the experiences of business owners in other
majority-Black neighborhoods in Chicago.
After the murder of George Floyd,
foot traffic increased disproportionately in
majority-white neighborhoods, reflecting
participants’ accounts of low protest ac-
tivity, at least in part due to political and
economic disinvestment in majority-Black
neighborhoods like Englewood. At the
same time, interviews revealed that looting
activity after the murder of George Floyd
injured Englewood’s physical storefronts
and further inhibited financial security for
participants in the sample. Clearly, political
protests — and police presence — are more
salient in Chicago’s majority-non-Black
neighborhoods,
while
majority-Black
neighborhoods like Englewood are de-
prived of the political infrastructure to
manage or prevent looting.
Although some business owners
experienced increased patronage from
customers in Englewood due to increased
awareness of BLM — and one participant
noticed that Englewood residents displayed
an increased propensity for patronizing his
business because it is Black-owned — the
movement was an insufficient force for
substantially increasing business visitation
at Black-owned businesses in Englewood.
Customers from majority-white neighbor-
hoods stopped using another participant’s
services due to COVID-19 safety concerns.
This aligns with some media accounts
that support for Black-owned business-
es because of the 2020 BLM movement
most benefited majority-white, north-side
neighborhoods. Future research and media
reports should clarify the effects of the BLM
movement on patronization by delineating
interactions among Black customers, white
customers, businesses in majority-white
neighborhoods, and businesses in majori-
ty-non-white neighborhoods.
The present discussion is limited due
to the range of businesses represented in the
study. This is especially true in analyses of
looting effects; according to participants,
liquor stores and corner stores were fre-
quently looted, but they were not included
in the sample due to outreach constraints.
I interviewed only two business owners
among the dozens of looted stores in En-
glewood. Additionally, a limitation to the
quantitative methods is my ability to dif-
ferentiate between protest foot traffic and
business visitation foot traffic due to the
inaccuracy of SafeGraph geospatial data.
However, the mixed-methods nature of this
research remedies some potential limita-
tions in that interview findings on protest
activity and business visitation suggest that
the quantitative results are accurate.
Fortunately, scholars will likely con-
tinue to document the impacts of 2020’s
crisis events on small businesses in Chicago.
However, the effects of these crises will last
for decades to come, especially in minority
and low-income communities, as has been
observed after recessions in the 20th centu-
ry and after Civil Rights-Era riots (Collins &
Margo, 2007; Williams et al., 2013). While
this paper demonstrates that business own-
ers’ experiences amid crises are highly com-
plex, it also forms a foundation on which
researchers can examine the potentially
enduring damages of 2020 crises in major-
ity-Black and low-income communities in
Chicago. Equally as important, the research
provides information for future policy-
making so that, as Participant 8 expressed,
policymakers, NGOs, and private firms can
“take action and be held accountable to bring
resources to the Englewood community.” ◆

F E AT U R E
Khoa Phan Howard is a second-year Ph.D. student in the Department of Sociology at Northwest-
ern University. He is also a Gender and Sexuality Studies Mellon Fellow in the Department of
Gender and Sexuality Studies and a Fellow in the Center for Legal Studies. His current research
focuses on how social institutions can shape the space of intimate relationships.
We were able to sit down with Khoa to gain insight into the experiences of conducting research
and securing funding and mentorship in the social sciences at both the undergraduate and grad-
uate levels through his own experiences.
[This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.]
Could you tell us a bit about yourself?
I went to college down the street at the University of Chicago, and I graduated in 2019.
I majored in English and sociology. My current research interests include looking at in-
timate relationships. I study institutional structures and how they are shaped, as well as
how people make sense of them within and beyond these institutions.
When did you get involved in research as an undergraduate student?
My first exposure to research happened during the summer between my first and second
years of school. I got a job as a research assistant for a sociology professor. The job was in
Vietnam and I’m Vietnamese, so the stars kind of aligned there. That project was a very
foundational experience for me in terms of exposing me to the subject of sociology and
the day-to-day work of doing research, and it was the starting point for my research path
towards sociology.
What was your experience in finding your first research assistantship
position?
My case was unique and I therefore wouldn’t generalize my case, but overall, I do not
think it was very difficult for me to acquire the job. I coincidentally
met this professor when I was in Vietnam the summer before. I was
interning at a newspaper, and the professor contacted the newspaper to
access their resources. I became connected to the professor through the
editor-in-chief. Generally, though, you are most likely not going to get
the first research job you apply to. However, I think if you are
persistent about applying, you can probably get a position to
do research somewhere.
Why did you decide to attend graduate school,
and what is something you think undergraduate
students should know when considering pursuing
graduate school?
When I went to college, I had no idea about academia or do-
ing a Ph.D. and that specific pathway, so that research assis-
tantship position was my introduction to this whole field. I
liked being in the field, interviewing people, observing, and
then analyzing that data. I find all these steps of the research process
very enjoyable. One of the biggest constraints about graduate school
that I feel should be more transparent is that for a good five to seven
years of your 20s, you’re not making that much money while your
friends … start very lucrative careers. Investment-wise, it’s almost like
a sacrifice. I think this is one of the many points of consideration that
students should think very carefully about if they are considering go-
ing to grad school.
What was your experience like applying for graduate school?
One resource I got was from my professors themselves, the ones who
I asked for letters of recommendation from. Professors in the depart-
ment who I had not noticed before gave me recommendations on
places to apply to, their reputations, etc. I applied for fewer graduate
schools than I think the average sociology applicant would aim for due
to geographical constraints with my partner. Something I really had to consider
was that I would be spending at least five to seven years in this one place. I think
this is another important point of consideration for students if they’re going
down the Ph.D. route.
Why did you decide to attend Northwestern University?
Northwestern was an overall good fit for me in terms of the topics in which I am
interested. Also, the stellar reputation of Northwestern appears to be true, specifically
for the Sociology Department; the community is collegial, the support system is good,
and the stipend is good, compared to other schools. It ended up being a good choice
and a good fit for me.
What was your experience like trying to secure funding for research
during graduate school?
One thing I have come to realize is that it is much easier to get undergraduate funding
than graduate funding. In graduate school, it seems as if everyone is applying for funding.
Applying for funding sources inevitably becomes a part of your academic career. The
process taught me a lot about how to write a strong research proposal and summarize
everything I want to study into a few pages.
What has your experience conducting research as a graduate student
been like so far, and what have you learned about graduate-level re-
search in the social sciences from it?
I am in my second year and have been mainly doing research more on my own. I think
most people in the social sciences conduct research on their own. There are also people
who express interest in working in a specific lab and aligning their theses/papers to that
lab’s research. Additionally, some people become research assistants for professors, and
the process becomes more involved when you are a graduate student. I think a friend of
mine is even doing manuscript preparation for one of her professor’s books. It might be
specific to sociology or maybe the social sciences in general, but this is how I see research
assistantships happening in graduate school.
F E AT U R E
Do you feel there is a difference in securing research funding, say in
comparison to STEM majors?
I think in the humanities and social sciences, research is much more individualistic in
that you do your own project. On the other hand, as STEM majors, you’re usually work-
ing under an existing research lab. From there, the student can pursue a specific line of
research within whatever resources are available in the lab.
Are there any other similarities or differences you noted in your expe-
riences with research as an undergraduate compared to as a graduate
student?
In graduate school, there is often an idea of mentorship. It’s a relationship with two
people involved and is based on how you are communicating and asking for mentorship
from the mentor. I think as an undergraduate, there is more hand-holding. For example,
I could be analyzing a set of quotes, and my adviser would nudge me towards a more pre-
cise way to analyze something. In graduate school, the adviser would not really prompt
you like that. You figure it out yourself. The advisers may give suggestions, but you are
also crafting your own identity and mindset as a scholar.
Do you have any advice for current undergraduate students trying to
pursue research in the realm of the social sciences?
I think research is, especially in the social sciences, a rewarding process. It is an opportu-
nity to explore and learn something new about the world and understand how the social
world works by using the tools that you have learned about in classes. You are creating
new knowledge. It is a rewarding process, but it is also a difficult one. There are other
dimensions of the experience of graduate school that are not just research: grant-writing,
learning how to network and how to navigate reaching out and getting mentorship from
other scholars in the field, or going to talks. All of these attributes of graduate school
could also be done during your undergraduate education as a precursor for graduate
school, and you could potentially start building some skills that can help you in the long
run when it comes to succeeding in graduate school. Even if you do not want to go to
graduate school, college is a very cool opportunity to learn new things, and so, if it means
pursuing a project just to learn something that you are interested in, I definitely suggest
going for it. ◆

Bridging the Youth
Movement-Electoral Divide
In recent years, it has been well docu-
mented that young people in the U.S. are
less involved in formal politics than older
people. According to the U.S. Census Bu-
reau, 18–29-year-olds are consistently the
least reliable voting bloc in the U.S.,7 and a
2017 study found that trends of low youth
participation extended to other political
activities like writing to representatives,
attending town halls and public legislative
meetings, and campaigning or working
for political parties.8 A 2000 survey by
Heather Bastedo found that young people
were less likely than any other age group
to express interest in traditional politics,
follow political news, or participate as a
member in an advocacy organization, but
the young people in this study were not
apathetic; instead of voting, subjects iden-
tified protest and community volunteering
as their preferred methods of social and
political engagement.9 These findings are
in line with the consensus among social
movement scholars that young people
have been critical to the operational suc-
cess of U.S. social movements over the
past half-century, even while exhibiting
low levels of interaction in formalized
politics.10 In other words, there has been
a youth participation gap: young people
are heavily involved in social movements
while exhibiting less consistent involve-
ment in more traditional electoral politics.
The 2020 elections, however, saw a sig-
nificant increase in youth electoral engage-
ment and participation, following a trend
of increased politicization in the nation as a
whole. In fact, the 2020 presidential election
garnered the highest voter turnout in over a
century at 66.3%, followed closely only by the

Framing in the Sunrise
Movement
For Sunrise and other organizations like it, a
crucial aspect of building both people power
and political power is telling a convincing
story, or in other words, political framing.
In the social movement scholarship in the
fields of sociology, political science, and
communication and media studies, a frame
is a way of looking at information.18 Fram-
ing describes the way that movement ac-
tors, like organizations or leaders, attempt
to publicly explain the problems they are
working to solve and the solutions that they
propose. There is a prevalent idea in social
psychology that people live in a perceived
world, meaning that they respond to exter-
nal events based on their built perceptions
of what is happening around them. This
suggests that, for social movements, fram-
ing has potential for real-world impact; if
people’s perceptions shape their responses,
then influencing those perceptions is a task
with great potential power.19
Benford and Snow’s seminal 1988 so-
ciological scholarship on social movement
framing provides a blueprint for social
movement organizations (SMOs) looking
to develop effective framing. The authors
write that frames for collective actions are
“intended to mobilize potential adherents
and constituents, to garner bystander sup-
port, and to demobilize antagonists.”20 In
other words, when SMOs strategize around
framing, they are looking to inspire partici-
pation amongst people who are aligned with
their cause, convert neutrals into support-
ers, and disempower those who disagree
with their cause from action. According to
Benford and Snow, there are three main
stages for this kind of frame: diagnostic
framing, or the identification and descrip-
tion of a problem; prognostic framing, or
the proposal of a solution; and motivational
framing, or the rationale for action.21
Sunrise’s framing falls clearly into
Benford and Snow’s three stages. First,
they diagnose the problem: the climate
crisis is here, and we have (now) less than
10 years before our habitat is damaged
beyond repair, but the fossil fuel execu-
tives and corrupt politicians who brought
about this crisis continue to enact their
decades-long strategy of blocking action
in protection of their profits. Meanwhile,
the dominance of neoliberalism over the
past several decades has cemented eco-
nomic and racial hierarchies that ensure
that poor communities of color are most
immediately in danger of the devastating
impacts of climate change.22

Digital Dimensions:
Disseminating the Frame
Sunrise’s use of contemporary social media
platforms — particularly Instagram, Twit-
ter, and sometimes TikTok — has been es-
sential in the organization’s dissemination
of its messaging, exemplifying how digital
tools create a more decentralized and par-
ticipatory information society. This paves
a way for new voices to be included in po-
litical idea generation and illustrates how
the bounds of what constitutes a political
stakeholder are being expanded.
At the time of this writing, Sunrise
uses Twitter and Instagram, along with (to
a lesser degree) TikTok and (even more
decreasingly) Facebook, to disseminate
its framing and communicate with the
public.25 Sunrise also engages with more
traditional media sources — members li-
aise with the press and place op-eds and
letters-to-the-editor in mainstream news
sources — but a significant portion of the
organization’s recruitment and commu-
nication efforts occur over social media
platforms. “I think a lot of Sunrise’s success
has been in … changing dominant cultural
narratives around climate justice topics,”
Sunrise’s Oregon-based video network
lead Allyson Woodward said, discussing
the way that the Green New Deal rheto-
ric has infiltrated mainstream media and
politics. “I do think that we could not have
done it without digital organizing,” she
added, suggesting that social media was a
key element of the organization’s strategy.

Digital Framing in Action:
#YoungAndNaive
Sunrise’s strategic use of digital commu-
nications as a tool for building power
and infiltrating mainstream media dis-
course was emblemized when videos27
of Pennsylvania gubernatorial candidate
Scott Wagner (who lost to Democrat
Tom Wolf) calling Sunrise activist Rose
Strauss “young and naive” went viral.
Sunrise used Twitter in conjunction
with traditional media outlets to cap-
italize on the moment — which could
otherwise have been seen as a blow to the
movement’s credibility — and start a con-
versation about the moral authority of
young people, claiming that the younger
generation has a unique perspective on
the future and challenging the prevailing
notion that young people should be kept
out of political ideation due to a lack of
knowledge or experience.28
The story began when, during a Q&A
at a campaign event, Sunrise member Rose
Strauss stood to ask Wagner a question.
“My name is Rose,” she began. “I’m 18,
and I’m really concerned about the future
of our country. Two-thirds of Pennsylva-
nians think that climate change is an issue
that needs to be addressed, but you’ve said
that climate change is a result of people’s
body heat and are refusing to take action
on the issue. Does this have anything to
do with the $200,000 that you have taken
from the fossil fuel industry?”
Wagner paused for less than a full
second before responding.
“Rose, I appreciate you being here,” he
said. “And you’re 18 years old. You know,
you’re a little young and naive. Let’s talk
about something else.” Wagner turned
away from Strauss and looked at the rest of
the people at the event, many of whom were
clapping and cheering, before continuing,
“Are we here to elect a governor, or are we
here to elect a scientist?” Multiple videos of
the exchange began to circulate online —
mostly on Twitter and YouTube — starting
some buzz about the candidate’s attitude.29
This was an opportunity for Sunrise
to take hold of the narrative, and the orga-
nization did just that. Sunrise took to Twit-
ter, starting the hashtag “#youngandnaive”
in order to weaponize Wagner’s words
against him and elevate its own platform.

Sunrise turned to traditional media. In an
op-ed for Teen Vogue, Rose Strauss de-

instead painted Wagner to be a symbol of
the establishment — old and out of touch.
By reframing the narrative around
Wagner’s words, Sunrise pushed back at
the idea that an 18-year-old should keep her
nose out of politics and instead asserted that
being “young and naive” was a designation of
moral authority: to be young and naive was
to be uncorrupted by money and the fossil
fuel industry, to be clear-eyed and strong.
This narrative resonated in both traditional
and participatory information spaces; the
exchange was covered by local and nation-
al publications including the Philly Voice,
The Guardian, and The New York Times,
and the hashtag was used by organizations
and public figures like NextGen America,
350 Action, Now This, and Al Gore. Dem-

Fetterman even adopted Wagner’s words
for a campaign t-shirt.32 The spreading
of the video — and the enthusiasm about
Strauss and Sunrise’s response — suggests
that Sunrise’s framing strategy was effective
at infiltrating public consciousness.
In this instance, social media allowed
Sunrise to send a clear message. A 2018
New York Times article featuring an inter-
view with Strauss introduced the exchange
by noting that “it quickly went viral on
social media,” using this as a justification
for its newsworthiness. Here, successful
framing on Twitter (a participatory plat-
form) gave Sunrise clout in the traditional
media realm, providing them with access
to a massive platform like The New York
Times. And there, in turn, Strauss — repre-
senting Sunrise — was able to use that plat-
form to publicize the movement, urging
young people like her to “join a movement,
not an isolated or singular thing. March-
ing, demonstrating is great, but we need
sustained action to really turn the tide.”33
That Sunrise was able to begin
spreading this story on Twitter, get no-
ticed by press, public figures, and political
actors, and then successfully transition
to traditional media sources, shows how
participatory media platforms can influ-
ence political discourse by giving voices
that might ordinarily be discounted — like
Strauss’ — the opportunity for greater
reach. On Twitter, politicians, activists,
and unofficial actors are using the same
platform; participatory social media dis-
rupts the previously entrenched dynamics
of who has access to spheres of political
idea-generation and persuasive messaging.

The Impact of Sunrise’s
Reframing: A People’s Politics
Video network lead Allyson Woodward
noted that in her mind, the proliferation
of the Green New Deal into mainstream
Democratic politics indicates a significant
shift in political ideology and a transition
around where political power is held:
Sunrise, in two years, has smashed the
climate versus jobs narrative among
Democrats. We’re still working on it for
culture as a whole, but when Joe Biden
gets up on stage to accept the presidential
nomination and he’s like, “we’re going
to create millions of good jobs — clean
union jobs — while addressing climate
change,” he’s basically parroting a
Sunrise talking point. And so, we didn’t
get the candidate we wanted, right,
we got Joe Biden.35 But our cultural
narratives have gained so much power
in our society that he can’t ignore them
because they are that powerful. Politics
is a game of power, not of persuasion.
And our narrative gained so much
power that Joe Biden has to parrot it,
even in his most important speeches,
because he knows he can’t ignore it.36
What Woodward describes here is a victo-
ry of framing. The Green New Deal rheto-
ric went from being derided by mainstream
Democrats as a “dream” to being invoked
by the party’s presidential nominee himself.
In fact, on Earth Day 2020, Speaker Pelosi
— who, as previously mentioned, once pub-
licly derided the Green New Deal as “the
green dream or whatever” — tweeted from
the @TeamPelosi handle, “Together, we
will create millions of good-paying green
jobs as we #BuildBackBetter and modern-
ize our infrastructure.”37 This phrasing of
“creat[ing] millions of good-paying green
jobs” is almost exactly the same as the words
in Sunrise’s mission statement38 and clearly
emulates the Green New Deal resolution’s
framework.39 The fact that Pelosi, who pre-
viously saw the Green New Deal as a pipe
dream, now sees its rhetoric as politically
viable enough to warrant its use suggests
that the narrative paradigm shift that
Sunrise seeks — changing the landscape of
formal politics to be a more participatory
movement space — is indeed in motion.
