Having grown up in New Delhi, India, Natasha Das — an under-
graduate student and researcher at Northwestern University in
Qatar (NU-Q) — has always had a particular interest in environ-
mental research. She recalls her personal experience with air pol-
lution in New Delhi: “The smog in New Delhi is so thick that
when you get off the airplane and you walk into the airport, …
your eyes will burn from the pungent smoke.” Given the severity
of pollution in her city, Natasha notes that her school experience
was marked by numerous projects designed to teach students
about environmental sustainability. In high school, however, Na-
tasha began to realize that “there was this huge disconnect between
all the science and what we’re being taught versus how much
people actually ended up doing.”
Combining this observation with her passion for com-
munications studies, Natasha began delving into the con-
nection
between
human
behavior
and
climate
change.
At NU-Q, she began to get involved in researching the politics of
climate change, the topic on which her senior thesis focuses. We
were able to sit down with Natasha to learn about her research
and gain more insight into her thoughts regarding climate change
and environmental policies. We feature key points from her the-
sis, The Politics of Climate Change (as seen by the quotations an-
notated in the margins throughout this piece), along with parts
of our conversation to bring together her thoughts regarding hu-
man action, or the lack thereof, in environmental sustainability.
[F]or decades, there has existed a dichotomy
between scientific consensus and human action.
Discussing the Politics of
Climate Change with
NU-Q Student Researcher
Natasha Das
by Rachel Chiu and Grace Lee
F E AT U R E
In her thesis, Natasha discusses the necessity of
increasing climate ambition. When asked about what
this specifically entails, she brings in her experience
working in public relations to expand upon the idea:
Companies will say something to seem like they’re
very environmentally friendly — say, ‘we’ve done
x, y, z initiatives.’ And I’ll be able to sell it to you
that this company is doing so much for the en-
vironment. … But the truth is: I’m making you
believe that because we’re persuasive enough.
This is what we’ve been trained to do. The ques-
tion you should be asking is: Why has this com-
pany only done x, y, and z, and why isn’t it more?
With this, Natasha calls for action on all dif-
ferent levels — from the government all the way
to the local level. She believes in the power of
collective action, envisioning a collaboration in
which individuals, neighborhoods, and schools can
work with small and big businesses to eventually
reach higher levels of policy change. She explains:
It’s really difficult for those policies on top to change
very quickly at the level that we need it to, so I
think our best hope right now is with local commu-
nities. … [W]e can set really high goals for ourselves
[and] then for … our neighborhood to meet certain
goals, and I think that’s really achievable as well.
Natasha’s vision for bottom-up, collective ac-
tion may seem idyllic to some, as it is often the case
that people are rather apathetic to environmental
issues. She acknowledges, “Unless you live in a place
like New Delhi, where there’s just smog hitting you
all the time, environmental issues are not necessar-
ily straight up in your face for you to care about it
every day — like in Doha, [the capital of Qatar,]
there’s so many times when I just forget.”
In her thesis, Natasha addresses some key fac-
tors that contribute to the “underwhelming amount
of action” in response to climate change. Lack of
belief in the science behind climate change, pre-ex-
isting cultural influences that skew scientific rea-
soning, and the prioritization of capitalistic success
over environmental sustainability are all factors that
“To stand a fighting
chance against climate
change, we need to
‘significantly increase
our climate ambition’
and contribute
towards this problem
more substantially
(Cantellano, 2020).”
“[T]o get organizations
to act in an
environmentally
friendly manner, there
needs to be a bigger role
taken by governments
or by local communities
taking initiative to be
climate friendly.”
“Climate change’s
very nature makes it
difficult for people to be
concerned because it is
invisible, seems distant,
and its effects are not
palpable enough to
cause action.”
contextualize human inaction against climate change.
Natasha stresses that these factors, along with the
seemingly intangible nature of climate change, make
it difficult for people to feel immediately concerned.
Despite the multitude of factors that discourage
concrete action, Natasha believes that there is a way
to get people to be more invested and involved in the
very real issue of climate change. This belief stems
from a personal anecdote from her high school days
in Doha. She shares, “I remember I was just so frus-
trated. … The focus in all these clubs [in my school]
would be to raise money for the cause, [but] we don’t
really know where all the money is going and ex-
actly how it works.” Natasha began to wonder what
would happen if the problem became more personal
for the students: “I just thought, … What if we just
focused on our own community and made it better?”
With this thought, Natasha began initiating
programs at her school that focused more on local
sustainability and community-based changes, and
the effects were immediate. “People immediately got
more engaged,” she reflects, “and within two years,
the school became drastically more sustainable because
people felt like they could relate to what was going
on, and suddenly, environmental issues seemed more
than just these theories that were floating in the air.”
Having seen firsthand the impact of creating a
more personal, common goal for people to work to-
wards, Natasha stresses the importance of inspiring
community-based action. “Human relations are some-
thing that’s important to all of us, regardless of where
we’re from,” Natasha states. She expands upon this by
saying that given the value that people tend to place
on human relationships and how they are perceived
by others, phenomena like the collective action theory
and the free-rider problem are “not very applicable to
local communities, where people know each other and
relationships are stronger.” Cooperation and willing-
ness to take action become stronger once the stakes
become more personal: “So if we could somehow tap
into that [aspect of human behavior] to create goals
and policies, … I think that could be a good solution.”
“Environmental
action requires
collective action,
which occurs when
individuals successfully
cooperate in pursuit
of one common goal
despite their diverging
self-interests.”
“People are more
likely to engage in a
local collective action
program because it
helps them feel [like] a
part of the community
and triggers emotions
such as benevolence and
conformity. … Within the
community, people want
to be seen in a positive
light and there is a
reputation to be gained
on a smaller scale.”
F E AT U R E
We ended our conversation with Natasha by asking her if
there is one thing she would change, if given the power, about
the discourse regarding climate change. Natasha answers, “The
thing that I would fix is the way that we’re talking about the
problem.” Especially as a communications major, Natasha is
greatly interested in the way in which the problem is framed:
From what I’ve seen in most environmentally themed mov-
ies or communication pieces, they try to make it sound like
if you don’t do something, then the world is going to end.
And usually, they’re not very clear on what that thing is,
and the focus is more on the ‘world end’ thing. That kind of
fear freezes people and makes them unable to do something.
Instead of framing climate change as a ‘doomsday-es-
que’ phenomenon and instilling fear in people’s minds,
Natasha believes in inspiring a collective approach towards
a positive reward. “I think the focus has to be more on we
should all do x, y, and z, and then something good will
happen,” she explains. Inspired by “the hope and all the
positive literature that’s out there about local communi-
ties doing something [together],” she envisions a future in
which a collection of small efforts eventually leads to mac-
ro-level, systemic change. She concludes, “I don’t know
how quickly it can happen, but I’m hopeful that [it will].” ◆
The Impact of Climate
Change on Energy Poverty:
by Ginny Ip
Department of Economics
Faculty Advisers: Prof. Mar Reguant, Ph.D.
& Prof. Jeffrey Lewis, Ph.D.
Abstract
Energy poverty can be understood as the inability or difficulty of a
household to meet their basic energy needs. While the condition is
already widespread across Europe, it will likely worsen in the near fu-
ture, as average temperatures increase due to climate change and there
becomes a greater need for heating and/or cooling. The present study
addresses the gap in research in this area by using Eurostat data on
energy poverty and changes in heating degree-days (HDD) and cooling
degree-days (CDD) across the 28 European Union (EU) Member States
from 2004–2019. These metrics are then used to create a composite
indicator of energy poverty based on a household’s inability to keep
warm, pay utility bills on time, and the presence of damp, leakage, or
rot in the home. The results indicate that an increase in the number of
days in which air conditioning is needed to be comfortable significantly
increases the share of energy-poor households, but there is no signif-
icant association with HDD. Additionally, a comprehensive analysis
of temporal and macroeconomic trends shows that energy poverty is
severely unevenly distributed across the Member States and that both
climate change and the ongoing energy transition will likely exacerbate
these inequalities. Thus, policy implications include increasing general
awareness of the phenomenon and implementing country-specific pol-
icies that directly address energy poverty in the context of a changing
climate, especially in Southern and Eastern European EU countries.
Evidence from the European Union,
I. Introduction and
Background
Awareness of energy poverty has been
rapidly growing in recent years and is
increasingly being recognized as a critical
social policy issue. Importantly, energy
poverty not only affects those living in
the poorest countries without any access
to power but also those in some of the
wealthiest countries in the world. While
the term “energy poverty” does not have
a universal definition, it is generally
understood as a distinct form of poverty
associated with households who have a
hard time meeting their basic energy needs
or spend a very high proportion of their
income to do so. For example, the United
Kingdom officially declares a household
energy-poor if it “needs to spend more
than 10 per cent of its income on fuel to
maintain a satisfactory heating regime”
(DTI, 2007). However, this definition of
energy poverty may be overly simplistic,
as the causes of energy poverty are often
multidimensional, stemming from a com-
bination of low household incomes, high
energy expenditures, and energy ineffi-
cient buildings and appliances (EU Energy
Poverty Observatory, 2016).
As a result, energy poverty is not
only a development issue but also involves
public health, environmental, and national
security issues, as its prevalence is often as-
sociated with adverse consequences rang-
ing from respiratory and cardiac illnesses,
exacerbated mental health problems,
increased air pollution, and higher levels
of social unrest and instability (EU Ener-
gy Poverty Observatory, 2016; Yumkella
& Bazilian, 2015). Additionally, energy
poverty often coincides with food pover-
ty, as energy-poor, income-constrained
households are forced to choose between
prioritizing their energy needs or food
needs (Omic, 2019). Thus, addressing
energy poverty has the potential to bring
many benefits, including healthier citizens,
a healthier environment, improved social
security, and higher levels of economic
productivity overall.
Energy Poverty & Climate Change
Recent decades have seen increasing
average temperatures and extreme tem-
perature days due to the onset of climate
change. For instance, a group of climate
scientists found that each of six European
heat waves since 2010 was significantly
more likely and intense because of climate
change (Schiermeier, 2019). This may
elicit an increase in household energy
demand, particularly for cooling purposes,
causing a positive feedback loop that fur-
ther perpetuates climate change and puts
a strain on existing energy services (Jessel
et al., 2019). However, most of the current
literature on household energy to date
have not sufficiently considered climate
change and its impact on vulnerable pop-
ulations (Jessel et al., 2019).
Moreover, subsequent global efforts
to undertake an energy transition, which
involves moving away from conventional
sources of energy such as oil and gas and
“towards a more sustainable energy system
characterised by universal access to energy
services … and security and reliability of
supply from efficient, low-carbon sourc-
es,” are also having a significant impact
on household energy bills (Bridge et al.,
2013). McGee and Greiner (2019) have
found that attempts to address climate
change through subsidies and other in-
centives for carbon mitigation, including
transitioning away from fossil fuels, have
disproportionately increased the percent-
age of household income spent on energy
by marginalized groups. Bouzarovski &
Herrero (2017) would agree, arguing that
European energy transitions in particular
have deepened existing regional inequali-
ties and energy poverty.
Acknowledging this gap, the pres-
ent study uses panel data to examine how
changing average temperatures as a result
of global climate change have impacted
energy poverty levels in European Union
(EU) Member States over the last few de-
cades. The principal finding is that an in-
crease in the number of CDD significantly
increases the share of energy-poor house-
holds, but there is no significant associa-
tion with HDD. Moreover, energy poverty
is indeed very unevenly distributed across
the Member States, and both climate
change and the ongoing energy transition
will likely exacerbate these inequalities.
Energy Poverty in the EU
I focused on the EU for three reasons.
First, an estimated 30 million people were
living in energy poverty as of 2019, with
the highest rates in Southern and Cen-
tral-Eastern European countries (Omic,
2019). Many countries are still suffering
the repercussions of the economic crisis of
2008/9, with high unemployment and in-
equality rates having serious consequences
on the living conditions of EU citizens
(Kyprianou et al., 2019). Second, there is
a high degree of geographic, social, and
economic variation across the Member
States, which means that climate change
will likely have very different effects on
energy poverty levels across the EU. Bou-
zarovski and Herrero (2017) note that the
“classic economic development distinction
between the core and periphery also holds
true in the case of energy poverty,” where
the Southern and Eastern European coun-
tries are simultaneously milder in climate
and poorer compared to the frigid but
wealthy Northern countries. At the same
time, the EU Member States share both a
common currency and an interconnected
power grid, which makes it easier to
compare and control for trends in energy
costs and prices. This unique combination
is particularly useful in understanding
the macro-scale spatial patterns of energy
poverty and how they relate to wider
economic and geographic disparities with-
in the EU, an area that is also currently
under-researched (Petrakos et al., 2011).
Finally, the Eurostat provides a rich body
of publicly available, highly reliable data
on energy poverty that is currently un-
matched in other regions of the world.
II. Data & Descriptive Statistics
The main data source was the EU Energy
Poverty Observatory (EPOV), launched in
2018 by the European Commission with the
goal of better monitoring and addressing
energy poverty across member countries
(EU Energy Poverty Observatory, 2019). It
recognizes the multidimensional nature of
energy poverty and thus includes a portfolio
of indicators that I used collectively. Specif-
ically, I combined three primary indicators
to create an Energy Poverty Index using the
following formula:
EP – Energy Poverty
W – Warm
A – Arrears
H – Housing Problems
The variables warm, arrears, and
housing problems measure the population
percentages of people who reported (1) not
being able to keep their homes adequately
warm, (2) having trouble paying their utility
bills on time, and (3) the presence of damp,
rot, or a leaking roof in the home, respec-
tively.1 This approach is based on Bouza-
rovski & Herrero’s (2017) energy poverty
index and previously developed efforts to
capture the multidimensional nature of en-
ergy poverty. However, while Bouzarovski
& Herrero’s index gives warm a weight of
0.5 and gives arrears and housing problems a
weight of 0.25 each, I gave the same weight
to warm and arrears and gave housing prob-
lems a lower weight. This was because the
latter is not necessarily a direct indicator
of energy poverty, while the former two
are. For instance, a household might have
a leaking roof but have no problem meet-
ing its energy needs. Likewise, a household
might have a perfectly functioning home
but can barely afford to pay the heating bills
in the winter. Additionally, I did not weigh
warm higher than arrears because the for-
mer does not take into account the inability
of households to keep cool in the summer,
which is highly relevant in the context of a
predominantly warming climate, while the
latter keeps track of late payment in energy
bills pertaining to both heating and cooling.
Other secondary indicators that were
included as controls are household electric-
ity prices and household gas prices, both of
which include taxes and levies and are mea-
sured in cents per kilowatt hour (ct/kWh);
the percentage of the population living in
an area with intermediate urbanisation; the
percentage of the population who are paying
tenure market rent; and the percentage of the
population with access to air conditioning
and heating in the home, respectively.
The other main dataset that tracks his-
torical temperature patterns was supplied
by the Eurostat (the Statistical Office of the
1 Note that data are available from 2004–2019 for the warm and arrears variables while only data from 2005–2016 are available for
the housing problems variable.
2 The United Kingdom is excluded from the sample even though the period covered is pre-Brexit. This is because the U.K. oper-
ated differently from the rest of the EU in many aspects even prior to Brexit, which may affect the reliability of the results. In its
place, I’ve included average observations for the European Union in general, which is why the sample size is still 28 and not 27.
European Union). The annual data series
covers the Member States of the EU and the
EU aggregated from 1975 to 2019, except
Cyprus, which only has data from 1978 to
2019. The two variables of interest were
Heating Degree Days (HDD) and Cooling
Degree Days (CDD). HDD measures the
difference between the daily mean outdoor
temperature (Ti) and 15°C, below which a
building is assumed to need heating; CDD
measures the difference between Ti and
24°C, above which a building is assumed
to need cooling. Both estimates are based
on daily observations from approximate-
ly 3,000 weather stations across Europe,
which are then added up to make yearly °C
temperature sums (Eurostat, 2019).
To control for differences in mac-
roeconomic conditions across the EU
countries, two additional datasets from the
World Bank and World Inequality Data-
base were included.
The former dataset includes infor-
mation on national GDP per capita (in
thousands of U.S. dollars) and the unem-
ployment rate from 1960 to 2019, while
the latter captures income inequality by
measuring the bottom 50% share of total
national income from 2004–2019.
A few weaknesses in the data sources
need to be acknowledged. First, while most
studies have used household-level micro-
data in their analysis of energy poverty, I
used individual Member States as the unit
of analysis, which means that the maximum
yearly sample size is 28.2 Nevertheless, this
approach is in line with the objective of the
analysis to uncover patterns across Member
States as a whole. I also supplemented my
macroanalysis with a case study on Spanish
households using micro-level panel data,
presented in Section V. Second, the EPOV
energy poverty indicators are based on the
consensual-based European Union Sta-
tistics on Income and Living Conditions
(EU-SILC) survey microdata that rely on
households’
self-reported
assessments,
which has received some criticism in the lit-
erature (Thomson et al., 2020). However, it
is difficult to think of other ways to go about
gathering the more qualitative data, such as
a household’s inability to keep warm, that
are not completely exempt of methodologi-
cal problems either. Further, the EPOV has
included a methodology guidebook on their
website which details the measures they
took to ensure full compliance with Eurostat
rules (Thomson et al., 2020). Finally, since
the main EPOV energy poverty indicators
only cover the period from 2004–2019, the
regression analysis was limited to this time
period, even though there is temperature
and macro data dating back to the 1970s.
Data for the percentage of the population
with access to heating and cooling were only
available for the year 2007, which means
that these two variables are time-invariant.
For this reason, they were omitted from the
regression models where fixed-effects were
added.3

in combination, according to equation

As an initial exploration of the differ-
ences in climate and characteristics of ener-
gy poverty across the EU, Table 2 reports
average CDD and HDD statistics, the pop-
ulation percentage unable to keep warm,
and energy poverty index by country. The
means confirm the paradox involving EU
members in the Mediterranean Basin: even
though winters are milder in Southern
Member States such as Cyprus, Portugal,
and Greece, households in these countries
consistently report higher percentages of
people who are unable to stay warm in their
home (Bouzarovski & Herrero, 2017). This
phenomenon is shown more clearly in Fig-
ures 2A and 2B, where the number of HDD
is highest in the Scandinavian and North-

Southern and Eastern European countries,
yet the opposite is true for the percentage of
households unable to keep warm.
A country's level of
income inequality seems
to be a huge predictor
of energy poverty
prevalence.
Additionally, one can see that energy
poverty levels are by far the highest in pre-
viously socialist states such as Bulgaria, Lat-
via, and Lithuania. This can be attributed to
the legacies of the centrally planned econ-
omy, including poor thermal insulation of
the housing stock and historically low en-
ergy prices (Fig. 1; Bouzarovski & Herrero,
2017). When these countries transitioned to
a market economy in the 1990s, energy tar-
iffs increased without accompanying social
welfare and energy-efficiency mechanisms,
which further exacerbated the problem
(Bouzarovski & Herrero, 2017).
Table 3 presents the correlation ma-
trix for central macroeconomic indicators
and energy poverty. As expected, GDP
per capita is highly inversely related to
both energy poverty and unemployment,
meaning that richer Member States tend
to have lower rates of both unemployment
and energy poverty-related issues. Also,
richer societies tend to have a more equal
distribution of income, with a higher share
of GDP going to the bottom 50% of the
population. Subsequently, a country’s level
of income inequality seems to be a huge
predictor of energy poverty prevalence —
the two are highly inversely related with a
correlation coefficient of -0.511.
In plotting average yearly unemploy-
ment rates and energy poverty in 2004–
2019 (Fig. 3), there is also strong evidence
for unemployment as a main driver of
energy poverty. In line with the literature,
the spike in unemployment following the
2008/9 economic recession drastically in-
creased energy poverty prevalence in Eu-
rope, especially in Portugal, Italy, Ireland,
Greece, and Spain (the PIIGS countries;
Halkos & Gkampoura, 2021). The gradual
drop in unemployment rate after peak-
ing at over 11% in 2013 is accompanied
by a similar drop in energy poverty rates,
suggesting that the two go hand-in-hand.
However, it seems that after the dramatic
spike in energy poverty rate from 6% in
2004 to 9% in 2005, energy poverty rate
did not decrease along with the unemploy-
ment rate in the years preceding the reces-
sion, suggesting that other factors might be
causing energy poverty to be sticky.
III. Empirical Model
I used a country-level approach and
regressed the energy poverty index on
cooling or heating degree days, macroeco-
nomic factors, and other relevant controls.
The general model was:

The dependent variable, yst, denotes
the energy poverty index as calculated by
(1) in Member State s and year t. In some
specifications, I also broke down the index
into its component parts and used either
inability to keep warm or arrears on utility
bills as the dependent variable. x(t-1)s is the in-
dependent variable of interest, either HDD
or CDD. I took degree days data from the
year before under the assumption that re-
spondents are thinking of their ability to pay
bills or comfort experienced in the months
leading to the survey, which could span the
previous year. z2007j is either the fraction of
the population with heating when the inde-
pendent variable is HDD or the fraction of
the population with air conditioning when
the independent variable is CDD. Similar-
ly, xt-1z2007s is the interaction term between
either HDD and heating or CDD and air
conditioning. Mst includes a vector of mac-
roeconomic controls, including the bottom
50% share of total national income (income
inequality), real GDP per capita, and un-
employment rate. Hst is a vector of housing
characteristics, including dwelling type and
Xrbanisation leYel. 7he Yectors γs and ǅt are
country and year fixed effects, respectively.
The former controls for unobservable vari-
ables that vary across countries but not over
time, such as national energy resources and
welfare policies, while the latter controls for
unobservable variables that vary across time
but not countries, such as oil shocks and
global recessions.
Some specifications also include
country-specific linear time trends, which
allow trends over time to differ across
countries. This is owing to the huge vari-
ation in development stage and economic
and political climate across different Mem-
ber States. For instance, we might expect
a steeper decline in those unable to keep
their houses warm for poorer Member
States compared to richer ones because
there is more potential for technological
progress in poorer countries.
As I discuss later, not all of these
controls are included in each specification.
My preferred specification includes both
country and year fixed effects but not time
trends. This is because time trends absorb
too much of the variation in the dependent
variables, leading to imprecise estimates
of the coefficients. For all of my models, I
used robust standard errors that are clus-
tered by country in order to eliminate the
possibility of heteroscedasticity, and I as-
signed weights to countries based on their
total population.
IV. Results
The main results for HDD and CDD on
energy poverty are presented in Tables 4
and 5, respectively. I provide four specifi-
cations to highlight the role played by the
control variables and fixed effects. In the
first column, neither interactions nor fixed
effects are included in the regressions. The
second column adds country fixed effects,
and the third column has both country and
year effects. The last column adds coun-
try-specific linear time trends.
The results show that the number of
HDD is not statistically associated with en-
ergy poverty but that the number of CDD
is consistently positively associated with
energy poverty. The CDD coefficients are
statistically significant below the 5% level
in every specification presented in Table 5,
except for specification 2. In my preferred
specification, which includes both country
and year effects (column 3), the results im-
ply that for every 100 °C sum increase in
CDD per year (which has a range of 0 to
812 °C/yr), mean energy poverty is expect-
ed to increase by an estimated 1.383%, all
other factors held constant. This result is
statistically significant at the 1% level.
Additionally, the increasing impor-
tance of household air conditioning is high-
lighted in Table 5. In column 1, the aircon
coefficient implies that a 1% increase in the
share of the population with air condition-
ing leads to an estimated 0.132% reduction
in energy poverty incidence. Moreover,
the interaction term between CDD and
aircon in column 3 suggests that for any
given number of CDD, a 1% increase in
household air conditioning reduces energy
poverty by a further 0.056%. Both results
are statistically significant at the 1% level.
However, the results for heating seem to
be less robust. Table 4 predicts that a 1%
increase in the share of population with
heating reduces energy poverty by 0.103%
(column 1), but once fixed effects are add-
ed, the interaction term between HDD and
heating is no longer significant (column 3).
As expected, controlling for coun-
try and year effects has a large impact on
estimated degree day effects. These fixed
effects control for unobserved differenc-
es across the Member States and across
time. Without these controls, the esti-
mated climate effect is biased upward;
the HDD coefficients drop from positive
to negative (albeit insignificantly), and
the CDD coefficient drops from 2.414
(column 1) to 1.383 when both fixed
effects are included (column 3). How-
ever, when country-specific time trends
are added (column 4), the coefficients
become imprecise, as they absorb too
much of the variation in the dependent
variable, which is reinforced by the ex-
tremely high adjusted R-squared value of
0.982 in both tables.
With regard to the macroeconomic
control variables, the results show that
many of them are significantly associated
with energy poverty (column 1) but have
insignificant effects once fixed effects are
added (column 3). Nevertheless, three
variables in particular stand out: house-
hold gas prices and the unemployment rate
are consistently positively associated with
energy poverty, especially for CDD, and
GDP per capita is significantly negatively
associated with energy poverty.
The main results using the preferred
specification (both country and time fixed
effects but no linear time trends) are pre-
sented in Table 6. I also include the results
when the composite energy poverty index
is broken down into its components, with
inability to keep warm (column 1) and ar-
rears on utility bills (columns 2 and 3) as
the dependent variables, respectively. The
regression tables showing the results of
the four different specifications for warm
and arrears can be found in Tables 4, 5,
and 6 in the Appendix.
The results in Table 6 are mostly ro-
bust across the three dependent variables.
The exception is the negative association
between HDD and both the inability
to keep warm and arrears on utility bills
(columns 1 and 2), which is significant at
the 10% level. This seems counterintui-
tive, since an increase in the number of
cold days should make it harder to stay
warm, not easier. Additionally, the inter-
action term between HDD and heating
is positively associated with both warm
and arrears and is significant at the 5%
level. Again, this is counterintuitive, as
it suggests that conditioning on HDD, an
increase in the share of households with
access to heating actually increases their
difficulty of keeping warm and paying
their utility bills on time. It is possible
that the Mediterranean Paradox is behind
some of these counterintuitive estimates,
but it is also likely that some important
explanatory variables are missing from
the model and are therefore limiting our
ability to see the full picture.
The fact that the presence of damp,
leakage, or rot is significantly associated
with warm and arrears only when HDD,
and not CDD, is concerned highlights
the importance of the energy efficien-
cy of the home during the cold winter
months. Additionally, the larger associa-
tion with warm than with arrears (where

a 1% increase in the presence of housing
problems is predicted to increase the
share of households unable to keep warm
by 0.274% compared to only 0.0458% for

utility bills) implies that households with
inefficient, poorly insulated homes find it
especially difficult to stay warm, even if

V. Conclusion
This paper has sought to investigate the
link between the climate crisis and energy
poverty in the EU against a backdrop of
existing regional spatial inequalities and
the ongoing energy transition. My theo-
retical approach has identified some of the
key dimensions that link climate change
and energy poverty: the need to position
increasing average temperatures and its
effect on overall energy poverty within
the context of existing patterns of uneven
geographic and economic conditions,
while keeping in mind the important role
that renewable energy policies play in
exacerbating existing or creating new dis-
parities. The empirical model has involved
regressing degree-days temperature data
on a multidimensional energy poverty
indicator and a vector of controls over
time and states to (1) uncover the aggre-
gate effect of a warming climate on energy
poverty incidence and (2) understand the
complex macro-scale spatial patterns of
energy poverty and how they relate to
wider disparities within the EU.
In relation to the first aim of the
study, a cross-country and time series anal-
ysis of Eurostat data showed that higher
average temperatures and more frequent
heat waves have increased the overall
share of energy-poor households across all
EU Member States and that this trend will
likely continue in the absence of targeted
policy intervention.
Addressing the second aim of the
study, the results support the findings of
previous studies by showing that there
is a clear regional and economic division
between the Northern and Southern EU
countries that is similarly reflected in
terms of an energy divide. In the colder
but well-off North, income inequality and
unemployment rates are lower, a higher
percentage of the population have access
to heating and air conditioning, and as
a result, energy poverty rates are much
lower. On the other hand, the warmer but
poorer South experiences a much higher
rate of energy poverty and population per-
centage that is unable to keep warm in the
winter; this is in part due to the legacies of
socialism, the 2008/9 economic recession,
and the low efficiency and quality of the
housing stock.
The results do not indicate that the
ongoing energy transition is having any
There is a need for greater general awareness
of the phenomenon of energy poverty at both
the national and international levels, as well as
recognition of the importance of implementing
policies that directly address energy poverty in the
context of a changing climate.
significant effect on energy poverty levels
in the EU as a whole, but there is reason
to suggest that they have or will have im-
portant impacts on regional inequalities
for individual Member States, given the
speed and direction in which the EU is
moving in this arena. This highlights a
need for more research into how specific
renewable energy policies and projects
are impacting energy poverty and overall
welfare levels in individual EU countries.
This also shows a general necessity to
acknowledge the energy poverty risks
associated with a long-term transition
towards a decarbonised future and the
necessary steps needed to overcome them.
Nevertheless, this paper serves as a
starting point in examining the relation-
ship between climate change and energy
poverty at the regional level. Further anal-
ysis could be done in other contexts, espe-
cially those in the global South that will be
hardest hit by climate change, to inform
a wider range of policy and development
projects. To this end, there is a need for
greater general awareness of the phenome-
non of energy poverty at both the national
and international levels, as well as recog-
nition of the importance of implementing
policies that directly address energy pover-
ty in the context of a changing climate. ◆

Abstract
Under the double oppression of the U.S.’ neocolonial occupation and the South Korean
state’s neo-Confucian patriarchy, Korean women experience an alienation from their
own bodies, becoming objects of sexual production. Although this is an issue that is
written about passionately within the banmi, or anti-American literary genre, it is an
issue that is often categorized under the greater narrative of national liberation from
U.S. forces. This male-centered utilization of female suffering is unfortunately also a
part of South Korea’s double colonialism.
Oh Jung-Hee’s Junggugingeori, a novella that delivers its anti-American criticism
indirectly through metaphors and juxtaposition, is uninterested in metaphorizing the
female experience to merely become a pawn in the drive towards a male-centered de-
colonization. Instead, Junggugingeori simultaneously criticizes the U.S. and the South
Korean state through the depiction of female characters’ suffering and resistance against
the double oppression of patriarchy and neocolonialism, partaking in the banmi literary
movement without offering the female experience up for male exploitation.
The purpose of this project is to examine how Junggugingeori portrays its protag-
onists’ individual bodily resistance to double colonialism. I propose that Oh portrays
resistance against the joint forces of patriarchy and U.S. neocolonial oppression through
the juxtaposition of the narrator’s witnessing of the sexualized violence that the adult
women in her life are forced to suffer with her own private and seemingly unrelated
physical resistance against her body.

act as props to expose and criticize the

Two state projects are key to under-
standing the double colonization of South
Korean women. First, in the years follow-
ing the Korean War, the South Korean
state invested in strengthening the patriar-

stripping women of wartime bread-win-

producers and home-makers to create
workers for the new nation (S. Moon 2).
Second, the Korean government legally
endorsed official sex workers to work for
U.S. G.I.s, establishing an otherwise illegal
prostitution industry for the U.S. military
(K. Moon 29-39). These measures created
a legal system in which Korean women’s
bodies could be utilized for the pleasure of
men, both Korean and American.

Finding a Space to Re-
belong: Resistance and
Protest Through the Body
The juxtaposition of feigned nonchalance
and the body divulging resistance
In Junggugingeori, the adult female char-
acters, Mother and Maegi, represent to
the young narrator the existing models of
womanhood that a girl may aspire to be in
South Korea. The narrator’s mother fulfills
her role as a sexual reproducer, endlessly
giving birth to children, and Maegi, a
young woman renting a room in the narra-
tor’s friend Chi Ok’s home, fulfills her role
in the larger national system that utilizes
women to satisfy U.S. military soldiers
through sexual labor (K. Moon 152). The
narrator frequently describes her mother
and Maegi in death-like, death-imitating,
or death-desiring states, weathered and
exhausted by their unbelonging to their
own bodies. In these states, as Spivak says,
the subaltern woman cannot speak. Even if
and when she speaks, she cannot offer her-
self in a way in which she is heard. What
results is, as the narrator describes of her
mother and Maegi, a shell of a human be-
ing, unable to resist and deadened.
The narrator interprets her mother
and Maegi’s lifeless lives as a future that
will irrefutably be hers. The narrator at-
tempts to resist this by resisting the site of
oppression: her own body. Her resistance,
materializing as an aversion to and a re-
jection of the maturation of her own body
into an adult female’s sexually reproductive
one, reads as her resentment of her body as
the root cause of her pre-determined fate.
Rather than allow the process of sexual la-
bor to alienate her from her own body, the
narrator rejects her body first, disallowing
any external force from having the power
to alienate her from herself. The narrator
masks her resistance against her own body
as growing pains, separated from her ob-
servations of the bodily labor her mother
and Maegi perform. Even the scenes in
which the narrator observes the ways in
which her mother and Maegi’s lives are
marked by their existence as sexual objects
only last a few sentences at most, often
reported in conjunction with surrounding
sounds or movements to further downplay
their significance. The narrator moves on
quickly from such moments and offers the
reader only her most unemotional and
detached observations. This uninterested
attitude seems to reduce the women even
further to the physical function of their fe-
male bodies — specifically, the body’s sex-
ual and reproductive potential. However,
the narrator’s nonchalant facade is inter-
rupted as Oh chooses to juxtapose scenes
in which the narrator witnesses the vio-
lence of sexual labor with scenes in which
the narrator is rejecting her own body. In
placing the narrator’s verbal nonchalance
alongside her visceral non-verbal reactions
to witnessing her mother and Maegi’s lives
of endless sexual labor, Oh ensures that the
reader senses the narrator’s apathy is an
effort to separate herself from her own in-
evitable female future of losing her body to
the structures of society. These sequential
but dissociated scenes may be read togeth-
er as such to unveil how they complement
and inform each other.
The final scene of the novella, when
the narrator’s mother gives birth to her
eighth child, is one such instance in which
the juxtaposition of two scenes unveils the
narrator’s resistance against the double col-
onization of the female body. Even though
the narrator hears her mother screaming
from labor, she proceeds about her day in a
seemingly unrelated manner:

their bloodsucking bites. Like bedbugs, the
parasitic presence of U.S. troops in South
Korea infiltrates the intimate space that
is the woman’s body, as U.S. G.I.s literally
get in bed with female sex workers. Here,
the bed is the very site of the nexus of the
invasion of the female body. The harmful
consequences of the U.S. presence is thus
revealed through the physical experience of
the body, much like the physical experience
of bedbugs’ bites on the body.9
The metaphor of the U.S. military as
a parasite reveals the connection between
the dehumanizing fate of women in Korea
to the narrator’s physical protest against
this loss of bodily autonomy. The fact that
the narrator fights bedbugs off her own
body during her sleep suggests again to the
reader that despite the narrator’s seeming
lack of concern for Maegi’s depressed state
or her eventual death, in reality, the narra-
tor is deeply affected by it. Her lack of con-
cern is an attempt to distance herself from
the woman’s fate of sexual labor, just as she
tries to do when her mother gives birth.
Most of the narrator’s descriptions of Mae-
gi are of her during the daytime when she
is off work, when she is lifeless and dull,
lying all day completely under her covers
and never once speaking to the narrator.
Though the narrator’s interactions with
Maegi are limited as such, in the narrator’s
sleep, a subconscious state, she fights the
bedbugs that represent the U.S. military
and their exploitation of sex workers, a
phenomenon she sees through Maegi’s
life. She imagines that she is fighting the
bedbugs “with poised nails” in an attacking
position rather than in a limp and uncon-
scious drowsiness, revealing that even in
her sleep, the narrator is actively attempt-
ing to ward the bugs away. That the bed-
bugs attack the body in its most vulnerable
state, in the dark, during sleep, reveals
why even in her sleep, the narrator must
maintain an attacking position, wary of
the problem of bedbugs, the pest has seemed to return to Korea through the U.S. A 2008 study on the re-emergence of bedbugs in
South Korea examined how after two decades of no reports of bedbugs, a woman who had arrived to Korea from New Jersey, USA
brought back the pest into Seoul. See: Lee, In-Yong et al. “Reemergence of the bedbug Cimex lectularius in Seoul, Korea.”
the domination of her body. If the bedbugs
represent the U.S. military, Oh is underlin-
ing the intimate and pervasive violence of
the U.S. military, leaving the female body
unable to rest alone, even in sleep.
Conclusion
I conceive of feminist resistance within the
Korean context as one that takes shapes
in clusters due to the fragmented nature
of women’s positionality within a doubly
oppressive environment. In resisting an
oppressive system, Junggugingeori’s narra-
tor uses the tools with which she is left to
resist through her individual body, even
against her own body. Change happens
whether or not external viewers believe in
it or are disappointed in it, as “resistance
is effective in that it produces a new real-
ity, a new condition from which to resist”
(Tuck and Yang 13). Maria Lugones argues
similarly for small-scale and non-public re-
sistance: resistance, often “expressing itself
infra-politically,” is not the end or goal of
political struggle, but rather the beginning
(746). These scholars show the multiplici-
ty of resistance within systems that do not
accommodate ‘others,’ underlining the ways
in which we must challenge the notion that
resistance is limited to the dramatic, public,
and visible domains. Though the lonely re-
sistance of Junggugingeori’s narrator may feel
merely like a pyrrhic victory, we can become
witnesses to the narrator’s seemingly invisi-
ble resistance if we make a “commitment to
“The feminist anti-American resistance portrayed in
Junggugingeori extends beyond literature and its history to
the non-literary politics of today’s South Korea.”
interpret [her] experience ‘against the grain
of power’” (Cruz, 2010, 7).
Importantly, the feminist anti-Amer-
ican resistance portrayed in Junggugingeori
extends beyond literature and its history
to the non-literary politics of today’s South
Korea. This paper highlights the neglect-
ed radical feminist resistance within an-
ti-American literature to emphasize that the
integration of women in anti-imperialist
political spaces in South Korea has already
been imagined and articulated. Though
this paper focuses on just one text in one
country in one short snippet of time, I have
written with the hope of transnational and
multiracial coalitions of resistance in mind.
In bridging together Gayatri Spivak, Ketu
Katrak, Cindy Cruz, etc. with feminist re-
sistance in Korean literature, I underscore
how the oppressions women face follow
similar patterns, surfacing in familiar logics.
Accordingly, to imagine that the individual
resistances revealed in Junggugingeori are
only Korean would be a shortcoming. As I
have attempted to show through a diversity
of sources, these methods of resistance have
sustained women of all kinds in varying
oppressive situations. We must read the
resistance of women against imperialism
as a legacy of work that must continue as
the problems of double colonialism con-
tinue, whether in their original or newfan-
gled forms. Although my essay highlights
a double colonialism that predates the
wealthy, globalized, technology-driven,
COVID-fighting, K-Pop making, so-called
“first-world” nation that South Korea is
today, the problems outlined within the
text have remained painfully with Korean
women. For example, the double colonial-
ism, previously geographically contained
within South Korea in my two texts, has
extended abroad, whether it be through the
direct international marriages between U.S.
G.I.s and former South Korean sex workers
or through the diaspora of Korean wom-
en who have immigrated to the U.S. Both
groups of Korean women have been and
continue to be subjected to the intersecting
oppressions of racialization, sexualization,
familial expectations, etc., rooted in the
double colonialism that originated within
the neo-Confucian patriarchy and U.S.
neocolonialism and its camptowns. It is also
important to think about the ways in which
Korean women have learned to oppress oth-
ers and each other, born out of the mentality
of patriarchy and of being colonized. Thus,
although the resistance of Junggugingeori’s
narrator may not necessarily need to be rep-
licated exactly today, these literatures and
their characters allow us Korean women to
belong to a long genealogy, whether imag-
ined into life through literature or written
into history through literature, of resisting
women. Indeed, Junggugingeori, written and
published during a time in which the South
Korean state and the occupying U.S. ren-
dered any potential anti-Americanism as a
threat, is, in and of itself, a resistance against
double colonialism.
In writing this paper, I hope to have
produced a small portion of knowledge,
courage, and a feeling of persistent legacy
that contributes to the history of Korean
feminist resistance against imperialism.
However, as Korean women, we are not
alone in this resistance. As we continue
to form coalitions with others who are
forging their own paths of decolonial re-
sistance, the resistance work we do will
flourish in the end. Together, from all
our different corners in the world, we are
imagining, building, and living a decolonial
futurity that dreams of the emancipation
of all peoples. Eventually, I believe that the
systems that oppress us will collapse under
our collective work. ◆

s one of the most prestigious research institutions in the United States, Northwest-
ern University (NU) is known to attract many students interested in conducting
some form of research during their undergraduate careers. Whether it takes place in
laboratories, dance studios, libraries, or online, student research life is notably vibrant on
the NU campus.
Among the many support systems in place to assist students in their pursuits, the
Office of Undergraduate Research (OUR) is the first stop that students should visit as
they begin their research journeys. Simply from their weekly newsletters and numerous
video series, one can tell that the OUR is nothing like the stereotypical college office that
any prospective student may imagine, but is instead an inviting place filled with spirited
and passionate advisors committed to helping students in any way possible to achieve
their research dreams.
One of the most prominent questions that surrounded the return to campus this year
was how different things would be as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. Concerns about
COVID-19 have dictated many changes to the way in which people live their lives, and it
is no surprise that the world of research has been affected as well. For the past two years,
COVID-19 restrictions have prevented students from pursuing research exactly according
to plan, especially in disciplines that require travel or in-person experimentation.
We had the pleasure of speaking to Outreach Coordinator and OUR Advisor Dia-
mond Jones, who also happens to be a recent graduate of NU. Regarding the effects that
COVID-19 has had on student research, Jones says that the OUR has made tremendous
efforts to mitigate as many COVID-19 related issues as possible.
Most grants that the OUR provides now have COVID-19 stipulations, meaning that
students must demonstrate a plan to continue their proposed research amidst anything
unexpected that may hinder their original ideas. The benefit of this additional policy is
that it allows students to think ahead so that “even if their perfect project can’t come to
fruition, they’re still not barred from using [the OUR’s] systems and money and making
their dreams come true.”

demic. However, she assures students that the OUR

Abigail Adams: Creating
a Literary, Pseudo-Public
Sphere
Adams employs literary performativity
not only to envision herself as occupying
roles that had traditionally corresponded
with republicanism, masculinity, and the
public sphere, but she does so in a way that
allows her to circumvent the Stoical narra-
tive of a modest and selfless entrance into
public service. By creating her own liter-
ary, pseudo-public sphere, Adams could
bypass the tenets of Stoical republicanism
and thus more directly and unabashedly
insert her voice into the public canon.
Engaging in a performance of any kind
requires the process of world building,
which includes establishing the rules of
the world by setting up the permissions. In
Adams’s epistolary correspondence with
Warren, she uses the pen name Portia to
establish that she is employing literary
performativity and to communicate a
sense of theatrical and literary permission.
Adams uses her Roman matron signature
to signal that, in her epistolary world, she
is capable of linguistically moving between
classical and contemporary roles, an action
that I will term “body hopping.” By com-
paring Adams’s April 10, 1776, letter to
John Adams with her April 13, 1776, letter
to Warren — two letters in which Adams
quotes the same passage in Shakespeare’s
The Tragedy of Julius Caesar — I will illu-
minate exactly what makes Adams’s and
Warren’s female-female correspondence

Adams pens letters to her husband on

the Battle of Bunker Hill and became known

oration by Mr. Morton” in which Warren’s
death was used to incite a recommitment to
the patriot cause, as the “heroic virtues of
the disceased” and “the noble cause to which
he fell a Martir” was very fresh in “the minds
of the Audience.”15 Adams uses a simile, re-

before their Eyes,” and then transcribes an
abridged version of Mark Antony’s solil-

play, The Tragedy of Julius Caesar, in order to
depict General Warren’s wounds:

By explicitly mentioning Caesar in her
letter to John Adams, Adams contextual-
izes the quote within Shakespeare’s play.
In The Tragedy of Julius Caesar, Brutus
and Cassius are worried by Caesar’s love
of power and his ambition to “turn the
republic into a dictatorship.”17 As a result,
they, along with some other conspira-
tors, assassinate Caesar by stabbing him
to death in order to “save Rome from
tyranny.”18 While Joseph Warren and
Caesar represent opposite agendas, the
former for liberation and the latter for
despotism, both become significant cata-
lysts that garner public support for their
respective causes in death. In order to
illustrate this parallel, Adams talks about
Morton’s eulogy directly prior to this
quote in order to assign Mark Antony’s
speech to Morton, consequently adapt-
ing Mark Antony’s statement of “Shall
cumber all parts of Italy” to “Shall cumber
all parts of Britton.”19 In fact, Morton’s
eulogy contains several parallels in both
vocabulary and imagery to this quote. For
instance, similar to how Mark Antony’s
quote uses a simile to transform Caesar’s
wounds into lips for his dead body to
speak, Morton revitalizes the voice of
the deceased General Warren when he
proclaims, “Ought we not to listen to
the Voice of our slaughtered Brethren,
who are now proclaiming aloud to their
Country.”20 Additionally, Mark Antony
exclaims, “Woe to the Hands that shed this
costly blood,” and Morton also uses hands
as a synecdoche for the enemy when he
says, “The Hand of British Tyranny!”21
Therefore, Adams’s letters to her husband
contextualize both Warren’s funeral and
the quote from Julius Caesar, overlapping
the former onto the latter in order to
place Morton, the orator, as the deliverer
of Mark Antony’s lines and highlight the
similarities between Caesar’s Civil War
and the American Revolution.
Alternatively, in Adams’s letter to
Warren on April 13, 1776, she decontex-
tualizes Joseph Warren’s funeral as well as
the Mark Antony quote in order to place
herself in the public, masculine roles of a
modern orator and a classical oracle. After
Adams discusses her new household re-
sponsibilities, she begins a new paragraph
in which she briefly mentions the passing
of a mutual, unnamed friend (which her
letters to John Adams identify as Warren)
with the line, “I have been much gratified
with the respect shewn to the remains of
our worthy Friend. I hope and believe that
the orator exerted himself upon the occa-
sion — he had a fine field to display himself
in.”22 While Adams mentions the presence
of an orator at the funeral, she does not
name the orator like she does in her letter
to John Adams before quoting Mark Ant-
ony’s soliloquy. Adams transcribes a longer
excerpt from Mark Antony’s soliloquy
in Act III Scene I of Julius Caesar, starting
from the moment when Mark Antony sees
Caesar’s dead body:
O pardon me, thou bleeding piece of
Earth!
That I am meek and gentle with these

Adams’s letter to Warren distances the
passage from its Shakespearean origins,
as she does not put quotes around the
passage, whereas she does use quotation
marks in her letter to John Adams. Fur-
thermore, the additional lines from Mark
Antony’s soliloquy that she chooses to
include in her letter to Warren add the
first-person pronouns “me” and “I,” which
make the language appear to fall under her
penmanship and represent her perspective.
Through claiming Shakespeare’s language
as her own, Adams is able to carry out
a literary performance as the orator at
Warren’s funeral, a role that women did
not have access to in the 18th century.
Not only does Adams transform into an
orator, but her audience accordingly shifts
from her correspondent, Warren, to the
American people. By assuming this role,
Adams is rewriting history, transporting
herself into the public sphere to publicly
eulogize and memorialize one of the most
prominent male martyrs of the American
Revolution. Unlike the Shakespearean
context of Mark Antony speaking these
lines to Caesar with no one else on stage,
in this new context of Adams as the orator
of this quote, she is speaking to the public
about how “brave a Man” Joseph Warren
was, asserting her loyalty to the General
and, ultimately, to the patriotic cause.
However, Adams does not stop
there. She uses the Roman roots of the
quote to body hop into the classical role
of an orator, granting herself another
position of masculine, public power. Ad-
ams explicitly takes on a prophetic tone
with the lines “Woe to [the] hand that
shed this costly Blood/Over thy Wounds
now do I prophesy,” but the following
parenthetical crucially reveals the source
of Adams’s oracular power. The simile of
“dumb mouths” with “Ruby lips” refers to
Warren’s bleeding wounds, portraying
these wounds as wanting to speak but
being unable to do so. Warren’s wounded
body “beg[s] the voice and utterance of a
Tongue,” or a spokesperson to speak on
his behalf. Thus, by framing this quote as
her own speech, Adams subsequently po-
sitions herself as the metaphorical “mouth”
of Joseph Warren, engaging in a clever
form of literary ventriloquism that gives
her the utmost level of contemporary and
classical authority in her epistolary public
sphere. As a modern orator and a classical
oracle figure who is authorized by War-
ren, Adams places a curse of “Domestick
fury and firce civil Strife” on Britain on his
behalf. Adams merges and blurs the private
and public spheres while simultaneously
blurring temporality by body hopping
between contemporary and classical roles.

Mercy Otis Warren:
Becoming a Sentimental,
Epistolary Playwright and
Historian
On one hand, it might appear that Warren
uses her epistolary correspondence not to
craft an alternate persona for herself but to
rather reaffirm her already existing public
authorship, using letters as “the testing
ground for different models of historical
explanation, narrative technique, and
character sketches.”24 Warren’s corre-
spondents thoroughly admire her skill in
“mental portraiture,”25 and John Adams
describes her responsibility to “delineate
Caracters” as one belonging to a “faithfull
Historian,” since “the public is so interested
in public Characters” that “it becomes the
Duty of every good Citizen who happens
to be acquainted with them to communi-
cate his Knowledge.”26 However, on the
other hand, Warren’s choice to identify
under her public roles as a playwright and
historian in her private, epistolary corre-
spondence to Adams accentuates that there
was something different that letter-writing
under these personas supplied her with.
When viewed from such a lens, Warren
uses letter writing to better actualize her
roles as a playwright and historian because
she is free to carry out her own sentimen-
tal philosophy and create portraits of real,
contemporary, female characters. War-
ren’s most prominent public plays, The Ad-
ulateur (1772), The Defeat (1773), and The
Group (1775), as well as her book, History
of the Rise, Progress, and Termination of the
American Revolution (1805), reflect on and
recount the American Revolution through
numerous allusions to Roman antiquity.27
For instance, in The Adulateur, Warren
names the revolutionary leaders and pa-
triots Brutus, Cassius, Junius, Portius, and
Marcus, who are “well-known and adored
heroes of the Roman Republic,” in order
to promote the revolutionary message of
expelling tyranny and restoring liberty.28
This apparent dichotomy between the
classical Stoicism of Warren’s published
works and the modern sentimentalism of
her epistolary correspondence with Adams
becomes more decipherable when think-
ing about the demographic that is rep-
resented in her public works: men. In all
three of these plays, every single character
is a man, as Warren uses “a cluster of Ro-
man republican heroes,” who are all men,
to embody public leaders in the American
Revolution, who are also all men.29 Simi-
larly, in Warren’s History, she only creates
literary portraits of public male figures,
such as her sections on the “character of
Mr. Hutchinson” and the “characters of
Samuel Adams and John Hancock.”30 In

the public sphere, unlike in the epistolary
sphere, Warren cannot renounce the tra-
ditionally male-dominated use of exemplar
theory. Her public roles as a playwright
and historian are constrained by the public
sphere’s perpetuation of its inextricable
link to republican Stoicism, patriotism,
virtue, and masculinity.31 Consequently,
Warren’s public works adhere to this same
classical, Stoical language of the masculine
public sphere. Nevertheless, Warren’s
private epistolary correspondence with
Adams enables her to modernize virtue in
the form of sentimentalism and ironically
actualize her public roles by playwriting
and history chronicling about contempo-
rary females for a female companion.
In her letters with Adams, Warren
first uses her new sentimental, epistolary
perspective as a playwright and histori-
an in order to bring to the forefront the
possibility that history’s classical models
may not be appropriate paragons for the
present. Warren explicitly narrates an
epistolary tonal shift that mirrors the
philosophical transition from Stoicism
to sentimentalism when she says, “I must
speedily descend from the Altitudes of
Heroism, and talk in the simple stile of the
Manufacturer and the Humbler Language
of the Domestic Dame: who seeketh Wool
and Flax and Worketh Willingly with her
hands.”32 Warren associates the “Altitudes
of Heroism” with Adams’s rhetorical strat-
egy of using her letters as a mode of classi-
cal, republican, and Stoical performativity.
Notably, Warren refrains from creating a
character portrait but rather uses the de-
scription of the “Altitudes of Heroism” to
represent Stoicism as an intangible, lofty,
and glorified public ideal that she wants to
leave in the past.
Warren then alternatively uses her
new epistolary role as a playwright and
historian to give voice to modern, female
characters, such as the private “Domestic
Dame,” treating the real world as her met-
aphorical stage. Warren uses language that
evokes vertical movement with the words
“descend” and “Altitudes,” building off of
the spatial dichotomy that she establishes
in her October 1776 letter between “sub-
lime qualities” and “Terest[r]ial” bonds,
in order to position the character of the
“Domestic Dame” as a foil to republican
Stoicism and antiquity. Warren highlights
how this persona requires a “descent” away
from past Roman fantasies and towards a
pragmatic contemporaneity grounded in
private domesticity and sentimentalism.
Furthermore, Warren updates this mod-
ern, female classification of the “Domestic
Dame” to reflect the present revolutionary
circumstances, as these women’s roles in
the late 18th century changed in response
to men’s shifting roles. Warren reveals that
this domestic classification is no longer
distinct from the role of “the Manufactur-
er,” since a housewife “seeketh Wool and
Flax” and also “Worketh Willingly with
her hands.” Since men were now “Wading
in the Field of Blood,” women needed to
enter the public sphere as manufacturers
in order to secure necessary materials for

appear to contradict her shift from classical
Stoicism to contemporary sentimentalism,
she substitutes the word “League” with
“Ladies,” modernizing the language to cre-

of female leaders rather than an ancient
council of men. Instead of fixating on the
past, Warren updates this classical term to
reflect a present classification of women,
showing how female manufacturers were
in an influential position to spur on a new,
modern lineage of female exemplars.
Thus, not only is Warren able to use
her epistolary roles as a playwright and
historian to overturn exemplar history,
but just like with patriotism and virtue,
Warren detaches this methodology from
its republican, Stoical, and masculine
roots, repurposing it to highlight a female
historical canon. Warren even explicitly
uses the word “Example,” not to focus on
imitating virtues from the past and ob-
serving masculine historical paradigms,
but rather to pose a new virtuous example
that is grounded both in the present and in
women. Finally, instead of using the words
“Look up” to continue the vertical, spatial
visualization of Stoical, Roman matrons as
an antiquated ideal to which women should
aspire, she replaces this ideal with the fu-
ture-oriented exemplar of the modern, fe-
male manufacturer. Therefore, while Ad-
ams’s letters strategically employ epistolary
performativity, Warren’s letters acknowl-
edge Adams’s literary world-building but
do not rhetorically position Warren as
occupying the role of a performer. Warren
complicates the idea of literary performa-
tivity by assuming the persona of a play-
wright and historian, two roles consistent
with her actual roles in the public sphere,
rather than embodying a character that is
located outside of her own sense of self. By
situating the roles of a playwright and his-
torian, occupations inherently tied to the
public sphere, within the private epistolary
sphere, Warren creates a space for herself
to criticize self-abnegation and classical
allusions. The epistolary sphere ironically
allows Warren to fully actualize her iden-
tity as a playwright and historian, opening
her eyes to these public roles’ potential to
capture the nuanced and constantly evolv-
ing classifications of modern-day women.
Through her epistolary correspondence
with Adams, Warrens taps into her new
historical and literary voices, paving the
way for a modernized use of the exemplar
theory of history that originates with the
female paragons of the present rather than
the Roman matrons of the past. Warren’s

Conclusion
As I argued in my introduction, just
because scholars have remembered the
“Remember the Ladies” letter, it does not
mean that we have properly remembered
and understood the literary legacies of
historical women like Abigail Adams and
Mercy Otis Warren. Examining Adams’s
and Warren’s 18th-century epistolary
correspondence as “Portia” and “Marcia”
through a literary perspective has served
to
complicate
historical
scholarship
by challenging the binary correlations
between women and the private sphere
and men and the public sphere. Through
her creation of a literary, pseudo-public
sphere, Adams transitions away from
historical parallels between antiquity and
contemporaneity, instead constructing her
own alternate reality as a means for her
to envision a world that is parallel to the
one in which she lived — in which she, as
a woman, has access to public positions of
political power. Warren’s private episto-
lary correspondence with Adams provided
“Warren ... moderniz[es] the language to create a new
contemporary portrait of a group of female leaders rather
than an ancient council of men.”
her with a new forum in which she could
explore her individual identity as a play-
wright and historian, liberating herself
from the republican, Stoical constraints
that these two roles possessed when
situated in the public sphere. Warren ac-
tualizes her individual, sentimental voice,
allowing her to use epistolary writing to
re-envision a public sphere in which she
can use her identity as a playwright and
historian to create literary characteriza-
tions of contemporary women. Adams and
Warren differed on exactly how to carve
out spaces for their historical and literary
voices, as Adams employs republican Sto-
icism and classical literary performativity,
while Warren employs sentimentalism
and a novel, modern adaptation of literary
performativity. Nevertheless, both women
ultimately rewrote the classical models of
republican Stoicism and the exemplar the-
ory of history. Adams’s letters to Warren
radically pushed the limits of epistolary
writing by envisioning an alternate ver-
sion of the public sphere, reimagining
the history of the American Revolution
entirely in order to grant women access
to the public sphere as well as public
positions of authority. Warren’s letters to
Adams created an alternate, female-ori-
ented literary lens to interpolate into the
historical documentation of the American
Revolution. I personally find hope in how
these two women, who lived within a re-
strictive and republican society, were able
to use epistolary writing as a tool to bridge
the literal spatial gap between them and to
figure out imaginative ways in which they
could bridge the public-propagated gap
between the private and public spheres.
Through complicating the relationship
between private and public spheres of
influence, Adams and Warren explore the
interconnected relationship between what
it means and should mean to have a public
voice as a woman in late 18th-century
America. ◆

Op-Ed: The Burgeoning
Academic Field of Existential Risk
by Manuel De Leon
T
he field of existential risk has grown rapidly in the last few years, with new research
organizations sprouting up all over the world. This work focuses on maintaining
humanity’s long-term potential by reducing the probability of catastrophic threats, such
as extreme climate change, nuclear winter, engineered pandemics, and unaligned artifi-
cial intelligence. While often disregarded by academics as fanciful or overly apocalyptic,
a brief glance at the literature shows that the risks we face in the next century are worth
further consideration. While the topic has not yet been widely discussed at Northwest-
ern University (NU), beginning steps have been taken towards researching existential
risk, and further initiative will hopefully be taken in the future to bring this important
subject to the forefront of research.
An existential risk is a risk that threatens the destruction of humanity’s long-term
potential.1 While mostly discussed in the context of extinction, this could also include
an unrecoverable collapse or dystopia. The stakes of such a catastrophe are literally
astronomical,2 not only harming the 7.8 billion people living now, but also foreclosing
the flourishing of all future generations. With so much at stake, thinkers in the dis-
cipline believe that even small reductions in the probability of existential risk would
generate massive expected value. This research has been undergirded by a philosophy
of longtermism,3 which argues that if one wants to do the most good, they should focus
on long time scales, perhaps thousands or millions of years into the future. Even if one
only examines impacts to people alive today, there seems to be a common-sense case4
for existential risk reduction. For instance, some in the field argue that the risk of
human extinction over the next century is around one in six,5 which could have
major implications within our lifetimes.
While pressing, many of these concerns are severely neglected in research
when compared with other, perhaps less threatening concerns (Fig. 1).
This lack of attention stems from an intuition that existential risks are
far-fetched. For instance, in the words of NU Economics Professor Scott

Ogawa, “Most of them are overblown.
… I think this idea of all life going out
is preposterous.”6 Once we look more closely,
though, it may be the case that this skepticality is the
work of cognitive biases. For instance, one must be wary
of the availability heuristic, a mental shortcut that assumes
something is important only if it can be readily recalled. Since
there have not been any catastrophes of this magnitude, these risks
are not salient to politicians and the public.7 Similarly, when the num-
bers become too large, people become numb to the effect of saving lives,
causing decision-makers to treat existential risks in a similar way to problems
that are less severe by many orders of magnitude.8
Fortunately, there are some strides being made at NU to address these risks.
For instance, in collaboration with Underwriters Laboratories, the University has
recently created the Center for Advancing Safety of Machine Intelligence9 in order to
lower the risk posed by emerging technologies. While progress has been granular, I am
optimistic about NU’s position in existential risk research and hope that more academics
