The Role of Habit in
Kafka’s “The Burrow” and
Proust’s Swann’s Way
by Nikol Kralimarkova
Department of Comparative Literary Studies
Faculty Adviser: Prof. Samuel Weber, Ph.D.
Across numerous fields of life, from psy-
chology through philosophy to literature,
habitude has been studied and reimagined
for centuries. Psychologically, a habit is
an energy-efficient behavioral response
to any repetitive context, a preservative
drive across living creatures, from humans
to animals. The term is synonymous with
automaticity, suggesting the learned exe-
cution of the behavior without involving
higher mental processes (Wood and
Rünger 291). Normally, habit functions
in parallel with a goal system, and the
frequency of repetition infers the inten-
tionality of a given behavior (Wood and
Rünger 289). Towards the end of the 19th
century, habit was explored as a pattern
across species and cultures. William
James, considered the father of American
psychology, famously studies habit in The
Principles of Psychology (1890), noting that
living creatures are first and foremost seen
as “bundles of habits” (James). James also
describes distinctions of habit as either an
innate tendency or instinct, or, if resulting
from education, “an act of reason” (James).
Further, external factors are shown to
affect the balance between habit and
goal-oriented behavior, with stress and
distraction suppressing decision making
and promoting reliance on habit (Wood
and Dennis 301). Although habit is often
regarded as a psychological term regarding
common and necessary behavior in living
beings, humans especially, it also remains
a complex phenomenon, often problema-
tized across the fields. James identifies the
limitation of studying habit externally and
as an objective, observable process despite
the mental aspect remaining covert: “It
thus appears that habit covers a very large
part of life, and one engaged in studying
the objective manifestations of mind is
bound at the very outset to define clearly
Introduction
just what its limits are” (James). While
psychology ends where the limits of the
mind are set, literature can dilute these
boundaries in fiction and offer a more dis-
turbing account of habit. Two examples of
that tendency of literature, also the critical
objects of my analysis, are Franz Kafka’s
short story “The Burrow” and Marcel
Proust’s first of seven volumes of In Search
of Lost Time, Swann’s Way.
Kafka and Proust both belong to the
modernist literary movement of the late
19th to early 20th century. Although of-
ten regarded separately due to their dif-
ferent linguistic traditions, German and
French respectively, both writers’ styles
can be characterized with their rejection
of traditional literary forms, experiment-
ing with language and narration and di-
recting literature towards the subjective
experience of reality. With the rise of the
bourgeoisie and the separation of private
space — as sensory and habitual space —
from the public, the theme of interiority
and the interior grew too, inevitably fol-
lowed by the importance of habit(-build-
ing). This inward focus on habitude and
its implications can be traced in the two
selected texts, making them key literary
and fictional case studies of the phenom-
enon. The narrator in “The Burrow,” for
instance, presumably a mole-like crea-
ture, is situated in the confined space of
the burrow he inhabits, obsessively aim-
ing to fortify it against external enemies
through continual digging and inspection.
The story’s peculiar animal first-person
narrative lacks continuous introspec-
tion and portrays the subordination of
habit to anxiety and the impossibility of
forceful habituation in the absence of a
feeling of safety. The visual landscape is
limited, further suggesting the mole-like
identity of the narrator, since moles are
blind. However, the auditory scene is
disrupted by the uncanny presence of an
unidentifiable sound, which sends him
on compulsive digging missions despite
the planned calculations he attempts and
always disrupts. The descriptive and dis-
continuous nature of the first-person nar-
rative further questions the perspective of
the narrator as external to himself, as he
reports habitual actions without being
able to reflect on them (Türk 152). The
discontinuity in conscious memory due
to the effects of habit is also illustrated in
Swann’s Way, the first volume of Proust’s
novel, in which the narrator Marcel is still
a child preoccupied with the feeling of
abandonment when his mother does not
kiss him goodnight during a dinner with
their friend Swann. The negative expe-
rience initially creates, similarly to “The
Burrow,” discontinuity in the first-person
narration (Türk 148). Although all seven
volumes are in the first person, the sec-
ond section of Swann’s Way, “Swann in
Love,” describing Swann’s problematic
romantic relationship with Odette, is ex-
clusively in the third person and disrupts
the narrator’s habitual mode. Swann, “the
While psychology ends where the limits of the mind are
set, literature can dilute these boundaries in fiction and
offer a more disturbing account of habit.
unconscious author of [the narrator’s]
sufferings,” and his role in the narrator’s
development thus push the boy to over-
come, or at least substitute, the habit of
his mother’s past presence (Proust 756).
In this light, habit is transformed from a
potentially painful and anxious experience
into a productive temporal medium upon
which the narrator’s imaginative, isolated
impressions of his familiar surroundings
can be created. To study the role of habit
in both texts, I will first briefly explore
how its spatial dimension relates to the
narratives and will then progress into
temporal analysis of habit as repetition
and discontinuity (of the narrative) in the
modes of anxiety or positive imagination
as a form of escapism.
(Subjective Experience of the)
Spatial Dimension of Habit
The familiar physical space of the narrators
in “The Burrow” and Swann’s Way makes
up the habitual landscape, but to position
oneself in space, sensory input from the
environment is key. Thus, the perception
of (the self in) the landscape and its sta-
bility need to be characterized in order to
introduce disruptions that problematize the
effects of habit. For the narrator in “The
Burrow,” the burrow is what he proclaims
as his “own house,” but the origin and loca-
tion of the place, as well as its exact relation
to the narrator, remain unclear (Kafka 163).
The German title of the short story is “Der
Bau,” which only means “building” since the
article only indicates the gender of the noun
and is not necessarily a definite article. The
phrase does not point to a specific building
or burrow (because a building is normally to
be found above the ground) to refer to as the
narrator’s home. Apart from the numerous
chambers he builds and modifies ceaselessly,
the auditory cues — rather their absence —
shape the narrator’s habitat: “The best thing
about my burrow is the silence; of course
this is deceptive, at any time the silence can
suddenly be shattered, … but at present, it
is still there” (Kafka 164). Even though the
narrator somewhat eagerly recognizes the
impermanence of the silence of the burrow,
he praises that negative state of the burrow
as ultimate and assumes it as the baseline
habitual environment. Nevertheless, even
in the opening pages of the story, the nar-
rator continues to describe his environment
rather carelessly: “I can hear nothing but the
occasional rustling of some lesser creature …
otherwise everything is quiet’’ (Kafka 164).
Although the described uncertain “rustling”
does not provide any certainty about the
nature of the sound or creature, it appears
that the silence is not at all absolute, and the
narrator’s reaffirmation that “everything”
is quiet is already refuted by his previous
report. Despite his controversial statements,
the narrator still discerns intruding sounds
from his desired regular, quiet, auditory
landscape that would maintain his peace. It
appears that the narrator is already trying to
impose a certain vision of what the burrow
[H]abit is
transformed from
a potentially
painful and anxious
experience into a
productive temporal
medium.
should feel and sound like, and the contra-
dictions he presents germinate his sense of
insecurity and anxiety.1
Similarly, the narrator in Swann’s Way
has a well-defined scenery of his room, which
is disturbed by the colorful magic lantern that
is placed on top of his lamp to entertain him
in his mother’s absence: “But my sorrows
were only increased, because this change
of lighting destroyed, as nothing else could
have done, the customary impression I had
formed of my room” (Proust 145). It becomes
more obvious through Proust’s narrator that
the customary landscape is a subjective im-
pression, rather than a mere physical quality,
of the place. Before the magic lantern, Marcel
would habitually be sitting in his room in ag-
ony, far from his mother, facing “the torture
of having to go to bed in [the room]” (Proust
145). In this case, the stable “customary”
scenery is where anxiety nests. The narrator’s
initial encounter with the magic lantern is
overwhelming because of the abrupt change
of scenery, which resembles the Burrow-
man’s response to the change of sound. Be
it a state of sound or light, the constancy of
subjective perception, or habituation, is only
realized when confronted with change, such
as a foreign sound or color. However, unlike
the narrator in “The Burrow,” Marcel is upset
by habit, and its invasive destruction by the
magic lantern only offers him an alternative
form of escapist habitude. Knowing how the
characters position themselves in their space
makes possible the exploration of the various
temporal effects of habit in the occurrence of
disruptions of the context’s stability.
Temporality of Habit in Kafka
Once habit is formed, the habitual re-
sponse to the given contextual cues occurs
without making a decision to perform it,
1 In Freudian terms, anxiety defines what is considered dangerous, especially based on occurrence in the past and the anticipated
repetition in the future (Türk 145).
indicating that a mental representation
of the habitual response is taking place as
soon as the cues are perceived (Wood and
Rünger 292). This mechanism of habitual
response suggests immediate reaction
upon presentation of a cue, such as the
Burrowman’s uncontrollably repetitive
springing into action. As the abnormal
reaction overrides the imagined order and
comfort, the narrator phases into a state of
thoughtless, already automized, habit:
[U]sually after I have been startled out
of my sleep, it seems that the current
distribution of provisions is completely
wrong, that it can lead to great dangers,
and that immediately, in all haste,
without regard for sleepiness and
fatigue, the situation must be corrected;
then I hurry, then I fly, then I have no
time for calculations, I … arbitrarily
seize whatever lands between my teeth,
dragging, carrying, moaning, groaning,
stumbling, and any random change in
the present situation, which seems to
me so extremely dangerous, it the only
thing that will satisfy me (Kafka 166).
This passage is one of the many re-
peating episodes of senseless, perhaps
compulsive, behavior of the narrator
when presented with a danger — even a
potential one. The frequency of “usually”
indicates that an unidentified reason
startles him out of his sleep habitually,
and his thoughtless actions are a reflex —
an instinctive unconscious response. If
there is a real threat, then strangely, his
actions do not produce truly self-preser-
vatory behavior, such as fight-or-flight,
but rather a stagnating repetitive circu-
lar pattern. The fact that the situation
is repetitive and the narrator still does
not have a learned, and therefore more
structured, response indicates the ab-
sence of true habituation and feeling of
comfort and only a spontaneous desire
for such.
These observations are further sup-
ported by the first-person narrative in the
passage. While Stahman claims that the
first-person narrative is self-reflective in
the story, another scholar suggests that the
first person does not serve this role well
because the overall descriptive nature of
the narrative, with the observable actions
of the mole (“then I hurry, then I fly”),
would normally be associated with a third
person narrative (Stahman 20) (Türk 152).
However, the narration creates distance
between the subject and his own actions
through the first person, demonstrating a
conscious break between his behavior and
his conscious judgement. According to J.M.
Coetzee, the iterative, habitual, present
tense drives the narrator’s existence in the
burrow entirely with only short glimpses
of realization beyond habit (Türk 152).
However, while a repeated, self-made,
goal-oriented decision can automate one’s
response to the same cue, the narrator in
“The Burrow” is subordinate to another
force that dictates his behavior — an antag-
onist of habit. The estrangement between
the narrator and the narrative becomes
most obvious later on when he is asleep:
“I remain here in deep sleep. I must have
slept for a long time, roused only from the
last sleep that already dissolves of its own
accord; this sleep must be very light, for a
hardly audible hissing wakes me” (Kafka
177). This passage is central to the story be-
cause of the paradoxical individual sentenc-
es and their discontinuity, which signify the
quality of the narrative and the narrator’s
2 Benjamin studies Kafka’s animals and suggests that an animal/beast could serve as a representation of Kafka’s deteriorating beast-
like symptoms of tuberculosis (Türk 153). This might explain why the mole believes there is an animal and not anything else that
might be making its way to his burrow, just like Kafka would be afraid of the “beast” taking over his body.
3 Habit, in this more lay, colloquial sense, doesn’t imply the psychological term in the introduction. Habit of anxiety is used in the
sense of the vicious circle of anxiety and the repetitive anxiety attacks observed in “The Burrow.”
relation to his existence in the burrow. The
first sentence is an impossible statement.
If the narrator is asleep, he is unconscious
and therefore cannot report his current
state. The following sentence then intro-
duces an abrupt grammatical and semantic
break from the previous statement. That
same sentence is internally contradictory
because of the cause of the narrator’s wak-
ing, for which the narrator initially blames
his naturally fading sleep, and then ascribes
it to the indefinite hissing2 sound, which
raises the question of whether the hissing
was already present upon his waking. The
passage, through the gaps of narration and
absurd conclusions of causality, illuminates
the narrator’s impossibility of protecting
himself and his sleep from the external
noise or of imposing control, comfort, and
therefore habit over his being in the bur-
row. Failing to habituate to the burrow, the
narrator exhibits the habit3 of anxiety.
The narrator’s logic of how to detect
the hissing again further reiterates the
claim that the narrator does not feel safe in
the burrow but wants to force habit onto
himself: “I had to feel completely at home
again in order to hear it; it is, so to speak,
only audible to the ear of the homeowner
who is truly exercising his authority” (Kaf-
ka 177). Here, the mole-like creature tries
to impose on himself to feel at home and
get into the habit of being home — but, if
he truly feels at home, then he wouldn’t
stay alert. His ear would be familiarized
with the noises, and his attention might
not even recognize the noise because of
habit. It is when he feels not at home in
his familiar living space that he steps out
of habit and can register differences in his
space. The uncanny experience of his (lack
of) authority upon realizing that the noise
has been there for a long time without him
realizing points to the conflicting dynam-
ics that drive the narrator’s existence. On
one hand, he desperately wants to cling to
the inexistent constancy of the burrow and
habituate, but on the other, his inability to
control it (and himself) traps him in the
habitual role of anxiety’s puppet. A further
question to ask then would be: Can the
intermittent hissing sound be a projection
of his own anxiety, creeping in when he’s
most vulnerable and least aware,4 as when
he is asleep?
Temporality of Habit in Proust
In Swann’s Way, habit and projections be-
yond it could look quite different. Proust’s
narrator realizes early on that the habits
his mother created for him — for example,
reading stories to him without including
the love scenes — altered his experience of
the world, but only after he is left alone in
his room. Having his mother around him
created “the gaps which this habit made
in [his] knowledge” (Proust 719). These
gaps in knowledge could also indicate the
gaps of his awareness, which is an effect of
habit. Thus, the discontinuity of the narra-
tor’s awareness in Swann’s Way, unlike the
discontinuous narration in “The Burrow,”
is imposed not by anxiety but by the moth-
er figure. The separation from his mother,
though, shapes the new setting to which
the narrator needs to accustom himself,
including
the
consequent
separation
anxiety: “Tomorrow night I should again
be the victim of anguish and Mamma
would not stay by my side. But when these
storms of anguish grew calm I could no
longer realise their existence” (Proust 756).
The serial repetition of the narrator’s pain
4 One is unconscious when asleep and in a way, that’s similar to being (partially) unconscious to your environment when habituated.
pathologizes the habitual cues to which
he responds. As Freud says, “Anxiety is a
mechanism that forms to compensate the
helplessness of the anthropologically weak
infant. … A danger-situation is a scene, in
which a situation of helplessness — which
is traumatic — is expected” (Türk 145). The
continuous disruption of the old habit of
having his mother around him becomes
the new traumatic habit of being alone.
Then, the reason for calming down is not
specified, but it is evident that habituation
to the traumatic stimulus occurs eventually
and the narrator becomes unconscious of
its existence, “no longer realizing” it. The
introduction of the magic lantern to his
troubled existence then produces a posi-
tive, imaginative effect on his perception:
[U]nsleeping, far from my mother and
grandmother, my bedroom became
the fixed point on which melancholy
and anxious thoughts were centered.
Someone has had the happy idea of
giving me, to distract me on evenings
when I seemed abnormally wretched,
a magic lantern … in the manner of
the master-builders and glass-painters
of gothic days it substituted for the
opaqueness of my walls an impalpable
iridescence, supernatural phenomena
of many colours, in which legends were
depicted, as on a shifting and transitory
window (Proust 145).
The magic lantern, the main disturbance
of the narrator’s static yet anxious habitat,
changes the scenery of the room and dis-
tracts him by opening up the space to new
imagery “as a window.” The magic lantern
is indeed detrimental to providing stabil-
ity of the narrator’s room and thus acts
against habit, which in Marcel’s case, is a
path to (habitual) escapism. The transience
of the magic lantern breaks habit apart
and offers ever-changing fragments to the
imagination. The habitual coexistence of
the traumatic separation with the happy
sensory impressions creates a complex
web around the narrator’s memories of his
early life in Combray, which fixates him on
the isolated painful memories (Türk 148).
However, the repetition and fragmen-
tation of instants open the imaginative
possibilities for the narrator in the form of
artistic manifestations, the culmination of
which is revealed in Time Regained, the last
volume of In Search of Time Lost.
These imaginative possibilities can
only exist upon the basis of habit whose el-
ements can be used to recreate alternative
visions of reality. A scene that beautifully
depicts the realized potential of habit’s mat-
ter in transcending it, or at least substitut-
ing it, is Marcel’s waking: “It is true, when
morning drew near, I would long have
settled the brief uncertainty of my waking
dream, I would know in what room I was
actually lying, would have reconstructed
it round about me in the darkness … as an
architect … , working upon an original”
(Proust 3403). Just like in “The Burrow,”
the narrator is situated just at the twilight
of consciousness upon waking. It is the fa-
miliarity of the room to which he is accus-
tomed that allows him to gain control over
the space, like an architect, and reconstruct
it in his mind’s eye in an instant — what
the Burrowman never accomplishes. Mar-
cel is able to perform this exciting waking
exercise because he has already learned to
manipulate the habitual and overcome the
traumatic, at least temporarily, with the
magic lantern. Instead of having the “mas-
ter builders and glass painters” project their
lantern’s images onto his habitual setting,
he can now be the creative master himself,
reshaping and decorating habitude. These
mental skills later open up the narrator’s
experience of the intermittencies of habit,
the break from routine, and the emergence
of involuntary memory, such as the most
celebrated madeleine-tasting episode.
Habit in literature can teach us much,
now even more than ever before. Literary
giants Kafka and Proust both bring the
theme of habit forward in “The Burrow”
and Swann’s Way, as well as in the rest of the
progression of In Search of Lost Time, that
the scope of this paper could not include.
They illustrate habit as either a driving
force of anxiety or a productive medium
for memory and imagination. As Kafka’s
peculiar creature illuminates the darkest
burrows of anxiety-driven life, his lack of
reflexivity and pathological habits allow us
to step away from the order of our routine
and wonder — wonder not only about the
nature of the Burrowman but also translate
his existence to any other “Bau” that any of
us could be inhabiting. Then, diminutively
viewing Marcel’s traumatized childhood
narrative, we are still drawn to experience
his developing world of impressions, con-
sidered a defense mechanism or simply a
beautiful, poetic way to master escapism.
Experiencing these alternative, fictional
realities of habit, we can hone what we
already know from psychology and trans-
late it to the human psyche and our own
lives. The direction of this project natural-
ly adapted to the current unprecedented
reality and reimagined the significance of
the discourse I wanted to join, bringing
science and literature closer together to
elucidate the powers of habit and promote
more mindfulness among us, “bundles of
habits” (James). ◆

THE FIRST
HOMOSEXUALS:
F E AT U R E
AN EXPOSITION OF
QUEERNESS IN ART
When you think about queerness and
you think about Islamic art, there [are]
two biases and cultural barriers you im-
mediately encounter: … [the] belief that
the Islamic art tradition is aniconic,” or
lacks figural representation, and the idea
that “the Islamic world, especially today, is
associated with being a place that is un-
accepting of queer people.” This is what
College Fellow (2021–22) and Assistant
Professor (Fall 2022–) of Art History
Thadeus Dowad explained to me when
we sat down to discuss an upcoming
exhibition that he is working on: a collab-
orative exhibit of global representations
of queerness in art. These assumptions, I
would later learn, are wholly incorrect.
The show, titled “The First Homo-
sexuals,” focuses on the time period im-
mediately after the word ‘homosexual’ was
coined in European sexological terms (ap-
proximately 1860–1950). The show takes
a broad definition of homosexuality and
queerness, examining “self-portraiture,
self-presentation, and the ways in which
queer desires figure even in abstract art,”
in addition to more traditional paintings,
sculptures, photographs, and drawings of
same-sex couples.
Professor Dowad was still in the pro-
cess of choosing the pieces that he wanted
to highlight for this exhibition — in fact, he
was putting together the final list the day
we spoke. He was able to show me a few
of the pieces he was considering, which is
when I truly learned the extent of my mis-
conceptions. I had gone into this interview
curious about how queerness could exist in
a culture that condemns figural representa-
tions. There’s a myth of a lack of represen-
tational art, as Dowad explained:
[It] presumes that all of Islam is
reducible to text, and it’s just not true.
The Islamic world, both historically
and today, is an incredibly rich,
contradictory space, so there’s tons of
figural representation — not only in
my particular area of specialty, in this
Eastern Mediterranean [region], but all
over the Islamic world.
One of approximately 20 curators
from all across the world for this exhib-
it, Dowad, compared to others, has a vast
amount of area to cover, quite literally. He
is in charge of assembling a collection of
queer works from a large part of the Islamic
world during this time period, namely the
Middle East and North Africa, including
Iran. In contrast, there is another curator
solely in charge of Poland.
Dowad is excited about the scope of
his responsibilities, though. “One of the
”What queerness
is, and even what
Islamic art is,
changes based on
your geography
[and] your period
in history.“
reasons I’m really excited about this show,”
he told me, “is because the period we’re
working on here, the 1860s to the first
half of the 20th century, is … the most un-
der-researched, unattended sub-field of
queerness in Islamic art.” Not only that, but
this century is also “a period of serious cri-
sis in [the Islamic world] because it’s being
actively colonized at this time.”
A major factor of the colonization
effort and colonial establishment in these
regions was building art schools to teach
European methods of depiction to the
artists in this region. Whereas earlier
Islamic art took the form of manuscript
or wall painting, this
period’s art is more
commonly
found
on canvas and more
traditional
Western
forms of the fine arts.
The effect of these art
schools is that “the kind
of art that gets produced
is highly disciplined by
the colonial context,
and those colonial
contexts are deeply,
deeply homophobic.”
In contrast to popular perception,
earlier generations of Islamic art were rich
with depictions of queer desire and same-
sex attractions. In this period, however,
explicit queerness was met with backlash
or was highly sexualized. Orientalist art, as
it is typically categorized, “has overt queer
themes, but always in a very denigratory
way. … Artists in this period are having
to fight back against [homophobic] stigma
against their region,” resulting in signifi-
cantly less “overt depiction of queerness
in Islamic art … so [that] it doesn’t cater
to these imposed stereotypes by colonial
powers.” Dowad noted, “queerness in Is-
lamic art, in this period especially, is not
happening in a vacuum but is happening
in a global and colonial context.” Dowad
also stressed, “An important takeaway here
is that when you think about queerness in
Islamic art, it’s not a single thing. … What
queerness is, and even what Islamic art is,
changes based on your geography [and]
your period in history.”
The international nature of this study
is what really makes it special. “There’s nev-
er been a show like this,” Dowad told me.
The show is planned to be split into themes,
rather than geographic regions, allowing
for artworks from all
different cultures to be
shown side by side.
In addition to
choosing pieces from
his region within this
time period, Professor
Dowad is also tasked
with writing an essay to
accompany the exhibit:
“The hope for the cata-
log [of essays written by
the curators] is that it
will be a little bit like a textbook, because
there’s no existing study like this.” When
asked what it is like to be working on an
exhibit that is truly the first of its kind,
Dowad responded, “It’s exciting. It’s daunt-
ing. But my hope is that this will be the
first stab trying to say something meaning-
ful and comprehensive” about queerness
and the themes of the time period.

Long Distance Nationalism:
by Akash Palani
Department of Political Science
Faculty Adviser: Prof. Julie Lee Merseth, Ph.D.
Abstract
What explains Indian American attitudes towards Hindu national-
ism? Following the election of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in
2014, Hindutva, or Hindu nationalism, has become a potent political
force in India. In the Indian diaspora, particularly in the United
States, the past decade has seen an increase in public activity related
to Hindu nationalism. From the World Hindu Congress in Chicago
to President Trump and Prime Minister Modi’s massive joint rally
in Texas to demonstrations against Hindu nationalist citizenship
laws in India, Indian Americans are now more vocal than ever about
politics in India. This study employs regression analysis to identify
key predictors of Hindu nationalism among Indian Americans. Reli-
gious identity and behavior, Islamophobia, and certain benchmarks
of assimilation emerge as statistically significant. Little empirical
work has been conducted on the subject of Hindu nationalism in the
United States, especially after the ascendance of the Bharatiya Janata
Party (BJP) in 2014. As one of the first surveys of Indian Americans
focused on Hindu nationalism, this work evaluates the existing the-
oretical explanations for the phenomenon and helps set the agenda
for future research. Furthermore, this study puts forth a method for
quantitatively measuring attitudes towards Hindu nationalism: the
index of Hindu nationalist sentiment.
Indian Americans and Hindutva
Section I. Introduction
What explains Indian American attitudes
towards Hindu nationalism? And, what
are the roles of religious behavior and
assimilation in the emergence of these
attitudes? Hindu nationalism and its
ideological foundation, Hindutva, have
become a powerful political force in India
in the past decade. With the election of
Prime Minister Narendra Modi of the
Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party
(BJP) in 2014, the movement became the
dominant strain in Indian politics, reified
by the BJP’s landslide wins in the 2019
parliamentary elections. Hindu nation-
alism itself has roots in colonialism and
confrontations with globalization, and
it is therefore unsurprising that the vast
Indian diaspora has a complex, varied re-
lationship with the movement and Indian
politics more generally.
Indian Americans who profess some
form of support for Hindu nationalism
are participating in the nationalism of a
nation in which they have not resided for
some time, or even never resided. Espe-
cially given the relatively recent entry of
Hindu nationalism into the Indian political
mainstream and the general rise of right-
wing political movements globally, Indian
Americans’ attitudes towards Hindutva are
a puzzling phenomenon. Few studies have
been published looking into this phenom-
enon in the past decade, during which
Hindu nationalism has come to dominate
national politics in India. By conducting
this research now, I hope to capture some
of the effects that this change in Indian
politics may have had on Indian Ameri-
cans’ attitudes towards Hindu nationalism.
I use regression analysis of original survey
data as the main methodological tool of
this research. The findings of this study
provide an empirical evaluation of existing
theories in the past decade’s new political
context. They also help direct urgently
needed future research regarding the pro-
cesses through which Indian Americans
form attitudes towards Hindu nationalism.
Section II. Literature Review
and Hypotheses
To identify key predictors of Hindu na-
tionalism among Indian Americans, I de-
velop a framework that considers religious
participation, identity, Islamophobia, and
assimilation. The attitudes of many Indian
Americans towards Hindu nationalism can
best be characterized as “tacit acceptance”
(Kurien 2007, 238). To be sure, there are
those who are avowed Hindu nationalists,
committed to the goals of Hindutva. Both
ardent nationalists and quiet supporters
are of interest to this study. In the follow-
ing pages, I present a theoretical frame-
work for how many Indian Americans are
exposed to the ideas of Hindu nationalism
and how they develop attitudes towards
the movement.
Religious Identity, Behavior, and Attitudes
Identification with and participation in
American Hinduism is likely related to
approval of Hindu nationalism. Hinduism
in the United States is far more ecumen-
ical and Sanskritic than the vast diversity
of Hindu practice found in India (Kurien
2007). These characteristics, while seem-
ingly incongruent with Hinduism in India,
are quite similar to the version of Hin-
duism espoused by the Hindu nationalist
movement. Kurien describes “popular” and
“official” aspects of American Hinduism
(2007), with popular Hinduism referring
to the daily devotional lives of American
Hindus and official Hinduism referring to
the version of Hinduism crafted by large
umbrella organizations. Some of these
umbrella organizations, such as the Vish-
wa Hindu Parishad of America (VHPA),
have explicit ties to the Hindu nationalist
movement in India (Rajagopal 2000, 479).
Many others are not explicitly linked to
Hindutva but espouse values and a version
of Hinduism that bears stark similarities
to those of the Hindu nationalist move-
ment (Rajagopal 2000). While these two
facets of American Hinduism, popular and
official, may appear disconnected, they
interact to shape Hinduism in the United
States to be reflective of Hindutva ideology.
The relationship between American
Hindu umbrella organizations and Hindu
nationalism is clear. Perhaps the most
prominent example is the VHPA. A direct
offshoot of the Hindu nationalist Vishwa
Hindu Parishad, VHPA — founded in 1970
— is one of the oldest Hindu umbrella or-
ganizations in the United States and has
chapters in 15 U.S. states (Rajagopal 2000,
473; VHPA 2020). VHPA publishes liter-
ature promoting a “Hindu way of life,” in
addition to organizing religious lectures,
seminars, and service projects in India.
The organization projects an image of cul-
tural authenticity and leverages this image
to shape the American public understand-
ing of Hinduism “almost entirely along
the grain of Hindutva thought” (Mathew
and Prashad 2000, 526). The influence
of Hindutva is clear in the literature pub-
lished by the VHPA. One recent blog post
about unrest in Delhi discusses Hindus
being “brutally killed” and portrays Mus-
lims involved in the unrest as organized,
militant anti-Hindus (VHPA 2020). The
post neglects to mention the 35 Muslims
killed during the unrest (Pasha 2020),
offering a prime example of the VHPA’s
Hindu nationalist slant.
The VHPA is not the only umbrella
organization that promotes Hindutva-in-
formed Hinduism in the United States.
The Hindu American Foundation, found-
ed in 2004, is not explicitly aligned with
any political movement and instead pur-
ports to educate the American public about
Hinduism and ensure that Hindus are
accurately represented in public discourse
(Hindu American Foundation 2021). Still,
its founding president and other staff have
been directly involved with the VHPA
(Rao 2003). Other major American Hindu
umbrella organizations include the Hindu
Students Council, the Infinity Foundation,
and more; see Kurien 2007 for a detailed
discussion. Many of these umbrella orga-
nizations share two key similarities: they
seemingly exist to promote awareness of
Hinduism and Hindu culture in the United
States, but their messaging is also close-
ly aligned with Hindu nationalist ideas.
Participation in these organizations is
Many of these umbrella organizations share two key
similarities: they seemingly exist to promote awareness
of Hinduism and Hindu culture in the United States,
but their messaging is also closely aligned with Hindu
nationalist ideas.
almost definitely related to higher levels of
support for Hindu nationalism, but most
Indian Americans are not active members.
The key takeaway is that American Hindu
umbrella organizations have a major role
in shaping American understanding of
Hinduism with a distinctly Hindutva slant.
Next, I turn to the interaction be-
tween Hindu umbrella organizations and
“popular” American Hinduism, or the
ways in which American Hindus practice
their religion in their daily lives. Through
her extensive ethnographic fieldwork,
Kurien finds that worshipping at tem-
ples, attending meetings of local Hindu
associations, and practicing Hindu rituals
at home are the primary ways through
which a large number of American Hindus
practice their religion (2007). These seem
to be strictly religious practices. However,
the connection between these seemingly
private practices and the aforementioned
Hindu umbrella organizations is intimate
and far-reaching. Rajagopal writes, “They
[VHPA] form a network of contacts and
affiliations with other Indian religious and
social organizations in the U.S., and often
their own members may occupy promi-
nent positions in these other organizations.
Thus, its influence extends well beyond its
enrollment.” Taken together, the synthesis
between official and popular Hinduism in
the U.S. makes Indian Americans who par-
ticipate in organized Hinduism more likely
to be exposed to Hindu nationalist ideas
and, in turn, more likely to express higher
levels of support for these ideas.
As a crucial tenet of Hindutva thought,
Islamophobia must also be considered.
From the 2000 riots in Gujarat to state
violence in Kashmir, Islamophobic policy
and action have been a prominent feature
of Hindutva praxis. The 2016 National
Asian American Survey found that Indian
Americans tend to be more Islamphobic
than the nation as a whole (Ramakrish-
nan et al. 2016). Kapur arrived at the same
finding in 2010. In fieldwork conducted
with Indian American lobbyists, Therwath
found “streaks of virulent Islamopho-
bia” and argued that Islamphobia unites
disparate professional Indian American
lobbyists to advocate for Islamophobic
U.S. foreign policy (2007). After the 2000
riots in Gujarat, Nussbaum found that In-
dian Americans played a significant role
in financing right-wing Hindu nationalist
violence during the riots and outlined a
number of networks through which Hin-
du nationalists in the U.S. offer material
support to their extremist counterparts
in India (2003). There is overwhelming
evidence that harboring Islamophobic at-
titudes is associated with higher levels of
Hindu nationalist sentiment.
Assimilation
Assimilation is both a process and an
outcome. The temporal dimension of
assimilation, both within and across im-
migrant generations, is quite important.
To measure assimilation, I draw from
the sociological literature on the subject,
with socioeconomic status, intermarriage,
linguistic patterns, and spatial dispersion
as key factors in assessing assimilation
(Waters and Jimenez 2007). I adapt these
factors in my own measures of Indian
American assimilation, discussed further
in the methodology section of this paper.
In the U.S., Asian Americans as a
whole are confronted with an ambiguous
racial positionality. Masuoka and Junn’s
prism model of the contemporary Amer-
ican racial hierarchy offers a useful frame-
work for understanding this ambiguity.
They posit that while Asian Americans’
proximity to whiteness is higher than
other minority groups, their relationship
to “Americanness” is still fraught. Their
position in the periphery of the in-group
of American society leads them to draw
stricter boundaries on American national
identity than their counterparts in the core
(white Americans), especially on charac-
teristics that are more accessible to Asian
Americans (Masuoka and Junn 2013).
I argue that this strict enforcement
of boundaries represents a desire, at least
in some Indian Americans, to assert their
belonging in the United States. Multicul-
turalism in the U.S. demands that immi-
grants construct an ethnic identity for
public performance (Walzer 1999). For
many Indian Americans, Hindu national-
ism and the neat, strictly defined version
of Hinduism espoused by its adherents
offers a convenient identity for those In-
dian Americans seeking to assimilate into
U.S. society. Rajagopal expands on this
approach, arguing that the development
of an ecumenical Hindu American identi-
ty provides a way for Indians to navigate
their ambiguous position in the polarized
racial hierarchy of the United States. He
writes, “For Indian [Americans], to be
‘Hindu’ is to bask in Orientalist visions of
an ancient civilization and so compensate
at the present time for its bygone glories
while muting the stigma of racism” (Ra-
jagopal 2000, 472-473). Mathew and Pra-
shad describe this turn to Hindu identity as
an “ontological reversal of racism” (2000).
When confronted with racism and white
supremacy, some Indian Americans assert
the superiority of their own perceived
Aryan identity in response (Mathew and
Prashad 2000). They argue that Indian
American support for Hindutva is as much
a response to racism in the United States
as it is an expression of affinity for the
Hindu Right in India.
Based on the preceding theoretical
discussion, the following hypotheses are
formulated and tested by this study:
1. Indian Americans who self-identify as Hin-
du are more likely to express higher levels of
Hindu nationalist sentiment.
Hinduism in the U.S. is characterized by
many of the Sanskritic, ritual-focused
aspects emphasized by Hindutva’s con-
ception of the religion. Self-identifica-
tion as Hindu by Indian Americans may
therefore be related to more agreement
with Hindutva broadly.
2. Higher levels of participation in religious
organizations are more likely to be related to
higher levels of Hindu nationalist sentiment.
Participation in Hindu religious or-
ganizations reinforces perceptions of
Hinduism that are closely aligned with
Hindu nationalist ideas. In turn, Indian
Americans who participate in such
organizations are more likely to support
Hindu nationalism more broadly.
3. Negative perceptions of Islam are more likely
to be related to higher levels of Hindu nation-
alist sentiment.
Hindu nationalist policy and activity are
deeply Islamophobic. Indian Americans
who express negative attitudes towards
Islam will be more likely to agree with
Hindutva ideology.
4. Higher scores on assimilation benchmarks
are more likely to be related to higher levels of
Hindu nationalist sentiment.
Highly assimilated Indian Americans
express support for Hindu nationalist ideas
as a consequence of their assimilation into
American society. Confronted with an
ambiguous racial positionality, they will be
more likely to use the cohesive definition
of Hindu offered by Hindutva to construct
an identity for themselves.
Section III. Research Design
The dataset for this research was con-
structed from an original survey of Indian
Americans. Using Ordinary Least Squares
(OLS) regression analysis, I tested the
hypotheses presented in the previous
section to identify statistically significant
predictors of Hindu nationalist sentiment
(HNS) in Indian Americans.
Survey and Data Collection
I developed an original survey instrument
to collect data for this project. The survey
was hosted on Qualtrics1 and fielded by
Bovitz, Inc., in the time frame of February
20, 2021, to March 1, 2021. A non-random
sample of 256 Indian Americans was se-
lected for data collection. To construct the
sample, Bovitz sent the survey to respon-
dents in its panel who self-identified as
Indian American. As an additional check, a
screener was included at the beginning of
the survey to ensure that respondents iden-
tified as Indian American. The surveyed
sample was not perfectly representative of
the population of all Indian Americans, but
I found a reasonable degree of consistency
with national characteristics.2
Dependent Variable: Hindu Nationalist
Sentiment
The dependent variable in this study was
the level of support for Hindu nationalism.
This was a difficult concept to measure,
especially in the context of the Indian
diaspora. I adapted an approach from
researchers at Lokniti, an Indian public
opinion research center (Kumar et al.
2018), to develop an index of Hindu na-
tionalist sentiment among Indian Ameri-
cans. This approach casted a wide net, as-
sessing attitudes towards a variety of ideas,
politics, and policies that can be classified
1 Access provided by Northwestern University Weinberg College of Arts & Sciences
2 See Table 2 for sample characteristics and discussion of external validity
as Hindu nationalist. Respondents were
asked to indicate whether they strongly
agree, somewhat agree, neither agree nor
disagree, somewhat disagree, or strongly
disagree with the following six statements:
1. India is the homeland and holy land
for all Hindus.
2. All Hindus should adhere to a certain
set of rituals and practices.
3. Prime Minister Modi and the Bhara-
tiya Janata Party (BJP) are taking
India in the right direction.
4. The demolition of the Babri Masjid
was justified.
5. The 2019 Citizenship Amendment
Act is good for India.
6. Hinduism is the one true path to
enlightenment.
Statement 1 addresses one of the
core ideological tenets of Hindu nation-
alism. The movement views India as both
home- and holy-land for Hindus only, an
idea which it uses to assert both the indi-
geneity of Hindus and the non-indigeneity
of Muslims, Christians, and others. This
forms the basis of the exclusionary politics
of Hindutva. Statements 2 and 6 address the
degree to which respondents agree with
Hindutva’s definition of Hinduism. While
there is vast diversity found in the practice
of Hinduism across India and the Indian di-
aspora, the Hindu nationalists’ idea of Hin-
du practice is more narrow, emphasizing a
specific set of rules and rituals that Hindus
must follow. Statement 3 addresses attitudes
towards Prime Minister Modi and the BJP.
The current Indian regime, in power since
2014, represents a major increase in political
power for Hindu nationalists. Modi and the
BJP have vigorously pursued Hindu nation-
alist rhetoric and politics, making attitudes
towards Modi and the BJP an important
measure of Hindu nationalist sentiment. Fi-
nally, Statements 4 and 5 address key events
that function as litmus tests for HNS. The
demolition of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya is
widely perceived as a landmark event in the
history of Hindu nationalism. A long-stand-
ing Muslim place of worship was destroyed
by militant Hindu nationalists who asserted
that the masjid was located on the site of
the Hindu god Rama’s birthplace (Buchetta
2000). Ayodhya re-entered the spotlight in
2020, with Prime Minister Modi breaking
ground on a Hindu temple on the site of the
demolished mosque (Gettleman and Kumar
2020). The 2019 Citizenship Amendment
Act (CAA) introduced changes to India’s
definition of citizenship that was exclusion-
ary of Muslims and was thus considered a
landmark victory for Hindu nationalist pol-
itics. The CAA sparked widespread, some-
times violent protests throughout India and
the Indian diaspora (Tandon 2020), making
it a useful litmus test for HNS.
Using these statements, I constructed
an index of Hindu nationalist sentiment
for each respondent. Responses to each
statement were assigned a weight on a
scale from 1 to 5, with 1 corresponding
with strong disagreement, 3 correspond-
ing with neutrality, and 5 corresponding
with strong agreement. These statement
weights were then averaged to assign an
HNS index score to each respondent. Thus,
higher scores on the index reflected stron-
ger agreement with Hindu nationalism.
Independent Variables
The independent variables in this study
were categorized into three sets: religion,
assimilation, and demographic controls.
Four variables were included in the reli-
gion set: religious identity, participation
in Hindu organizations, Islamophobia
towards Muslims in the United States, and
Islamophobia towards Muslims in India.
Religious identity was measured by a cate-
gorical variable constructed from a survey
question in which respondents were asked
to report their religious identity from a
set of options or to report an identity not
included in the options. To measure the
level of participation in organized Amer-
ican Hinduism, I constructed an index.
Respondents were asked to report the
frequency with which they participated
in the five major types of organizations
identified by Kurien in 2007: local associ-
ations, temples, internet forums, student
organizations, and umbrella organizations.
As an additional measure of participation,
I adapted questions from the 2016 Nation-
al Asian American Survey (Ramakrishnan
et al. 2016) regarding leadership positions
in religious organizations and attending
temples for reasons other than worship.
In all, the following seven statements were
presented to respondents.
1. Attend a local Hindu organization
meeting (Balavihar, satsang, etc.).
2. Pray at a temple.
3. Participate in Hindu internet forums.
4. Engage in Hindu identity-based
activism/advocacy.
5. Participate in a Hindu student
organization.
6. Serve in a leadership position in a
religious organization.
7. Visit a temple with people for reasons
other than worship.
For each statement, participants were
asked to report the frequency with which
they participated in each activity (Daily,
Weekly, A few times per month, Monthly,
A few times per year, Never). A weight
from 1-6 was assigned to each response,
with 1 corresponding with never, 2 with a
few times per year, 3 with a few times per
month, and so on. As I discussed above,
there was a great degree of interaction be-
tween different types of organizations, and
in this study, I was interested in assessing
the relationship between overall level
of participation in organized American
Hinduism rather than the impact of spe-
cific organization types. To capture this,
I computed the mean of each participant’s
response to each of the seven statements
and assigned that mean as an index of
participation. To measure Islamophobia,
participants were asked to indicate the de-
gree to which they thought Muslims were
a threat to the United States and to India.
I relied on Waters and Jimenez’s
framework for assessing immigrant as-
similation. According to their review of
the sociological literature, key metrics
of assimilation include socioeconomic
status, residential segregation, intermar-
riage, and English language acquisition
(2005). The most widely used measure
of residential segregation was the index
of dissimilarity, D (U.S. Census Bureau
2016).3 I adopted the idea of capturing
dissimilarity as a measure of residential
segregation. Each respondent was asked
3 See White 1986 for details on how the index of dissimilarity
is computed.
to report approximately how much of
their neighborhood is Indian and/or Indi-
an American. I also constructed variables
measuring perceptions of inter- and in-
tra-generational socioeconomic mobility,
English language acquisition, and interra-
cial/inter-ethnic relationships.
To
operationalize
confrontations
with ambiguous racial positionality, I in-
cluded perceptions of discrimination as an
additional measure of assimilation based
on Vijay Prashad’s work (2000). There are
a variety of scales used to measure percep-
tions of discimination (see Williams 2016).
I used a common scale for everyday discrim-
ination put forth by Williams et al. (1997)
and computed an index of discrimination
for each respondent using a similar meth-
odology to those outlined for other indices
in this study. Lower scores indicated more
frequent perceptions of discrimination.
I also included a set of controls. Hin-
du nationalist imagery and messaging is
dominated by masculinity. Banerjee termed
the image of India projected by Hindu na-
tionalists a “masculinized vision of a nation”
(2006). I included gender as a control fac-
tor to account for the possible effects that
the masculinity of Hindu nationalism may
have had. I included another control for the
immigrant generation, constructed from
questions on self, parent, and grandparent
nativity. Finally, I included a control for
U.S. political ideology. The exclusionary
stance that Hindu nationalists take towards
minorities, especially Muslims, is incompat-
ible with American liberal ideology (Heth-
erington and Weiler 2010), so self-identi-
fied liberals may be less supportive of Hindu
nationalism on the whole. Furthermore,
the closeness of Prime Minister Modi and
President Trump may have led conservative

Indian Americans to view Hindu national-
ism more favorably. The results of the 2020
Indian American Attitudes Survey showed
that there may not have been a significant
consistency between their attitudes towards
U.S. and Indian politics (Badrinathan et al.
2020). So, while there is some empirical
ambiguity about the relationship between
U.S. political ideology and Hindu national-
ist attitudes, the strength of the theoretical
relationship justifies the inclusion of this
control. Finally, I included a control for
North vs. South Indian origin, as the BJP’s
electoral performance in North India is gen-
erally much stronger than in South India.
Regression analysis
Table 1 summarizes the OLS regres-
sion models used in this study. This
iterative approach to model building in
multivariate regression analysis allows
for the demonstration of relationships
that persist even in the presence of ad-
ditional factors, an indicator of a strong
correlation. With a quite limited body of
work on the subject, this large-N correl-
ative approach yields insights into more
population-level trends than have been
previously identified. Therefore, while
the results of regression analysis do not
imply causality, the identification of sig-
nificant predictors of Hindu nationalist
sentiment allows for an empirical test
of existing hypotheses and helps set the
tone for future research.

Implications
Below, I present a discussion of my findings
from the regression analysis and an examina-
tion of descriptive statistics. For full regres-
sion output, see Appendix B. For detailed
variable characteristics, see Appendix C.

is the index of HNS. HNS is computed on

Figure 1 represents the distribution

Evaluating Hypotheses
Religious Identity, Behavior, and Attitudes
I find strong evidence in support of Hy-
pothesis 1, leading me to conclude that In-
dian Americans who self identify as Hindu
are more likely to express positive attitudes
towards Hindu nationalism. It is worth
noting that the self-identified Hindu group
had the highest coefficient magnitude of
any predictor and that no other religious
identities had a significant relationship with
attitudes towards Hindu nationalism.
Figure 2 is a box plot depicting the
HNS index broken down by religious iden-
tity. This plot underscores the extent to
which self-identification as Hindu affects
attitudes towards Hindu nationalism. Not
only is the mean response for the Hindu
group quite a bit more positive than other
S Figure 2. Hindu Nationalist Sentiment by Religious Identity
groups, but the entire distribution also
skews more positive compared to any oth-
er group. It would be reasonable to expect
that, for instance, Indian American Mus-
lims would be less likely to support Hindu
nationalism due to the movement’s explicit
Islamophobia. While the descriptive sta-
tistics shown in Figure 2 do offer some
evidence for this expectation — Muslims
are the group with the most generally
negative attitudes towards Hindu nation-
alism — no religious identity other than
Hindu emerged as statistically significant
in regression analysis. With only Hindu
identity emerging as significant, the ev-
idence suggests that the characteristics of
Hinduism in the United States, not of oth-
er religious identities, are one of the key
mechanisms at play.
Hypothesis 2 is also supported by the
results of regression analysis. Increased
overall levels of participation in Hindu
organizations in the United States make
Indian Americans more likely to express
agreement with Hindu nationalist ideas.
This confirmation of Hypothesis 2 offers
an important complement to Hypothesis
1. There is clear evidence that American
Hindus’ acceptance of Hindu nationalist
ideas is not a result of some endogenous
feature of Hinduism as a religion. Rather,
the evidence suggests that Hindu umbrella
organizations in the U.S. have developed
a Hindutva-oriented outlook on the Hindu
religion and identity through multiple pro-
cesses. From the organized Hindu Right’s
efforts to promote Hindu nationalism
through the VHPA to immigrant selection
through the U.S. immigration system,
numerous factors unrelated to Hindu the-
ology have shaped official American Hin-
duism to be accepting of Hindu nationalist
ideas. Confirmation that Indian Ameri-
cans’ participation in and identification
with Hinduism increases their likelihood
of expressing agreement with Hindu na-
tionalism demonstrates the extent of the
influence that official American Hindu
organizations have in day-to-day life for
Indian American Hindus. This synthesis of
popular and official Hinduism, then, offers
a strong explanation for Indian American
attitudes towards Hindu nationalism.
Finally, I find compelling evidence in
support of Hypothesis 3, which states that
Islamophobic attitudes are associated with
higher levels of HNS. Negative percep-
tions of Muslims in India and in the U.S.
both emerged as significant predictors of
stronger HNS. Earlier in this paper, I cit-
ed the Modi regime’s passage of the 2019
Citizenship Amendment Act as an example
of Hindu nationalism’s fundamental Islam-
ophobia. The COVID-19 pandemic offers
another recent illustration. Many of India’s
television news channels harbor a heavy
pro-BJP slant. As the deadly coronavirus
spread through India, TV anchors scape-
goated Muslims, referring to them with
epithets ranging from “virus villains” to
“human [COVID-19] bombs” (Yasir 2020).

Given the virulent Islamophobia present
in Hindutva ideology, rhetoric, and praxis,
it is not particularly surprising that Indi-
an Americans who harbor Islamophobic
attitudes are more likely to support Hindu
nationalist ideas. Somewhat troubling,
though, is the fact that negative perceptions
of Muslims both in India and in the U.S.
are associated with higher HNS. I discuss
Islamophobia in the American context in
more detail in the final part of this section.
Assimilation
Perceived loss of socioeconomic status,
intermarriage, and English language
proficiency did not emerge as statistically
significant. Therefore, I refrain from
drawing definitive conclusions regarding
the direction of the relationship between
assimilation and HNS. Still, two com-
ponents of assimilation — perceptions
of discrimination and residential segre-
gation — do hold statistical significance.
Higher levels of both of these measures
are associated with greater support for
Hindu nationalism.
The positive relationship between
higher levels of discrimination and higher
levels of support for Hindu nationalism
lends support to Mathew and Prashad’s
proposed “reverse racism” mechanism
(2000). Taken alone, it would be an over-
reach to argue that perceptions of dis-
crimination alone are sufficient to draw
conclusions
about
assimilation
more
broadly. Still, the significance of perceived
discrimination deserves a nuanced discus-
sion. Experiences of discrimination may
serve to remind many Indian Americans of
their ambiguous position in the racialized
hierarchy of U.S. society, thereby creat-
ing a desire for belonging. As I explained
earlier, Hindutva’s Hinduism offers this
feeling of belonging by crafting a version
of Hinduism that is compatible with, or
even desired by, American society. Thus,
Indian Americans who experience higher
levels of discrimination may be drawn to
Hindu nationalism as a way to grapple with
desires for belonging in American society.
Especially in the context of rising
anti-Asian racism in the United States, this
finding is particularly important. In April
2021, a white mass shooter in Indianapolis
killed eight workers at a FedEx facility,
four of whom were Sikh Indian Americans
(Mervosh et al. 2021). While the motive of
the shooter remains under investigation,
he is reported to have accessed white
supremacist websites (Contreras 2021).
Combined with the general climate of
anti-Asian sentiment in the U.S., it is likely
that Indian Americans have perceived
higher levels of discrimination during this
recent wave of violent acts and rhetoric.
Some of these individuals, including those
who have not previously supported Hindu
nationalism, may turn to the movement to
find a sense of belonging in an American
society that has increasingly alienated them.
While residential segregation is one of
the benchmarks of immigrant assimilation
“The Hindu Right ... has both effectively shaped public
perceptions of Hinduism and influenced the day-to-day
religious lives of American Hindus in favor of its religious-
nationalist agenda.”
outlined by Waters and Jimenez (2005), I
refrain from arguing that the association
found between higher concentrations of
Indian Americans in an individual’s neigh-
borhood and higher levels of support for
Hindu nationalism provides sufficient
evidence to reject Hypothesis 4. This is
especially true given the moderate effect
of segregation and the disappearance of
statistical significance in the most robust
model. Still, some interesting implications
emerge. Immigrants living in areas with
higher ethnic concentrations are more
likely to be exposed to ethnic community
organizations and media, thereby lower-
ing the cost of the political mobilization
for these residents (Ramakrishnan 2005).
For Indian Americans, living in areas with
higher concentrations of co-ethnics may
lead to greater exposure to Hindu nation-
alist ideas through Hindu organizations.
More generally, I do not form any de-
finitive conclusions regarding the nature or
direction of the relationship between assim-
ilation and support for Hindu nationalism.
At the same time, I do not conclude a truly
null relationship. Issues with how assimila-
tion was operationalized in the quantitative
portion of this study may be an explanation
for the mostly null results I found. As both
a process and an outcome, the temporal di-
mension of assimilation is important when
assessing its effects. Capturing variation
over time and between generations of im-
migrants within a single survey is difficult.
Implications
The findings of this research hold nu-
merous implications regarding the future
of Hindu nationalism in the U.S. and
the study of Indian American political
attitudes and behavior. In this study, I
have shown how the Hindu Right, op-
erating through organizations of official
Hinduism in the U.S., has both effectively
shaped public perceptions of Hinduism
and influenced the day-to-day religious’s
lives of American Hindus in favor of
its religious-nationalist agenda. Hindu
nationalism will likely continue to be an
important component of Indian American
politics, and it is reasonable to expect that
it will become increasingly popular in
Indian American communities.
Even in this study’s sample, in which
native-born Indian Americans were over-
represented (see Table 2), there is signifi-
cant, well-distributed variation in attitudes
towards Hindu nationalism. Therefore, it is
unlikely that Indian Americans will simply
“age out” of affinity for Hindutva as the na-
tive-born population grows and matures.
Immigrant generation was not a significant
predictor of HNS in the regression analysis.
Figure 3, which shows HNS index scores bro-
ken down by immigrant generation, further
underscores how the strategies employed by
the Hindu Right are effective regardless of
nativity or immigrant generation.

Although neither a perfectly representative nor truly random sample, this sam-
ple still generally aligns with national Indian American population characteristics on a
number of parameters. Notably, foreign born Indian Americans are underrepresented,
with 69% of the population being foreign born and only 47% being foreign born in the
surveyed sample. This holds important implications for the interpretation of regression
results presented in this section — and will be discussed further in the next sections.
While median income appears to be slightly lower in the sample, respondents were asked
to self-report income based on predetermined categories. Combined with respondents’
potential disinclination to accurately report income and the lack of more granular data,
the lower median income present in the sample should not be taken as a serious issue
for external validity. Educational attainment and age distributions in the sample broadly
align with national characteristics with minor deviations. Taken as a rough proxy for
Indian American political attitudes, the consistency of sample and population partisan-
ship characteristics on this measure is a positive indicator of the external validity of this
study. With the exception of nativity, which will be discussed later, most of this sample’s
characteristics suggest that this study holds a strong degree of external validity, though
the results are clearly not perfectly generalizable.

In short, demographics alone fail to ex-
plain Indian American support for Hindu
nationalism. This failure, coupled with the
evidence I have presented regarding the
efficacy of Hindu nationalist strategies in
the U.S., makes it clear that Hindu nation-
alism will likely continue to be a persistent
force in the Indian American community.
For critics of Hindu nationalism, the
intuitive response to this study may be to
advocate for heightened policing and scru-
tiny of American Hindus and American
Hindu organizations writ large. Recent U.S.
history demonstrates that this would be a
disastrously misguided impulse. In the af-
termath of the September 11, 2001 attacks
on the World Trade Center, the U.S. un-
dertook unprecedented mass policing and
surveilance of Muslim Americans, leading
to significant, long-term negative conse-
quences for those involved (see Quinlan
2015 for a case study of NYPD surveilance
and its negative consequences of Muslim
New Yorkers). This should not be replicat-
ed. The consequences of Islamophobia are
present even in the regression analysis pre-
sented above, with higher levels of Islam-
ophobia being associated with more posi-
tive attitudes towards Hindu nationalism.
Continued research into this phenomenon,
further challenges to the racist and Orien-
talist foundations of Hindutva, and commu-
nity-based organizing will prove far more
productive for those interested in engaging
critically with Hindu nationalism.
From Indian Americans’ financing
of early-2000s Hindu nationalist violence
in Gujarat (Nussbaum 2003) to Hindu
nationalists’ successful campaign against
a 2021 Chicago City Council resolution
condemning the Indian regime’s nationalist
violence (Husain and Byrne 2021), harbor-
ing HNS holds real-world ramifications for
politics at all levels. If Indian Americans’
Hindu nationalist support is to persist, so
too will its real-world consequences. Indian
Americans are widely understood to be a
generally Democratic voting bloc. Although
they overwhelmingly favored President Joe
Biden in the 2020 U.S. presidential election, a
growing minority of Indian Americans have
been voicing support for more conservative
Republicans (Gjetlen 2020; Sirohi 2020).
At some level, this is very surprising,
especially given the closeness of Modi and
Trump. However, should there indeed prove
to be a broader rightward shift in the voting
behavior of Indian Americans in the coming
years, the results of this study may offer some
insight. Immigrant community organiza-
tions, including religious organizations, are
important vehicles for political mobilization
(Wong 2006, 119). The influence of the Hin-
du Right on American Hindu religious orga-
nizations, then, may be related to changing
Indian American voter behavior. At the same
time, partisanship and political ideology did
not emerge as significant predictors of HNS
in the regression analysis presented above.
Figure 4 shows a more detailed
breakdown of HNS by political ideology. It
appears that conservatives and even mod-
erates lean more in favor of Hindu nation-
alism than liberals do. However, given the
lack of statistical significance underneath
this relationship, the question of the effect
of political ideology on HNS remains unan-
swered. The relationship between support
for Hindu nationalism, political ideology,
and voting behavior presents an urgent line
of inquiry with immediate implications.
Section V. Conclusion
There are a number of limitations to this
study that should be discussed. The index
of Hindu nationalism I construct as the
dependent variable is unique in a number of
ways. Few have constructed such an index
for measuring sentiment in India, and this
study is the first to construct such an index
in the diasporic context. My construction
of an index for Hindu nationalism is an
important caveat for the interpretation of
findings presented above. I emphasized
capturing the wide set of ideas and political
phenomena that can be classified as “Hindu
nationalist.” Further research should look to
refine measures of this concept and should
also consider developing measures for senti-
ment intensity. While I capture variability, I
was not able to capture how strongly Hindu
nationalist sentiment is held among Indian
Americans. Assessing knowledge of Hindu
nationalism would be a useful place to begin
measuring the strength of that sentiment.
Understanding how strongly Indian Amer-
icans hold Hindu nationalist beliefs would
enable researchers to unpack what makes a
committed Hindu nationalist.
From Table 2, it is clear that for-
eign-born Indian Americans are underrepre-
sented in the sample I used. The explanations
for HNS I put forth in this study are robust
in that they persist even when controlling for
immigrant generation. However, it is high-
ly likely that factors such as organizational
participation and discrimination operate
differently on different generations. For in-
stance, second-generation immigrants may
have quite different motivations for partici-
pating in Hindu religious organizations than
their first-generation counterparts (parental
insistence, for example). However, given
the underrepresentation of first-generation
immigrants in the sample, I am unable to
quantify these differences, and future studies
should look to sampling techniques that al-
low for better representation in this regard.
Caste and Hindu nationalism are in-
extricably linked. Indeed, many argue that
caste and Hinduism itself are fundamentally
related (Ambedkar 1936). I have discussed
how Hindu nationalist ideology relies on
a narrow set of Vedic, Sanskritic, and up-
per-caste rituals and practices in its pur-
portedly universal definition of Hindu-ness.
With upper-caste rituals playing such a
crucial role in the very definition of Hindu
nationalism, it is only reasonable to expect
that attitudes towards caste factor into Hin-
du nationalist attitude formation. Caste is
far from a relic of Indian history. It contin-
ues to play a major role in the lives of those
living in India and in the diaspora. In 2020,
a wave of caste-based discimination alle-
gations swept through Silicon Valley (Rai
2020), providing just one example of caste’s
relevance in the Indian American context.
I included two questions about caste iden-
tity and the salience of caste identity in the
survey instrument, but these data were ulti-
mately excluded from the main dataset due
to significant concerns over data quality and
response bias. Undoubtedly, caste must play
a prominent role in future attempts to ex-
plain attitudes towards Hindu nationalism,
and the experience of this research shows
the major methodological hurdles that exist
for such an endeavor.
Ultimately, this research lays the
groundwork for future investigations of the
relationship between Indian Americans and
Hindutva. With little large-N empirical work
conducted on this subject since 2014, or
even at all, this study marks one of the first
large-scale tests of existing theories about di-
asporic attitude formation regarding Hindu
nationalism. By examining religious identity,
attitudes, and behavior, as well as assimila-
tion, I have conducted a wide — although not
comprehensive — analysis of different factors
that may be related to Indian American HNS.
Building an understanding of this phenome-
non not only advances academic understand-
ing of the subject but also helps mitigate its
more harmful effects. ◆
Appendix A: Definitions of Key Terms
Hindu nationalism — A political, social, and religious movement that aims to build a
Hindu Rashtra (lit. “Hindu nation”) in India.
Hindutva — Literally “Hinduness,” Hindutva forms the ideological basis for the Hindu
nationalist movement. Hindutva’s defines “Hindus” as the people for whom India is both
homeland and holy land, emphasizing indigeneity through connection to the land and
Aryan ancestry.
HNS — Throughout this study, the abbreviation HNS is used to refer to “Hindu Nation-
alist Sentiment,” a measure of the level of approval or disapproval an individual holds
towards Hindu nationalism.
RSS — Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (lit. “National Volunteer Organization”). The
civil society arm of the Hindu nationalist movement, the RSS works to promote Hindu
values and Hindutva.
Sangh Parivar — An umbrella term referring to the collection of organizations
spawned by and/or affiliated with the RSS.
BJP — Bharatiya Janata Party. The political arm of the Hindu nationalist movement, the
BJP pursues a Hindu nationalist agenda and is the ruling party of India as of April 2021.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi is the Parliamentary Chairperson of the BJP.
VHP — Vishwa Hindu Parishad (lit. “World Hindu Council”). The religious arm of the
Hindu nationalist movement, the VHP works to “organise, consolidate, and serve Hindu
society” (VHP 2020).
VHPA — Vishwa Hindu Parishad of America. An offshoot of the VHP, VHPA shapes
the public image of Hinduism in the U.S., promotes what it considers Hindu values, and
engages in various service projects in the U.S. and in India.
CAA — Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019. A controversial piece of legislation passed
by the Indian Parliament in December 2019, the CAA makes various changes to Indian
citizenship rules, notably excluding certain persecuted Muslims from Muslim-majority
countries.
Immigrant Generation — First-generation immigrant is defined as a foreign born
individual who has immigrated to the U.S. Second-generation immigrant is defined
as a native born individual with at least one foreign born parent, and third-generation
immigrant is defined as a native born individual with native born parents and at least
one foreign born grandparent (Rumbaut 2006).
