by Nolan Fizoires Robinson II
Department of Theatre
Faculty Adviser: Prof. Gail Shapiro, MFA
Abstract
The following paper seeks to explore and discover how the
tools and resources that actors gain throughout their training
are applicable to vocations outside of just performing and in the
process of everyday life. By conducting interviews with current
Northwestern students, current and former Northwestern acting
professors, as well as Northwestern alumni who are at the pinnacle
of their fields in both the entertainment industry and professions
outside of this particular industry, I use anecdotes and qualitative
applications to dive into the substance, and not just the form, of
acting — in short, this paper will share how techniques and skills
related to the entertainment industry are crucial to more than just
the actor. Furthermore, I argue that being an actor is akin to being
a scientist and that the process an actor undergoes in preparing to
play a role is a process one should try to implement in their own
walk of life.
Transcending the Stage:
Exploring the Applicability of an
Actor’s Training to Other Vocations
and Our Everyday Lives
I. Introduction
“I like to say that if medical professionals
get it right, we live longer and healthier lives.
If economists get it right, we enjoy higher
material standards of living. But without the
arts — literature, dance, music, the visual arts,
cinema, etc. — life loses its meaning. The arts
inspire us, inform us, and help us understand
differences. Nothing else comes close.”
— Northwestern University President
Morton O. Schapiro
The impetus of this project began to grow
from several places throughout my time
at Northwestern University, the first of
which was a class I registered for in the
winter of my junior year: “Economics and
the Humanities: Understanding Choice in
the Past, Present, and Future.” The course
— offered in the College of Arts and Sci-
ences and taught by Morton O. Schapiro,
American economist and University Presi-
dent, and Gary Saul Morson, American lit-
erary critic and internationally renowned
scholar of Slavic studies — required its stu-
dents to engage in conversations among
various disciplines.
Throughout the quarter, I grew in
the knowledge that in order to understand
the world as I wish to and to connect with
those around me, I must be willing to
engage in conversations that encourage
me to switch points of view and examine
questions in perspectives and disciplines
different from my own. This prospect fas-
cinated me, as it pertained to my studies as
an actor. I related this understanding of the
world and attitude towards interactions to
an essay written by Yale Professor Elinor
Fuchs, “EF’s Visit to a Small Planet: Some
Questions to Ask a Play,” that provides
1 Fuchs, EF’s Visit to a Small Planet (Some Questions to Ask a Play).
2 Ibid.
actors with the tools to analyze and under-
stand the world of a play when discovering
it for the first time, as well as what the play
itself demands of the actor. She states:
The play asks us to focus upon a total
awareness, to bring our attention and
curiosity without the censorship of
selective interpretation, “good taste,”
or “correct form.” Before making
judgments, we must ask questions. This
is the deepest meaning of the idea, often
repeated but little understood, that the
study of art shows us how to live.1
This idea of “selective interpretation,” as
Fuchs shares, can be akin to the refusal to
integrate ideas other than our own in com-
ing to the conclusions that we do in argu-
ments — that, essentially, no other world
exists but the one we have grown accus-
tomed to through our studies, upbringing,
and ways of living. The scholarship taken
from my humanities class shares the same
logic as that of Fuchs’: through breaking
out of uncertainty, we cannot focus solely
on what we already know, as this keeps us
from asking questions — questions that
“are intended to light up some of the dark
matter in dramatic worlds,” or the worlds
in which we live every day.2
As acting is a very specialized path,
its power in connecting human beings to
the world, to each other, and to their own
humanity is seldom understood by those
who are not in the craft and sometimes
even forgotten by those who have received
training, like me. Given this understand-
ing, I followed my impulse to dive deeper
into what an acting education truly teaches.
The interviews integrated into this paper
are conversations I have had with actors,
writers, producers, doctors, managers,
financial advisors, etc., who have all stud-
ied or taught acting at Northwestern Uni-
versity and discovered how their training
has appeared throughout their daily lives.
I hope to be in constant communication
with the reader through the material that
follows, and I hope readers will be able to
discover themselves within this work and
within these people.
II. Exploring What Acting Is
“We believe to study theatre is to seek to
understand what it means to be human.”
— Lookingglass Theatre Founding
Ensemble Member and Northwestern
Head of Acting David Catlin
The process I developed in conducting this
research first required me to step outside of
what I already know about the art of acting.
As this paper analyzes the tools of an actor,
what they know, and how this work and
knowledge continue to be present even
outside of acting, I began to try to unlearn
this craft as if I were discovering it for the
first time. I desired for anyone reading this
to do the same — to discover, or rediscover,
the power and magic behind what acting is.
With this, it became crucial that I presented
this work for both the seasoned actor and
one who has no idea what it is that actors
actually do and learn, other than perform-
ing and how to perform. So, in examining
the factors that propelled me into wanting
to pursue acting professionally, the starting
point of this thesis naturally gravitated to-
wards acting teachers themselves and what
they believe they are teaching their students
from the study of acting.
The role of an acting teacher is to,
obviously, teach acting. However, just as a
mathematics professor strives to teach their
students how to analyze the mathematical
complexities that surround human beings
in everyday life or how political science
does more than just encourage students to
understand politics and explains through
analytical frameworks why political ac-
tions are conducted, acting, too, contains
more than what many may believe it does.
One of the teachers to whom I had the
pleasure of speaking is an Emeritus Profes-
sor of Acting at Northwestern University,
David Downs. Downs was an acting pro-
fessor from 1973 to 2000 and, during his
tenure, taught actors who would go on to
become world-renowned artists, including
David Schwimmer, Greg Berlanti, Harry
Lennix, and Dennis O’Hare. To begin our
conversation, I asked him to break down
what his job was as an acting teacher, as
this profession can have several meanings
attached to it. He explained that there was
always an impulse in him to be an acting
teacher. The paths that “[spun] around in
his life” included being an actor and writer,
but teaching was the thing that he wanted
to do the most. He credited Alvina Krause,
former Northwestern University acting
professor and the driving force behind the
acting sequence still continued today at the
university, for contributing to that choice:
“As acting is a very specialized path, its power in
connecting human beings to the world, to each other, and
to their own humanity is seldom understood by those who
are not in the craft and sometimes even forgotten by those
who have received training.”
I met [Alvina Krause] during her
career in the 30s, 40s, and 50s, and early
60s. And suddenly, what she believed
that acting was, and theater was, hit
my heart deeper than anything else
that I had done, even all the acting
experiences that I’d had. And that’s
what I wanted to teach and the reason
why was just what you’ve articulated:
that beyond the skills that are needed
for a certain kind of profession, there
was something that the art of theater
and the art of acting dealt with
[and] developed in people that was
profoundly about what it means to be
a human being in a culture, in a society.
And teaching that in a liberal arts
education environment, made great
sense. I wouldn’t have wanted to teach
in a professional studio in the city,
where what acting is is much more
specific than what I just described.3
An aspect of training that all actors experi-
ence is approaching the question “who am
I?” In the process of being able to accurately
portray the life of another person in a piece,
it is of the utmost importance to know,
to the greatest depths, who this person is.
“Who am I?” encompasses all of the ques-
tions that we ask ourselves every day: who
am I? How do I see myself? How does the
world see me? How does my family see me?
What do I want? How do I get it? How do
I feel if I do or do not get it? The processes
we use in discovering who we are as indi-
viduals are no different from the processes
that trained actors use in discovering who
they are within the worlds they inhabit.
Acting, in a way, is a mode in which those
who practice it are able to understand a
person made real through the words of a
playwright. While we maneuver through
3 Downs, David Downs Conversation.

portion of the people I have spoken with attended or taught at the university before it was renamed. The school was renamed to
reflect its ever growing catalog of academics, including: Communication Sciences & Disorders, Digital Media, and Health Commu-
nication, for example.
this process every single day of our lives, in
one of my conversations with Tom Swift,
an alumnus, it was fascinating to see just
how the “who am I?” comes up in practice
and how he uses it in his daily work life.
Swift is a graduate of Northwestern
University’s School of Speech,4 where he
earned a Bachelor of Science degree in
theatre. He completed his studies under
the instruction of David Downs. He is the
co-founder of the Financial Avengers, a fi-
nancial planning and investment manage-
ment firm based in Oakland, CA, and has
worked in this position for over 20 years.
As of today, the Financial Avengers man-
age over $300 million in client assets. In
our email interaction before our interview,
Swift mentioned that without his training
and background in acting, he would not
have succeeded and that all he ever does
and will ever do is framed by his acting
degree and theatre education. This relates
to Downs’ philosophy stated earlier about
instilling acting into his students’ lives so
that it may become a central part of who
they are as educated human beings. Swift
said this in relation to Downs’ point:
The work that we do with clients
is literally based entirely on acting.
So when we do financial planning,
everyone thinks, “Oh it’s, you know,
all this detailed shit,” and it is — I mean
… you know, there’s mathematics and
economics, and economics is incredibly
fascinating and the numbers don’t lie.
But it’s, you know, only ever about
how people operate around money,
how people operate around finance,
how people operate in the world,
how people operate relative to their
relationship, how people operate based
on, you know, what their parents told
them they could and couldn’t do, what
their parents made them, you know,
become. Their fears are steeped in all of
those human relationships and if you
don’t untangle that, then you’ll never
fundamentally create a financial plan
that addresses their actual needs.5
Part of what Swift is describing lies in the
“who am I?” How people operate around
money is akin to how characters operate
in the environments of their pieces.
Questions such as “why does a character
act this way towards their partner?” and
“why do they think certain ideas about
themselves and about the world?” all
relate directly to questions about why
a person may act the way that they do
around money. The accompanying an-
swers lie in the actors discovering their
relationship to all the factors that make
up their lives, and Swift’s comment ar-
gues that the aforementioned questions
are continuously present even outside the
art of acting.
III. Words, Subtext &
Naturalism
“Death and life are in the power of the
tongue,
And those who love it will eat its fruit.”
-Proverbs 18:21
Words create the universe of a play — they
breathe life. They build the foundations of
civilizations and the flow of thoughts from
one character to another. These words
move the actors through a story and create
images for both themselves and the audi-
ence to follow. To use this manifestation
of power means to create.
5 Swift.
6 “Subtext.”
7 Hensher, “Incomparable Naturalism: Only an Artificer of the Highest Skill Could Have Produced so Seamless an Illusion of Reality.”
8 Borny, Interpreting Chekhov.
With this, it is important to under-
stand the unspoken words that actors are
trained to understand in their studies,
also known as the subtext. Defined by the
Oxford Dictionary, subtext is the “hidden
meaning or theme in a piece of writing or
conversation.”6 Subtext, as per the defini-
tion, is the meaning that lies behind the
mask that explicit words inherently put
over themselves — they are what someone
means to say but decides not to. One of
the most prolific writers known for allow-
ing actors the opportunity to dig into the
meaning lying behind the words is Anton
Chekhov. Throughout his career, Chek-
hov used a naturalistic view of the world
in his writing. In a 2002 piece from The
Atlantic, journalist Philip Hensher said this
about his writing:
His
stories,
like
life,
have
no
beginnings, middles, or ends; they
do not deal in crises and happy
endings; they are simply glimpses of
ordinary lives in their untidiness and
irresolution.7
Having been a practicing physician
before he became a writer, and drawing
from his scientific training, Chekhov be-
lieved early on that literature should show
life as it is. As a materialist, he believed
that in exploring and creating new artistic
worlds, he must employ the “concept of
scientific objectivity in all of his writing” in
order to “depict life as it actually is.”8
The challenge, though, that Chekhov
faced throughout his quest of crafting his
writing to depict life as it is — and where
we may now cue the actors — came from
needing to express life “as it ought to be,
while avoiding being overtly judgemental
or polemical.”9 This then encouraged him to
integrate subtext in the characters’ speech.
Among the various ideas I discussed
with Broadway actress Kate Baldwin,
subtext was one of them. A graduate from
Northwestern’s School of Speech, Kate
Baldwin is a renowned actress noted for
her work in musical theatre. Having made
her Broadway debut in 2000 with the pro-
duction of The Full Monty, she was featured
in several shows following that, including
Big Fish, the 2009 revival of Finian’s Rain-
bow, and the 2017 revival of Hello, Dolly!,
the last two of which garnered her Tony
Award nominations.
I asked her, “What have you learned
about subtext, and how do you think the
knowledge that not everything is seen
as face value has shown up in your life?”
Baldwin replied:
Hmm, that’s — mm-hmm — yeah.10 I find
— I don’t know if you have experienced
this too, but I find even with a close close
friend, if they’re not an actor, I have to ask
them three times how they are to get the
truth. The first answer is always, “I’m fine.”
Are you, though? You know, I mean like.
Actually, a friend of mine talked about
a phrase that he heard that was called
“COVID good.” “How are you?” “Oh, I’m
COVID good.”(laughs) Which is different
from just, like, regular good. I mean, just as
an observant human, you can see a person
— their body can, like, revolt when they
lie, you know? So you say, “Hey, how are
you?” and they go, “Fine.” And then look to
the side and you’re like, “You’re not fine;
you just lied and your eyes are going —
you’re darting to the left,” you know.11
9 Borny.
10 I wish one could hear the inflection she gave of this line. Read as if the subtext is “Oh boy, do I know how this has shown up in
my life.”
11 Baldwin, Kate Baldwin Conversation.
12 As of the COVID-19 pandemic, and as of our interview, this class has been discontinued. Per Uziel-Miller, struggles ensued with
figuring out how to conduct the class virtually, but “hopefully it will get replaced with something similar and maybe even better.”
13 Uziel-Miller.
14 Woodworth, “Acting for Your Life: Ann Woodworth at TEDxEducationCity.”
This technique is all the more fasci-
nating when it comes to discovering how
all of these ideas continue to appear within
another profession: clinical psychology. I
had the privilege of speaking with Nina
Uziel-Miller, a School of Speech class of ‘92
graduate who studied under Dawn Mora.
Working primarily in private practice, Uz-
iel-Miller currently has offices in Chicago
and Evanston, IL. She is a faculty member
at Northwestern’s Feinberg Medical School
and has, for a number of years, taught a class
in which she worked with students in navi-
gating the transition to the medical profes-
sion, addressing topics like work-life bal-
ance and inequities in medicine and helping
them understand themselves and their goals
as they move into working with patients:12
You know, it reminds me of this incident
with a woman and her husband, where
she was just carrying on about apples he
had bought, you know, and, and I said,
“You know, I don’t think we’re talking
about the apples. I don’t think it’s the
apples that matter,” right? And so,
being able to sort of hone in on that and
articulate it is probably informed by my
work as an actor.13
All of these ideas in regard to subtext
connect to the theme of a TEDx Presenta-
tion by Ann Woodworth — kindly directed
to me by Ms. Baldwin — titled “Acting for
Your Life.” In it, Woodworth shares that
social science studies indicate that “86% of
what we communicate … is non-verbal.”14
She goes on to say that of the 14% remain-
ing, 7% is the tone of voice, and only 7%
is content. Just as Uziel-Miller was able to
deduce that her patient’s story about apples
was truly not about apples, this awareness
of subtext requires an understanding of
what these statistics share. Human beings
rarely ever say what they mean directly;
what we truly mean lies in how we say it
and how we show it — through our ac-
tions. Actors are keenly aware of this, for
discovering words and how human beings
present them are part of what they are
trained to know.
IV. Acting as a Science
For quite some time, I have related what
actors do in their training and perfor-
mance to what physicists learn in their
own studies. In order for the following to
make sense, it is necessary to understand
that the process of performance and
human life is the process of motion and
that life is in constant motion: past with
the present and the future, one person
to another, etc. When a play begins, the
plot does not end until the last line, and
even then, the piece’s contents are still in
constant motion with the audience. The-
atre, in this sense, is always moving. Isaac
Newton’s third law of motion states that:
For every action (force) in nature, there
is an equal and opposite reaction. In
other words, if object A exerts a force

V. Conclusion
When speaking to my acting teacher,
who also served as my thesis advisor,
about this research, she asked me to dig
deeper into why I chose this particular
subject — why am I exploring these
questions and these ideas? From studying
under her, I have learned that all actions
have intentions, that I had intention
behind this action — researching these
ideas and writing this thesis — and that I
needed to discover more of that. Truth-
fully, I chose this topic out of annoyance
and anger. Very often, in approaching the
world as an artist, I often receive verbal
or non-verbal responses of “why acting?”
In the early stages of the COVID-19 pan-
demic, I also asked myself this question.
There was a part of me that felt selfish in
exploring this art when I could be invest-
ing my time in what — at that moment
— I had thought to be more “important”
career paths. Needing to consistently jus-
tify to the world and to myself (albeit less
frequently) that my studies and training
as an actor carried with it just as much
merit as other professions made me tired
and also made me question, “Why is this
profession viewed as it is?”
This thought made me think of
Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, pictured below:
20 McLeod, “Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs.”
This pyramid is a motivational theory
in psychology that comprises a five-tier
model of human needs in order of their
importance to a human being. Basic needs
must be met in order to reach the self-ful-
fillment needs. These basic needs are those
close to the bottom of the pyramid: physi-
ological needs, such as food, water, shelter,
etc. The self-fulfillment needs are closer to
the top, involving the achieving of one’s
full potential and including creative needs.
One theory that I have developed
throughout this research relates to why
some believe the study of acting needs to
be justified: it just is not important enough.
I argue that society is in a constant state of
physiological and safety needs, especially
during this pandemic. When one is starv-
ing, everything that they do and every-
thing they strive for becomes about finding
food. They care about nothing else, and as
long as it never truly becomes fulfilled, we
never reach the top, where creativity lies.
Once we as a society, hopefully after this
pandemic, remember the pyramid has five
tiers, we can remember that in order to be
fulfilled as human beings, all of these needs
must be met.
On the other hand, through this proj-
ect, I found myself doing the very thing
that I said I hated doing when explaining
to others my career in acting: justifying it.
In many ways, this paper was a justification
for why acting is important and why it is
more than what many think it is. It allows
us to observe, to discover, to connect, to

any way?

In Indian society, the social divides of
caste, class, gender, and urban/rural
groups fall along the same fault lines as
linguistic divides. These linguistic divides
largely fall into two categories: the elite
and the vernacular. Language — both elite
and vernacular — is always actively chang-
ing; the manner in which it is wielded
defines it as much as the language itself.
A primary example of elite language is the
authoritative discourse found in places of
heteropatriarchal dominance: education,
state government, medical facilities, and
even traditional marriages and households
in India where literature shows agency
and identity usually being wrested from
the woman. In contrast, those not tradi-
tionally given power/authority in society
— lower castes, lower classes, women,
and the rural populations — find them-
selves unable or unwilling to represent
themselves with the elite languages and
ideologies made available to them. Thus,
they are driven to make themselves heard
through a vernacular language instead
(Gupta et al., 812). Though the vernacular
is traditionally thought of as culturally
substandard — in large part because any
subjectivity not sanctioned by the societal
elite is considered illegitimate — it nev-
ertheless has become a way for voices in
these margins to make themselves heard
(Lemke 5). The vernacular emphasizes
the everyday lived and spoken language of
the masses and margins; it is “consistently
anti-hierarchical and anti-exclusionary”
by Tara Shirvaikar

The Rise of the Female
Vernacular:
Contemporary Indian Women
Authors and the Subversion of

Introduction
(Lemke 5). This thesis will further narrow
this definition of vernacular to one of po-
litically gendered identity. This gendered
vernacular centralizes female subjectivity
through the self-expression of embodied
experience and the self-affirmation of the
politics of womanhood and resistance.
Working through a lens of feminist agen-
cy, the vernaculars analyzed in this thesis
deconstruct and reappropriate the central
social concept of female shame.
In English Heart, Hindi Heartland, Rash-
mi Sadana posits that “literature reflects and
represents, but it is also produced and con-
sumed under particular social and political
conditions” (Sadana 27). Through examin-
ing these particular social and political con-
ditions, this thesis will analyze the work of
contemporary Indian women writers, all of
whom explicitly engage with the gendered
politics of language and the overlaps of (and
distances between) their vernacular and
the elite. We will consider an array of gen-
dered vernaculars: tribal languages trans-
lated to Bengali and then to English, Tamil
translated to English, Hindi translated to
English, and then finally original works in
both English and Hindi. All of the authors
discussed in this thesis have deconstructed
elite linguistic structures in some way —
some by repopulating these structures with
their own lived experience and others by
communicating through an embodied ver-
nacular instead. Through undercutting and
mocking the ostensible cultural and socio-
political authority denoted by elite languag-
es like Sanskrit and English, these authors’
1 The particularity and singularity of these literary texts work to ground this essay in a hyper-contextualized space, thus avoiding
any harmful false generalities; as such, the feminine, female experience, woman’s body, or Indian feminisms discussed will always be
that in literature.
feminized vernacularization1 of the elite
language critiques the language’s role in
sustaining heteropatriarchal authority and
colonial power structures, all while working
to subvert these forms of dominance.
Further, Meenakshi Thapan points
out that “oppression, in its psychological
form, is then an experience of a disjunc-
tion between a woman’s body image and
the male constructions of it” (Thapan and
Nehru Memorial Museum and Library
19). Essentially, female internalizations
of the patriarchal constructions of the
female body then inform their own un-
derstanding of their body, agency, and
sexuality. The heteropatriarchal authority
is not external but is an oppressive force
that actually exerts its power from within
the woman through social expectation. In
India specifically, the discourse of shame is
intricately tied with womanhood and hon-
or; shame is the internalized punishment
for transgressing moral codes imposed
and policed by the dominant male social,
cultural, and political ideology. As such,
women are forced to define their identi-
ty within these purely male discourses of
shame and purity/honor (Viswanath 318).
Thus, this thesis locates shame within the
framework of heteropatriarchal power and
understands that these authors are part of
the movement to challenge its political and
social existence/validity.

I. Revealing English
Linguistic Oppression:
“Draupadi” (1981) and
“Neela Scarf” (2014)
The original story of Draupadi from the
Hindu epic The Mahabharata illustrates the
type of female representation and patriar-
chal control that these writers are fighting
to subvert. Indian epics and religious texts
were partially responsible for the sanskri-
tization of norms and cultural values that
are a primary source of violence towards
women even today. By creating female
characters who are forced to uphold re-
alistically impossible standards of purity,
devotion, and compliance, violence is per-
petrated in multiple ways. First, holding
the female body to these heteropatriarchal
standards snuffs out any possibility for fe-
male subjectivity because now the woman
is forced to be the site upon which social
and national ideology and politics are car-
ried out. Second, by worshipping women
as shakti, or goddess, society is able to
justify putting them on a pedestal and then
judge and punish them harshly when they
fail to meet these standards of perfection.
Thus, these works established — and con-
tinue to establish — unreasonable social
expectations for the female body.
In The Mahabharata, Draupadi2 is
forced to marry five brothers by her moth-
er-in-law after a misunderstanding. After
one of the brothers stakes everything —
including his wealth, power, and finally,
Draupadi — in a gambling game to a jeal-
ous king and loses, the king demands that
all of the brother’s possessions, including
Draupadi, appear before him. The king
tries to humiliate Draupadi further by
publicly disrobing her in the court, but the
2 In Hinduism, she is praised as one of the panchakanya (“five virgins”), archetypes of female chastity whose names are believed to
dispel sin when recited. She regained her virginity each year after bearing her five husbands’ children (Bhattacharya).
Hindu god Krishna responds to Draupadi’s
desperate pleas, intervenes, and blesses
her with a never-ending sari. Now, no
matter how much the king pulls her sari
off, Draupadi’s honor is preserved (“The
Story of Draupadi”). This story sets the
tone for the expectation of the treatment
of a female body and character; Draupadi is
never given any choice in husband, home,
or fate, and as a character, she is given no
emotional or sexual subjectivity/desire.
Using Draupadi as an introduction to dis-
cuss the nexus of elite language, religious
and cultural authority and the conventions
of appropriate/pure womanhood, Mahas-
weta Devi reimagines Draupadi through a
feminist lens in her story “Draupadi.”
Mahasweta Devi, a prominent Bengali
author and tribal activist, wrote “Draupa-
di” originally in Bengali and a tribal dialect
(Swaminathan). Later translated to En-
glish with a foreword written by Gayatri
Chakravorty Spivak, “Draupadi” is situated
against the Naxalite movement, the Ban-
gladesh Liberation War in 1971, and the
Hindu epic The Mahabharata. Written in
the style of a military report about the ap-
prehension of tribal rebels, the short story
is about Draupadi (Dopdi) Mehjen, a fight-
er who, along with her erstwhile husband
Dulna, murders the wealthy landlord in the
area to gain access to and democratize the
well water during a seasonal drought. She
is then apprehended by Officer Senanayak
who demands that she be raped by his offi-
cers so he can break her resistive silence and
find out more information about the rebel
uprisings that the military is there to quell.
Dopdi Mehjen brings English closer
to a lived language, not just a language
of colonial and state domination. When
Draupadi is captured and raped by multiple
men, she is described like a wounded wolf,
with raw animalistic power — she rips
the clothes they give her to cover up her
wounded body with her teeth and pours
the water they give her to clean her wounds
on the ground. By refusing the narrative of
shame placed upon women’s bodies, Dopdi
retools the language of rape, refusing the
silence that often excuses that violent be-
havior, and as an ultimate subversion of
power, she refuses to cover herself in the
clothes they give her.
Dopdi finally goes to meet Officer
Senanayak, unclothed, and Senanayak’s
theoretical knowledge of the tribals col-
lides with the reality of a wounded tribal
woman, turning the tables, and leaving
him afraid and ashamed:
The object of your search, Dopdi
Mejhen. You asked them to make me
up, don’t you want to see how they
made me? Draupadi wipes the blood
on her palm and says in a voice that is
as terrifying, sky splitting, and sharp
as her ululation, “What’s the use of
clothes? You can strip me, but how can
you clothe me again? Are you a man?
… There isn’t a man here that I should
be ashamed. I will not let you put my
cloth on me. What more can you do?
Come on, counter me – come on, counter
me.” Draupadi pushes Senanayak with
her two mangled breasts, and for the
first time Senanayak is afraid to stand
before an unarmed target, terribly
afraid (Spivak and Devi 402).
This is the most powerful moment in the
story where Dopdi has the last word, and
Officer Senanayak is reduced to silence.
Dopdi refuses to be shamed into being
dominated by masculine subjectivity and
instead asserts her own. She places blame
on Senanayak and mocks him by referring
to herself as “the object of [his] search.”
The italicization and repetition of “counter”
foregrounds Dopdi’s vernacularization
of the word officially used by the army,
“encounter.” A technical, passive term that
obscures the actual violence that the army
does to bodies, “encounter” is an example
of exactly the way in which English is
used to dominate a subjugated population
through, in this instance, rape or sexual
assault. Dopdi actively challenges this, and
then by mirroring his violence with her
body, she reverses the semiotics of shame
and thrusts it back into the face of Sena-
nayak. She refuses to be covered by that
language and instead names the violence
inscribed on her body, her land, and her
people; she turns the verb from passive
to active. “Draupadi” draws attention to
the feminine vernacular of Dopdi and
contrasts it with the masculine violence
of English. Initially, the reader sees the
officer’s desire to dominate or conquer
the subaltern by dominating her linguistic
meaning, and the story ends with Dopdi’s
By creating female
characters who are
forced to uphold
realistically impossible
standards of purity,
devotion and
compliance, violence is
perpetrated in multiple
ways.
refusal to succumb to violence at both a
bodily level (indicated by her refusal to
cover up) and a linguistic level (by sub-
verting “encounter” with “counter”). Though
she is unclothed in a camp of men, she
subverts the physicality of her body from
weakness and vulnerability to power by
calling into question the masculinity and
humanity of Senanayak’s actions and
making him come face to face — literally
— with his actions and the consequences
of his theory of “knowledge” dominance
through her appropriation of English.
Describing her presence and power as
“terrifying, sky splitting, and sharp as her
ululation,” Devi is once more calling into
mind the tribal connection to land and
tight community as well as reminding
the reader that the female power and
naturalistic vernacular upon which Dopdi
draws comes from there. Dopdi daring
Senanayak to “counter” her is to dare him
to counter all of those reserves of power
and is her taking his agency into her own
self. He is unable to even question her
presence and assert his power because
she is reappropriating his English as her
vernacular and recreating her body as a
space for feminine resistance by using it
to assert her socio-political subjectivity.
Thus, the link between the vernaculariza-
tion of language and a woman’s embodied
experience is made clear: she refuses both
with her words and with her body to
submit to the violent appropriation that
both the English language and a rape/
assault demand from her, and her refusal
and reimagination of that conventional
script causes fear.
Whereas English plays an active, mil-
itaristic role in “Draupadi” to perpetuate
physical violence, the medicalized English
in the Hindi-language short story “Neela
Scarf” highlights a different form of physical
and emotional violence grounded in female
isolation. Applauded for its unfiltered look
into the female mind, “Neela Scarf” by Anu
Singh Chaudhary is a collection of short
stories published in 2014 that depicts female
narratives across different classes and geog-
raphies in India (Fazili). The eponymous-
ly-named short story is centered around the
protagonist’s refusal to submit to the for-
malized heteropatriarchal violence and clin-
ical isolation that English represents, so she
revolts by only communicating through her
embodied experiences. The story is centered
around a newly married couple, Shambhavi
and Amitesh, and the breakdown of their
trust in each other and eventually their rela-
tionship. Three months into their marriage,
Shambhavi gets pregnant, and Amitesh,
claiming that he is not ready, forces her to
get an abortion even though she wants to
keep the unborn baby. After the abortion
procedure, Shambhavi retreats from the
marriage both mentally and emotionally.
The second time she gets pregnant three
years later, Amitesh wants to keep it, but
there are pregnancy complications because
of the previous abortion, and she must un-
dergo another abortive procedure and loses
her fallopian tubes in the process. After she
recovers, she decides she needs a break from
her strained, barely standing marriage and
pursues an opportunity for a fellowship
abroad. The story ends with Shambhavi not
knowing whether she will return.
Although no words are written in Ro-
man script, there are many English words
integrated into the Hindi prose in Devana-
gari script. Categorized by frequency, En-
glish medical and physical language is the
most common, followed by the language of
money and business,3 and then the language
of technology and departure.4 Since the
medical language is the most common, this
thesis will focus on analyzing that, starting
with how both Amitesh and Shambhavi
refer to the abortion. It is clear that one is
able to note a greater level of comfort and
intimacy denoted here through the use of
Hindi versus English. Whenever Amitesh
refers to abortion, he calls it an “अबॉर्शन”
(the English word “abortion” written in
Devanagari), while Shambhavi refers to it
as “उसके विदा हो जाने की दुआ माँगे” (praying for
its departure;5 Choudhary 107). When
Amitesh uses “abortion” in English, he dis-
tances himself from the child and any emo-
tional complications that would be associ-
ated with its loss. The constitution of the
fetus’s body is negated; Amitesh’s dismissal
of the baby’s body through the medicalized
language becomes a “key locus for … [his]
exercise of power” (Berg and Bowker 533).
However, in Shambhavi’s vernacular con-
struction, she is already giving the child
some subjectivity by wondering whether it
will take some action (in this case, depart).

The third-person descriptions of her visits
to the hospital are saturated with clinical
English words6 such as “pregnancy kit,”
“bleeding,” “ultrasound,” and “sanitary
napkin” (Choudhary). Further, the diag-
nosis of Shambavi’s Obsessive Compulsive
Disorder (OCD) is again indicative of the
cold, medical Western vocabulary of scien-
tific diagnosis and clinical procedure. This
clinical English disavows the embodied ex-
perience she is going through; no thought
is given to offering emotional, personal
support for having gone through an abor-
tion or for living life with OCD. Instead,
in a form of epistemic violence, her own
life is articulated to her in a foreign, for-
malized English.7 She is categorized and
“configured” with English words of proce-
dure and diagnosis (Berg and Bowker 514).
Once her mental and physical “disorder[s]”
are named, she is cast aside by both her
husband and Western medical procedure.
Then, when she does not behave as her
husband expects and begins retreating
from the marriage because of the forced
abortion, Amitesh uses English words
“She no longer has any need for her own body and
subjectivity to be validated — and governed — by the
specter of heteronormativity, embodied ignorance, and
apathy.”
once again to describe her silence and push
her further away. Describing Shambhavi,
he says, “Formal. Curt. Ceremonious. Si-
lent. Amitesh did not want to believe it”8
(Chaudhary 104). The concept of negative
space plays a large role in showcasing the
growing distance between the two people
and also the helplessness that Shambhavi
later becomes ashamed of. The auditory
manifestation of this negative space is the
silence present in their relationship, the
physical manifestation of the space is her
empty womb, and emotionally, it rep-
resents the lack of space she is allowed to
take up in her and Amitesh’s marriage and
home. Notably, the only way in which she
is able to escape her feeling of helpless-
ness and betrayal to her child is by leaving
the space that Amitesh occupies, and she
drives this point home by leaving the blue
scarf she bought to impress him on one of
their first dates back in the airport when
she departs. She no longer has any need for
her own body and subjectivity to be vali-
dated — and governed — by the specter of
heteronormativity, embodied ignorance,
and apathy.
However, instead of accepting the de-
humanization and isolation that follows the
procedural dialects of English, she rejects
this language and thus refuses to obfuscate
her unborn child through the medicalized
English language. Instead, Shambhavi’s
articulation of her state of mind and heart
is through a specific discourse of the body.
When she does speak or emote, it is either
through embodied emotion (for exam-
ple, her teary eyes) or through vernacular
language that calls into being the body of
her absent baby. Most of Shambhavi’s di-
alogue is assumed to happen off the page

or is made up of curt sentences traded with
Amitesh. However, here she is given the
opportunity to verbalize the baby’s life into
the world for the first time. Shambhavi’s
longest dialogue by far is with her doctor,
who tells her she is pregnant. She replies,
“I know. And I also know that by this time,
the heart of the child must have started to
form, and the brain as well. I know that her
eyelashes must have started forming, and
she may too have a twist in both elbows”9
(Chaudhary 108). By listing its body parts,
she characterizes the physical space and
shape the baby inhabits in her womb and
also the negative space that will be left when
it is gone. Unlike Amitesh, who wishes to
remain clinically abstracted and detached
from the fetus, Shambhavi refuses to use
the word “abortion” throughout the whole
story. She only ever asks forgiveness from
the unborn child and prays that it stays well
after it “departs.” For everyone else, focus-
ing on the humanness of the unborn body
is a problem, but she insists on verbalizing
it and their connection into reality.
II. Rejecting Sanskritized
Shame: “Mitro Marjani”
(1967) and “When I Hit You:
Or, A Portrait of the Writer as
a Young Wife” (2017)
Supported by culturally and religiously
fundamental stories such as “Draupadi,” the
notion of the ideal woman as chaste, pure
of body and mind, and loyal to the patriarch
became the popular one. Even in contem-
porary literature, we see an expectation of
the woman to behave this way, as well as a
justification of violence towards the woman
if she does not. The characterization of Mi-
tro in “Mitro Marjani” allows the reader to
explore shame as a social discourse as well
as its deconstruction by Mitro both in her
articulation of her body and in her physical
uncovering of it. Building upon Mitro’s
exploration of her femininity, Meena Kan-
dasamy’s “When I Hit You: Or, A Portrait
of the Writer as a Young Wife” further
explores the gendered language of sexuality
through the protagonist’s radical rejection
of her husband’s violent representation of
female sexuality.
In 1967, Krishna Sobti — one of the
leading female Hindi authors of the twen-
tieth century — wrote “Mitro Marjani,”
arguably her most famous work. In it, she
depicts a family drama centered on the
defiant daughter-in-law of a middle-class
Punjabi family. The middle daughter-in-
law, Sumitravanti (whose nickname is
Mitro), is the most outspoken of all the
daughters-in-law, constantly facing threats
of violence from Sardarilal (her husband),
harsh reprimands from Dhanvanti (the
matriarch), and scorn from Suhag (the first
daughter-in-law) for her improper behav-
ior. The most controversial aspect of “Mi-
tro Marjani” is the fact that the dialogue
is imbued with such potent female sub-
jectivity. At various points in the novella,
Mitro speaks freely about her sexual desire
and her body. After a family argument
10 “मित्रो, तेरी देह क्या निरा शीरा है-शी-रा ! उस नास-होने से कहती हूँ... -अरे, इसी शीरे में तेरी जान को डंक मारते सर्पों की फौजें पलती हैं !” (Sobti).
11 “मँझली लेटी-लेटी उठ बैठी । हाथों से छातियाँ ढँक मग्न हो कहा-सच कहना, जिठानी सुहागवन्ती, क्या ऐसी छातियाँ किसी और की भी हैं ?...सुहाग का तन-बदन फुँकने लगा ।”
(Sobti).
about Mitro’s behavior, she speaks to the
first daughter-in-law, Suhag, mocking her
husband: “Banwari [the eldest son, Suhag’s
husband] says — Mitro, your body is all
honey, pure honey! I tell the rascal — in
this milk and honey of mine, there writhe
the serpents of your own desires!”10 (Sobti
trans. Yadav 17). Then after taking all of
her clothes off, Mitro asks Suhag, “‘Tell me
the truth, Jethani, does any other wom-
an have breasts like these?’ Rage blazed
through Suhag”11 (Sobti trans. Yadav 18).
First, it is pointedly cruel of Mitro to
talk about her sexual power over Suhag’s
husband with Suhag. With Suhag repre-
senting the “ideal” daughter-in-law, Mitro
posits herself as superior to Suhag and thus
positions herself above the expectations
of the household. Through the repetition
of “honey,” the reader gets the sense that
Mitro is reveling in her own body. Mitro is
intimately aware of her body, of the phys-
ical space it takes up, and of its powerful
capabilities as a sexed body; she dismisses
Suhag’s normativity as simple hypocrisy.
Even while Mitro is unapologetically cele-
brating the female body, she still emphasiz-
es that the male eye is more sinful than the
female body. In recognizing that and thus
taking power away from the male gaze,
she begins to reassert her own subjectiv-
ity. By discussing her body parts, bodily
Mitro is empowering herself because she is creating
a space where she does not have to suppress her
subjectivity and submit to sanskritized notions of purity
and honor.
processes such as menstruation, and sexual
innuendos, Mitro reclaims the female body
for herself. She does not let the family —
or any other authority — dictate what she
wears, how she acts, and what she says.
By not suppressing these thoughts and by
verbalizing this body-centric, sexualized
discourse, Mitro is empowering herself
because she is creating a space where she
does not have to suppress her subjectivity
and submit to sanskritized notions of puri-
ty and honor.
One of the most remarkable parts of
Sobti’s novella is how she constructs the
clash between the patriarchal gaze and
Mitro’s sexuality. In the novella, Mitro not
only lays claim to her own body but also
turns an accusatory eye towards Sardari-
lal’s body and sexuality. Her deliberate and
continual provocations of Sardarilal spring
from her unfulfilled sexuality. She says,
“The dullard! Had [he] any manhood, [he]
would have either licked me all over with
relish or torn me apart like a lion” (Sobti
trans. Yadav 16-7). Sobti problematizes the
phallocentric view of sexuality by showing
Mitro taking control of the sexual dynamic
between the two; though her takeover is
steeped in stereotypical images of man-
hood, hypermasculinity, and male sexuali-
ty, she nonetheless is able to turn a reverse
gaze to Sardarilal and his supposed author-
ity over her body. He, in turn, is thrown off
guard because the sex is not on his terms.
In response, Sardarilal becomes physical-
ly abusive whenever Mitro misbehaves.
This violence is another manifestation of
his own male insecurity due to Mitro now
controlling the narrative and discourse
of shame within the novel, as well as his
inability to verbalize his problem with her
objectification of him (Hoque). Incredibly,
Mitro is able to dominate the subjectivi-
ty within their relationship through her
embodied language and fully reappropriate
her body through language of desire.
Written exactly half a century after
“Mitro Marjani,” Meena Kandasamy’s
English novel “When I Hit You: Or, a Por-
trait of the Writer as a Young Wife” also
reveals the dynamics of a heteropatriarchal
household. Similar to Mitro, this unnamed
protagonist finds power in the verbaliza-
tion of her body and subjectivity, with one
key difference being that in Kandasamy’s
novel, the protagonist’s husband uses that
same female sexuality to abuse and shame
her in a far more violent and explicit way
than Mitro’s husband ever does. Set during
the first couple of months of an increas-
ingly manipulative and abusive marriage,
the unnamed female protagonist details
the burgeoning emotional, physical, and
sexual violence she faces. Although the
protagonist falls in love with a passionate
Marxist professor in a whirlwind romance,
she quickly realizes after their marriage
how abusive and controlling he really is.
Initially forcing her to give him her email
and social media passwords, he eventually
controls her internet time, clothing, job
prospects, phone time with family, and ev-
ery single other aspect of her life until the
only respite she has left is her writing.
As the relationship gets increas-
ingly violent, the protagonist’s husband
uses specifically female sexed language to
harm her because he feels threatened. Fe-
male sexuality has a negative, insatiable,
and dangerous connotation because, like
other independent female functions (i.e.,
menstruation, childbirth), it cannot be
controlled by the man. Thus, it provides
a significant threat to the level of control
the husband wants to have over the pro-
tagonist (Viswanath 315). In an effort to
“control” her, he constantly shames her for
being a dirty, sexually loose woman. After
getting mad that his provocations are no
longer garnering a reaction from her, he
rapes her so she can “prove it to [him]
that [she is] not thinking of another man.”
Over her screams, he continues, “You are
a whore. This is what whores do. … How
many men took you from behind? How
many? … Fucking cheap whore” (Kan-
dasamy, When I Hit You 102). In the whole
passage, “bitch” is repeated twice, “whore”
is repeated seven times, and “cunt” three
times. The sheer onslaught of slurs that are
meant to demolish the female spirit and to
disrespect and violate the female body is
significant. The husband twists the gen-
dered language of women’s bodies in order
to inflict pain and bring shame to his wife.
The narrator later writes:
The coarseness of my husband’s insults
makes me cringe. I’m ashamed that
language allows a man to insult a
woman in an infinite number of ways.
… Every part of my body is a word spat
out in disgust. My cunt, sequestered and
quarantined, is nothing but a spittoon
for his insults. Once, this language
… was a secret place of pleasure
(Kandasamy, When I Hit You 106).
Kandasamy reveals language to be gen-
dered, steeped in heteropatriarchal ideol-
ogy, and predetermined towards favoring
the man. The narrator recalls parts of her
body as if she is dismembered but also to
preserve them by verbalizing them. The
final body part — the cunt — is forced
into submission, as if a wild animal, to
take whatever the man chooses to throw
at it. The image of a “spittoon” used in the
quote is exacting here: the female body is
dismembered and then, in turn, made into
the passive receptacle for those very body
parts as they are turned into insults that
are hurled back at the woman.
However,
the
protagonist
in
Kandasamy’s “When I Hit You: Or, A
Portrait of the Writer as a Young Wife” is
able to further reappropriate English as her
own vernacular. Since the protagonist is
an author by trade, this novel also discuss-
es her shifting relationship with English,
Tamil, language in general, and writing as
a form of resistance and self-preservation.
While an authoritative abuse of English
(emerging from colonialism) is one form
of perpetuated heteropatriarchal violence
against women, another far older form is
using the cultural discourse of female own-
ership under the guise of a familial bond.
Where before, the protagonist was violat-
ed physically by her husband and by En-
glish, she now uses English as a vernacular
form of self-expression and preservation.
As her husband slowly erases all semblance
of autonomy from her life, including the
ability to write without incurring violence,
the protagonist starts writing these letters
to imaginary lovers and herself as a form of
private rebellion: “Each of my letters, I de-
lete after I have finished typing them. Ev-
ery line I have written to you is a thought-
crime, a crime that does not leave a trail of
evidence, a crime that is not even a crime”
(Kandasamy, When I Hit You 67). The repe-
tition of the word “crime” four times high-
lights the simple absurdity and desperation
of a situation where writing letters would
be considered an act so offensive as to be
labelled a crime. The only crime is that the
protagonist is daring to retain some sense
of identity and subjectivity through the act
of writing these love letters. Here, she is
rebelliously reoccupying the English space
with which she was so intimate before her
marriage turned it against her. In one of
her letters, she writes:
I imbue the word kiss with the idea of
clandestine; I smuggle the thought of
me into the word caress. You can never
dislodge me from each of the words
I’ve meticulously occupied. … English
makes me a lover, a beloved, a poet.
Tamil makes me a word huntress, it
makes me a love goddess (Kandasamy,
When I Hit You 60).
In regaining a semblance of power through
a repossession of both of her vernaculars
— English and Tamil — she begins to feel
empowered once more. English becomes
a space with reciprocal love and physical
affection, a concept so foreign to her that
she feels she must “smuggle” herself back
into the word “caress.” Tamil goes one step
beyond the English docility and makes her
a warrior; she feels so uplifted by being
able to communicate her desires and
thoughts through her own vernacular that
she secures in herself the subjectivity that
her husband is trying to snuff out.
III. Concluding Thoughts
As women writers begin to understand
how our language shapes thought, they
can then begin to push back and repop-
ulate our uses of the language — their
vernaculars — with their own agency/
identities instead of mirroring the male
subjectivity which social discourse tends
to follow. This is exactly what Mahaswe-
ta Devi and Gayatri Spivak, Anu Singh
Chaudhary, Krishna Sobti, and Meena
Kandasamy are able to accomplish with
their produced literature. Whether in
English, Hindi, a tribal language, or the
language of the body, this vernacular
creates space for the female subjectivity
to exist and be heard in contemporary
literature and society. Looking ahead,
in her book of essays “My Friend, My
Enemy,” Ismat Chughtai, one of India’s
most foundational feminist writers in
the twentieth century, writes about
her wish for women in India to achieve
true equality in name, in reality, and in
language, stating that “the heroine of the
future will be neither heartless nor op-
pressed. She will be only a woman, and
instead of giving her the title of ahramen
[Satan] and yazdaan [God], writers will
bless her with the title of woman. And
then the process of construction will
begin” (Chughtai and Naqvi). ◆
As women writers begin
to understand how our
language shapes thought,
they can then begin to
push back and repopulate
our uses of the language
— their vernaculars —
with their own agency/
identities instead of
mirroring the male
subjectivity which social
discourse tends to follow.
Steubenville Ghazal
Steubenville, Ohio 2013
It was hard not to notice the style of him.
We were all mesmerized by the smile on him.
Snaps, sexts. He might. I might not.
Friends teased, Post a pic of your thigh for him.
There’s a strip mall, a steel mill, the long Veteran’s Bridge.
The white picket grin was the lie of him.
A basement. The music. Coats draped on the couch.
I kept drinking and thinking, don’t be shy with him.
He posed for the camera, his hand on my neck.
I lay still underneath the hard guile of him.
I dream I’m clear wind, I dream I’m blank space,
I dream of the girl who’s surviving him.
Skank. Slut. Cunt. Whore.
What did you expect? is the cry from them.
Skank. Slut. Cunt. Whore.
These are the facts from the trial of him.
In Delhi, a bus. In Houston, a bridge.
There’s New Bedford, Toronto, Dubai for him.
For a girl to be innocent she has to be dead.
The newspapers await a reply from him.
My name is redacted, it no longer applies.
I end every line writing him, him, him.

Department of International Studies
Faculty Adviser: Prof. Lauren Stokes, Ph.D.
The Cultural Legacy of American
Atrocity Against Civilians During the
War in Vietnam
Introduction
It is Strange How War Never Ends For
Those Involved.1
On March 16, 1968, American soldiers
carried out a search-and-destroy operation
in the Son My village of South Vietnam.2
Quang Ngai province, called Pinkville by
American GIs, had a “reputation as a Viet
Cong hotspot.”3 The village includes the
hamlets of My Lai, My Khe, Tu Cung,
and Co Luy; each hamlet includes several
sub-hamlets. Though the province was sup-
posed to be an “enemy bastion … American
forces encountered no organized resistance
on the morning of March 16th, either in
My Lai 4 or My Khe 4.”4 US troops killed
an estimated 567 Vietnamese civilians.5
Though the massacre did not occur entirely
in either My Lai or My Lai 4, the atrocity is
known as the My Lai Massacre.
The troops at My Lai 4 belonged
to Charlie Company, led by Lt. William
Calley. Calley was ultimately the only
person convicted for his involvement in
the massacre. Lt. Calley’s conviction was
received with bipartisan backlash.6 People
opposed to the verdict believed either that
the military was using Calley as a scape-
goat or that he had done nothing wrong.
President Nixon felt justified in pardoning
Calley because of the outcry. He shared
“the opinion of many Americans” that My
Lai was “an aberration, unrepresentative
of our country.”7

Real American War in Vietnam (New York: Picador, 2013), 51–53.
3 Howard Jones, My Lai: Vietnam, 1968, and the Descent into Darkness, Pivotal Moments in American History (New York, NY: Oxford

However, Nick Turse argues in his
book Kill Anything That Moves that the My
Lai Massacre was not an aberration but
“part of a consistent pattern of criminality
resulting from policies set at the top.”8 In
order to reframe it as an anomaly, the mili-
tary and the Pentagon focused their investi-
gations only on the killings at My Lai 4 and
the subsequent cover-up of those killings;
they did not investigate the killings at My
Khe 4. According to Turse, the “killings of
civilians … were widespread, routine, and
directly attributable to U.S. command pol-
icies.”9 While there were codes of conduct
that were supposed to protect noncomba-
tants, they mostly functioned to give the
military deniability, since actual conduct
differed greatly from what was on paper.10
Officials were desperate to reach the so-
called ‘crossover point,’ which was when
they killed more guerilla fighters than the
Viet Cong could recruit; that goal, along
with the military’s intentional indoctrina-
tion of racism against Vietnamese people,
led to the ‘mere-gook rule,’ or MGR, which
held that Vietnamese people were less than
human. Success was measured by the num-
ber of Vietnamese killed-in-action, and
“the mere-gook rule promised that any
dead Vietnamese would do.”11
Turse’s point that the military used
racism as a tool to instill in soldiers the abil-
ity to kill readily and ruthlessly connects
to two concepts that Mimi Thi Nguyen
employs in The Gift of Freedom. Nguyen’s
work studies how America’s promise to
deliver freedom to populations around the
world, often through war and violence, in-
evitably and inescapably colonizes the sub-
jects of that freedom by imposing on them
an unpayable debt. Nguyen deploys the
Vietnamese refugee as a double target of
the gift of freedom: the first time through
war and the second time through refuge.
Two ideas Nguyen employs are necropo-
wer and Foucault’s economy of biopower.
The former is “the idea that some deaths
don’t matter,” and the latter views racism as
“the politics of disposability.”12 To learn to
kill without hesitancy is to learn that cer-
tain people are disposable.
In the following chapter of my thesis,
I examine the work of Vietnamese-Amer-
ican writers about the war and their ex-
periences as immigrants in the United
States. I use Mimi Thi Nguyen’s book The
Gift of Freedom: War, Debt, and Other Refu-
gee Passages to frame my close readings of
Viet Thanh Nguyen’s The Sympathizer and
Qui Nguyen’s Vietgone. Many Vietnamese
victims of the massacre at My Lai are not
living and are therefore unable to share
their side of the story. Given this reason, I
examine works by Vietnamese-Americans
for their perspective of American involve-
ment in Vietnam and the Vietnamese ref-
ugee experience.
Before I begin my analysis, I would like
to first address how I choose to reference
the war, since the name itself has inescap-
able implications. Both the ‘Vietnam War,’
the term Americans use, and the ‘American
War,’ the term many Vietnamese use, over-
simplify the conflict. For example, Laotians

among others, in his book Nothing Ever Dies,
Viet Thanh Nguyen refers to the conflict as
“the war.” He argues, “to deny it a name …
clears a space for reimagining and remem-
bering the war differently. Denying this war
its name also acknowledges what everyone
who has lived through a war already knows:
their war needs no name, for it is always
simply the war.”14 Renny Christopher ar-
gues that calling the war “Vietnam” erases
“all distinctions between enemy and ally
and among Vietnamese individuals,” con-
flating the country with “war and evil,” and
is another way of victimizing U.S. soldiers
by placing blame on the amalgamation of
country and war itself. To challenge typical
connotations associated with the name ‘the
Vietnam War,’ I will instead use the term
‘the war in Vietnam,’ or simply ‘the war.’
Chapter: We Could Never
Forget
We have been the subjects of that
experiment they call, with a straight
face, the Cold War. What a joke, given
how hot the war has been for us.15
Biopower, Necropower, and PTSD
American stories about the war do not de-
pict Vietnamese people or their experiences
accurately or empathetically. Whether
Vietnamese people are stereotypical sup-
porting characters or extra bodies to be
blown up in the background, their lack of
humanity and complexity suggests that
they are ‘other,’ ‘alien,’ and less than white
Americans. This attitude seeps into and
shapes cultural narratives about the war
and Vietnamese refugees. I will perform
close readings of excerpts from Viet Thanh
Nguyen’s The Sympathizer and Qui Nguyen’s
Vietgone, using Mimi Thi Nguyen’s reading
of trauma as a tool of neoliberal war-mak-
ing as a framework for my analysis in order
to understand how these works counteract
cultural narratives that dehumanize Viet-
namese people and humanize and center
perpetrators of violence.
Mimi Thi Nguyen, like Nick Turse,
also critiques the erasure of systemic vio-
lence from the American consciousness.
She examines how the idea of trauma op-
erates differently on American veterans
than on Vietnamese refugees in ways that
ultimately absolve not only the soldiers
who committed the violence but American
war-making itself. Put simply, she argues
that American veterans can be divorced
from their trauma, which reinforces their
humanity by highlighting their mental and
emotional pain. However, refugees are
defined by their trauma and limited to the
category of ‘displaced person,’ a permanent
status which they must perpetually work
to overcome but can never overcome. As
Nguyen states, “to be given freedom is a
process of becoming without being.”16
Foregrounding
Post
Traumatic
Stress Disorder (PTSD) in American vet-
erans reframes American violence against
racial others, transforming perpetrators

(USA: Duke University Press, 2012), 18.

what they had witnessed and by what they themselves had done.” Didier Fassin and Richard Rechtman, The Empire of Trauma: An
Inquiry into the Condition of Victimhood, trans. Rachel Gomme (United States: Princeton University Press, 2009), 91.

of brutality into victims of “unimaginable
pain.”17 The victimization of perpetrators
humanizes them by using their pain and
suffering as proof of their humanity.18 In
addition, their victimhood eclipses the
people toward whom they committed
violence and obscures the effects of the
violence inflicted on their victims. Finally,
the emphasis on their pain “rescue[s] lib-
eral empire[s] from the criminality of its
wartime conduct” by framing American
violence against racial others (in this case,
Vietnamese civilians) as an aberration
rather than a fundamental tool of Ameri-
can foreign policy.19 Because of the harm-
ful psychological consequences soldiers
experience after perpetrating violence, lib-
eral war is able to claim that such violence
is an anomaly. In fact, “public disclosures
about cruelties committed by U.S. military
forces — including the My Lai massacre …
were hugely influential in the diagnosis’s
codification.”20 The diagnosis of PTSD,
regarded as a psychological abnormality,
makes such violence seem aberrant and
atypical. Using Nguyen’s understanding,
it is no surprise that the My Lai Massa-
cre is turned from “insensible destruction
wrought by a supremacist empire” to “a
regrettable failure to discern between the
good racial subject and the bad one” and
“an accident, the unfortunate symptom of
soldier’s unbearable experiences.”21
In contrast, under liberal empires,
the refugee cannot be separated from their
trauma. The refugee becomes not only
a person who is traumatized but also a
displaced person who responds to violence
‘abnormally’ and is defined by their ar-
rested potentiality. Refugees are divorced
from the situations that traumatized them
(i.e., political repression or war). Trauma
comes to signify abnormality and failure in
refugees, rather than the experiences that
harmed them. Unlike veterans, refugees
are burdened with the necessity of reacting
to violence ‘correctly’ or ‘normally’; with-
out a response that is deemed as such, they
are seen as deficient or incapacitated.
If the American military uses racism
as a weapon to engender in its soldiers the
capacity to kill Vietnamese without hesi-
tation, then PTSD absolves the system of
American war-making of blame after the
war ends. In other words, biopower and
necropower operate both during and after
the war. During the war, they enable and
encourage the perpetration of violence;
after, they give way to exoneration over
accountability.
The Sympathizer
The end of the war is near, and a little
Vietnamese boy is “crowned with a Yan-
kees cap … and airlifted into the heavens,
his ultimate destination being [an Amer-
ican soldier’s] family in St. Louis, where
he would be given a golden retriever and
the nickname Danny Boy.”22 This quote
frames the refugee’s passage from the dis-
tant nation of Vietnam to America as an
act of salvation. The young boy’s passing
22 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 157.
23 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 157.
24 Nguyen, The Gift of Freedom, 24–5.
to America is depicted as a spiritually
purifying journey. “Danny Boy’s” method
of travel via helicopter is an act of sanc-
tification; it takes him “to the heavens.”23
The destination — in this case, St. Louis
— and the gifts that await him there are
wholesome and thoroughly American. His
new American family welcomes “Danny
Boy” with open arms, a baseball cap — a
reference to America’s favorite pastime —
and the most idyllic pet possible: a golden
retriever. After his salvation and his pic-
turesque homecoming, Danny Boy’s life is
full of possibility.
Danny Boy’s tale comes from a story
within a story, satirizing America’s refugee
parable. Danny Boy is a character in The
Hamlet, a fictional Hollywood blockbuster
in Viet Thanh Nguyen’s novel The Sympa-
thizer. The film parodies many aspects of
American cinema and American ideology.
Danny Boy’s narrative illustrates not the
genuine refugee experience but rather a
mocking critique of America’s idealistic
understanding of what it has to offer the
disadvantaged racial ‘other.’ For Mimi
Thi Nguyen, America’s gift of freedom
is “composed of pipe dreams, bogus con-
cepts, and moral luck as well as violence at
its origin.”24 By juxtaposing Danny Boy’s
story with The Sympathizer’s main plot,
Viet Thanh Nguyen exposes the refugee
parable and shows that it is in fact what
Mimi Thi Nguyen says it is: a “pipe dream,”
America’s involvement in Vietnam and its ‘rescue’ of
South Vietnamese civilians and soldiers engenders in
him a deep sense of powerlessness.
“bogus,” and born from violence. Instead of
following a young child whose Vietnamese
identity and experience of the war are eas-
ily and effectively erased by a picturesque
American welcome, the novel follows
adult men who take active roles in the war
and are destroyed by it.
The Sympathizer follows an unnamed
North Vietnamese mole — referred to as
the Sympathizer — working for a South
Vietnamese general who relocates to
America after the Communists take over
Vietnam. The book begins days before the
fall of Saigon. Though the Communists
take the capital by the third chapter, the
struggle over Vietnam continues for the
rest of the book. The war is technically
over, but it hasn’t ended strategically or
emotionally for any of the Vietnamese
characters. Specifically, Bon, one of the
narrator’s closest friends and a true be-
liever in democracy and South Vietnam,
suffers a great loss just before their escape
to America. The Sympathizer uses his close
relationship with an Army of the Republic
of Vietnam (ARVN) general to get spaces
for Bon, his wife Linh, and his child Duc
on a plane to America, but Linh and Duc
are shot and killed as they run across the
tarmac towards the plane that will take
them out of Vietnam.
Bon’s story juxtaposes and under-
mines the refugee parable represented by
Danny Boy. Bon and the Sympathizer are
not ‘purified’ or ‘fixed’ by their passage
to America. In contrast to Danny Boy’s
passage — his salvation — after Linh and
Duc are killed on the tarmac, Bon and the
Sympathizer bring their bodies onto the
plane. Their passage is far from purifying
or healing. Bon literally carries his family’s
bodies with him to America, and he is un-
able to leave his pain behind. Leaving their
25 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 223.
bodies is not an option: the Sympathizer
takes Linh’s body and runs onto the plane
without discussion. There is no question
that both he and Bon will bear this pain;
there is no possibility that their passage to
America will heal Bon’s heartbreak.
Once in America, Bon’s loss and his
experiences in the war cannot be smoothed
over or forgotten. In fact, he regrets leav-
ing Vietnam at all, and not only because
Linh and Duc were killed. Fighting for his
country gave him a sense of purpose that
he was willing to give up in order to save
his family, but he ends up losing both. To
him, life in America is not a life worth liv-
ing. Their apartment in Los Angeles is “a
jail cell,” rather than an idyllic new home;
the Americans are their rescuers, but Bon
says, “they just didn’t tell us that they’d
cut off our balls and cut out our tongues
along the way … If we were real men, we
wouldn’t have let them do that.”25 America
offers Bon neither freedom nor possibility.
His escape to America not only costs him
his identity as a father and a husband but
also his identity as a man. Bon’s anger over
his lost masculinity is indicative of his lost
autonomy and control. America’s involve-
ment in Vietnam and its ‘rescue’ of South
Vietnamese civilians and soldiers engen-
ders in him a deep sense of powerlessness.
Bon’s decision to return to Vietnam
underscores America’s inability to heal
him. He volunteers to take part in an oper-
ation to go back to Vietnam in an attempt
to overthrow the Communist government.
The operation is widely acknowledged to
be a suicide mission by characters in the
novel. However, Bon would rather die in
Vietnam than live in America. His faith
in democracy has disappeared, as has his
commitment to any kind of cause. Bon tells
an anticommunist admiral in Thailand, “I
don’t give a damn about saving anybody,
including myself. I just want to kill com-
munists.”26 Bon no longer values his life or
anyone else’s life.
Bon’s experience of coming to and
living in America differs greatly from Dan-
ny Boy’s. In The Hamlet, Danny Boy leaves
behind an older brother who died and a sis-
ter who was sexually assaulted by the Viet
Cong and subsequently disappeared from
the movie. Neither the death of his brother
nor leaving behind his sister impacts Dan-
ny Boy’s quixotic salvation. His potential
pain and regret for leaving them behind is
never even suggested by the movie’s finale.
Instead, a new life with an American fam-
ily offers a simple, neat, and happy ending.
Nguyen’s novel also works against
the narrative propensity to center ex-
periences of the war around those of
Americans. Though implicated, Amer-
icans are not held directly responsible
for any of the main characters’ suffering.
Bon’s wife and child are shot by either the
North Vietnamese Army or South Viet-
namese soldiers (neither is confirmed).
However, Bon’s loss is just one example
of intra-community violence. The pro-
tagonist’s other close friend, Man, was
a Communist double agent working in
the South Vietnamese Army up until the
Communists took over. The day Saigon
falls, Communist planes drop Napalm
bombs on Man and his South Vietnamese
unit. The bomb permanently disfigures
him; as a result, he distances himself from
his wife and children who are disgusted
by and terrified of him. The Sympathiz-
er, who is half-Vietnamese and identifies
as Vietnamese (though other characters
torment him for his biraciality), kills two

dominant American-centric narratives
about the war, the novel remains very

Vietnamese; war is one tool of America’s

national ideology, Nguyen suggests that
Hollywood is more influential.
Hollywood’s ideological and cultural
power are intrinsically linked to violence
and exploitation in Nguyen’s novel. The
Sympathizer often uses violent words and
metaphors involving weapons to describe
the film’s ideological rule in that the mil-
itary-industrial complex and Hollywood
both contribute to “the obliteration of
natives.”31 He describes Hollywood as “re-
lentlessly assaulting the mental defenses of
audiences” and being “the launcher of the
intercontinental ballistic missile of Amer-
icanization,” which ultimately succeeds in
the “lobotomization and pickpocketing of
the world’s audiences.”32 Nguyen creates
an association between America’s military
power and its cultural power. The lan-
guage itself (e.g., the phrases “relentlessly
assaulting” and “obliteration”) is violent
and aggressive. All of these metaphors

The Hamlet also satirizes Hollywood’s
“Vietnam War” movie tropes, including
its inaccurate, shallow, and stereotypical
portrayals of Vietnamese people. Even
though The Hamlet contains speaking roles
for Vietnamese characters, it denies them
full humanity and cultural and ethnic
specificity. The Auteur, the director of the
Movie, adds Binh (nicknamed Benny by
the Americans), his sister Mai, and their
little brother (whose real name is never

Boy by the Americans). None of the Viet-

inaccurate ethnicities and their characters’

tifiably Vietnamese about Binh, Mai, and
Danny Boy. The fact that these characters
are Vietnamese is ultimately not as im-
portant as the fact that they are non-white

These Vietnamese characters are vio-
lently exploited in order to add intrigue to a
story about white Americans. Each of their
plotlines reinforces that the film is, as the
Sympathizer calls it, “an epic about white
men saving good yellow people from bad
yellow people.”36 Binh’s extended, grue-
some death scene underlines the brutality
and viciousness of the Viet Cong while his
body is brutalized and tortured. Mai’s sex-
ual assault, also perpetrated by Communist
soldiers and shown in detail on screen,
functions as shock value and justification
for the annihilation of the Viet Cong.37
Danny Boy’s rescue establishes America’s
benevolence and superiority over this
war-ravaged ‘other’ country. Nguyen is
clear and unequivocal in his determination
that American media — specifically Holly-
wood — is an essential and powerful tool of
American power and ideology.38

Vietnamese-American sources regarding
the war clearly counter the racist tropes of
American narratives by reclaiming agency,

work against America’s refugee parable,
which depicts refugee passage to America
as a spiritual rebirth. Furthermore, The
Sympathizer criticizes Hollywood not only
for the violence against and exploitation
of Vietnamese people within its films but
also for its powerful and destructive role as
a weapon of American power.
The racism that the U.S. military
inoculated in its troops during the war
in Vietnam is not contained within the
specific time and place of war. Mimi Thi
Nguyen’s analysis shows how PTSD is used
to forgive systemic American violence af-
ter wars end. That is one manifestation of
racism, and outright violence is another.
Anti-Asian violence and sentiment has a
long history in the U.S., not beginning or
ending with involvement in Vietnam.
Over the past year (2020), Anti-Asian
violence in the United States has been
exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic,
especially in the Bay Area (San Francisco
and Oakland). The Atlanta Spa shooting
is one recent example, but the reports are
numerous. Vicha Ratanapakdee, who was
84 years old, was pushed to the ground and
died two days later; a 64-year-old Vietnam-
ese mother was robbed in San Jose; and
Noel Quintana, who is 61, was cut across
the face with a box cutter on the New York
City subway.39 American leaders are only
recently beginning to name and address
the issue. President Joe Biden called the
attacks “wrong” and “un-American,” while
Vice President Kamala Harris stated that
the violence is part of a “larger issue.”40
After the Atlanta spa shootings, there has
been an attempt by news outlets and across
social media platforms to highlight the vic-
tims, rather than focus on the shooter.41

Literature Review
Gender-based violence (GBV) is defined
by the United Nations High Commission-

an umbrella term for any harmful act

(i.e., gender) differences between males
and females. It includes acts that inflict
physical, sexual or mental harm or
suffering, threats of such acts, coercion,
and other deprivation of liberty. These
acts can occur in public or in private.4
GBV includes any type of violence that
stems from gender identity or presenta-
tion, including violence against men and
violence experienced by gender non-con-
forming people, who are especially vul-
nerable due to the marginalization of their
gender identity. I discuss eradicating GBV
as the long-term goal in the anti-violence
movement. Eradicating, eliminating, or

olence. This language is adapted from the
