Methodology
Feminist Ethnography and Fieldwork
In this section, I provide my intellectual
genealogy of utilizing feminist ethnogra-
phy. Feminist ethnography grounded in
CRT was employed to guide data collec-
tion and analysis for this project. Christa
Craven and Dána-Ain Davis (2011) define
feminist ethnography as “a project com-
mitted to documenting lived experience
as it is impacted by gender, race, class,
sexuality, and other aspects of participants’
lives.”8 The aim of feminist ethnography is
not to presume an egalitarian relationship
between research and research subjects,
but to acknowledge the power dynamics
at play.9 Anthropologists should be contin-
uously interrogating their role in meeting
the needs of their female and non-binary
subjects. My interlocutors were generous
with their time and knowledge because
they believed that I was doing impactful
work simply by listening to them and
bringing visibility to GBV in immigrant
communities
through
my
academic
research. I argue for the use of feminist
ethnography because this approach can
broaden our understanding of the con-
ditions that lead to violence and map the
intersections between race, ethnicity,
gender, and justice.
Ethnographic Fieldwork (Participant
Observation)
Participant observation involves the day-
to-day aspects of people’s activities, rituals,
and interactions to uncover their culture.10
While participant observation is a common
component of qualitative research and
ethnographic fieldwork, I resist the premise
of the “self” and the “other.” In early ethnog-
raphies, the “self” has historically been the
detached, privileged anthropologist who is
merely present to examine the peculiarities
and deviations of the “other.” Given my
salient identities and personal history with
GBV, I questioned the prevailing dichot-
omy between “self” and “other.” Instead, I
was focused on being an active participant
who was reflexive of my own coexistence
within the same context.
My ethnographic account begins with
a brief history of the South Asian Support
Center and continues with a description of
my involvement and the shelter environ-
ment. The South Asian Support Center is
located in Uptown Chicago, a north side
lakeshore neighborhood home to “Asia on
Argyle,” and has a concentration of Chi-
nese, Vietnamese, Cambodian, Laotian,
and Thai businesses and residents. In the
1970s, the women’s anti-violence move-
ments gave rise to community-organizing
institutions, including domestic violence
shelters.11 In the United States, many Asian
American women spearheaded specific
organizational responses to domestic vio-
lence in the 1980s after questioning their
own communities’ lack of access to main-
stream programs.12 In 1989, the South

to ensure the well-being of residents, meet

My positionality as a researcher
blurred with my roles as an intern and
colleague. I did not interview any clients in
a thesis researcher capacity, yet all of my
interactions with clients created greater
empathy and emotion for their stories. I
experienced vicarious trauma as I spent
countless hours researching gender vio-
lence and poring over transcripts of clients’
and staff members’ interviews. I was fear-

my apartment and scared of alleyways and
men who could emerge from the shadows
at any time. My participant observation
informed my reflexivity as an anthropolo-
gist and reinforced the importance of lived
experiences. I also became acutely aware of
the limits of compassion and the exhaus-
tion of professional care, which influenced
my empathy for frontline workers. In the
later sections of analysis, I will discuss how
the specific limits are reflected in the pro-
fessional experiences of frontline workers.
Interview Process
From August to December 2020, I con-
ducted 14 semi-structured, key informant
interviews
with
frontline
workers.13
Purposeful sampling was used to recruit
female or non-binary identifying frontline
workers within Asian-serving agencies
in Chicagoland.14 My co-workers at the
South Asian Support Center connected me
to other staff members within this small
but mighty community. At the end of each
interview, I used snowball sampling to
recruit additional participants. Once inter-
viewees had a sense of my questions, they
would introduce me to their co-workers if
my interviewees thought that they would
be a good fit.
Interviews ranged from thirty to
eighty minutes, depending on the inter-
viewee. Due to the ongoing pandemic, all
interviews were conducted virtually via
phone or Zoom to follow COVID-safe re-
search protocols. A pre-designed interview
guide with 15 questions was used to frame
the direction of the interview. Follow-up

Enacting Radical Care
The themes discerned from the qualita-
tive analysis will be discussed on the indi-
vidual level. I employ the socio-ecological
framework to highlight how the work
of frontline workers is crucial and inter-
connected on these levels for combating
GBV. The integrated socio-ecological
framework for violence prevention by
the World Health Organization (WHO)
views GBV as the outcome of interactions
at the four levels.15 This provides a holis-
tic approach to understanding the needs
of survivors and contextualizes the range
of factors affecting the lives of women
and non-binary people of color.
Locating Frontline Workers. I define front-
line workers as direct service professionals
who “comfort, advocate for, and assist
victims and survivors of gender-based vio-
lence.”16 They are the “actors who provide
care and support to survivors of violence:
from volunteer-run domestic violence
shelters or community-based organiza-
tions to the increasingly professionalized
service providers giving psychosocial,
therapeutic and legal aid.”17 Within this
ethnography, frontline workers range
from shelter advocates and counselors
to program supervisors and directors. I
focus on the roles that are derived from
and exist within community organizations
rather than public service roles (e.g., police
officers), which intrinsically reproduce
systems of violence and oppression. With-
in my research, I focus on the frontline
workers of five total organizations — three
multi-service organizations (Arab Ameri-
can Family Association, Pan-Asian Health
Center, Korean Community Center) and
two domestic violence (DV) agencies
(Asian Women’s Services Center, South
Asian Support Center).
Individual Level
The first level identifies the life histories
of frontline workers to understand their
motivations and hopes for their work. As
previously stated, they are often the first
line of help in efforts to respond to GBV.

Anthropological scholarship has his-
torically theorized culture in a myriad of
ways. Culture refers to the values, attitudes,
and behaviors that determine definitions
and descriptions of norms within distinct
societies. Within GBV literature, culture is
often scapegoated as the primary influence
of violence. It undeniably plays an important
role in how such societities “view, perceive,
and process sexual acts as well as sexual vi-
olence.”18 However, “culture-blaming” is an
incorrect narrative that does not accurately
reflect the power dynamics at play.
First, “culture-blaming” designates a
perceived dichotomy between “tradition-
al” and “modern” cultures. “Traditional”
cultures, such as immigrant communities
within the United States, have not fully
understood the notions of modern, civi-
lized culture. Therefore, it is argued that
gender violence continues to occur within
these communities; however, this is an
oversimplified argument that overlooks
social, political, and economic inequalities.
Modern societies and cultures are located,
both physically and imaginarily, within
First World nations, many of which are
former colonizers or current neo-coloniz-
ers. Reckoning with the historical implica-
tions of oppression is crucial in doing the
work of radical caring.
First-Generation Immigrants. Of my 14
interlocutors, seven of them — Soo Jin,
Hong, Sharon, Shaima, Sun Hee, Hye
Jin, and Munira — were first-generation
immigrants who immigrated from Asia.
By first-generation, I refer to individuals
who were born to one or both parents
in a country outside of the U.S. and
later immigrated to the U.S. for various
reasons. Studies on the ethnic identity de-
velopment of first-generation immigrants
in educational settings19 have ascertained
that students who have left the comfort of
homes seek affirmation of their ethnicity
and have a strong relationship between
ethnic identity development and self-es-
teem. I believe that my interlocutors seek
similar affirmations through their current
and ongoing work. By serving their cul-
tural and ethnic communities in the U.S.,
they can continue to remain connected to
their parent cultures despite being situated
in the dominant white American culture.
Hong was born in Vietnam and came
to the United States when she was 7 or 8
years old with her then-17-year-old aunt
as a refugee. She recalls leaving Vietnam
in the 1980s as “boat people’’ and going to
refugee camps before finally arriving in the
U.S. This was a formative experience for
her that led to her pursuit of roles that could
give back to her community. She went on to
receive a bachelor’s degree in fine arts and
a master’s degree in expressive art therapy.

then, she has built many relationships
with individual and group clients. Hong
describes how she was able to learn how
to process her emotions, memories, and
experiences through art therapy:
My beliefs in the process of nonverbal
expression or communication mean
that expressive art is not just visual
art but writing and poetry; it could be
music or video; it could be any form
of expression a person may have to
express or explore themselves, or
communicate with another person or
be a part of a community …
Certainly my own experience with
doing art and writing for myself since
I was younger and seeing the power of
that. The process of working with clay
and this particular process triggered
a memory that I was really surprised
by and just seeing how powerful that
process is because I do a lot of work
in understanding myself and my
experiences. Firsthand I see the power
of that, and it’s kind of endless with
infinite possibilities.
Expressive art was an important part of
her journey in understanding her own

Conclusion
This research began out of my curiosities
about the perspectives of female frontline
workers of color within the work of com-
bating GBV. My conversations with my
14 interlocutors — Amina, Diana, Farah,
Hong, Hye Jin, Jang Mi, Jasmin, Jennifer,
Keerthi, Munira, Shaima, Sharon, Soo Jin,
and Sun Hee — demonstrate the complex
interactions between personal, social, and
professional factors that translate in their
radical caring for their ethnic communities.
I have the utmost respect for the
care, compassion, and labor of frontline
workers in addressing and preventing
GBV, often at the expense of personal
trauma to themselves. In the process of
combatting state and interpersonal vio-
lence, however, their stories and labor
also become marginalized and co-opted
through the professionalization of the an-
ti-violence movement. Furthermore, their
roles are often made invisible by the over-
whelmingly white feminist anti-domestic

Elana is a rising senior studying Psychology and Global Health Studies. During her sophomore
year, Elana joined the Development of Identities in Cultural Environments (DICE) Lab, with
Dr. Onnie Rogers. Through her research and extracurricular involvement in Peer Health Ex­
change and the Undergraduate Psychology Association, she has become interested in studying
how human development is shaped by the broader social context.
At the undergrad research expo, Elana and her partner Yola Mzizi presented their findings
from a research project in the DICE Lab, which was led by Dr. Ursula Moffitt. The objective of
this project was to examine how emerging adults made meaning around their racial identities
in a sociopolitical context marked by inequity. To explore this question, they used the lens of
critical consciousness, which suggests that recognizing social inequity contributes to a strong
racial identity and can prompt individuals to take action against injustice. The varying degrees
to which white and BIPOC college students critically engaged in conversations about race were
shaped by their positionality within the system of racism.

Yola Mzizi is a rising senior from Durban, South Africa, majoring in journalism and sociology
and minoring in global health studies. During her undergraduate career, Mzizi has participated in
the Kaplan Humanities Scholar’s Programme, the Undergraduate Research Assistant Programme
(URAP) and she currently holds the position of  creative director for STITCH Magazine, and is a
writer at The Daily Northwestern. Mzizi’s interests in cultural and political reporting, whereby,
she hopes to elucidate complex concepts and issues for the public in order to inspire social justice
action, has motivated her research experience.
Mzizi joined the Development of Identities in Cultural Environments (DICE) lab, a social
psychology lab under the leadership of Dr. Onnie Rogers, in January of 2021 as a research assistant
and member of the URAP cohort. In the lab, Mzizi worked with post-doctoral fellow Dr. Ursula
Moffitt and fellow research assistant Elana Charlson. Mzizi, Moffitt and Charlson’s work hoped to
understand how racial identity development in a time marked by racial violence and political po­
larisation occurred. Mzizi and her co-researchers were interested in how young people gain critical
consciousness and how this enables them to better resist and challenge the systems of racial inequity.
In their project titled “Talking About Race in the Sociocultural Moment: Emerging Adults’ Critical
Consciousness and Racial Identity in Context,” Mzizi and her co-researchers found that in order to
actively resist systemic racism, one needs to have developed a strong racial identity which allows
them to see their racial identity as inextricably tied to the larger socio-political context. This was
particularly imperative for young white people, who, as their data showed, saw race as something
other people had, and racism as individual acts they could sympathise with, rather than seeing how
their racial identity is implicated in the systems of inequity we see today.

Kade Kelley is a third-year student from Falmouth, Maine majoring in biological sci­
ences and chemistry. In addition to research, he is also involved on campus as a Peer
Advisor for incoming first-year students and as a Peer-Guided Study Group Facilita­
tor for Organic Chemistry through the Office of Academic Support and Learning
Advancement (ASLA). Kade first got involved with research in Spring 2021 when he
joined the Radhakrishnan Lab ahead of working over the summer on a Northwestern
Undergraduate Research Grant. Since then, his work has focused on the screening and
computational docking of small molecules in proteins and the experimental assessment
of these interactions.
Kade’s expo project focused on a protein implicated in Parkinson’s disease, Nurr1.
Nurr1 is a nuclear receptor (NR) — a protein that responds to environmental signals,
modulating gene expression through binding small molecule ligands. Unlike other
NRs, however, Nurr1 is an “orphan” NR, lacking the typical ligand-binding pocket.
Instead of binding Nurr1, Kade’s project explores the hypothesis that ligands can bind
a different protein, a coactivator, in order to control NR activation and gene expres­
sion. Although more work is needed to characterize the effect of ligand-binding on the
coactivator-nuclear receptor interaction, current results propose a likely group of lipid
ligands and their binding configurations to the coactivator protein. Since orphan NR
mechanisms have yet to be discovered, and such proteins have vital roles in cellular
metabolism, development, and homeostasis, the research could hold potential implica­
tions for other maladies, too.

Sophie

Black-Owned Small
Businesses in Englewood,
Chicago: Documenting
the Effects of COVID-19
and the Black Lives
Matter Movement in 2020
In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
To better understand the obstacles minority
business owners face and how they are
working to overcome them, my research aims
to document the effects of the COVID-19
pandemic and the 2020 Black Lives Matter
(BLM) movement on Black-owned small
businesses in Englewood, Chicago. The
research employs a mixed-methods approach
by examining foot-traffic data across Chicago
Community Areas and gaining perspective
from Englewood’s Black-identifying small
business owners in one-on-one interviews.
How did you come to your research topic?
When considering topics for my senior thesis
prior to 2020, I took interest in examining the
impacts of crisis events, particularly natural
disasters, on minority communities. When
COVID-19 became a global pandemic and a
simultaneous crisis of police brutality emerged
at the forefront with the BLM movement,
I rewrote my thesis proposal. I hoped that
research on contemporaneous crises would
enhance scholarly understanding of minority
communities’ needs amid crises, which to date
are under-documented. I was eager to leverage
my background in both social policy and
statistical analyses to examine these topics with
a mixed-method approach, as well as apply skills
from my certificate with the Kellogg School of
Management to analyze business operations.
Where do you see the future direction
of this work leading? How might future
researchers build on your work, or what is
left to discover in this field?
Research on the effects of COVID-19 and the
BLM movement will undoubtedly continue
for decades to come, but it is my hope that
academics will prioritize examining minority
communities’ experiences in 2020. Researchers
can specifically build on the present research to
examine policy solutions based on the obstacles
documented in this paper: looting, intra-
community asset building, police response,
and inter-community business visitation.
Because economic disparities are rooted in
systematic racism, the recovery of Black-owned
small businesses from the COVID-19 and
BLM protests is of paramount importance in
supporting the global movement to eliminate
racism. As one participant in the research
expressed, it is my hope that the present
research will not “just be a study,” and it can be
used as a basis for future policy research and
recommendations.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
I will be working as an Associate Consultant
at EY-Parthenon. I completed an internship
at the firm in summer 2020 and look forward
to continuing my education on business
operations.
Keerti Gopal
Framing and Youth Participation in the Sunrise
Movement
In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
I studied the Sunrise Movement’s (Sunrise)
use of narrative framing tactics in digital
media to encourage youth electoral
engagement, arguing that the group provides
an example of how organizations can bridge
the youth movement-electoral politics divide
through a framing that brings outsider,
movement mentality into insider, formal
politics.
How did you come to your research topic?
I started researching Sunrise in 2019 through
a project on youth motivation for activism,
and I joined the organization myself the
same year. Through my experience at the
organization, I started growing curious about
the dissonance I saw between narratives of
youth political apathy and the high levels of
electoral engagement I saw in my peers at
Sunrise. I formulated this project to look at
that gap and soon found Sunrise’s narrative
framing to be incredibly intriguing, leading to
the eventual focus of the project.
Where do you see the future direction of this
work leading? How might future researchers
build on your work, or what is left to
discover in this field?
Since I focused my study on Sunrise alone, it
would be interesting for further research to
look at additional case studies to see if similar
patterns emerge. As digital communication
tactics are constantly evolving, their use in
movement and electoral politics has not yet
been thoroughly studied. There is much left
to discover with regard to how digital tactics
(like social media) are used and what impacts
they might have.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
This year, I will be going to Taiwan for a
Fulbright-National Geographic Storytelling
fellowship to continue my research on youth
climate change activism in a different context.
Ginny Ip
The Impact of Climate
Change on Energy
Poverty: Evidence from
the European Union,
In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
My research uses historical climate data
to explore the potential impacts of climate
change on the proportion of EU households
who find it difficult to meet their basic energy
needs. As average temperatures rise and
both the intensity and frequency of extreme
weather events increase due to the onset of
climate change, there will be a greater need
for heating and cooling. In the absence of
drastic policy changes, how will this affect the
share of energy poor households?
How did you come to your research topic?
During the last two years of my
undergraduate career, I worked as a research
assistant for Professor Reguant, an energy
economist. Our work investigated the
distributional impacts of real-time electricity
pricing in Spain as opposed to a fixed rate.
What we found was that real-time pricing
can often be regressive, meaning that it
disproportionately places a bigger burden
on low-income households. This made me
wonder how this might change against a
backdrop of climate change, not only in Spain
but across Europe and the rest of the world.
Where do you see the future direction of this
work leading? How might future researchers
build on your work, or what is left to
discover in this field?
My work only serves as a starting point in
examining the relationship between climate
change and energy poverty at the regional
level. Future researchers can build on my
work by conducting further analysis in other
contexts, especially those in the global south
that will be hardest hit by climate change.
Additionally, climate change is an ongoing
process. This means that as the world
continues to change and more data becomes
available, it is important to update these
findings to inform more accurate and reliable
policies and development projects.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
I will be heading to Boston after graduation
and starting my career at Charles River
Associates as an economic consultant in the
energy industry.

Reformulating Korean

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
My research is about feminist resistance
against the double colonialism of U.S.
imperialism and South Korean patriarchy in
anti-American literatures of South Korea.
How did you come to your research topic?
In 20th century Korea, literature has often
been a tool of resistance (for example,
against Japanese colonization). However,
I found that there has not been as much
research focusing on anti-American
literature in the 1970s and 1980s in South
Korea, particularly within Anglophone
scholarship. As such, I was drawn to
researching literary manifestations
of resistance against the U.S. military
occupation in South Korea. During this
research, I found that anti-American
resistance within Korea has been very male-
centered. So, I decided to focus on female
authors who wrote anti-U.S. novels from a
feminist perspective.
Where do you see the future direction
of this work leading? How might future
researchers build on your work, or what
is left to discover in this field?
I believe that we must continue to connect
and analyze together the various resistance
literatures produced in the numerous
countries that have experienced the U.S.’
occupations, interventions, wars, coups,
etc. As a Korean person, I wish to draw
connections between the Korean literary
resistance movement against the U.S.’
militarization and war in Korea with those of
other countries around the world. Although
there is a lot I still have not read, I hope
that researchers may continue to study the
commonalities and differences between anti-
American literary movements in order to
read patterns about the sort of impact the U.S.
has had through its foreign policies, not just
through an American light, but through local
and indigenous eyes.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
I will be working in an immigration law firm
in Chicago as I apply to PhD programs.
Lauren Katz
Revolutionary Women:
Literary Performativity,
Classical Pseudonyms,
and the Public Sphere in
the Correspondence of
Abigail Adams and Mercy
Otis Warren
In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
In my thesis, I examine the epistolary
correspondence between Abigail Adams and
Mercy Otis Warren from 1775–1777. During
this time, these women engaged in a nuanced
dialogue and literary performance in which
they reimagine the relationship between the
classical and the modern, the Stoical and the
sentimental, the public and the private, the
national and the domestic, and the masculine
and the feminine as a means to actualize their
historical and literary voices.
How did you come to your research topic?
During the spring of my sophomore year
at Northwestern, I took an English course
entitled “Visionary Women and the American
Colonies.” I was struck by a line in the first
section of Caroline Wigginton’s journal,
Transatlantic Feminisms in the Age of Revolutions:
“In a moment when America was boldly
pronouncing its rejection of British tyranny,
Adams called for the end of tyranny of men
over women.” I loved the idea that Adams was
strategically repurposing America’s fight for
her own use, which ultimately led me to her
lesser-known performative correspondence
with Warren under the respective Roman
matron pseudonyms “Portia” and “Marcia.”
Where do you see the future direction of this
work leading? How might future researchers
build on your work, or what is left to
discover in this field?
With my thesis, I want to show future
researchers that they can shine a light on
historically marginalized groups, such as
women, by examining mediums that have
not traditionally been regarded as “high-end
literature.” I also want to encourage researchers
to work to question and challenge simple
binaries that trivialize the complexity of human
nature/thought, especially when exploring
historically marginalized groups. I believe that
it is important to work against the stereotypical
models into which women are collapsed and
the reproduced narratives that pin women
against one another. Furthermore, the concept
of repurposing an intended limitation as a
medium for discovery and ultimately defiance
is so powerful and can definitely be applied to
other topics throughout our past and present-
day history. In terms of opportunities to
expand upon the insights made in my thesis,
my work on Warren unveiled a whole new
avenue of research concerning her potentially
new role as a modern biographer that I hope
others research further.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
I will be working in New York City as a Client
Experience Associate at Broadway Plus.
Nikol
Kralimarkova
The Role of Habit in
Kafka’s “The Burrow”
and Proust’s Swann’s Way
In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
The topic of my senior thesis was habit as a
psychological and perceptual phenomenon
and its role in two major texts, namely Franz
Kafka’s short story The Burrow and Marcel
Proust’s Swann’s Way. I studied habit and its
spatiotemporal dimensions that shape the
two narrators’ realities and their respective
thoughts and/or behaviors. More concretely, I
explored both the constructive and destructive
effects of habit or its absence, such as the
creative possibilities to recreate and paint over
one’s reality as well as the anxieties that could
arise if a habit is disturbed.
How did you come to your research topic?
I had been studying Kafka in a couple of
Comparative Literary Studies courses and
Proust, I immediately fell in love with.
Given my diverse background, speaking
five languages, two of which French and
German, I fell for the intersection between
two distinct literary worlds. Still immersed
in times of a pandemic and lockdowns, I
was strongly drawn by a recurring theme in
many of Kafka’s short stories and Proust’s
In Search of Lost Time, specifically habit,
something that all of us faced in its essence
in the past two years. The familiarity of the
theme of habit and the literary mastery of
the authors and texts on which I focused
convinced me to pursue this research topic
whilst fighting COVID-19 myself.
Where do you see the future direction of this
work leading? How might future researchers
build on your work, or what is left to
discover in this field?
There is a lot more that literature can teach
us about the effects of habit and its absence,
especially in the times in which we have
been living, where we are more isolated and
constrained than the previous generation(s)
have ever been. Through such literary
pieces, we can (re)gain consciousness about
the processes of habituation that drive us a
majority of the time. Academically speaking,
Kafka’s creatures could also be studied
individually, as well as Proust’s narrator in the
progression of all volumes of In Search of Lost
Time to construct more detailed case studies of
the habitual existence of the narrators in their
literary worlds.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
I will be heading to medical school. I’m
currently residing in my home country,
Bulgaria, and am applying to medical schools in
the U.K., where my family and best friends live.
Akash Palani
Long Distance Nationalism: Indian Americans and
Hindutva
In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
In the context of Hindu nationalism’s entry
into the Indian political mainstream during
the past decade, my research seeks to identify
the mechanisms through which the Indian
diaspora, particularly Indian Americans,
form their attitudes towards the movement.
Public expressions of Hindu nationalism have
become increasingly frequent in the United
States, from the World Hindu Congress
in Chicago to the prevalence of Hindutva-
aligned campus groups. Many Indian
Americans may have lived outside of India
for decades or may even have been born and
raised outside India altogether. This presents
a fascinating puzzle: how do they form such
attitudes?
How did you come to your research topic?
I came to my research topic through
studying Indian history and Asian American
activism. The literature on these subjects
was compelling, and I saw from my own
experiences the need for the questions I put
forth to be addressed.
Where do you see the future direction of this
work leading? How might future researchers
build on your work, or what is left to
discover in this field?
There is a serious dearth of literature on this
subject in American academia, especially in
recent years. Future researchers should look
to connect the work I put forth with studies
of immigration, political polarization both
domestic and foreign, and transnational
political activism.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
I will be working in Chicago after graduation,
with plans to pursue graduate work in
political science in the near future.
Nolan Fizoires Robinson II
Transcending the Stage: Exploring the Applicability
of an Actor’s Training to Other Vocations and Our
Everyday Lives
In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
My research topic explores how the tools an
acting education and training gives its students
are not conducive to just acting, but they can
also be used in a variety of professions that lie
outside of the theatrical arts and teach us all
about the fundamentals of being human.
How did you come to your research topic?
I came to my research topic due to the
COVID-19 pandemic. After a year of being
unable to perform, I really had to reflect on
why my education and training as an actor
was crucial to the landscape in which we were
and currently are. The arts were suffering and
many Americans thought this industry was
expendable, but I knew there existed a power
inside this art that I needed to unlock — that
acting, in its essence, is less about being on a
stage and more about being present and human.
Where do you see the future direction of this
work leading? How might future researchers
build on your work, or what is left to
discover in this field?
I hope this work allows other actors to
discover what their art does for them
and how it connects them to their own
humanity and others to theirs. Maybe
future researchers can dive deeper into the
psychological implications of acting and
the psyche of an actor, as it takes a certain
level of psychological dedication in order to
efficiently do one’s job as an actor. It would be
interesting to see data on what it does to our
brains/the brains of those on stage with us
and discover how artificial emotions that an
actor creates relate to the moments in which
we may actually feel those emotions in real life
(fear, anger, sadness, joy, etc.)
Where are you heading to after graduation?
After graduation I am heading to New York to
start/complete work on Broadway! I hope to
have a bi-coastal career, working in both New
York and Los Angeles as an actor and writer.
Tara Shirvaikar
The Rise of the Female Vernacular: Contemporary
Indian Woman Authors and the Subversion of the
Heteropatriarchal Linguistic Establishment
In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
I researched how vernacular could be used
to dislocate shame as the place where female
sexuality resides, in contemporary Indian
literature.
How did you come to your research topic?
I wanted to learn more about how feminism
located itself within Indian literature and,
more than that, what role language (both elite
and vernacular) played in the formation of
the female social body and female sexuality.
With the guidance of my thesis adviser, I used
a lot of older, fundamental feminist works
published in India for my senior paper in
the CLS department and decided to focus on
contemporary literature for my senior thesis.
Where do you see the future direction of this
work leading? How might future researchers
build on your work, or what is left to
discover in this field?
There is so much more contextualizing work to
be done — locating the female body in literature
within different regional, linguistic, class, and
caste attributes would be the next step.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
I am headed to the Bay Area to work as a
hardware engineer at Intel.
Saidie Stone
Exoneration of American Violence: The Cultural
Legacy of American Atrocity Against Civilians During
the War in Vietnam
In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
I examined the representation of American
violence against civilians during the war
in Vietnam from three different categories
of sources: American veteran narratives,
Vietnamese-American narratives, and high
school American history textbooks.
How did you come to your research topic?
In the fall of 2019, I took Dilemmas of
American Power with Medill Professor Peter
Slevin. During the week we spent on the war
in Vietnam, we learned about the My Lai
Massacre of 1968, during which American
civilians killed 500 Vietnamese civilians,
including elderly people, women, children,
and babies.
Where do you see the future direction of this
work leading? How might future researchers
build on your work, or what is left to
discover in this field?
Ideally, researchers and educators will read
my work and understand the necessity for
incorporating more Vietnamese sources and
perspectives into high school and collegiate
curriculum.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
Chicago!
Chloe Wong
Radical Caring: A Qualitative Study on the Role of
Frontline Workers in Eradicating Gender-Based
Violence in the Asian American Communities
In a nutshell, what is your research topic?
My research topic is on the role of Asian-
identifying, female or non-binary identifying
direct service professionals (hereby referred
to as frontline workers) in preventing
gender-based violence in Asian American
communities. By incorporating their salient
identities and life histories, they actively
serve survivors on individual, relationship,
community, and societal levels.
How did you come to your research topic?
I was interested in the topic of gender-based
violence because of my personal experiences
of the topic. I was further inspired by my
internship experiences in Vietnam and
Chicago in conducting research and working
with survivors.
Where do you see the future direction of this
work leading? How might future researchers
build on your work, or what is left to
discover in this field?
Anthropological perspectives in gender-based
violence are crucial in centering the voices of
frontline workers and building a decolonial
praxis that restores the agency of survivors.
Future researchers can continue allocating
resources towards similar works in various
communities of urban settings, as well as
exploring options of transformative justice.
Where are you heading to after graduation?
I will be participating in the Management
Rotational Program in McMaster-Carr.

volumes.label: Deconstructing Global Wellbeing and the World Happiness Report
volumes.nurj_title: Deconstructing Global Wellbeing and the World Happiness Report

blocks: Deconstructing Global Wellbeing and the World Happiness Report
Anika Wilsnack
Department of Psychology, Northwestern University
Introduction

The measurement of happiness has been a key topic in popular psychology for the past several decades. In recent years, a particular interest in international comparisons of happiness has come to the forefront of this discourse. The practice of measuring a nation’s happiness originated in the 1970s with Bhutan’s Gross National Happiness Index, a nine-domain measure intended to inform the development, policy, and legal prioritization of societal well-being[0]. The Gross National Happiness Index was formalized as a development indicator in Bhutan’s 2008 constitution and served as the foundation for the 2011 UN General Assembly Resolution calling for a “holistic approach to development”[1]. The UN’s push for more comprehensive measurement and policy surrounding social wellness produced the World Happiness Report, the most dominant international happiness index on the global scale[2]. The WHR was constructed by an international committee of psychologists and includes cross-nation comparison and ranking of happiness based on six dimensions of happiness: GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy at birth, freedom to make life choices, generosity, and perception of corruption[3]. These six factors are predicted to account for about 75% of variation in subjective well-being globally, leaving at least a quarter of variation unaccounted for[4].

The WHR measurement approach establishes a norm for which components of well-being are of highest priority, which contributes to a standard of happiness for which Nordic European cultures are the epitome[5]. Beyond the Nordic region, WHR’s narratives more broadly align with the values of Western cultures. In doing so, the methodology neglects emotional experiences of the less frequently studied regions of the Global East and South[6], in addition to homogenizing the experience of positive affect[7]. These norms influence the domain of well-being psychology, social development policy, and even the general public’s perception of what it means to be a ‘happy nation’. In an attempt to understand the breadth of ‘happiness’ internationally, we have accepted a criterion heavily dependent on a country’s wealth, political state, and individualism.

By taking a cultural psychology approach to the measurement of happiness, we may deconstruct the idea of what a global definition of ‘happiness’ really means, and how current measures may fail to represent the breadth of culturally specific experiences of wellbeing. Analyzing cultural variation from the general psychological theory of a universal ‘happiness’ will better inform culturally specific wellbeing policy initiatives and address common biases in what makes a nation ‘happy’.

I will argue that the World Happiness Report’s measurement of happiness is ineffective at representing the diverse manifestations and significances of well-being globally, and that the narrative of a universal happiness fails to represent the breadth of cultural contexts of wellbeing. I will explore my thesis through three culturally specific examples, each highlighting different issues in the standardized definition and measurement of happiness. I will argue that Finland as a consistent winner of WHR’s ‘happiest nation in the world’ does not prescribe to a universally standardized definition of happiness, which results in a disconnect between a statistically happy nation and a population skeptical of this evaluation. I will then argue that Bhutan, as the originator of happiness indexing and a consistently low scoring nation on the WHR, represents a culture with a high value of well-being without alignment with WHR’s standard of happiness. Lastly, I will argue that Costa Rica, as the highest-scoring non-Western nation on the WHR, shows cultural disparity in definitions of happiness and provides an alternative model of a high-wellbeing culture.
Case Study I: Finland – The Paradox of the ‘Happiest Nation’

Finland’s disconnect in being the statistically ‘happiest nation in the world’ complicates our understanding of what ranking first on the WHR really signifies. Analysis of Finnish popular media and news reveals distinct patterns in reaction to the WHR. While some readers treat the ranking akin to a ‘sports victory’, many display skepticism or discontent referencing issues such as high national rates of depression and lack of consideration of the nuances of Finnish definitions of happiness[8]. In characterizing Finland as a global beacon of happiness, residents fear their experiences of struggle are being discredited and their understanding of what it means to be well misconstrued. The WHR mechanism of life evaluation which Finns are scoring exceedingly high on does not reflect much of an emotional experience of ‘happiness’, and rather reflects a value of accepting and making peace with one’s current life conditions[9]. When such findings are reported as ‘happiness’ this nuance is lost, leading to disconnect between the reality and idealized representation of a culture.

Finnish discourse regarding happiness measurement addresses both a lack of cultural prevalence of positive emotionality, as well as a discrepancy between Finland and those nations with less global privilege who experience and display positive emotions at higher frequencies. These members of the happy ‘other’, largely nations from the Global South, are positioned as more successful at manifesting happiness against environmental odds in comparison to Western and wealthy nations such as Finland[10]. In this sense, Finnish skepticism in their ranking appears as not only recognition of how Finnish affect tends to be less outwardly positive, but in discourse of how having less (or more) resilience should be reflected in wellbeing measurement. The resilience disparity between Western and non-Western nations which the Finnish public is picking up on is further solidified in cultural research. Watters ethnography of Sri Lanka in 2004 shows high resilience in regions where conflict and disaster have been prevalent, due to cultural mechanisms that allowed for integration and meaning making of terrible events[11]. Watters’ case study identified cultural mechanisms that emphasized a community-based, rather than individual-based, approach to addressing trauma. This highlights a key aspect of wellbeing in high-resilience cultural contexts—an aspect that must be considered for any analysis of culturally specific wellbeing to be complete.

Finland’s happiness is also qualitatively distinct in terms of autonomy and agency. Ninomiya and colleagues demonstrate that Finnish children tend to define happiness through autonomous involvement in activities, personal achievement, and success, which deviated from Mongolian and Japanese children’s definitions which relied more on family and authority respectively[12]. While this trend aligns with Western cultural literature beyond Finland, it is an important consideration for understanding that in a global context, this perspective is still the minority. In addition, the Finnish public seems split on a definition of happiness more grounded in positive affect versus one grounded in terms of agency[13]. This perspective of agency and happiness goes beyond the norms of American Western culture (where the majority of Western happiness research is produced) to qualitatively change the meaning of happiness being observed.

The conflation of Finland’s status as a modern and advanced society, as responsible for their high wellbeing measurement, diminishes the influence of tradition and spirituality in supporting wellbeing. One such instance of the role of spirituality is the prevalence of belief in angels and practice amongst Finnish women[14]. Belief in angels and spirituality is a more salient cultural feature than in the majority of high-happiness Western cultures, and yet this attribute of Finnish happiness is lost in translation. All in consideration, Finland as a national leader in happiness is not the straightforward case of Western cultural happiness it may appear to be.
Case Study II: Bhutan – Misaligned Metrics and the Legacy of GNH

Bhutan as the originator of happiness indexing and a consistently low scoring nation on the WHR represents a culture with a high value of wellbeing without alignment with WHR’s standards. Bhutan contrasts Finland and the greater Western happiness ideal in the dimensions of collectivism and indulgence, which both contribute to mismatch in measurement of happiness values[15]. Bhutan’s Gross National Happiness Index (GNH), which inspired the WHR, continues to operate and reflect national wellbeing using a measure built specifically for its cultural context. The GNH assesses 33 indicators across 9 domains, and notably includes categories neglected in the WHR like community vitality, cultural diversity and resilience, and ecological diversity and resilience[16]. NPR journalist McCarthy’s report on research by  Dr. Penjore reaffirms “This is no Western-style satisfaction survey on a scale from zero to 10… Bhutan asks about 300 questions”[17]. The greater breadth of questions, as well as the reflection of additional wellbeing domains, contributes to a more tailored report on Bhutanese happiness.

The GNH index is also deeply tied to Mahayana Buddhist principles, prioritizing communal happiness over the individual experience[18]. The integration of wellbeing with religious principles is a common global phenomenon, and Buddhist frameworks particularly have allowed for processing of hardship and giving structure and meaning to healing[19]. While the mechanism of national happiness indexing and the appeal of a Buddhist approach to happiness may have attracted global interest during Bhutan’s UN presentation, the underlying value system would be lost in attempts to appropriate measurement and policy to less collectivist cultures[20]. The attempt to globalize the GNH structure through a Western measurement system may misconstrue the intentionality behind such measurements, and leave nations like Bhutan misrepresented in global happiness discourse.

Bhutan as a historical center for wellbeing science has presented solutions for more equitable global representations of happiness through mechanisms like the WHR. Bhutanese happiness researcher Dr. Penjore suggests if the WHR and GNH were to validate and use the same within-nation data, Bhutan’s placement would jump to 20[21]. This claim aligns with his broader research on disparities between data collection and wellbeing values present in the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals, where he argues the UN model puts outsized pressure on developing nations without the culturally informed knowledge required to accurately measure progress on wellbeing goals[22]. Although rooted in the Bhutanese context, the idea that nations possess the perspective and tools to most accurately collect their own wellbeing data holds promise for other countries that have been similarly marginalized in wellbeing research. Bhutan is positioned uniquely at the crossroads of high cultural value of happiness with low WHR measurement and has the potential to change the approach to a globalized study of happiness.
Case Study III: Costa Rica – Sustainable Wellbeing in the Global South

Costa Rica as the highest-scoring non-Western nation on the WHR shows cultural disparity in definitions of happiness and provides an alternative model of a high-wellbeing culture. Costa Rica took the top spot on the Happy Planet Index from 2006-2019, a measure that uses similar self-report wellbeing measures but calculates overall wellbeing in the context of environmental impact[23]. This evaluation mirrors the elements of wellbeing highlighted in the WHR, while giving weight to the ways in which Costa Ricans are producing a more sustainable and collective experience of happiness than those nations who score higher on WHR domains. In addition to values of sustainable wellbeing, interconnectedness within communities is an important Costa Rican wellbeing value that goes underrecognized on an international scale. Amongst Costa Rican subjects, interconnectedness is a predictor of higher wellbeing in aging populations, a value with great potential to improve longevity and societal wellbeing[24]. Interconnectedness is not directly addressed via the WHR as the measure prioritizes individual rather than collective experience, which misses a relevant part of the experience of wellbeing in Costa Rica and other cultures with high interconnectedness.

Costa Rica’s placement on the WHR highlights significant disparities in the evaluation of Western versus Globally Southern experiences of happiness. As a nation with both a reputation for high values of wellbeing as well as validation from various non-WHR measures, Costa Rica’s omission from the top tiers of happiness measurement is puzzling to many. One way to understand this disparity is to problematize the characterization of wellbeing frameworks from the Global North as being capable of accurate and seamless application in the Global South, where we must consider variations in environments, circumstances, and relationships due to variables often outside of one’s control[25]. Rather than experiencing less happiness, the qualitative differences in the context and manifestation of happiness in Costa Rica create a distinct kind of happiness from that of the Global West. As with the lower-ranking Global South, Western wellbeing frameworks used in the WHR do not know how to make sense of diverse experiences of happiness. It is important to consider that the Global South is not a geographical monolith; instead, it is an epistemological form linked inseparably from histories of colonialism and international capitalism via the Global North[26]. This history constructs a kind of wellbeing discourse focused more on social structures and connectedness, political state, environment, and power, than on experiences of individual wellbeing.
Conclusions & Future Directions

The World Happiness Report’s attempt to quantify happiness fails to represent the diversity and significance of wellbeing globally. Without problematizing such research, a popular psychology definition of ‘universal’ happiness prevails, which distracts from the contextual considerations of wellbeing in individual nations and cultures. Through exploring the unique relationships that nations of Bhutan, Costa Rica, and Finland have with the WHR and the emotion of ‘happiness’, we begin addressing the diversity underlying the accepted oversimplified definition of happiness and method of measurement.

In my review of existing literature and application of cultural psychological frameworks to the global measurement of happiness, there are important gaps that must be addressed to construct a holistic understanding of the subject matter. While there are differences in experiences of wellbeing across cultures, my research has failed to directly test what causes these differences, leading to vulnerability to the cultural attribution fallacy[27]. Home-field disadvantage is another important consideration; the majority of wellbeing research comes from U.S. institutions, yet not bringing into conversation our values of wellbeing may be skewing our ability to nuance a global conversation of wellbeing[28]. There must also be a more explicit distinction of the diversity across cultures than the simple dichotomy of Western and non-Western, grouping together all cultures who do not fit a slim-minority criteria. The lack of specificity in these categories makes any overarching claims of its culture of happiness difficult; while I begin to address this through complicating Finland as an outlier Western nation, further attention is required to breaking down this categorization[29].

Additionally, this discussion should not disregard the concerns of discussed nations regarding their wellbeing. While recognizing nuance in Finland’s definition of wellbeing is important, the public’s concerns with the label of ‘happiest nation on earth’ including the lack of recognition of the ongoing mental health crisis, deserves greater attention[30]. Bhutan’s historical connection to wellbeing has been oversimplified into a narrative of a ‘trouble-free and blissful’ kingdom in the minds of the West; in reality wellbeing is complicated by factors such as unemployment and environmental change[31]. Similarly, Costa Rican happiness can not be studied in a vacuum of the environmental and historical factors that shape a post-colonial conception of wellbeing; even as Costa Rica is adopted as a diversifying representative of global happiness, we cannot conflate experiences across cultures[32]. Directly studying the proposed factors leading to cultural differences in understanding of happiness is an essential next step to minimize the effect of the Cultural Attribution Fallacy and to begin to unpack the ways in which happiness is defined in such diverse ways. Beyond this, I believe conducting further research about self-perceived national happiness would illuminate more of the discrepancy between the WHR and the experience of happiness in diverse settings. Advancing cultural psychology research will be essential to creating more equitable and well societies across the globe.
