The secondary hydroxyl was then activated with nosyl chloride,
10, and used for an Sn2 reaction with tBuDO3A.13 Base de-
protection with LiOH/THF was used to remove the methyl
ester, and the reaction was adjusted to acidic conditions with
TFA and TIPS as scavengers. It is essential to perform the base
deprotection before adjusting to acidic conditions as the phos-
phodiester has a higher rate of hydrolysis under basic con-
ditions, especially intramolecularly.19 The metalation was per-
formed with GdCl3 and the resulting product was purified by
HPLC to yield Gd-3PG. The polar endcap, phenyl ester (C18),
required an isocratic method in acid buffer to retain Gd-3PG.
Higher substitutions of Gd-3PG would require a form of anion
exchange or ion-pairing to purify similar to oligonucleotides
and mononucleotides.20
Relaxivity measurements
r1 measurements were taken under different magnetic fields
and at different temperatures (1.4 T at 37 °C and 7 T at 21 °C).
Typically, the r1 decreases with an increase in magnetic field
strength, but since the temperature is lower at 7 T, the r1 of
Gd-3PG appears the same (Table 1). The r1 of Gd-3PG is higher
than that of common gadoterate and more similar to the trend
of gadobutrol. The increase in Gd-3PG could either be due to
the increase in molecular weight or attributed to the secondary
sphere effects of the hydrogen bonding moieties, specifically
the phosphodiester, hydroxyl, and carboxylic acid groups.
Gd-3PG was then extrapolated with data from previously
published phosphodiester incorporated GBCAs (Fig. 1b).14
While Gd-3PG is above the trendline, indicating a higher sec-
ondary sphere effect, there is significant uncertainty in the
relationship between molecular weight and r1.
Enzymatic assays
Enzymatic kinetics was determined using the 3PG-Arm,
which showed phosphorylation by PGK. A Michaelis–Menten
constant of Km = 240 ± 30 µM was obtained, similar to that of
the known 3PG metabolite9 (Fig. 1a). This demonstrates that
even modified 3PG metabolites can be phosphorylated enzy-
matically. When compared to controls without PGK, Gd-3PG
showed no change in r1 under active buffer conditions with
PGK (Fig. S3†). This could be due to the low influence of
phosphorylation on r1 or the decreased activity of PGK
caused by the macrocyclic chelator. During these experi-
ments, it was determined that ATP concentrations increase
the r1 for both gadoterate and Gd-3PG with similar slopes
(Fig. S2†). The effect of ATP on r1 is therefore independent of
the 3PG-arm.
Conclusion
The synthesis of a GBCA conjugated to a glycolytic metabolite
(3PG) is reported to afford a relatively high yield of the syn-
thetic 3PG-arm (10, 29% linear yield). The r1 of Gd-3PG was
higher than that of common gadoterate due most likely to
secondary sphere effects or molecular weight enhancement
from the 3PG-arm (5.39 ± 0.14 mM−1 s−1 at 1.4 T and 37 °C).
The 3PG-arm demonstrated enzymatic activity, showing the
possibility of modifying metabolites for future MRI probes.
These results demonstrate the potential to use glycolytic
metabolites conjugated to GBCAs for investigating metabolic
function.
Data availability
The authors confirm that the data supporting the findings of
this study are available within the article and its ESI.† Raw
data that support the findings of this study are available from
the corresponding author, upon reasonable request.

blocks: AAPI Women and Workers Rights in Reality
Kaylyn Ahn
Northwestern University
Introduction

The Victims’ Economic Security and Safety Act (VESSA) was enacted in Illinois in 2003. It provides up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave to an employee who is a victim of or who has a family member who is a victim of domestic or sexual violence (“820 ILCS 180/ Victims’ Economic Security and Safety Act.”). It is granted to enable employees to maintain the financial independence necessary to leave abusive situations, pursue medical help, or obtain order of protections from their abusers. However, as it stands, no public record or study exists pertaining to the effectiveness of VESSA. Sexual and domestic violence affects millions of Americans every year. One out of every 6 American women has been victim of attempted or completed rape (Scope of the Problem: Statistics | Rainn, n.d.). One in every 3 women have experienced some form of physical intimate partner violence (Ncadv | National Coalition against Domestic Violence, n.d.). Intersectionality is important in understanding sexual violence because 55% of Asian women in the US report experiencing intimate physical and/or sexual violence (“Statistics on Violence Against API Women”).

If employers do not give survivors time off to successfully transit to safety and stability because employment laws fail to protect them, survivors risk poverty. Asian women in particular have endured some of the harshest economic effects of the pandemic, including the closing of small businesses, job loss, and increased caregiving responsibilities (“The Economic Status of Asian American and Pacific Islander Women”). Asian women have experienced a larger drop in their employment after COVID-19 than did both women and men overall (“The Economic Status of Asian American and Pacific Islander Women”). Poor women of color are segregated into low paying occupations, pink collar jobs (teaching, child care, waitressing), and spend more time providing unpaid caregiving than men (Cawthorne, n.d.). In 2019, more than 1.4 million AAPI women in the labor force worked in jobs that had hourly earnings below $15 an hour (“The Economic Status of Asian American and Pacific Islander Women”). Working class jobs often have little state regulations to protect workplace discrimination or exploitation. This renders working class women of color especially vulnerable to economic insecurity due to domestic or sexual violence. According to a 1988 report by the United States General Accounting Office on the effects of domestic violence on employed victims, 55% to 85% missed work because of domestic violence and 24% to 52% lost their jobs as a result of the abuse (Tarr, 2007). Furthermore, sexual and domestic violence have severe health consequences that affect a survivor’s job performance, such as post-traumatic stress disorder which may cause the survivor to re-experience trauma through flashbacks or recurrent nightmares (Jina & Thomas, 2013). Women who must escape domestic violence are often forced to leave their employment to find shelter, seek medical attention, or attend court proceedings for order of protections or child custody (Diaz, 2003). Thus, survivors are pushed into a cycle of poverty: experiencing domestic/sexual violence can lead to poor health and missed shifts, leading to job loss, and thus homelessness (Cawthorne, n.d.).

There are little federal protections to prevent survivors from being fired because they experienced domestic or sexual violence. In the United States v. Morrison, the Supreme Court held that gender motivated violence had an insufficient impact on interstate commerce that would grant Congress the ability to create a civil cause of action (Tarr, 2007). Employment protections survivors are thus reliant on state law, such as the Illinois law (Tarr, 2007).

While many survivors of sexual and domestic violence are at risk for economic insecurity, no research currently exists pertaining to the effectiveness of VESSA protections nor the law’s effectiveness for AAPI women in particular. In this light, my project evaluates how the ‘Victims’ Economic Security and Safety Act’ is or is not implemented in the workplace through the perspectives of victim service providers. I examine the experiences of Asian survivors to interrogate the financial barriers they face when seeking VESSA leave.

Based in the Chicagoland area, KAN-WIN is a nonprofit organization founded in 1990. It is the first domestic violence agency in Chicago to serve the Korean American community. KAN WIN works towards a “world free from gender-based violence through direct service, community education, and organizing within Asian American communities” (KAN-WIN). Its services are designed to empower immigrant survivors to tackle the unique and complex challenges they face and transition from crisis to long-term empowerment. KAN-WIN’s direct services include legal advocacy, case management, support groups, multilingual hotlines, transitional housing, and children's programs. Its community outreach includes education, training, peer advocate leadership, youth programs, advocacy initiatives, information and research development, and a multilingual advocacy program.
Method
This project utilizes qualitative data collected through a focus group with KAN-WIN staff based in the Chicagoland area.

There were 12 participants in the focus group. The participants were all various staff members from KAN WIN who work directly with survivors of violence. The participants’ specialities ranged from a general case worker, legal advocate, housing program lead, counselors, to translators. The participants were from a wide range of age groups, spanning from individuals in their early twenties to those over the age of fifty. Every participant was female identifying and Chinese, Korean, Mongolian, or Filipina.

A focus group was employed with KAN-WIN staff to protect the privacy and confidentiality of the survivor clients. In order to refrain from retraumatizing survivors through direct interviews, researchers chose to create a group discussion to engage how service providers navigated VESSA. A focus group was conducted also to foster collaboration and conversation amongst staff.
Procedure

Participants were identified as service providers at a domestic violence nonprofit meant to serve AAPI survivors and were asked to participate in a focus group in person. The focus group was scheduled to last 90 minutes and participants received a disclaimer that they are allowed to exit at any point and time in the focus group, that they do not have to answer any questions they do not feel comfortable with, and that they have the right to omit personal information. One researcher took notes during the focus group and another researcher facilitated the discussion. The focus group was transcribed by zoom software. Qualitative data was then coded, labeled, and organized to identify different themes and the relationships between them.
Results

The victim advocates discussed four different themes regarding AAPI women’s access to VESSA leave: lack of awareness and assistance in applying for leave, stigma and confidentiality, lack of enforcement, and structural barriers for undocumented and immigrant women.
Lack of Awareness and Assistance

Many survivors, employers, and service providers are unaware of the existence and details of VESSA, making it difficult for survivors to access its benefits. Several participants were not aware of eligibility expansions of VESSA, such as the amount of unpaid time off survivors can take and the minimum number of employees a company needs to employ for a survivor to take leave. One provider stated that "I think if there’s also any helplines or any government to help for the client to exercise their rights instead of they have the burden to actually tell the employer and so, it's kind of grievance procedure, so if their employer does not follow then they can like report to the human rights, office of whatever, so they can follow up with their employer so that they can follow this act."
Stigma and Confidentiality

Survivors often face challenges in applying for VESSA leave, including the need to explain their situation to their employer, which can be uncomfortable and risky. One provider discussed how disclosure is difficult in cases in which the employer or another coworker was the perpetrator of violence. Survivors may hesitate to disclose their situation to employers due to fear of stigmatization and a desire to maintain confidentiality.

Some survivors who experience victimization may get fired, face discrimination, or encounter hostile work environments. For example, “It is not just that she got fired, but they make her-make her to leave that job. Because they spread rumors and all the others, they were gossiping behind the client so that victim blaming culture is very very prevalent.”

One provider discussed the cultural stigma of accessing time off, one worsened for victimization reasons: “For example, I got in a car accident right? So my car was damaged or totaled so I need to do take care of my car stuff, related to insurance, and if I’m injured I need to go get checked, with my doctor…they can’t use as many days off as they want from their workplaces because there’s gonna be blaming from their employer, coworkers, even if workplace is small in size, you know under 50 or so. Many of our clients are working in a very small business and then especially you cannot just talk to your employer, Oh I need to take time for this thing, for my car accident, so I have to check with insurance and this and that. And even if it is not related to your personal thing, your personal violence, domestic violence, but still there’s shame on that.”
Lack of Enforcement

The certification requirement creates additional barriers for survivors because it violates their privacy and confidentiality and employers may falsely claim that their proof does not satisfy the requirement. One participant stated that "the certification requirement creates an additional barrier, as survivors must provide proof of their situation." Another stated that a survivor was denied “because not enough proof of incident.” Participants support simplifying or modifying the certification requirements to make it more accessible and survivor-centered. In order to satisfy the certification requirement for VESSA, the survivor can send to their employer documents that include but are not limited to documentation from an employee, agent, victim services organization, or medical professional verifying the incident(s). Even though the survivor provided a letter from a victim services organization, the employer denied leave and violated VESSA statute. The penalties for employers who do not comply with VESSA may be perceived as too lenient, leading to a lack of enforcement.

Participants supported more days off for survivors and paid time off. One participant stated that “I think DV and SA is ongoing problems but VESSA is up to how many days they can take off, not much right? I mean it's helpful, but it's not enough days to take off.”
Structural Barriers for Immigrant and/or Undocumented Women

Immigrant and/or undocumented women face structural barriers to accessing VESSA leave. Even when survivors are eligible, VESSA is often not practical for those working in service sector jobs, such as restaurants and nail salons. Immigrant and/or undocumented women who may be paid “under the table,” or paid off the record, do not have access to paid time off and may not be able to afford unpaid time off. One participant stated that “A lot of our clients work under the table or illegally, I think the issue on hand is that our clients without status are not able to work high-paying jobs that provide PTO or any kind of reputable assistance." Without paid time off, survivors living paycheck to paycheck cannot take advantage of VESSA leave. Another stated "Even if we can tell our clients that there is this law, that they can take their time off of work, but I haven’t seen any of my clients use it just because all clients come in they have their financial struggles and the fact that they are taking time off work, unpaid, like when they don’t have any other resources and when there aren’t any other financial resources, and that many of them are undocumented, working under the table, getting cash jobs, their employers are not going to be happy about them taking time off for any reason.”

Language barriers and the lack of VESSA resources in multiple languages pose additional obstacles for survivors in understanding and applying for VESSA. The participants looked at the City of Chicago’s online available resources regarding VESSA and found translations in English, Spanish, and Polish. Participants suggest that providing multilingual resources and information about VESSA would be beneficial.
Discussion

The sample from which the participants were chosen influenced the results. The results focused on employees in small businesses, language barriers, and employer non-compliance because participants serve mostly undocumented and/or immigrant survivors. Results did not focus on how survivors navigate obtaining VESSA leave but the barriers to considering VESSA leave in the first place. This is relevant to the framework of intersectionality; undocumented AAPI women are forced to work illegally and are segregated to low paying jobs where there is higher risk of noncompliance to employer regulations. Furthermore, negative perceptions and victim blaming of survivors cause hostility and insensitivity.

This study could have been improved by increasing the number of participants recruited to gain a wider understanding of VESSA. Focus group questions could be altered to focus less on how survivors logistically navigated VESSA and more on the systemic barriers undocumented survivors face in general. More research should be conducted on the complex context undocumented survivors are situated in, such as where they are employed, how they obtain employment, and how they are treated by their employers.

This research suggests possible avenues of legislative changes to increase penalties for noncompliance, simplifying certification requirements, increasing paid time off, and increasing unpaid time off. The research also suggests changes within the current laws to increase awareness and education about VESSA, multilingual resources, and advocacy to better the cultural understandings of survivors.

The discussion highlights the need for greater awareness, improved accessibility, and systemic changes to ensure that VESSA effectively protects survivors of domestic violence in the workplace. These quotes highlight the challenges survivors face, the barriers they encounter in accessing VESSA benefits, and the need for systemic changes to make the law more effective and accessible.
Conclusion

Gender-based violence has severe financial consequences; the lifetime economic cost of rape across all US victims is nearly $3.1 trillion (Merrefield, 2019). Since its passing in 2003, the Victims’ Economic Security and Safety Act has served as a seminal piece of legislation for expanding survivor rights in Illinois and inspiring other states to adopt similar protections. With no federal workplace protections for domestic violence victims, the state legislature and their corresponding departments of labor serve as social safety nets for survivors, one that often lets marginalized survivors slip through the cracks.

blocks: On the Immoral Nature of Capitalistic Unfreedoms
Melissa Canales
Introduction

Political philosopher G.A. Cohen makes the succinct and powerful argument that “To think of capitalism as the realm of freedom is to overlook half of its nature.”[0] By this, he means that capitalism, like any other man-made social or economic structure, protects a certain set of freedoms by permitting another set of unfreedoms.

An important capitalist freedom is the right to private property. Many leftist theorists argue that the freedom of private ownership has, in turn, made it such that non-owning workers—the proletariat—are unfree because they are forced to sell their labor. Cohen denies this assertion. Instead, he argues that proletarians under capitalism retain the individual freedom to become capitalists, at which point they would no longer be forced to sell their labor. Yet, he concedes that capitalism requires a large working class that does sell its labor that then collectively forces the proletariat to sell its labor. Still, if all societies must have some set of unfreedoms, it is not immediately apparent that we should take issue with proletarian collective unfreedom if, in exchange, we remain individually free to own capital and not sell our labor.

This paper takes up the assertion that the proletariat is merely collectively unfree to argue that this mere collective unfreedom poses serious moral concerns about the individual rights of all people under capitalism, proletarians and capitalists alike. I argue that people are unconditionally entitled to a kind of respect that protects them from domination. When one sells their labor under capitalism, though, they are necessarily dominated by their capitalist employer, depriving them of the respect they are owed. Moreover, I argue that collective unfreedom forces people to continuously compete for a position in the capitalist class where they can be free from domination. This competition, however, makes freedom from domination contingent on one’s class status, meaning that even individuals who successfully become capitalists or inherit a position within this class are also not respected as equal persons who are unconditionally entitled to this freedom. In this sense, the proletarian collective unfreedom deprives individuals of their right to respect.
Proletarian Unfreedom

It will be helpful to clarify first what is meant by capitalism. I distinguish capitalism from other economic systems by its two necessary components: property relations, whereby the means of production are privately owned by individuals or collectives who are distinct from the people who operate them, and a dominant market economy.[1]

Because the workers under capitalism do not own capital, there is a common leftist thought that workers, to survive, are forced to sell their labor. Cohen denies this.[2] Instead, he defends the meritocracy of capitalism; workers, he argues, maintain their individual freedom to not sell their labor because all workers are free to work hard, acquire capital, and ascend into the capitalist class, at which time they could choose to labor for themselves or purchase the labor of some other worker. Given that any worker could earn their way into the capitalist class, it is not true that any of them are individually forced to stay a proletarian and sell their labor. Thus, to the delight of pro-capitalist readers, Cohen argues that capitalism upholds the individual freedom of workers in that they are not, as leftists would claim, individually forced to sell their labor.

Still, Cohen acknowledges that capitalism structurally demands a “substantial hired labor force” that limits the number of opportunities available for workers to exit the proletariat.[3] This scarcity of exits produces a different kind of unfreedom that Cohen diagnoses in the proletarian condition: collective unfreedom.

Collective unfreedom, in short, means that one is free only on the condition that others do not exercise their similarly conditional freedom.[4] The collective unfreedom of the proletariat, then, stems from the scarcity of opportunities to be a capitalist; though they are all theoretically individually free to become capitalists, one’s individual freedom to do so is threatened by the others’ individual freedom to do the same.

It is not immediately obvious, though, why this collective unfreedom is immoral, especially if our individual freedom remains intact. There are endless trivial instances of collective unfreedom, such as our collective unfreedom to all labor in the same occupation.[5] Most people would find it morally permissible that we are not all able to be bus conductors as long as those who wish to be conductors can pursue this path. Further, it is not true that collective unfreedom is always a cause for concern, even when its individual freedom equivalent is morally troubling. Even if we would not raise a moral eyebrow at our society being collectively unfree to work as bus conductors, we would be right to be concerned if we found that some of us were individually unfree to pursue this occupation as a result of discriminatory hiring practices. Thus, we must question if the proletarian collective unfreedom that forces workers to sell their labor is of moral concern, especially considering that individuals within this class remain individually free to leave and not sell their labor.
Lamenting the Proletarian Condition

While the last section largely followed Cohen’s lead in discussing the nature of collective unfreedom and the ways in which freedom under capitalism pits people’s exercise of freedom against one another, it will go beyond Cohen in arguing about the immoral nature of this collective unfreedom the proletarian class suffers under capitalism.

Cohen argues that the lamentable aspect of the conditions of proletarian unfreedom forces the proletariat to subordinate themselves to the bourgeois class, something that other, morally irrelevant kinds of collective unfreedoms do not force individuals to do.[6] I will make a similar, though distinct, argument in this section and propose that the proletarian condition is morally troubling to us because, when workers sell their labor, they are necessarily dominated by their employer. Later, Section V will detail how proletarian collective unfreedom deprives all people of their right to respect as equal persons, not merely by forcing some into dominated work, but by conditioning freedom from domination on class status.

According to Philip Pettit, a person dominates over another when they have the capacity to interfere with another’s choices on an arbitrary basis[7]; interference is arbitrary when the dominating person is not forced to track the interests of the person they are interfering with. Further, a person need not actually interfere with another to hold dominating power over the other. It suffices that they have the mere capacity to interfere without having to track the interests of the other.

Pettit argues that freedom from domination requires having the proper recourse to contest it.[8] Should someone exercise power over another, then, this would not constitute a dominating form of power if their actions and decisions could be contested, and they could be held accountable to the interests of those they have power over. A police officer, for instance, while seemingly not tracking the interests of the bank robber when he detains the criminal, would not constitute as dominating over the robber if he is held up to the same legal standards as his fellow citizen and is not permitted to abuse his power through excessive force.

A tyrant, however, does dominate over the citizens of their nation. They control the means to create and enforce legislation and do not answer to any system that might keep them accountable to the nation’s citizens. The tyrant has the capacity to interfere with citizens through legislative and judicial means and can regulate how their citizens engage in their public and private spheres; they can enforce these regulations by deploying militaristic forces to ensure obedience; they can oversee trials for the accused. Furthermore, the tyrant responds to no outside party or governing body that might hinder their ability to interfere with their citizens. Citizens, having no legal recourse to contest the tyrant’s legislative decisions, are subject to the tyrant’s arbitrary will and are, thus, dominated by the tyrant.

Without any limitations on their power, even if the tyrant were sympathetic to the interests of their people and ruled in such a way that improved their standard of living, or if a tyrant simply did not enact any legislation and allowed their citizens to go about their lives, it would still follow that the tyrant dominates their people, given that they retain the capacity to interfere at their pleasure and remain unaccountable to the interests of their citizens.

Under this account, domination is concerned with the power that mediates the relationship between dominating and dominated. In the capitalist workspace, such roles are performed by the capital-owning employers and the capital-deprived workers, respectively.

Under capitalism, employers fulfill the requirements for domination. Having control over a worker’s employment status, the employer has the capacity to interfere with employees within the workplace and, in certain cases, outside of the workplace. Employers determine when and how employees work, including the tasks they will undertake, the hours they will work, and the places they will work. In more dominating workplaces, employers also control how employees must live outside of the workplace by, for instance, dictating acceptable forms of online presence and political participation or affiliation. These decisions can be made by the employer irrespective of the interests of their workers.

Workers also have little to no means of properly contesting the decisions dictated by their employers. Employers alone control the continued and future employment status of their workers within a given workplace, leaving workers vulnerable to the decisions of their employers if their contestation put them at risk of retaliation, such as demotions or firings. Further, workers seeking to enter an employment relationship have limited, if any, means with which to contest their employment conditions. Workers’ interests are, at best, suggestions for employers, but the latter are never forced to track these interests when making company decisions and outlining employment relations. Even if employers do track their workers’ interests in individual cases, they would still dominate over their workers if they were not required to do so in a more general, systemic manner. The police officer, for example, would dominate over a criminal even when peacefully arresting him if the police officer were not held accountable to the justice system that would hold him liable for excessive force. In this same sense, the employer would still dominate over their workers even when they tracked individual worker interests if they were not held liable to a system that forced them to track these interests more generally.

Though the employer does not have the same absolute power as the tyrant, they do have the capacity to arbitrarily interfere with their employees in the workplace. The employer dominates their workers.

Consider, for example, Silvana and Ernesto, two workers at different companies. On a given day, Ernesto and Silvana wake up to discover that their respective children have fallen ill and need their parents to monitor them and ensure they don’t need further medical attention. To take time off work, both workers must request permission from their employers.

Silvana speaks with her employer, a cold individual with no sympathy for the hardships of parenthood, and is denied her time-off request. It is clear that Silvana’s interests are disregarded by her employer, who is not forced nor voluntarily moved to track such interests. Silvana can either deny her ill child’s needs and go to work or tend to her child and risk retaliation at work for which she has no means of contesting. After all, it is a generally uncontroversial practice that employers alone dictate operational matters such as time off requests. Silvana is dominated by her employer.

Imagine, however, that when Ernesto speaks to his employer, a kind-hearted individual who sympathizes with the challenges of parenthood, his time-off request is granted. His interests are tracked, and he spends the day taking care of his child. While Ernesto, fortunately, does not find himself in the same compromising position as Silvana, it does not follow that Ernesto is not dominated in the same way as Silvana. That the kind-hearted employer does track Ernesto’s interest does not mean that the employer is forced to do so. If, on this particular day, Ernesto’s workplace had had a shortage of workers, the kind employer might have denied Ernesto’s time-off request to keep the business running efficiently. In this sense, Ernesto is dominated by his employer even when his interests are tracked because his employer retains the ability to deny such interests, and Ernesto, like Silvana, would not have the means to contest this power conferred onto capital-owning employers.

Of course, time-off requests are not the only way in which employees are dominated. Samuel Arnold distinguished between two kinds of decision-making powers that employers have sole control over and that dominate workers. The first is operational decisions, which outline what workers will produce, how they will do it, and the compensation they can expect to receive for their labor. The second is strategic decisions, which include questions on how a company will spend its revenue, the investments it will make, and the like.[9]  On these matters, capitalists are not forced to track the interests of their workers. An employer may choose to invest in new products, open new storefronts, or pocket more profit while their workers, naturally, are interested in getting their own paycheck bonuses. The employer, however, has the power to make the final rulings on these matters.

That capitalist employers hold the power to make these decisions irrespective of the interests of the workers is a truth about capitalism. Without the right to control the operational and structural decisions of a workplace, private ownership of capital would be meaningless. The right to private ownership of capital is a meaningful one only insofar as it allows individuals to make use of their capital as they see fit without the interference of others. Forcing an employer to track the interests of their employees would require them to surrender significant control over their property, rendering their ownership a meaningless one.

In fact, Arnold argues that conflicting interests between capitalists and workers are structural, and capitalists must dominate their workers to continue being capitalists: “Capitalists who do not resolve key operational and strategic conflicts in profit-maximizing ways do not long remain capitalists.”[10] A kind-hearted capitalist responding to workers’ interests may offer higher wages and work benefits in place of personally profiting, but even these employers must eventually answer to the demands of the market over the interests of their workers.
Thus, workers, once engaged in an employment relationship, are necessarily dominated by their employers.
IV. Deprivation of the Right to be Respected

So far, I have established that when workers sell their labor, they are necessarily dominated by their capitalist employer. However, it remains to show that it is a moral concern that the proletariat are merely collectively forced to be dominated.[11] This final section will argue, first, that domination is immoral because such treatment is incompatible with the respect that people are owed because of their equal personhood; and, second, that the collective unfreedom through which this domination occurs deprives all individuals under capitalism, including those who ascend into and exist in the capitalist class, of the respect they are owed by conditioning their unconditional right to freedom from domination to class status.

Individuals are owed respect on their basis as equal persons. Respect in this sense does not capture “appraisal respect”, or positive attitudes felt toward one another, such as admiration for another’s attributes or accomplishments, nor does it capture holding another in high esteem.[12] Instead, it consists only of the treatment that I owe to others because of their innate status as persons of equal standing to myself.[13] This treatment, then, is an unconditioned obligation I have to others and that others have to me; respect in this sense is not earned and cannot be lost.

There are plausibly many forms of treatment that one must abstain from to respect others in the ways that they are owed, such as by abstaining from manipulation or causing unwarranted physical harm. While these may be true, I will focus on freedom from domination as a kind of treatment that people of equal standing are entitled to; as such, when one is dominated, or threatened with domination, one is deprived of the respect they are owed.

To suggest that domination has deep implications on the respect given between peers of equal standing is not far-fetched, even for the republican thinker. Pettit wrote that, when one is free from domination, one can see oneself “as possessed of a comparable social standing with the other. They can look the other in the eye; they do not have to bow and scrape.”[14] Conversely, when one is dominated, one is vulnerable to another’s capacity to arbitrarily interfere with one’s choices; one’s equal standing to others is undermined by another’s ability to override one’s own interests with the interests of the other. To treat someone in such a way that they are vulnerable to another’s arbitrary interference, then, is inherently incompatible with the treatment of them as a person of equal standing to others. To dominate someone is to fail to treat them with the respect they are owed.

Workers toiling under a capitalist labor market do bow and scrape before their dominating employers. Even when reforms eliminate particularly egregious forms of domination and provide workers with some bargaining power to demand better work contracts and conditions, workers must generally conform to the orders and demands of their employers who enjoy arbitrary power by virtue of their ownership of capital and who are structurally obligated to dominate their workers. Workers who assume this subservient role through the employment contract are denied the respect they are owed by their employers in their workplace.[15]
Respect, however, is not denied only to workers nor exclusively through active domination. It is also denied to all individuals through the capitalist competition to be free from domination.

Proletarian collective unfreedom creates a situation in which individuals must compete for the limited spots in the capitalist class if they wish to be free from domination. Imagine that a proletarian works hard to scrape up the money with which to purchase capital. At this time, she can free herself from domination by being self-employed and/or by profiting through the domination of her own set of employees. This proletarian’s freedom from domination is contingent on her ability to earn it through capitalist competition, meaning that even when she is free from domination, it is not because she is treated with the unconditional respect owed to her as a person of equal standing. In fact, she is not treated with this respect at all because her freedom from domination under capitalism is never the result of her right to respect and is always the result of her continued success in being a capitalist.

Further, because proletarian collective unfreedom does not require the unfreedom of particular individuals, even those who have successfully entered the capitalist class are not completely saved from the proletarian condition. After all, class mobility under capitalism, insofar as everyone retains the individual freedom to be a capitalist, operates in both an upward and downward direction. Workers can earn their way into the capitalist class, and existing capitalists may be run out of business by an up-and-coming entrepreneur. This constant competition highlights the precarity of the capitalist's position: freedom from domination is not given out of respect for the capitalist as an equal person, but rather it is given as a reward that is always contingent on her ability to maintain her class status. If she fails to do this—if she loses her capital and must earn a living by selling her labor—she will be dominated through the employment relationship just like any other proletarian. The fact that she is perpetually threatened with the possibility of being dominated reveals that she, like the proletariat, is not respected as an equal person. She is protected from domination merely through her class status.[16]

Even modern-day elites whose immense wealth assures them that they will never have to sell their labor and fall victim to domination cannot escape the lack of respect they are shown by their peers. Their protection from domination is not guaranteed through their treatment as equal persons by their peers, but rather through their class status.

Thus, while it might seem that capitalists are not deprived of the respect of others because they are not dominated, the collective unfreedom of the proletariat makes it such that they, too, are always, at least theoretically, at risk of being dominated, of being kicked back down into the proletariat if someone successfully replaces them or drives them out of business. If capitalists were respected through their status as equal persons rather than their status as capital owners, such precarity in their freedom from domination would not exist. Capitalists, just like proletarians, lack the respect they are owed.

It becomes the case, then, that all people—capitalists and proletarians—suffer from a deprivation of the respect they are owed by others because of their status as equal persons. The collective unfreedom of the proletariat, with its indifference as to who will be forced into dominated employment relations, threatens everyone’s right to be respected, making it a moral concern to even those who only concerns with individual unfreedoms

It is reasonable to think, then, that if workers owned the means of production—ending the current property relations that distinguish non-working capitalists and propertyless workers—workers would no longer be collectively forced to sell their labor. They could, instead, work for themselves and engage in productive activity with fellow worker-owners. In light of this radical shift in property relations, we would have not only the end of the collective unfreedom that currently plagues the proletariat but also the end of the immoral treatment of all people under capitalism.

[2]  Cohen, G.A. (1983). The Structure of Proletarian Unfreedom. Philosophy and Public Affairs, 12(1), 3-33.
[3]  Cohen’s understanding of this structural need fits the given necessary conditions of capitalism that this paper focuses on.
[4]  See footnote 3.
[5]  See footnote 3.
[6]  See footnote 3.
[7]  Pettit, P. (1997). Republicanism: A theory of freedom and government. Oxford University Press.
[8]  See footnote 8.
[9]  Arnold, S. (2016). Capitalism, class conflict, and domination. Socialism and Democracy, 1-19.
[10]  See footnote 10.

[11]  The account of domination I’ve sketched above has largely relied on the philosophers of the republican tradition, who argue that freedom is freedom from domination. Yet, the central unfreedom in this paper has been the negative collective unfreedom of the proletariat, who are forced to sell their labor under a capitalist system where they are then dominated. The issue of domination, then, as I understand it, is not an issue of unfreedom. Though the proletariat are forced to be dominated when they are forced to sell their labor, they are not, by extension, forced to be unfree. As such, one of the virtues of the view expressed in this paper is that it can be accepted by readers who do not buy into the republican notion of freedom as non-domination.
[12]  Darwall, S.L. (1977). Two kinds of respect. Ethics, 88(1), 36-49.

[13]  Darwall (1977)  calls respect of this sort “recognition respect.” Recognition respect requires that my treatment of others is constrained to that which is morally permissible of treatment of persons. While he does not make the explicit distinction of equal personhood that I do in my understanding of respect, I take it that to acknowledge another’s personhood very likely requires reckoning with their equal standing to myself and acting accordingly. My distinction of equal personhood, then, is simply helpful in emphasizing how domination undermines the respect that we are owed to one another by treating the dominated as less-than.
[14]  See footnote 8.

[15]  Briefly, I want to clarify that there are, of course, many facets in life in which one expects to be treated as an equal by their peers. Many people, then, find equal treatment and respect from others in areas outside of their work life, from their neighbors or friends. While these are important parts of one’s life, they cannot substitute the respect that one is also owed within their workplace. Conversely, if one were to experience domination in aspects of life outside of the workplace, that would also be morally troubling, even if one did not experience domination in the workplace.

[16]  One might think that if a capitalist receives the same end as the respected person, namely that they are both free from domination, the capitalist is also respected, at least in some sense. However, the capitalist and the respected person differ in treatment given that, unlike the capitalist, the respected person is never threatened with the possibility of domination if they do not own capital. They are granted freedom from domination because of their inherent status as an equal person. The capitalist, though, receives only a conditional freedom from domination.

blocks: Rai 1
चिपको की छोरियां
(Chipko ki chhoriyaan)*
How peasant women in India became self-empowering political actors
through their use of performative protest in ecological activism
Aashna Rai
American Society for Theatre Research: Ecologies of Theatre & Change
Seattle, WA
November 14th, 2024– - November 17th, 2024
*Translation: The women of Chipko
मेट्रो बनाने उखाड़ो तुम झाड़
जब झाड़ ना बचेंगे, कैसे लोगे सांस?
घर मेरा जंगल, खुला आकाश
तुम आये त्रास देने, करने इसका नाश
प्रकृति का बनाओ मज़ाक
यही प्रकृति से बनी मानव जात
तुम आज रहे हो हमे भगा
छिन के हमसे तुम हमारी जगह
बस बचा है ये जीने का तरीका
तुम वो भी छिन के करे हमें तबाह
सज़ा पक्षी-प्राणी की है क्या?
क्यों इन्हे बेदखल कर रहे ऐसा?
To build a metro you’re killing the trees.
When they are gone then how’ll you breathe?
The jungle and sky are my home.
You come here, mess with us and destroy our home.
Nature for man has lost its worth but she is the one who truly gave us birth.
Today you are trying to throw us out snatching away our home and ground
All we have left is the way we live now, but you want to steal that too, somehow mess with our lives.
What did our birds and animals do? Why are you evicting them too?
The Warli Revolt (an anthem against the
destruction of the Aarey forest) by Swadesi,
featuring Aarey tribal chieftain Prakash Bhoir
As theatre exemplifies the politics of embodiment, it is inherently political;1
protest—involving tropes of human action, body, land and community, and figures of speech and
1 Jane Chin Davidson, “Performance Art, Performativity, and Environmentalism in the Capitalocene,” Oxford Research
Encyclopedia of Literature, 2019, https://doi.org/10.1093/acrefore/9780190201098.013.93.
function—is inherently theatrical.2 The line between the theatrical and the political actor became
blurrier in the eighteenth century: both roles involved embodying fictional entities and realizing
the abstract, whether that was through artistic realism or through representative legislation.3
Augusto Boal, through his creation of the spect-actor, created theatrical arenas for sociopolitical
change where oppressed communities could reclaim their personal and collective agency by
blurring audience-actor (and sometimes people-politician) boundaries.4 Boal’s philosophy lives
on in the current intersections of politics and performance. Benjamin Page defines a political
actor to be performing “observable action that is purposive … and sufficiently unified so that it
makes sense to speak of a single actor.”5 Frederick Frey, alternatively, places emphasis on a
“sentient entity” that affects or responds to other actors, whether as an individual or a collective.6
Performative protests allow the exploration of the relationship between the human actor
and political subjectivities. Eco-indigenous protest, usually built upon environmental
philosophies of justice and respect for nature,7 can be interpreted as a performance that
acknowledges indigenous forms of cultural knowledge and the importance of integrating nature
and culture to address the ecological crisis. Tribal social systems in India are built upon the
harmony between man and nature, viewing the earth as a sacred living organism. However,
colonization by the British caused the destruction of this relationship and of indigenous cultural
ecology.8
8 Chandra N D R. and Nigamananda Das, Ecology, Myth and Mystery: Contemporary Poetry in English from Northeast India
(New Delhi: Sarup & Sons, 2007).
7 Krishna Mallick, Environmental Movements of India: Chipko, Narmada Bachao Andolan, Navdanya (Amsterdam: Amsterdam
University Press, 2021).
6 Frederick W. Frey, “The Problem of Actor Designation in Political Analysis,” Comparative Politics 17, no. 2 (1985): p. 127,
5 Benjamin I. Page, “The Mass Media as Political Actors,” PS: Political Science &Amp; Politics 29, no. 1 (1996): pp. 20-24,
4 Augusto Boal, Rainbow of Desire (Routledge, 2015).
3 Paul Friedland, Political Actors: Representative Bodies and Theatricality in the Age of the French Revolution (Ithaca: Cornell
University Press, 2003).
2 Pramod K. Nayar, “Indigenous Cultures and the Ecology of Protest: Moral Economy and ‘Knowing Subalternity’ in Dalit and
Tribal Writing from India,” Journal of Postcolonial Writing 50, no. 3 (February 2013): pp. 291-303,
In my essay, I view indigenous peasant women protestors as political actors, in an equally
political and theatrical sense of the term, based upon their exhibition of four primary
characteristics: (1) their action is observable; (2) it is performed with conscious purpose,
sentience, and an unconventionally high level of autonomy; (3) it consists of enough cohesion to
perceive them as a singular force; and, (4) it gained them entry into eco-political dialogue, with
long-lasting impact in fields of postcolonial environmentalism, ecofeminism, and indigenous
ecologies. In analyzing the role of these women in the Chipko movement as an act of political
performance, I will consider five aspects of their protest: physical action and body, dialogue and
language, religious context, location, and the theatricality of suffering. I argue that each of these
characteristics transforms the Chipko protests into political performance art, presenting it as an
empowering endeavour for a largely marginalized community. Considering their level of formal
political influence, indigenous tribal women fall into the bottom tier of categories of political
actors: “members of the public … encapsulat(ing) public opinion via their own work.”9 They are
also political outsiders: actors, usually from vulnerable and disadvantaged communities, who are
excluded from institutional political decision-making processes either due to political strategy or
marginalization.10
While familial structures vary from one tribal community to the other, the ‘social
contract’ between state and citizen was largely built upon the exclusion of women11— a form of
subordination that was intensified by the intrusion of British patriarchal structures. This
intersection of identities—that of the tribal peasant and of the woman—is integral to my
11 Carole Pateman, The Sexual Contract (Stanford, CA: Stanford University Press, 2018).
10 Salvatore Paolo De Rosa, Joost de Moor, and Marwa Dabaieh, “Vulnerability and Activism in Urban Climate Politics: An
Actor-Centered Approach to Transformational Adaptation in Malmö (Sweden),” Cities 130 (2022): p. 103848,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cities.2022.103848.
9 Nikki Soo, Alexandra Anderson, and Charlie Heywood-Heath, “Exploring Public Opinion and Why It Matters to Political
Actors,” Politics Blog, May 13, 2021,
http://politicsblog.ac.uk/2021/05/13/exploring-public-opinion-and-why-it-matters-to-political-actors/.
analysis. In discussing the role of these women as political actors, I attempt to avoid the
reduction of their actions to solely eco-feminist or poverty-protest, instead examining how the
synthesis of their identities was reflected in their performance in the Chipko protest. Their
approach to environmental activism reflects a transformational approach to climate
adaptation—one that is opposed to the neoliberal, mainstream, urban, and technocentric of the
Global North—by challenging social drivers of climate vulnerability.12
Ideas of development, modernity, and progress in postcolonial India led to land
encroachment and displacement of tribal communities, placing their ecosystems and economies
in jeopardy. British colonialism had also ‘de-industrialized’ many indigenous technologies,
leaving the country more underdeveloped and economically insecure than it was in the
eighteenth century.13 Subsistence systems of farming and forestry, distinguished by the
involvement and even leadership of tribal women, were remodeled into a Western commercial
economy that resulted in vast forest destruction.14 Members of indigenous communities became
ecological refugees; unfamiliar Western systems of labour further escalated deprivation and
suffering caused by unfair land allocation, widespread deforestation, and inadequate wages.
Peasants were excluded from the market economy with no contribution to political decisions and
no access to any form of sociopolitical transparency.15 Environmental protest in India was thus
concerned with the intersection of social and ecological survival: the life of the poor and the life
of nature were intertwined, and one required the other.
When the government of India continued these forestry practices even after
Independence, local communities were resentful and unhappy that their forests were being
15 Firdaus Fatima Rizvi, “Why People Protest: An Analysis of Ecological Movements,” Social Change 39, no. 3 (2009): pp.
14 Vandana Shiva, Staying Alive: Women, Ecology, and Development (Berkeley, CA: North Atlantic Books, 2016), 61-65.
13 Subhash Sharma, “Why the Marginalised Protest: Environmental Movements as a Critique of Dominant Development
12 De Rosa, de Moor, and Dabaieh, “Vulnerability and Activism in Urban Climate Politics” Cities 130 (2022): p. 103848
exploited for commercial gain while their own needs were unmet. After the 1970 flooding of the
Alakananda valley—which led to great loss of human, agricultural, and pastoral life—villagers
realized that landslides were occurring on land where felling operations had taken place; the
connections between deforestation, floods, and landslides were increasingly evident. In 1973,
they asked for and were denied access to ash trees for agricultural purposes, while the Symonds
Co.—a British sporting goods firm—was allotted ash trees in the Mandal forest only a short
distance away. Then, Chandi Prasad Bhatt, a leader of the movement, suggested embracing the
trees to prevent Symonds from cutting them down; thus, the Chipko movement (chipko means
“to stick or hug”) was born. Employees of Symonds were forced to leave the Mandal forest
without chopping a single tree.16
Tribal women were particularly affected by British ecological policy because their
livelihood depended on stable forest ecologies that they had established through years of
experience.17 They entered the Chipko movement in the struggle at the Reni forest through
spontaneous action when the men of the village were absent. When workers from the lumber
company were spotted in Reni, the women of the village—led by Gaura Devi—approached the
men themselves, even staring down the barrels of their guns in their encounter. In another
instance, the women of Dongri Paintoli village opposed their own fathers, brothers, and husbands
as they held a Chipko demonstration in a nearby oak forest that was to be felled for oncoming
commercialization. The women, as well as associated male leaders of Chipko, faced defamation
and threats after the Dongri protests; yet, they were ultimately successful.18
18 Shobhita Jain, “Women and People's Ecological Movement: A Case Study of Women's Role in the Chipko Movement in Uttar
Pradesh,” Economic and Political Weekly 19, no. 41 (October 13, 1984): pp. 1788-1794,
https://doi.org/https://www.jstor.org/stable/4373670.
17 Mallick, Environmental Movements of India (Amsterdam: Amsterdam University Press, 2021).
16 Ramachandra Guha, The Unquiet Woods: Ecological Change and Peasant Resistance in the Himalaya (Ranikhet: Permanent
Black, 2010).
The physical action of the Chipko movement is distinctive and powerful in establishing a
bodily relationship between the tribal women and nature. The South Asian woman’s relationship
with her body can be complex. Colourism is rampant in both rural and urban
households—especially in poor or lower-caste communities.19 Nutritional insecurity,
malnutrition due to poverty and illiteracy, gender discrimination in intrahousehold food
allocation, high domestic workloads, and prevalence of chronic energy deficiency are common in
tribal women.20 Lack of bodily integrity and forced conformity to sociocultural norms and codes
often render women physically powerless, especially when it comes to their own body.21
Therefore, the action of hugging the tree can be interpreted as a pioneering act of bodily
autonomy, especially in a symbolic sense. This presence of physicality is also significant in
lending the protest an overt aspect of theatricality—creating what is ultimately the defining
feature of the Chipko movement. The act of “tree-hugging” has become globally popular as a
manifestation of ecocentric views; although extrapolated and commodified by Western neoliberal
environmentalism,22 the power of the physical action cannot be ignored. The entire protest is
based upon physical security: the body of the protestor protects the body of the tree. The
relationship of these women to the trees has trifold significance: the tree can be perceived as a
mother, an equal, or a child. Gaura Devi was known to refer to the forest as her maika (mother’s
home).23 In Maria Mies’ argument that the relationship of man and nature was necessarily violent
23 Jain, “Women and People's Ecological Movement” Economic and Political Weekly 19, no. 41 (October 13, 1984): pp.
22 Siddhartha Shome, “The New India versus the Global Green Brahmins,” The Breakthrough Institute, February 7, 2012,
https://thebreakthrough.org/journal/issue-2/the-new-india-versus-the-global-green-brahmins.
21 Kanchan Mathur, “Body as Space, Body as Site: Bodily Integrity and Women's Empowerment in India,” Economic and
Politics Weekly 43, no. 17 (2, 2008): pp. 54-63, https://doi.org/https://www.jstor.org/stable/40277391.
20 Ridhima Kapoor, Manisha Sabharwal, and Suparna Ghosh-Jerath, “Diet Quality, Nutritional Adequacy and Anthropometric
Status among Indigenous Women of Reproductive Age Group (15–49 Years) in India: A Narrative Review,” Dietetics 2, no. 1
19 Sammy Pleiza, “Exploring the Relationship between Hinduism, Body Image, and Maladaptive Eating Behaviors among South
Asian Individuals: A Qualitative Study,” Brown Undergraduate Journal of Public Health, December 12, 2021,
https://sites.brown.edu/publichealthjournal/2021/12/12/image/.
and destructive, similarities are drawn between the female body and the natural
world24—especially in the context of Indian tribal women, who are more likely to face sexual
violence and rape, with no help or justice offered by police forces and political leadership.25
Likening women to nature, the Chipko action can thus be perceived as the woman physically
protecting her own kind, equalizing the environment to herself and to humankind. From another
ecofeminist perspective that views women as sustainers and protectors of the earth, the Chipko
action can also be compared to women—mothers—protecting their child. However, I believe
that forcing the female political actor into the limited sphere of motherhood in every action is
orthodox and unnecessary. Thus, I prefer to interpret this physical action as individual, political,
and empowering—consciously opposing its reduction to “motherly.” ​
The use of language and song in the Chipko movement creates a sense of political
dialogue, revealing ecological community and security in women as well as the power dynamic
between politician and protester. Chipko was not a singular event, and thus existed in multiple
instances and versions of itself, each of which incorporated unique strategies of performance to
achieve the group’s political purpose. While some of this dialogue was explicitly theatrical in
form, such as chants or prayers, every use of language that led up to and occurred beyond the
Chipko action is a part of its performance. The use of language as an organizing strategy is
significant in the Reni protest. A young girl first spied workers arriving at the Reni forest with
their logging equipment; she quickly relayed this information to Gaura Devi, head of the village
Mahila Mandal (women’s club); Gaura Devi then mobilized fellow women in the community
and headed to Reni quickly enough to render the felling efforts unsuccessful.26 In 1979, a logging
26 Guha, The Unquiet Woods (Ranikhet: Permanent Black, 2010).
25 Amit Singh, “Does India Care to Protect Her Tribal Women?,” The Citizen (January 29, 2017),
https://www.thecitizen.in/index.php/en/NewsDetail/index/7/9799/Does-India-Care-To-Protect-Her-Tribal-Women.
24 Maria Mies, Patriarchy and Accumulation on a World Scale: Women in the International Division of Labour (Critique.
Influence. Change) (Zed Books, 2014).
contractor responded to early hints of protest with a challenge: “hum ped ka koi hissa nahin
chodenge.” (“We will not leave any part of the tree behind.”) Therefore, the political actors in
this movement spoke to each other constantly, often through direct address—unintentionally
supplementing the Chipko action with dialogue. Additionally, the protest abounded with songs.
“Matu Hamru, Paani Hamru/Hamra hi chhan yi bhaun bhi!” (“Ours is the earth, ours is the
water, ours is the fields, forest and fodder!”) and other choruses were popular.27 Often
accompanied by the Bajgi people—a caste of musicians—these songs were used to rouse and
mobilize other villagers, exemplifying the use of performance as a communal activity.28
An eco-dramaturgical perspective to the Chipko resistance recognizes the reflections of
these women’s actions in the feminine principle and ethical dimensions of Hinduism. Hinduism’s
attitude towards nature is sacred and devotional, evident through the worship of multiple animals
and plants as deities. The earthly manifestation of all primordial energy and power is called
Prakriti, which directly translates to “nature”; Prakriti is worshipped as a female goddess, and
the action of Chipko’s women is connected to the femininity of the earth. This is further
exemplified by the women tying rakhees (religious wrist threads) around the trees to signify
kinship with them.29 However, one should be careful to not attribute the actions of the women to
such religious or feminine connections only: doing so would discredit their ecological knowledge
and political reasoning. A patriarchal perception of Mother Earth might view her as a passive
entity who simply accepts all that happens to her—a persona often forced upon marginalized
women too. But, in Shiva’s explanation of the feminine principle, Prakriti is embodied by
creativity, activity, diversity, productivity, and interconnectedness with all beings. The women of
29 Shiva, Staying Alive (Berkeley, CA: North Atlantic Books, 2016)
28 Shiva, Staying Alive (Berkeley, CA: North Atlantic Books, 2016)
27 Sunandita Mehrotra, “A Walk down Memory Lane with Sudesha Devi,” Sahapedia, January 2, 2017,
https://www.sahapedia.org/walk-down-memory-lane-sudesha-devi.
the Chipko movement almost seem to encapsulate her character in their action, producing a
metaphorical theatricality that escapes both patriarchal gender roles and religious tradition.
According to the Arthashastra, an ancient Hindu philosophical text, “agricultural administration,
disaster management, and environmental policy” would all fall under responsibilities of a central
“monarch.” The text also mentions environmental offenses such as littering and inappropriate
treatment of animals.30 I contend that it was the tribal women who undertook the “monarch’s”
work of maintaining the earth and supporting the social and environmental well-being of the
community; through their protest, they upturned the patriarchal value of ancient Hinduism,
proving that the woman isn’t just the caretaker of homes but of nations and ecologies.
The Chipko movement consisted of various actions—performed in specific
locations—that employed the theatricality of suffering to convey urgent need for political
initiative. In the Pulna village, women saved 621 trees by traipsing through 40 centimetres of
snow to the felling operations, surrounding the workers, and taking away their tools. In
Badyagarh, three thousand men, women, and children (“one for every chir tree in the forest”)
participated in a fast to stop the logging of the Malgaddi forest.31 Protestors also undertook a foot
march along the full length of the Himalayas to encourage people to understand the importance
of protecting their forests.32 The location of these protests is significant in interpreting them as
site-specific performance: place, as an element of one’s ecological identity, is significant in
eco-theatre.33 A sense of place is ultimately a sense of self. It is particularly vital to the tribal,
lower-caste communities of India as it connects individual suffering to communal locality: the
scars on the ecological place are linked to the scars on the social body of the tribe, especially its
33 K. Mary Elizabeth, “Performing the Elements in Indian Eco-Theatre: Deepan Sivaraman’s The Legends of Khasak,” Modern
32 Mallick, Environmental Movements of India (Amsterdam: Amsterdam University Press, 2021).
31 Guha, The Unquiet Woods (Ranikhet: Permanent Black, 2010).
30 Christopher Key Chapple and Mary Evelyn Tucker, Hinduism and Ecology: The Intersection of Earth, Sky, and Water
(Cambridge: International Society for Science and Religion, 2007).
women.34 Multi-sited protests also suggest embodiment beyond the biological body through “in
situ performance”—the human body and the ideology remain the same while the environment
keeps changing. Additionally, the theatricality of suffering, through liveness and physical body,
was used as a tool to draw nationwide attention to the issue. In Julie Peters’ essay “Theatricality,
Legalism, and the Scenography of Suffering,” she argues that the use of rhetoric,
self-characterization, and dramatic setting by witnesses in a courtroom trial produced an implicit
assertion of the priority of universal justice over national justice—with the witnesses themselves
representing the values they stood for.35 A parallel can be drawn to the Chipko protests, where
impactful setting (forest as the stage), characterization (dynamics of us versus them, powerful vs
powerless, men vs women), and rhetoric (silence, chanting, prayer, or dialogue) were used
effectively—if unintentionally—to elucidate the desire for political and ecological justice
through the theatricality of suffering.
“The tribal women in the Chipko protests refused to remain passive victims and let things
happen to them; instead, they became speakers, disruptors, and leaders.” For many of them, their
actions were “an act of defiance against their own families”; although aware of this, they went
ahead and participated anyway.36 Amidst India’s highly collectivistic, patriarchal, joint family
model, their autonomy is striking. These women were supported by years of experience and
knowledge in subsistence farming, forest economy, and ecological tradition.37 Their involvement
changed the implications of the movement; it has been extensively romanticized and
sensationalized by both Indian and Western media. After all, “the environmentalism of female
37 Jain, “Women and People's Ecological Movement” Economic and Political Weekly 19, no. 41 (October 13, 1984): pp.
36 Mehrotra, “A Walk down Memory Lane,” Sahapedia, January 2, 2017,
35 Julie Stone Peters, “Theatricality, Legalism, and the Scenography of Suffering,” Law & Literature 18, no. 1 (January 2006):
34 Nayar, “Indigenous Cultures and the Ecology of Protest” Journal of Postcolonial Writing(February 2013): pp. 291-303
indigenous postcolonials” holds a certain appeal.38 Yet, there is little understanding of the
influence of these women’s intersectional identities on their political action, and the impact it had
on traditional gender relations in tribal peasant communities. Research conducted on the
after-effects of the Chipko movement found that there is currently a dearth of natural resources
for forest communities.39 The sensationalization of the issue resulted in strict governmental bans
on tree-logging that left no space for the women’s original systems of self-sufficient subsistence
agriculture.
The Chipko movement has resulted in women becoming pro-active agents against
climate change; their extensive knowledge systems, open communal economies, efficiency and
care, and collective solidarity uniquely suit this role.40 Women-led adivasi (tribal) movements for
environmental protection have provided them opportunities to enter agricultural politics and thus
economic structure.41 The performativity of the Chipko protests thus included theatrical devices
that generated solidarity, gathered attention and response, and held strong implications for the
intellectual and political empowerment of the tribal peasant woman. Performances of protest are
symbolic and influential in emphasizing the dynamics between the powerful and the
marginalized—providing the “common (wo)man” in contemporary political society a path to
emancipation and equality.
