volumes.nurj_title: Asceticism in Early Fiqh and Medieval Sufi Text: Shaybānī and Ghazālī Compared

blocks: Asceticism in Early Fiqh and Medieval Sufi Text: Shaybānī and Ghazālī Compared
Rizwanul Islam
Northwestern University in Qatar
Introduction: Zuhd Between Misinterpretation and Authenticity

There was once a prevalent concept of considering Sufism as a sect of Islam in oriental studies, which to some extent still affects the idea of zuhd (asceticism) being a quintessential theme within Sufism. Some think of it as an aberration from a Christian perspective of monastic practices; others think that these practices are what amounts to the mainstream understanding of zuhd or asceticism in Islam. Most of these misinterpretations also arise from a secularized analysis of history, where the past is seen as an unavoidable influence on the context as it builds upon previous understandings of a particular subject matter. This essay aims to present the idea of asceticism in Islam as an independent theme from a fiqh (legal) perspective through Kitāb al-kasb of Muhammad b. al-Hasan al-Shaybānī (d. 189/805) and compare it with the later Sufi text Kitāb al-faqr wa’l-zuhd of Abu Hamid al-Ghazālī (d. 1111) to understand the distinct legal and spiritual dynamics within this theme.
Zuhd and the Legal Framework: Al-Shaybānī’s Kitāb al-Kasb

Asceticism is one of the many practices (e.g., zikr, muraqaba, khalwa, sama) through which Sufism or tasawwuf, aims to purify the nafs or emotional state of humans to remove the veils on their ruh (spirit) and attain ma’rifa (gnosis). It requires a constant practice of avoiding physical desires that arise through the emotional or psychological faculties of humans. The crux of the matter is to what extent this avoidance is sanctioned and recommended by the Prophetic narrations and legal injunctions of Islam. Contrary to what the orientalist narrative was about the smooth osmosis of monasticism into early Sufis due to their constant interaction with vast numbers of Chrisitians spread around the centers of the Islamic world, there is a harsh rejection of self-abasement, celibacy, and reclusion in the Prophetic narrations.[0] Shaybānī mentions a narration from the Prophet saying, “I was sent with tolerant Hanifism, and I was not sent with difficult monasticism.”[1] It reflects the Quranic verse 25:67—“They are those who spend neither wastefully nor stingily, but moderately in between.”

Shaybānī very explicitly names a section of his book “The Ruling on Earning Livelihood and Its Excellence” where he mentions the Prophetic traditions—“Seeking livelihood is incumbent upon all Muslims” and “Seeking livelihood is mandatory after the mandatory prayer.”[2] He writes that it is not possible to fulfill the mandatory duties to God without livelihood; hence, it has been made mandatory.[3] He brings examples of prophets and messengers to exemplify its necessity. In a section called “The Permissibility of Halal Livelihood and the Deviant Opinion of Some Sufis,” he explicitly attacks some ascetics in his time who tried to emulate the monastics by calling them “imbecile” and writes that they say that earling livelihood is impermissible (haram) and it is only permissible when there is no other way, the way eating from dead animals in certain situations is sanctioned.[4] He goes on to mention the revealed texts and examples of the Prophets; these so-called Sufis try to back their claim with and refute them with the left-out texts from the Quran and Prophetic narrations.[5] He mentions that there are examples of the Prophet earning livelihood; however, the matter of the Prophets was special as their primary objective was to spread the message of God, and they too sought livelihood at times to leave examples for the people to follow.[6]

After establishing the obligation to earn a livelihood, the later part of the book deals with the extent of earning and abstaining. Here is where Shaybānī finds moderation in the example of the Seal of the Prophets rather than Sulayman, the Prophet and ruler of the Israelites. After mentioning the verse where Sulayman asks God, “My Lord! Forgive me, and grant me an authority that will never be matched by anyone after me. You are indeed the Giver of all bounties,” he mentions in two narrations, the first from the Prophet, where he says, “The poor of my nation will enter paradise before half a day, and that day would equal five hundred years on earth,” and the second from the companions—“Sulayman would be the last to enter paradise among the prophets because of his royalty.”[7] He balances it with the saying of the beloved Prophet, “Oh God! Give me a life of need, give me a death in a needy state, and resurrect me with needy people on the Day of Resurrection,” and mentioning the incident—“The keys of the treasures of the world were presented before me. When I asked the advice of my brother Jibreel about what decision to make, he humbly pointed to me that I make my own decision. Then I said, I will be a slave prophet; one day I will be hungry; and one day I will be satisfied. I will be patient when I am hungry, and I will express gratitude (to Allah) when I am satisfied.”[8] There is a similar narration of the Prophet choosing milk over honey when given the keys to the treasures. Preferring the example of the Prophet, Shaybānī writes, “If people are content with the indispensables in life and focus on the hereafter through extraneous things, then that will be the best for them.” In another place, he says, “Man will be interrogated (on the Day of Resurrection) about matters beyond what is necessary for man's life. On the other hand, no one will be questioned about poverty.”[9]

Shaybānī recognizes that the state of wealth and livelihood is one that is dictated by the qadr (power) of God, and humans have no free will over it except making supplications, which can change even the writing of taqdeer or fate. The status of the Prophets made their supplications necessary to be manifested, which is why the Prophets were given the scope to decide on their worldly state. Shaybānī considers both states of both the prophets in the middle as the reason why Sulayman wanted the worldly status out of remembrance for his Lord.[10] Hence, what mattered in Islam, according to Shaybānī, was the intention or state of the heart of humans when they are positioned at different levels of worldly status and when they supplicate for it. He goes deeper when he mentions other scholarly opinions that considered both the states of shukr (gratitude) and sabr (patience) to be equal and shukr to be in a higher state than sabr. He mentions the revealed texts those scholars use and finally provides some proofs in support of his verdict while considering it a valid difference amongst the scholars.[11] In the following sections, he expounds on the practical legal injunctions involving worldly needs and status. His verdict can be summarized into four principles: 1) Contrary to monasticism, it is compulsory for everyone to consume the minimum amount of food, clothing, or subsistence necessary for living. 2) It is desirable or mustahab to occasionally eat expensive food, wear expensive clothes, or use expensive means of living after the minimum necessities. 3) It is makruh or undesirable to perform these on a regular basis. 4) Waste of means of livelihood, i.e., eating beyond one's satisfaction, wasting, and, in the case of clothes and other means, leaving them idle, showing off, competing for pride or abundance, is haram or prohibited.[12]
Spiritual Asceticism in Ghazālī’s Kitāb al-Faqr wa’l-Zuhd

Ghazālī's Sufi perspective on zuhd, or abstinence, and poverty also draws from the teachings of the Prophet. The thirteenth chapter of Ghazālī's Ihya' Ulum al-din, titled Kitāb al-faqr wa’l-zuhd (Book of Poverty and Abstinence), delves into the intertwined themes of poverty and abstinence, highlighting their spiritual significance and the path they offer to seekers of God's closeness. According to Ghazālī in the Islamic tradition, poverty and abstinence have a profound connection, with poverty often seen as a manifestation of abstinence.[13] The Prophet's teachings encourage believers to love the poor, emphasizing that such love is a key to attaining heaven. The tradition even suggests that the poor will enter paradise ahead of the rich by five hundred years, underscoring the significance of poverty in the spiritual journey, as also mentioned by Shaybānī.

Ghazālī clarifies that the essence of the quest for poverty lies not in outward contrariness to the world but in an indifference to worldly allurements. True poverty, according to Ghazālī, is not an accidental state of destitution but a disciplined approach to life, emanating from an internal center of gravity, irrespective of one's material possessions or status. Ghazālī categorizes those who are “poor” into various groups, ranging from those who are repelled by material gain to those who hunger for wealth.[14] The highest degree of poverty, he argues, is embodied by those who are completely indifferent to material gain or loss. The term poverty, in this context, is semantically close to indigence, with the Prophet praising the indigent person who owns nothing that might enrich him and is ashamed to beg before God.

Importantly, Ghazālī distinguishes between true poverty and beggary. Poverty, as practiced for spiritual benefit, is not synonymous with dependence on others but rather signifies reliance on God. In contrast, beggary, especially for personal profit, is viewed as demeaning. Ghazālī emphasizes the importance of sincere poverty leading to inner wealth and highlights the three properties that sincere fuqara (poor) should adhere to: not asking when in need, not refusing when given, and not being bound by anything after acceptance.[15] The opposite of poverty, according to Ghazālī, is wealth, which is one of God's attributes. He explores the debate on whether it is better for human beings to have wealth or to be poor, concluding that the key to sincere poverty lies in accepting the Divine decree and maintaining an absence of resentment or rejection regarding one's state.[16] Ghazālī highlights that true poverty lies in accepting the Divine decree without resentment or resistance. In this context, poverty is valued for the spiritual wealth it brings and encourages individuals to compare their condition with that of those less fortunate rather than those more affluent.

Transitioning to the theme of asceticism or abstinence (zuhd), Ghazālī explains that it has a semantic range comparable to that of poverty. Zuhd involves refraining from the world and its temptations. Ghazālī illustrates the usage of the term in the Qur'an and draws on earlier themes to emphasize that abstinence is not about refraining from what is already prohibited but from what is licit and attainable.[17] He clarifies that abstinence does not imply refraining from prohibited things but rather abstaining from excessive attachment to what is lawful and attainable. He underlines the importance of avoiding excess and highlights that some things may be legitimately enjoyed in this world but could pose a moral danger. Ghazālī argues that worldly attachments separate humans from the Hereafter, considering the world and the Hereafter as alternate states of the human heart. He contends that "the world" and "the hereafter" represent different emotional states within the human heart, with the worldly state being closer and lower, while the hereafter is more distant, extending beyond death. Ghazālī underscores that worldly desires can distract the heart from God, and the objective of practicing abstinence is to redirect the heart away from the world, promoting closeness to God and the Hereafter. Furthermore, he suggests a higher level of abstinence where one forsakes both the world and the hereafter, solely seeking proximity to God. Ghazālī condemns the world when it becomes a distraction from God, highlighting that excessive aversion or love for the world can lead to spiritual neglect and inattention to God.[18]
Zuhd at the Intersection of Law and Spirituality

The exploration of asceticism in Islam through the lens of fiqh (legal) perspectives, as presented in Al-Shaybānī's Kitāb al-kasb and Al-Ghazālī's Sufi text Kitāb al-faqr wa’l-zuhd, reveals nuanced dynamics between legal and spiritual dimensions. Al-Shaybānī, one of the two principal disciples of Imam Abu Hanifa, emphasizes the mandatory nature of earning a livelihood, grounding his arguments in prophetic traditions that highlight the obligation of seeking sustenance. His legal framework establishes principles such as moderation in consumption, occasional indulgence in luxuries, and the prohibition of wastefulness. Al-Shaybānī recognizes the divine determination of wealth, asserting that supplication can influence fate. In complement to Shaybānī, Ghazālī's Sufi perspective delves into the spiritual significance of poverty and abstinence. Ghazālī too draws from the teachings of the Prophet to elucidate the profound connection between poverty and abstinence, emphasizing that true poverty is not a mere outward state but an internal disposition of indifference to worldly allurements. Ghazālī categorizes different degrees of poverty, aligning with various spiritual attitudes toward material possessions.
Conclusion: Toward a Unified Understanding of Zuhd

Both texts acknowledge the Prophet’s teachings on the significance of zuhd in the spiritual journey, yet they differ in approach. Al-Shaybani's legal perspective provides a framework for permissible and impermissible actions related to livelihood to apply externally, whereas Ghazālī's Sufi perspective focuses on what is at stake in terms of the internal transformation and spiritual significance of the practice of zuhd. The legal-spiritual dynamics within this theme rooted heavily in the Islamic textual tradition showcase its originality and a continuum where the science of legal obligations intersects with the science of spiritual aspirations, offering complementary insights into the same objective of immersing all human faculties into the essence of God.

volumes.nurj_title: Policing Italy: Neoliberal Authoritarianism, Racial Stigma, and the Emerging Thin Blue Line

blocks: Title: Policing Italy: Neoliberal Authoritarianism, Racial Stigma, and the Emerging Thin Blue Line
Introduction: Italy’s Policing Crisis in Context

Policing in Italy stands at the crossroads of a deeply rooted history and rapidly shifting contemporary challenges. From its inception during the unification of Italy to its transformation under fascist rule and evolution in the neoliberal era, Italian law enforcement has mirrored the nation’s broader struggles with power, identity, and inequality.² Unlike other European nations, where policing traditions often evolved alongside democratic reforms, Italy’s law enforcement has been repeatedly shaped by authoritarian legacies, colonial practices, and militarized structures that continue to influence its operations today.³

At the same time, Italy’s policing culture is increasingly influenced by global trends, such as the rise of the “Blue Lives Matter” movement and the symbolic adoption of the “thin blue line” rhetoric. These narratives, emphasizing police victimhood and moral superiority, have provided new frameworks for resisting public criticism and accountability. Combined with far-right political ideologies, these global influences have exacerbated systemic discrimination, widened social divides, and entrenched militarized approaches to public order.⁴

This paper explores the historical foundations and contemporary dynamics of policing in Italy, offering a critical examination of how past and present intersect to perpetuate authoritarian practices and socio-economic inequalities. From the violent suppression of peasant uprisings during the Risorgimento to the hyper-surveillance of marginalized communities in the neoliberal era, the history of Italian policing offers a lens through which to understand the ongoing tensions between state authority, public trust, and civil liberties. By investigating these patterns, this research seeks to highlight pathways for systemic reform and alternative approaches to public safety that prioritize equity and justice over coercion and control.⁵
Historical Foundations of Policing in Italy

The development of policing in Italy reflects a complex interplay of colonialism, authoritarianism, and socio-political upheavals. The modern Italian policing system evolved from its deep-rooted historical foundations in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, shaped by the unification of Italy (Risorgimento), fascist rule under Benito Mussolini, and post-World War II democratization.⁶ These historical forces not only defined the structure of Italian law enforcement but also embedded authoritarian tendencies, militarized models, and patterns of discrimination that continue to shape contemporary policing practices.⁷
Policing Under the Risorgimento and the Liberal State (1861–1922)

The unification of Italy in 1861 marked the emergence of a centralized state, and with it, the need for a unified system of law enforcement to control diverse regions that had previously been under separate rulers. Before unification, policing in Italy was fragmented, consisting of localized military forces such as the Carabinieri (established by the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1814) and municipal militias.⁸ The Carabinieri Reali (Royal Carabinieri), functioning both as military and civilian police, played a critical role in consolidating state authority after unification.⁹

The liberal state’s approach to policing focused heavily on maintaining public order and quelling local revolts, particularly in the agrarian and industrializing south. In the late 19th century, Italy experienced frequent uprisings, particularly among the southern peasantry, who resisted harsh economic and land reforms. The police often functioned as enforcers of elite interests, using repressive tactics to suppress movements like the Sicilian fasci (a peasant labor movement that demanded fair wages and land redistribution). Between 1893 and 1894, for example, the liberal state unleashed the military and Carabinieri to violently repress the fasci uprising, killing hundreds of peasants and imprisoning thousands.¹⁰

During this period, the Italian police were marked by a strong militarized structure and a focus on preventive policing rather than investigative work. This was a deliberate strategy to monitor and preempt political dissent, leading to the establishment of extensive networks of informants, surveillance systems, and political police units. The roots of distrust between marginalized communities—particularly peasants, workers, and anarchist groups—and law enforcement were firmly planted during this era.¹¹
Policing Under Mussolini’s Fascist Regime (1922–1943)

The most significant period in the development of policing in Italy came under Benito Mussolini’s fascist regime. Following his rise to power in 1922, Mussolini transformed Italian policing into a hyper-militarized and authoritarian apparatus to enforce fascist ideology and maintain control over society.¹² The creation of the Milizia Volontaria per la Sicurezza Nazionale (MVSN), better known as the “Blackshirts”, marked the blending of paramilitary and police forces. The Blackshirts, nominally an auxiliary force, terrorized political opponents, labor unions, and ethnic minorities, particularly targeting socialist and anarchist groups in urban centers.¹³

At the heart of Mussolini’s policing strategy was the Organizzazione per la Vigilanza e la Repressione dell'Antifascismo (OVRA), established in 1927 as a secret police force. OVRA was tasked with surveillance, infiltration, and repression of anti-fascist movements.¹⁴ It developed a vast intelligence-gathering network, including informants embedded in communities, labor unions, and universities. The OVRA’s methods—arbitrary arrests, torture, and executions—left a legacy of institutional brutality within Italian law enforcement that shaped policing culture for decades.¹⁵

Mussolini’s regime also expanded colonial policing practices in Italy’s African colonies, particularly in Libya and Ethiopia. Italian colonial forces combined military and policing functions, using brutal methods to suppress resistance movements. This included mass executions, concentration camps, and chemical weapons.¹⁶ Colonial policing fostered racialized practices and a sense of police superiority that later permeated domestic policing, particularly in dealings with Italy’s growing migrant and Roma populations in the postcolonial period.¹⁷
Post-War Reconstruction and the Democratic Transition (1945–1960s)

Following the collapse of the fascist regime and the end of World War II, Italy embarked on a significant period of political and social reconstruction. The 1948 Constitution officially established the country as a democratic republic, emphasizing civil liberties and placing formal limits on police powers.¹⁸ However, the transition to democracy was far from a clean break. Many institutional structures and personnel from the fascist period were retained, resulting in a continuity of authoritarian practices in law enforcement.¹⁹ This institutional inertia ensured that repressive policing tactics persisted, even as Italy sought to redefine itself as a modern democratic state.²⁰

During the fascist era, the Carabinieri and the state police (Polizia di Stato) had been key instruments of authoritarian control, enforcing strict public order through surveillance, suppression of dissent, and violence. Despite the fall of Mussolini’s regime, these institutions remained central to post-war law enforcement, carrying forward their militarized ethos.²¹ The Carabinieri, in particular, continued to function as a gendarmerie with dual responsibilities for military and civilian policing, ensuring that policing in Italy retained a quasi-military character.²²
Cold War Dynamics and the Suppression of Leftist Movements

The Cold War had a profound influence on Italy’s approach to law enforcement, shaping the priorities and tactics of the state. As a frontline state in the ideological battle between the Western bloc and Soviet-aligned communism, Italy was a key battleground for competing political ideologies.²³ The Communist Party of Italy (PCI) was one of the largest and most influential communist parties in Western Europe, with significant support from labor unions, intellectuals, and working-class communities.²⁴ This made Italy’s political landscape a focal point of Cold War tensions.

To counter the perceived threat of communism, the Italian government, often with tacit support from the United States and NATO allies, prioritized the suppression of leftist movements.²⁵ The police were frequently deployed to break up labor strikes, protests, and demonstrations, particularly during the 1950s and 1960s. Industrial regions such as Turin, Genoa, and Milan became hotbeds of labor unrest, as workers demanded better wages and conditions in the wake of post-war economic challenges.²⁶

The violent repression of these movements was emblematic of the state’s priorities. For example, during the Genoa strikes of 1960, police forces used batons and tear gas to disperse peaceful demonstrators, resulting in widespread injuries and public outcry.²⁷ Such incidents reinforced the perception of the police as protectors of elite economic and political interests rather than neutral public servants. This era of police violence created a deep mistrust between law enforcement and left-leaning segments of the population, a rift that would persist for decades.²⁸
The Years of Lead and the Rise of Terrorism (1970s–1980s)

The 1970s and 1980s, known as the Years of Lead (Anni di Piombo), marked a period of intense political violence and terrorism in Italy. Radical leftist groups, such as the Red Brigades (Brigate Rosse), and far-right factions both engaged in bombings, assassinations, and kidnappings.²⁹ These groups sought to destabilize the state and provoke revolutionary change or authoritarian crackdowns.

In response, the Italian government expanded police powers and adopted highly militarized strategies. Special anti-terrorism units were established within the Carabinieri and Polizia di Stato, and the intelligence services played an increasingly prominent role in counter-terrorism efforts.³⁰ The Legge Reale of 1975 granted police broader authority to use firearms and conduct searches without warrants.³¹ While these measures were effective in dismantling many terrorist networks, they also led to widespread abuses of power, including extrajudicial killings and the targeting of non-violent activists.³²

The Years of Lead further entrenched a militarized policing culture in Italy. Law enforcement agencies began to view themselves as the last line of defense against societal chaos, fostering a siege mentality that persists to this day.³³ This era also deepened public mistrust of the police, particularly among leftist and marginalized communities, as excessive force and surveillance became normalized tactics.³⁴
Neoliberalism and the Regulation of Working-Class Spaces

The rise of neoliberalism in Italy brought significant changes to urban and rural policing strategies, focusing on regulating working-class spaces and enforcing socio-economic divides.³⁵ Since the 1990s, urban redevelopment projects in cities such as Milan, Rome, and Turin have prioritized gentrification, displacing working-class and immigrant communities from central areas.³⁶

Neoliberal policies have also introduced aggressive policing in marginalized neighborhoods, where officers routinely conduct identity checks, surveillance, and stop-and-search operations.³⁷ Areas like Via Padova in Milan and Tor Bella Monaca in Rome have become symbols of over-policing, where residents—primarily migrants—face systemic discrimination and heightened scrutiny.³⁸

In rural regions, such as Calabria, policing strategies target migrant laborers employed in exploitative agricultural jobs.³⁹ Under the guise of cracking down on undocumented workers, law enforcement often ignores systemic exploitation by agribusinesses, instead criminalizing vulnerable populations.⁴⁰

Technological advancements have further entrenched inequities. Predictive policing systems and biometric tools disproportionately target minority neighborhoods, perpetuating racialized enforcement practices.⁴¹ Algorithms used by law enforcement rely on biased historical data, creating a feedback loop that justifies continued over-policing in these areas.⁴²
The Rise of Far-Right Influence in Policing

The infiltration of far-right ideologies into Italy’s police forces has significantly shaped the nation's law enforcement practices, amplifying systemic discrimination and perpetuating authoritarian policing.⁴³ Far-right political groups, such as Lega Nord and Fratelli d’Italia, have fostered alliances with police unions, often framing law enforcement as protectors of traditional values and national security.⁴⁴

Police unions like Sindacato Autonomo di Polizia (SAP) have actively adopted far-right rhetoric, including anti-immigrant sentiment and the defense of "Blue Life" victimhood narratives.⁴⁵ These unions frequently campaign for expanded police powers and immunity from prosecution, often with the support of far-right politicians who use these platforms to appeal to their voter bases.⁴⁶

The rise of far-right influence is also evident in the normalization of extremist symbols and ideologies within police ranks.⁴⁷ Investigations have uncovered cases of officers sharing fascist slogans, displaying Nazi memorabilia, and participating in far-right demonstrations.⁴⁸ These actions not only deepen public mistrust but also erode democratic norms within law enforcement institutions.⁴⁹
Pandemic Policing and Securitized Governance

The COVID-19 pandemic provided a pretext for the expansion of police powers and the normalization of securitized governance in Italy.⁵⁰ Under the guise of public health and safety, the Italian government imposed strict lockdown measures, which were among the most stringent in Europe.⁵¹ These regulations, while ostensibly aimed at controlling the virus, disproportionately targeted marginalized communities and entrenched pre-existing inequalities.⁵²
Extraordinary Powers and Policing Tactics

During the pandemic’s initial phases, Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte’s administration introduced emergency measures that granted law enforcement significant authority to enforce movement restrictions.⁵³ Citizens were required to carry self-certification forms (autocertificazioni) justifying their movements, and penalties for non-compliance included steep fines and, in some cases, criminal charges.⁵⁴ These measures led to widespread enforcement campaigns, with police conducting roadblocks and identity checks throughout the country.⁵⁵
Policing, Inequality, and Spatial Control

The pandemic further deepened socio-economic inequalities, and law enforcement practices exacerbated these disparities.⁵⁶ Marginalized groups, including migrants, Roma communities, and low-income workers, bore the brunt of pandemic policing.⁵⁷ Migrant laborers, essential to industries like agriculture and domestic work, were disproportionately fined for failing to produce valid self-certification documents.⁵⁸ Language barriers and unclear guidelines made compliance particularly challenging for these populations.⁵⁹

Roma settlements were similarly targeted under the guise of pandemic regulations. Local authorities exploited lockdown measures to justify the forced evictions of informal camps, leaving families homeless and without access to basic resources.⁶⁰ In Rome, for example, officials dismantled Roma camps, framing their actions as necessary for public health.⁶¹ Human rights groups criticized these evictions, noting the use of heavy-handed police tactics and rhetoric portraying Roma communities as vectors of disease.⁶²
Militarization of Policing and Authoritarian Trends

Pandemic policing in Italy also saw a marked shift toward militarization.⁶³ The government expanded the deployment of soldiers under the “Operation Safe Streets” (Operazione Strade Sicure) program, initially established to combat organized crime and terrorism.⁶⁴ By mid-2020, over 7,000 soldiers were stationed across Italian cities to patrol public spaces, enforce curfews, and conduct identity checks.⁶⁵ This increased reliance on military personnel blurred the lines between civilian law enforcement and military operations, raising concerns about the erosion of civil liberties.⁶⁶
Legislative Changes and Surveillance Expansion

The pandemic accelerated the adoption of surveillance technologies and legal measures that expanded police powers.⁶⁷ Emergency decrees (decreti emergenziali) introduced during the crisis allowed the government to bypass traditional democratic oversight, granting police broader discretion in enforcing public health measures.⁶⁸ These temporary provisions raised concerns about their potential to establish long-term securitization frameworks.⁶⁹

Municipalities like Florence and Turin adopted facial recognition software and big data analytics to monitor public compliance with lockdown measures.⁷⁰ While marketed as tools for enhancing public safety, these technologies lacked robust safeguards against misuse.⁷¹ Civil rights groups warned that such measures could be repurposed for broader surveillance post-pandemic, threatening civil liberties and privacy.⁷²
Conclusion: Resisting Authoritarian Policing in Italy

Italy’s policing crisis is deeply entrenched in a web of historical authoritarian legacies, neoliberal governance, and racialized socio-political structures.⁷³ The militarized and repressive nature of Italian law enforcement is not merely a vestige of the past but an actively evolving apparatus that continues to perpetuate systemic inequities.⁷⁴

Addressing this multi-faceted crisis requires transformative reforms that dismantle entrenched structures of coercion, inequality, and impunity.⁷⁵ Central to this effort must be the demilitarization of Italian policing.⁷⁶ This involves a fundamental shift away from the reliance on military forces like the Carabinieri for civilian policing roles.⁷⁷

Combatting the rise of far-right ideologies within police forces is another pressing challenge.⁷⁸ This necessitates a comprehensive de-radicalization strategy, including mandatory anti-racism and anti-extremism training for all officers.⁷⁹

Reimagining public safety in Italy involves investing in alternative approaches that prioritize community care over coercion.⁸⁰ Without addressing the intertwined structures of racial stigma, economic dispossession, and militarized policing, Italy risks deepening the social fractures that law enforcement is purportedly designed to address.⁸¹ By embracing transformative change, Italy can move toward a vision of public safety that values equity, community care, and democratic accountability over repression and control.⁸²

blocks: Dain 1
Beyond the Shoes: How the Running Industry Affects Run Culture
Lauren Dain
Originally Published in womensmarathonhistoryproject on 08/22/2024
Dain 2
Introduction
Running shoes and apparel are essential for any runner. Therefore, the running industry,
which consists of companies, race organizers, and advertisers targeting runners and influencing
running culture, is similarly essential to a runner’s sports experience. The running industry has been
dramatically growing in the last half century, in tandem with the recreational running boom. The
industry is known for adapting to new technology, trends, and fashion. Chicago Area Runners
Association Senior Development Manager of Community Development Dominique Sabbs speaks to
the recent ways the running industry has worked to mold itself to the time it’s in: “For many years,
running marketing was shifting to being very gendered, and now there is also a huge change in unisex
clothing and shoes to add an extra layer of inclusion.”1 Throughout the past 50 years, many of the
changes in the running industry to be inclusive and welcoming to runners have resulted from the
advocacy and ingenuity of running consumers. There are many instances when women have taken
control of their sports participation and made space for themselves, even if the existing running
industry did not provide it for them first.
Despite the prevalence of brands like Lululemon, Athleta, Fabletics, and others targeting
female consumers with athletic and athleisure apparel, sports bras were just hitting the marketplace
only fifty years ago. In 1977, Lisa Lindahl, Honda Miller, and Polly Smith invented the jog bra by
sewing two jock straps together.2 These women sought to address their personal needs after Lindahl
started running and found traditional bras not compressive or comfortable enough. Their invention
revolutionized all women’s sports, so much so that the Smithsonian houses a prototype of the jog bra.
2 Murashima, C. (2023, July 22). As the Women's World Cup gets underway, a look at the history of the sports bra.
NPR WBEZ Chicago. Retrieved January 13, 2025, from
https://www.npr.org/2023/07/20/1188869644/as-the-womens-world-cup-gets-underway-a-look-at-the-history-of-the-
sports-bra
1 Sabbs, D., & Dain, L. (2024, June 18). Interview with Dominique Sabbs [Personal Interview].
Dain 3
The prototype of the Jog Bra was made from two jock straps sewn together.3
The jog bra exemplifies how women have had to fill in the gaps for themselves in sports
designed around men. When women began to compete in marathons in the 1960s and 1970s, they
found creative ways to use non-running or athletic clothing for their performance, such as the jog bra
invention. Kathrine Switzer has written about pulling together her marathon outfit for her first Boston
race in 1967 from her old sports uniform and ballet tights. Regarding her outfit choice, she said, “I got
the idea from my old hockey tunics, which were easy to run in as they allowed total leg movement
and, with ballet tights, no chafing.”4 Switzer goes on to express that the construction of men’s running
shorts was made from canvas and was uncomfortable even for men. Her commentary is important:
running was just becoming a widespread recreational sport in the United States, and there were not
nearly as many shoe and apparel brands on the market as there are now. However, men still had some
official running options, mainly with shoes, while women had no specified running gear. Women had
to hodgepodge together running outfits, mainly pulling from the uniforms of more established female
4 Switzer, K. (2007). Marathon Woman: Running the Race to Revolutionize Women's Sports. De Capo Press.
https://www.amazon.com/Marathon-Woman-Running-Revolutionize-Womens/dp/0738213292
3 Keen, C. (2015, April 13). The First Jogbra Was Made by Sewing Together Two Men’s Athletic Supporters.
Smithsonian Magazine. Retrieved January 13, 2025, from
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smithsonian-institution/first-jogbra-made-sewing-together-two-mens-athletic-sup
Dain 4
sports, such as field hockey, and had to wear men’s shoes until the 1980s. I interviewed Nancy
Rollins, who has run over 100 marathons, starting with the 1980 Chicago marathon. When she began
running, Rollins remarked on the lack of gear availability: “The gear just was not in great shape for
quite a long time,” Rollins said, “There was not a lot of variety; it was nothing like what it is today.”5
The first women’s running shoe was the Waffle Racer by Nike, which debuted in 1978 and featured
the signature Nike waffle sole.6 The basis for the sole and design of the shoe are made from molds
called shoe lasts. While women can wear men’s shoes comfortably in many cases, female feet are
typically narrower and shorter. These distinctions can affect the arch's placement, the toe box's size,
and the shoe's width. Therefore, a shoe designed around a woman’s foot benefits overall foot health
and comfort, especially when running 26.2 miles. Creating a running shoe with a female last and
female-specific workout apparel, such as the jog bra, marked a revolutionary moment in women’s
athletics. Women were now seen as viable consumers in the running industry, enough that the industry
made products for them. Women are now major consumers in the United States, making up sixty
percent of all annual activewear sales.7
7 Bailis, R. (2016, November 16). Why Millennials Love Activewear — The Numbers Behind This Explosive
Growth. Retrieved January 13, 2025, from
https://multichannelmerchant.com/marketing/why-millennials-love-activewear-the-numbers-behind-this-explosive-g
rowth/
6 Alger, K. (n.d.). The History of the Running Shoe. Retrieved January 13, 2025, from
https://www.zappos.com/c/history-of-the-running-shoe
5 Rollins, N. (2024, June 13). Interview with Nancy Rollins [Personal Interview].
Dain 5
This photo is from the 1972 Boston Marathon, the first with an official women’s field.
Switzer ran the race with the bib number F6. Patrick A. Burns, The New York Times via
ESPN8
The Rise of Women’s Running Brands
Today, women are driving consumers, yet until the late 1990s, there was still not a significant
amount of availability in the activewear marketplace. That changed with the rise of companies like
Lululemon, Athleta, and Oiselle. In the 2000s, a surge of women’s activewear brands began to pop up
and dominate the clothing market. While leaving shoes to Nike, Brooks, Saucony, and the other
dominant brands of the twentieth century, these new brands sought to address comfort and style issues
in the running clothing sector. Oiselle is a Seattle-based women’s running apparel company founded
by Sarah Bergeson. It started because Bergeson was unhappy with the waistband fit of her running
shorts after having a baby and sought to create shorts that had more comfortable features for all ages
8 Minsberg, T. (2017, November 4). How 6 Women Changed the New York City Marathon Forever. Retrieved
January 13, 2025, from https://www.nytimes.com/2017/11/04/sports/women-new-york-marathon.html
Dain 6
and types of runners. In doing so, she took what was then an unusual approach in the running industry:
asking women what they wanted in their products. Bergeson is among the only female CEOs or
executives in the running industry. The leaders in the running industry are historically white and male,
which reflects how they produce their products and materials. Retired professional long-distance
runner Lauren Fleshman wrote in her memoir, Good For A Girl, about the ways the running industry,
specifically her former sponsor Nike, tried marketing towards women without their input. She says
that John Hoke, the designer of the female-specific Nike Goddess store in the early 2000s, said:
“Women weren’t comfortable in our stores, so I figured out where they would be comfortable—most
likely in their own homes.9 The [women’s] store has more of a residential feel.” Fleshman explains
that efforts such as Nike's have not been well-received because, ultimately, these PR stunts emphasize
the company’s historic tone-deafness toward women.10
Internally, in the running industry, sponsored female athletes feel the effects of sexist
practices towards women in the sport, such as through maternity leave policies. Retired professional
distance runner and Olympic marathoner Kara Goucher has advocated in the running industry for
better maternity benefits and overall treatment of female athletes. During her pregnancy in 2010, she
faced suspensions and pay cuts from Nike, which caught her off guard because she continued to train
and engage in marketing and advertising throughout her pregnancy. Goucher documented her
experience in her memoir The Longest Race, exposing the abuse she experienced on Nike’s elite
running team, the Oregon Project.11 She notes that Nike even monetized her pregnancy, having her
pose for a billboard shot to catch new consumer demographics, yet Nike still used its contract powers
11 Strout, E. (2023, March 29). Why Kara Goucher's Story Matters. Women's Running. Retrieved January 13, 2025,
from https://www.womensrunning.com/culture/people/why-kara-gouchers-story-matters/
10 Fleshman, L. (2023). Good For a Girl: A Woman Running in a Man's World. Penguin Random House.
9 MAD Design (n.d.). A Nike exclusively for women. Retrieved January 13, 2025, from
http://madesignllc.com/project/nike-goddess/
Dain 7
to find ways to reduce her salary.12 Since then, other professional athletes, such as former Nike runner
and multi-time Olympian Allyson Felix, have come forward with similar stories about Nike using
their pregnancy to make irrecoverable pay cuts despite these women continuing to be monetary assets
to the company while pregnant.13
Kara
Goucher, holding her son after The 2012 USA Half-Marathon Championships.  Duluth News
Tribune14
14St George, L. (2016, June 16). Goucher at forefront of runners seeking to change system. Retrieved January 13,
2025, from https://www.duluthnewstribune.com/sports/goucher-at-forefront-of-runners-seeking-to-change-system
13 Felix, A. (2019, May 22). Allyson Felix: My Own Nike Pregnancy Story. Retrieved January 13, 2025, from
https://www.nytimes.com/2019/05/22/opinion/allyson-felix-pregnancy-nike.html
12 Goucher, K., & Pilon, M. (2023). The Longest Race: Inside the Secret World of Abuse, Doping, and Deception on
Nike's Elite Running Team. Simon & Schuster.
Dain 8
Fleshman has experienced two sides of the running conglomerate’s approach towards
women. In her memoir, she discusses how Nike was willing to hear her ideas about improving their
female-targeted advertising and vocalized how they wanted to improve their image with women. Yet,
their approach to making these changes and the sexist practices within the company, such as maternity
policies, eventually forced Fleshman to leave the brand. A positive Fleshman takes away from her
work with Nike is the famous ‘Objectify Me’ ad campaign, which publicized Nike’s first shoe solely
designed for women (this differs from the women’s waffle racer since it was initially a men’s shoe just
inserted with a women’s last). Fleshman wrote most of the Objectify Me ad, showing her standing up
and staring at the camera. In an interview with her current sponsor, Oiselle, Fleshman discusses how
the initial concept Nike presented her was a photo of her in the nude with the words “Nike Objectifies
Women.”15 She found this not to be targeted to women but rather the “male gaze,” so she presented an
alternative that Nike was receptive to. Nike then turned the Objectify Me ad into posters that lined the
bedrooms of thousands of aspiring female teenage runners, showing them a representation of power
not completely laced with the sexualization of women.
15 Lesko, S. (n.d.). The Story Behind 'Objectify Me' - Lauren Fleshman Tells It. Retrieved January 13, 2025, from
https://www.oiselle.com/blogs/oiselle-blog/the-story-behind-objectify-me-lauren-fleshman-tells-it
Dain 9
The Nike “Objectify Me” ad featuring Fleshman. Google Images16
Female Runners in the Media
Combatting the sexualization of women in athletics is a pervasive problem in all sports, often
leading to advertisements that fail to celebrate and inspire women and instead present unrealistic and
unhealthy standards. An article published by the University of Calgary analyzes how advertising
16 Nike Objectify Me Print Ad [Photograph]. Google Images. https://www.pinterest.com/pin/353954851960575287/
Dain 10
targeting female runners sends mixed messages to consumers.17 Author Carly Drake found that in the
sixty advertisements she studied from January and February 2017, the issues of Runner's World,
Women’s Running, and Canadian Running, women’s mental and physical fortitude is “celebrated” but
in possibly unhealthy ways that perpetuate physical and beauty standards. For example, Drake defines
“obligatory running” as a “run at all costs mentality akin to exercise addiction.” This theme appears in
many advertisements Drake looked at, where advertisers layered images of women running alone at
dawn with messages such as “I will not run away from pain.” Drake notes that most advertisements
show elite athletes or women who fit the conventional physical standards of an elite athlete: lean, tall,
and fast. The connection a consumer can make from this type of marketing is that to belong in the
distance running culture, you must fit this mold. By flooding billboards, magazines, and online ads
with images of either elite athletes or lean models, women, especially young women, will internalize
that that is what they need to look like to be a runner, leading to increased drop-out rates of female
runners.
17 Drake, C. (2018, April 9). Boston Marathon: How advertisers target female runners. Retrieved January 13, 2025,
from https://ucalgary.ca/news/boston-marathon-how-advertisers-target-female-runners
Dain 11
An ad that Drake analyzed. The ad originally ran in an issue of Women’s Running. University of
Calgary18
Often, running carries a feeling of elitism and exclusion regarding speed. Barriers to entering
a race based on your finishing time exacerbate this elitist belief. In response to running brand Track
Smith’s annual ‘Boston Qualifiers (BQ) Only’ gear, they released after the Boston 2024 entries were
released, the organization Diverse We Run released a statement summarizing the effect that
exclusionary aspects of the running industry can have on the greater culture of the sport:
18 Drake, C. (2018, April 9).
Dain 12
“No one is saying we shouldn’t celebrate achievements or have standards. No one is saying a
race can’t have qualifying times. The problem is when a brand (or race event, or governing
body … etc.) claims to be a ‘champion for the AMATEUR RUNNER‘“(i.e., ‘for everyone’) in
theory but still reinforces exclusion and elitism in practice.”19
The leaders at Diverse We Run identified companies like Track Smith's influence on
consumers. Track Smith has released the BQ-only gear since 2015 and has received criticism in the
past for the gear only being made for time qualifiers and not registered charity runners. The company
has also faced critiques about its available sizes since its sizing only goes up to a woman’s 32-inch
waist. All of this frustration reached a boiling point in 2023 since their Instagram post introducing the
gear began with the quote, “This is not a jogging race,” from former Boston Marathon race organizer
Jock Semple, who notoriously advocated against the inclusion of women in the marathon, and is
infamously pictured trying to pull Kathrine Switzer out of the race in 1967. The brand quickly
removed the post and issued an apology for not considering the effect that using a quote from Semple
would have.20 However, the moment still acted as a push for more conversations around how the
running industry continues to celebrate certain types of athleticism, such as pushing past pain and
highlighting those with the most incredible speed, which is isolating to recreational and amateur
runners who similarly feel a great sense of accomplishment completing their races, but do not receive
the same accolades from the media and running culture broadly.
20 Carney, A. (2023, October 10).
19 Carney, A. (2023, October 10). Tracksmith’s BQ Singlet Raises Questions About the Marathon’s Most Exclusive
Race. Retrieved January 13, 2025, from
https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a45486207/tracksmith-boston-marathon-qualifier-singlet-controversy/
Dain 13
The Running Industry and Amateur Runners
In conversations with amateur and recreational runners, specific themes arose when asked
about their relationship with the running industry. Many women said they had noticed a dramatic shift
toward racial and body-type inclusion in the past decade. They see a broader range of clothing sizes in
activewear and see themselves more accurately represented in advertising. The growing popularity of
marathons may account for the change toward more inclusive gear, apparel, and race practices.21
Chicago area runner Lindsey Gerba ran her first marathon in 2003, and she speaks about the change
she has noticed since then:
“Before I did a marathon, I had this preconceived notion that marathon runners looked a
certain way, and I think one of the most interesting things is that if you go to a marathon start
line, you see every type of person. Now, you see every body type, every age, all of it. I think that
is such a powerful thing. Popularity in the sport has gone up, and from that, I think people see
other people they can relate to and think, ‘Oh, maybe I can do that too.’”22
A barrier to entering running is the belief that it is only for “certain people,” which is why
the way media and companies portray running is essential to the culture of the sport. If people do not
see themselves reflected in the sport’s messaging, they do not feel welcomed into that space. Sabbs
speaks to her observations in the running industry:
“Especially speaking as a woman of color, when it comes to inclusive sizes, we are seeing way
more than we ever did, but I do think there is a way to go in terms of quality and price. There is
a lot more investment in creating shoes for women and plus-size runners.”23
23 Sabbs, D., & Dain, L. (2024, June 18).
22 Gerba, L., & Dain, L. (2024, June 18). Interview with Lindsey Gerba [Personal Interview].
21 Goldman, J. (2024, May 10). The reasons behind the unprecedented spike in marathon runners. Retrieved January
13, 2025, from The reasons behind the unprecedented spike in marathon runners
Dain 14
The investment Sabbs refers to comes in many forms, such as running apparel, but also in
how the running industry works to address deeper structures of racism and privilege present in
running culture. A moment of reckoning for the running industry came after the tragic murder of
Ahmaud Arbery, a Black man who, while out for a run, was murdered by two white men; in Running
While Black, Alison Désir discusses how, in the wake of the murder of Arbery, she worked as a
consultant on an industry-wide task force to address racism in the sport.24 What she discovered was a
lack of willingness to take accountability for how running has participated in racism and white
supremacy. Even after the tragic murder of Arbery, Désir expressed the challenge and frustration she
felt in having to explain to the white members exactly how racism is prevalent in running culture. She
wrote about the isolating feeling of being “the only” in predominantly white running groups and the
differences in freedom white people feel when running compared to the fear that People of Color feel
in public spaces.25 Chicago area runner Maria Coleman expresses that “when you are in a running club
that is a white running club, there is a difference in how you feel, greater than that of male versus
female. There is a difference in the interactions in a running club when it comes to race.”26 Due to the
long history of exclusion in long-distance running, deeply rooted social structures perpetuate distance
running as a white space.
The Running Industry Diversity Coalition was formed in 2020 and is working to identify and
reckon with these stereotypes and racist practices within the sport.27 The formation of the RIDC marks
a tangible step towards accountability in the running industry; however, many brands have not yet
partnered with the coalition, such as some of the largest running shoe companies in the world, like

(2024, June 18). Interview with Lindsey Gerba [Personal Interview].

Nike and Adidas. It is essential to address current runners by including all levels of athletes in
conversations about apparel, shoes, and other facets of the running world to combat the intimidation
that runners feel about “looking the part.” The companies that greatly influence long-distance running
culture must take responsibility for the sport to repair the systems of elitism and exclusion that have
prevented people from participating in the past. While this discussion has focused on the running
industry as a company, it is also the duty of the runners, predominantly white runners, to identify how
we have maintained this culture, whether intentionally or not. As the marathon continues to grow in
numbers and diversity, it is the running industry and its runners' responsibility to be accountable for
transforming the future of running culture. A lesson I took away from my research into the running
industry is that there is success when the industry collaborates and listens to its runners of all levels.
As demonstrated by how women have broken into the running world, when runners of all
backgrounds have agency and control in running culture, the gaps and failures in the industry begin to
be filled.

blocks: The Negative Cultural Externalities of Transnational Economic Regulation
A Case Study of the US-China Trade War’s Potential Negative Cultural Effect and Possible Interactions with Policymaking Efforts
Michael Staller
December 9, 2024
Introduction

As of August 2024, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) is the United States’ third largest trading partner and largest trading partner outside of the Americas, constituting 11.3% of all net exports in the U.S. (U.S. Census Bureau, 2019). The economic interdependence between the two nations cannot be overstated; many of the goods and services that flow into the United States from the PRC and vice versa are fundamental to how each country has operated. Yet, economic interdependence has decreased to its lowest extent since 2010, as U.S. imports from the PRC have decreased by over $100 billion year over year (U.S. Census Bureau, 2019).

Concurrently, political tensions have risen between the two countries to an unprecedented extent; concerns regarding military presence, technology and security risks, and human rights issues have created an environment of contention not only between political leaders, but also each nation’s general population. According to a 2023 Gallup poll, only 15% of Americans view China “favorably,” decreasing from 53% in 2018 and 72% in 1989. Additionally, 50% of Americans name China as the nation’s greatest enemy (32% named Russia, 7% named North Korea), stating that China poses a “critical threat” to American interests over the next decade (Brenan, 2023). This sentiment is not just generalized among the American populace either; a Pew Research Center poll found just 42% of Chinese Americans view China “favorably,” compared to 72% who view the US “favorably.” Most notably, Chinese Americans are the only major Asian origin group in the United States in which the majority of people do not have a favorable opinion regarding their ancestral homeland (Pew Research Center, 2022). Similarly, an anti-American ideology is shared among the Chinese populace as well; the Global Times, a CCP affiliated newspaper, found that only 2% of Chinese adults view the United States as their “most favorite foreign nation,” down from 7.5% in 2010 (Xie et al, 2024).

The spillover of this simultaneous rising political tension coupled with the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on political psyche may have impacted another function of prosperous codependence in the form of student flows; the number of undergraduate and graduate students studying abroad in each country has a significant effect on the way in which cultures are exchanged, future leaders between countries interact with each other, and political peacefulness between countries is signaled. Consequently, the magnitude of student flows between the two countries has decreased dramatically as well; the number of Chinese students studying abroad in the US has decreased 22% since 2019 (Ross et al, 2023). As such, cultural connectedness in the form of academic exchange between these two countries has decreased significantly over time.

The observed effects outlined in this introduction include economic disassociation, political antagonism, and the halting of student flows. It is hard to predict how these factors and their direction will impact the future of PRC and U.S. relations. As such, a more comprehensive and answerable question may be the extent cultural connectedness between these two countries is correlated to economic interdependence. This in turn may help determine the extent of these factors’ impact on political opposition. Additionally, the results from this regression may highlight an unanticipated impact on the broader international political arena; by examining the way in which economic ties have correlated with cultural connections, we may be able to more accurately predict how cultural barriers will evolve as economic variables fluctuate. Highlighting these results may indicate ways in which these findings can help determine how certain economic trajectories may impact political ideology and how these ideologies may impact future policy making efforts.
Methods

The method of this paper explores the relationship between economic ties between the PRC and the United States and cultural ties connecting the two nations. This examination can teach us important information about the future of cultural exchange in the 21st century transnational political arena. The disciplinary framework of this paper is the way in which macroeconomics interplays with Asian cultural studies. This paper will utilize a macroeconomic ideology by highlighting a regression analysis between these two concepts in order to gauge how much of a correlation exists, and this will explain the explanatory power and the direction of the magnitude of each of the variables that will be examined. The Asian cultural studies framework outlines how this correlation may provide a glimpse into the evolution of cultural connectedness between these two countries.

This study will specifically focus on this past decade’s U.S.-China trade war  to highlight how economic correlations with cultural components can be applied to a policymaking level. From 2018 to 2019, the United States and the PRC enacted mutual escalations of trade tariffs, resulting in a trade war that affected an approximate value of $450 billion in the inflows and outflows of goods (Fajgelbaum & Khandelwal, 2021). As such, measuring the volatility of imports and exports from each country to the other over a significant time frame may be able to signify economic interconnectedness and its fluctuations. This data can be collected through the U.S. Census Bureau and the Office of the United States Trade Representative. The independent variables used to measure economic connectedness in this study will include import and export figures from both countries before, during, and after the 2018–2019 trade war, and U.S. FDI into the PRC from 1985 onward. The dependent variable used to signify cultural connectivity is the rate of change of exchange students from the PRC to the United States. This paper uses the rate of change for exchange student enrollment because student foreign exchange is a great indicator of societal integration between groups of people of foreign descent. Not only is it a direct indicator of people to people relations, but also reflects diplomatic and educational cooperation and reflects a symbol of openness and trust.

Initial research on historical educational exchange rates shows a slow but gradual increase in Chinese international students studying at American universities from 1985 to 2007, a rapid increase from 2007 to 2015, a more gradual increase from 2015 to 2017, flat rates from 2017 to 2020, and decreasing rates from 2020 onward (IIE Open Doors, 2021). The number of U.S. students studying abroad in China from 2000 to 2016 follows a similar but more extreme fluctuation pattern; the amount of American students studying at Chinese universities began to increase in 2004, essentially flatline in 2012, and plummeting from 2012 to almost none in 2022 (Wang et al, 2020, Tang & Kang, 2024)[0]. The results indicated are consistent with heightened United States and Chinese economic tensions; decreasing exchange student rates for Chinese students at American universities from 2017 onward are consistent with the Trump administration’s more stern approach to diplomatic relations with the PRC, including the ensuing trade war in the following year. Concurrently, decreasing exchange student rates for American students at Chinese universities follows a similar path with American students plummeting throughout the Trump administration. Granted, one cannot appreciate these results without acknowledging the presence and impact of COVID-19 on the years following 2020. However, very initial indications of a correlation between fiscal relations seem to exist.

The regression highlighted in this paper will determine how the rate of change of net exports and foreign direct investment affect the rate of change of Chinese students studying in America year over year. The increasing or decreasing rate of change can help establish important nuances in the data that may provide a more accurate interpretation of the ways in which this dynamic relationship isn’t just changing, but determining how fast this relationship is changing over time related to the baseline. Additionally, measuring the rate of change over time as opposed to nominal values of student flows adds an element of stationarity to the data. Thus, one interpretation of the regression run may be the extent to which the growth (or decline) in net exports and FDI have affected an accelerating (or decelerating) rate of growth (or decline) of Chinese students studying abroad at U.S. universities.
Findings

Figure 1. Regression of the percentage change in Chinese students studying in the United States on the  percentage change in imports into the United States  from China and percentage change in U.S. FDI into China.

Results of the regression indicate minimal to moderate correlation (R squared = .2998). This result can be interpreted as meaning ~30% of the variance in the rate of change of Chinese students studying abroad at American universities can be explained by the rate of change of net exports from the United States into China and the rate of change of FDI from the United States to the PRC. Yet, this study highlights more significant information, including significance tests of the regressors; this test is conducted by studying the statistical significance of the coefficients of the two regressors (‘Imports’ and ‘FDI’). By comparing the magnitude of the coefficients of each variable to the Margin of Error Formula[1], we can determine the statistical significance of each variable.
(1.96[2])*(Standard Error of the coefficient)
Formula 1: Margin of Error Formula

Thus, this study finds that the yearly percentage change in imports from the PRC into the United States has a statistically significant, positive effect on the percentage change in the number of Chinese students studying abroad at American universities. However, the yearly percentage change in foreign direct investment from the United States into the PRC has an insignificant, indistinguishable effect on the percentage change in the number of Chinese students studying abroad at American universities.

The results of this regression highlight a few key findings; first, progress toward the initial question of to what extent do economic ties between the PRC and the U.S. influence cultural connections between the two countries may have been achieved; this in turn suggests that the economic connection of trade flows does has a statistically significant effect on cultural ties between the two countries; in other words, each incremental increase in the percentage change of imports into the United States from China leads to a positive change in the percentage change in the number of Chinese students studying in the United States by a factor of about 0.48. Additionally, this study helps specify the extent to which another sector of the international economy, FDI, influences cultural ties. The percentage change in the FDI has an insignificant effect on the percentage change on the number of Chinese students studying in the United States. Thus, this regressor’s effect on the percentage change in the number of foreign students is insignificant, if at all. In sum, the most significant factor regarding the interpretation of these significance tests is that while percentage change in FDI has an insignificant positive or negative effect on the percentage change of students, percentage change in net exports does have a statistically significant, positive effect on this regressand.

Secondly, these findings may help distinguish other factors that could contribute to cultural progress; while the major explanatory factor may not be trade, others such as American/Chinese businesses operating within the PRC/U.S., acquisition of American/Chinese treasury bonds by the PRC/U.S., and many other factors may be of particular interest when trying to provide further color to this topic of choice. As noted before, the insignificance of percentage change on FDI on cultural ties indicates that this variable may not be the best regressor; therefore, opportunity for other regressions exists that study other variables that may signify economic connections to a different extent.

One potential explanation for the lack of definitive correlation between FDI and student flows may be a significant disconnect between the parties in charge of FDI and monetary transfers and the students and families of students who are hoping to study abroad at American universities. If this connection proves to be strongly divisive, the cultural correlation between the two variables would have no connection. Additionally, it is possible that FDI may not be the best representation of economic ties between the PRC and the U.S.; the United States has been heavily reliant on the Chinese manufacturing economy since the early 1980s. The continuum of FDI from the U.S. to China therefore may have no indication of political openness or dissent; the monetary investment abroad may just be a purely transaction occurrence without any cultural significance whatsoever. One way in which to alter this research would be to determine the opinion of the U.S. of the general public within the PRC and determine how this opinion has changed over time.

While evidence suggests a correlation exists to an extent, it is important to note that this does not indicate causation to any extent; the statistically significant, positive effect of trade flows on student flows is merely a positive effect; the R-squared value of roughly 0.30 is just an indication of the explanatory power of the regressors on the variance of the regressand. Thus, this study cannot be interpreted as indicating that the economic connections between the U.S. and China are positively causal in the direction of student flows between the two countries, as that would be an overstatement and incorrect.
Discussion

I argue that determining a positive correlation between U.S. and PRC economic interconnectedness and cultural ties can have a drastic impact on the way in which economic policymaking efforts influence cultural acceptance and inclusivity. By exploring the ways in which changes in economic policy are connected to changes in cultural policy, policymakers can understand the extent and magnitude of a potential cultural effect stemming from new policy. By considering the way in which economic ties are correlated with cultural affiliations, policymakers have a concrete datapoint on the way in which transnational economic policy and cultural barriers are connected; a higher percentage change in trade flows between these two countries is correlated to a higher percentage change in student flows between them. Conversely, as the yearly percentage change of trade flows decreases, the yearly percentage change of student flows decreases as well. This is uniquely important because the existence of this relationship can inform policymakers regarding how economic policy toward other countries will affect cultural exchange, cultural barriers and the growth of each countries’ inclusivity and understanding of others. This may help policymakers when determining the impact of potential policy he or she is hoping to enact; by exploring the ways in which economic policy may impact cultural connectedness, policymakers can understand a cultural effect when determining the efficacy of an economic policy.

The extent to which this study is useful is determined by how applicable this information is to predicting how cultural barriers will evolve as future economic ties continue to fluctuate throughout time. Over the past decade, rising political conflict between the U.S. and China has led to a more contentious political arena than either country has experienced in their relationship before. Yet, the extent to which economic ties may act as an indicator or predictor of student flows is one attempt to observe factors that could impact the way in which cultural barriers are constructed or torn down. As noted in Section II, the intuition behind using educational exchanges as a signifier of cultural exchange is not only due to the fact that student foreign exchange is a great indicator of societal integration between groups of people of foreign descent, but also reflects diplomatic and educational cooperation and reflects a symbol of openness and trust.

The process of examination for potential policymaking using this study is as follows: firstly, one needs to recognize trends in the data, determine the direction and magnitude of trade flows and educational exchanges, and examine the effects on populations’ cultural affinity to others. One can deduce this by synthesizing external polling metrics to determine populations’ cultural harmony and views. Lastly, policymakers can deduce the extent to which past policy and potential future policy has and will impact cultural rapport so that this can be included in the process of policymaking when determining the effectiveness of provisions.

This case study, highlighting the U.S.-China trade war starting in 2018, begins with an understanding of the trends between the economic and cultural data of choosing; in this case, trade flows and educational exchange. As such, an interpretation of this data shows that there has been a consistent deceleration in the yearly rate of change of net exports since 2005 with a significant decrease starting from 2016 onward. This downward trend could highlight increasing legislation from the U.S. and PRC over the past decade. Concurrently, a significant and consistent deceleration is present in the yearly rate of change of student flows since 2011, decreasing to a much more significant extent in 2017.
Figure 2. Percentage change in yearly student flows.             Figure 3. Percentage change in yearly trade flows.

As the direction and magnitude of both student flows and trade flows experienced an accelerating decline between 2019 and 2020, one can then view the way in which public opinion has changed to determine the extent to the impact of these economic barriers. The Global Times, a PRC-affiliated news source, conducted a poll in October 2022 that surveyed 1,655 people from ages fourteen to thirty five to determine the extent to which public opinion toward ‘the West” has changed in the last decade; the results show, “43.9 percent of Chinese young people have become less favorable toward Western countries. More than 90 percent of young people say they “equally look” at (39.3 percent) or “look down” on (54.6 percent) Western countries. The poll found only 3.9 percent of respondents “look up” to the West and theUnited States, and the Global Times story said that was a marked decrease from five years ago when 37.2 percent looked up to the West” (Tang, 2022). As such, though a definitive causal link is not established, one can interpret the timing of heightened U.S. and Chinese turmoil with the timing of the trade war between the two countries as to not be coincidental.

Concurrently, this sentiment is shared across the Pacific Ocean as well. A Pew Research Poll conducted in 2021 studied American popular sentiment toward China on a “feeling thermometer,” indicating their assessment of general sentiment toward the PRC on a scale from zero to one hundred. The poll found that, “67% of Americans have “cold” feelings toward China… rating the country less than 50 on a 0 to 100 scale. This is up from just 46% who said the same in 2018. The intensity of these negative feelings has also increased: The share who say they have ‘very cold’ feelings toward China (0-24 on the same scale) has roughly doubled from 23% to 47%” (Pew Research Center, 2021). This poll has determined that within a roughly three year timeframe (2018 to 2021), a 104 percent increase in very negative sentiment toward China has occurred in the United States. However, understanding the academic and cultural realm within which this paper was written is crucial to understanding the biases of Americans regarding Asian cultural studies. Kuan-Hsing Chen, a critical theorist based in Taiwan and former professor in the Graduate Institute for Social Research and Cultural Studies at National Chiao Tung University, discusses the idea of colonialism and imperialism cultural studies within former imperialist centers, such as the US and Great Britain. Kuan argues that work regarding uncovering the implications of imperialism is inescapable for scholars who reside in places where neoimperialism continues to exercise power, whereas these studies have not been central to scholars in former imperialist nations (Kuan, 2010). As such, when discussing the role of American perceptions of the PRC, it is important to understand the context of the American survey responder. The effects of imperialism are hardly a concern for the average American, who likely doesn’t interact with the lingering effect of imperialism in China. As such, these responses toward the PRC are not likely fully informed regarding the amount of cultural and historical understanding necessary to embrace the PRC’s position. Nonetheless, the cultural responsiveness of the publics of these two nations to each other is most certainly a reflection of the political agendas of both nations; thus, decreased trade flows and decreased student exchange between these two countries have shown a connection with heightened tension among each country’s population and an association with increased cultural barriers.

This understanding could induce economic policymakers to make a more holistic decision about the effectiveness of potential future policy by recognizing its indirect effect on cultural components. The importance of cultural affinity in society cannot be understated; social cohesion, deeper interpersonal relationships, cultural preservation, political stability, and societal advancements depend on a societies’ ability to maintain cultural openness and coherence. Thus, in the cost benefit analysis of potential future policy, policymakers can determine the extent to which these factors may be inhibited.
Conclusion

Determining the causal link between governmental political agendas and public sentiment would be indicative of many factors, including determining how geopolitical tensions between two populations can rise to a significant level; yet, this study is merely answering the question of to what extent can economic ties predict one indication of a cultural connection. However, this data may be useful in a broader context; by determining this connection, future research may be able to predict future predicaments in the arena of transnational politics. Decreased economic connectivity is correlated with decreased cultural affiliations, which leads to deteriorating public sentiments and ultimately the construction of cultural barriers. This disallows the free flow of ideas and shared experiences. If the United States and the PRC continue in the economic direction that has been expected over the past decade, one can expect cultural connectivity to follow suit. As such, fewer cultural connections will be made and less cohesion will be experienced within each population.
