volumes.nurj_title: VAI O LE OLA: SĀMOAN WOMEN'S WATER ECOLOGIES

blocks: VAI O LE OLA:
SĀMOAN WOMEN’S WATER ECOLOGIES
Lula Blas Fox
Northwestern University
SIT Sāmoa: Social and Environmental Change in Oceania
Fall 2024
ADVISOR
Anita Latai-Niusulu
ACADEMIC DIRECTOR
Fetaomi Tapu-Qiliho
INTRODUCTION

Sāmoan identity is intimately tied to Indigenous relationships with water, as water sources, such as natural springs, are rich in ancient legends, myths, meanings, and practices.[0] In the ancient Sāmoan belief system, water is genealogically connected to man, as well as lands, the cosmos, and the gods. This shared genealogy is considered sacred, and establishes a, “legacy of responsibility on all living things (trees, clouds, volcanoes, water, animals, people) to respect through reciprocity, the divine balance or harmony they share.”[1] The relational space that binds responsibility between creator, created, and all of creation is known as the vā––the foundation of most Polynesian societies––as it “governs all things and holds all things together.”[2] The vā thus represents a crucial ethical and religious orientation for Sāmoan interactions with the environment. In the context of water sources, natural springs are particularly important within Sāmoan relations, as it was often believed that the gods inhabited these spaces. The presence of natural springs became the defining characteristic of many communities, as they named themselves, “after the aitu who created, and often inhabited, springs or acted as guardians of springs in pre-Christian times.”[3] The village was thus defined by those who shared the springs and communally cared for them.

Water sources eventually became the foundation of the village-wide fa’amatai (chiefly) structure, where chiefly titles became directly tied to land and water sources. Sites such as mangroves and natural springs were placed under the pule (authority) of a matai (chief), and the stewardship of the water sites by the matai therefore verified and validated their honorifics as village leaders.[4] The fono a matai (village council), for example, “met regularly to manage all activities in the village and, in this process, enacted regulations to maintain springs and their surroundings and to control human conduct around the pools.”[5]  In the present day, over 80% of the land in Sāmoa is considered customary, collectively owned by matai that represent each ‘āiga (family) (Macpherson & Macpherson, 2009). Thus, stewardship of local water sources remains a village-wide endeavor, as the matai, village women, and elders contribute towards sustaining Sāmoan water stewardship.

The deep, millenia-maintained connections to water have cultivated a system of reciprocity amongst all Sāmoans, where they care for and honor the water systems that nourish them.[6] Stewardship of the springs was institutionalized in ancient Sāmoan spiritual and religious beliefs; many Sāmoan villages described the presence of aitu (human spirits), who would punish any individual that did not treat the springs with respect. In order to maintain the va fealoa’i, or the relational space between humans, the spirits, and the environment, Sāmoan villagers strived to “ensure quietness and respect for the spirit,” by managing human conduct around the springs.[7] The introduction of Christianity to the Sāmoan archipelago in the mid-19th century initiated rapid change amongst Sāmoan religious practices, challenging and reshaping the ancestral values that influenced human interaction with the environment.

Throughout these various periods of change, natural springs sustained the cultural and historical significance they held in Sāmoan communities, especially amongst Sāmoan women. For women of the villages in particular, collecting water was an, “...established part of daily routines for young women because, ‘Sāmoans refuse to drink river water, which they called suamalō.’”[8] The pools of the springs were often divided into specific areas for women’s daily tasks, such as collecting drinking water, bathing, and cleaning laundry. As everyday frequenters of these pools, Sāmoan women have always played a crucial role in stewarding local water sources, however, little academic work focuses on documenting their participation in the management of village ecosystems. This research seeks to add to existing scholarship on the implicit feminisms of Sāmoan women, where they are the, “backbones of families and villages.”[9] By emphasizing core Sāmoan values, such as community care, good relations, and collective self-determination, Sāmoan women play a crucial role in perpetuating cultural systems of reciprocity and environmental stewardship.[10]

This research project sought to understand the role of Sāmoan women in village-wide environmental management systems by examining women’s participation in protecting the natural springs of Faleapuna, a village located on the northeast coast of Upolu. Utilizing a Pacific Research Framework that emphasized Sāmoan conceptions of feminism, semi-structured interviews were conducted with multiple Sāmoan women of different age groups, as well as one elder male matai. All interviewees were from the village of Faleapuna, and held a significant stake in protecting the natural environment as community members. Lengthy conversations with women in the village revealed the deeply entrenched desire to care for the environment, in order to protect and preserve the land for future generations. This research seeks to position the case-study of Faleapuna in the broader context of Indigenous governance, feminism, environmental health, and climate resilience, examining the socio-cultural and spiritual beliefs that drive Indigenous stewardship––an essential institution amidst the current climate crisis.
FALEAPUNA: HOUSE OF SPRINGS
Organization of the village

Faleapuna is a Sāmoan village on the north coast of Upolu. The name of the village stems from the words fale (house) and puna (to boil, swell, as in a natural spring/pool), indicating the presence of natural springs.[11] Adjacent to the sea, the village is separated into four pitonu’u (districts) that are demarcated by their proximity to the main natural pools. The village economy is largely subsistence based; family-operated plantations abundant in taro, bananas, and breadfruit are found throughout the village. Less than a mile from shore, there is also a coral reef where men, women, and children alike fish. Day-to-day life in the village therefore consists of fishing, farming, household feau (chores), and swimming in the natural springs, while a majority of children attend school in Faleapuna, other nearby villages, or in Apia (Personal Interview #1, 2024). Food is often shared communally throughout the village, and once the seafood or agricultural products are distributed, a member of the family may sell any surplus goods at the nearby market in Apia for additional income.

The village is organized around the fa’amatai (Sāmoan chiefly system), where each ‘āiga (family) has a matai (family chief) representing them in the village fono (council). Both men and women can become matai in the village, and there are currently, as of November 2024, at least two women matai in the village.[12] Women matai are not allowed to join the women’s committee, another crucial institution towards running the village. Women’s committees, or komiti tuamama, were first formed in the 1920s, during New Zealand’s military occupation of Western Sāmoa. Women in the committee are responsible for cultivating respectful relations amongst villagers and the environment, increasing public health awareness, and keeping the village clean––all of which are crucial aspects of environmental and community health.[13] Elder non-matai women in the ‘āiga, including those that are not genealogically from Faleapuna but rather married into the village, often participate in village decision-making through the women’s committee. Faith is an equally important institution in Faleapuna, in addition to fa’amatai and the women’s committee; the village has multiple churches in the village, each catering to different denominations, such as the Catholic Church, the Congregational Christian Church (LMS), and the Church of Jesus Christ and the Latter-Day Saints (LDS). These institutions all play a significant role in the stewardship of the natural pools.
Rules of the Puna

There are four main springs in Faleapuna: Vai levi, Vai alae, Vai apo’a, and Vai punaleilei. The pools are divided into four main districts, with each district defining its respective boundaries around a centrally-located pool. Since they are located on village land, the pools are largely open to all people, including tourists. They are primarily cared for by the women’s committee, who organize monthly village-wide beautification initiatives of the pools, invest tourist money into infrastructure upgrades, and cultivate respectful behavior that protects the pools from disturbances, such as pollution. Women are additionally responsible for passing down the stories of the pools, and ensuring the village youth learn about the importance of taking care of them.

The leadership of the women’s committee in maintaining the natural pools is linked to women’s everyday presence at the pools throughout village history. In the past, the other four main pools were used for bathing, laundry, and swimming, with stones, “laid around the springs to form small pools one yard across that are used for drinking water.”[14] Women in the village spent a significant portion of their day at the pools, completing household feau (chores) such as fetching water for the family, cleaning laundry, and bathing the children. The women always made sure to clean the pool before they left, washing out any remnants of their daily activities: “We always cleaned the pools. In the olden days, our ancestors always cleaned them after using them. We never left them dirty. We take care of them.”[15] In this regard, the pools were central towards women’s everyday life in Faleapuna.

Over the last decade, the use of the pools has shifted as Faleapuna adopted different amenities associated with Sāmoa’s integration into the capitalist market, resulting in changes to the village lifestyle. Now, villagers have increased access to alternate water sources, such as tap water and bottled plastic water from Apia and other surrounding villages, so most of Faleapuna no longer requires drinking water from the pools.[16] The exception is during times of storm, when water is collected from the pools and boiled to be used for cooking and drinking.[17] Around a decade ago, the women’s committee helped upgrade the pools for tourists, so village members no longer wash laundry or bathe in them to ensure they remain clean.[18] Community members continue to use the springs for recreational purposes, however, with many families going to the pools after finishing their daily feau, swimming between the hours of 12:00 p.m. and 6:00 p.m.[19] The responsibilities of the women’s committee includes managing money given from tourists to swim in the pools (however, there is no set charge to use the pools), ensuring people are not polluting the pools with rubbish or other materials, and enforcing behavioral rules/norms that are considered respectful ways of acting in the presence of the pools.

The rules, which both tourists and locals alike are suggested to follow, comprise of: no fishing in the pools (except for ceremonial purposes); no swimming in the pool after 6:00 p.m. or sunset (most villagers seem to obey); no yelling or loud voices used in the pools; no jumping in the pools; and no disorderly behavior, such as consuming alcohol.[20] The rules were created to, “protect the springs and have people respect them.”[21] Since these rules are partially rooted in pre-colonial notions of tapu and maintaining the vā between humans and aitu, the women told me that most people in the village follow the rules, but some villagers do not truly believe in them because of Faleapuna’s conversion into a Christian village.
Sacred Ecologies: Legends of Aitu

Derived from the ancestral Sāmoan religion, etiquette codes that guided human behavior and tapu (sacredness) were established at the natural springs due to the presence of certain aitu (human spirits/Gods). Remaining quiet and respectful while in the space of an aitu was crucial so as not to anger them; thus, the rules instituted at the springs were created in consideration of the vā between humans and ancient spirits.[22] The primary goal of the pool rules was to prevent any sort of human-caused disruptions at the springs, as ancient Sāmoan proverbs, “...warned Sāmoans to leave springs as their spirit guardians had created them and not attempt to alter them.”[23] In Faleapuna, one of the stories that was shared with me concerned an aitu that was an old male ghost, said to lurk at one of the pools. He was easily angered, so in order to respect the aitu, ancient villagers remained quiet when at the pools, ensuring they did not disrupt the spirit.[24] Villagers also did not swim at the pool after dark, as they believed the aitu came out while the sun set––hence why some women still do not enter the pools after 6:00 p.m.

Another story consisted of a tele sā, or a ‘spirit woman’ that guards specific forests, pools, villages, and falls in Sāmoa. Tele sā are considered protectors of the earth that get easily intrigued or angered by beautiful women.[25] Sāmoan women and girls are often told to cover their mirrors at night, and to have their hair up so as not to attract or provoke the tele sā. Tay,[26] one of my interlocutors, a younger mother who was not a member of the women's committee, told me about a tele sā that lived in Saleimoa, a nearby village on the northwest coast of Upolu. In the old days, despite the distance between her and Faleapuna, the tele sā was acutely aware when a girl was being “naughty” at one of the pools by wearing a sei (flower worn in the ear) with her hair hung down. She also got angry when people disrupted the pools or left rubbish in them. In response, she would “transform into an animal and tell the person to stop what they are doing.”[27] If one did not comply with the words of the tele sā, there would be severe consequences, ranging from the person’s hair falling out to the tele sā even creating storms or flooding; “When she gets angry, the water rushes and the wind gets rough.”[28] In the old days, one would apologize to her before they left the pools, pick up any rubbish they left, and go straight home. If their actions angered the tele sā to a severe extent, the villager would have to formally apologize to the fono.

When discussing the rules of the pools with my interlocutors, all of them emphasized the importance of the rules in protecting the pools, but some explained to me that the rules did not matter as much to them since they no longer believed in aitu.[29] Despite all of my interlocutors following the rules with great caution, even teaching them to their kids, many of them had complex emotions regarding the fact that the rules stemmed from aitu. One of my interlocutors said to me about the aitu, “Samoa is Christian now. The [ancient] ancestors are gone, and so are their rules.”[30] Tay, however, who notably did not subscribe to either of the dominant churches in the village (Congregational and Catholic), said to me, “You must respect the tele sā and the ancestors in the olden days. Now Sāmoa is Christian, but still you must respect the rules and what came before.”[31] Tay told me a story about her experience of seeing a woman from her husband’s village disrespect tapu, wearing a sei and singing at one of the village pools. The tele sā warned the woman to stop, but she did not listen. “She disrespected the tele sā and she got sick. Her hair even fell out, and her ears bled. You have to learn about the tele sā and respect her.”[32] Most Sāmoans I spoke with have heard of similar experiences between humans and aitu, and many can describe the aitu located in other villages. Despite holding Christian beliefs, most Sāmoan women I spoke to still chose to respect the stories of the aitu, regardless of whether or not they personally believed in them.

The connection between aitu and environmental protection can be located within a greater body of academic literature that has described the linkage between faith and Indigenous stewardship as a form of ‘sacred ecology.’ Within the concept of sacred ecology, Indigenous ecological knowledge includes “spiritual or religious dimensions” that fall outside the realm of western science, as the use of resources is regarded as, “an exchange and a privilege that comes with stewardship responsibilities, and the knowledge that to waste has direct consequences on the web of interactions that sustain life.”[33] These spiritual beliefs are largely responsible for the regulation of human interactions with the environment––known as tapu in the Sāmoan context.[34] Within a sacredness ethic, Tapu, or rules restricting human behavior in sacred spaces, became essential in the island context, where resources were understandably finite and islanders learned to follow the seasons and migrations in earthly and aquatic harvest so as to allow regrowth and regeneration amongst non-human life. Tapu thus ensured that all forms of life were not overexploited, polluted, or desecrated by human activity. In this regard, tapu represented the marriage between spirituality and sustainability ethics, consecrating balance and harmony into the Indigenous human-environment relationship.

Due to the large-scale, village-wide conversion of Sāmoans into Christians, however, the dynamic between ancestral sacred ecology and contemporary Christian faith has resulted in complex socio-cultural beliefs where elements of both spiritual systems are present.[35] The introduction of Christianity in the Pacific Islands did not wholly result in the demise of belief in spirits, but rather it, “altered the beliefs in certain kinds of spirits and their powers.”[36] Spirits that regulate human-environment relationships have, “diminished in the eyes of Christians,” but the underlying ideologies and practices related to environmental management have persisted, albeit, “challenged and reshaped.”[37] Thus, while Sāmoans abandoned many aspects of the ancestral religion, stories of the aitu and notions of tapu remained present within Sāmoan society, although they were communicated in continuously evolving forms that coexist with Christianity. The sacred nature of the pools is reaffirmed in church practices, for instance, since the water from Faleapuna’s springs is often used to baptize babies.[38] The continued utilization of spring water into Christian practice reflects how sacred entities have taken on new meaning as they are adapted into Christianity; within the Christian belief system, water is purifying agent that cleanses of sin.

Christian institutions in the village are essential towards fostering environmental stewardship. Since all village matters are discussed in church, church pastors play a significant role in informing Faleapuna’s residents on the importance of conservation. The pastor in the Catholic church, for example, regularly reminds the village youth to refrain from polluting the pools or acting disrespectfully. “The pastor tells them not to leave rubbish and to act good, and the youth listen because that is their pastor.”[39] Churches are central to contemporary Sāmoan society, and by wielding their influence to inform their congregations on the value of preserving the environment, they are able to positively contribute to local Indigenous stewardship in ways that may have been overlooked by previous researchers (Wildermuth, 2012).
Transcending Generations: Women as Environmental Storytellers

As primary caretakers of the children in the village, Sāmoan women in Faleapuna rely on spiritual and historical stories to describe the importance of the pools to the younger generations. While not all of the women I interviewed necessarily believed in the continued existence of the aitu, they all shared stories of the spirits with their children in order to scare them into acting properly at the pools.[40] When telling their children about the rules of the pool, such as no jumping or screaming, the kids, “mostly listen, but some don’t,” however, “they listen more when they are told the old stories about the aitu in the pool. They get scared, so they follow the rules.”[41] The women in the committee emphasized to me that they were responsible for teaching their kids about respecting the environment, and that their own mothers first taught them about the history of the pools, and how to treat them with respect.[42]

For the women in the village, caring for the pools therefore represented the continuation of ancestral practice, as women were raised by their mothers, grandmothers, and other elders to become stewards and maintain the generational commitment of protecting the pools. In this respect, the passing of knowledge was linked to the processes of relationality through the vā; “The giving and receiving of information is closely dictated by observance of the vā.”[43] The vā is relationship, stewardship, affiliation, and in this application, the transcending of environmental stories across time is a practice associated with sustaining the vā between humans generationally; respect is taught, passed down, learned, and subsequently perpetuated. The women I spoke to all went on to raise their own children and ensure they understood the significance of protecting the pools as well. When asking my women interlocutors about how they taught their own children about the pools, they explained that passing on the knowledge imparted to them by their own mothers was extremely important to them:

I teach my kids about the pools just like my mom taught me. I don’t let them go in the pools until they’re older. They go with me to the pools when they are six or seven. I tell them they will get punished if they act naughty or leave rubbish at the pools. They learn from me how to respect the pools and the tele sā.[44]

Stories of a religious nature were also critical towards the environmental education imparted on children, as my women interlocutors emphasized to me the importance of having children understand they had a responsibility to protect God’s creation; “The water is sacred to us and we have to remind the kids that.”[45]

The women in the village considered it their responsibility to not only educate the village children, but also share the stories of the pools with tourists: “We have to tell tourists about the rules to make sure they respect them, and so that they know the story of the pools. Then they know about the village.”[46] Since women largely act as custodians of the pools, they have also taken on the crucial role as storytellers and historians of the pools, sharing with both future generations, as well as visiting tourists, the rules, stories, and legends of the natural springs. In this regard, women play a pivotal role in sustaining the local, everyday ecologies of the springs by ensuring that Indigenous knowledge systems are sustained amongst all people who use them; “...As people retell village histories embedded in tala le vavau (ancient stories of myths, legends, and customs), their sense of place is affirmed, and the meanings they give to their connections to fanua persist.”[47] By combining contemporary Christian narratives with tala le vavau, the women of Faleapuna engage in oral storytelling that effectively furthers the importance of Sāmoan ecological conservation.
DISCUSSION: SĀMOAN WOMEN’S WATER ECOLOGIES

As this research has revealed, the women of Faleapuna comprise an essential role in the management of the village’s natural springs. By regularly maintaining the springs, preserving and passing down the springs’ histories and legends, and affirming the spiritual and socio-cultural beliefs of the springs, the women of Faleapuna embody a successful Indigenous stewardship system that has transcended generations.

The case study of Faleapuna’s natural springs ecologies fits well into the growing body of literature that emphasizes Indigenous eco-spiritual relationships as a necessary element of land management. Eco-spiritual relationships are instrumental in localizing Western sustainability science, which have already largely invested in dispossessing Indigenous peoples of their lands, cultural autonomy, and sovereignty for the sake of conservation.[48] Sāmoan theologian Reverend Dr. Upolu Lumā Vaai, for example, has written extensively on the need to address the spiritual and religious components in community-based environmental knowledge and relationality systems: “relationality sees the world as an eco-relational multidimensional whole that sustains itself only through a healthy flow of connections and deep relationships.”[49] The notion of eco-relational spirituality is akin to the Indigenous Pasifik vā, or the relational space in between the creator and the created, the visible and the invisible.[50] The principles of the vā reveal that all aspects of life are, “multi-dimensional, distinct and different yet mutually and inextricably related,” and thus, there must be balance and harmony between them.[51] According to Rev. Dr. Vaai, Pasifik multi-dimensionality can be seen within the dual meanings of terms such as fanua/vanua/fenua, which indicate both land and placenta, showing how the life of humans and the land are therefore intertwined.[52] This eco-relational understanding is experienced within the village of Faleapuna, where the protection of the natural springs is a labor of respect––for the springs, God, the elders, and the ancestors who have passed––a labor of faith, and a labor that extends past the despiritualized Western perception of ‘preserving resources’ and thinking of land only as a commodity, rather than a living, breathing extension of the people themselves.

The commodification of nature, ingrained in capitalism and stemming from Western colonial ideologies that view the land as both separate and below humans––thus rendering it subject to human expansion and exploitation––continue to pervade Western climate and sustainability science. Western climate science often ignores the spirituality of Indigenous environmental knowledge, deeming it superstition and instead advancing secular notions of rationality that originated in the Enlightenment period.[53] Instead, western sustainability science is largely dedicated toward infrastructural and economic development to maintain access to resources.[54] The disregard for Indigenous spirituality in the Western sustainability ethic has removed ecosystems from their human context and rendered Indigenous management systems inferior to Western conservation. Pasifik academics and climate activists, however, emphasize the importance of “embracing the sacred”:

When we reclaim and embrace the sacred in everyone and all around us, when we act in ways that maintain spirit-focused relationships with family, with community as an extension of our family, and with environment as an extension of our community, we grow out capacity to love and attain a soulful state––joyful, fulfilled, connected, and undeniably sustainable.[55]

Indigenous frameworks of “embracing the sacred” are already embodied in the village of Faleapuna, where the management of the natural springs is just as much about Sāmoan relationality as it is about protecting a ‘resource.’ The springs were and continue to be considered sacred by Faleapuna visitors, who have protected them from human-related disturbance even after no longer requiring them for daily activities.[56] The entire village works together to maintain the springs, with every individual playing a role; whether this means collecting the rubbish, building cement fixtures around the springs, educating tourists about the springs’ histories, or enforcing the pool rules, the women, the youth, the taule’ale’a (untitled men), and the matai all aid in sustaining the local water ecologies.

Within Sāmoan and other Indigenous Pasifik communities, “beliefs about the sacred are tightly coupled to place-based knowledge systems and culturally driven management practices.”[57] These knowledge systems take effect within a set of, “shared responsibilities that bind communities… and are transferred across generations through regular community practice.”[58] Through Kealiikanakaaoleohaililani and Giardina’s description of sacred ecologies, it is evident that the village of Faleapuna demonstrates a form of place-based management with knowledge systems and practices intimately connected to the land that villagers reside on. The naming of the village itself reinforces the notion that the ecology and place are central; Faleapuna translates to house of springs, representing how the springs are integral towards village identity and everyday life.

In Indigenous communities across the globe, it is widely held that the land is not only a provider, but it is an extension of us. The land holds our ancestors, our histories, our practices, and our genealogies. This sentiment is echoed in Sāmoa where Indigenous connection toward the earth can be explained by the phrase: “‘O le faavae o le mau nei, o le sootaga ma le ‘ele’ele,’” or, “our cultural claim to any land or earthly inheritance is premised on a genealogical connection with the earth.”[59] As this statement articulates, humans are not separate from their environment, but rather genealogically connected. In this regard, Indigenous kinship and stewardship are integral in the status quo, as they challenge the hegemony of colonial logic entrenched in the Western capitalist worldview, which emphasizes the exploitation of land––an entity subject to relentless domination––for profit.[60]

Ultimately, this case-study of Faleapuna serves to demonstrate a form of community-based sacred ecologies, where faith-based and religious orientations are crucial towards local land management systems. Uplifting these forms of Indigenous ecologies are integral at a time when conservation zones across the globe are being established on Indigenous lands, but excluded from Indigenous peoples.[61] This form of ecocolonialism, however, predicated on the forcible transfer of, “resource rights from their traditional owners and managers to a relatively new ‘nation state,’” displaces Indigenous peoples from their ancestral lands, interrupting the continuation of ecological knowledge.[62] As Cox and Elmqvist reveal, Western conservation systems alienate Indigenous forms of collective land management, where land is not owned by an individual but rather genealogically connected to a family title. The commodification of land into private property that can be sold or usurped by a dominating political entity, such as a nation-state government, therefore disrupts communal land practices and Indigenous genealogies. Rather than continuously violate Indigenous stewardship and its associated worldviews, global and local environmental policy must reorient itself similar to the model of Sāmoa and emphasize community-based initiatives that reaffirm Indigenous land rights, sovereignty, and self-determination.
CONCLUSION

This case-study of Faleapuna reaffirms the necessity of women in building climate resilience and sustainable land management systems. As stewards, educators, culture keepers, and protectors, Sāmoan women’s participation in environmental initiatives is critical towards fostering a healthy ecosystem. Through the cultivation of generational knowledge and practice and stewardship rooted in ethics of care, faith, and reciprocity for their people and their land, the women of Faleapuna exhibit how Indigenous stewardship is central toward building a sustainable Indigenous future. Environmental, cultural, and spiritual health are intertwined, as the women of Faleapuna reveal. By not only cleaning the springs regularly, but by telling the stories and legends of the springs, and caring for the springs to sustain ancestral practice––while simultaneously teaching future generations––the women villagers of Faleapuna depict how protecting their environment is also an act of community care that nurtures Indigenous understandings of eco-spiritual relationality. In an era where Indigenous peoples across Oceania continue to face land dispossession, environmental racism, and the denial of sovereignty and self-determination from colonial powers, the success of Faleapuna in maintaining traditional land tenure and empowering community-led environmental management is an essential model for Indigenous-led climate resilience.

blocks: Zhou 1
The Idea of Tibet:
Forms and Functions of Narrative Storytelling in Exile
Audrey Zhou
Professors Arthur McKeown and Sarah Jacoby
December 7th, 2024
Zhou 2
Our Shared Stories
The air was crisp that Wednesday morning, but I was uncomfortably sweaty. A few
wrong turns and Google Maps misreadings resulted in an unexpected morning spent scaling a
neighboring hillside in a fruitless attempt at finding an easy shortcut. Pushing past tall pine trees
and prickly underbrush, I prayed that I was heading in the direction of Jampaling Elder’s Home,
known by locals as ‘Old People Home.’ It was here that I met Sonam Lhundup, an 82-year-old
former cowherd for the Dalai Lama. Sitting on a small green bench outside his simple room,
exhausted by my unexpected climb, I asked him to tell me his story.
With a slight reluctance, Sonam-la1 began. Originally from a small village at the foothills
of Mount Kailash —  the mountain of Milarepa legend —  Sonam-la crossed the Himalayas in
1959 when he was only fifteen years old, step-in-step with approximately one hundred thousand
other Tibetans and His Holiness, the Dalai Lama.2 The story of this treacherous crossing is one
shared by many of the Tibetans I met and interviewed during my time in Dharamshala, a small
town in the north Indian state of Himachal Pradesh and home to the Tibetan
Government-in-Exile. Dhondup Gyalpo —  now Headmaster of the Junior School at the Tibetan
Children’s Village school —  made the crossing when he was six years old;3 Bhuchung D.
Sonam, poet, writer, and founder of TibetWrites — a publishing house for Tibetan writing — at
eleven years old;4 Kunsang Tenzin-la, creator of the Stories of Tibetans project and Tibet Hope
4  Bhuchung D. Sonam quoted by Tenzin D. Tsagong, “An Exiled Publisher Creates a
‘Brotherhood across Tibetans.’” The New York Times, The New York Times, 12 July 2023.
3 Personal interview with Dhondup Gyalpo. Headmaster of the Junior School at Upper Tibetan
Children’s Village. Mcleodganj, India. November 30th, 2024.
2 Personal interview with Sonam Lhundup, Elder residing at Jampaling Elder’s Home and former
cowboy for the Dalai Lama, Mcleodganj, India. Personal Interview. November 27th, 2024.
1 -la is a common Tibetan honorific added to the end of names to convey respect.
Zhou 3
Center, at six years old.5 In Dharamshala and its neighboring suburb of Mcleodganj, nearly every
Tibetan I met spoke of their relationship to their homeland, speaking of either a longing to return
or a dream to see a place they have never been before. It is clear that this shared story of the exile
experience is central to the Tibetan-in-Exile community, a narrative which holds, bridges,
crosses, contains, and colors each individual’s life narrative.
The purpose of my inquiry is to further understand how the creation of this shared
narrative occurs through storytelling. In asking the very broad and open question, “How does
storytelling function within the Tibetan-in-Exile community?,” I have found a diversity of
rejoinders unique to the political context and history of this community. Separated from the lands
of Tibet, the Tibetan diaspora in Dharamshala and Mcleodganj must instead actively construct a
rich and complex idea of Tibet, one that becomes real in the active process of storytelling. It is
through the vehicle of narrative that diasporic Tibetans unlock full potential for creative
transformation. In an interview for the New York Times, Bhuchung D. Sonam sums it up best:
“Until we find a political solution, we have to hold and build this idea of Tibet — whether you
call it a home or an idea, . . . and art does that.”6 The voice of writer and editor Tenzin Dickie
echoes this sentiment, succinctly expounding on the power of Tibetan prose: “It’s not like I can
live my life on Tibetan land . . . but I can live it in Tibetan literature.”7
In this paper, I synthesize my observations from three weeks in the field. By weaving
together fresh art, literature, and stories directly from people themselves, I aim to show how
storytelling in exile functions cohesively in three broadly construed ways — as reclamation,
protestation, and creation — to construct a real ‘idea of Tibet.’
7 Tsagong.
6 Tsagong.
5 Personal interview with Kunsang Tenzin, Founder of Tibet Hope Center and Stories for
Tibetans. Mcleodganj, India. December 2nd, 2024.
Zhou 4
Theory and Praxis
Initially, I had approached this assignment with a much simpler hypothesis, one rooted in
my practice and study of chaplaincy last summer, which posits that storytelling is the key to grief
processing and psychological healing. Through storytelling, actors gain both the critical distance
and the necessary empowerment to fully claim their narrative in an act of radical transformation
from passivity toward activity. In the words of Arthur Frank in The Wounded Storyteller: “The ill
person who turns illness into story transforms fate into experience.”8 Further, storytelling
requires at least two parties — one to tell and one to hear. Chaplaincy capitalizes on the
dialectical nature of this dynamic, often using the mere presence of a ‘story-hearer’ to prompt the
patient to embody the role of storyteller. In psychologist Honey Oberoi Vahali’s book Lives in
Exile: Exploring the Inner World of Tibetan Refugees, she expounds on the therapeutic nature of
these forms of encounters, explaining how a “dialogical aperture enables a person to articulate
certain aspects of her inner experience in the presence of an empathetic ‘other’ . . . [thus]
creati[ng an] inter-subjective, intermediary ‘third’ space [that] makes it possible . . . to gain fresh
understandings about the past.”9 Though her argument refers to the relationship between
researcher and research-participant, I believe that it applies to any encounter between a
storyteller and empathetic listener — especially when that ‘third space’ of healing is
intentionally contrived, as is between chaplain and patient.
And thus, it is with therapeutic aims that narrative theory and the practice of chaplaincy
encourages the ill to reframe their life story in a way that is both communicable and palatable to
themselves and to their audience. Scholar Anne Hansen explored this practice in her work in
9 Honey Oberoi Vahali, Lives in Exile: Exploring the Inner World of Tibetan Refugees.
(Routledge India, 2023), xx-xxi
8 Arthur W. Frank, The Wounded Storyteller: Body, Illness, and Ethics. (The University of
Chicago Press, 2013), Prologue, xi.
Zhou 5
narrative therapy with Khmer refugees and trauma victims, explaining in her article “Narrative,
Sub-Ethics, and the Moral Life: Some Evidence from Theravāda Buddhism,” co-authored with
Charles Hallisey, that a key ‘refiguration’ may be achieved through narrative “insofar as it
enables us to cultivate a crucial distance from our own circumstances and gives us a way of
seeing our lives with a degree of detachment.”10 Hansen reflects further, noting how at times
when reflecting on one’s own life may be too painful, Khmer refugees often found solace in the
telling of well-known Buddhist stories of grief and loss (e.g. the story of Patacara11 or Kisa
Gotami), stories they found their own life narratives reflected in.12
Additionally, once the story has been heard and told, psychiatrist and anthropologist
Arthur Kleinman’s narrative theory expounds, the chaplain is able to respond with their own
interpretation. Together, the dyad can begin to build a collaborative retelling of the person’s lived
experiences.13 With proper training and skill, these critical revisions can disrupt cycles of grief,
working to liberate patients from many of illness’s trappings.
The potential of the dynamic, dialectical act of storytelling is one propounded not only in
the Western psychological cannon but also reflected in some of Buddhism’s oldest tales. Kisa
Gotami’s mustard seed story is one famous for its universal resonance. A young mother, Kisa
Gotami’s story begins with the deeply grieved loss of her son. Unable to process this personal
tragedy, she goes mad with anguish. An ‘empathetic story-hearer,’ the Buddha witnesses and
guides, offering her a simple instruction: Bring me a pinch of mustard seeds from a house which
13 Daniel H. Grossoehme, “Chaplaincy and narrative theory: A response to risk’s case study.”
Journal of Health Care Chaplaincy, vol. 19, no. 3, July 2013, pp. 101
12 Hallisey and Hansen, pp. 323.
11 Suffering the loss of her husband, two sons, her parents, and brother, Patacara falls mad with
grief. It is only through the kindness and wisdom of the Buddha that she is redeemed and attains
arhathood.
10 Charles Hallisey and Anne Hansen. “Narrative, Sub-Ethics, and the Moral Life: Some
Evidence from Theravāda Buddhism.” The Journal of Religious Ethics, vol. 24, no. 2, 1996, pp.
Zhou 6
has not experienced grief, and I’ll bring back your son. And thus, Kisa begins her journey
knocking door to door in an attempt to find such a household. Gradually, as each house tells her
their own stories of loss, Kisa begins to see outside her own grief, realizes the suffering of others,
and moves forward. In her essay, “Searching for Mustard Seeds and Flickering Flames: A Guide
to Reading as a Mode of Care,” Harvard Divinity School student Sarah Fleming explains that “it
is not just the content of the teaching that enables her to move on — it is also the process, the
relationships that her impossible quest draws her into, . . . [and the] sustained attention required
in moving through the narrative of another, that allows [Kisa Gotami] to move through her
grief.”14 Fleming argues that in this story, Kisa herself holds a chaplain-like role, illustrating a
more overlooked process: one in which in the receiving of grief stories, the chaplain herself is
transformed.
When presented with the opportunity to spend three weeks traveling on the other side of
the world to investigate any topic I might be interested in, I jumped at the opportunity to
continue my investigation of spiritual care and grief processing. I had heard of an opportunity to
shadow at Delek Hospital, a small allopathic hospital founded in 1971 with the blessing of His
Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama, and the support of the Central Tibetan Administration.15 Delek is
a Buddhist hospital by and for the Tibetan community, with an emphasis on equity and
compassion. I was curious how staff attitudes and behaviors, institutional policy differences, and
its specific patient population would affect the flavor of care provided here.
However, arriving in Dharamshala with these questions, an attitude of openness, and a
just-show-up mentality, I was able to discover far more than I had initially imagined— though I
15“About Us - Who We Are.” Delek Hospital, delekhospital.org/about-us/. Accessed 7 Dec.
14Sarah Fleming, "Searching for Mustard Seeds and Flickering Flames: A Guide to Reading
as a Mode of Care." Harvard Divinity School. 2021.
Zhou 7
found some evidence for my original thesis of storytelling as a vehicle for transformative healing
— such as Bhuchung D. Sonam’s reflections on why he writes:
Left in a foreign country without kin . . . everything was new. Writing and literature
became a salve to help survive the loss of homeland and family. The writing seals the
pain. It’s a process of negotiating this really harsh and endless barrage of
obstacles and challenges that exile throws at you.16
And the words in poet Ten Phun’s introduction to his collection Sweet Butter Tea: “The truth is
that a mere exercise of putting pen to paper creates necessary values through which the mental
void and trauma of dislocation can get streamed out.”17 What truly struck me was the sense of
joyful unity, determination, and collective protest embodied by the Tibetan-in-Exile community I
met in my time at Dharamshala.
In the remainder of this paper, I strive to accurately capture the current lived attitudes and
movements of this group, along with distilling a sense of the ‘idea of Tibet’ that is created in
Vahali’s ‘third space’ of narrative storytelling. Though with the scope of this project it would be
impossible to make wide and sweeping generalizations, I hope to have captured a semi-realistic
snapshot informed by a diversity of voice. In the last three weeks, I conducted nine formal
interviews and countless informal conversations with students, monastics, business owners,
teachers, doctors, nurses, artists, and storytellers. My interviewees range from ages 30–82. The
stories I have collected span generations. I read widely, seeking out the voices of Tibetan authors,
poets, and activists. I participated in both the second annual Dharamshala Khadhok Art
Exhibition: Unsettled, and the inaugural Tibetan Artists Festival. Visiting historic institutions
such as the Central Tibetan Administration, upper Tibetan Children’s Village (TCV), the Tibet
17 Ten Phun. Sweet Butter Tea. Square One Classic, 2017.
16 Tsagong.
Zhou 8
Museum, and the Dalai Lama’s Temple, I attempted to receive the rich stories and harrowing
history of this community with openness and clarity.
In this abridged version of my thesis, I hope to introduce and discuss how narrative is an
important vehicle for reclamation, allowing actors not only to transition from passivity toward
activity in an Arthur Frank-ian sense of the idea, but creating the space necessary for them to
re-define and tell their own complex stories, refuting the predominant and reductive stereotype.
Further, returning to the specific context and history of Tibet and the ongoing conflict with
China, I explore how the mere circulation and preservation of Tibetan literature and language is
an act of protestation, actively challenging oppressive powers. Finally, I explore these ideas in
the context of Tibetan children, those of whom were born in exile and have never stepped foot in
Tibet. For them, narrative functions as creation, constructing an ‘idea of Tibet’ from the stories
they learn from their families and schools.
Reclamation
In one of the first conversations I had in Mcleodganj, I spoke with artist and founder of
Khadhok Art Collective Tashi Nyima about the symbolism and story behind his painting Lost in
Searching, the only piece he decided to showcase at Unsettled, a two-week gallery showcasing
Tibetan Contemporary Art. A massive painting, Lost in Searching depicts a young Tibetan man
meditating under the Bodhi Tree (where the Buddha himself sat when he attained
enlightenment), with a rainbow and map of a Buddhist pilgrimage circuit behind him. Next to
and below him are painted a naked woman, a box of pizza, scattered cash, and a boombox.
Compositionally inspired by traditional thangka paintings, Lost in Searching contrasts the
highest, most spiritual subjects near the top of the painting with the realities of desire and
attachment as a young person near the bottom. Nyima-la explained how this painting was a
Zhou 9
reaction to frustratingly one-dimensional stereotypes of Tibetans as highly spiritual and
untouched people he has encountered. “You don’t know me,” I recall Nyima-la explaining with a
laugh, “I may have more temptations and desires than even you!”18 In completing this painting
and organizing the large gallery space it was displayed at, Nyima-la expresses a complex lived
experience, directly challenging popular conceptions. With one painting, Nyima-la deconstructs
an abstract and nebulous stereotype to a real and personal level.
The many writings of Tenzin Tsundue, red-bandana-ed activist and co-founder of
TibetWrites and Blackneck Books, echo a similar sentiment. In his February 2005 article
“Celebrating Exile II: Our religion and the struggle,” Tsundue-la speaks about the
disappointment he has noticed in his non-Tibetan friends when they realize that he does not pray,
prostrate, or do other rituals19 — and yet he proudly claims to be Buddhist: “That’s why the
reality disappoints them: Tibetans in jeans, enjoying discos, monks on motorbikes, doing the
things they do in their lives. Their imagined glass idol is broken. For me kindness and sincerity
are guiding principles of Buddhism in life. One’s service in action for society is true worship.”20
As new young voices strive to elevate themselves and be heard, they work directly to dispel old
stereotypes. In many ways, these individual stories humanize this community, impelling readers
to relate to the authors themselves instead of focusing on larger historical and cultural contexts.
Individual stories, however, are often overlooked or overshadowed by competing
narratives. One of my interviewees, Kunsang Tenzin—  the producer, director, and interviewer
behind Stories for Tibetans—  spoke about the importance of a platform to highlight the voices
20 Tsundue.
19 Tenzin Tsundue. “Celebrating Exile II: Our Religion and the Struggle.” Tenzin Tsundue,
Tibetbridges, 1 Feb. 2005. Accessed 9 Dec. 2024.
18 Personal interview with Tashi Nyima. Artist and founder of Khadhok Arts Collective.
Mcleodganj, India. November 27th, 2024.
Zhou 10
of Tibetans-in-Exile as a collective.21 Having made the crossing to India when he was only six
years old, Tenzin-la went to the Tibetan Children’s Village (TCV) for education, an environment
he claims spoiled him — failing to instill in him the drive to take responsibility to do his part for
the Tibetan cause. It was only in university, after a fight with Indian peers and a sharp jab of
“you refugees don’t have anything” that everything changed for Tenzin-la. Initially planning to
immigrate to America with his family at 23, Tenzin-la decided instead to stay and invest all his
energy into building something for his community.
Tenzin-la began by teaching English classes of 10–15 students. Over the years, these
classes grew and grew, until eventually, Tenzin-la founded the Tibet Hope Center in 2000, a
volunteer-powered NGO which works to further education, aid, and cultural exchange. Almost
twenty years later, inspired by Humans of New York, an American storytelling project, Tenzin-la
started the Humans of Dharamshala project, and then Stories of Tibetans — a platform designed
to give people the flexibility to share however they want. Tenzin-la explained how traditional
interviewees are always those who have already accomplished something. Stories of Tibetans, on
the other hand, hopes to capture raw stories of people wherever they are, real people whose
work-in-progress projects and goals could use the help and connections this exposure might
bring, in real time. Tenzin-la is humble, explaining how though his weekly hour-long videos may
not currently receive much attention or money, their true importance will shine twenty, fifty
years in the future — as an important record of how people live now. In these stories, he
explains, there is the power to dispel the judgements that people in small communities inevitably
have of each other, and act as an important force in “uniting our own people.” In the now over
200 videos up on the Stories of Tibetans YouTube channel, it is clear that Tenzin-la not only
21 Personal interview with Kunsang Tenzin.
Zhou 11
believes in the philosophy at the center of his work but has put in countless hours toward
working toward its realization: “All stories should be documented; all stories matter.”22
Protestation
In every interview I have conducted as part of this project, politics has inevitably come
up. And how could it not? With the urgency, continuation, and every-present nature of the
ongoing political situation in Tibet, every attempt to preserve Tibetan language and culture
becomes an inherently political act. Burning the Sun’s Braids: New Poetry from Tibet, is a slim
volume of poetry translated by Bhuchung D. Sonam and published by Blackneck Books in 2017.
To protect writers that may face detention if the People’s Republic of China (PCR) suspected
them of collaborating with Tibetans-in-Exile, Sonam-la chose not to seek any copyright
permissions from the poets of the original works. The translator’s note at the beginning of the
book reads, “None of the poets featured in this collection knows his/her work is rendered into
English and published in exile. I decided not to get in touch with or relay to anyone of them
about this translation project for reasons that Beijing knows best.”23
While this book strongly alludes to the political implications of its existence, I believe
that it could also be argued that, in the context of Chinese occupation, every production and
circulation of Tibetan language and literature is an act of protest. The afterword featured in
Burning expounds on the reality of being an artist or writer in Tibet. Tenzin Dorjee — lecturer at
Columbia University and former executive director for Students for a Free Tibet — explains how
“for anyone living in a political tinderbox like Tibet, where every attempt to live . . . is choked by
23 Bhuchung D. Sonam, Burning the Sun’s Braids: New Poetry from Tibet. Blackneck Books,
22 Personal interview with Kunsang Tenzin.
Zhou 12
an inescapable web of rules, restrictions and penalties . . . even nonpolitical matters like love,
friendship and leisure are never truly free from the tentacles of politics.”24
While this reality paints a bleak picture, conversely, it also means that Burning can be
read as a triumph, “evidence that the Chinese state has not won the battle for Tibetans’ hearts and
minds.”25 In a very real way, these poems challenge “Chinese colonial power by naming the
poverty of life under its rule and in refusing the colonized present,” while also providing a
rallying impetus for action. I have noticed that in the narratives I have engaged with, actors are
always careful not to paint an entirely discouraging picture, always coupling the honest, and at
times bleak, picture of Tibet’s reality with encouraging calls to continue fighting for a Free Tibet.
In the words of Tsering Wangmo Dhompa, the first female Tibetan poet published in English, “It
is through reminders of a shared history that the poets speak as though to be with the people and
to rouse the people to consciousness . . . The present is the space and place in which a national
community and a collective consciousness is generated by Tibetian people about Tibetan
struggles.”26
Creation
Dreaming Tibet, one of Khadhok Art Collective’s new projects this year, asked 200
hundred students across five different schools to create an artwork in response to the prompt, ‘If I
were in Tibet . . .’ For these children, artist Tashi Nyima-la explained, though they have never
stepped foot into Tibet, they share a common longing for this place they have learned about
through the stories of their parents and cultures. For them, Tibet exists only as an intangible
26 Dhompa, pp. 18.
25 Tsering Wangmo Dhompa.“Revolutionary Literature: Writing from Tibet.” Burning the Sun’s
Braids: New Poetry from Tibet, Blackneck Books, Gamru Village Dharamsala, HP India, 2017,
24 Tenzin (Tendor) Dorjee. “Rain, Fire and Freedom.” Burning the Sun’s Braids: New Poetry
from Tibet, Blackneck Books, an Imprint of TibetWrites, Gamru Village Dharamsala, HP India ,
Zhou 13
‘idea,’ one constructed through the narratives of others. A grassroots project, Dreaming Tibet
selected fifty artworks from all that was submitted to be showcased at the Gangra Art Museum.
Inviting the Tibetan community, press media, and local Indians (Nyima-la emphasized the
importance of sharing Tibetan stories outside of the community), Dreaming Tibet was an
exhibition that celebrated the pure expression of these children’s work. For Nyima-la, after
struggling himself to resist societal and familial academic pressures and find the courage to
pursue artistry, being able to give these children a real exhibition and, for some, opportunities to
interview with the press, has been immeasurably rewarding.27
Inspired by Dreaming Tibet, I found myself suddenly curious about how Sonam-la’s ‘idea
of Tibet’ functions differently among children born in exile who have never entered Tibet
compared to older folks who may still retain faint memories of Tibet. Unsure of what I would
find, I decided to make a trip up to upper Tibetan Children’s Village, a place where so many of
the Tibetans I had interviewed or spoke with had personally attended school. On my first day,
Mr. Tsultrim Dorjee-la gave me a personal tour of the TCV campus and a brief overview of the
history of this unique place. Founded in 1960 when the Dalai Lama crossed the Himalayas with
51 young students, TCV’s initial operations were headed by the Dalai Lama’s elder sister,
Tsering Dolma Takla, and Diki Tsering, his mother. A charitable school created to provide a
Tibetan education for exiled Tibetan orphans and destitutes, TCV strives to preserve Tibetan
language and culture through education. Now, upper TCV serves over 1000 students with most
of them boarding in 32 homes, each with 24 children and an ‘ama-la,’ a Tibetan word for mother,
who, living in housing quarters in the home and on call 24 hours, helps enforce the daily
schedule and teaches life skills including cooking and cleaning.28
28 Tsultrim, Dorjee. Director of Upper Tibetan Children’s Village. Mcleodganj, India. Personal
interview. November 29th, 2024.
27 Personal interview with Tashi Nyima.
Zhou 14
The next day, I returned to spend the morning with Mrs. Jampa Palmo-la’s Montessori
class. From 8:45–11:00 a.m. every weekday and every Saturday (except every second Saturday),
these twelve three-to-five-year-olds spend most of their morning reading, either aloud to each
other or listening to Palmo-la’s expressive and patient narration. Palmo-la said she recently
counted and found that the kids and her have already gotten through 80 books together this year.
All the books available in her classroom were printed in Tibetan. Some featured classic fairy
tales, one that I had similarly grown up with, while others were familiar contemporary titles. But
a curious subsection was entirely new to me. As it turns out, there is a rich library of children's
books written, illustrated, and published by the Department of Education of the Central Tibetan
Administration in partnership with The Tibet Fund. Since 2014, these two organizations, along
with Manjushri Educational Services, Tibetan Children’s Village, the Library of Tibetan Works
and Archives, Shasta, and USAID have together supported more than 200 volumes of original
and translated children’s books. Determined to increase access to “high quality, age-appropriate,
culturally relevant books in Tibetan language . . . critical for Tibetan children to achieve literacy
and reading proficiency in their mother tongue,”29 570,000 copies have been distributed to
schools and families in India and Nepal. These books cover a wide range of topics from original
works explicitly about Tibetan culture — Green Chupa and His Holiness the Dalai Lama’s
Birthday and Making Gyathuk — to translations of other children's literature including Fat Cat:
A Danish Folktale and The Very Wiggly Tooth.
In conversation with Mrs. Tsering Dolkar-la, I learned that much of TCV’s philosophy in
preservation of culture is linked explicitly to the Tibetan language. Children here are raised with
Tibetan first. English is only introduced in grade four, and Hindi in grade six. Concepts and
29 “Children’s Literature.” The Tibet Fund,
tibetfund.org/what-we-do/publications/childrens-literature/.
Zhou 15
ideas, she explains, are better learned in one’s own native tongue.30 Though TCV is still bound
by many Indian education requirements, a recent project is translating textbooks of subjects such
as social studies for older students into Tibetan, to continue the emphasis on Tibetan first.
Beyond language, TCV also incorporates cultural immersion and study in many other ways. For
example, Wednesdays are Lhakar, His Holiness the Dalai Lama’s auspicious day, and children
are required to attend class on Wednesdays dressed in traditional dress. Cultural songs and
dances are also taught, morning Buddhist prayers are part of the daily routine, and the food
cooked and served is Tibetan-ized Indian food — think rice and dal, but also tingmo’s and
thukpa.
But beyond the beautiful celebration of Tibetan language and culture practiced here, there
is a sense of complexity. In 2008, China began cracking down on borders, leading to much fewer
influx of Tibetan immigrants and Tibetan children coming into the exile community. Now, TCV
is faced with a growing lack of students, a problem which threatens to shut down other schools in
this district permanently. The demographic of the children here has now changed, with more
children coming from other Himalayan regions to take advantage of the cheap and quality
education offered here. “Earlier this was a school for Tibetan children,” Dolkar-la explained,
“and we had a strong sense about doing something for our culture and language.”31 Now, there is
a diversity of children who still don traditional Tibetan clothing every Wednesday, and there is a
shared sense that “maybe this does not make sense.” But generally, Dolkar-la is careful to
explain, these are not things that come to mind often and certainly are not something that affects
her teaching. It will be an ongoing curiosity to see how things in this community continue to
31 Personal interview with Tsering Dolkar.
30 Tsering Dolkar. English teacher at Upper Tibetan Children's Village. Mcleodganj, India.
Personal Interview. November 30th, 2024.
Zhou 16
change — how much rests on an assumed homogeneity of the community here, and how much it
will adapt and transform to the ever-changing nature of our conventional realities.
Conclusion
Initially inspired by my long-time academic interests, it was only when I got out into the
field, spoke with all the people I met there, and cultivated an openness to receiving what was
presented to me, that this project revealed itself as a much larger, more nebulous endeavor. It is
unclear to me whether I have been able to synthesize my findings in a clear and linear fashion. It
has, however, been an illuminating process. In writing this essay, I myself have embodied a role
like Kisa Gotami, and garnered a front-row seat to observe the playing-outs of the abstract
theories I have studied. I feel incredibly grateful to have been so welcomed into the
Tibetan-in-Exile community in Dharamsala. This project rests squarely on the shoulders of all
those willing to share their lives and stories with me — I know it is not always an easy task.
In my original outline, I had more space dedicated to exploring the identity and
responsibility of being on the receiving end of storytelling, questioning what it means to be a
listener outside of the illness narrative context. It is an interesting question, one I wish to
continue to explore, of what it means to be a complete outsider to this community receiving these
stories. And what it means, specifically in my case, to be a Chinese-American student traveling
next to visit my distant family in China. How can I, now knowing so much more about Tibet's
history, still make the crossing across that impossible border, in a journey I now know so many
can only dream of. What is my place — our collective places — in the fight for a free Tibet? In
the liberatory fight for all oppressed people? I suppose these are questions the poets know we
will ask ourselves. The ending of Dhompa-la’s article, positioned as the introduction to
Sonam-la’s Burning, ends with a haunting warning: “The poems in this collection are
Zhou 17
heartbreaking, groundbreaking and revolutionary; readers need courage.”32 So have courage, dear
readers! And continue to question your place in the order of things. If any insights arise, do let
me know. I would love to hear your story.
32 Dhompa, pp. 20.
Zhou 18

blocks: Manufactured Color: An Analysis of the Euro-American Historic Decorated Ceramics of the Montgomery Site
Laurel Anderson
Introduction

Industrially produced European and American ceramics produced throughout the 18th and 19th century are an invaluable resource for the dating of historic sites, as the extensive records left by their increasingly standardized production provide known dates that can be used to situate the site from which these artifacts are recovered in a broader temporal context.
Figure 1. Areas of the Montgomery Site: (1) 1836 Log House, (2) Parsonage Northwest Midden, (3) Parsonage, (4) Cabin 1, (5) Cabin 1 Southwest Midden, (6) Trails and General, (7) Cabin 2.
The Montgomery Site

The Montgomery cabin, reported to be the earliest documented Euro-American structure in Kenosha County, is located within Petrifying Springs County Park in the township of Somers, Wisconsin. Initial excavations of the site were conducted by the Kenosha County Archaeological Society (KCAS) between 1975 and 1977. From 2013 to 2023, the University of Wisconsin-Parkside has worked in conjunction with the Kenosha Public Museum to reconstruct the methods and findings of the prior group, as well as conducting further investigations across the site. These periods of work have generated a collection of 1,342 earthenware historic ceramic sherds, which form the basis for this analysis.

The investigations of the Montgomery site have yielded artifacts from seven main areas, which are laid out in Figure 1. Cabin 1 is the eponymous Montgomery family’s residence, which was occupied from approximately 1834 to 1839. This structure was likely razed before 1855 and has a midden nearby. Cabin 2 was built around 1855, occupied for a year by John Soutour. Following this, Edward Cooley then occupied the building for around 15 years. The 1836 Log House is recorded on an 1836 survey map; however, investigations have currently yielded no signs of foundations. Building materials and household items have been recovered from the area. The parsonage was built in 1855 and eventually served as a private residence until it was razed in 2014 (Sasso 2023). North of the parsonage, there is a structure shown on two maps from 1861 and 1873 respectively. Survey of the area has yielded domestic refuse and construction materials. The category “Trails and General” refers to any material found during survey outside of these specified areas, or objects whose provenience was not recorded.
Elements of Nineteenth Century Ceramics
Ware Types

The primary terms for non-vitreous, white-bodied wares (creamware, pearlware, and whiteware) do not possess mutually exclusive definitions within literature concerning historical ceramics and are often used interchangeably. Part of the reason for this discrepancy is the differences in language used by those who are primarily interested in ceramics from a collector’s perspective and those who approach this form of classification from an archaeological background.
Figure 2. An illustration of the difference in surface appearance among white-bodied wares.

Majewski and O’Brian (1984) outline the historical developments in the creation of white-bodied ceramics, as well as the contemporaneous ambiguity with which terms describe this style of ware. Roughly, what has been termed creamware was typically manufactured prior to the late eighteenth century. Pearlware introduced ca. 1780, is considered by some to be only a subtype of creamware, the primary difference in manufacturing being the addition of cobalt oxide to the glaze used on a very similar clay body. This created the illusion of a whiter appearance compared to the coloration of creamware, as well as creating the primary visual characteristic associated with pearlware: a noted pooling of blue pigment in areas of heavy glaze, which is noticeable around the foot or base of a vessel. This can also present as a greenish cast to the surface of the vessel. Further refinement in the early nineteenth century led to what is referred to as whiteware, which may have been a result of the addition of cobalt to the body of the vessel in tandem with a lesser amount in the glaze. The body of this type is much closer to a “paper white” color, rather than the yellow or blue leaning hues of the wares that preceded it.

The ceramics outlined in these categories comprise a large portion of the white-bodied decorated ceramics of the Montgomery site. Type distinction is also of less use when attempting to distinguish between whitewares produced after the 1820s, as whiteware dominated the ceramics produced after this point. The relative similarity of the visual appearance of these ware types, in addition to the fact that they were not distinct lines of production, but rather broad areas in a temporal continuum representing advances in commercial manufacturing, lead to the conclusion that a categorization based on these factors would be of relatively little use within this analysis.
Application of Color

Beginning in the early nineteenth century, commercial ceramic production likely would have relied upon color preparations manufactured by specialists (Majewski and O’Brian 1984: 139). The various metallic oxides used as the basis for color application all have differing levels of volatility and stability, meaning that not all colors were equally suitable to being subjected to high firing temperatures.

The application of these colors could be done before the application of a layer of clear glaze or after the addition of a glaze. Underglaze coloration would have to withstand the full firing temperature of the finished vessel. Overglaze coloration, though less durable, could be hardened in several steps at potentially lower temperatures, greatly increasing the range of colors that could be reliably used. The use of overglaze enamel decoration was particularly common in the production of porcelain. The firing temperatures to which underglaze colors could be reliably subjected allowed the decoration of non-vitreous and semi vitreous whitewares to utilize a larger palette of colors compared to the few colors that could be used in the decoration of vitrified wares such as porcelain.

The main components of the ceramic stains used in both these methods are colorants, diluents, and fluxes. The properties of a given coloring agent could be modified by changing the composition of the flux to suit the application that was intended. The most common color used for both hand painting and transfer printing prior to 1820 was cobalt blue, due to its high stability in both underglaze and overglaze decoration. This dominance was partially disrupted in the late 1820s, with the expansion of available underglaze colors from classic blue to include black, red, green, and yellow. Majewski and O’Brian (1987:139) attribute the explosion of colors available that took place from 1820 to 1830 to a rapidly increasing understanding of the properties of the flux and color used in decoration rather than the introduction of lead-free glaze, as proposed by Lofstrom et al. (1982). The market demand for more exclusive table wares distinct from the blue transfer print motif that had become commonplace by the 1820s may also have contributed to the motivation for applying these new chemical developments (Samford 1997).
Methods

The scope of this analysis encompasses all non-vitreous or semi-vitreous decorated earthenware recovered from the Montgomery Site over the course of the 1975-1977 KCAS excavation and the field school sessions held from 2013 to 2023 by U.W.-Parkside in conjunction with the Kenosha Public Museum. All sherds had been washed, broadly sorted, and assigned catalogue numbers prior to the beginning of this examination. The initial stage of the study involved sorting the sherds into broad types of decoration, as well as verifying previous assessment of decoration type. Multiple decorative techniques could be used on a single surface, but the size of sherds recovered from the Montgomery site makes reconstruction of individual vessels impractical, and thus sherds were sorted by their individual characteristics.  These groupings were then further separated by the location from which they were recovered. For the purposes of this study the Montgomery site was divided into seven major areas: Cabin 1, Cabin 1-Southwest Midden, Cabin 2, Parsonage House, Parsonage-Northwest Midden/Structure, 1836 Log House, and Trails & General Areas. The catalogue number of each sherd was then recorded under its decoration type and general location.

Though there are many ways to go about the classification of historic ceramics, and merits to forgoing the system of taxonomy entirely, this study focused on decoration type almost exclusively, with some allowance for wares of a different ceramic body entirely. The classification system used within this analysis is a modified version of that outlined in the DAACS Ceramic Genre Appendix, with further specification added to groups within categories which have established documentation.

Median dates were drawn from established literature regarding the general manufacturing period for any given type of ceramic. For types whose manufacture continues until the present, end production dates were taken from the end of the period of popularity. In order to complete the Mean Ceramic Dating process, a tally was taken of the number of sherds of each decoration type that was found in each area. This was then multiplied by the mean (average) production date and added to the sum for each site area, which was then divided by the total number of sherds in that location, yielding an approximate mean ceramic date for each area. Although vessel counts provide a more accurate estimation of the occupation date of a site (Lofstrom et. al. 1982), no complete ceramic objects were found at the Montgomery site, and very few could be absolutely confirmed to be from the same vessel. Using mass of sherd rather than count is also potentially problematic, as it would be disproportionately informed by those decoration types that covered the whole of a vessel and thus are likely to have more sherds attributed to them when categorizing by decoration type.

Differential breakage is also not a particularly relevant source of error, as the sample of sherds analyzed is composed of similar paste types and shares roughly the same physical properties. Porcelain, though represented at the Montgomery site, was not accounted for. This is because of the size of the sample it represents, as well as the fact that its vitrification would mean that vessels are more likely to fracture into several large pieces rather than many smaller ones. This difference would artificially inflate the weight of any non-vitreous or semi-vitreous ceramics in the averaging process, hence porcelain’s exclusion.
Figure 3. A Taxonomic tree representing the process of how decorative types were assigned. For more information on the characteristics of each type, see Appendix.
Figure 4. Timeline of Production Ranges for Nineteenth Century Ceramics.
Results
Table 1. Mean Ceramic Dates Generated by Area.
Area | Mean Ceramic Date (Sample Size)
Parsonage NW Midden | 1843.502 (n = 203)
Parsonage | 1863.333 (n = 6)
Cabin 1 SW Midden | 1841.422 (n = 457)
Trails and General | 1839.600 (n = 10)

Overall, the mean ceramic dates generated align with the known occupations of the Montgomery site. Though the first recorded structure in the Cabin 1 area was built ca. 1834, and occupied for about five years, the mean ceramic date for that location reflects an estimated occupation of 1849. This discrepancy may be explained by the limits of mean ceramic dating as an analytical tool. The formula applied relies on initial dates of manufacture, which are not necessarily reflective of when an object was used or discarded. Particularly with ceramics of this era, the lifespan of a piece could easily extend to ten or more years past the date that it was initially made.

Furthermore, the pattern in the ceramics found at the Montgomery site represents the disposal of sherds, not necessarily how objects were used as the site was occupied. These potential errors in blanket application of mean ceramic dating are also documented within existing archaeological literature (Majewski and O’Brian 1987). It is also known that the Parsonage House’s residents used the abandoned Montgomery Cabin’s cellar (Cabin 1) as a place to discard refuse during the mid to late 1800s. Applying these considerations to an analysis of the mean ceramic dates produced reveals the more likely reconstruction of the temporal trends in disposal of ceramics within the Montgomery site.

The later date indicated by the ceramics, in conjunction with analysis of other artifacts found in Cabin 1 indicates that it was likely used as a rubbish dump by later inhabitants of the site after its original occupants had left the area and it had ceased to be used as a home. The fact that the proposed date of 1847 for Cabin 2 also predates any recorded building in this area of the site by almost ten years is also reflective of the lag between the dates of manufacture and the period during which ceramic objects were used and discarded. Bearing in mind that mean ceramic dating commonly generates a period of at least ten years before the actual occupation of the site, the dates produced by this analysis are consistent with both the historically documented occupation of the Montgomery site and archaeological analyses previously conducted.

An additional consideration for the results of this study is that most sherds recovered are also of a relatively small size. More sizable fragments are usually associated with the breakage of this type of ceramic. Their absence strongly indicates that larger pieces were disposed of in a privy whose location has not yet been identified during archaeological surveys of the area.

The completion of this aspect of ceramic analysis for the Montgomery Site excavations not only provides further insight into both the past of the area and potential avenues for future work but may also serve as a case study in the application and modification of the technique of mean ceramic dating.
Figure 7. Montgomery site ceramic assemblage by location and decoration type.
