Appendix: Guide to Decorated Ceramic Types
Transferware
Standard

Based on the description given by Majewski and O’Brian (1987:141-146): In general terms, the process of transfer printing involved the application of ink or paste to an engraved plate, which then fills all of the indentations in the pattern. Excess ink is then removed, and a piece of paper or glue bat is used to take an impression of the inked pattern and then pressed onto an unfired ceramic surface. The transfer medium is then removed, leaving the color pattern behind, which is hardened through a preliminary firing. In the case of underglaze ceramic, the piece is then dipped in the final coat of glaze and fired once again. Changes in value within transferware are produced through the use of cross hatching or stippling, details which often appear less distinct on earlier examples of transfer printing. In the early 1800s, the industry had largely moved to the use of line and stipple engraving. Other technical improvements from the same period made the use of bats for transferring impression of engravings the most common mode of production, as it allowed the use of even finer detail (Samford 1997). Polychrome, or decoration with multiple colors within the same pattern, may have been applied through multiple steps of transfer printing, or by the application of color by hand to specific areas of a transfer printed outline, though the latter is more common. Transferware in the following colors was identified from the Montgomery Site collection: red, green, black, brown, blue, purple, and polychrome. Figure . Blue transferware sherdFigure . Example of early transferwareFigure . Polychrome TransferwareFigure . Black transferware with handpainted color detailsFigure . Flow blue and flow mulberry sherds
Flow

This variation of transferware was introduced in the mid-1830s. The effect of flow decoration was produced “by firing vessels in an atmosphere into which Figure . Slip decorated sherdsvolatile chlorides were introduced” (Majewski and O’Brian 1987). Though other colors of flown transferware have been produced, the two colors featured in the Montgomery site assemblage are blue and mulberry. Within the subcategory of flow blue, denser and darker motifs are associated with earlier examples, ca. 1835-1860, while lighter patterning is more common in the later decades of the nineteenth century (Peterson 2015).
Slipped Wares
General

Rather than being a distinct type of decoration outlined by previous work on ceramic analysis, this label was used as a category for sherds exhibiting a marbled or swirled pattern of slip not consistent with any other subgroup identified below.
Annular

Refers to a technique through which colored slip is used to apply stripes to the body of a vessel, the results of which are often slightly raised or otherwise distinguishable from flat or hand painted stripes (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:45). Within analysis of the Montgomery site, sherds that exhibited uniform bands or striping associated with this method, as well as those that contained solid colors only otherwise observed in annular wares, were placed within this group.Figure . Slip decorated sherds, annular
Rouletted

An additional decorative technique used on some annular ware in which a shaped instrument is pressed into damp slip, thus lifting the color and exposing the body below (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:45).  Only one sherd of this type is known within the existing Montgomery site ceramic assemblage.Figure . Slipped Sherds, Annular (Left and Right), Rouletted (Center)
Mocha

A variation of annular ware in which “decoration is created when an acidic mixture (consisting of various combinations of tobacco juice, hops, urine, dry printer's black, turpentine, citric acid, and water) is dripped on an area of colored slip, where it spreads into dendritic forms resembling trees, seaweed, fronds, etc.” (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:45).Figure . Slip sherds, mocha
Sponge

Figure . Sponge decorated sherds, assortedWhat is most often termed “spatter ware” was achieved by tapping a brush full of paint against the side of a vessel, creating a dotted effect (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:44). Sponge ware refers to the application of glaze by use of a sponge, which typically resulted in a pattern like that of spattering, though more densely packed. Both methods were also used in combination with stencils in order to create a desired result.” (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:44). These patterns could both be either monochrome or have multiple colors applied to the same vessel, as with the striping on the characteristic tricolor spongeware, which typically features bands of red, green, and blue around a central hand painted motif (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:44). Though some authors make a distinction between the groups of “sponged”, “spattered”, and “splattered” wares, the terms do not have distinct definitions within ceramic literature, and so the general category of sponge decorated wares was not subdivided further, except for one very specific and well-defined pattern.Figure . Sponge decorated sherds, red
Open Sponge

Figure . Open sponge patterned sherdsA subset of sponge decorated wares within the Montgomery assemblage fit the characteristics of what has at times been referred to as “flowing spatter”, “kitchen”, or “cottage spatter” ware, which was likely manufactured by both British and American companies from 1860 to 1935 (Majewski and O’Brian 1987:162). The term open sponge is taken from the Diagnostic Artifacts in Maryland database, which uses that label to describe several vessels with very similar patterns to the sherds from the Montgomery site (Samford and Miller 2015).
Edge Decorated

The term “edge decorated ware” refers to all sherds that have distinct patterning or glaze decoration that is consistent with application exclusively to the rim or edge of a vessel. A large portion of these fall under the “shell edge” pattern described by Majewski and O’Brian (1987:148). This motif is comprised of short, perpendicular, impressed lines along the edge of a vessel, to which the characteristic stripe of colored glaze is applied by hand. Edge decorated shreds from the Montgomery assemblage all feature blue glaze, although green coloration was utilized during the same era.Figure . Edge decorated sherds
Hand PaintedFigure . Hand painted sherds

Hand painted ware is a category with a large amount of internal variety, including broad and narrow brushstrokes, and possibly also exhibiting stenciled designs. Motifs could be large or small, and applied Figure . Hand painted sherds, spriggedFigure . Hand painted sherd

to the entire body of a piece or only a small portion. The most common pattern observed in the Montgomery Site assemblage are sherds with what is referred to as a “sprig” pattern often “composed of a black hairline stem with small green leaves and stylized red and blue flowers and berries” (Majewski and O’Brian 1987). Vessels with hand painted features may also include border stripes along the rim of a vessel, which may cause some to identify them as annular, even though they share most of the traits attributed to the general hand painted category. In these cases, the characteristic pigments used in hand painted ceramics were used as the distinguishing factor of categorization. When cataloging the Montgomery Site ceramics, those sherds only exhibiting a stripe in chrome red, a color rarely observed in true annular ware, were determined to be hand painted. Lofstrom et al. (1982) remark that the colors observed in sprig decoration are exceedingly similar in appearance to those used in tricolor sponge or splatter ware.Figure . Hand painted sherds
Victorian Majolica

Named for its imitation of 15th century Italian maiolica, Victorian Majolica is characterized by its unusually vivid colors applied to a molded base. The decorative motifs with which a piece was embossed are frequently floral or botanical in nature. All sherds under the Majolica category from the Montgomery Site are consistent with a specific pattern of vessel produced by Simon Fielding’s Railway Pottery company from ca. 1880-1890 (Majolica International Society 2014). This specific pattern had a larger counterpart used to produce decorative umbrella stands, but the specific placement of design elements on the more complete sherd that were recovered indicates that what was found at the Montgomery Site was likely the remains of a smaller object used in table service, such as the hexagonal kettle or pitcher produced with the same motif.Figure . Majolica sherds, exteriorFigure . Majolica sherds, interior and exterior
Decalcomania

Decal decoration differs from transfer printing in how the decoration is prepared before being applied to the surface of the ware. For decal wares, a pattern is transferred to the ceramic body in some sort of adhesive, and color is then brushed or dusted over it. The visual signifiers of decalcomania are clearer lines, the presence of shading rather than stippling or hatching, and the use of colors that differ dramatically from those observed in transferware (Majewski and O’Brian 1987). Though decal decoration had existed for some time prior, the style gained popularity at the end of the nineteenth century, which Majewski and O’Brian (1984) attribute to its use as an alternative to hand painted motifs which were more costly to produce. Decalcomania refers to the period of intense popularity experienced by decal decoration.Figure . Decal decorated sherds
Yellow Ware

Yellow ware is a broad category that encompasses all ceramics found that display a distinctly yellow past color, both unrefined and decorated (Majewski and O’Brian 1984). Yellow ware was produced in England during the Figure . Yellow ware sherdseighteenth century but was not introduced to America until ca. 1820 (Majewski and O’Brian 1984). Yellow ware was produced in the United States, beginning ca. 1830, and was used for heavy-duty utilitarian wares in addition to more specialized vessels. When categorizing the Montgomery assemblage, all sherds with a yellow paste body (that did not otherwise possess a decorative characteristic belonging to another type) were labeled as yellow ware. It is to be noted that styles such as annular decoration were practiced on yellow ware, and that yellow ware sherds that bore these styles were categorized as annular for the purposes of quantification.
Rockingham Ware

Rockingham is the name given to a particular type of slip-glaze finish, most often practiced on yellow ware, that results in mottled brown coloration. A brown glaze was applied to a vessel with a light-colored paste by spattering or dripping, causing the glaze to streak, and resulting in a distinctive tortoise shell finish (Majewski and O’Brian 1984). Rockingham glaze is notable for its application to body molded vessels, on which the thin glaze pools in low-lying areas and accentuates the embossed detail. Figure . Rockingham ware sherds
Redware

Redware refers to unrefined earthenware with a red coloration to the ceramic body. It is the softest category of unrefined earthenware and was produced in America beginning in the seventeenth century, though the majority was produced in the nineteenth century (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:21). If it is glazed, the coating is typically lead-based, with manganese pigments, which can include “shades of brown and yellow, copper-green, and brownish black” (Majewski and O’Brian 1984:21).

Abstract
This paper investigates the historical impacts of water pollution on downstream
communities along the Mississippi River during the late 19th and early 20th centu-
ries. As industrialization and urbanization intensified, urban centers and industries
along the river increasingly discharged untreated pollutants into the water, thereby
transforming the river from a residential amenity into a significant disamenity.
Drawing from historical surveys and census data, this study examines how changes
in pollution levels influenced population shifts in downstream counties relative to
their upstream counterparts. I found that increased levels of upstream pollution
had significant and economically meaningful effects on downstream populations,
with pollution levels correlating negatively with population sizes. These findings
are robust across a range of pollution specifications. Furthermore, I found that the
impact of upstream pollution became more severe between 1880 and 1900 before
declining from 1910 onwards. I hypothesize that the intercity effects of upstream
pollution contributed to the urban mortality penalty before declining in the early
20th century as cities began adopting modern water purification technologies to
mitigate the adverse effects of pollution and water-borne diseases. This paper
contributes to the broader economic discourse on environmental externalities and
neighborhood amenities by detailing the intercity effects of water pollution.
Urban Currents: Upstream
Pollution and its Impacts on
Intercity Populations Along the
Mississippi River
Faculty Adviser: Dr. W. Walker Hanlon
Department of Economics
by Darran Shen
Introduction
The Mississippi River powered commerce
and industry in the United States for a
significant portion of American history as
early superhighways that supported trade,
transportation, and industry. Urban areas
and trading centers such as New Orleans
and St. Louis were developed and grew
along the riverbanks, aided by water
access for both consumption and travel.
The introduction of the Second Industrial
Revolution accelerated the role of rivers:
Beginning in the late 19th century, the
Revolution marked a period of rapid
industrialization, urbanization, and tech-
nological innovation that fundamentally
transformed the American economy and
society. Bodies of water, specifically rivers,
suddenly offered a new kind of industrial
amenity as a fertile avenue to both situate
and spread innovations from the Second
Industrial Revolution: Rivers offered the
water required to power steam factories
and machinery. The Mississippi River also
offered direct access to a natural super-
highway for steam-based transportation;
by 1840, steam-based river transportation
had made New Orleans the fourth-larg-
est port in the world, surpassed only by
London, Liverpool, and New York.1
Importantly, rivers also served as an
outlet for waste disposal. Over the next cen-
tury, this natural resource would become
increasingly polluted as cities, factories,
and industrial mills directly released pollut-
ants into rivers, including human effluent,
industrial waste, and animal byproducts. In
this paper, I study how downstream pop-
ulations shifted in response to upstream
pollution in the late 19th and early 20th
centuries to understand this phenomenon.
1 Frank Haigh Dixon, A Traffic History of the Mississippi River System (Govt. Printing Office, 1909), 15.
Are there significant differences in the
size of communities living downriver
compared to upriver communities? What
are the channels that caused this popula-
tion change? While the impact of river
pollution across communities and cities is
highlighted in policy debates and historical
research, the economic consequences are
less well-known. Even today, upstream
pollution remains a concern, with its
ongoing relevance reflected in the reports
that regularly make the news, from con-
flicts over fertilizer runoffs to the dumping
of forever chemicals.
I find that upstream industrial and
urban pollution had a statistically and
economically significant impact on down-
stream populations, robust across a wide
range of pollution estimates. A longitu-
dinal analysis of census data from 1880
to1930 further demonstrates that the
adverse effects of pollution on population
levels intensified between 1880 and 1900
but began to diminish after 1910 following
the introduction of contemporary water
treatment technologies such as filtration
and chlorination which were introduced
in the early 20th century. My results imply
“Upstream industrial
and urban pollution
had a statistically
and economically
significant impact
on downstream
populations.”
that upstream pollution contributed to the
urban mortality penalty with its impact
diminishing concurrently with the reduc-
tion in mortality rates, aligning with exist-
ing research on the topic.
Background
What Pollution?
The Second Industrial Revolution precip-
itated a dramatic expansion of urban areas
and industrial development along the
banks of the Mississippi River, an indus-
trial growth that was typified by the mas-
sive increase of pollution in the nation’s
waterways, reflecting the contemporary
theory of pollution control: “The solution
to pollution is dilution,” the erroneous
belief that one could empty untreated
sewage, waste, and effluents into the
nearest fast-moving stream of water and
hope that the water would clean itself. The
prevailing belief that rivers could dilute
any and all waste meant that every city and
industrial plant dumped untreated waste
and sewage into the nearest watercourse.
By the mid-1920s, Minnesota had already
declared the Mississippi River a health
hazard; District Engineer Major Williams
reported that “all of the cities and towns
located on the Mississippi River from
Minneapolis to Hastings now empty their
untreated sewage into the Mississippi
River.”2 In a 1925 study, author H.R.
Crohurst concluded that industrial waste
could be found over 50 miles downriver
from the Twin Cities.3 Figure 1 shows
a 1932 map of sewage systems in urban
areas of the Upper Mississippi region.
2 Raymond H. Merritt, The Corps, the Environment, and the Upper Mississippi River Basin, Environmental Review, vol. EP 870-1-19
(United States. Army. Corps of Engineers, Historical Division, 1984), 51.
3 H. R. Crohurst and U.S. Treasury Department Public Health Service, A Study of the Pollution and Natural Purification of the Upper
Mississippi River (Govt. Printing Office, 1932), 31.
4 Paul Hesterman, “The Mississippi and St. Paul: Change Is a Constant for River and the City That Shaped It,” Ramsey County
5 William W. Folwell, “The Disposal of City Cleanings,” The Minnesota Horticulturist 16 (1888): 173–89.
6 Joseph Manulik, “Establishment of the Minneapolis Waterworks, 1867–1910,” Minnesota Historical Society.
Note that most communities on the River,
including the largest Upper Mississippi
cities of St. Paul and Minneapolis, did not
have sewage treatment of any kind and
simply emptied their effluents into the
river. Contemporary reports found that
the combined pollution dumped into the
Mississippi from the Twin Cities was now
over two and a half times the volume of
the flow of the river.4
The Health Calculus
River pollution, then, was a well-docu-
mented phenomenon along the Missis-
sippi, and upstream pollution was a noted
problem. As early as 1888, William W.
Folwell, a professor at the University of
Minnesota, issued a warning in the Min-
nesota Horticulturist: “The spectacle of …
emptying into the Mississippi river thou-
sands upon thousands of tons of solid and
liquid filth and offal yearly is one to make
angels weep and men blaspheme.”5 Thus,
the effects of river pollution on health
were noted, even if river residents did not
fully understand the relationship. In Min-
neapolis, where water was pumped from
the Mississippi River, residents began
complaining about the color and taste of
their water as early as 1880.6
The most significant impact of pol-
luted water was the spread of water-borne
diseases. In 1900, these diseases accounted
for nearly a quarter of all deaths from infec-
tious diseases in major cities, which them-
selves caused 44% of total deaths. As cities
discharged untreated waste into rivers,
downstream communities used the same
water for drinking and cooking, allowing
diseases like typhoid and cholera to spread
easily. Existing economics research by Cut-
ler and Miller (2004), Ferrie and Troesken
(2008), and Anderson, et al. (2022) exam-
ine how the interaction between environ-
mental pollution and public health shaped
demographic patterns and contributed to
the urban mortality penalty. The concept
of the “urban mortality penalty” refers to
the increased risk of death associated with
living in urban areas compared to rural
ones; in the late 19th and early 20th centu-
ries, rapid urbanization led to densely pop-
ulated cities that struggled with inadequate
sanitation infrastructure. This lack of infra-
structure resulted in the direct discharge of
untreated sewage into rivers, which were
often the same sources from which down-
stream communities drew their drinking
water. A lack of infrastructure and poor
understanding of disease theory and bacte-
riology also meant that water drawn from
cesspool sources allowed pathogens such as
those causing typhoid and cholera to thrive
and spread, exacerbating the incidence of
water-borne diseases. The urban mortality
penalty during this period can be attributed
primarily to these diseases, which prolifer-
ated due to the crowded living conditions
and poor environmental management
inherent to urban settings.
Literature Review
My paper contributes to existing literature
in several notable ways. First, it joins the
substantial volume of research that looks
at the negative impacts of water pollu-
tion on populations, both long-term and
short-term. Second, it contributes to the
body of economic history that identifies
pollution as an amenity (or in this case,
a disamenity) that may result in sorting
or migration effects. Third, my paper
adds a results-centered take on existing
economics and hydrology research that
looks at the upstream and downstream
effects of water pollution.
Existing research has firmly identified
the negative health effects of water-related
pollution. Unprecedented improvements
in urban health from 1900 to 1940 elim-
inated the so-called “urban penalty” asso-
ciated with living in cities, with mortality
rates falling by 40% during this period
(Cutler and Miller 2004). Cutler and Miller
find that the introduction of major public
health interventions and specifically new
clean water technologies such as filtra-
tion and chlorination played key roles
in eliminating or reducing the spread of
water-borne pollution-related diseases
such as typhoid, pneumonia, and tubercu-
losis by preventing infected effluent from
polluting clean water sources. My research
expands on these findings by looking spe-
cifically at intercity water pollution, which
Cutler and Miller acknowledge as an issue.
Heblich et al. (2021) look at temporal
disamenities, finding that high levels of
temporary pollution from coal factories
during the Industrial Revolution altered
the spatial organization of cities in the
long run, wherein different households
express their environmental preferences
and willingness-to-pay through reloca-
tion. Other literature that looks at air
pollution-induced
neighborhood
sort-
ing includes Banzhaf and Walsh (2008),
who find that households will “vote with
their feet” for better environmental qual-
ity, entering and leaving communities in
response to environmental disamenities.
My paper seeks to expand on the study
of pollution-related sorting by looking at
river pollution, which may offer similar
environmental amenity decisions but must
contrast with the inherent commercial and
recreational value of rivers.
Finally, my paper contributes to
research that looks at the upstream and
downstream effects of water pollution.
Existing research approaches water pol-
lution with both economics and hydrol-
ogy. Existing economics approaches to
upstream and downstream water pollution
famously address the question through
the study of externalities. Lewin (1982)
offers a neoclassical approach to pollu-
tion externalities by creating a theoretical
framework of social costs, property rights,
and optimal levels of pollution. Ferrar
and Sassone (1975) and Sokoloski (1967)
address the externality issue of effluent
charges in the specific context of upstream
and downstream firms. Cutler and Miller
(2004) and Beach et al. (2016) do acknowl-
edge, but do not substantively address, the
potential issue of upriver pollution, indi-
cating that cities that dump sewage into a
river would increase future typhoid rates
for cities downstream.
Research stemming from the field of
hydrology grapples more with the upstream
and downstream effects of pollution but is
primarily focused on modeling pollution
itself instead of linking pollution with eco-
nomic outcomes and focusing on modern
events. Shrestha and Kazama (2007) and
Singh (2004) assess upstream and down-
stream water quality relations, focusing on
modeling the quality of river water when
transporting municipal and industrial
wastewater and agricultural runoff. Chen
et al. (2021) find that the severity of water
pollution is closely related to the popula-
tion size of cities. Glinska-Lewczuk et al.
(2016) is one of few papers that recognizes
multi-city effects, analyzing the river as an
environmental path that links urban areas
into an “urban river continuum.” I bridge
the economic and hydrology approaches to
upstream and downstream pollution, on
one hand borrowing a water quality anal-
ysis framework and multi-city approach
from hydrology, while focusing more on
the economic impacts of water pollution.
My paper ties together the ideas of
health-related water pollution effects,
neighborhood choice and migration, natu-
ral disamenities, and upstream and down-
stream pollution models to identify how
downriver counties fared in a new era of
urbanization and industrialization.

I assume that pollution concentration has
a 1:1 relationship with population density.
I construct my upstream pollution
concentration figure using three elements.
First, I use each county’s aforementioned
population density as a measure of pollution
density. This data is pulled from the U.S.
Census. Second, I aggregate the pollution

Finally, I use an exponential decay function
to model the varying levels of pollution
over distance and severity. As effluents
flow through a river, they are subject to
various decaying forces such as decompo-
sition, oxidation (the chemical process by
which organic materials are broken down
when they react with oxygen), dilution,
and sedimentation. In the context of my
paper, I model the decay of river pollution
using the recorded distances between each
county so that pollution from County A
will impact County B the most, County C
the second most, and so on.
For each census, I construct a dataset
using my list of counties along the Missis-
sippi River and their associated population
densities, population levels, and %Urban
observations. There are a total of 112
counties (111 in 1880) used in my dataset.

Most notably, the regression results beg an

Discussion
The consistent direction and magnitude
of my findings indicate that upstream
pollution concentration had both sta-
tistically and economically significant
impacts on population levels over a long
period in the late 19th to early 20th cen-
turies. A logical next step in interpreting
these results would be to understand the
channels by which populations declined.
There are a few possibilities. First, one
could interpret the decline in population
to represent an increase in mortality.
That is to say, increases in pollution
concentration increased the incidence of
deadly water-borne diseases, increasing
mortality and reducing population levels.
This is not unreasonable, given the find-
ings from Cutler and Miller (2005), Ferrie
and Troesken (2008), and Beach et al.
(2016). In the absence of mortality data,
however, it is difficult to directly prove
this hypothesis. Another way to interpret
the results is to argue that populations
reacted to the presence of a disamenity,
manifesting in the form of negative health
effects or low aesthetic value, and decided
to move elsewhere. This is the explanation
that my amenity model predicts in section
4. Therefore, a second channel could be
that populations declined as a result of
migration. The most likely case is that
both channels were valid and active.
It is also worth discussing my finding
that the effect of water pollution on the
population began declining after 1910.
From 1880 to 1900, the effect of upstream
pollution concentration on population lev-
els increased in magnitude. The increasing
magnitude of pollution makes sense: The
river was increasingly polluted, resulting
in increasing deaths from water-borne
diseases. The sudden declining effect
of pollution from 1910-1930 defies this
explanation. I propose that one potential
explanation for the observed directional
change in Figure 3 may be linked to sig-
nificant exogenous developments in clean
water technologies. As demonstrated by
Cutler and Miller (2005), breakthroughs
in bacteriology and clean water tech-
nologies such as chlorination during the
early 20th century played pivotal roles
in reducing urban mortality rates. These
technological
innovations
effectively
mitigated the health risks posed by pol-
luted water sources, thereby diminishing
the negative impact of upstream pollu-
tion on population health. As cities and
smaller communities implemented these

new technologies, they not only curbed
the prevalence of waterborne diseases but
also enhanced the overall quality of life,
contributing to increased amenity levels
of urban environments. Consequently, the
reduction in the upstream pollution coef-
ficient can be interpreted as a response to
these public health improvements and the
subsequent decline of the urban mortality
penalty caused by intercity pollution.
Indeed, many cities on the Mississippi
River began filtering and chlorinating
water in the early 20th century as part of
broader trends in U.S. water treatment
practices; to gain a more complete under-
standing of these developments, I build a
timeline of water-related interventions
in selected cities along the Mississippi
River referencing papers published in the
Journal of the American Water Works
Association (Journal AWWA) as well as
data drawn from local city government
websites. Figure 4 shows the timeline of
a selection of 12 river cities that adopted
clean water practices and sanitation tech-
nologies from 1880-1940. A detailed list
of cities used for this survey is listed in
Appendix A. As Figure 4 shows, cities on
the Mississippi River began implementing
water purification technologies at around
the same time the pollution coefficients in
Table 1 began to decline. These findings
track with both the historical record and
the aforementioned research showing that
such efforts to purify water sources for
safe consumption were indeed effective
enough to address the negative effects of
water pollution.
Conclusion
My paper looks at how increased
urban and industrial pollution in the late
19th and early 20th centuries in the Mis-
sissippi River affected the population size
of river communities. I find that upstream
pollution had a statistically and economi-
cally significant impact on downstream
populations. My findings add to existing
economic research that (dis)amenities, and
specifically environmental disamenities,
have a powerful effect on where people
choose to live. Furthermore, I find that
the effects of water pollution worsened
from 1880-1900 before declining from
1910 onwards. I argue that upstream river
pollution likely contributed to the urban
mortality penalty by increasingly polluting
the same water sources from where down-
stream cities often drew their water. By the
same token, the implementation of new
water technologies such as filtration and
chlorination in cities along the Mississippi
in the early 20th century, which helped
mitigate the urban mortality penalty, also
explains why my pollution concentration
effect declined after 1910.
This paper is one of few that look at the
economic relationship between upstream
and downstream communities, and there
are numerous opportunities to expand and

time and access to historical records (spe-
cifically local or state-level records), one
could analyze the effects of pollution at a
more precise scale than my existing coun-

differential effects of pollution between
inland communities and communities on
the river. I also propose future directions
of study. One extension of this research
may analyze the relationship between up-
stream pollution and population sorting
(i.e., changing income, property values,
and literacy in downstream communi-
ties), which would also be an interesting
application for a hedonic pricing model or
externality analysis. Another extension lies
in investigating the differential mortality
rates of smaller industrial towns, which
often lagged behind in implementing
modern public health mechanisms (Leon-

the Mississippi that did implement water

Northwestern’s Office of Undergraduate Research (OUR) is the pin-
nacle hub on campus for young, aspiring scholars to access the innumerable
resources in pursuing projects both independently and with a faculty. A
unique initiative from OUR is the Emerging Scholars Program (ESP), which
is composed of 8-10 students
The Arthur Vining Davis Foundation grant launched the Emerging
Scholars Program in 2021, and it has subsequently become a core, formally
offered program within the OUR. It can be tough for students to get involved
in research, especially within subjects like the social sciences or journalism
without a formal lab-based component. Thus, ESP aims to provide an easier
entry point for these students while also providing a $10,250 stipend for the
completion of the 15-month program.
The program’s cohort of 8 - 10 students start during the summer of
their freshman year, and they continue through the end of their sophomore
year. During the first summer, they support a professor’s research from the
list of Emerging Scholars Program faculty. Professors come from a wide
array of disciplines, supporting students of all interests.
Diamond Jones, the Education Program Manager at OUR, supports
students in their undergraduate research journey from guiding them
through workshops about research opportunities all the way to helping
them eventually pursue their research interests at a greater depth.
As a 15-month commitment, the longest offering at OUR, Diamond
Jones explains that the dedication required by the program encourages
major leaps in academic and research development for students. The addi-
tion of professional development sessions during the cohort’s sophomore
summer guides students from this program to future academic and career

Opening Doors to Undergraduate Research

development afterwards: research is a transferable experience, and OUR guides
students to discover industry parallels from their experience at ESP beyond just
graduate school.
Valentina Parra, an undergraduate sophomore majoring in Learning
Sciences and Latinx Studies, is a testament to the Emerging Scholars Program’s
transformative power. When asked about the impact of this program, she says, “It
exposed me to a world I would not have stepped into as early as I did.”
She worked with Dr. Alyssa Garcia in the Gender and Sexuality Studies
department last summer, studying an interdisciplinary approach to feminist the-
ory’s application in Cuban sex work and race. Valentina says that students are not
expected to know how to conduct research going in, and the mentors help guide
students through the entire process. This experience helped her see new possibil-
ities in academia, as the program “demystified the spaces that are exclusionary of
backgrounds like [hers].”
A key component of the Emerging Scholars Program for Valentina was
the mentorship she received. She appreciated that the environment “made space
for [her] in a way [she] did not have to assimilate.” Diamond Jones also touched
on this point – since the program serves many students from underrepresented
backgrounds, such as First Generation Low Income (FGLI) and racial minorities,
students often put their identities into the research that they “wished existed
for them.”
Through the skills she developed this past summer, she now has the founda-
tion to conduct her own research, now transitioning into her last summer with the
program. Her research focuses on analyzing race and class impacts in the Mexican
2024 presidential election discourse on X through a satirical account.
For students interested in research, Valentina advises students to consider
the Emerging Scholars Program as a pathway to exploring their research and
academic interests. She notes that 15 months is much less intimidating than at first
glance, and participants are able to develop a strong connection to their community
of fellow academics.
Abstract
In this study, we employ a conjoint analysis to assess what factors influence the
likelihood of male and female candidates being perceived as leaders. In partic-
ular, we consider the influence of agency and communality stereotypes in terms
of personality, emotionality, and parental status. Participants evaluated a set of
fictitious employee profiles of a consulting firm, selecting which employees they
considered most deserving of being promoted to managers. Participant evaluations
were then analyzed to determine the relative importance of eight study attributes
in influencing the probability of managerial promotion (i.e., leadership selection).
In this paper, we discuss two of our main findings. First, when emotional control is
described as fair, female candidates are less likely than male candidates to be chosen
as leaders. Second, certain agentic female leaders benefit from being described as
mothers: bossy, but not ambitious, female candidates are more likely to be chosen as
leaders when described as having children compared to when described as childless.

corporate pipeline: while women hold a
slim 36% of senior manager positions, they
hold just 28% of C-suite positions (Cata-
lyst, 2022; McKinsey & Company, 2023).
If female employees are as prevalent
and as qualified as male employees, why
then does there exist a disparity between
men and women in positions of authority?
For decades, psychologists have investi-
gated a myriad of stereotypes as potential
sources of this gap. Such research has un-
covered that the traits comprising society’s
traditional leadership prototype are mas-
culine, and the stereotypical traits associat-
ed with women are inconsistent with this
prototype (Eagly & Karau, 2002). Leaders
are typically described as ambitious, inde-
pendent, confident, and assertive; while
men can display these traits without pen-
alty, women face backlash. Women are
expected to be warm, friendly, nurturing,
and sensitive—traits that are rarely used
to describe leaders. Women who violate
these societal norms (e.g., by being cold or
acting assertively) face various penalties
for being stereotype-inconsistent (Eagly &
Wood, 2002; Eagly & Wood, 2012; Rud-
man et al., 2008).
Thus, a woman in the workplace is
subject to a double-edged sword: act too
submissively, and she will not be seen as a
leader, but act too dominantly, and she will
not be desired as a leader. This research
seeks to address how women can best nav-
igate this paradox in order to be seen and
desired as leaders.
Agency and Communality
In this study, we utilize Bakan’s (1966)
agentic-communal framework. Bakan’s
model posits that humans can be described
using two constructs: agency and com-
munality. Agency can be understood as
independence, while communality can be
understood as interdependence. Although
the prototypical traits used to describe suc-
cessful leaders are agentic, social identities
like gender appear to play a critical role
in governing the effectiveness of agentic
displays as a means of demonstrating lead-
ership quality (Eagly & Karau, 2002).
Agentic stereotypes are prescribed
for men and proscribed for women; hence,
agentic male leaders are stereotype-con-
gruent, while agentic female leaders are
stereotype-incongruent (Eagly et al., 2020;
Sczesny et al., 2018). When individuals
violate their prescribed stereotypes, they
prompt psychological discomfort, which
often results in negative evaluations
(Moss-Racusin et al., 2010). Since agentic
female leaders are inconsistent with the
stereotype of women being communal,
they experience various forms of backlash,
including being seen as less likable, hirable,
and competent (Eagly & Karau, 2002; Rud-
man et al., 2012; Rudman & Glick, 1999).
Due to this backlash, when compared di-
rectly against one another, agentic male
leaders are typically perceived as better
than agentic female leaders. However,
when leaders are described as communal,
male and female leaders are typically evalu-
ated similarly (Heilman & Okimoto, 2007;
Rudman et al., 2012).
Agentic female leaders appear to be
able to mitigate the backlash they face by
being mothers, or more precisely, through
evaluators’ awareness of their motherhood.
When agentic female leaders are described
as having children, they are perceived
significantly more favorably than when
described as being childless[a] (Heilman &
Okimoto, 2007). Having children appears
to mitigate the penalties incurred by agen-
tic women due to the fact that they are now
perceived as sufficiently communal (i.e.,
stereotype-congruent).
Emotionality stereotypes can further
explain differences in leadership percep-
tion between men and women. Commu-
nality is tied to emotional attunement, such
that communal individuals are regarded as
warm, sensitive, and empathetic (Keck,
2019). In that women are stereotyped as
being more communal than men, they
are also stereotyped as being more emo-
tional than men (Shields, 2002). In fact, a
majority of men and one-third of women
believe that women are underrepresented
in leadership positions in business and
politics because they are too emotional
(Dolan, 2014). Research, however, has
shown that men and women do, in fact,
experience the same amount of emotion,
but since women are more likely to ex-
press it, women are commonly believed
to be more emotional than men (Durik
et al., 2006; LaFrance & Banaji, 1992).
As female leaders are more likely
to express emotion, it is assumed that
they allow their emotions to influence
their thoughts and decisions. This per-
ceived biasing effect of emotions on deci-
sion-making hurts female leaders because
it is widely believed that emotion detracts
from rational thought, despite a robust
body of research indicating that emotion
does not impede decision-making and,
in some cases, actually helps it (Damasio,
When leaders are described as emo-
tional, female leaders are more likely than
male leaders to be perceived as overreact-
ing and unable to regulate their emotions
[b](Shields, 1987). Even when no evidence
pertaining to a leader’s emotionality is
made available, individuals are still more
likely to evaluate an identical managerial
decision as emotion-driven and, conse-
quently, rate that decision as inferior and
that leader as less employable when told
the leader is female compared to male
(Brescoll, 2016).
Present Study
With a novel methodological application,
this research aims to fill a gap in the
existing literature and contribute to a more
multifaceted understanding of leadership
perception. With a conjoint survey design,
we examine the influence of several
attributes to better assess how potential
leaders are judged. This project addresses
“When agentic female leaders are
described as having children, they are
perceived significantly more favorably
than when described as being childless.”
the following overarching question: under
what criteria are male and female leaders
perceived differently, and how can agency
and communality stereotypes explain
these differences?
In previous comparable leadership
studies, only a small number of variables
have been examined within a single exper-
iment. With conjoint analysis, however,
it becomes possible to precisely evaluate
a significantly larger number of variables,
referred to as attributes. While conjoint
survey experiments are common in fields
such as product testing and political sci-
ence research, they have never before been
applied to study leadership using the agen-
tic-communal framework, allowing us to
provide novel insights.
In order to better understand the
basics of conjoint analysis, consider the
following example in which a group of
researchers conduct an experiment to
inform the development of a new smart-
phone. The researchers decided to evaluate
three core smartphone features to deter-
mine their relative importance and the
optimal combination of features (i.e., the
smartphone with the highest likelihood of
purchase). As such, they create a conjoint
survey design with three attributes: color,
length, and price. The color attribute lev-
els are silver and black, the length attribute
levels are five inches and six inches, and
the price attribute levels are $600, $700,
and $800. With a forced-choice conjoint
survey design, participants see a series of
tables each depicting two phone profiles
in terms of color, length, and price, with
a randomly selected level for each of the
attributes. Because conjoint designs are
within-subjects, the profile tables are com-
pletely randomized across participants. For
each selection task, participants consider
the two phone profiles and select which
phone in the pair they would rather pur-
chase. The subsequent analyses are repeat-
ed-measures comparisons of participant
responses to each of the tables. In other
words, respondents’ preferences are com-
pared to each other to examine how they
vary as a function of the attributes of inter-
est. This analysis enables the researchers to
determine which phone to produce based
on the feature combination yielding the
highest probability of selection.
Conjoint analyses allow for the cal-
culation of average marginal component
effects (AMCEs) for each attribute level.
AMCEs can be understood as the individual
effect of each attribute level on the proba-
bility of a profile being selected. Moreover,
interaction AMCEs can be calculated to
show how differing combinations of attri-
bute levels impact the overall probability
of a profile being selected. With this meth-
odology, we were able to assess leadership
perception via the agentic-communal
“When leaders
are described
as emotional,
female leaders are
more likely than
male leaders to
be perceived as
overreacting and
unable to regulate
their emotions.”
framework across several attributes, more
than ever previously examined in a compa-
rable singular experiment. This study tests
the following hypotheses: (1) Gender and
emotional control will interact to affect
leadership perception, (2) Gender and per-
sonality will interact to affect leadership
perception, and (3) Gender, personality,
and parental status will interact to affect
leadership perception.
Methodology
Participants
Participants (n = 301) were recruited
through
the
online
data
collection
platform Prolific. The average age of
participants was 39.9 years (SD = 13.54).
Participants were limited to U.S. citizens
18 years and older. Although an a priori
power analysis suggested that for 10 selec-
tion tasks, 200 participants were needed to
detect a medium-sized effect, to increase
the robustness of our study results, we
increased our sample size to 301.
Design and Materials
A forced-choice conjoint survey design
was employed; see Table 1 for a full attri-
bute breakdown.
In total, this design had eight attri-
butes: race, gender, relationship status,
parental status, personality, emotional
control, industry experience, and high-
est education. Three attributes served to
analyze agency and communality percep-
tion. First, the personality attribute most
directly indicated the candidates’ agentic or
communal nature. This attribute had four
levels, two levels being communal traits
(collaborative, empathetic) and two levels
being agentic traits (ambitious, bossy).
Second, parental status served as a poten-
tial indicator of commonality, particularly
among female candidates. This attribute
denoted the number of kids a candidate had
with four levels (0, 1, 2, 3). Third, the emo-
tional control attribute served to indicate
agency and communality through emo-
tionality associations. This attribute had
four levels (poor, fair, good, and excellent).
In order to create a more realistic
employee evaluation experience for par-
ticipants, the emotional control attribute
was renamed to “performance under pres-
sure” during the experiment. Similarly, to
explain how candidates’ personality traits
and abilities to perform under pressure
were determined, the task description
explained to participants that this infor-
mation was pulled from previous perfor-
mance evaluations.
Procedure
Participants began the experiment by
reading a short passage that described a
consulting firm and explained their task of
evaluating current firm employees up for
a promotion to a managerial role. More
specifically, participants were informed
that each selection task would consist of
assessing a pair of candidate profiles and
selecting which candidate they believed
to be more deserving of a managerial (i.e.,
leadership) role. While this company and
the employees were entirely fictitious,
participants were not given this infor-
mation until after completing the study.
Participants completed 10 selection tasks.
See Figure 1 for a sample task.
After the candidate selection compo-
nent, participants provided demographic
information, including two scales to assess
gender bias. The Benevolent Sexism in the
Workplace (BSW) scale (Warren et al.,
2023) consisted of 19 items and assessed
participant endorsement of complemen-
tary gender differentiation (e.g., “When
employees have personal problems, they
prefer to go to their female coworkers
to get emotional support”) and protec-
tive paternalism (e.g., “Women should
work less than men so they can serve as
a caretaker for their families”). For each
item, participants indicated their agree-
ment using a 7-point Likert scale (1 =
strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree);
higher scores indicated stronger endorse-
ment. A modified version of the 13-item
Color-blind Racial Attitudes Scale (Neville
et al., 2000), in which racial terminology
was replaced with that of gender, assessed
participant endorsement of gender-blind
ideology (e.g., “Sexism may have been a
problem in the past, it is not an important
problem today”). For each item, partici-
pants indicated their agreement using a
6-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree
to 6 = strongly agree); higher scores indi-
cated stronger endorsement.
Results
A complete overview of the average mar-
ginal component effects (AMCEs) of all
attribute levels is shown in Figure 2.
Note. Figure 2 shows percentage
point change in probability of being
selected. Sample size N = 301 respondents,
or at candidate level N = 6020.
Candidates with college and with
graduate degrees were evaluated signifi-
cantly better than candidates with a high
school degree, experiencing a sizable bump
of about 10 percentage points (p < .001).
Similarly, candidates with eight years of
experience and 12 years of experience
were evaluated significantly better than
candidates with only four years of experi-
ence, experiencing a bump of about 10 per-
centage points (p < .001). Considering the
personality attribute, results indicated that
compared to empathetic candidates, col-
laborative candidates experienced a boost
of about 6 percentage points (p < .001),
ambitious candidates experienced a drop
of about 6 percentage points (p = .002),
and bossy candidates experienced an even
larger drop of about 24 percentage points
Emotional control played a significant
role in determining candidate perception.
Compared to candidates with poor emo-
tional control, candidates with fair emo-
tional control were roughly 25 percentage
points more likely to be selected for the
promotion, candidates with good emo-
tional control were roughly 36 percentage
points more likely to be selected for the
promotion, and candidates with excellent
emotional control were roughly 51 per-
centage points more likely to be selected
for the promotion (p < .001).
Figure 3 shows how the gender
attribute interacted with each of the seven
other candidate attributes to affect the
probability of candidate selection. For each
attribute level, the presence of a signifi-
cant difference between male and female

Comparing the interaction AMCEs

all attribute levels revealed one signifi-

a significant evaluation gap between male
and female candidates emerged. Female
candidates with fair emotional control
were evaluated roughly 7 percentage points
more negatively than male candidates with

Participant characteristics generated
additional insights into this interaction.
Figure 4 shows the effects of the inter-
action between gender and emotional
control when conditional on partici-
pant BSW scores. The effects for the top
50th percentile scorers (high BSW), the

between the effects (high BSW minus

Among participants with the strongest
ideological adherence, female candidates
with fair emotional control were signifi-
cantly less likely to be promoted: high
BSW participants evaluated female candi-
dates with fair emotional control about 10
percentage points behind low BSW partic-
ipants (p = .036).
Transitioning to the parental status
attribute, analyses showed no significant
evaluation differences between candidates
with zero, one, two, or three children.
However, when personality interacted
with parental status, significant evaluation
differences emerged within one person-
ality trait: bossy. The interaction AMCEs
between parental status and personality
can be seen in Figure 5. Compared to bossy
candidates without children, bossy candi-
dates with children were evaluated signifi-
cantly more favorably. (see: Appendix)
Bossy candidates with one child
experienced a boost of about 9 percentage
points (p = .007), bossy candidates with
two children experienced a boost of about
7 percentage points (p = .022), and bossy
candidates with three children experienced
a boost of about 8 percentage points (p =
.018). For no other personality trait did
parental status produce a significant effect
on the probability of candidate promotion.
Considering the influence of gender
on this interaction, results showed the
agentic male and female candidates expe-
rienced some key differences in evaluation.
This analysis revealed that the significant
evaluation boost of having children expe-
rienced by bossy candidates applied only to
female candidates. Bossy male candidates
were evaluated similarly with or with-
out kids, while bossy female candidates
were evaluated significantly better when
described as having kids. Compared to
childless bossy female candidates, bossy
female candidates with one child were
more likely to be promoted (13.6%, p =
.003), and bossy female candidates with
three children were more likely to be
promoted (15.3%, p = .001). While bossy
female candidates with two children were
also more likely to be promoted, this effect
was not quite significant (8.3%, p = .065).
Discussion
The results of this study support
Hypothesis 1 (Gender and emotional
control will interact to affect leadership
perception). While we had expected that
female candidates would be evaluated
more negatively than male candidates
across all emotional control levels, we
found only a significant gender difference
within the fair level. When both were
described as having fair emotional control,
female candidates were significantly less
likely than male candidates to be pro-
moted, but when both were described as
having poor, good, or excellent emotional
control, female candidates were evaluated
similarly to male candidates.
A possible explanation for this effect
is that the “fair” descriptor is a rather
ambiguous term to indicate a candi-
date’s ability to regulate their emotions,
while the “poor”, “good”, and “excellent”
descriptors are more explicit and tangible.
In the absence of a clear indication of a
candidate’s ability to regulate their emo-
tions, participants may be forced to rely
on gendered emotionality stereotypes. It is
possible that as a result of subscribing to
the stereotypes that (1) women are more
emotional than men and (2) emotionality
impedes leadership quality, individuals
evaluate leadership candidates described
as having “fair” emotional control more
harshly when that leader is female com-
pared to when the leader is male. In other
words, when a candidate’s emotionality is
left vague to individuals, they may resort
to the use of gendered emotionality ste-
reotypes to inform their decision-making,
leading to female candidates suffering pen-
alties avoided by male candidates.
Our reasoning that emotional con-
trol being described as “fair” results in
biased evaluations against women due to
stereotyping is further supported by our
analysis of the effect of participants’ ideo-
logical beliefs. For the fair emotional con-
trol level (and this level only), a significant
difference in evaluation emerges between
participants with strong adherence to
workplace benevolent sexist ideology and
participants with weak adherence. We find
that individuals who more rigidly endorse
this form of sexism are significantly less
likely to select a female leader over a male
leader when both are described as having
fair emotional control, compared to indi-
viduals lower in sexism endorsement. The
lack of significant evaluation differences
between these participant groups within
the poor, good, and excellent levels can
once again be explained using the reason-
ing that with more explicit indications
of emotionality, individuals do not need
to resort to gender stereotypes to inform
their decision-making.
Our results do not support Hypothe-
sis 2 (Gender and personality will interact
to affect leadership perception). Based on
previous research, we had expected that
when described communally, there would
be no difference in evaluation between
male and female candidates, but when
described agentically, male candidates
would be perceived more favorably than
female candidates (Rudman et al., 2012;
Rudman & Glick, 1999). Our results indeed
show that individuals perceive leadership
capability similarly between communal
male and communal female candidates.
However, contrary to our expectations,
our results also show that individuals
perceive leadership capability similarly
between agentic male and agentic female
candidates. Hence, we find some evidence
that may suggest that the United States
populace is moving away from a dominant
alpha male as its leadership prototype, such
that agentic women are no longer at such
a significant comparative disadvantage
(Wiezel et al., 2024).
The results of this study support
Hypothesis 3 (Gender, personality, and
parental status will interact to affect lead-
ership perception). While, for bossy male
candidates, we find no significant evalua-
tion differences based on whether or not
they have children, we find that bossy
female candidates experience significant
improvements in evaluation when they
are described as having kids compared to
when described as childless. This evidence
supports previous research indicating that
agentic female leaders benefit from being
described as mothers, with motherhood
serving to remedy a perceived commu-
nality deficit (Heilman & Okimoto, 2007).
However, we had expected that all agen-
tic female candidates would benefit from
being described as mothers, but we only
see this among bossy female candidates.
Ambitious female candidates do not appear
to experience significant evaluation differ-
ences based on their status as mothers.
We reason that ambitious female
leaders may not experience a mother-
hood boost because the perception of
these leaders’ ambition is reduced by the
knowledge that they are parents. Pre-
vious research suggests that parents are
typically perceived as less committed to
their jobs and less achievement-oriented
than non-parents (Allen & Russell, 1999;
Fuegen et al., 2004; Heilman & Okimoto,
2007). An explanation for why ambitious,
but not bossy, female candidates do not
experience a motherhood boost is that any
improvement in perception they receive
for being considered sufficiently commu-
nal is counteracted by the punishment in
perception they receive for being seen as
less professionally dedicated.
Building on previous studies for a
more nuanced perspective, we suggest
that not all agentic female leaders experi-
ence improvements in perception when
described as being mothers. We reason that
when female leaders are defined by moti-
vation-based agentic traits (e.g., ambitious,
dedicated, persistent, go-getter), having
children calls these traits into question,
resulting in similar evaluations between
mothers and non-mothers. Conversely,
when female leaders are defined by agentic
traits tangential to motivation (e.g., bossy,
decisive, assertive, dominant), having chil-
dren does not call these traits into question,
resulting in mothers being perceived more
favorably than non-mothers.
Conclusion
We hope this study can highlight the value
of examining a familiar research question
in an unfamiliar way. Decades of research
have
applied
the
agentic-communal
framework to understand how male and
female leaders experience differences, yet
through novel methodological applica-
tions, we become capable of generating
new insights and showing that this
question remains to be fully answered.
Where in most of the previous literature,
leaders were either classified as agentic or
communal, emotional or non-emotional,
parents or non-parents, in conjoint
experiments, leaders not only have more
facets but also more specific levels within
facets. Participant evaluations of the truly
multifaceted candidate profiles unique
to conjoint experiments can facilitate a
more precise understanding of percep-
tion. With the results of our conjoint
survey design consisting of 13,284 possible
candidate profile combinations, we con-
clude with two testimonies to this point.
First, considering the interaction
between gender and emotionality, our
results show that not all female leaders
are evaluated more negatively than male
leaders when emotional control is held
constant. When emotional control is
described explicitly, we find no evaluation
differences between genders, but when
described ambiguously, we see that female
leaders are at a disadvantage. Yet, in the
real world, a person’s ability to control
their emotions is ambiguous; people do
not walk around with a one-word label
on their shirt or a numeric score on their
resume designating such an ability. Had we
not included “fair” as a level and opted only
for explicit levels, we would not have seen
any way in which female leaders suffer a
penalty, let alone the most critical way —
that which is most true to life.
Second, considering the interaction
between gender, personality, and parental
status, our results show that not all agentic
women see an improvement in leadership
desirability when described as having
children. While we find that bossy female
leaders experience a motherhood boost, we
do not find this to be the case for ambitious
female leaders. If both “bossy” and “ambi-
tious” are agentic traits, why do we see this
difference? We explain this discrepancy
through the reasoning that within the
agency umbrella, there may exist different
types of agency, and the perception of cer-
tain types can be jeopardized by the knowl-
edge of a female leader having children. If
instead of having two levels to encapsulate
agentic personality, we had only used one,
we would have missed out on this nuance.
These findings help to illustrate the
salience of extracting and empirically eval-
uating multiple levels within leadership
criteria. Follow-up research is necessary to
sketch out more of the complexities with-
in agency and communality. As we find
evidence to support the existence of unique
dimensions within agency, we are left
wondering what dimensions within com-
munality may likewise uniquely affect how
leaders are perceived. When interpreting
these results, it is important to keep in
mind that although conjoint analyses are
extremely useful in illustrating what fac-
tors influence leadership preference and
factor interactions, there are critical dif-
ferences between theoretical preference
and real-world choice. Moreover, we can
not rule out that any number of our find-
ings would differ if we were to repeat this
experiment using a participant pool made
up of actual employees in the business
world tasked with these kinds of leader-
ship personnel decisions. ◆
