Green Chemistry with
Dr. Mark Aparece
Impacts of Chemistry
Beyond the Lab:
By Hannah Xu
FEATURES
Dr. Mark Aparece is an Assistant Professor of Instruction in the Department of
Chemistry at Northwestern University. After completing his master’s and PhD work
on transition metal catalysis, he began teaching organic and green chemistry at North-
western, which sparked his interest in the environmental impacts of modern chemistry.
In addition to his research on soil contamination in Chicago, Dr. Aparece is innovating
new ways to incorporate green principles in his curriculum, emphasizing the impacts of
chemistry beyond the lab.
What sparked your interest in green chemistry?
During my undergraduate education, some green chemistry principles (such as atom
economy and reducing waste) were introduced in my organic chemistry teaching lab,
but green chemistry itself wasn’t really incorporated in the broader curriculum. Then,
in my first year at Northwestern, I was assigned to teach the Green Chemistry class in
the spring quarter of 2023. To prepare for the class, I read a lot of books and articles
about green and environmental chemistry, which really opened my eyes and made me
passionate about the subject, as well as environmental justice in general. I’ve really liked
teaching the class—I’ve learned a lot, and I’m excited to learn more!
Could you describe your research?
I’m currently collaborating with Dr. Shelby Hatch, collecting soil samples from different
neighborhoods in Chicago and digesting them in nitric acid to analyze the inorganic
heavy metal content (lead, arsenic, etc.). My research assistants and I have also started
looking into organic pollutants, like “forever chemicals” and polychlorinated biphenyl
compounds. These are toxic to the human body and the environment in a complemen-
tary way to inorganic heavy metals, and many of these compounds are carcinogenic or
can be metabolized as endocrine disruptors, causing health issues like fatigue, cancer,
infertility, and other conditions. To build upon existing methods, we are trying to
develop new ways of detecting these contaminants in Chicago soils.
Beyond analyzing soil contamination, we are also collaborating with a Chicago Public
Schools teacher and a historian to look into demographic data and historical archives. By
learning what kinds of people and places (factories, stores, etc.) have been in a specific
area throughout the last 10, 20, 50, or 100 years, we can better understand how these
contaminants were introduced to the soil in the first place.
How have you been incorporating green chemistry principles in the labs
you teach?
Last quarter was my third time teaching the accelerated organic chemistry lab at North-
western, and I actually switched out three experiments! The first two were for a two-
part Grignard experiment. Originally, students were given a Grignard reagent to use
for their reaction, but this time, students were asked to make it themselves and to use
dry ice as the electrophile. This change was not only a pedagogical choice, but also one
that made the reaction more green—the dry ice sublimes into small quantities of carbon
dioxide once used, instead of producing harmful waste.
The final lab of the quarter was also changed. It was an epoxidation with green reagents.
Traditional epoxidation involves using mCPBA, but the byproduct from this reaction
has higher mass and complexity than the product itself. It is also uncommon and toxic, so
it needs to be disposed of in a very specific way. However, after changing the procedure
and using oxone and base, the byproduct was simply potassium bisulfate, a harmless salt
that can simply be washed down the drain. I’m happy to say it worked really well! And
besides being greener, this reaction also served a pedagogical purpose, as the students
learned how to do more complex NMR analysis.
What are your future goals for incorporating green chemistry
into the curriculum?
I hope to develop new green reactions, which could be a future undergraduate research
project of its own! If any undergraduate students want to help test out these reactions,
I would love to work with them to figure out how to further incorporate green experi-
ments into the organic teaching lab sequence.
Do you have any advice for undergraduate students looking to get
involved with research?
Cast a wide net! There’s a lot of interdisciplinary work, so don’t be limited to projects
within your home department or school. I’m in the Department of Chemistry, but
there are professors in Earth and Environmental Sciences, as well as ones in Civil and
Environmental Engineering, who have worked on research related to mine. There are
always cool research opportunities in every department, so make sure to be open-minded
and stay curious!
By: Avery Morawa
The work of Dr. Sarah Rodriguez - a professor of global
health, the Co-Director of Undergraduate Studies, and
a medical historian - is a testament to curiosity, critical
inquiry, and persistence. With an undergraduate back-
ground in history and American studies, her academic
journey began with a fascination for understanding how
society navigates complex issues. This culminated in an
honors thesis focused on the history of medicine and
reproductive health. This laid the foundation for a career
spent uncovering stories that illuminate the intersection
between medical ethics and social history.
Exploring the Complex History
of Reproductive Health:
Insights from Dr. Rodriguez
FEATURES
Researching the Past to Inform the Present
For Dr. Rodriguez, research is more than a search for an answer —
it’s a process of exploration that often raises new and unexpected questions
along the way. “You can go in with one question and leave with another,”
she explains, emphasizing the importance of maintaining an open mind
and remaining inquisitive. The process of her work often involves diving
into archives, medical journals, court records, and historical newspapers to
search for the threads that connect medical practices to broader social and
political contexts. “Historical research is looking at ‘stuff’,” she describes.
Dr. Rodriguez’s research on maternal mortality is particularly strik-
ing. “Counting maternal deaths is difficult,” she notes, describing the chal-
lenges of obtaining reliable numerical data. It’s difficult to evaluate exactly
how many deaths in or near childbirth are caused by maternal inflictions
versus other factors, making this quantitative data burdensome to work
with. Instead, her work examines how states and organizations — ranging
from individual nations to the World Health Organization — have histor-
ically responded to maternal death rates and what those responses reveal
about societal values. Changes to law code, establishment of supportive
programs such as the Department of Maternal Health, and the creation of
private companies such as the Rockefeller foundation are all changes that
Rodriguez seeks to investigate and reflect upon.
One persistent theme uncovered by her work is the historical pri-
oritization of infant health over maternal health. Dr. Rodriguez attributes
such to systemic sexism. Maternal and child health are heavily linked:
trends in maternal mortality often follow on the heels of trends in infant
mortality. However, despite their codependence, Rodriguez points to his-
torical patterns in which women’s health becomes a priority only when it’s
seen as essential to the well-being of children or to addressing population
concerns. Confronting this pattern may help develop more effective treat-
ments, better data, and greater equity in healthcare in the future.
The Intersection of Medicine, Ethics, and History
Dr. Rodriguez’s knowledge extends beyond medical history and into
the ethical dimensions of medical practices. In her book The Love Surgeon:
A Story of Trust, Harm, and the Limits of Medical Regulation (2020), she
dives into the controversial career and operations of a physician whose sur-
gical procedures sparked public outcry due to a lack of informed consent.
Through court documents, medical files, and interviews, Dr. Rodriguez
explores questions about accountability in medicine, the responsibility of
physicians to regulate their peers, and societal conditions present during medi-
cal ethics dilemmas.
Her findings reveal that this physician’s actions were not inherently
isolated or malicious, rather they were reflective of broader systemic and social
issues within medical practice at the time. “This wasn’t normative behavior,
but it wasn’t an outlier either,” Dr. Rodriguez explains, highlighting the
importance of understanding historical context to address challenges in medi-
cal ethics and regulation.
Reflections on Research and Its Impact
Research is as much about the process as the findings according to
Rodriguez. “You need to be open to change and thinking about things differ-
ently,” she says, emphasizing the importance of recognizing gaps in knowl-
edge and adapting the research to evolving questions. Whether exploring
the evolution of maternal health policies or the ethics of surgical
practices, her work is a reminder of the complexities that shape
medicine today and the ongoing need to question, learn, and
advocate for change. Through her meticulous research and
thoughtful analysis, Dr. Rodriguez continues to illu-
minate the ways history informs present-day
discussions on reproductive health.
Abstract
State merit-based scholarships are a large source of funding for many college
students, and the effects of this aid on families, students, and states’ economies
is a topic of continued interest and research. There are 22 states with merit aid
programs, and because eligibility includes graduating from an in-state high school,
students and parents in some states can depend on this aid while others cannot.
I use this variation, documented by the InforeED State Financial Aid Dataset,
together with survey data on people’s decisions to save for college, provided by the
National Financial Capability Survey, to assess the effect of merit aid programs on
college savings. I find mixed evidence, some suggesting that living in a state with a
merit aid program meaningfully decreases the likelihood of saving for college, and
some suggesting that it has no effect. I assess whether the scholarships change the
amount parents save using the College Savings Plan Network data on 529 accounts.
My results are inconclusive, and I propose redoing my analysis with the Survey
of Consumer Finances confidential dataset. My analysis is limited by the fact that
data sets containing both a measure of college savings and the state of residence
are difficult to obtain and/or to use because of the structure of the available data.
The purpose of this paper is, in addition to quantifying the effect of scholarships on
savings, to describe the potential data sources, limitations, and possible strategies,
to inform future related work.
The Effect of Merit
Scholarships on Saving
for College
Faculty Adviser: Dr. Scott Ogawa
Departments of Economics and
Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
by Emilya Ershtein
Introduction
Government funding for college has the
following direct effects: pushing students
slightly below the margin of affording
college to attend college, reducing families’
financial burden, reducing students’ finan-
cial burden, increasing student charges
(increasing tuition or decreasing insti-
tutional aid), and replacing other forms
of financial aid. The manner in which
the funding is distributed between these
areas is not, however, decided by the gov-
ernment. Instead, it is determined by the
interaction of choices made by students,
parents, universities, and various loan and
scholarship providers. Theory has helped
make predictions and guide the decisions
of state and federal governments. But the
unpredictability of preferences about col-
lege and the complexity of factors playing
into funding for college make it difficult to
know how exactly government funds are
distributed.
In this paper, I focus on the effects
of aid on family savings for college. I look
at one type of government funding for
college: merit-based scholarships given to
undergraduate students. I use merit schol-
arships administered by U.S. states because
eligibility for merit aid is determined by
residence, and states in various regions of
the country have adopted these programs.
As a result, outcomes can be compared
across states and over time, providing a
plausible identification strategy for the
treatment effect of government-funded
merit-based aid.
The size of the effect on savings is rel-
evant for several reasons. First, it is an in-
teresting behavioral question. Do parents
carefully optimize the amount they put
into college savings, changing their behav-
ior as they learn more about their child’s
scholarship possibilities? Or do they go by
some default idea of how much they should
save, or by a worst-case scenario savings
scheme? It can also be a question about
information and certainty about future
scholarships. Do parents know enough
about merit aid programs and feel that the
programs are stable and certain enough to
depend on?
My question also relates to the trade-
off between benefiting colleges and helping
families faced by any government funding
for education. If families reduce their sav-
ings for college, and are thus expecting
to pay less, this would counteract tuition
increases, especially because the reduction
in savings has already happened at the time
that colleges set their tuition. However, if
families do not reduce their savings due to
uncertainty about receiving the merit aid,
colleges are likely able to demand higher
charges from parents.
Another reason to study this question
relates to the common criticism that merit
aid programs benefit wealthier families.
Families that have college savings funds
are often more wealthy and can afford col-
lege more easily to begin with, so a finding
that aid reduces savings could confirm that
criticism. The extent to which merit aid
decreases savings would help clarify how
much the funding is helping to reduce the
burden on families who would have paid
for college regardless, as opposed to mak-
ing it affordable for more students.
The theory that merit aid would affect
savings is simple: when parents anticipate
lower future costs, they save less. It is pos-
sible that a parent would not change their
saving behavior because of uncertainty
about their child’s future qualification for
the scholarship; however, one reason to
believe that parents can reliably predict eli-
gibility for the scholarship is that the GPA/
SAT requirements for these scholarships
tend to be fairly low, so it may be clear
early on whether a student will qualify.
For example, for the Louisiana TOPS
scholarship, which covers full tuition, a
2.5 GPA and approximately a 1000/1600
SAT or 20 ACT score are required. A 2.5
GPA is achievable with half B’s and half
C’s, which is generally a very low standard
for public schools in the United States. A
1000 SAT score and a 20 ACT score cor-
respond to getting approximately half of
the questions correct. The Georgia HOPE
scholarship, which covers full tuition, re-
quires a 3.0 GPA (B average). New Mexico,
covering full tuition, has no requirements
aside from successfully graduating. (See
Table 1 for eligibility requirements of all
states.) However, it is still possible that
parents don’t change their savings deci-
sions due to behavioral explanations, lack
of information, or correct expectations.
For example, they could correctly expect
future tuition increases, lack of eligibil-
ity for need-based aid in these states, or
lack of availability of other scholarships.
1 These statistics come from National Center for Education Statistics’s National Postsecondary Student Aid Study.
2 These statistics come from the Education Data Initiative.
The Status of Merit Aid Programs
in the U.S.
State scholarships constitute a fairly large
portion of funding for U.S. college stu-
dents. In 2023, 23% of students received
state grants, as compared to 40% receiving
federal grants, and 28% receiving insti-
tutional grants. The average state grant
was $3,500, average federal grant was
$4,300, and average institutional grant
was $9,900.1 The average cost of in-state
tuition was $9,700 and out-of-state was
$27,000.2 Students received an average
of around $5,000 in scholarships, with
low-income students receiving more fed-
eral and state aid because much of the aid
is based on demonstrated need.
Between 1991 and 2006, 27 states
implemented merit aid programs, and five
of them have been terminated at some point
since. These programs give scholarships to
seniors graduating in the state who meet
certain merit criteria. The largest program
is the Georgia HOPE Scholarship, followed
by Tennessee HOPE and Louisiana TOPS.
The first one was the Arkansas Academic
Challenge Scholarship in 1991, Georgia
HOPE in 1993, 12 others starting in the
1990s, and eight starting in the 2000s.
The stated goals include reducing families’
and students’ financial burden, as well as
increasing the number of students who
attend college. Nine states have programs
classified as strong by Sjoquist and Win-
ters (2014), a classification that I borrow
in this paper, which identifies large par-
ticipation rates and large average awards.
I add Arkansas into the strong category as
they expanded in 2011, a year outside of
the range that Sjoquist and Winters stud-
ied. Each program has specific eligibility
requirements, but the requirement shared
“The theory that
merit aid would
affect savings
is simple: when
parents anticipate
lower future costs,
they save less.”
by all programs is being a resident of that
state at the time of graduation. Programs
differ slightly in their merit criteria, but
not drastically. They differ in funding
amounts, number of students affected, and
some have other miscellaneous rules. Ta-
ble 1 gives a summary of the characteristics
of each state’s program.
Literature Review
One of the most common criticisms of
merit aid programs is that they do not
increase college access because they tar-
get students who would attend college
regardless. Consequently, there are several
papers assessing average effects on college
enrollment
and
college
completion.
Various papers in the literature find con-
tradictory results for the average effect
on college enrollment, with more recent
literature generally finding smaller effects.
Cornwell, Mustard, and Sridar (2006)
estimated that between 1988 and 1997,
the Georgia HOPE Scholarship increased
college enrollment by 5.9%. This corre-
sponds to 15% of HOPE recipients being
people who would not have gone to a
college in Georgia otherwise. These per-
centages refer to increase in enrollment
in Georgia, so some of the effect may be
coming from students choosing to stay in
Georgia instead of going out of state, and
may not be reflecting enrollment of stu-
dents who would have not gone to college
otherwise. Dynarski (2004) estimated that
merit aid programs in Georgia, Arkansas,
Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi,
and South Carolina had an average effect
on in-state enrollment of 5%. Binder and
Genderton (2004) find an enrollment
effect of 6% in New Mexico.
A comprehensive analysis conducted
by Sjoquist and Winters (2014) uses data
from 25 states, and distinguishes between
weak and strong programs. It finds no
effects on college enrollment as well as
no effects on college completion. Most
recently, Chakabarti, Nober, and Klaauw
(2023) use the most granular data yet and
find no effect on propensity of attend-
ing college or of degree attainment, in
the general population as well as among
low-income and racial minority groups.
Scott-Clayton
and
Zafar
find that marginal recipients of the West
Virginia merit scholarship have higher
incomes, and are more likely to complete
graduate degrees. Despite finding no effect
on their enrollment in college, it appears
that the scholarship decreased the time it
took to complete the degree, and improved
life outcomes. Cornwell and Mustard
(2006) find that Georgia HOPE increased
the portion of high ability students choos-
ing to go to in-state colleges, and increased
selectivity in universities.
To the best of my knowledge, there
have been few attempts to examine
which sources of funding the scholarships
replace, and none have examined the effect
on savings. Chakabarti et al. (2023) find an
average effect of about -$1,000 on student
“One of the most common criticisms of merit
aid programs is that they do not increase
college access, as they target students who
would attend college regardless.”
loan originations. Long (2004) finds that
the Georgia HOPE Scholarship allowed
universities to increase student charges
by increasing tuition, increasing room
and board fees, and reducing institutional
scholarships.
There is also an array of past litera-
ture looking at other unintended effects of
statewide merit aid programs for college,
some of which counteract some of the goals
of the programs. For example, research-
ers have investigated if grade inflation
occurred in high schools, counteracting
the intended impact of improving student
achievement to qualify for the scholarship.
Sjoquist and Winters (2015) give evidence
that merit aid scholarships have diverted
students away from STEM majors, but
were unable to identify the mechanism
behind this trend. Cornwell and Mustard
(2007) showed evidence that car regis-
trations in richer counties increased as a
result of HOPE, suggesting that HOPE
was helping families be less burdened by
college costs, allowing them to spend on
other consumption goods.
Data
Close to half of states, varied in demo-
graphics and geography, give merit aid,
which presents the opportunity to use the

and pre-2001 data on college savings is

I compile two main data sets for my
analysis. The variables contained in each

The saved dummy dataset contains

529 Data
The College Savings Plan Network
(CSPN) works with state sponsored 529
programs to compile data on the total
amount of assets and number of accounts
in each 529 plan. Every 529 plan is admin-
istered by a state, and some states have
multiple 529 plans. The data is provided
on the CSPN website in separate PDF files
for each year/quarter. The New York Fed
compiles data on total assets, aggregating
over states’ multiple plans into a CSV file,
and this is what I use.
There are two types of 529 accounts:
prepaid and savings. About 95% of 529
assets are in savings plans, and the other 5%
are in prepaid plans. Prepaid plans allow
you to prepay tuition, locking in current
lower tuition rates for attending the par-
ticipating universities in the future. Typ-
ically, participating universities include
all in-state universities. If a child ends up
not going to a participating university,
funds can typically be transferred to other
uses. Prepaid plans do not pay interest, and
money must be used to pay tuition or fees.
These plans have declined over the years;
22 states used to offer prepaid plans, which
has decreased to nine in 2023.
The 529 savings plans, on the other
hand, allow account holders to choose
from a range of investment portfolio
options. Money in a savings plan may be
used to pay for room and board expenses in
addition to tuition and fees. Incentives for
putting college savings into a 529 savings
account include federal tax exemptions
and state tax benefits, described further in
Table 4. There are also disincentives from
putting savings that may not be used for
educational expenses into 529 accounts. If
money in either a savings or prepaid plan
is used for nonqualified expenses, it incurs
taxes and a 10% penalty.
The first issue with the CSPN data is
that it is not available for 1991–2000, the
years when some of the largest merit aid
programs started, so it is not possible to
use difference in difference methods. For
the years covered, 2001–present, there
is not a lot of variation or jumps in merit
aid. I searched merit aid data from 2001–
present for jumps (See Figure 1), and the
only large jump is Arkansas, which jumped
from about 1,000 students receiving $8,500
in their merit aid to about 35,000 students
receiving $3,000.
However, data directly from 529 pro-
grams on savings prior to 2000 likely exists.
Different states started their 529 programs
at different times, and many states started
these programs several years before a merit
aid program, so if this data were obtained it
might be possible to do a difference in dif-
ference analysis. Unfortunately, however,
the rapidity of the uptake of these 529 pro-
grams is influenced by many different fac-
tors in different states, and so it is unclear if
even this analysis would be possible.
The second issue for both panel and
cross-sectional analysis is that most pro-
grams accept out-of-state account openers.
As a result, the state of the 529 program
doesn’t correspond perfectly to merit aid
eligibility. There is still reason to believe
that this data may be fairly representative
of states’ residents for certain states. First-
ly, 6 states (New Jersey, South Dakota,
Florida, South Carolina, West Virginia,
Louisiana) do not allow out of state resi-
dents to enroll in their program. Second,
online sources like Morningstar, which
give advice regarding choosing a 529 plan,
typically suggest choosing the home state’s
529 program if that state provides tax ben-
efits (39 states), so it is possible that many
states’ residents primarily use their home
Even if a state’s residents use their
own 529 program, the issue remains that
the data could overestimate residents’
529 savings due to out-of-state account
holders. The 529 programs offer differing
investment portfolio options as well as dif-
fering fee structures, making some more
desirable, depending on people’s circum-
stances. One way to get around this issue
is to exclude the states that have non-neg-
ligible out of state investment. It seems as
though there are a handful of states which
attract the majority of out-of-state inves-
tors. Morningstar provides ratings of the
529 programs, and rates only two to three
of them as Gold level. Online advisory
sources typically recommend one of sev-
eral programs including Virginia, Maine,
Nevada, and Utah. In my analysis, I exclude

The CSPN data is desirable for

Addressing the issue of resident/non-resi-

specifications. The first set of regressions
uses the NFCS survey data with the binary

check that the regression specification
does not alter my results, and I report
the linear probability results as my main
results. There are various ways to measure
the largeness of a merit aid program, and
I use average merit aid per student and
recipients as a percentage of all undergrad-

for having a strong-classified merit aid
program as the input variables, because
savings decisions may not be sensitive to
fluctuations in the exact amounts, but may
instead respond to the general knowledge
that a strong merit aid program exists.

NFCS Data
Results for regression 1 are shown in

living in a state with more merit aid per
student on the probability of saving, in

less negative in regressions without the

education is an important factor and re-

Table 2 summarizes the results for
regressions 3–4. There are no statistically
significant coefficients on the merit aid
variables. However, the coefficient for
median income is negative in four out of
the six regressions, and the coefficient on
percent of college graduates is negative in

Because the NFCS data demonstrates that
people with more education and higher
income typically save more, I believe the
issue is that the assets in each state’s 529
account are not truly representative of the
college savings of parents in that state. It
is likely the case that there are a lot of out-
of-state 529 accounts.
Arkansas Program Expansion
In 2011, the Arkansas Academic Challenge
Scholarship expanded significantly, going
from funding around 1,000 incoming
students per year to 30,000. The scholar-
ship currently gives $1,000 the first year,
$4,000 the second the third, and $5,000
for the fourth year. Figure 3 shows that
Arkansas is the only state to have a big
jump in the amount of merit aid given out
per child during the time period for which
college savings data is available.
The trajectories of states’ savings
measures over time are shown in Figures
2 and 3. The red lines represent strong
program states, the black line is Arkansas,
and the gray are all others. There is a lot
of heterogeneity in the trends of states in
both 529 savings and percent of people
who save for college. For the percentage of
parents saving, neither merit aid states nor
non-merit aid states seem to have a com-
mon trend. It is unclear whether Arkansas’
trend is more like one or the other. In 529
assets, merit aid states have less overall
growth 2007–present than non-merit aid
states. Arkansas saw one of the smallest
growth rates throughout, with no visible
changes after 2011. The case of Arkansas
does not give any evidence that merit aid
affected college savings.
Conclusion
I primarily assessed whether merit aid
programs decreased the probability of
parents saving for college. The National
Financial Capability Survey provided the
most reliable source of publicly available
data on savings, and formed the core of my
analysis. While results from regressions
across different years had different results,
the majority had statistically significant
negative coefficients, and I conclude that
merit aid programs likely do decrease the
likelihood of parents saving by around
1–3%. $1,000 of merit aid per student
decreases the probability of saving by
2–7% and a 10% increase in merit aid
recipients decreases the probability of
saving by around 1%. While I control
for many demographic variables in my
regression, there are endogeneity concerns
with potential policy omitted variables.
My results tell us about the likeli-
hood that a parent will save, but it remains
unclear whether parents who do save
decrease the amount that they save when
they expect to benefit from a merit aid
program. I attempted to assess this us-
ing 529 data, but the results appear to be
unreliable. The fundamental issue with
529 data is that many people hold accounts
in states they do not reside in, and thus the
assets in a certain state’s 529 program does
not necessarily correspond to merit aid
availability. For further work, the Survey
of Consumer Finances confidential data
could be a good alternative way to assess
this question. ◆

An Interview with Dr. David N. Rapp
Comprehension and
Misinformation:
By Katie Fu
FEATURES
Dr. David N. Rapp, the Walter Dill Scott Professor of Education in the Depart-
ment of Psychology and the School of Education and Social Policy, focuses his
research on examining memory, language, and the cognitive mechanisms associ-
ated with learning. Dr. Rapp received his Masters in Psychology from New York
University (NYU), a PhD from Stony Brook University, and completed a post-
doc in Classics and Psychology at Tufts University. In the following interview,
Dr. Rapp discusses his research in cognitive psychology, its limitations, and the
importance of an interdisciplinary view.
[This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.]
Interviewer: Could you tell me about your research in graduate school
and what sparked your interest in cognitive psychology?
Professor Rapp: In graduate school, I was very interested in how people under-
stand stories, so I started doing work on reading comprehension and inferencing.
I focused on how people understand the themes of a text, how they take away
ideas from what the authors are trying to say, and how they add information to
what’s left out of the text. A lot of my early work was in memory and language in
people’s experiences with fictional stories. Then, I became interested in nonfic-
tion and focused on how we can help people not only become better readers with
different kinds of materials, but also better at discourse experiences that involve
conversation, such as watching videos and movies. While there are many people
studying what happens when what you know is wrong but a text tells you the
right thing, I became interested in the opposite: what happens when what you
know is correct, but the text tells you the wrong thing?
When I was going for a master’s at NYU, I worked with a researcher who studied
implicit memory tests, which focus on what people remember when they are not
aware that they are being tested. I thought it was really interesting that you could
design studies to understand how people are thinking and what they are remem-
bering. She was amazing and it really got me excited about this being a career
because the kind of research she’s doing contributes to theoretical understanding.
I could see the ways in which it could be applied and that got me excited about
cognition.
Interviewer: What are some valuable lessons you learned along your
journey in academia?
Professor Rapp: The most valuable lesson I learned was trying many things
because you don’t just want to find out what you are interested in, but also want
to figure out what you might not like. When I was an undergraduate, I worked in
a lab where I did research but did not like it, and I’m glad I did because it helped
me figure out that that’s not something I want to do as a career. It would have
been disappointing if, after four years of undergraduate, I went to graduate school
to do that work and only figured out I did not enjoy it after all that had happened.
So, you want to try many different things and get a lot of experience to see what
areas you will be interested in; maybe research is exactly what you want to do, but
you need to figure out what kind. Another lesson I learned was treating everyone
respectfully because it is not only important and something we should care about,
but also some of the best ideas have come from talking to people who aren’t even
in psychology. Talking to authors, cartoonists, students, families, teachers, and all
different kinds of people who have interesting ideas and intuitions about thinking
has been very informative for me to think about what could become projects that
help make the world better.
Interviewer: What insights has your research provided about the way
people learn from different types of media?
Professor Rapp: Yeah, there’s a lot. Our research has really helped demonstrate
that when people are exposed to inaccurate information, even if they know it’s
wrong, it could still impact their thoughts and behavior. For a while people
thought, well, it doesn’t matter if I already know what’s correct and someone tells
me the wrong thing. Our research actually shows it can be influential, which is
bad. Some of our research has also described ways in which you can help people
become more evaluative, which has been great in terms of talking with teachers
in schools to think about how you would build media literacy experiences. It’s
also been important in discussing with authors how to write material to help peo-
ple really understand the world or in talking to journalists trying to help people
change their minds when they have to refute an idea that’s already out there. I’m
really proud that the work has had theoretical implications and think that there’s
still a lot to do so there will be more applications.
Interviewer: What are the challenges of studying the processes involved
in understanding and how does this relate to the consequences of being
exposed to inaccurate information?
Professor Rapp: You can’t see the things that people are doing. They can tell you
what they think they’ve done and you can assess their comprehension, but to really
know what they are doing, you need to come up with sophisticated techniques or
use expensive technological tools like eye tracking. Getting a sense of both what
people do and where they do it is what my lab focuses on. Because we want to
understand how the mind works when you can’t see it, we have to ask a lot of
questions through introspection interviews. We use a lot of different methods,
such as surveys, experiments, and eye tracking, and hope they will all converge
on our understanding to help us get a better idea of where people see inaccurate
information, how they deal with it, and if there are ways for us to address these
experiences. We try to understand from multiple directions what’s going on and
maybe, from that, we can build better experiences for people.
Interviewer: How does the interdisciplinary view contribute to
our understanding of the mechanisms associated with reading
and comprehension?
Professor Rapp: There are psychologists who are studying this information, but
we also have to collaborate with linguistic researchers, educational researchers,
teachers, and journalists, because they’re all going to have a different set of expe-
riences and a different set of investments in understanding that space. And if we
can all come together and understand things from each other’s perspectives, that
will allow us to build better models and better accounts. I’m part of the Cognitive
Science program here at Northwestern and that’s really what they do at their
heart. People from across different units on campus come together, talk about
ideas, and share methodologies, because if only one person and one method is
used to study an issue, you’re not going to get as rich of an understanding as with
multiple people with multiple methods. By bringing computer scientists, anthro-
pologists, educational psychologists, learning scientists, and music theorists in
to discuss, then you will get a better chance since the folks who are having the
biggest impact tend to have multiple disciplines behind the work they’re doing.
Interviewer: What advice would you give to the undergraduate
students at Northwestern?
Professor Rapp: You should do research as an undergrad because Northwestern
has amazing resources and faculty so you can gain more experience. You might
find that it is not something you want to do, but you might also find that it is
something that’s really exciting. I only figured it out because I did a lot of research
in undergrad and in grad school that helped me figure out what I liked and what I
didn’t like. I’m still learning what kind of things I want to do, so doing research is
really important. I’m always excited to hear that there are so many Northwestern
undergraduates doing research but I also think that more of them should do it
because it is so important.
Abstract
When the United States (U.S.) entered World War II in 1942, 12,000 men refused
uniformed service through the draft. These conscientious objectors (C.O.s) were,
however, willing to perform alternative service. This project focuses on the Min-
nesota Starvation Experiment, which was conducted between 1944 and 1945 at the
University of Minnesota’s Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene and used C.O.s as
volunteer human subjects. In conducting the experiment, the doctors (led by Ancel
Keys) and subjects hoped to understand the biological and psychological effects
of starvation and illuminate best practices to nourish the starving populations of
Europe after World War II. In order to accomplish these aims, the 36 C.O.s under-
went a control period of three months, a systematic semistarvation of six months,
and a rehabilitation period of three months. This project integrates the Minnesota
Experiment with the social and political landscapes of an America engaged in total
war, bridging a gap between scholarship that discusses the experiment as a micro-
history and broader scholarships of World War II that mention it only in passing. It
does so by demonstrating and analyzing the parallels between specific groups in the
experiment and specific groups in the military, showing how the character of total
war became part of an experiment that was defined by its separation from combat
and military institutions. In demonstrating these parallels and contextualizing
the experiment in the climate of total war, the Minnesota Starvation Experiment
emerges as both extraordinary and unprecedented while also deeply ordinary in the
context of its own time.
The Protect of Total War and
the Minnesota Starvation
Experiment, 1944-1945
Faculty Adviser: Dr. Ken Alder
Department of History
by Aimee Flanigan
Introduction
Everyone agreed that the University of
Minnesota’s Laboratory of Physiological
Hygiene was an odd place. Due to the lab’s
unassuming entrance at Gate 27 of the
university’s football stadium, most people
passed by without a second glance. When
36 C.O.s reported to the lab in the winter
of 1944, most could not find the entrance
and walked the perimeter of the stadium,
or looked aimlessly around the parking lot,
before finding Gate 27. Gate 27 was deeply
significant, however, to the small group of
people who worked at, lived in, and visited
the Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene.
The lab comprised a maze of tunnels
located beneath the stadium. Alongside
these tunnels were offices, exam rooms,
and a staggering collection of laboratory
equipment.1 On Saturday afternoons, the
noise of fans enjoying the football game
above the researchers’ heads became an
ambient rumble. With its exposed pipes,
drab walls, summer and winter drafts,
and inconspicuous entrance, the lab was
certainly utilitarian.2 Suffice it to say
that decor was not a priority for the lab’s
founder, Dr. Ancel Benjamin Keys.
Keys led a team of physicians who
designed and conducted the Minnesota
Starvation Experiment. The 36 men who
arrived in 1944 were human subjects, all
of them draft-age men who had declared
themselves to be C.O.s and had agreed to
an alternative form of wartime service:
systematic starvation in the Laboratory of
Physiological Hygiene at the University of
Minnesota. The C.O.s volunteered for the
chance to be of service and to tangibly help
others. The experiment, sponsored by the
1 Henry Blackburn, If It Isn’t Fun: A Memior from a Different Sort of Medical Life (Wordpress, 2000), https://henryblackburn.
wordpress.com/stories/professional-memoirs/if-it-isnt-fun-volume-i/.
2 “Medicine: The Fat of the Land,” Time, January 13, 1961,
https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,828721,00.html.
3 “Arsenal of Democracy,” Fireside Chat, https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/node/209416.
U.S. government, mimicked the meager
diets starving Europeans suffered as a
result of World War II. To study how they
could most effectively be rehabilitated,
the 36 C.O.s were starved together. They
were then divided into four groups of nine
and revived by different diets of proteins
and vitamins.
Scholars have portrayed the Minne-
sota Starvation Experiment as an extraor-
dinary experiment. Indeed it was, insofar
as nothing quite like it has been attempted
before or since. Perhaps for this very reason,
scholars have largely neglected to place the
Minnesota Starvation Experiment within
the broader social and cultural landscape
of wartime America. Rather, scholars have
either touched on the experiment as a piece
of evidence or have examined it in isola-
tion. This thesis bridges this gap, integrat-
ing the Minnesota Starvation Experiment
into the American story of World War II.
In illustrating how the experiment took on
the character of total war, this thesis ana-
lyzes parallels between the experiment and
wartime America to emphasize the degree
to which total war permeated American
society.
Central to the understanding of the
project of total war is World War II’s
consumption of American society. When
President Roosevelt announced U.S. entry
into the war on Dec. 9, 1941, he made it
clear to the American public that “we
are now in this war… Every single man,
woman, and child is a partner in the most
tremendous undertaking of our Ameri-
can history.”3 World War II was an era of
collective commitment and absolutes that
effectively rallied the country. Resources
and factories were used to manufacture
guns, trucks, tanks, and aircraft engines
rather than Fords, Cadillacs, and Chevro-
lets.4 Author Mark P. Parillo wrote that
“No war before or since touched so many
Americans and so many aspects and facets
of their lives.”5 From Pearl Harbor until
Victory in Europe Day, Americans ded-
icated themselves, their time, and their
money to the war effort.
The 11,996 men who declared them-
selves C.O.s stood out from this intense
and collective mobilization: they were
the men who refused noncombatant,
uniformed military roles but were willing
to contribute to the country’s war effort
through alternative forms of service. This
group, of which the Minnesota men were
a part, made up the Civilian Public Service
(CPS).6 In 1942, the CPS allowed these
C.O.s to participate as human subjects in a
variety of government-sponsored medical
experiments that reflected the conditions
soldiers might have faced in combat.
Although the Minnesota Starvation
Experiment was part of a broader net-
work of human medical experiments that
used C.O.s as human subjects, it stood
out from these other ventures. The Star-
vation Experiment’s duration—one year
living at the Laboratory of Physiological
Hygiene—was much longer than other
experiments in which C.O.s participated.
Furthermore, every day of the experi-
ment required significant personal effort
on the part of its human subjects. Indeed,
while many of the other experiments that
utilized C.O.s were strictly biological, the
Starvation Experiment depended not only
on the C.O.s’ willingness to sacrifice their

fense, March 27, 2020, https://www.defense.gov/News/Feature-Stories/story/article/2128446/during-wwii-industries-transi-
tioned-from- peacetime-to-wartime-production/.
5 Mark P. Parillo, We Were in the Big One (Wilmington, Del: SR Books, 2002), 6.
6 Tucker, The Great Starvation Experiment, 42.
bodies but also on their mental and emo-
tional willingness to dedicate themselves
to the experiment. They would be required
to take draining tests of intelligence, to
honestly report private information such
as their dreams and psychological changes
to the experiment’s doctors, and to remain
on the strict experimental diet as those
around them continued eating as normal.
The men would be faced with countless
choices every day that would test their
self-sacrifice and dedication to the exper-
iment. Because of this dynamic, the C.O.s
became active participants, partners, and
drivers of the Starvation Experiment.
They continuously committed themselves
to the experiment and to each other in a
way that C.O.s engaged in other medical
experiments did not.
As this thesis will show, the experi-
ment partook of the character of Amer-
ican wartime. Its execution hinged upon
the lead doctors’ ambitious goals and
expansive moral license during a period
of total warfare and human suffering.
The experiment likewise depended on
the willingness of the C.O.s to voluntarily
subject themselves to intense hardship and
medical risk for a prolonged period of time
to serve a larger humanitarian purpose.
Finally, the risks the C.O.s took captured
the public’s attention in ways that can only
be understood in light of contemporary
reports from Europe, where a five-year
war
against
fascism
had
wrought
unheard-of devastation.
This thesis argues that the Starva-
tion Experiment, though unique in many
aspects, also contained deep parallels that
connected it to the experience of American
military leadership and goals, which drafted
all able-bodied young men as combatants
and enlisted the entire nation at home in
the project of total war. These parallels
include the mixes of voluntarism and com-
pulsion, war-fighting and peace-planning,
and individual initiative and group cohe-
sion that existed in the larger experience of
World War II and in the microcosm of the
Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene and
the Starvation Experiment.
The Doctors and the
Direction of the Experiment
The condition of total war influenced the
events of the Minnesota Starvation Exper-
iment in that, throughout the experiment,
the doctors’ actions, priorities, and con-
cerns mirrored those of American military
officers engaged in World War II. Like
their officer counterparts, those involved
in the experiment established and operated
in an environment with a strict hierarchy,
with Ancel Keys at the top, followed by
the rest of his doctors, staff, and finally,
the C.O.s. Similarly to officers, Keys and
his team had a complicated and dynamic
relationship with the men beneath them in
this hierarchy. Their relationship mirrored
that between officers and the enlisted men
under them, both of which were at times
characterized by tension and a constant
separation of the two groups. The doctors
noticed that the subjects had, over time,
developed a “tremendous in-group” iden-
tity that excluded the doctors and staff.7
Similarly, when enlisted men bonded with

loneliest job in the world.”9
Furthermore, the doctors of the Star-
vation Experiment were concerned with
the morale of the C.O.s, reflecting similar
battlefield concerns of those commanding
enlisted men. In 1943, the Special Search
Division published its first issue of What
the Soldier Thinks, which compiled the
results of numerous surveys of soldiers
conducted between 1942 and 1943. The
motivation behind the project, according to
the Special Search Division, was “to probe
underlying factors affecting morale” as the
Army expanded with America’s entry into
the War and the ensuing Draft.10 Clearly,
the military considered the morale of its
soldiers important and devoted resources
to assessing it. Similarly, in the Laboratory
of Physiological Hygiene, Keys was so con-
cerned about morale that he took action:
On May 26, he organized a “relief meal.”
The men chose the foods they wanted for
this one glorious break from the semistar-
vation diet. Though Keys restricted the
quantity of each food in order to maintain
the experiment’s integrity, the relief meal
was still by far the most food the C.O.s had
seen since the start of the experiment.11 The
strategy was effective, and the C.O.s’ mood
noticeably improved as the men enjoyed
the meal. Reluctant to conclude the meal
and return to semistarvation, many of the
men consumed the peel of an orange that
had been part of it. Keys, who had metic-
ulously measured and recorded the specific
caloric content of each food item in the
meal, was furious when he found out this
unmeasured consumption of calories he
had not predicted.12
Finally, Keys and his team had to
adapt to changing and unforeseen cir-
cumstances to keep the experiment run-
ning and on schedule, just like officers in
the military. As the doctors embarked on
their unprecedented experiment, various
conditions forced them, over time, to alter
their conception of the experiment and its
purpose, the ways in which they related
to the subjects and interacted with them,
and their own understanding of nutrition’s
effects on the human body. While it was
not easy to overcome the difficulties that
arose beneath the university’s football sta-
dium between 1944 and 1945, the doctors
ultimately managed to bring the experi-
ment to completion in accordance with
their original schedule.
The Conscientious Objectors
and the Experience of
the Experiment
As World War II and the feeling of total
war
reverberated
through
American
society, everyone—even C.O.s—played a
part. As a result, aspects of the Starvation

and individual sacrifices of the battlefield.
The C.O.s of the Starvation Experiment
suffered in their bodies, just like com-

Both groups shared analogous motivations
for the larger purpose of their mission,
whether it involved combat or human

battling starvation. Both groups experi-

comradeship lingered in both the subjects’
and soldiers’ recollections of their wartime

efforts.”17 The C.O.s’ understanding of the
experiment and its legacies of suffering and
comradeship paralleled that of American
soldiers. Despite their differing stances on
war and pacifism, the wartime experiences
of both groups were similar in ways that
left a lasting impression on the participants.

drafted soldiers’ experiences, despite their
different views of war, showed how both

Conclusion
With the conclusion of the Starva-
tion Experiment on Oct. 20, 1945, the
Minneapolis C.O.s spread out across the
country and entered an array of careers.
When 19 of the men gathered in 1998,
all of them had college degrees, and six
had PhDs. Among the group, six were
college professors, four were teachers,
and two were ministers. There was also
an architect, a lawyer, an engineer, and a
social worker.18
The former subjects all carried
reminders of the experiment with them
long after they left the Laboratory of Phys-
iological Hygiene. Even 50 years later, the
men perfectly recalled their exact body
weights throughout the three phases of
the Minnesota Experiment. Their weights
had dictated their lives for almost a year,
and they never forgot them. Many were
staunchly against food waste, insisting that
their children and grandchildren finish
every bite on their plates.19 Some subjects
also fixated on providing others with the
plenty they had been deprived of during
the experiment. Subject Lester Glick, for
example, developed an obsession with
cinnamon rolls during the experiment that
never quite went away. Every Sunday for 20
years, he baked around 400 cinnamon rolls
and distributed them to his congregation.20
Finally, although some men fell
out of touch, others met lifelong friends
through
the
Starvation
Experiment.
Towards the end of their lives, many of the
C.O.s reconnected through reunions and
personal outreach. When researchers Leah
Kalm and Richard Semba interviewed 18
of the men in 2005 as part of an oral history
for the Library of Congress, the records of
which form an important source base for
this project, the former subjects referred to
one another as friends. Their excitement at
hearing which C.O. was being interviewed
next is palpable in the recordings of their
conversations. They often asked Kalm and
Semba to pass on messages or greetings to
the man next on the researchers’ list. In
2005, the C.O.s all felt that the experiment
was a major life event. They unanimously
agreed that they thought the Starvation
Experiment was ethical and that they
would volunteer again.21
As for Keys and his team, they
worked tirelessly to publish The Biology
of Human Starvation in 1950. The work
went on to deeply impact science, specif-
ically in the sciences of nutrition and eat-
ing disorders. The Starvation Experiment
remains the only exploration of the biolog-
ical and psychological effects of prolonged
semistarvation, making it part of the
bedrock of these fields. The experiment
proved that the psychological symptoms of
starvation are so significant that they are
often impossible to distinguish from the
symptoms of the eating disorder itself. As
a result, doctors learned to treat patients
for starvation before treating the eating
disorder.22

and Review of the Minnesota Study of Human Starvation and its Relevance to Eating Disorders,” Archives of Psychology 2, no. 3
(March 2018): 2, http://www.archivesofpsychology.org.
23 Zohar Lederman and Teck Chuan Voo, “The Minnesota Starvation Experiment and Force Feeding of Prisoners—Relying
on Unethical Research to Justify the Unjustifiable,” Journal of Bioethical Inquiry 18, no. 3 (2021): 409, https://doi.org/10.1007/
24 In the Willowbrook Experiments, doctors injected mentally ill children at the Willowbrook State School with live hepatitis in
order to develop a vaccine. The children’s parents gave permission for their children to participate, usually because it guaranteed a
child’s acceptance into the overcrowded school.
Interestingly, the field of bioethics has
also been notably silent on the experiment,
suggesting an area for further exploration
and analysis. Bioethicists Zohar Lederman
and Teck Chuan Voo note that “the [Min-
nesota Starvation Experiment] seemingly
has no mention in the bioethics litera-
ture.”23 Indeed, as bioethics has shifted to an
explicit condemnation of unethical human
experiments, especially after World War
II, the Minnesota Starvation Experiment
seems to have largely been left out of such
discussions. Perhaps this is because the
experiment prompts scholars to grapple
with complex issues such as volunteerism,
social and group pressure and consent, and
conflict between the principles of benefi-
cence and individual autonomy.
The Starvation Experiment is also
challenging in its subversion of the
villain-victim narrative bioethics often
uses to discuss human experimentation,
in which doctors and researchers uneth-
ically impose their will and risky science
on a vulnerable population. This is not to
say that the villain-victim narrative does
not have its place in bioethics and history
more generally—cases like the Nazi and
Japanese experiments on prisoners of war
during World War II, the Tuskegee Syph-
ilis Experiment, and the Willowbrook
Experiments can and should be analyzed
via this binary.24 This view does not—and
never has—fit the Minnesota Starvation
Experiment, however. The C.O.s who
Fi
F
faced the challenges of semistarvation held
complicated and changing relationships
with the laboratory’s doctors and staff, but
ultimately shared their dedication to the
experiment. In many ways, they actively
cultivated a partnership with one another.
The context of the experiment within
a time of total war makes these tensions
even more nuanced. For example, the Star-
vation Experiment exemplified changes
to the bioethical principle of beneficence,
defined as the obligation of a physician to
act for the benefit of the patient. In know-
ingly placing the C.O.s of the Starvation
Experiment in such physical, mental, and
emotional distress, the doctors threatened
to contravene this principle. For a nation
horrified by Nazi atrocities and mobilized
to fight a just war, everyone, including the
medical establishment, doctors, and C.O.s,
was expected to contribute to an unprec-
edented degree. Military historian and
professor Hew Strachan wrote that World
War II was a period in which “the ends
justified the means.”25 In such a context,
the Minnesota Starvation Experiment be-
came necessary, regardless of the sacrifice
of beneficence it required. The difficult
choices made by the C.O.s of the Starvation
Experiment—to declare their conscientious
objection, participate in the experiment,
and to repeatedly commit to it—reflected
the difficult choices made by many of their
enlisted peers and even other Americans,
all of whom took various actions and made
25 Hew Strachan, “Essay and Reflection: On Total War and Modern War,” The International History Review 22, no. 2 (June,
2000): 359, http://www.jstor.org/stable/40108371.
life choices within the unique context of a
total war environment. They engaged in
and endured circumstances that may not
have been permissible or accepted in times
of peace and stability.
The most famous human experi-
ments and those most readily discussed by
the field of bioethics lack the nuance that
is foundational to the Minnesota Experi-
ment. For a field like bioethics, which has
been shaped so heavily and reactively by
atrocities and makes lessons out of cau-
tionary tales, the Starvation Experiment
hovers uncomfortably in the gray area.
This analysis shows that, while the
Starvation Experiment was an endeavor
defined by its use of C.O.s and its separa-
tion from military institutions and combat,
it was a part of the U.S. war machine all
the same. Somewhat ironically, the group
of men who declared themselves C.O.s,
entered the CPS, and volunteered for the
Starvation Experiment in the end partici-
pated in wartime activities that deeply par-
alleled that of their enlisted counterparts.
The Starvation Experiment shows how a
particular group of Americans, set apart by
their pacifist principles, engaged with the
war effort and, in their own way, sacrificed
for the project of total war. Just like so many
stories that emerge from war, the story
of the Minnesota Starvation Experiment
is one that is intrinsically human, full of
difficult sacrifices, and situated in its own
history and complexities. ◆

Palmy Lamsam’s Journey
from Figure Skating
to Research
From Blades to
Breakthroughs:
By Evan Hostetler
FEATURES
Seven-year-old Thita “Palmy” Lamsam rushes past the bustling shops of the
Imperial World Samrong in February of 2007, her excitement growing with each
hurried step towards the ice rink that sat in the middle of hustling crowds. With
a gift for her friend Vanessa wrapped tightly in her hands, Palmy was ready to do
something she had never done before, despite her longing to do so: skate. Influ-
enced by Disney movies, like the Ice Princess, that showed the beauty and artistry
of the sport, Palmy had been waiting for the chance to experience it herself, and
she was finally able to at Vanessa’s birthday party. After strapping on her skates
and taking her first few wobbly and unsteady strides, Palmy fell in love with the
magical feeling of being on the ice. The afternoon passed in a blur of youthful joy
and revelry, and that day, a little girl went home with a newfound passion.
From that moment on, Palmy was hooked on the sport of figure skating and
would find any opportunity to explore it. She would beg her parents to take her
to the rink on the weekends, and if they wouldn’t, she would create her own rink
at home, coating her wooden floors with baby powder and “skating” countless
hours away with her older sister, Rada. Whether it was her persistent pleading or
multiple fiascos with baby powder, her parents eventually relented and enrolled
her in recreational skating lessons on the weekends. With each glide, spin, and
stumble, Palmy’s talent for the sport deepened quite quickly, and it was clear she
was meant to shine on stages bigger and brighter than her living room rink.
As Palmy grew in age, her commitment and passion to the sport grew as well.
When she turned eight years old, her recreational coach pushed her to find other
coaches that could foster and grow her talent even more, and she and her parents
did just that. As she transitioned to her new coaches, she went from skating one
or two times a week to three or four times a week.
When she turned nine a year later, her schedule changed again, shifting to five or
six practices a week for two hours each day. Eventually, when Palmy reached her
peak at about 15 years old, she was practicing six days a week for three hours on
the ice, and an additional two hours were spent doing some sort of conditioning
(working out at the gym with a personal trainer, taking a dance class, etc.).
This hard work and busy schedule would eventually pay off. Due to her confi-
dence on the ice and immense artistry, Palmy was able to win the Thai National
Championship five times. Each time she was able to skate at these championships,
Palmy was grateful—grateful that she was skating on home ice, grateful that her
body still allowed her to skate (considering she won her last Championship at 20
years old), and grateful she got to compete in the sport she loved so dearly.
Despite her love for the sport, Palmy still yearned to learn about the world
around her—not just the best technique to do a double axel or the proper posi-
tioning needed to do a flying camel spin. She wanted to understand the reason
behind successful coach and skater relationships, as well as the physics behind a
double axel or flying camel spin.
To Palmy, it became perfectly clear that she would have to make certain sac-
rifices in order to strike a balance between her life on the ice and her life in
the classroom. She couldn’t complete the International Baccalaureate Diploma
at her high school because she consistently missed class for skating competi-
tions, so she had to settle for a regular high school diploma. When she was
applying to colleges, despite the myriad of opportunities that called out to her
at more rigorous institutions, she compromised by attending Michigan State
University. This was so she could balance the increased academic workload
that came with being a college student with her meticulous skating schedule,
especially considering the fact that MSU offered strong student athlete support.
One day, Palmy realized that if she wanted to progress any further in skating,
she would have to choose between her skating or academic career. Therefore,
she decided that she would take a gap year from her studies, spending all 365
days as a professional athlete. She wanted to understand what her life would be
like if she treated figure skating as her full time job in an attempt to discover if
it should be the endeavor she dedicated the rest of her life to.
During this gap year, she increased her training regimen ten fold and pushed
her body to its limits. Every day was a test of endurance, discipline, and
passion—early mornings at the rink, grueling conditioning sessions, and hours
spent perfecting the smallest details of her routines. Yet, as the months passed,
Palmy began to reflect on what truly fulfilled her, and she realized it was not a
life focused solely on skating. Palmy missed the intellectual challenges she had
put on hold and found herself looking for some academic outlet.
Around this time, Palmy received a letter from Northwestern University’s
Marriage and Family Therapy Program. From her time at Michigan State, she
had developed a deep interest in psychology, particularly in the social threads
that connect the millions of relationships humans form each day. When she
discovered the therapy program at Northwestern, she thought it would be
the perfect outlet to continue her academic studies, and sure enough, she was
accepted! That day, Palmy decided that she would no longer sacrifice her future
in academics for a future in figure skating; she would no longer settle when it
came to the pursuit of her interest in psychology. In February 2023, she retired
from the sport of figure skating entirely, ready to take advantage of the plethora
of opportunities Northwestern had to offer.
Although she no longer had to dedicate hours and hours to her jam-packed figure
skating schedule, Palmy still found many ways to keep busy, fitting right in with
the hustle and bustle of Northwestern’s campus. She has become quite involved
with the Thai Student Association and has given back to the community through
multiple service organizations. She is connected with Professors like Claudia
Haase, helping out in her research lab and assistant teaching for her classes.
However, her involvement as a Student Therapist at Northwestern’s Family
Institute has played a major role in defining her experience at Northwestern, as
it helped her discover her own special research topic. In this position, she has
had the opportunity to talk to families whose loved ones have been incarcerated,
and she has seen the first hand effect this has had, not just on their relationships,
but on their mentality as well. Right now, there is very little psychological
research that focuses on how to help families in this position. Therefore, she has
decided to write a research paper on the psychological and emotional impact of
incarceration on relationship dynamics, with a particular focus on how people in
relationships navigate the challenges of separation and what kinds of treatment
or support might help them do so. Right now, she is in the literature review
stage, trying to understand all the current research that has already been done on
the subject.
Although Palmy doesn’t compete on the ice anymore, the characteristics she
developed as a figure skater continue to shape her approach to research. For
one, she uses the time management skills she developed while balancing her
hectic life as a figure skater. Palmy is involved in every corner of Northwestern’s
campus, yet, she is able to perfectly manage and complete all of her activities,
largely due to this experience. Further, she developed a fine-tuned attention to
detail from years of perfecting every jump, spin, and glide—she uses this skill
everyday in her research. Whether she’s analyzing data, reviewing psychological
theories, or fine-tuning her writing, Palmy approaches each task with the same
precision she once applied to her routines, ensuring that every detail is up to her
standards. Finally, her ability to perform and exceed under pressure has served
her immensely, especially as a student at Northwestern. Just as she once thrived
under the scrutiny of judges and the intensity of competition, Palmy now excels
in high-stakes academic settings—whether it’s presenting her research, engaging
in deep, trauma-heavy therapy sessions, or meeting tight deadlines.
Despite the fact that, most days, you’ll find Palmy in an academic or clinical
setting, remnants of the former skater within her are expressed a couple times
a week at the local ice rink. There, she lets her inner artist flourish, using the
skills and tricks developed over the past 18 years of her life. Moreover, Palmy
has now added another, instructional aspect to this passion of hers, creating
social media videos to share her knowledge and experience when it comes to
figure skating.
When that little, seven-year-old girl stepped on the ice for the first time at her
friend’s birthday party, she had no idea she would climb the ranks and become
one of the best figure skaters in Thailand. Moreover, she probably didn’t expect
to transition from the sport all together, becoming a researcher at one of the
best institutions in the world. Her journey from a young girl mesmerized by
the magic of skating to a dedicated researcher at Northwestern University is
a testament to her resilience, adaptability, and passion for learning. Though
her skates may be retired, her drive for excellence remains as strong as ever,
propelling her forward as she carves a new path—one that is just as meaningful
and rewarding as the one she left behind.
Abstract
While global economic growth rises, international poverty also continues to
increase. From 2022-2023, the population living below the international poverty
line increased by 4%, now estimated at 31.4% of the global population. Indeed,
poverty is multidimensional, and the multilateral allocation of resources is contin-
uously reevaluated at the household-level. Founded around this guiding principle,
alongside modern development theory on poverty traps (Duflo’s “poor but neo-
classical”), it is hypothesized that the regular occurrence of economic shocks—e.g.
natural disasters, global pandemics, and political, ethnic, and religious conflicts—
keep poor households poor by forcing such households to respond by reducing
caloric intake, limiting cognitive development and long-term health. We find that
short- and long-term effects differ with respect to these outcomes. In particular,
significant short-term decreases in nutritional status are found, prominently guided
by age-effects, as well as significantly lower assessed cognitive ability. While some
long-term differences are reported with regard to physical activities of daily life,
more studies must be done in this area to confirm relevance and results.

bounce back, shocks may have significant
impacts on short- and long-term out-
comes. Moreover, economic shocks have
the ability to affect household welfare,

perhaps exemplified by the COVID-19
pandemic, recent hyperinflation, and the
globally
disproportionate
distribution
of natural disasters.1 With comprehen-

Within the context of protecting
and supporting human capital formation
in poor populations, we consider the
consequences of early childhood shocks
in Ghana. Rapid biological and cognitive
growth occurs during early childhood and
adolescence; thus, deficiencies in nutri-

may have long-lasting consequences on
cognitive development and educational
attainment. Even more so, the reallocation
of household resources necessitated by
unanticipated economic shocks may have
consequences on investments in nutrition,
health care, or education. This paper focuses
on the effect of early childhood shocks on
short- and long-term physical health and
youth cognitive development. It is moti-
vated by the limited economic evidence we
have about early childhood circumstances
on both short- and long-term outcomes,

Since the Ghana cluster is a relatively
novel dataset which comprehensively

producing estimations with less bias. The

Ghana has made significant progress in
recent years to invest in economic and pol-

in support of those efforts supports ongo-

for further research.

Literature Review
Applied Models: Difference-in-Difference
Approach
Studies examining the impacts of eco-
nomic shocks vary widely in the shock
types and outcomes measured. One of
the most frequently applied econometric
approaches exploits the occurrence of a
national shock via natural experiment
(i.e. natural disaster, war), often offering
a large sample size, fixed time effects, and
stronger reliance on the exogeneity of
a shock.
Cas et al. (2014) take the 2004 Indian
Ocean tsunami as a framework for exploit-
ing an unanticipated shock: parental death
in Indonesian households.11 Their specifi-
cation measures the wellbeing of the same
individuals before and after the tsunami,
via child fixed effects, to estimate the effect
of parental death on children’s wellbeing.
Differences are averaged between children
who lost one or both parents and children
whose parents both survived. Cas et al.
find significant differences in wellbeing
due to the shock, with variation between

In general, short-term impacts are less
pronounced than long-term impacts for
children who lost one or both parents.
Frankenberg and Thomas (2017)
examine early life shocks on human capital
formation through the lenses of in-utero
shocks, prenatal nutrition, national finan-
cial shocks, and natural disasters.12 Cov-
ering an array of shock types, their work
demonstrates the complexity in isolating
shock effects on human capital develop-
ment and wellbeing in both short- and
long-run analyses and across shock types.
Nonetheless, following a similar econo-
metric DiD specification using child fixed
effects, Frankenberg and Thomas isolate
the effects of the 1998 financial crisis and
the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. Franken-
berg and Thomas conclude that house-
holds respond to shocks multilaterally to
mitigate shock effects on younger genera-
tions; households choose either to expend
all resources possible in order to avoid
falling into poverty traps or to rationally
reallocate resources on a micro-level to
best recover from shocks. As we examine
the effects of early childhood shocks in
Ghana, we consider cross-sectional panel
data to similarly achieve child fixed effects
and to account for differences in short- and
long-term outcomes.

Theoretical Foundations
The literature discusses two distinct
interpretations of poverty. The first is that
those in poverty are exactly like those who
are not: the poor have the same abilities
and capacities for rational decision-making
as the nonpoor—their position within
cyclical poverty is attributed to external
adversities. The second is that, while the
poor and nonpoor may face similar objec-
tive functions, poverty changes the set of
options and constraints that individuals
face, affecting individual behavior.18 Mod-
ern development economics largely rests
on the second view, reframing empirical
structures to account for market ineffi-
ciencies in a neoclassical environment.
Although we proceed with this rel-
atively novel paradigm, it is important to
situate contemporary theory within its
foundations, first examining poverty as
singularly determined by external adver-
sities. In this case, the decision-making
agent is considered “poor but rational,”

19 UNICEF, “Poor Diets Damaging Children’s Health Worldwide,” 2019.

a term coined by Ted Schultz with the
publication of Transforming Traditional
Agriculture (1975), and developed con-
currently with Sir Arthur Lewis’ work on
surplus labor market transfers.19 In the
mid-20th century, it was widely accepted
that the marginal product of labor in agri-
culture was zero such that labor transfers
between agricultural and industrial sectors
would not impact agricultural production
in developing countries. Prior—distinctly
biased—beliefs also held that markets in
developing countries did not respond to
economic incentives.20 Schultz’s central
thesis argued against these beliefs—the
extreme poor are “efficient but poor”—
efficient in their rational decision-making
and poor due to “friction-driven” market
conditions. In other words, the poor ratio-
nally optimize resources, even when facing
extreme constraints; the phenomenon of
cyclical poverty must then be attributed to
the inequity and inefficiency of the market,
not of the individual. As clarified by Duflo
(2006), “efficient but poor” describes the
fact that “the poor certainly have bad lives,
but there is nothing special about them;
they just do the best they can under the
difficult circumstances in which life has
placed them and their fields are as produc-
tive as possible—they just cannot be very
productive.”21
As empirical evidence has grown
in the field, particularly through natural
experiments and RCTs, recent reevalua-
tion of the “poor but rational” theory fails
to adequately account for observations
of inefficient resource allocation among
the extreme poor, making way for a sec-
ond view of poverty. This second view
suggests that while the poor face similar
objective functions to the nonpoor, pov-
erty changes the set of constraints that
individuals face. Such constraints refer
to behavioral, self-reinforcing choices
which are encountered as a result of cir-
cumstances. For example, a poor house-
hold may allocate resources counter to
rational expectations, resulting in a market
failure: “poor but neoclassical (but not
necessarily efficient)” as coined by Duflo
(2006).22 Further, facing extreme scarcity
on a daily basis, a household must make
subsistence-oriented decisions that serve
present and near-future needs while lim-
iting investment in future payoffs as we
might expect. Hence, this view of poverty
is considered “scarcity-driven.”23
Furthermore, there exists a broad
range
of
empirical
and
theoretical
evidence that links household shocks to
poverty traps.24 Take, for instance, the
nutrition-wage hypothesis: a household
with very low income will struggle to
obtain adequate nutrition, and in turn, be

Poverty is multidimensional, and

Stemming from Schultz’s “poor but ratio-

reallocate resources following an economic
shock diluting long-term consequences;
however, it would perhaps be ignorant
to overlook alternate internal constraints
at play. We proceed with such theoretical
foundations at the forefront of the empiri-
cal agenda to follow.

Frankenberg and Thomas (2018) identifies

resource allocation in anticipation or
response to shocks are not generalizable
as households may differ significantly and
multilaterally; (iii) the short- and long-run

For short- and long-run effects, we
examine physical metrics, activities of dai-
ly living, and health in the last two weeks.
We construct a weight-for-height mea-
sure, setting a lower-bound of minimum
premature weight and height32 to account
for measurement error. Since physical
health outcomes are considered in Period
2, we focus on activities of daily living in

physical wellbeing. In particular, two

had to carry a heavy load (e.g. size 34 Bucket
of water) without any help for 20 meters,
could he/she do it?, and (2) If [Name] had to
bathe him/herself without any help, could he/
