blocks: The Impact of COVID-19 Cognitive and Emotional Experiences on Increases in Anxiety
and Depression in Youth
Abigail O. Ayemoba1, Katie L. Burkhouse, Ph.D1.2.
1University of Illinois Chicago, Department of Psychology, Chicago IL 60607
2University of Illinois Chicago, Department of Psychiatry, Chicago IL 60612
email: aayemo2@uic.edu *PI: kburkho@uic.edu
The COVID-19 pandemic poses a significant and unique stressor to the mental health of families and children.
Recent studies reveal that adolescents are exhibiting higher levels of depression and anxiety than ever before.
However, little is known about how the COVID-19 pandemic produces these effects on youth. In the current study, we
examined the potential role of cognitive difficulties and emotional experiences during the COVID-19 pandemic as
predictors of increased depression and anxiety in youth. We predicted that increased cognitive (e.g., forgetfulness,
disorganization) and emotional (e.g., worry, stress) experiences during COVID-19 would be associated with increases
in anxiety and depressive symptoms pre-to-peri pandemic among children and adolescents. Participants of 43
children and adolescents participated in an ongoing longitudinal study of the intergenerational transmission of
depression. To assess cognitive and emotional experiences during COVID-19, youth completed the COVID-19
Symptom & Psychological Experience Questionnaire (CASPE). To assess change in depression and anxiety, youth
completed the Centers for Epidemiological Studies-Depression (CESD) and the Screen for Child Anxiety Related
Disorders (SCARED) pre- and peri-pandemic, respectively. Linear regression analyses revealed that greater
cognitive experiences (e.g., difficulty concentrating) during COVID-19 predicted increases in anxiety symptoms in
youth (t= 2.135, p= .039) pre-to-peri pandemic. These findings were maintained when adjusting for child sex and
gender. COVID-19 emotional experiences were not significantly associated with increased anxiety or depression
among youth. Results from this study suggest that cognitive experiences during COVID-19 may be one route through
which the pandemic increases symptoms of anxiety in children and adolescents.

volumes.label: Personality Traits and the Narration of Spiritual Experiences among African American and White Adults in Late Midlife
volumes.nurj_title: Personality Traits and the Narration of Spiritual Experiences among African American and White Adults in Late Midlife

blocks: Personality Traits and the Narration of Spiritual Experiences among African American
and White Adults in Late Midlife
Ahmadu Simpson
Department of Psychology, Northwestern University
PSYCH 398: Senior Thesis Seminar
Dr. Dan McAdams
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
Abstract
For over a hundred years, psychologists have sought to understand the role of spirituality
in human behavior and experience, and how it might relate to features of personality. This study
considered personal narration of spiritual experience and how it relates to the personality traits of
Openness to Experience, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism.
Over 400 narrative accounts of spiritual experiences given by mid-life adults (approximately half
of whom were white and half African American) were analyzed and coded for themes of (1)
Narrator Agency (NA), which tracks how participants describe their own efficacy and
responsibility; (2) Spiritual Action/Intent (SA), which tracks how much participants attribute
agency to spiritual beings; and (3) Spiritual Proximity (SP), which tracks how much participants
view spiritual forces as omnipresent and accessible. Openness was positively associated with
themes of NA, and negatively associated with SA.  Gender and race proved to be strong
predictors of narrative themes, with men showing higher scores on narrative agency (NA) than
women and African American adults scoring higher on spiritual action/intent (SA) and spiritual
proximity (SP) than white adults.  After controlling for demographics, Extraversion predicted
greater NA while lower Openness was associated with higher SA. Furthermore, themes of NA
and SA were inversely related, which has implications for the importance of spiritual paradigms
in understanding how people narrate their lives.
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
Personality Traits and the Narration of Spiritual Experiences
In The Varieties of Religious Experience, William James (1902) famously argued that
religious sentiments are so distinct, profound, and universal that they can be considered a unique
product of the human mind. Religiosity is expressed through institutional and social
organizations, and it is a foundational motivator and emotional component in individuals’ lives.
According to James (1902), considering the motivational and emotional dimensions of religion
illuminates why various life events can project a mystical or transcendent significance for some
people, while they may seem entirely ordinary to others. In other words, the existence of
personal religiosity means that humans have the capacity to experience life events and their
associated emotions in one of two ways: as being transcendentally significant or not being so.
James suggested that religious emotional experience is, in many ways, similar to regular
emotional experience on the behavioral surface, but religious emotions are always felt in relation
to what the individual considers “divine.” This element of divinity causes religious sentiments—
and religiosity more broadly—to adopt a tone of severity and urgency (which may be positive or
negative in valence) that is not broadly characteristic of secular emotions or experiences.
Many psychologists today believe that religious experience is a natural feature of human
life, perhaps unique to our species. Imparting religious significance on life experiences may be
an evolutionary product of the human inclination to seek intent and meaning in random,
unexplainable events (Bering, 2006; Willard & Norenzayan, 2013).  Religion also functions to
bind people together into communities, promoting cooperation and solidarity within groups
(Wilson, 2002). It is clear that personal religious experiences and their associated emotions are
widespread and persistent in nearly all contemporary societies. Even as conventional religious
observance has waned somewhat in the United States and Europe in the past few decades, all
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
societies nonetheless showcase strong religious traditions, and billions of human beings today
consider themselves to be “religious” and report personal experiences that have a religious or
spiritual quality (Baker et al., 2016; Labbé & Fobes, 2009; MacDonald, 2000).
In the current study, we explore people’s narrative accounts of religious experience
through a life-story approach (McAdams & McLean, 2013).  In the spirit of James’s (1902)
effort to document the varieties of religious experience, we aim to identify salient themes in
different stories people tell about religious or spiritual experiences in their lives. In addition, we
aim to discover links between the varieties of religious experiences people describe and their
self-reported dispositional personality traits. In what ways do differences in people’s narrative
accounts of religious experience map onto their basic traits? Can we predict specific variations in
religious narratives from people’s particular trait profiles? In this study we seek to answer these
questions and examine how race and gender influence individual differences in the narration of
religious experience.
The Study of Spirituality and Religion in Psychology
In modern research, personal religious feelings and their interpretations have come to be
broadly referred to as “spirituality,” as such experiences and emotions do commonly occur
independent of conventional religion. Different researchers use different meanings for
“spirituality,” but the most common uses of the term are represented by a definition offered by
Baker and colleagues (2016), which defines spirituality as that which is related to a search for
“transcendent connection and sacred meaning.” This definition of spirituality is also very similar
to James’s (1902) definition of religion, which he defines as “the feelings, acts, and experiences
of individual men in their solitude, so far as they apprehend themselves to stand in relation to
whatever they may consider the divine” (p. 31). James (1902) defines divinity quite broadly, but
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
for him—independent of religion or practice—it also refers to a grand quality of fundamental,
transcendent, and all-encompassing interconnectedness and importance. In this study, I use
“spirituality” in place of James’s notion of “religion” in order to maintain specific emphasis on
the personal relationship with the “divine” while keeping some distance from discussions of
organized institutions and formal practices also denoted by the term “religion.”
James’s (1902) discussion of religiosity is also deeply concerned with the individual
differences in spiritual experience and the unique qualities that differentiate spiritual emotions.
He believed that by guiding the way people seek sacred meaning and universal connection,
organized religion functions as a powerful, emotive motivator that works uniquely in conjunction
with an individual’s conception of the divine. Yet as important as certain emotional experiences
may be to a person’s religiosity, it is only once these feelings interact with logical and cognitive
factors—normally offered through doctrine or creeds—that religion fully gains its motivational
power to guide various behaviors and decisions in daily life (James, 1902). Thus, many
formalized aspects of organized religions ultimately become key components in how individuals
consciously interpret their religious emotions or mystical phenomena.
James (1902) offered some preliminary illustrations of how varying individual
dispositions create different patterns of spiritual experience and emotionality, exemplified by his
“healthy mind/sick soul” distinction. According to James (1902), people with a “healthy mind”
are more inclined towards seeking religious experiences that validate and encourage connection
to the world around them, which in turn promotes jubilant emotions and feelings of
empowerment and acceptance associated with spiritual experiences. On the other hand, those
with a “sick soul” are more inclined towards feelings of guilt and angst, so they more frequently
seek salvation or an alleviation of internal suffering in their religious experiences.
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
James (1902) felt that a consideration of personal religious or spiritual accounts would
provide the richest insights into the nature and causes of these divergent religious experiences.
He stressed the importance of individual accounts because spiritual experiences are necessarily
individualized due to their ineffable and noetic qualities. These features of spiritual experience
make them difficult to understand, communicate, or quantify for those who have not had them.
Furthermore, such experiences are transient and hard to induce intentionally, making it a difficult
task to study these experiences and their associated sentiments in an objective laboratory setting
Nevertheless, psychologists have tried to undertake this task of studying spirituality by
employing highly constrained and conventional methodologies. Most commonly, researchers
have used self-report questionnaires designed to measure an individuals’ levels of spirituality
according to various conceptual dimensions. Examples of these spirituality dimensions include
‘existential well-being,’ ‘cognitive orientation towards spirituality,’ and a tendency to accept
paranormal beliefs (Hill & Pargament, 2003; MacDonald, 2000; Saroglou, 2002). Meta-analyses
by Saroglou (2002) and MacDonald (2000) show that these, along with a litany of other
measures, have been developed to differentiate certain aspects of religiosity, religious
participation, and spirituality. Though it is common for researchers investigating the psychology
of spirituality to define their own parameters and dimensions, there have been three distinct
dimensions of religiosity which have enjoyed more widespread popularity and use: intrinsic,
extrinsic, and quest-oriented religiosity (Allport, 1966; Batson, 1993; Saroglou, 2002, 2010).
First proposed by Allport (1966), the distinction between intrinsic and extrinsic
religiosity describes different motivations for participating in religious practice. People who are
intrinsically religious view connecting with the divine as an end in itself and are motivated by an
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
internal desire to understand their faith, live by their religion’s moral principles, and maintain a
personal connection with the higher force at the center of their belief (Allport, 1966). People who
are more extrinsically religious engage in religious practice as a means to procure external
benefits such as an organized social alliance or securing basic life needs like food and shelter
(Allport, 1966).
Beyond intrinsic and extrinsic motivations for religiosity, Batson and colleagues (1983)
identified a third orientation, which they named quest religiosity. In quest religiosity, individuals
view their religiosity as an ongoing search for truth or supreme meaning. They see spirituality as
an adventure to be pursued over time. All of these motivations—intrinsic, extrinsic, and quest—
may govern aspects of an individual’s personal religiosity or spirituality, and indeed a great deal
of empirical research on spirituality has been organized around these concepts, especially in the
field of social psychology (Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Jagers & Smith, 1996).
Religion, Spirituality, and Well-being
Several research studies and meta-analyses have found significant and consistent effects
of religiosity on physical and psychological well-being.  Beyond The Varieties of Religious
Experience, research has consistently found that religiosity of any sort is a protective factor
against mental illness and psychopathology, promoting positive coping strategies for dealing
with negative life events, and predicting physical health benefits, too, likely through the
promotion of healthy lifestyle habits. Studies have found that these benefits hold true across
different age groups (Berry & York, 2011; Wink & Dillon, 2008), gender and ethnicity/race
categories (Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Jagers & Smith, 1996), and different religious traditions
(Hill et al., 2000; Hill & Pargament, 2003). This line of research suggests that the internal and
motivational features of religion are largely responsible for its associated health benefits. It may
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
also be true that the communal aspects of participating in organized religion promote some of
these health benefits (Wink & Dillon, 2008), but the social elements of religious practice may
not fully account for the tendency of some people to more frequently employ positive, spiritual-
grounded coping strategies in their daily lives (Berry & York, 2011).
Indeed, some studies have found that intrinsic religiosity, rather than overall religiosity, is
the feature of religion/spirituality primarily responsible for the positive association with well-
being (Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Jagers & Smith, 1996). The internal and personalized
experiences of religious belief and spiritual emotion offer benefits that ordinary experience and
emotion do not. The association between intrinsic religiosity and associated health benefits
seems to be especially strong for Black Americans (Jagers & Smith, 1996), who consistently
report higher levels of both intrinsic and extrinsic religiosity than whites. African Americans,
along with other members of the African diaspora, generally tend to view spirituality as being
central to their personal and cultural identities as well as instrumental to much of what happens
in ordinary life (Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Jagers & Smith, 1996). Black Americans are also more
likely than white Americans to make spiritual attributions in their everyday lives, thereby more
frequently inducing their own spiritual emotions and experiences, likely to the benefit of their
own health.
Hill and Pargament (2003) argue that the relationship between intrinsic religiosity and
well-being is driven by differences in attributional styles, which reflect profound qualitative
differences in the spiritual frameworks people use to interpret life events—something James’s
predicted with his healthy mind/sick soul distinction. Hill and Pargament (2003) propose that
viewing religiosity as a cognitive schema helps explain the effects of different spiritual
orientations on health. Cognitive schemas are mental representations of life events that help
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
people bridge gaps in knowledge or memory to better understand causality and derive meaning
from various events (McIntosh, 1995). Therefore, a more intrinsically religious individual would
be more likely to employ religiously grounded schemas when trying to understand events in their
life and relate them to a divine will or process (Hill & Pargament, 2003). This is exactly what
Hill and Pargament (2003) found in their study, which reports that people who use religion or
spirituality to enhance their connection to God, motivate their actions, and frame their individual
or interpersonal struggles enjoy more of the psychological benefits associated with religiosity. A
schematic implementation of religious belief is also consistent with earlier hypotheses that
cognitive components of religious belief interact with one’s spiritual sentiments to motivate and
justify behavior (James, 1902).
Employing a religious schema to explain a life event like personal failure or the
unexpected loss of a loved one can help individuals attribute the causes of negative outcomes to
fundamentally positive spiritual forces, helping people reframe their understanding of random or
painful events. In this regard, Spilka and Schmidt (1983) found that people are more likely to
make religious attributions in situations of greater importance and personal concern, especially
those that are negative, potentially maximizing the benefits of religion as a coping mechanism.
Similarly, Chang and colleagues (2012, 2014) have found that perceptions of one’s own ability
and self-efficacy mediate the spirituality–well-being relationship, suggesting that the mental
health benefits of spiritual schemas are strongest when employed to help strengthen the
perception of one’s own ability to succeed and overcome hardship.
In sum, psychological research into the effects of religiosity and spirituality show that
they do serve a special function for the human mind and body by providing people with new
schemas through which they can understand their lives and emotions and relate them to what
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
they believe to be sacred truths. Yet despite the robust benefits of spirituality on health, the
nature of its effects varies greatly with the individual’s internal experience of spiritual
phenomena and emotion. Thus, as useful as the extrinsic, intrinsic, and quest distinctions have
been in organizing quantitative research, scholars have known since James (1902) that the
qualitative differences in individual spirituality vary in ways beyond what is described by the
motivational paradigm used in modern empirical research. More research is still needed,
therefore, to document this variation and to understand what predisposes people towards
qualitative differences in how they interpret life events through a spiritual framework.
Personality Traits
Due to the deeply personal and idiosyncratic nature of spiritual experience, the present
study aims to examine personal spirituality by analyzing people’s unique narrations of spiritual
experiences. This study also aims to examine how dispositional personality traits relate to the
characteristic manner in which people narrate these kinds of experiences.  Because intrinsic
religiosity is strongly related to an internal tendency to recognize divine or spiritual influence on
various aspects of life (Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Hill & Pargament, 2003), we expect that
dispositional traits related to intrinsic religiosity will correspond to narratives which portray
spiritual or divine forces embodying a more active and normative role in their lives.
Additionally, we expect that dispositional traits related to greater mental-well-being and self-
confidence will be associated with narratives that portray spiritual forces which aid and
strengthen the self, consistent with findings on the link between perceived self-efficacy, spiritual
attributions, and well-being (Berry & York, 2011; Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Chang et al., 2012;
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
This study draws on the Five Factor Model of personality (FFM) to assess variation in
dispositional traits. The FFM is a widely adopted framework for understanding and
distinguishing broad personality differences (McCrae & Costa, 2008). The five traits which
comprise the FFM are Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Neuroticism, and
Openness to Experience. Agreeableness captures tendencies toward being compassionate,
cooperative, trusting, and compliant, versus their opposites (e.g., lack of compassion,
distrustfulness, aggression), while Conscientiousness taps into variation on dimensions of
orderliness, industriousness, responsibility, and self-control (John, 2021). Extraversion is about
dominance, assertiveness, sociability, and positive-emotionality (John, 2021). Neuroticism
measures negative emotionality, emotional instability, and lower self-esteem (John, 2021).
Finally, Openness assesses the overall tendency to seek novel stimuli and engage in fantastical or
imaginative thinking, as well greater intellect and cognitive flexibility (John, 2021).
Psychologists have already begun to investigate the relationship between these traits and
religiosity using empirical studies that quantify trait personality levels and various aspects of
religiosity using self-report questionnaires. The most consistent findings to date have been strong
associations of both Agreeableness and Conscientiousness with religiosity (Saroglou, 2002).
Two meta-analyses by Saroglou (2002, 2010) and one by McDonald (2000) found that higher
levels of Agreeableness and Conscientiousness consistently correlate with higher levels of
general religiosity, intrinsic religiosity, religious fundamentalism, and spirituality.
A potential explanation for these associations may be that since Agreeableness is related
to being trusting and compliant, it may also predispose people to be more likely to trust and
comply with the authority of a more powerful and knowledgeable spiritual being (Labbé &
Fobes 2009; Womble et al., 2013). However, this explanation is premised on the predominantly
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
Christian population used for these studies, who may be more likely to view the divine as a
willful figure to be obeyed. Likewise, it may be true that people who are higher in
Conscientiousness may be more likely to adhere to the standards of behavior associated with
their spiritual belief system, including participating in prayer services, following certain lifestyle
customs, and trying to maintain a personal connection with spiritual beings (Labbé & Fobes
2009; Womble et al., 2013).
Extraversion and Neuroticism also relate to religiosity and spirituality, though these
relationships are found less frequently and often show weaker associations (Beitel et al., 2004;
Labbé & Fobes 2009; MacDonald, 2000; Saroglou, 2002, 2010; Womble et al., 2013). In fact,
the associations that have been found between religiosity and Extraversion and religiosity and
Neuroticism are almost opposite to one another. Extraversion correlates positively but weakly
with intrinsic religiosity and a cognitive tendency towards spirituality (MacDonald, 2000;
Saroglou, 2002), but Neuroticism only correlates positively with extrinsic religiosity (Saroglou,
2002). Furthermore, research into the effects of spirituality on stress response and existential
well-being has found that Neuroticism is often negatively associated with these benefits of
spirituality, though it remains unclear whether this is because highly neurotic people less
frequently employ spiritual schemas or because less spiritual people are more likely to have
difficulty coping with existential stress and thus exhibit increased neuroticism (Labbé & Fobes
2009; MacDonald, 2000; Womble et al., 2013). On the other hand, these same studies have
found that Extraversion is positively associated with the mental-health benefits of spirituality,
which may be due to Extraversion’s role as a protective factor because of its connection to
positive emotionality and greater self-confidence (Labbé & Fobes 2009; Smillie et al., 2019;
Womble et al., 2013).
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
With respect to Openness to Experience, the most consistent finding is that Openness is
negatively associated with intrinsic, extrinsic, and fundamentalist religiosity, but it is positively
associated with quest religiosity (Saroglou, 2002; 2010). People who are higher in Openness are
generally more attracted to more complex and abstract ideas (John, 2021), which may explain
why they are more to engage with religiosity an inquisitive and curious manner, associated with
quest religiosity (Saroglou, 2002). Other findings relating spirituality to Openness are slightly
more varied, but a meta-analysis by MacDonald (2000) has found that Openness correlates with
a greater tendency to believe in paranormal or supernatural phenomena, as well as a greater
tendency to emphasize the experiential elements of spiritual belief. These findings are also
consistent with a finding by McAdams and colleagues (2004) that people higher in Openness
tend to give more complex narrative accounts of life experiences that include descriptions of
unusual or fantastical experiences and sensations. Fantastical and ineffable sensations are also a
common component of mystical experiences as noted by William James (1902), so it may be that
spiritual people higher in Openness are more likely to accept these types of sensations and
incorporate them into a spiritual framework.
Narrative Accounts
In order to investigate how individuals describe the presence and influence of divine
forces in their lives, this study will analyze narrative accounts given in response to one section of
the Life Story Interview (LSI) dealing with a spiritual, mystical, or transcendent experience. The
LSI was used as part of McAdams and Guo’s (2015) longitudinal study of personality and
narrative identity in midlife adults (see also, Manczak, Zapata-Gietl, & McAdams, 2014). One
advantage of using autobiographical narratives to study spirituality is that it allows researchers to
focus on the internal and personal components of spiritual or religious belief. In the responses
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
given to the LSI, participants are encouraged not only to describe a spiritually significant event
but also to discuss their emotional reactions and interpretations of the event. These added
elements of narration can better help researchers understand the varying nature of religious—or
spiritual—sentiment in different people, beyond simply measuring their degree of adherence to
certain spiritual or religious beliefs.
Another benefit of a narrative approach is that it allows researchers to more easily track
how adults describe divine influence in relation to themselves, which is understood to be an
important component of the link between spirituality and psychological well-being (Berry &
York, 2011; Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Chang et al., 2012; 2014; James, 1902). Agency is
considered one of two primary motivational themes in autobiographical narratives (McAdams,
1996), and is reflected in the way people describe intentionally and effectively initiating change
in their lives according to their own goals and motivations (Adler, 2012). Tracking how
individuals narrate their own agency in the context of a spiritually significant event allows us to
directly observe how and when spiritual schemas are invoked in reference to the self, and
whether they describe a strengthening or pacifying impact of divine intervention (Berry & York,
2011; Blaine & Crocker, 1995; Chang et al., 2012; 2014).
The autobiographical narratives used in this study are excerpts of transcribed responses to
the LSI used in McAdams and colleagues’ Foley Longitudinal Study of Adulthood (FLSA:
McAdams & Guo, 2015). The FLSA was a nine-year study of personality and narrative identity
in midlife adults, where participants, initially aged between 55 and 57, were asked to describe
key scenes from their lives three times over the course of nine years. As part of participation,
participants also completed a series of self-report measures, including the NEO-FFI, a valid and
reliable questionnaire used to measure dispositional personality according to the FFM. For this
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
study, I focus on each participants response to the section of the interview in which they are
asked to narrate key spiritual, mystical, or transcendent experiences. Since participants were
asked to discuss such experiences all three times they completed the LSI, data from the all three
interviews are analyzed and aggregated in order to create the most robust assessment of how
adults narrate spiritual experiences. Then I compare these scenes with FFM personality traits for
each participant taken form their NEO-FFI scores.
Because of previous research that finds both Agreeableness and Conscientiousness
predict intrinsic religiosity, which is associated with a greater personal adherence to spiritual or
religious frameworks (Blaine & Crocker, 1995), I hypothesize that (1) participants higher in
Agreeableness will be more likely to describe divine or spiritual forces that actively and
normatively influence their lives, and participants higher in Conscientiousness will also be more
likely to exhibit this tendency. I also examine how much participants describe themselves as
exhibiting agency, which is strongly linked with well-being (Adler et al., 2008) and is associated
with dominance and self-confidence, both of which are positively linked with Extraversion and
inversely with Neuroticism (Ghaed & Gallo, 2006). Since spirituality seems to aid well-being
through attributions that enhance a sense of personal responsibility (Blaine & Crocker, 1995)
while externalizing blame for failure and hardship (Spilka & Schmidt, 1983), I hypothesize that
(2) participants higher in Extraversion will be more likely to describe spiritual experiences that
emphasize their personal agency, while participants lower in Neuroticism will be more likely to
emphasize their own agency.
Finally, because of the finding that people higher in Openness narrate more elaborative
and fantastical personal experiences (MacDonald, 2000; McAdams, 2004), and because of its
negative relationship to religious fundamentalism (Saroglou, 2002; 2010) I hypothesize that (3)
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
participants higher in Openness to Experience will give narrative accounts that describe divine
or spiritual forces as more fluid, flexible, and accessible.
Method
Participants
The participants in this study were the 164 adults who took part in the Foley Longitudinal
Study of Adulthood, aged between 55 and 57 years old. Participants were recruited from the
greater Chicago area in Illinois to participate in a study, a majority of whom were female (63.6
% female, 36.4% male), and slightly more than half of whom were White (55%). The rest
predominantly identified African American (43% African American, 1% interracial, 1%
“other”). There was significant variation of annual household incomes among participants,
ranging from a minimum of under $25,000 a year to a maximum of over $300,000 a year, with
the median household income falling between $75,000-$100,000 a year. A large majority of the
sample had at least some college education: 44% had some graduate education, 24% graduated
college, 27% had some college education, and 5% had only a high school diploma.
Materials
The materials and data used in this study were taken from Foley Longitudinal Study of
Adulthood with the permission of Dan McAdams, the lead researcher in the study. This study
worked with a specific section of the LSI dealing with spiritual experiences, which was
administered as part of the FLSA. These scenes (S/T scenes) asked participants to describe as
spiritual or transcendent moment using the prompt:
“The next question is a religious, spiritual or mystical experience. Whether they are
religious or not, many people report that they have had experiences in their lives where
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
they felt a sense of the transcendent or sacred, a sense of god or some almighty or
ultimate force or a feeling of oneness with nature, the world or the universe. Thinking
back on your entire life, please identify an episode or moment in which you felt something
like this.  It may be an experience that occurred within the context of your religious
tradition if you have one, or it may not be connected to religion at all, and it may be a
spiritual or mystical experience of any kind.  Please describe this transcendent
experience, where and when, who was involved.”
This prompt was used all three times the LSI was administered, during the first, fifth, and ninth
years of the FLSA. Here I refer to the first year of the FLSA study as Time 1, the fifth year as
Time 5, and the ninth as Time 9. In order to develop a more robust picture of the what narrative
themes are typically included in response to this section, and how they related to personality, this
study analyzed responses from all three times the LSI was administered.
Participants also completed a small battery of self-report questionnaires, including the
NEO-FFI-3, which is an abridged version of the NEO personality inventory with generally
accepted validity (Guo, Klevan, & McAdams, 2016). The scores on the NEO-FFI-3 indicate the
degree to which participants exhibit each of the traits from the FFM. The NEO-FFI contains 60
items, each of which is phrased as a statement about the self to which participants must indicate
how much they agree or disagree using a five-point scale (1=strongly disagree; 5=strongly
agree). Each of the big five personality traits is measured by set of twelve specific items on the
NEO-FFI, meaning each item corresponds only to one trait. Responses to the twelve items for
each trait were used to provide an overall score for that trait, with higher scores indicating that
the survey’s respondent exhibits higher levels of that personality trait (Guo et al., 2016). Given
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
the prior evidence that personality traits are relatively stable in the later stages of adult life (John,
2021), this study only considered data from the responses given at Time 1 of the FLSA.
Procedure
As the first step in deriving thematic categories for the data, I read the S/T scenes from
Times 1 and 5 in order to understand how participants described the experience of spiritually or
religiously significant events in their lives. Three major themes were identified relating to how
participants characterize spiritual influence, the relationship between spiritual influence and
personal action, and the fluidity and omnipresence of spiritual beings. In order to codify how
these themes are discussed by each participant, I developed coding schemes using five-point
scoring systems in order to quantitatively describe differences in spiritual narration. This
approach then allowed for direct comparison of the prominence of these narrative themes with
personality data, which has been quantified using the scores on the NEO-FFI-3.
Establishing Interrater Reliability for the Coding Systems
The Spiritual Action/Intent and Spiritual Proximity schemes were developed specifically
for the purposes of this study, while the Narrator Agency scheme was merely adapted from a
preexisting for use with the S/T scenes. As part of the development of these coding systems, and
second coder used the coding systems to score the S/T scenes independently of the primary
coder. Initially, 20 of the S/T scenes from Time 1 were coded together by both coders in order to
develop the specificity and precision of the coding schemes. Then, five groups of 10 - 15
narratives from Time 1 were coded by each coder independently, and after each round, scores
were compared and discussed, and the coding schemes were adjusted for clarity and specificity
to achieve more coding consistency and reliability. Afterwards, the rest of the of the Time 1
narratives—roughly half—were coded independently by both coders, and once all Time 1
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
narratives had been coded twice, all scores completed independently were compared using a
Pearson’s correlation coefficient to establish interrater reliability. The S/T scenes from Times 5
and 9 were only coded by the primary coder.
Spiritual Action/Intent (SA). The Spiritual Action/Intent system was designed to
measure whether participants narrate divine or spiritual influence as more active or passive.
Spiritual causality was scored on a 5-point scale (0 – 4), where higher scores correspond to S/T
scenes in which spiritual forces are narrated as actively and intentionally influencing the lives of
participants. Lower scores corresponded to scenes in which spiritual forces are described as
passive or inactive, and the minimum score of 0 was reserved for scenes that attribute no
spiritual influence.
The application of the Spiritual Action/Intent scale followed a similar logic for scoring as
that of Adler’s (2012) scale for codifying narrator agency, which is discussed in more detail
below. This decision was made since some psychologists theorize that humans are innately
predisposed to imagine spiritual beings as agentic actors because of our ability to understand and
infer the intentions behind the action of others, referred to as the Theory of Mind (TOM) (Bering
2006; Willard & Norenzayan, 2013). Furthermore, many religions do describe divine forces
which act intentionally to bring about a specific goal or divine order (James, 1902). Therefore,
according to the TOM, if humans invoke the TOM to understand spiritual influence, then they
will likely describe spiritual or divine action in a way which mirrors the way they describe
human action. The reliability for this scale, containing 139 items, was acceptable (r = .63).
Narrator Agency (NA). The Narrator Agency system was developed so that we can
track the way participants describe the relationship between spiritual forces and their own ability
to act and affect change. Agency is a common motivational theme used in narrative research,
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
which relates to how much the participant believes in the efficacy of her own abilities and
attributes outcomes to her own intentional actions (McLean et al., 2020). Highly agentic
narratives emphasize the protagonist’s autonomy and ability to achieve success primarily
through one’s own efforts, while narratives low in agency often attribute outcomes to external
causes or factors (McLean et al., 2020). The coding scheme used for this study was a 5-point
scale (0 – 4), with 0 given to responses that describe the protagonist as exhibiting practically no
agency, and 4 given to responses that depict highly agentic protagonists. The reliability for this
scale suggests the adjustments made to fit this study may have limited used elsewhere (139
items; r = .41)
Spiritual Proximity (SP). The Spiritual Proximity scale was used to codify the degree to
which participants describe divine or spiritual forces as omnipresent and accessible. Spiritual
Proximity will be scored according to five-point scale (0 – 4). Higher scores will correspond to
narratives that depict spiritual forces which can commonly interact directly through ordinary
people or are inextricably linked to ordinary life. A narrative with a higher score in the Spiritual
Proximity scale may include more descriptions of personalized contact with spiritual forces (e.g.
a participant believes Jesus spoke with him directly) and specific sensations related to the
interaction with spiritual beings. Lower scores were given to scenes in which the divine or
spiritual forces were narrated as more rigid, localized, and inaccessible to ordinary people. A
minimum score of 0 was reserved for scenes that do not describe any spiritual influence or event.
Table 1 includes paradigmatic examples of high and low scores for all coding schemes. The
interrater reliability for this scale was also acceptable (139 items; r = .63).

Results
For the narrative themes of Narrator Agency, Spiritual Action, and Spiritual Proximity,
participant’s scores for each coding scale were averaged across Times 1, 5, and 9. A second
coder provided independent scores for all coding scales at Time 1, which were combined with
the first coder’s scores and then an average was taken for Time 1.
On average, across all time points, participants tended to narrate spiritual experiences
with slightly more emphasis on their own agency (NA: M = 2.16, SD = .70), while also being
slightly more likely to attribute events and experiences to the deliberate action of spiritual forces
or beings (SA: M = 2.19, SD = 1.10). A Pearson’s correlation coefficient revealed an inverse
relationship between the tendency to emphasize one’s own agency and an inclination to
emphasize the presumed agency of spiritual beings. The correlation coefficient for this
relationship is displayed in Table 2. Participants were also somewhat more likely to describe
spiritual beings and forces as accessible or proximal to the ordinary world (SP: M = 2.73, SD =
1.00). A Pearson’s test revealed a significant relationship between the themes of Spiritual Action
(SA) and Spiritual Proximity (SP), indicating that the inclination to narrate spiritual beings as
proximal and accessible was strongly associated with a tendency to describe such beings as more
deliberate and agentic. The correlation coefficient for this relationship, as well as those for SP
and Narrator Agency (NA) are shown in Table 2.

Focusing on bivariate relations between traits and narrative themes, the first hypothesis—
that higher levels Conscientiousness and Agreeableness will predict a greater tendency to
emphasize the deliberate nature spiritual phenomena—did receive some support from the data.
Significant correlations were obtained for both Conscientiousness and SA scores, and
Agreeableness and SA scores. This finding is consistent with previous studies that show a
relationship between higher levels of Conscientiousness and Agreeableness and spirituality
(Beitel et al., 2004; Labbé & Fobes 2009; MacDonald, 2000; Womble et al., 2013). Scores on the
SA scale were also significantly correlated with Extraversion, but inversely with Neuroticism
and Openness to Experience. The findings about Neuroticism are also consistent with previous
research that shows the usefulness of religiously grounded coping mechanisms for managing life
stressors (Labbé & Fobes 2009; MacDonald, 2000; Womble et al., 2013). The tendency of
people higher in Openness to deemphasize any possible intentionality behind spiritual
phenomena may be reflective of the finding that Openness is negatively associated with more
fundamentalist forms of religiosity, which emphasize the primary importance of a divine will
(MacDonald, 2000; Saroglou, 2002; 2010).
The second hypothesis—that participants higher in Extraversion and lower in
Neuroticism would narrate their spiritual experiences with greater emphasis on their own
agency—did not receive significant support from the correlational data. Neither Neuroticism nor
Extraversion predicted the degree to which participants emphasized their own agency in the S/T
scenes. However, Openness to Experience was positively associated with more agentic narration
of spiritual experience.
Yet despite the finding that Openness positively predicted NA scores and negative
predicted SA scores, Openness was not found to be significant related to SP scores. Thus, the
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
third hypotheses—that Openness will predict an inclination to view spiritual phenomena as more
omnipresent and related to ordinary phenomena—was not supported by the correlational data.
However, as Table 2 shows, Extraversion was weakly but significantly associated with a greater
tendency to view spiritual forces and beings as more proximal to the ordinary world.
Multiple Regression Analysis
In order to better understand the interacting influences of all personality and demographic
variables on the narration of spiritual experience, a simultaneous multiple regression analysis
was conducted for all three narrative themes. For each test, race, gender, and all Big 5
personality traits were considered as predictors, and the narrative theme was treated as the
dependent variable. The first test, which considered whether personality, race and gender impact
how much intention participants attribute to spiritual forces, found that 32% of the variance in
SA scores were predicted by these variables (F(7,148) = 9.78, p < .001, R2 = .32). The largest
contributor to his relationship was race, and when controlling for all personality variables and
gender, Black participants were more likely to emphasize spiritual action and intent (β = .35, p <
.001). When controlling for personality and race, gender also still significantly impacted SA
scores, with female participants being more likely than males to emphasize spiritual action (β =
.18, p < .05). Furthermore, lower Openness was the only personality trait to predict higher SA
scores, independent of the effects of race, gender, and other personality variables (β = -.22, p <
.01). The reported beta coefficients are standardized to the same unites of measure, so beta
coefficients with absolute values closer to 1 indicate stronger influence of the predictor on the
prevalence of the narrative themes.
The simultaneous multiple regression analysis also revealed a significant impact of
personality, race, and gender on NA scores in the narration of spiritual experience, with these
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
variables predicting roughly 13% of the variance (F(7,148) = 3.07, p < .01, R2 = .13). Regardless
of race and personality, male participants were more likely than females to emphasize their own
agency when recounting spiritual experiences (β = -.18, p < .05). Additionally, when
demographic variables and all other personality variables were controlled for, higher
Extraversion did predict higher NA scores (β = .19, p < .05), though it was the only Big 5 trait to
do so. Nonetheless this finding does offer some support for the hypothesized relationship
between Extraversion and personal agency in the narration of spiritual experience.
Themes of spiritual proximity were also significantly associated with race, gender, and
the Big 5 personality traits, which predicted 16% of the variance in SP scores (F(7,148) = 3.94, p
< .001, R2 = .16). Race was the only variable which predicted the prominence of SP themes, with
black participants being more likely than whites to describe spiritual beings as accessible and
omnipresent regardless of personality or gender (β = .33, p < .001). Overall, it seems an that the
ways adults narrate their experiences are influenced not only by personality variables, but also
significantly by race, and gender as well.
Discussion
Whereas the study’s main aim was to document associations between personality traits
and particular narrative themes in accounts of spiritual experiences, the demographic
characteristics of gender and race ended up accounting for much of the variance in narrative
themes. According to the multiple regression analysis, men showed significantly higher levels of
narrative agency (NA) than women, while African American adults scored significantly higher
than their white counterparts on both spiritual action/intent (SA) and spiritual proximity (SP).
With the influence demographics being considered, only Extraversion and Openness proved to
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
be significant predictors of narrative themes.  Extraversion was positively associated with NA (as
hypothesized), and Openness was negatively associated with SA (contrary to hypothesis).  The
traits of Neuroticism, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness were not significantly associated
with the narrative themes in the multiple regression analyses.
Spiritual Narration and the Big 5
Personality and the Narration of the Self in Spiritual Scenes
The relationships discovered in this study between personality traits and the ways adults
narrate spiritual experiences offer new evidence to the claim that spiritual reasoning is
qualitatively different form ordinary autobiographical reflection. Though Extraversion and
Neuroticism were expected to predict how much participants emphasize their own agency since
both traits are related to assertiveness and self-confidence (John, 2021), only Extraversion
showed the predicted relationship. This finding suggests that the agentic narration of spiritual
experiences is not strongly related to emotional stability but is (as hypothesized) positively
associated with an upbeat, outgoing, and assertive disposition. Moreover, in the correlational
analysis, Openness was also significantly associated with NA.
James (1902) argued that spiritual experiences uniquely push individuals to reflect on
deeper, universal truths, and he reported that such reflections are closely associated with
questions of morality and personal responsibility. As Openness is the Big 5 trait most closely
associated with cognition and intellect (John, 2021), it is plausible that more Open individuals
would be more willing to engage with such cerebral questions regarding morality when
reflecting on spiritual experiences. Consequently, people higher in Openness may be more
inclined to reflect on the moral implications of their spiritual experiences, reflecting more agentic
themes like personal responsibility, whereas others may be more concerned with the concrete
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
elements of these experiences and consider their concrete influence on real-life events. Consider
a response given by one participant high in Openness as she discusses how her connection with
God makes her feel. In her response, she reflects on the observation that strangers seem to find
her approachable, and she emphasizes her belief that she can leverage this perception to fulfill a
moral responsibility to be kind and supportive of others:
“No, but I -- you know I sometimes when you meet people and you can sense the joy and
the sadness if you open to them when they talk to you. […] And people always like to be
around me cause I'm always smiling and laughing, so -- even strangers will walk up to
me and want to talk to me. I'm like okay, what do you want to talk about? And I'll just
listen to them. […] And this one guy, he was strung out but I didn't know that, I was, you
know, I been through all that. I just listen to him. And he say I keep trying. I say well you
just got to keep trying. And just keep trying, don't give up you know.”
This interpretation is also compatible with the finding that Openness to Experience is
strongly associated with quest-religiosity (Saroglou, 2002; 2010), which means that more Open
individuals are somewhat more likely to view transcendent experiences within the context of a
life-long search for spiritual understanding. McAdams and colleagues discovered that people
higher in Openness generally tend to give more elaborative, reflective, and cohesive narrative
accounts during life-story interviews (2004). Thus, agentic narration of spiritual experiences
might be reflective a more quest-like orientation towards religiosity. The association between
Openness and agency may be driven by a tendency of people higher in Openness to position
themselves at the center of their spiritual experiences, emphasizing what they learned from each
experience and how it contributed to a life-long search for spiritual understanding. One
participant high in Openness narrated his spiritual experience in this way, highlighting his self-
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
directed search for spiritual meaning when asked to reflect on what his transcendent experience
says about him:
“It says I am a seeker and in my heart a mystic and a non-conformist and, and that has in
fact been a problem my whole life and will continue to be […] So, again, but, it
reinforced this idea of a seeker, that this, this is really what I'm interested in. And to this
day now, since I've had that experience, I don't see the world the same, I just don't.”
Personality and the Narration of Spiritual Elements
With respect to the agency of spiritual forces themselves (the theme of SA in narrative
accounts), Openness to experience showed a negative association in the multiple regression
analysis. In the correlational results, Neuroticism, was also negatively associated with the
tendency to emphasize the presumed agency or intention of spiritual forces. In the correlational
analyses (but not in multiple regression), Extraversion, Conscientiousness, and Agreeableness
were all positively related to this theme. Given that the majority of religious participants in this
sample practiced Abrahamic religions (e.g. Judaism and Christianity), which often characterize
spiritual forces as anthropomorphic and deliberate (Kay et al., 2009), it is likely that many of the
narrative accounts which attribute intentionality to spiritual phenomena reflect these belief
systems. Such an interpretation is consistent with the consistent finding that these two traits—
Agreeableness and Conscientiousness—are strongly related to conventional religious practice
and belief (Saroglou, 2002; 2010).
Openness was the only trait associated with the spiritual action/intent theme when all
other personality and demographic variables were controlled for. Openness is already negatively
associated with more fundamentalist forms of religiosity in previous literature (MacDonald,
2000), so the results regarding Openness and spiritual action/intent probably reflect an
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
inclination of more Open individuals to eschew fundamentalist frameworks offered by these
religions that imagine the divine as highly anthropomorphized.  People high in Openess may
adopt an abstracted and intellectualized form of religion, which might incline them toward less
personification of the divine, and less projected agency. For adults high in Openness, religion
and spirituality may be more about abstract principles and quests of self-actualization than about
the intentional actions of spiritual beings.
Regarding the associations between Neuroticism and Extraversion and the theme of
spiritual intent, there is a smaller body of prior research investigating these relationships. Some
studies suggest that more Extraverted people are attracted to communal elements of religious
worship (Saroglou, 2002; Womble et al., 2013), yet this does not fully account for narrative
styles employed by more Extraverted people in this study. Perhaps it is more useful to consider
spiritual action/intent’s relationship with Extraversion alongside its negative relationship with
Neuroticism. Many personality psychologists describe Extraversion as a protective factor against
mental illness because it is associated with an inclination to experience more positive emotions,
whereas Neuroticism is viewed as a risk factor because of its relationship to negative
emotionality (Labbé & Fobes 2009; Smillie et al., 2019; Womble et al., 2013). Therefore, the
relationship discovered in this study between Extraversion, Neuroticism, and a tendency to view
spiritual phenomena as deliberate may actually speak to a profound, positive, and self-affirming
emotional quality of adopting such spiritual schemas. In fact, the data shows that an emphasis on
spiritual agency may be as or even more strongly connected to emotional stability and self-
affirmation than an emphasis on narrator agency in these scenes.
With respect to spiritual proximity (SP), no personality variables predicted this theme
once demographic effects were taken into consideration. But in the correlational analyses,
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
Extraversion related to the theme of spiritual proximity, suggesting that viewing spiritual forces
as deliberate, normative, and omnipresent may be related to more emotionally positive and self-
affirming dispositions. This also seems likely when considering that Openness was not
associated with spiritual proximity, despite the initial hypothesis. As discussed, Openness to
Experience is more associated with intellect and cognitive styles, whereas Extraversion is
somewhat more related to emotional dispositions. Evidently, the tendency to describe
omnipresent and accessible spiritual forces is more closely linked with an energetic, upbeat
disposition than an imaginative and inquisitive mind. For example, consider the response given
by one participant who was relatively high in Extraversion, low in Neuroticism, and average in
Openness compared to the rest of the sample as she describes the feeling of discovering a direct,
personal relationship with God:
“I said everything is going to be okay. And it was that power; it was the -- I know it was
[…] God talking to me. A calm.  I was feeling calm.  I was feeling okay. You know, it's
okay. Everything's gonna be okay. It was probably one -- another one of those turning
points in my life where I realized there were something greater than myself […] I had to
rely on that faith. I had to turn to God at that point in my life. And that is the point in my
life where everything became not religious but became very spiritual.”
This participant’s response is rife with themes of spiritual intent and spiritual proximity and
reflects the profound sense of peace and acceptance that she associates with feeling that her life
is in God’s hands. These strong emotional expressions are characteristic of many of the
responses given to this section of the LSI, further substantiating William James’s (1902) claim
that experiences of divine insight or connection come with their own unique pattern of emotional
experiences.
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
Spiritual Action/Intent vs. Narrator Agency
Regarding the narrative themes investigated in this study, there is more consideration to
be had regarding the relationship between Spiritual Action/Intent and Narrator Agency. While
NA is a long-standing and well-established theme used in life stories research, the SA coding
scheme was developed specifically for the purposes of this study. As it turns out, an inclination
to emphasize one’s own agency was moderately associated with an inclination to deemphasize
the deliberate intention of spiritual beings (see Table 2). On the surface, it seems that NA and SA
are mutually exclusive themes, which parallels how psychologists understand locus of control
(LOC). Locus of control refers to whether a person believes control over events in their lives lies
primarily in themselves or in external forces such as other people, luck, or nature (Holder &
Levi, 1988). Narrator Agency and LOC do seem to be similar themes, as agentic storytelling
does often reflect an internal LOC. Furthermore, more agentic storytelling is associated with
mental health benefits (Adler, 2012), whereas an external LOC appears linked to higher levels of
anxiety and depression (Holder & Levi, 1988). It seems then, that by extension, having an
external LOC would be analogous to SA in the same way having an internal LOC is analogous to
more agentic storytelling.
However, I caution against this comparison for a couple of reasons. First, NA is
conceptually distinct from having an internal LOC because it also involves describing one’s
realized actions and successes, whereas LOC only refers to beliefs about who has potential
control over a given outcome (Adler, 2012). Secondly, the finding that SA is related to
Extraversion and low Neuroticism in the correlational analyses actually suggests that including
some degree of SA in personal narration is reflective of a more emotionally stable personality
profile, rather than one prone to anxiety or depression (Smillie et al., 2019; Womble et al., 2013).
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
Indeed, an inclination for a narrative style high in SA may even be a protective factor against
anxiety and depression because it offers superior coping mechanisms for stress relief (Berry &
York, 2011; Labbé & Fobes, 2010).
Thus, it seems that SA may be its own, unique complement to NA, and that a balance of
the two is ideal for psychological health and existential well-being. Almost all participants in this
sample were able to offer a unique spiritual experience, regardless of whether or not they viewed
themselves as religious or spiritual. This suggests that with only minimal prompting, all healthy,
developed adults are able to engage with ideas of spiritual action and intentionality to some
degree, much like how they are able to engage with ideas about their own agency. I propose that
further life stories research would benefit from including a spiritually grounded framework that
carefully tracks how people make sense of the forces and phenomena beyond their control, and
relating it to how humans describe causality, responsibility, and empowerment.
Gender and Race
The results from this study indicate that the demographic variables of gender and race
are highly associated with certain ways of discussing spiritual experiences. Men in this study
were significantly more likely than women to emphasize their own agency when narrating
spiritual experiences, whereas women were much more likely to emphasize the intentional action
of spiritual forces. These effects were shown in especially sharp relief when all personality
variables and race were controlled for. The multiple regression analysis revealed that race was
the strongest independent predictor of narrative styles, more so than gender and any personality
trait. Black participants were much more likely than white participants to narrate spiritual forces
as actively influencing their lives and working closely with them to achieve their desired
outcomes or further their spiritual understanding.
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
Developmental research has found that all Big 5 personality traits undergo some degree
of change over the course of a life time, with certain stages of life inducing especially strong
directional changes in most people (John, 2021). On the other hand, demographic variables like
gender and race are typically stable over a lifetime and do not change from birth. Therefore,
using correlations to study the relationship between personality and spirituality does little to
uncover the mystery of one’s causal influence on the other. However, since gender and race do
not change throughout a participant’s lifetime, it seems that these variables precede the
development of one’s spiritual beliefs. Perhaps a life time of socialization associated with being
male or female, or Black or white, strongly contributes to how participants develop their spiritual
beliefs.
As it pertains to gender, some previous studies have found that women tend to report
higher levels of religiosity than men. Some researchers have hypothesized that this finding may
be driven by a relationship to psychoticism, since women are typically lower in psychoticism
than men (Lynn & Martin, 1997; Penny et al., 2015). That women were more likely than men to
also narrate spiritual beings as active and intentional further supports the argument that viewing
spiritual beings in this way may be reflective positive mental health. Yet, it was men who were
more likely than women to emphasize their own agency in these themes, a narrative tendency
which has already been shown to be significantly related to positive mental health (Adler, 2008).
Once again, it seems that some mix of both narrative tendencies is ideal from a mental health
perspective.
Regarding race, the finding that Black participants seem to employ more concrete and
encompassing spiritual frameworks when describing their spiritual experiences is not surprising,
considering the previous literature which has documented the profound role of spirituality and
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
religiosity for many communities across the African diaspora (Jagers & Smith, 1996). The
results of this study are consistent with the findings that Black communities, across the globe,
traditionally place very high value in spiritual connection and understanding and tend to view
most or all ordinary phenomena as having some spiritual impetus or consequence (Jagers &
Smith, 1996). The results of this study are also consonant with the enduring finding that Black
Americans are the most religiously involved racial group in the country (Blaine & Crocker,
1995). That Black participants so strongly reflected these spiritual beliefs in their narration of
spiritual experiences serves as one illustration of how this religious engagement is not only
extrinsic, but also deeply intrinsic in nature.
Furthermore, race was not a significant predictor of narrator agency, which strengthens
the notion that narrator agency and spiritual action/intent are compatible, complementary themes
in autobiographical reasoning. Even though black participants were much more likely to view
spiritual forces as active and having infinite agency, this did not necessarily come at the cost of a
decreased emphasis on personal agency. This is even further evidence that spiritual reasoning is
a profound component of the autobiographical understanding of the self, integrated to varying
degrees with other established themes autobiographical reasoning. The strong correlation
between Spiritual Proximity and Spiritual Action/Intent observed in the sample further
strengthens this notion, as it might be that those who believe spiritual beings to be more
omnipresent and accessible are more likely to view spiritual actions as relevant to their own
actions. Conversely, those who feel unable to communicate with or understand the actions of
spiritual beings may come to view spiritual forces as essentially external, independent, and even
conflicting with their own agency. This could mean that the Black and white participants in this
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
study demonstrated alternative frameworks for understanding the relationship between spiritual
phenomena and one’s own power, agency, and decision making.
Limitations
One of the primary limitations to this study is the narrow population from which this
sample was drawn. This study only considered the spiritual beliefs of midlife adults living in the
Midwest, many of whom were slightly more educated than the average American citizen. Further
research is needed to see whether these described associations are true of Americans across a
wider variety of ages, income and education levels, racial groups, and geographic locations.
Additionally, developmental psychologists have found aging to impact personality variables in a
similar fashion across all individuals, especially Conscientiousness and Neuroticism (Hopwood
et al., 2011 & Shiner, 2019; Jackson & Hill, 2019), which may obscure subtler relationships
between personality and the narration of spiritual belief that may be observable in a younger
sample.
Secondly, although initially conceived as separate narrative themes, the spiritual
action/intent and spiritual proximity coding systems were highly correlated (see Table 2),
meaning that there was significantly more overlap between these themes than initially
anticipated. The spiritual action coding system was intended to track how much participants
believe spiritual forces intentionally move them towards a new goal or realization, regardless of
whether the participant anticipated receiving spiritual aid. The logic of this system was to track
how much participants’ descriptions of spiritual forces resemble the popular conception of God
shared by many Abrahamic religions as an omniscient, omnipotent, and morally pure entity with
infinite agency. Lower scores do not necessarily indicate that participants do not have an
extensive and highly developed spiritual worldview. For instance, an individual who views
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
spiritual forces as latent reservoirs of power, which can be controlled through means like magic
or witchcraft, may narrate their spiritual experience with little emphasis placed on spiritual action
or intent. However, this person’s narrative could be high in spiritual proximity if they believed
they could access these magical powers at will, at any place. On the other hand, a participant
who is not intrinsically religious, but still holds many fundamentalist Christian beliefs may
narrate an instance where God acts intentionally to affect change, while also implying that such
events are confined to specific religious ceremonies or holy locations. This participant’s
narrative would them be high in themes of spiritual action but low in themes of spiritual
proximity since he believes God can act independently, but only does so in limited instances.
That these coding systems were highly correlated is likely due to the population of the
sample, the majority of whom subscribe to Abrahamic religious beliefs that depict good as
highly active and intentional, and highly accessible (Kay et al., 2009). Therefore, for many
participants in this sample, both the spiritual action/intent and spiritual proximity themes are
likely a part of their spiritual belief systems, so it follows that these themes would be correlated
in this study. However, the coding systems for these themes were developed to track what people
say, rather than what they believe, since the scenes used for this study do not ask participants to
elaborate extensively on the features of their spiritual belief systems. That these two coding
schemes are so highly correlated does likely reflect a flaw in the coding system, in that there is
too much overlap in the language we used to distinguish high spiritual action and high spiritual
proximity. Future research would benefit from revisiting these coding systems and reconfiguring
them so that they account for more distinct verbiage.
Furthermore, the data in this study was taken from a short section of a long interview
about participant’s lives. More research is needed to understand how participants discuss their
PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
spiritual beliefs in other scenes in the LSI, and how this may differently relate to personality
variables and the Big 5. Since this study was designed to be a preliminary investigation of the
narration of spiritual experience in the LSI, religious denominations were not considered in data
analysis. Future research into the narration of spiritual experiences may benefit from a
consideration of how people of different denominations employ different spiritual schemas and
narrative tendencies, such as what settings, events, and characters are included in the scene.
Directions for Future Research
In this study, Black and white participants demonstrated two distinctly different ways of
understanding how spiritual phenomena relate to one’s own actions and sense of agency. This
finding complicates prior research which has investigated the usefulness of spiritual or religious
belief systems for promoting positive mental, emotional, and physical health. Perhaps future
research could stand to reexamine the ways individuals employ their spiritual beliefs as coping
mechanisms with added attention paid to the ways participants conceive of spiritual agency, their
own agency, and the accessibility of spiritual forces. Such findings could have significant
implications on clinical practices that seek to empower clients and renew their sense of control,
responsibility, and agency while also balancing the reality that some events are simply beyond
our control.
Additionally, at a social communal level, these findings have strong implications for
understanding the ways communities respond to successes, hardships, and collective traumas.
The understood relationship between spiritual power and human agency demonstrated by Black
participants in this study offers a glimpse into psychological factors that facilitate collective
organizing, healing, and celebration in various communities, even in the face of overwhelming
hardships.

Background

Context variable pairs other than the ones pictured were: Number of people whose names begin with “T”/Number of trees in a neighborhood, and Total amount of rain in the US/Number of US lawyers.
Methods

In predicting error through considering the different between no-context and context correlation ratings of the same scatterplot, no significant effect of condition or topic was found. However, there was a significant effect of belief, as can be observed

through the general upwards trend of average difference visualized below. Participants with stronger beliefs in the relationship depicted tended to judge the scatterplots with context as having a stronger correlation than the same scatterplots without
context.

So, a real-world application or context on a scatterplot can alter correlation estimation in comparison to the very same scatterplots without said context. This difference may depend on the strength of the belief around the topic, with greater belief showing
overestimation. Future work should examine other types of visualizations, as well as investigate more precise impacts of belief on judgment and interpretation of visualizations.

Shreya Sriram, Kristi Ward, & Tina Grieco-Calub
1The Roxelyn & Richard Pepper Department of Communication Sciences & Disorders, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL
email: shreyasriram2022@u.northwestern.edu
• Crandell, C. C., & Smaldino, J. J. (2000). Classroom Acoustics for Children With Normal

• Oberfeld, D., & Klöckner-Nowotny, F. (2016, August 31). Individual differences in selective

• Shreya Sriram would like to thank the Northwestern Hearing and Language Lab for the
support in data collection and guidance, especially from her mentors Dr. Tina Grieco-Calub
and Kristi Ward and members of the lab, especially Natalie Sliskovich. Shreya is incredibly
grateful for the opportunity to spearhead this related initiative and for the time and effort of
the participants in this study. Lastly, Shreya would like to extend her gratitude to the
Northwestern Office of Undergraduate Research for the chance to present her research.
Listeners have difficulty understanding speech in environments that have multiple sound sources (i.e.,
background noise). To improve speech perception in these scenarios, listeners must allocate more of
their attention to the speech signal and inhibit their attention to the background noise. Thus, the inability
to selectively attend to speech would likely further impair speech recognition accuracy.
This is especially important for listeners with hearing loss, who have difficulty understanding speech even
with the use of hearing devices (e.g., hearing aids or cochlear implants). In considering the proposed role
of selective attention in speech recognition, it is possible that part of the reason listeners with hearing loss
experience poor speech understanding is due to impaired selective attention.
Previous research has demonstrated this relation in children with hearing loss. However, the extent of this
relation in adulthood remains unknown. As selective attention is known to improve with age, the
maturation of attentional processes may compensate for differences that are seen in children.
This preliminary study investigates whether adults with
hearing loss demonstrate greater difficulty attending to a
target stream than adults with normal hearing.
Future research is needed to delineate these possibilities. Testing this phenomenon with
adults with less severe hearing loss or with better aided hearing functionality would
allow distinction between audibility and selective attention.
Furthermore, using a larger sample size would allow for more quantitative conclusions
to be drawn.
